apps\\admin\\app\\api\\content-queue\\ru.summary: This file defines a Next.js App Router API route at `apps/admin/app/api/content-queue/run/route.ts` that acts as a thin server-side proxy for triggering the content-queue processing job in the admin backend. apps\\admin\\app\\api\\bookings\\route.t.summary: This file defines a Next.js API route handler for the admin app's `/api/bookings` endpoint, acting as a thin server-side proxy to the backend admin API. apps\\admin\\app\\api\\content-queue\\au.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router route handler for the admin app that acts as a thin server-side proxy for triggering automatic posting of queued content. Its sole exported handler, POST, forwards the request to the backend admin API at the `/api/v1/admin/content-queue/auto-post` endpoint, then relays the upstream response verbatim—passing through the raw body text, status code, and content-type header (defaulting to application/json). It depends on the internal `lib/api` module, specifically the `adminApiBase()` and `adminApiHeaders()` helpers, which supply the backend URL and any required authentication headers so secrets stay server-side. The exported `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` config disables Next.js caching, guaranteeing every call actually hits the backend rather than serving a stale result—essential since this endpoint performs a mutating action rather than returning cacheable data. A notable gotcha is that the handler performs no error handling of its own: network failures from `fetch` will propagate as unhandled rejections, and upstream errors are simply mirrored back to the client with their original status codes.

This file is a Next.js App Router route handler in the admin app that serves as a thin server-side proxy for checking the content-queue auto-post status. Its single exported `GET` handler forwards incoming requests to the backend admin API at `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/content-queue/auto-post/status`, attaching authentication/context headers produced by `adminApiHeaders()`, both imported from the shared `lib/api` module. apps\\admin\\app\\api\\donations-export\.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router route handler (`GET` at `/api/donations-export`) that exists purely as a server-side proxy so the admin frontend can download a donations CSV from the backend admin API without exposing upstream credentials to the browser. It reads optional `from` and `to` date filters from the incoming query string, rebuilds them into a new `URLSearchParams`, and forwards the request to `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/donations/export.csv` using authenticated headers from `adminApiHeaders()`, both imported from the shared internal module `lib/api`. The upstream response body is buffered as an `arrayBuffer` and returned verbatim via `NextResponse`, preserving the original status code, `content-type` (defaulting to `text/csv; charset=utf-8`), and the `content-disposition` header so the browser still treats it as a file download. Its key dependencies are Next.js's `next/server` and the internal `lib/api` helpers; no external services are called directly beyond the upstream admin API. Notable constraints: the route is marked `force-dynamic` and both the fetch and the response carry `no-store` caching directives, ensuring exports always reflect live data and are never cached — a deliberate choice for a data-export endpoint, though buffering the whole file in memory means very large exports could be a memory concern.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\content-queue\\ro.summary: This Next.js App Router route handler (`apps/admin/app/api/content-queue/route.ts`) exists as a server-side proxy that lets the admin frontend read the content draft queue without ever exposing the backend API bearer token to the browser. It exports a single `GET(req: NextRequest)` handler plus `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` to disable static optimization. The handler reads an optional `status` query parameter, URL-encodes it, and forwards the request to `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/content-queue/` with credentials supplied by `adminApiHeaders()` and `cache: "no-store"`. Both helpers come from the internal module `apps/admin/lib/api`; the only external dependencies are `NextResponse` and `NextRequest` from `next/server`. Authentication is split across two layers: the app-root `middleware.ts` gates page access via the `darshya_admin_session` cookie, while this route injects the service bearer token server-side. Notably, it passes the upstream response through verbatim — streaming the raw text body, mirroring the status code, and copying the `content-type` header (defaulting to `application/json`) — so it performs no validation, error normalization, or shape transformation. Only GET is supported, and the combination of `force-dynamic` and `no-store` means every call hits the backend fresh, which is intentional for queue data but worth noting for load.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\leads\\conversion.summary: This file defines a Next.js App Router API route at `/api/leads/conversion/timeline` in the admin app, serving as a thin server-side proxy that forwards GET requests to the backend admin API. Its single exported `GET` handler preserves the incoming query string (`req.nextUrl.search`) and passes the request to `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/leads/conversion/timeline`, returning the backend's raw response body, status code, and content-type unchanged. It depends on two internal helpers from `lib/api`: `adminApiBase()` for resolving the backend service URL and `adminApiHeaders()` for attaching authentication/identification headers, plus `NextResponse`/`NextRequest` from `next/server`. Notable design choices include `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` and `cache: "no-store"` on the fetch, both ensuring the timeline data is never cached and always fetched fresh, and the deliberate use of `res.text()` rather than `res.json()` so the proxy is content-agnostic and can pass through any response format without parsing.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\content-queue\\[i.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router route handler in the admin app that acts as a thin server-side proxy for POST actions on a single content-queue item. Its sole export is a `POST` function (plus the `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` config and a local `RouteContext` interface) which extracts the `id` route parameter, reads the incoming request body as raw text, and forwards it verbatim to the backend admin API at `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/content-queue/{id}`. It depends on `NextRequest`/`NextResponse` from `next/server` and on the internal `lib/api` module (`../../../../lib/api`), which supplies `adminApiBase()` and `adminApiHeaders()` to locate and authenticate against the backend service. Notable design choices include passing the body through as unparsed text so the proxy never mutates the payload, and mirroring the upstream response's status code and `content-type` header (defaulting to `application/json`) so clients see the backend's answer unmodified. The `id` is URL-encoded before being embedded in the path, and `force-dynamic` opts the route out of any static caching since it is purely a live proxy. Finally, the handler uses the newer Next.js convention of awaiting `ctx.params` as a Promise, which matters for anyone copying this pattern on an older framework version.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\payouts\\pending\.summary: This file defines a Next.js App Router API route at `apps/admin/app/api/payouts/pending/route.ts` that acts as a thin proxy for fetching pending payout data. The handler also deliberately streams the raw response body back as text while preserving the upstream status code and content-type, meaning it performs no validation or transformation—any backend errors pass straight through to the client unchanged.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\refunds\\pending\.summary: This Next.js route handler (`apps/admin/app/api/refunds/pending/route.ts`) exists solely to proxy requests from the admin frontend to the backend's pending-refunds endpoint, avoiding direct browser-to-API calls. It exports a single `GET` handler that forwards the request to `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/bookings/refunds/pending` using credentials from `adminApiHeaders()`, both imported from the shared internal module `lib/api`, and it re-exports Next.js config via `dynamic = "force-dynamic"`. Its dependencies are minimal: `NextResponse` from `next/server` and the two `lib/api` helpers that resolve the backend base URL and attach admin authentication headers. Notably, the handler is a transparent pass-through — it reads the upstream response as raw text and returns it verbatim with the same status code and content-type (defaulting to `application/json`), doing no parsing, transformation, or error handling of its own. apps\\admin\\app\\api\\refunds\\[booking.summary: This Next.js App Router route handler exists to let the admin frontend approve a booking refund by acting as a thin proxy to the backend admin API, avoiding direct browser-to-backend calls. Its single export is an async `POST` function (plus a `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` config export) that extracts `bookingId` from the awaited route params, reads the raw request body as text, and forwards it via `fetch` to `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/bookings/refunds/{bookingId}/approve`. It depends on the internal `lib/api` module for the `adminApiBase()` URL helper and `adminApiHeaders()` (which presumably injects authentication), and on `next/server`'s `NextRequest`/`NextResponse`. Notable design choices: the body defaults to `"{}"` if reading fails, the `bookingId` is URL-encoded before interpolation, and the upstream response is passed through verbatim — same status code, raw text body, and content-type (falling back to `application/json`) — so the route adds no validation or transformation of its own. The `force-dynamic` setting prevents Next.js from caching or statically optimizing the handler, which is appropriate for a mutating approval action.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\whatsapp\\deliver.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router API route that acts as a thin server-side proxy for the admin dashboard's WhatsApp deliveries listing. It exports a single `GET` handler that takes the incoming request's query string (`req.nextUrl.search`) and forwards it verbatim to the backend admin API at `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/whatsapp/deliveries`, then streams the backend's response body, status code, and content type back to the browser unchanged via `NextResponse`. Its only dependencies are the internal `adminApiBase` and `adminApiHeaders` helpers from `../../../../lib/api`, which supply the backend URL and authentication headers, plus Next.js server primitives. Notable design choices include `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` and `cache: "no-store"` on the fetch, both of which disable caching so delivery data is always fresh, and the deliberate pass-through of the raw response text (rather than parsing JSON) so errors and payloads from the backend reach the client untouched. The route exists to keep admin API credentials server-side while letting the frontend call a same-origin URL.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\temples\\[slug]\\.summary: This Next.js route file (`apps/admin/app/api/temples/[slug]/route.ts`) exists as a server-side proxy that lets the admin dashboard's client components read and update temple timings without ever exposing the `ADMIN_API_BEARER` credential to the browser. It exports two route handlers, `GET` and `PATCH`, both of which forward requests to the upstream admin API at `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/temple-timings/{slug}`, passing the slug URL-encoded and returning the upstream response body, status, and content-type verbatim. Notable choices include `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` plus `cache: "no-store"` on the fetch to prevent any caching of timing data, raw text pass-through of both request and response bodies (avoiding JSON re-serialization), and awaiting `ctx.params` as a Promise, reflecting the Next.js 15 async-params convention.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\refunds\\[booking.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router API route handler that acts as a thin server-side proxy for rejecting a refund on a specific booking in the admin application. Its sole export is a `POST` handler (plus a `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` config disabling static caching), which extracts the `bookingId` from the route's async `params` and forwards the incoming request to the backend admin API endpoint `/api/v1/admin/bookings/refunds/{bookingId}/reject`. It depends on the internal `lib/api` module, specifically the `adminApiBase()` helper for resolving the backend base URL and `adminApiHeaders()` for attaching authentication/service headers, and communicates with the external admin backend service over HTTP. Notable design choices include reading the raw request body as text and passing it through unchanged (defaulting to `"{}"` when empty), using `encodeURIComponent` on the `bookingId` to guard against malformed path segments, and mirroring the upstream response faithfully by copying its status code and content-type header (falling back to `application/json`). The `RouteContext` typing with `params` as a `Promise` reflects the Next.js 15 async-params convention, and the handler performs no validation or error mapping of its own, making the backend solely responsible for business logic and failure responses.

apps\\admin\\app\\api\\whatsapp\\broadca.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router API route (`apps/admin/app/api/whatsapp/broadcast/route.ts`) that exists purely as a server-side proxy: it forwards WhatsApp broadcast requests from the admin frontend to the backend admin API at `/api/v1/admin/whatsapp/broadcast`, keeping backend credentials and the base URL server-side. Its only export is the `POST` handler, alongside the `dynamic = "force-dynamic"` config that disables static optimization and caching so every request hits the backend fresh. It depends on `next/server` (`NextRequest`, `NextResponse`) and on the internal `lib/api` module, which supplies `adminApiBase()` for the backend URL and `adminApiHeaders()` for authentication headers. Notably, the handler reads the incoming body as raw text and passes it through verbatim without parsing or validation, and it mirrors the upstream response's status code and content-type back to the caller, defaulting to `application/json` if the upstream omits a content-type. Only POST is supported; any other method will receive Next.js's default 405. The main gotcha is that this layer adds no error handling of its own — network failures from the `fetch` call will surface as unhandled 500s rather than structured errors.

apps\\admin\\app\\experiments\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the admin app's `/experiments` route, rendering a read-only dashboard of PostHog feature flags and A/B tests. The default exported async server component `ExperimentsPage` calls `fetchFeatureFlags` from the internal `../../lib/posthog-experiments` module and branches on the returned union type (`missing_config`, `error`, `empty`, or success with `FeatureFlagSummary[]` data), rendering either an `EmptyState` helper or a `FlagsTable` that displays each flag's key, name, active/paused status, rollout percentage, and multivariate variant breakdowns. It depends on the PostHog REST API indirectly through that lib module, which requires the `POSTHOG_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` environment variables. Notable design choices include ISR with `export const revalidate = 300` so flag data refreshes at most every five minutes, a deliberate read-only posture that links out to the PostHog dashboard for editing, and a static conventions section documenting kebab-case flag keys, a 95% significance threshold, and a pointer to `docs/ab-testing.md` for guardrail guidance.

apps\\admin\\app\\bookings\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the admin panel's bookings list, rendering the latest 100 puja bookings as a server component at the `/bookings` route. Its default export `BookingsPage` is an async server component that calls the internal `fetchBookings()` helper, which hits the backend REST endpoint `${adminApiBase()}/api/v1/admin/bookings/?limit=100` using `adminApiHeaders()` from `../../lib/api`, then formats money with `formatPrice` from `../../lib/format`. Two local types shape the data: `BookingRow` (booking number, status, scheduled date, price/currency, plus nullable `pujaType`, `temple`, and `user` relations) and `ListResult`, a status-tagged union that lets `fetchBookings` return API or network errors as data instead of throwing, so the UI renders an inline error panel, an empty state, or a table with a "showing X of total" footer. Notable gotchas: the fetch uses `cache: "no-store"`, which makes the page fully dynamic and effectively negates the exported `revalidate = 60`, despite the header copy claiming a 60-second refresh. The limit is hardcoded to 100 with no pagination controls, nullable relations are rendered as em-dashes, dates are formatted via `toISOString().slice(0, 10)` (UTC date, which can shift a day relative to local time), and the brand saffron color `#E16318` is hardcoded inline rather than coming from a theme.

apps\\admin\\app\\broadcast\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the admin dashboard's WhatsApp broadcast page (`BroadcastPage`), a force-dynamic Next.js route at `apps/admin/app/broadcast` that lets staff send pre-approved message templates to opted-in devotees of the Darshya platform. Its main job is to declare a static `TEMPLATES` array of five Meta-approved templates—`daily_aarti_reminder`, `new_puja_listed`, `booking_reminder_24h`, `booking_video_proof_ready`, and `welcome_devotee`—each with a name, label, description containing `{{variable}}` placeholders, and a variables list, which it passes as props to the client component `BroadcastClient` imported from `./broadcast-client` where the actual interactive sending logic lives. The only external dependencies are React/Next.js conventions and the sibling `broadcast-client` module; no backend calls happen in this file itself. Notable design points: `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` forces per-request rendering rather than static caching, the brand color `SAFFRON` (#E16318) is hardcoded for the header, and the page copy documents operational constraints imposed by Meta—templates are rate-limited to 50 messages per second and user opt-outs are enforced automatically—making this purely a presentational shell with template metadata.

apps\\admin\\app\\broadcast\\broadcast-c.summary: This file is a Next.js client component (`"use client"`) for the admin app's WhatsApp broadcast tool, exporting the single component `BroadcastClient`, which receives a list of message `Template`s from its server-rendered parent and lets an operator compose, confirm, and dispatch a bulk WhatsApp send. The admin picks an audience (`waitlist`, `bookings`, or `all`), a template, and a language code, fills in per-template variables via inputs generated from `tpl.variables`, then confirms through a modal warning that the send is irreversible before the component POSTs to `/api/whatsapp/broadcast`. It also polls `/api/whatsapp/deliveries?limit=50` to render a "Recent deliveries" table of `DeliveryRow` records, and re-fetches that list whenever a new `BroadcastResult` arrives so the table reflects the just-completed send. Local types `Template`, `DeliveryRow`, and `BroadcastResult` describe the prop shape, the delivery log rows, and the API's send summary (total/sent/skipped/optedOut/failed/enabled) respectively; the component depends only on React hooks and the two internal `/api/whatsapp/*` routes, with no external client libraries. Notable details: empty variable strings are filtered out before submission, delivery-fetch failures are silently swallowed, the variable inputs are reset via an effect keyed on the selected template, and the brand color `SAFFRON` (#E16318) is hardcoded for action buttons. The component assumes the parent page supplies at least one template, defaulting `templateName` to `templates[0]?.name`.

apps\\admin\\app\\funnel\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the admin dashboard's conversion funnel view, rendered at `/funnel` in the `apps/admin` app. The default-exported `FunnelPage` is an async server component that calls `fetchFunnel` from the internal `lib/posthog-funnel` module, which queries PostHog's API for event counts across the canonical `FUNNEL_STEPS` definitions, and the route uses ISR via `export const revalidate = 300` so data refreshes every five minutes. It renders one of four branches based on the result status: a `missing_config` empty state naming the absent `POSTHOG_API_KEY`/`POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` env vars, an `error` state when the PostHog request fails, an `empty` state when no events were recorded in 30 days (still showing the zeroed chart), or the populated `FunnelChart`. `FunnelChart` is a pure-CSS bar visualization—no charting library—that shows per-step counts, each step's percentage of step one, and drop-off versus the previous step, using helper functions `pct` and `widthPct` and a hardcoded saffron brand color (`#E16318`). A `Step → PostHog event` legend section maps each funnel step to its underlying PostHog event name and description, which is useful for verifying tracking. Notable gotchas: failures never throw the page—they degrade into empty states that retry on the next revalidation—and bar widths are normalized against step one's count with a 2px minimum so tiny nonzero steps remain visible.

apps\\admin\\app\\gurukuls\\GurukulModer.summary: This file defines GurukulModerationClient, a Next.js client component ("use client") in the admin app that renders the gurukul moderation table, letting admins review listings and toggle their verified and active status. It receives an initialRows prop of GurukulRow objects (a locally defined interface mirroring the API payload, including slug, location, tradition, owner info, and programCount) from a parent server component, then manages client-side state for the rows, an all/pending/verified filter, and a busyId flag that blocks concurrent mutations. The toggleVerified and toggleActive functions issue PATCH requests to the backend endpoints /api/v1/admin/gurukuls/:id/verify and /api/v1/admin/gurukuls/:id/active, then update local state with the server's returned flag rather than trusting the optimistic value. The API base URL comes from clientApiBase(), which prefers NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL, falls back to NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL, and finally defaults to http://localhost:4000. Authentication relies on cookie-based sessions via credentials: "include", so no token handling appears here. Notable gotchas: error handling is a bare alert() with the response body truncated to 200 characters, the busyId guard disables all interaction for a row while a request is in flight, and the GurukulRow type is duplicated locally instead of imported from a shared types package, so it can drift from the API schema.

apps\\admin\\app\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the root index page for the `admin` Next.js app (`apps/admin/app/page.tsx`). Its sole export, the default `AdminIndex` component, exists only to send visitors to a real screen: it calls `redirect("/funnel")` from `next/navigation`, so hitting the admin app's root URL lands on the funnel page. apps\\admin\\app\\gurukuls\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the server-side Next.js page for the admin app's gurukul moderation dashboard (`/gurukuls` route), responsible for loading all owner-submitted gurukul listings and handing them to an interactive moderation UI. Its default export, `GurukulsAdminPage`, is an async server component that calls the local `fetchGurukuls` helper, which hits the backend endpoint `/api/v1/admin/gurukuls/?status=all` and wraps the outcome in a `FetchResult` union that carries either the rows or an error message. It also defines the `GurukulRow` interface describing each listing (identity, location, verification/active flags, contact and owner info, and program count). Internally it depends on `adminApiBase` and `adminApiHeaders` from `../../lib/api` for backend configuration, and delegates all interactive behavior to the `GurukulModerationClient` component, which receives the data as `initialRows`. Externally it talks to the admin REST API over HTTP. Notable design choices include forcing dynamic rendering with `force-dynamic` and `cache: "no-store"` so moderation data is never stale, and graceful error handling that renders a styled inline error banner instead of throwing, keeping the page shell usable when the API fails.

apps\\admin\\app\\content-queue\\page.ts.summary: This file is the Content Queue admin page (`ContentQueuePage`, a `"use client"` Next.js App Router page in `apps/admin`) that gives humans a review workflow for AI-generated Reddit and Quora posts: drafts are listed under `STATUS_TABS` (DRAFT, APPROVED, POSTED, REJECTED), can be edited inline, then approved — which copies the title and body to the clipboard via `navigator.clipboard` — manually pasted onto the target site using the `targetUrlHint` helper's Reddit submit / Quora topic URLs, and finally marked POSTED with the resulting URL. It defines a local `Draft` interface and talks exclusively to sibling API routes in the same app: `GET /api/content-queue` for listing, `POST /api/content-queue/[id]` for status transitions (approve, reject with a `window.prompt` reason, mark posted), `POST /api/content-queue/run` to generate a batch on demand, plus `GET /api/content-queue/auto-post/status` and `POST /api/content-queue/auto-post` for automated posting. React `useState`/`useEffect` and Tailwind classes are the only real dependencies; there is no external data-fetching library. Notable constraints: auto-posting is Reddit-only and gated on `REDDIT_*` environment variables being configured (the button is disabled and the status badge reflects this), while Quora remains manual-copy only. Inline edits live in per-draft `edits`/`titleEdits` state maps and are only persisted when the draft is approved, so unsaved edits are lost on tab switch or reload. UX feedback runs through a transient `flash()` toast that auto-dismisses after three seconds, and all fetches use `cache: "no-store"` to keep the queue fresh.

apps\\admin\\app\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the root layout for the Darshya Admin app, a Next.js App Router application, and it wraps every page in the admin dashboard. It exports a `metadata` object setting the site title to "Darshya Admin" with the description "Internal admin dashboard", plus a default `RootLayout` component that renders the HTML shell (`<html lang="en">` and `<body>`) around all page content. Its key dependencies are the global stylesheet `./globals.css` and the internal `AdminNav` component imported from `../components/admin-nav`, which is rendered above the page `children` on every route. Styling relies on Tailwind CSS utility classes applied to the body — a `stone-50` background, `stone-900` text, full minimum viewport height, and font antialiasing — establishing the app's baseline visual theme. Because there is no `"use client"` directive, `RootLayout` runs as a React Server Component, so any interactivity must live in child components like `AdminNav` rather than here.

apps\\admin\\app\\donations-export\\page.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page (a client component) for the admin console's "80G donations export" screen, letting finance staff download a CSV of paid donations over a chosen date range. Its single export is the default `DonationsExportPage` component, backed by a small `isoDate` helper; the UI offers From/To date inputs (pre-filled to a 90-day window ending today), client-side range validation, and a download button that surfaces inline error messages. It depends only on React hooks (`useState`, `useMemo`) and browser APIs — it calls the internal `/api/donations-export` route with `from` and `to` query params using `fetch` with `cache: "no-store"`, then converts the response to a Blob and triggers a download via a temporary anchor element named `darshya-donations-{from}-to-{to}.csv`. The page documents the CSV schema (receipt_number, donor_name, donor_pan, donor_email, donee_name, amountInr, donation_date, gaushala_id) and notes that every export is recorded in an audit log, implying server-side auditing in the API route. Notable details: the brand saffron constant `SAFFRON` is applied inline rather than via Tailwind theme, the button is disabled when `from > to`, and failed requests throw an error containing the HTTP status plus the first 200 characters of the response body. One subtle mismatch: the helper text claims a 90-day default applies "when both dates are blank," but the inputs are actually pre-populated, so blank values only occur if the user manually clears them.

apps\\admin\\app\\refunds\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js server component for the admin app's pending-refunds page (`/refunds`), listing cancelled bookings whose payments remain captured so staff can process refunds. It exports the default `RefundsPage` component (plus a `revalidate` of 60 seconds), and internally defines the `RefundBooking` and `RefundResult` interfaces and a `fetchRefunds` helper that calls the backend endpoint `GET /api/v1/admin/bookings/refunds/pending` with `cache: "no-store"`. It depends on internal helpers `adminApiBase` and `adminApiHeaders` from `../../lib/api`, `formatPrice` from `../../lib/format`, and the client component `RefundActions` from `./refund-actions`, which renders per-row refund action buttons for each booking. The UI renders a table of booking number, devotee name, puja type, cancellation date and reason, and formatted amount, with distinct empty and error states. Notable details: fetch failures are caught and surfaced as an inline error banner rather than throwing, an optional `schemaNote` from the API is displayed as a "schema gap" warning (suggesting known backend schema drift), and monetary amounts are typed as `string | number` to accommodate serialized decimals. The 60-second revalidate conflicts somewhat with `no-store` fetching, so the page effectively refreshes on each request rather than serving cached data.

apps\\admin\\app\\leads-conversion\\page.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`LeadsConversionPage`, default export) renders the admin dashboard's lead outreach conversion funnel, showing how cold leads progress through emailed → opened → clicked → replied → interested → converted stages. It fetches two endpoints in parallel from the admin API — `/api/v1/admin/leads/conversion` and `/api/v1/admin/leads/conversion/timeline?days=30` — using the shared `adminApiBase()` and `adminApiHeaders()` helpers from `../../lib/api`, with no external charting or data libraries (all visualizations are hand-rolled CSS bars). The page composes several local components: `KpiCards` for open/click/reply/conversion rates, `FunnelChart` for stage drop-off, `RoleTable` breaking stats down per role via the `ROLE_LABELS` map (TEMPLE, PRIEST, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, GAUSHALA — indicating a spiritual-services lead domain), `TimelineChart` for 30-day activity, and `RecentInterested` listing replies classified as INTERESTED with links to `/leads?id=`. Data shapes are defined locally as `RoleStats`, `ConversionResponse`, and `TimelineResponse`, and both fetchers return a `FetchState<T>` discriminated union so failures render inline error banners instead of throwing. A notable wrinkle: the module sets `revalidate = 60` (advertised to users as "refreshes every 60s") but both fetches pass `cache: "no-store"`, which opts out of ISR caching, so the page is effectively rendered fresh per request rather than every 60 seconds. Styling is Tailwind with hard-coded brand constants `SAFFRON` (#E16318) and `STONE` (#E5E0D8). The empty-state copy in `RecentInterested` reveals that intent classification arrives asynchronously via an external outreach webhook, which this page only consumes.

apps\\admin\\components\\admin-nav.tsx.summary: This file defines the top navigation bar for the Darshya admin dashboard app. Its single export, the `AdminNav` React component, renders a branded "Darshya admin" home link followed by a static list of section links (Funnel, Retention, Experiments, Bookings, Payouts, Refunds, Leads, Conversion, Temples, Gurukuls, Broadcast, Content queue, and 80G export) declared in the module-level `LINKS` constant. It depends only on Next.js's `next/link` for client-side navigation and uses Tailwind utility classes for styling, with a couple of inline style overrides for the border color (`#E5E0D8`) and brand orange (`#E16318`). Notably, the nav is purely presentational: it has no active-route highlighting, no role- or permission-based filtering of links, and the link set is hardcoded, so adding a new admin section requires editing this file; the horizontal container uses `overflow-x-auto` to accommodate the long link list on narrow screens.

apps\\admin\\app\\temples\\[slug]\\page..summary: This file is a client-side Next.js admin page (`TempleEditPage`) for editing a single temple's aarti (ritual) schedule, reached at the route `/temples/[slug]` in the `apps/admin` app. Its default export, `TempleEditPage`, loads the temple and its audit history from the internal REST endpoint `/api/temples/[slug]`, renders an editable list of named time-range rows plus free-text `closedOn` and `specialDays` fields, and persists changes via a `PATCH` request to the same endpoint. It defines local TypeScript interfaces (`Temple`, `TimingInfo`, `AuditEntry`, `DetailResponse`) describing the API contract, and a helper `rowsFromTiming` that converts the `timingInfo.regularHours` map into editable row state. Dependencies are limited to React hooks and Next.js navigation utilities (`useParams`, `Link`); it talks only to the app's own API routes, not directly to a database. Notable design choices include strict client-side validation via the `HHMM_RANGE` regex enforcing 24-hour "HH:MM - HH:MM" values, rejection of empty or duplicate slot names, and a save guard requiring at least one row; empty `closedOn`/`specialDays` strings are omitted from the PATCH body rather than sent as blanks. The page also displays a read-only "Recent changes" audit list (showing `changed_by` and timestamp only, ignoring the `before`/`after` payloads), and uses a cancelled-flag pattern in its fetch effect to avoid state updates after unmount.

apps\\admin\\app\\payouts\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page in the admin app renders the "Pending payouts" dashboard, a server component that lists money owed to service providers aggregated per provider. Its default export `PayoutsPage` fetches data via the internal `fetchPayouts` helper, which calls the backend endpoint `/api/v1/admin/bookings/payouts/pending` using `adminApiBase()` and `adminApiHeaders()` from `../../lib/api`, and renders a table of `PayoutGroup` rows (provider name, role, booking count, total owed) with a summed footer formatted by `formatPrice` from `../../lib/format`. Errors are captured into a `PayoutResult` union (`status: "ok" | "error"`) rather than thrown, so API failures and empty states render as inline panels, and an optional `schemaNote` from the API surfaces as an amber "schema gap" banner. The header copy hardcodes the commission rules — PRIEST/WELLNESS net 75%, ASTROLOGER net 70%, GAUSHALA net 100% — and the brand saffron color `#E16318` is applied inline. One notable tension: the file exports `revalidate = 60` for ISR, but the fetch uses `cache: "no-store"`, which opts out of caching entirely, so the revalidate setting is effectively dead and data is fetched fresh on every request. Styling is plain Tailwind with a responsive overflow-x table.

apps\\admin\\app\\refunds\\refund-action.summary: This file defines `RefundActions`, a client component in the Next.js admin app (`apps/admin`) that renders the Approve and Reject buttons shown for a pending refund request, keyed by a `bookingId` prop. It exists to let operations staff resolve refund requests directly from the refunds page without leaving it. The component calls two internal API routes: a POST to `/api/refunds/{bookingId}/approve` for approvals, and a POST to `/api/refunds/{bookingId}/reject` with a JSON body containing a `reason` for rejections, then triggers `router.refresh()` from `next/navigation` so the server-rendered page re-fetches updated booking state. Its only dependencies are React's `useState` and Next.js navigation; all side effects go through those same-origin fetch calls, with no external services touched directly. State management is deliberately minimal: a single `pending` field tracks which action is in flight and disables both buttons to prevent double submission, while failures are surfaced as inline error text built from the HTTP status and the first 120 characters of the response body. Notable design choices include using native `confirm()` and `prompt()` dialogs instead of modal components, and enforcing that rejections must include a non-empty trimmed reason before the request is sent.

apps\\admin\\app\\temples\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js admin page (route `/temples`) that lists all temples along with a summary of their aarti timing configuration, serving as the entry point for editing per-temple timings. Its default export, the async server component `TemplesAdminPage`, renders a table of temples (slug, name, city/state, aarti slot count) with an Edit link to `/temples/[slug]`, plus error and empty states; the internal types `TempleRow` and `TempleListResult` shape the data, while the helper `fetchTemples` loads the list and `regularHoursCount` derives the slot count from the untyped `timingInfo` JSON blob. It depends on `next/link` for client navigation and on the shared internal module `../../lib/api`, using `adminApiBase()` and `adminApiHeaders()` to call the backend admin API at `/api/v1/admin/temple-timings/`. Notable decisions: the page opts out of caching twice—via the `force-dynamic` export and `cache: "no-store"`—so the listing is always fresh, and `fetchTemples` never throws, instead returning a discriminated `status: "ok" | "error"` result (truncating error bodies to 200 chars) so the UI can render a friendly banner. Because `timingInfo` is typed as `unknown`, the slot count is computed defensively by checking for a `regularHours` object and counting its keys.

apps\\admin\\app\\retention\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the admin dashboard's cohort retention view, rendered as an async React Server Component with a 5-minute ISR cache (`revalidate = 300`). Its default export `RetentionPage` calls `fetchRetention` from the internal `lib/posthog-retention` module and renders one of four UI branches based on the result's status: `missing_config` (naming the absent `POSTHOG_API_KEY`/`POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` env vars), `error`, `empty`, or the data grid. The `RetentionGrid` component renders the `RetentionCohort[]` data as a weekly heatmap table with a sticky cohort-label column, one column per interval (W0–W7), and a color legend; helper functions `pctValue`, `pctLabel`, `heatmapColor`, and `textColorFor` compute clamped percentages, alpha-scaled saffron (`#E16318`) cell backgrounds, and contrast-aware text colors. `EmptyState` is a small shared presentational component for the non-data branches. Notable details: retention is defined entirely by PostHog `$pageview` events (first `$pageview` as the cohort-signup event, any subsequent one as return), week 0 is hardcoded to display "100%", missing future cells render as a middot placeholder, and PostHog failures are tolerated gracefully with a note that the next revalidation will retry rather than crashing the page. Styling is pure Tailwind utility classes with inline styles only for the dynamic heatmap colors.

apps\\admin\\lib\\format.ts.summary: This file provides a local price-formatting utility for the admin app, deliberately duplicating the convention from `packages/shared` rather than adding a cross-package dependency. Its sole export, `formatPrice`, accepts a number, string, null, or undefined amount plus an optional currency code (defaulting to `"INR"`) and returns a human-readable currency string. It coerces string inputs with `Number`, treats nullish values as zero, and renders non-finite results as an em-dash so bad data never reaches the UI. Formatting relies on the built-in `Intl.NumberFormat` API—there are no external library dependencies—choosing the `en-US` locale for USD and `en-IN` for everything else, and always rounding to zero fractional digits. Notable gotchas: the whole `Intl` call is wrapped in try/catch with a `` `${currency} ${n.toLocaleString()}` `` fallback for unsupported currency codes, and any non-USD currency is displayed with Indian digit grouping regardless of the actual currency, which is a conscious simplification rather than a bug.

apps\\admin\\lib\\posthog-funnel.ts.summary: This module powers the admin app's conversion-funnel dashboard by querying PostHog's funnel insights API for a fixed five-step booking funnel on darshya.online. The exported `FUNNEL_STEPS` constant declares the funnel definition (`FunnelStepDef`) — from `$pageview` on the home page through `temple_viewed`, puja page views, `booking_started`, and `payment_success`, with optional property filters like `$pathname` matching — while `fetchFunnel()` is the sole async entry point, returning a discriminated union `FunnelFetchResult` that distinguishes ok, empty, missing_config, and error states rather than throwing. It depends on the PostHog REST API (`POST /api/projects/{id}/insights/funnel/`, hardcoded to the `us.i.posthog.com` host) authenticated via `POSTHOG_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` environment variables, and uses `zod` schemas to validate the response. Notable choices include a fixed 30-day window, graceful degradation when env config is absent, tolerance of two PostHog response shapes (flat `result[]` and nested `result[][]`) since the API format varies, a Next.js fetch cache hint (`next.revalidate = 300`), and a heuristic that treats an all-zero funnel as a distinct "empty" status so the UI can message it separately from errors.

apps\\admin\\lib\\posthog-experiments.ts.summary: This file is a read-only client for listing PostHog feature flags (experiments) in the admin app, hitting the PostHog REST endpoint `GET /api/projects/:project_id/feature_flags/` against the hardcoded host `us.i.posthog.com`; creation and editing are intentionally left to the PostHog dashboard. Its sole exported function, `fetchFeatureFlags`, returns a discriminated union `ExperimentsFetchResult` (statuses `ok`, `missing_config`, `empty`, `error`) so callers can render each failure mode without exceptions. Supporting exported types include `FeatureFlagSummary` and `FlagVariant`, which normalize raw PostHog rows into UI-friendly shapes with camelCase fields like `rolloutPercentage` and `createdAt`. The only external dependency is `zod`, used to validate the API response via `ResponseSchema`/`FlagSchema` before mapping, and configuration comes from the `POSTHOG_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` environment variables, with missing values reported through the `missing_config` result rather than thrown. Notable details: the request uses Next.js's `next: { revalidate: 300 }` fetch caching so flag data is cached for five minutes; the helper `topRollout` reduces a flag's filter groups to the maximum rollout percentage as a summary metric; and any schema mismatch, HTTP failure, or network exception is converted into a structured `error` result instead of propagating.

apps\\admin\\next.config.mjs.summary: This file is the Next.js configuration for the `admin` application, defined in `apps/admin/next.config.mjs`. It exports a single default `config` object typed against the `NextConfig` interface from the `next` package, which is the framework's standard way of validating config shape. The only option set is `reactStrictMode: true`, which enables React's Strict Mode to surface potential problems — such as unsafe lifecycles and legacy API usage — during development. Everything else is left to Next.js defaults: no custom webpack overrides, rewrites, redirects, image domains, or environment variable exposure are declared. The file has no internal dependencies and talks to nothing beyond the Next.js framework itself. Notably, its minimalism means any future build customization (e.g., transpiling shared monorepo packages via `transpilePackages`) would need to be added here.

apps\\admin\\lib\\api.ts.summary: This file provides server-side helpers for the admin Next.js app (apps/admin) to make authenticated calls to the Darshya API. It exports three functions: `adminApiBase()` resolves the API base URL from `ADMIN_API_BASE_URL`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, or `API_BASE_URL`, throwing in production if none is set and defaulting to `http://localhost:4000` in development; `adminApiBearer()` returns the admin token from `ADMIN_API_BEARER` or `ADMIN_API_TOKEN`; and `adminApiHeaders()` builds a JSON content-type plus Authorization bearer header, optionally merged with extra headers. The auth model is layered: `middleware.ts` already gates the admin app via the `darshya_admin_session` cookie checked against `ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN`, but the Darshya API still requires its own bearer token, which these helpers supply. A key design decision is that there is deliberately no silent demo-token fallback — `adminApiBearer()` throws if the env vars are missing — so deployed environments must set `ADMIN_API_BEARER` explicitly; local developers are expected to use `demo-admin` in `apps/admin/.env.local` together with `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS=true` on the API side. The main gotcha is the asymmetric fallback behavior: a missing base URL is tolerated only outside production, while a missing bearer token is never tolerated anywhere.

apps\\admin\\next-env.d.ts.summary: This file is the standard auto-generated TypeScript declaration file for the `apps/admin` Next.js application, and it exists solely to wire Next.js's ambient type definitions into the TypeScript compiler. It contains no exported functions, classes, or types of its own; instead it pulls in three sets of declarations via triple-slash reference directives: the core `next` types, the global types for `next/image` (which enable importing image assets like PNGs and SVGs as typed modules), and the generated route types at `./.next/types/routes.d.ts` that power typed routing in the App Router. Its only dependencies are the `next` package's bundled type definitions and build artifacts produced in the `.next` directory when Next.js runs. The key gotcha is stated in the file itself: it is regenerated by Next.js on every dev or build run and must not be hand-edited, since any manual changes will be overwritten. The reference to `.next/types/routes.d.ts` also means type checking will fail or be incomplete if the project has never been built or started, because that generated file won't exist yet.

apps\\admin\\lib\\posthog-retention.ts.summary: This module fetches weekly user-retention cohort data from the PostHog insights API for the admin app. Its single exported function, `fetchRetention`, POSTs a retention query (eight weekly intervals, `retention_first_time` on `$pageview` events) to `https://us.i.posthog.com/api/projects/{id}/insights/retention/`, then normalizes each row into the exported `RetentionCohort` shape (`date`, `label`, `cohortSize`, `values`). Results are returned as the exported discriminated union `RetentionFetchResult`, with statuses `ok`, `missing_config`, `empty`, and `error`, so callers never see thrown exceptions. It depends on `zod` to validate the external response against `RetentionResponseSchema` and on the environment variables `POSTHOG_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID`, whose absence short-circuits to a `missing_config` result. Notable decisions include using Next.js fetch caching with a 300-second revalidation window, treating a response whose cohorts sum to zero users as an explicit `empty` status, and coercing malformed or schema-mismatched responses into plain `error` messages rather than crashing. A small `formatCohortLabel` helper trims ISO timestamps to `YYYY-MM-DD` for display labels.

apps\\admin\\postcss.config.mjs.summary: This file is the PostCSS configuration for the `apps/admin` application, existing solely to wire Tailwind CSS into the app's CSS build pipeline. It exports a single default `config` object typed against the `Config` interface from `postcss-load-config`, which gives editor autocomplete and type checking for the configuration shape. The only registered plugin is `@tailwindcss/postcss`, invoked with default (empty) options, indicating the project uses Tailwind CSS v4's dedicated PostCSS plugin rather than the older `tailwindcss`/`autoprefixer` plugin pairing. There are no internal module dependencies — the file is self-contained and references only external build tooling. A notable implication is that Tailwind-related customization (theme, content sources, plugins) must live elsewhere, likely in a CSS entry file or a shared Tailwind preset, since this config passes no options. Because it is an `.mjs` ES module, it relies on PostCSS's native ESM config loading, which fits a modern bundler setup such as Next.js or Vite in the admin workspace.

apps\\admin\\middleware.ts.summary: This is the Next.js edge middleware for the `apps/admin` app, and it exists to gate every admin route behind a shared bearer-style token stored in the `darshya_admin_session` cookie. It exports a `middleware` function that reads the `ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN` environment variable and compares it against the cookie value using a local `timingSafeEqual` helper, plus a `config` export whose matcher excludes only `_next/static`, `_next/image`, and `favicon.ico` — so all 14 admin pages are covered. The only dependency is `next/server` (`NextRequest`/`NextResponse`); there is no database or auth-service call, which keeps the check fast at the edge. Two fail-closed behaviors are deliberate: if `ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN` is unset the middleware returns a 503 rather than passing traffic through (fixing a prior misconfiguration that exposed the whole dashboard), and on token mismatch it returns a plain-text 401 with instructions rather than redirecting. The hand-rolled `timingSafeEqual` is a documented P0 hardening (#B4) against timing side-channels in the old `===` comparison, including a length-mismatch branch that still walks the expected string to avoid leaking its length. The comments flag the shared-token model itself as technical debt: the intended end state is per-user Supabase JWTs with `requireRole('admin')`, a migration deferred and tracked separately in the docs.

apps\\api\\prisma\\content-data.ts.summary: This file is the seed data source for Darshya's devotional content catalog, exporting a single `contentData` array of typed content records intended to be loaded into the database via Prisma. Each record represents an aarti, chalisa, or similar devotional text (e.g., 'Om Jai Jagdish Hare', 'Hanuman Chalisa', 'Shiv Chalisa', 'Durga Chalisa') with fields for `type`, `title`/`titleLocal`, `slug`, markdown-formatted `body` containing Hindi/Sanskrit verses plus English transliteration, `deity`, `language`, `durationSeconds`, `tags`, `isPremium`, `status`, `imageUrl`, `audioUrl`, `videoUrl`, and `sortOrder`. It has no runtime dependencies — it's pure static data consumed by the Prisma seeding pipeline in `apps/api` — though it references external media hosted on `images.darshya.online` and YouTube video URLs. A notable design decision is that `audioUrl` is deliberately set to `null` for all entries, with the file header documenting that the client `AudioPlayer` handles missing audio gracefully by showing "Audio coming soon" until real CDN-hosted audio is available. All content ships as published and non-premium, bodies embed attribution footnotes (e.g., Tulsidas for the Hanuman Chalisa), and tags encode recitation guidance like day-of-week and festival associations.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260427_.summary: This Prisma migration creates the `service_ratings` table, which stores 1-to-5 star post-call or post-delivery ratings that devotees leave on a `chat_conversations` record. The table holds a uuid primary key, foreign keys to `chat_conversations` (`conversation_id`) and to `users` twice (`devotee_id` for the rater, `provider_id` for the rated provider), a `stars` integer, optional free-text `body`, and a `created_at` timestamp defaulting to `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`. It depends on the pre-existing `chat_conversations` and `users` tables, both of which must already exist in the schema. All three foreign keys use `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so ratings are automatically cleaned up when either the conversation or the associated user accounts are removed — a deliberate choice to avoid orphaned rows at the cost of losing rating history on account deletion. A `CHECK` constraint enforces that `stars` stays between 1 and 5, and a unique index on (`conversation_id`, `devotee_id`) guarantees at most one rating per devotee per conversation, meaning re-rating attempts must be handled as updates or rejected at the application layer. A composite index on (`provider_id`, `created_at`) is included to support efficient provider-facing queries, such as listing a provider's recent ratings or computing aggregates over time.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260426_.summary: This Prisma migration (`20260426_pgvector/migration.sql`) sets up the database foundation for semantic search by enabling the pgvector extension on the Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL instance and adding a 1024-dimension `embedding` column to the `content_items`, `temples`, and `puja_types` tables. It also creates IVFFlat indexes (`content_items_embedding_idx`, `temples_embedding_idx`, `puja_types_embedding_idx`) using `vector_cosine_ops` so approximate nearest-neighbor queries over cosine similarity stay fast. The dimension count is hard-coupled to Cohere's `embed-multilingual-v3.0` model, so switching embedding models requires altering all three columns and reindexing. The migration is intended to run before the companion `scripts/backfill-embeddings.ts` script, which populates the vectors. A noted tuning constraint: the IVFFlat `lists = 100` parameter is calibrated for up to roughly 100k rows (the ~sqrt(rows) heuristic) and should be revisited as content volume grows. Key dependencies are the pgvector extension, Supabase/PostgreSQL, Prisma migrations, and the Cohere embedding service used by the backfill script.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260428_.summary: This Prisma migration (apps/api/prisma/migrations/20260428_donations/migration.sql) creates durable Postgres storage for gaushala donations and their 80G tax receipts, replacing a previous in-memory Map that lost all rows on every Render restart. It defines the DonationStatus enum ('created', 'paid', 'failed') and the donations table, which tracks amount_inr, razorpay_order_id, razorpay_payment_id, receipt_number, status, and paid_at for each contribution. The user_id column is a UUID foreign key to users with ON DELETE CASCADE, but gaushala_id is deliberately a free-form text string rather than a foreign key, because gaushala profiles may be deleted while donation history must persist for tax-receipt traceability. It depends on the existing users table and on Razorpay as the external payment provider whose order and payment IDs anchor each record. Uniqueness is enforced via unique indexes on razorpay_order_id and receipt_number (the latter allowing NULLs), and composite indexes on (user_id, created_at) and (gaushala_id, created_at) support per-donor and per-gaushala history queries. A notable gotcha: the primary key id is plain text rather than a UUID or serial, so ID generation is handled by application code rather than the database.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260427_.summary: This Prisma migration (applied manually via the Supabase SQL editor, after the pgvector migration) creates the schema for human-to-human chat between devotees and providers, intended for post-payment service delivery conversations. It defines three enums — `ChatConversationKind` (puja_booking, astrology, wellness, temple, gaushala, store_order, support), `ChatConversationStatus` (open/closed), and `ChatMessageKind` (text/system/call_link) — plus three tables: `chat_conversations`, `chat_messages`, and `chat_call_sessions`. Conversations reference the `users` table twice (as `devotee_id` and `provider_id`, both cascade-deleting) and carry denormalized inbox state: `last_message_at` and per-participant unread counters (`devotee_unread`, `provider_unread`), with composite indexes on (user, `last_message_at`) to serve inbox listing queries. Messages belong to a conversation, store free-form `metadata` as JSONB (used for things like call-link payloads), and track read state via a nullable `read_at`. The `chat_call_sessions` table records Jitsi video calls, storing a unique `room_name` and `jitsi_url`, making Jitsi the external service dependency for in-chat calling. Notable gotchas: `linked_booking_id` is a plain UUID with no foreign key to any bookings table (so referential integrity must be enforced in application code), and `chat_conversations.updated_at` has no default or trigger, meaning the application layer must maintain it on every write.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260428_.summary: This Prisma migration (apps/api/prisma/migrations/20260428_phone_nullable/migration.sql) relaxes the users table schema by dropping the NOT NULL constraint on the phone column, enabling social-login users — specifically Google sign-ups — to register without supplying a phone number. It contains a single ALTER TABLE statement and exports no functions or types, as it is a plain SQL migration applied by Prisma Migrate against PostgreSQL. The file builds on the existing users table defined in the Prisma schema, where phone carries an @unique constraint, and it depends on Postgres behavior where unique indexes permit multiple NULL values, so uniqueness among real phone numbers is preserved without requiring every row to have one. A notable design note, documented in the header comment, is that the team explicitly verified this NULL-friendly unique-index semantics before relaxing the constraint, avoiding the pitfall seen in some other databases where NULLs are treated as conflicting duplicates.

apps\\api\\prisma\\fix-seed-urls.mjs.summary: This file is a one-off Node.js maintenance script (run via `node apps/api/prisma/fix-seed-urls.mjs`) that rewrites the sibling `seed.ts` Prisma seed file in place, swapping placeholder `images.darshya.online` and `stream.darshya.online` URLs for real, working ones. It exports nothing; instead it loads `seed.ts` with `readFileSync`, applies a large table of literal string-pair replacements, and writes the result back with `writeFileSync`. The replacement groups cover temple images for Kashi Vishwanath, Tirumala Tirupati, Siddhivinayak, Somnath, and Jagannath Puri (mapped to Wikimedia Commons), puja and content images plus priest avatars (mapped to Unsplash), and live-darshan stream URLs (mapped to YouTube `embed/live_stream` channel URLs); it also flips Somnath's `liveDarshanEnabled` flag to true and rewrites the `playbackUrl` template in the seed logic to fall back to `t.streamUrl`. Dependencies are limited to Node built-ins (`fs`, `path`, `url`), with the actual data flowing to external hosts: upload.wikimedia.org, images.unsplash.com, and youtube.com. Notable gotchas: `content.replace(old, replacement)` with a string pattern only replaces the first occurrence, so duplicated URLs in `seed.ts` would survive, and the end-of-run "remaining darshya.online references" check is buggy—it regex-matches `/poojly\.com/g` (a leftover from a renamed project) instead of `darshya.online`, so it will always report zero and the per-line diagnostic never triggers. Because it mutates source code rather than the database, it must be run before seeding, and it silently logs a warning for any pattern not found rather than failing.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260502_.summary: This migration introduces Layer AT, the antim sanskar (death rites) booking feature, for the API's Prisma-managed Postgres schema. It creates the `antim_sanskar_bookings` table, which stores deceased and contact details, city, `preferred_ghat`, `preferred_date`, `package_tier` with `package_price_inr`, and an optional `asthi_visarjan_river`, with `status` defaulting to `pending_coordinator` and fields for `assigned_pandit_id` and an optional `user_id`. Indexes are added on `city`, `preferred_date`, and `status` to support coordinator queue lookups, and `booking_number` is enforced unique. The migration also alters `pandit_profiles` with an `available_for_antyeshti` boolean flag (default false) plus a matching index, enabling city-based matching against a dedicated pandit pool. Notable business constraints documented inline: bookings are high value (₹15K–50K) with no upfront online payment — collection happens on-site to avoid distressing grieving families — coordinators must call within 30 minutes, severity is treated as critical regardless of time of day, and antyeshti-opted pandits commit to a one-hour response window. All DDL is idempotent via `IF NOT EXISTS` guards, and `user_id`/`assigned_pandit_id` are plain UUID columns without foreign key constraints, suggesting referential integrity is handled at the application layer.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260428_.summary: This Prisma migration (in apps/api) creates the `provider_kyc` table, implementing provider KYC stage 2: collecting bank account details and PAN before payouts can be processed. The table is keyed by `user_id` with a cascading foreign key to the `users` table, and stores `aadhaar_last4` plus `aadhaar_hash`, `pan_number`, bank fields (`bank_account_number`, `bank_ifsc`, `bank_holder_name`), and verification state (`verified`, `verified_at`, `rejection_reason`), with an index on `verified` to support payout-eligibility lookups. Aadhaar is deliberately stored only as last-4 digits plus a SHA-256 hash of the full number, since the system only needs to confirm a match if challenged, never reverse it — the legal team owns the hash policy. KYC is intentionally per-user rather than per-role: even though a provider may hold multiple roles, a single payout flow uses one bank account, which is why `user_id` is the primary key. The CHECK constraints enforce loose format validation for PAN (AAAAA9999A pattern), IFSC (11 chars with a 0 in the fifth position), and Aadhaar last-4 (exactly 4 digits), but full validation with friendly error messages is deliberately left to the route layer. Deleting a user cascades to remove their KYC record via the `provider_kyc_user_id_fkey` constraint.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260502_.summary: This raw SQL migration (labeled "Layer AM") introduces multi-tenant organization accounts so the API can support B2B SaaS for Temple Trusts. It creates three tables: `orgs` (organization records with a unique `slug`, an `owner_user_id`, a `plan` column constrained to free/pro/enterprise, and an optional `razorpay_subscription_id` for billing integration with Razorpay), `org_members` (membership rows joining users to orgs with roles OWNER/ADMIN/MEMBER and a uniqueness constraint on the org/user pair), and `org_invites` (token-based email invitations with `expires_at`/`accepted_at` lifecycle timestamps, restricted to ADMIN/MEMBER roles). It also adds an optional `org_id` column to the existing `temples` table as a soft foreign key, deliberately not enforced so Temple records can be linked to orgs without a hard referential constraint. Supporting indexes are created on owner, user, email, and org foreign-key columns, all guarded with IF NOT EXISTS for idempotent re-runs. Notably, the migration is written as hand-authored SQL rather than via Prisma schema changes — a deliberate workaround to avoid a `prisma generate` cycle due to Windows DLL-lock issues used elsewhere in the repo — which means the Prisma client schema must be kept in sync separately.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260428_.summary: This migration is the Phase 2.4 performance pass for the API's PostgreSQL database: it adds four indexes covering hot query paths on `content_items` (filtering by `status`), `daily_panchang` (composite lookup on `date` + `location_city`), `puja_types` (filtering by `is_active`), and `temples` (composite search on `city`, `state`, `status`). Rather than going through `prisma migrate dev`, it is applied manually via `prisma db execute` — a deliberate choice because the Prisma schema diff also surfaces unrelated drift from the pgvector extension and the `provider_kyc` table, which the team explicitly does not want to apply, so this file is the surgical subset of safe changes. Every statement uses `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS`, making the script idempotent and safe to re-run against environments where some indexes may already exist. There are no exports in the code sense; the index names themselves (`content_items_status_idx`, `daily_panchang_date_location_city_idx`, `puja_types_is_active_idx`, `temples_city_state_status_idx`) are the durable artifacts, and the column choices reveal the expected access patterns (date-plus-city panchang lookups, city/state temple browsing with status filtering). The main gotcha is operational: because the file bypasses Prisma's migration runner, it may not be recorded in the `_prisma_migrations` history table, so teammates must apply it manually per environment and be aware that the pgvector/provider_kyc drift remains unresolved and will keep showing up in future diffs.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260502_.summary: This Prisma migration for the API's PostgreSQL database adds three tables supporting 80G donation CSV export auditing and the weekly devotee digest email. DonationExportAuditLog records one row per admin CSV download—who exported, the queried date range, row count, and IP address—retained indefinitely for tax/audit traceability, with a composite index on exported_by and created_at for forensic lookups. WeeklyDigestOptOut is a side-table keyed by user_id (with a foreign key to the users table and ON DELETE CASCADE) for opting out of the digest; the comments explain the opt-out design was chosen because digest enrollment is implicit at signup per the ToS, and because a side-table avoids forcing a Prisma client regenerate, which intermittently fails on Windows due to DLL locks. WeeklyDigestRun is a singleton table (enforced by a CHECK constraint that id must equal 1) tracking when the digest job last ran plus sent and skipped counts. The migration relies on gen_random_uuid() for primary keys and uses CREATE TABLE/INDEX IF NOT EXISTS guards throughout, making it safe to re-run.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260511_.summary: This Prisma migration (`20260511_user_blocked`) implements the P0 #6 user-blocking gate, giving admins a way to suspend accounts without deleting user data. It alters the `users` table to add three columns: a `blocked` boolean (non-null, defaulting to false) used for the auth-time check, plus nullable `blocked_reason` and `blocked_at` columns for audit purposes. It also creates `users_blocked_idx`, a partial index covering only rows where `blocked` is true, so the hot-path query in `auth.ts` — which checks the flag on every authenticated request — can be answered without scanning the full table. The design deliberately makes every column nullable or defaulted so the migration is safe to apply while traffic is in flight, and the partial index keeps the index tiny on the assumption that blocked users are a very small fraction of the user base.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260502_.summary: This Prisma migration (`20260502_fcm_notifications`) sets up the database schema for "Layer AE": Firebase Cloud Messaging push notifications that remind users 15 minutes before aarti begins at temples they follow. It creates two PostgreSQL tables — `fcm_device_tokens`, which stores each user's device token, `platform`, preferred `language`, and an `aarti_opt_in` flag, and `temple_follows`, which records which `temple_id` each `user_id` subscribes to. The only dependencies are PostgreSQL built-ins (`gen_random_uuid`, `TIMESTAMPTZ(3)`); the actual push delivery depends on the external FCM service and an as-yet-unscheduled job that must join these tables against temple aarti times. Notable design choices: `device_token` is globally unique while `temple_follows` enforces a composite unique key on (`user_id`, `temple_id`) to prevent duplicate follows, and indexes exist on `fcm_device_tokens.user_id` and `temple_follows.temple_id` to support fan-out lookups by temple. A key gotcha is that neither table declares foreign key constraints, so referential integrity to the users and temples tables is left to application code. Also note `aarti_opt_in` defaults to `true`, making notifications opt-out rather than opt-in, and all statements use `IF NOT EXISTS` so the migration is safely re-runnable.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260503_.summary: This Prisma migration (ticket TD8) adds composite indexes to Postgres for the API's hottest query paths, targeting tables backing PujaBooking, Lead, OutreachLog, DailyPanchang, Temple, PujaType, ContentItem, Donation, and ServiceRating. Every statement uses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS so production deploys via `pnpm prisma migrate deploy` on Render avoid table-level exclusive locks and are safe to re-run; a commented block of matching DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY statements at the bottom serves as the manual rollback path. Key gotcha: CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, so the file must not be wrapped in BEGIN if applied by hand via psql. The header also warns that the indexes only pay off once table stats pass the planner's seq-scan threshold, recommending ANALYZE after applying and a pg_stat_user_indexes check after a week of traffic. Several comments document schema corrections against the TD8 spec: the leads index uses `last_contacted_at` (not `last_emailed_at`), the outreach_logs index uses `channel` (the OutreachChannel enum, not `type`), and service_ratings has no `is_hidden` moderation column yet, so it gets a plain `(provider_id, created_at DESC)` index with a TODO to add a partial index once such a flag exists. A few indexes (temples, daily_panchang, puja_bookings temple calendar) deliberately re-declare indexes already defined in schema.prisma or a phase2 migration, relying on IF NOT EXISTS to make them idempotent no-ops so the migration stays self-contained.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202605140.summary: This Prisma migration creates the `reading_progress` table, which persists a user's position while reading a book so reading state can be restored across sessions. The table stores `user_id`, `book_slug`, `chapter_slug`, and `chapter_number` to identify the location, plus `scroll_percent` (defaulting to 0) and an optional `last_verse` integer for finer-grained position tracking, along with standard `created_at`/`updated_at` timestamps. It builds on the existing `users` table via a foreign key on `user_id` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, meaning a user's progress rows are automatically removed when the user is deleted. The key design decision is the unique composite index on (`user_id`, `book_slug`), which enforces one progress record per user per book — implying the application upserts a single row as the reader advances rather than appending history. A separate non-unique index on `user_id` supports efficient lookup of all books a user is reading. Note that `updated_at` has no default, so the application layer is responsible for setting it on writes.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202605200.summary: This Prisma migration creates the `priest_puja_offerings` table, which stores the catalog of puja (ritual) services that individual priests offer through the API, including each offering's name, optional description, associated deity, base price, and duration in minutes. The table uses a UUID primary key generated via `gen_random_uuid()`, stores `base_price` as `DECIMAL(10,2)` to avoid floating-point money errors, and includes an `is_active` soft-toggle flag defaulting to true plus standard `created_at`/`updated_at` timestamps. Its key dependency is the existing `priests` table: `priest_id` is a required foreign key referencing `priests(id)` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, meaning removing a priest automatically deletes all of their offerings rather than orphaning rows. Indexes are added on both `priest_id` and `is_active`, indicating the expected query patterns are "list offerings by priest" and "filter to active offerings only." Because this is a raw SQL migration rather than application code, there are no exported functions; the schema itself is the deliverable, and it should correspond to a `priest_puja_offerings` model in the Prisma schema for the apps/api service.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\20260502_.summary: This Prisma migration (`apps/api/prisma/migrations/20260502_content_drafts/migration.sql`) creates the `content_drafts` table, which backs "Layer O" — a draft queue for AI-generated devotional posts destined for Reddit and Quora that must pass manual admin approval before being published. The table stores each draft's `type`, `title`, `body`, and `target` platform, and tracks its moderation lifecycle via a `status` column (defaulting to `DRAFT`) plus nullable timestamps and metadata: `generated_at`, `approved_at`, `posted_at`, `posted_url`, and `rejected_reason`. Rows use a UUID primary key from `gen_random_uuid()`, which requires PostgreSQL 13+ (or the pgcrypto extension on older versions). Two indexes support the expected query patterns: a composite index on `(status, generated_at)` for the admin review queue and a single-column index on `type` for filtering by content category. Notably, `status` is plain `TEXT` with no CHECK constraint or Postgres enum, so the valid states are enforced only in application code, not at the database level. All DDL uses `IF NOT EXISTS`, making the migration idempotent and safe to re-run against an existing database — unusual for Prisma-generated migrations. Since this is raw SQL under the Prisma migrations directory, the corresponding model must exist in `schema.prisma` for the Prisma client to expose the table to the API layer.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202605200.summary: This Prisma migration (`20260520020000_e7_followups`) closes leftover W2/W4 TODOs from the prior `20260520010000` admin bundle by replacing temporary JSON-marker and empty-array shims in the bookings/from-offering, temple-portal/donations, store/reviews, and priest/pujas routes with real schema columns. It adds a nullable `priest_puja_offering_id` foreign key on `puja_bookings` referencing `priest_puja_offerings`, a `product_id` FK on `reviews` pointing at `store_products` to enable per-SKU reviews instead of provider-level ones, and a `temple_id` FK on `donations` alongside the existing `gaushala_id`, which is loosened to nullable so donations become polymorphic across temples and gaushalas. It also gives `priest_puja_offerings` slot-capacity fields—`max_bookings_per_slot` (default 1) and a JSONB `available_slots`—mirroring the existing `TemplePujaOffering` model. The script is deliberately idempotent, using IF NOT EXISTS guards and `pg_constraint` checks so it can be replayed against Supabase without conflicting with `prisma migrate deploy`. A notable gotcha: the invariant that exactly one of `donations.temple_id` or `donations.gaushala_id` is set is enforced only at the application level, since a database CHECK constraint would fail on partially back-filled rows mid-migration.

This Prisma migration (apps/api/prisma/migrations/20260520010000_admin_p0_p1_bundle/migration.sql) is a bundled "W2 admin P0/P1" schema patch for the Supabase Postgres database, applying several small, unrelated fixes in one idempotent script that can be run manually ahead of a Render redeploy without conflicting with a later `prisma migrate deploy`. Its most urgent change re-asserts the `blocked`, `blocked_reason`, and `blocked_at` columns on `users` to fix auth-time 500 errors seen in production when the earlier 20260511_user_blocked migration was skipped on at least one Supabase instance. It also adds a free-form JSONB `availability` column to `astrologer_profiles` (deliberately schemaless so the portal can iterate on slot shapes), adds `nri_price` (an override for the 9–10× NRI pricing business rule, falling back to `PujaType.nriPrice` when null) and an `assigned_priest_id` foreign key to `priests` on `temple_puja_offerings`, and adds manager-authored `title`, `description`, and `camera_location` fields to `live_darshan_streams`. Finally it creates a new `store_products` table — one row per SKU owned by a `store_profiles` record — with CASCADE delete so account closure doesn't leave orphaned products, plus indexes on `store_profile_id` and `is_active`. The key design constraint is pervasive idempotency: every statement uses IF NOT EXISTS guards (with foreign keys wrapped in `pg_constraint`-checking DO blocks so partial earlier runs are handled gracefully), making the script safe to re-run manually or via Prisma.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202605190.summary: This Prisma migration (`20260519000000_gaushala_cows_volunteers`) creates the schema for cow and volunteer management in a multi-tenant gaushala (cow shelter) system, adding three tables: `cows`, `cow_health_records`, and `volunteers`. The `cows` table stores per-shelter animal records with fields like `tag_number`, `breed`, `health_status`, and `arrival_date`, enforcing that tag numbers are unique within a shelter via the `cows_gaushala_id_tag_number_key` composite unique index. The `cow_health_records` table holds vet visit or medical event logs per cow, linked by a foreign key with `ON DELETE CASCADE` so health history is removed when a cow is deleted, and indexed on `(cow_id, recorded_at)` for chronological lookups. The `volunteers` table tracks shelter staff/volunteers with contact info, `role`, and an `active` flag, indexed on `(gaushala_id, active)` to support filtering active members per shelter. All tables use UUID primary keys generated by `gen_random_uuid()` and are scoped by `gaushala_id`, but notably this migration declares no foreign key from `gaushala_id` to a parent gaushalas table, so tenant referential integrity is left to the application layer. Enum-like fields (`gender`, `health_status`, `record_type`, `role`) are plain TEXT columns with defaults rather than database enums or CHECK constraints, meaning valid values are enforced only in application code.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202605210.summary: This Prisma migration adds the gamification data model for the Sanskrit learning feature in the API: per-user lesson completion records, daily activity streaks, and earned badges. It creates three tables — `user_lesson_progress` (score and completion timestamp per lesson, unique on `user_id` + `lesson_id`), `user_streaks` (one row per user keyed by `user_id`, tracking `current_days`, `longest_days`, and `last_active_day`), and `user_badges` (unique on `user_id` + `badge_key`) — each with a foreign key to the existing `users` table using `ON DELETE CASCADE` so gamification data is cleaned up automatically when a user is deleted.
