apps\\api\\scripts\\leads\\_shared.ts.summary: This file is the shared toolkit for the lead-scraping scripts under `apps/api/scripts/leads`, giving each scraper a database client, polite HTTP fetching, and idempotent persistence. On import it hand-parses a `.env` file from the working directory — never overriding already-set variables and silently tolerating a missing file so CI works — then exports a shared `PrismaClient` instance (from `@prisma/client`, along with the `LeadRole` enum type), the `RawLead` interface describing scraped contact data, and the constants `USER_AGENT` ("Darshya Outreach Bot") and `SLEEP_MS` (200ms). `politeFetch` wraps the global fetch to attach that user-agent and enforce a 200ms courtesy sleep after every request, accepting an optional `fetchImpl` override for testing. `upsertLead` normalizes emails (lowercased, regex-validated) and phones (stripped to digits and `+`), skips leads lacking both, and dedupes via the compound unique keys `role_email` or `role_phone` — preferring email — merging only `metadata`, `sourceUrl`, and `whatsappNumber` on existing rows so reruns are no-ops; notably it never refreshes name, city, or state on updates, defaults `country` to 'India', and uses `as any` casts on `client.lead` to accommodate the compound-unique where clauses. `runScrape` is the runner each scraper script calls: it injects an `upsert` callback bound to a `LeadRole`, tallies created versus skipped counts into an `UpsertResult`, logs a summary line, and always disconnects Prisma in a `finally` block. The file also exports `TOP_INDIAN_TEMPLE_CITIES`, a hardcoded list of roughly 30 Indian pilgrimage cities (Varanasi, Tirupati, Ayodhya, etc.) that scrapers iterate over as targets.

apps\\api\\scripts\\ops\\cs005-resend-st.summary: This is a one-off operations script (ticket R-Q1-CS-005) that re-sends roughly 230 stale leads stuck in EMAILED status after a Resend DNS deliverability incident, and it hard-refuses to run unless the `RESEND_DOMAIN_VERIFIED=true` env var is set, enforcing the IT-004 DNS-verify runbook before any send. Its exported surface is deliberately split into pure, dependency-free functions — `skipReason` (eligibility: EMAILED status, has email, prior contact, no replies, not already resent via `metadata.cs005_resent_at`, last contact older than 30 days), `templateForLead`/`TEMPLATE_KEY_BY_ROLE` (routing PANDIT, TEMPLE_MANAGER, GAUSHALA_MANAGER, ASTROLOGER roles to four Hinglish warm-followup templates), `buildPlan` (filters, counts by role, and chunks into per-day batches), `renderTemplate` (inline HTML/text with darshya.online unsubscribe links), and `parseCliArgs`/`checkDomainVerifiedGate` — plus the async `sendBatch`, which isolates per-lead failures so one bad email never aborts the batch. At execution time `main()` lazily imports the internal `../../src/lib/prisma.js` client and the external `resend` SDK, keeping the module importable by tests (via the `__testing` export and a bare-execution guard) without side effects. Idempotency is achieved by stamping `lead.metadata.cs005_resent_at` and incrementing `contactCount` after each successful send, so re-runs skip completed leads. The plan respects Resend's free-tier cap of 100 sends per UTC day (default `--limit=100`, clamped to 1–500), with the founder expected to run it three times over three days. Notable gotchas: the templates are inlined rather than read from the canonical `docs/cs/templates/cs005-warm-followup-{role}.md` files so the script has zero filesystem dependencies at send time, the `RESEND_API_KEY` is only required for live sends (not `--dry-run`), and the sends go out from `founder@darshya.online`.

apps\\api\\scripts\\ops\\sla-breach-outr.summary: This ops script (spec R-Q1-CS-003 v2) generates a daily SLA-breach outreach report: it fetches overdue bookings from the Darshya API endpoint `/api/v1/admin/ops/sla-overdue-bookings` (authenticated via the `ADMIN_OPS_TOKEN` env var), narrows them with `filterBreaches` to bookings in `priest_assigned` status more than 7 days past `scheduledDate` with no `videoProofUrl`, and writes a CSV to `docs/agent-reports/sla-breach-<YYYY-MM-DD>.csv` that the founder uses for manual WhatsApp Business and Gmail outreach. Key exports are the `BookingRow`, `SlaResponse`, and `CsvRow` types plus the pure functions `csvField`, `filterBreaches`, `groupByPriest`, `toCsv` (deterministic, sorted by `bookingCode` so output is byte-identical and commit-safe), and `summarize`, which reports refund-at-risk totals and flags priests with ≥2 breaches; legacy wrappers `transformToCsvRows` and `renderCsv` survive as back-compat shims for older tests, and `__testing` re-exports everything for test access. The script depends only on `node:fs`, `node:path`, and global `fetch` — no internal modules. Notable constraints: it is strictly observational (no production writes or auto-sends), always exits 0 even on fetch failure (emitting a header-only CSV so the founder still gets an artifact), and deliberately leaves devotee name/phone/email and puja name blank because the endpoint withholds that PII to keep it out of commit-able files. The `suggestedAction` column encodes escalation tiers referencing internal response macros (Macro 1, Macro 11, Macro 3) based on `daysOverdue` and per-priest `repeatBreachCount`, and a bare-execution guard on `process.argv[1]` prevents `main()` from running when the file is imported by tests.

apps\\api\\scripts\\ops\\__tests__\\cs00.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the behavior of the `cs005-resend-stale-leads` ops script, which re-emails stale leads for the Bhaktisetu product, by importing its internals through the `__testing` export along with the `LeadRow` and `SendCandidate` types. It tests `checkDomainVerifiedGate` (which refuses to send unless the `RESEND_DOMAIN_VERIFIED` env var is exactly `true`), `skipReason` lead eligibility rules (status must be `EMAILED`, `lastContactedAt` older than 30 days, no `reply_count` in metadata, no prior `cs005_resent_at` marker for idempotency, `contactCount` > 0, and a non-blank email), and `templateForLead` role routing from `PANDIT`, `TEMPLE_MANAGER`, `GAUSHALA_MANAGER`, and `ASTROLOGER` to their respective templates. `buildPlan` is checked for role segmentation, spreading sends across UTC days at a 100-per-day cap matching the Resend free tier, honoring a `--limit` flag, and recording skip reasons per lead, while `parseCliArgs` is verified to parse `--dry-run` and clamp `--limit` to 500. `renderTemplate` tests assert that each role's copy includes name/city interpolation, safe fallbacks for null fields, and explicit unsubscribe language pointing at `darshya.online/unsubscribe` for compliance. `sendBatch` is exercised with a mocked Resend client (no real API calls) to confirm failure isolation: successful sends trigger an `onSuccess` callback that stamps `metadata.cs005_resent_at`, individual send failures route to `onFailure` without aborting the batch, and the batch survives even when the `onFailure` audit-log callback itself throws. A notable gotcha documented in the tests is that `--dry-run` is enforced in the CLI's `main()` before `sendBatch` runs, so the suite only asserts the flag threading rather than the short-circuit itself. The suite depends only on `vitest` and the module under test, with all Resend and database interactions stubbed via injected callbacks.

apps\\api\\scripts\\probe-razorpay-mode..summary: This standalone Node.js CLI script (`apps/api/scripts/probe-razorpay-mode.mjs`) exists to satisfy requirement R-Q1-F-003: it probes whether the Razorpay payment integration is configured for test, live, or unset mode in the current environment. It exports nothing and has no module dependencies — it reads only the `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` environment variable and classifies it by key prefix (`rzp_live_` for live, `rzp_test_` for test), emitting a JSON object with `status`, `mode`, `ok`, and a human-readable `note`. A deliberate design decision is the "env-or-noop" contract: the script makes no network calls and never leaks the key value, making it safe to run in CI pipelines. Exit codes form the machine-readable contract — it exits 0 when the key is unset (treated as a noop, with the note flagging that a "demo-fallback path" is active) or when live mode is confirmed, and exits 1 for test mode or unrecognized prefixes, so CI can fail the gate until R-Q1-F-003 is closed. Gotchas worth noting: an unset key is a silent pass rather than a failure, and the live-mode note reminds operators to verify `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS` is unset and the webhook signature secret has been rotated, though the script cannot actually check either of those conditions itself.

apps\\api\\scripts\\smoke-fcm-push.mjs.summary: This is a standalone smoke-test script that verifies Firebase Cloud Messaging push delivery end-to-end by sending a single test notification to a device token, closing out the founder verification step for roadmap item R-Q1-E-011. It follows an env-or-noop pattern: if `FCM_PROJECT_ID`, `FCM_CLIENT_EMAIL`, or `FCM_PRIVATE_KEY` are missing it exits 0 with a "skipped" message so CI never red-fails, but it hard-fails (exit 1) when creds are present yet `FCM_TARGET_TOKEN` is absent. Its only export-level behavior is the script itself, built around two internal helpers: `getAccessToken()`, which manually constructs and RS256-signs a JWT bearer grant using `node:crypto` (avoiding the `firebase-admin` dependency entirely), and `sendTestPush()`, which POSTs to the FCM v1 `messages:send` endpoint. Externally it talks to two Google services: `oauth2.googleapis.com/token` for the token exchange and `fcm.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{projectId}/messages:send` for delivery. Notable details: the private key's escaped `\n` sequences are normalized to real newlines (a common Render env-paste gotcha), the target token is masked in logs via `maskToken()`, the title/body can be overridden via CLI args, and failures matching `UNREGISTERED`/`INVALID_ARGUMENT`/`NOT_FOUND` print a hint that the device token is likely expired and should be re-fetched from the mobile app's debug surface in `apps/mobile/app/_layout.tsx`.

apps\\api\\scripts\\seed-demo-users.ts.summary: This standalone seed script (run via `pnpm --filter @poojly/api exec tsx scripts/seed-demo-users.ts`) inserts the eight hardcoded demo accounts from `DEMO_USERS` as real database rows so that demo tokens like `demo-pandit-token` resolve to genuine UUIDs, which the Phase A+ routes (conversations, messages, calls) require to pass Prisma's UUID validation. It depends only on `PrismaClient` from `@prisma/client` plus `node:fs`/`node:path` for a manual `.env` load (deliberately copying the pattern from `backfill-embeddings.ts` to avoid a dotenv dependency). The `main()` function iterates the `DemoSpec` entries and, because both `email` and `phone` are unique columns that could collide independently, it first does a `findFirst` matching either field and then updates or creates the `user` row accordingly, making the script idempotent. Demo phones deliberately use the `+910000000XXX` block to avoid clashing with real seed data, which occupies `+91-9876543XXX`, and new users default to `preferredLanguage: 'hi'` and `subscriptionTier: 'bhakti_pass'`. Roles are granted through `userRoleAssignment` via a composite-key upsert on `userId_role`, with a defensive fallback to `findFirst` + `create` in case the deployed schema lacks that unique constraint. Finally, it promotes `pandit@demo.com` to a full `priest` row (verified, active, with specializations like `rudrabhishek`) so that chat-on-`priest_assigned` flows can find a provider for puja bookings. Failures exit with code 1, and the client disconnects in a `finally` block.

apps\\api\\scripts\\seed-sample-gurukuls.summary: This SQL seed script, part of the `apps/api` service, populates the Postgres `gurukuls` and `gurukul_programs` tables with three verified sample gurukuls (identified by the slugs `sampurnanand-sanskrit-vidyalaya`, `poornaprajna-vidyapeetha`, and `parmarth-niketan-rishikul`) and eight associated study programs, providing demo data for development or staging environments. It has no exports in the traditional sense; its "interface" is the two tables it writes to, using `gen_random_uuid()` for primary keys and `NOW()` for timestamps. The script is designed to be idempotent: gurukul inserts use `ON CONFLICT ("slug") DO UPDATE` to upsert in place, while programs are first deleted for the three sample slugs and then reinserted via a `VALUES`-derived join that resolves each `gurukul_id` by slug lookup. A notable constraint is that `owner_id` is deliberately left NULL, relying on the owner relation being nullable with `onDelete: SetNull` behavior defined in the schema. The delete-and-reinsert strategy for `gurukul_programs` is flagged in a comment as safe only because no applications are expected on sample records — implying a foreign key from an applications table would make re-seeding fail otherwise. All contact URLs and emails use `example.org` placeholders, so the data is clearly non-production. The script depends on the database schema (table and column names, the unique `slug` constraint) staying in sync with the API's data layer, and on the pgcrypto extension for UUID generation.

apps\\api\\scripts\\ops\\__tests__\\cs00.summary: This Vitest suite covers the sibling ops script cs007-reset-stale-temple-leads.js, a maintenance job that finds stale temple leads (role=TEMPLE, status=EMAILED, reply_count=0, last_contacted_at over 30 days old) and resets them to status=NEW with contact_count=0 so they re-enter outreach. It exercises internals exposed through the script's `__testing` export: `selectStaleLeadsSql` (SELECT against the snake_case `leads` table with validated LIMIT and a `cs007_reset_at IS NULL` idempotency check), `cs005UnsentGuardSql` (counts EMAILED leads missing the `cs005_resent_at` marker from the prior cs005 campaign), `buildResetUpdate` (parameterized UPDATE embedding a JSON metadata snapshot of `cs007_reset_at` plus `cs007_prior` status/contact_count/last_contact_at), `buildAuditLogInsert` (writes a `cs007_reset` action row to `ops_audit_log`), `parseArgs` (`--dry-run`, `--limit=N` defaulting to 200 and capped at 500), and `summarize` (tallies scanned/reset/skipped). The only external dependency is vitest, and the assertions imply a Postgres-style backend (NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days') whose `leads` table name comes from a Prisma `@@map`. Notable constraints locked in by these tests: injection discipline (lead ids bound as parameters rather than concatenated, non-positive or non-integer limits rejected), the 500-row safety cap on batch size, and idempotency via the `cs007_reset_at` marker so already-reset leads are skipped on reruns.

apps\\api\\scripts\\_apply_payout_migrat.summary: This is a one-off operational script that manually applies the `provider_payout_requests` Prisma migration to the production database, created because Prisma's `$executeRawUnsafe` cannot run multi-statement SQL while the `pg` driver can via simple query mode. It reads `.env.production` directly (stripping null bytes and quote-wrapping) to extract the `DIRECT_URL` connection string, loads the SQL from `prisma/migrations/20260806000000_provider_payout_requests/migration.sql`, and executes it with a `pg` `Client` using SSL. It then manually records the migration in the `_prisma_migrations` bookkeeping table with a hardcoded checksum of `manual-20260806-payouts` and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for idempotency, since Prisma Migrate itself is bypassed. Finally it verifies success by checking `information_schema` for the `payout_requests` table and the `commissions.payout_request_id` column, printing EXISTS/MISSING status. Gotchas: it has no transaction wrapping, truncates fatal error messages to 300 characters, and exits 0/1 for shell scripting, so it's meant to be run once by hand and then retired.

apps\\api\\scripts\\verify\\razorpay-web.summary: `razorpay-webhook-sim.mjs` is a standalone Node CLI utility in `apps/api/scripts/verify/` that simulates Razorpay webhook signatures so developers can test the local `/webhooks/razorpay` endpoint without waiting for real sandbox events; it is Step 6 tooling for the R-Q1-F-005 runbook documented in `docs/finance/razorpay-sandbox-e2e-runbook-v1.md`. It exposes two modes: `sign`, which reads a JSON payload from stdin and prints the HMAC-SHA256 hex digest Razorpay would send in the `X-Razorpay-Signature` header (with a `--raw` flag for clean shell substitution into curl commands), and `verify`, which compares a provided signature against the computed one and reports PASS/FAIL. Its only dependency is `node:crypto`, it requires the `RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` environment variable (matching both the Razorpay dashboard webhook config and the API's `.env`), and it deliberately uses the same `crypto.timingSafeEqual` comparison as the production verifier in `apps/api/src/services/payment.service.ts`, including an explicit length check before comparison to avoid a timingSafeEqual throw. Exit codes are a contract: 0 for sign success or verify PASS, 1 for signature mismatch, 2 for usage/env/input errors, and the payload must be piped via stdin rather than passed as an argument. The key gotcha is that the HMAC is computed over the exact raw JSON body, so any whitespace or reformatting between signing and POSTing will invalidate the signature.

apps\\api\\scripts\\smoke-all-roles.mjs.summary: This is a standalone Node smoke-test script (`smoke-all-roles.mjs`) that verifies the production deployment end to end: it logs in eight seeded demo accounts (devotee, priest, store, astrologer, wellness, gaushala, temple, admin — all using the hardcoded password `demo123` via `POST /api/v1/auth/login`, which must return a `session.accessToken`), then exercises role-specific API surfaces such as `/api/v1/priest/dashboard`, `/api/v1/store-admin/revenue`, `/api/v1/gaushala-portal/cows`, and `/api/v1/admin/pending-approvals`, plus public GETs like `/health`, `/api/v1/temples`, and `/api/v1/panchang/today`, and matching web pages on the frontend. It defaults to the live hosts `https://api.darshya.online` and `https://darshya.online` (overridable via CLI args), uses only the global `fetch` with no external dependencies, prints a per-role PASS/FAIL report, and exits non-zero if anything fails. Two guard checks go beyond simple status assertions: `permsCheck` confirms a devotee token is denied (401/403) on `/api/v1/admin/gurukuls`, and `adminGurukulMutation` toggles a gurukul's `isVerified` flag as admin and restores it — deliberately distinguishing a real auth-guard bug (401/403 on the list call) from merely missing seed data (200 with an empty list). Notable gotchas: it mutates production data (the verify toggle), depends on demo accounts being seeded in prod, treats web redirects 307/308 as success, and runs all requests sequentially.

apps\\api\\scripts\\verify\\astrologer-s.summary: This standalone verification script enforces the R-Q1-S-007 spec by asserting that the Postgres `astrologer_profiles` table exposes every column the astrologer lead-gen and onboarding flow depends on, and it is run manually via `pnpm tsx` rather than as part of the app runtime. It connects through `PrismaClient` from `@prisma/client` and uses `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe` to read `information_schema.columns` for the `public` schema, then diffs the result against a hardcoded `REQUIRED_COLUMNS` list covering `approved`, `kyc_status`, `sample_reading_url`, `price_per_minute`, `aadhaar_verified`, and `payout_blocked`. A notable design decision is the spec-to-repo column mapping: the spec's `verified` and `active` columns both map to the single repo column `approved`, and `price_per_minute_inr` maps to `price_per_minute`, with the spec names kept only for traceability in the gap report. The script is deliberately read-only — if the table or any column is missing it prints a gap report, points to `docs/sales/astrologer-schema-gap-2026-06-12.md`, and exits 1, explicitly stating that the sales queue item must not ship a schema migration and that founder/eng action is required. Exit codes carry meaning: 1 signals a schema gap, 2 signals an unexpected runtime error, and 0 means all columns are present. There are no exported symbols; the only internal dependency is the generated Prisma client, and the only external service is the Postgres database whose connection comes from Prisma's configured datasource. One gotcha: because `verified` and `active` collapse into `approved`, the check cannot detect a future divergence where those two spec concepts need separate columns.

apps\\api\\scripts\\verify\\razorpay-web.summary: This file is a dependency-free smoke test for the sibling script razorpay-webhook-sim.mjs, confirming that its HMAC sign/verify roundtrip and tamper detection behave the same way as the server's timing-safe signature comparison for Razorpay webhooks. It deliberately avoids vitest and runs as a plain Node script, using spawnSync from node:child_process to invoke the simulator as a subprocess with a fixed RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET and a canned payment.captured JSON payload. The assertions cover five behaviors: sign --raw emits a 64-character lowercase hex digest, verify exits 0 and prints PASS for a matching signature, verify exits 1 and prints FAIL for a single-character-tampered signature, a length-mismatched signature fails fast with an explicit "length mismatch" message, and a missing secret aborts with exit code 2. It exports nothing and defines only two small helpers, run (subprocess wrapper) and assert (tallying reporter that prints ok/FAIL lines and exits 1 if any check failed). Its only dependencies are Node built-ins (node:child_process, node:url, node:path) plus the simulator script itself, which it locates relative to its own directory. A notable gotcha is that the contract under test is partly string-based — the suite greps stdout for PASS, FAIL, and "length mismatch" — so renaming those messages in razorpay-webhook-sim.mjs would silently break this test's coupling even if the exit codes stayed correct.

apps\\api\\src\\db\\n-plus-one-detector..summary: This Vitest test file defines the expected behavior (marked "RED," indicating TDD-first development) for the N+1 query detector module at `apps/api/src/db/n-plus-one-detector.js`. It exercises four exported functions: `normalizeSql`, which must strip integer and string literals into `?` placeholders (including inside `IN` lists); `recordQueryForNPlusOne`, which counts queries against the active request scope; `runWithRequestScope`, which establishes that scope; and `reportNPlusOne`, which emits a structured warning once per offending template. The core contract is a threshold of five: identical normalized SQL templates at five executions stay silent, but six or more trigger a `warn` call with message `n_plus_one_detected` and a payload containing the route, normalized template, and count. Tests also pin down edge cases — reporting is a no-op when no scope is active, concurrent scopes via `Promise.all` must stay isolated (implying an AsyncLocalStorage-style implementation), and multiple templates exceeding the threshold in one request each produce their own warning. The file depends only on `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`, `vi`) and the detector module itself, so it documents intent without constraining how the detector is wired into the actual database layer.

apps\\api\\scripts\\verify-mail-dns.ts.summary: This is a standalone ops/diagnostic script in the `@poojly/api` package that verifies inbound-mail DNS configuration for `darshya.online` (or any domain passed as a CLI argument), intended for CI steps or a pre-launch checklist. It performs three checks via internal async functions — `checkMx` (MX records exist, sorted by priority), `checkSpf` (a TXT record starting with `v=spf1`), and `checkDmarc` (a `v=DMARC1` TXT record at the `_dmarc` subdomain) — each returning a `CheckResult` that `main` prints as green/red OK/XX lines. Its only dependency is Node's built-in `node:dns` promises API; there is no auth, no external service, and nothing imported from the rest of the codebase, though failure output points readers to `docs/support-email-setup.md` for remediation. The script is executed with tsx (e.g. `pnpm --filter @poojly/api tsx scripts/verify-mail-dns.ts`) and signals results through exit codes: 0 when ready, 1 when required records are missing, and 2 on unexpected errors. Notably, only MX and SPF are treated as required while DMARC is advisory, and that requirement is enforced by `checks.slice(0, 2)` — so the "required" set is implicitly coupled to the ordering of the `Promise.all` array, a subtle fragility if checks are ever reordered or added.

apps\\api\\src\\db\\instrument-prisma.ts.summary: This file connects Prisma's `$on('query')` event to the API's database observability tooling, so every SQL statement is fed to both the slow-query logger and the N+1 detector. The exported `instrumentPrisma` function attaches the event callback once per process (guarded by a module-level `wired` flag, making repeat calls a no-op), forwarding each query's SQL, duration, params, and current route to `recordQuery` from `./slow-query-log.js` and to `recordQueryForNPlusOne` from `./n-plus-one-detector.js`. The second export, `registerNPlusOneRequestScope`, installs Fastify `onRequest`, `preHandler`, and `onResponse` hooks on a `FastifyInstance` so that each inbound request runs inside an `AsyncLocalStorage` scope (via `runWithRequestScope`), letting the detector attribute query templates to a single request and emit findings through `reportNPlusOne` after the response. Route attribution works by stashing `request.routeOptions.url` on the request object as `_route` in `onRequest`, then re-entering it via `routeStorage.enterWith` in `preHandler` so the Prisma callback can read it. Notable constraints: the whole instrumentation is disabled when `DB_QUERY_INSTRUMENTATION=off` (an incident escape hatch), and it silently stays inactive if the Prisma client lacks `$on` or query events aren't enabled in Prisma's log options, surfacing only a single `prisma_query_event_unavailable` warning. Errors from `reportNPlusOne` are swallowed in `onResponse` so detector failures can never block a response. Dependencies are limited to the two sibling modules, `fastify` types, and `node:async_hooks`.

apps\\api\\src\\db\\slow-query-log.test..summary: This is a Vitest test suite for the `slow-query-log` module in the API's database layer (`apps/api/src/db/`), written in TDD "RED" style to pin down expected behavior before implementation. It exercises four exports from `./slow-query-log.js`: `recordQuery` (the main entry point that inspects a finished query's duration and conditionally logs), `getSlowQueryThreshold` (returns the cutoff in milliseconds), `resetSlowQueryLog` (clears captured state between tests), and `__testGetEntries` (a test-only accessor to the in-memory entry list). The suite establishes that the default slow-query threshold is 100ms and that the `SLOW_QUERY_MS` environment variable overrides it, with the override honored both by `getSlowQueryThreshold` and by `recordQuery` itself. It also locks in the emit contract: queries under the threshold produce no output, while over-threshold queries trigger exactly one `logger.warn` call whose message is the literal string `'slow_query'` and whose payload object carries `{ sql, durationMs, route, timestamp }`, with `timestamp` required to be a parseable date string. Each test injects a stub logger (`{ warn: vi.fn() }`), so the module is expected to accept a caller-supplied pino-style logger rather than importing one directly. The only external dependency is `vitest`; the module under test is otherwise self-contained apart from reading `process.env`.

apps\\api\\src\\db\\n-plus-one-detector..summary: This module implements per-request N+1 query detection for the API's database layer: it counts how many times each normalized SQL template executes within a single request and warns when any template exceeds a configurable threshold. It stores per-request state in a Node `AsyncLocalStorage` scope, created by `runWithRequestScope`, so counts are isolated across concurrent requests without explicit context passing. The key exports are `runWithRequestScope` (opens a fresh counting scope), `normalizeSql` (collapses queries differing only in literals into one template via regex stripping of quoted strings and numeric literals), `recordQueryForNPlusOne` (increments the counter for the current scope, silently no-oping outside one), `getNPlusOneThreshold` (reads `N_PLUS_ONE_THRESHOLD` from the environment, defaulting to 5), `reportNPlusOne` (emits a structured `n_plus_one_detected` warn log per offending template), and the `NPlusOneLogger` interface describing the logger shape it expects. Its only dependency is the Node built-in `node:async_hooks`; it deliberately contains no Fastify or Prisma wiring, which the header notes lives in the sibling `instrument-prisma.ts` module. Notable constraints: the SQL normalization is intentionally conservative regex-based rather than a real parser, so unusual literal forms may not collapse; both recording and reporting are no-ops if called outside a request scope; and the threshold is strictly greater-than, meaning exactly 5 identical queries will not trigger a warning.

apps\\api\\src\\db\\slow-query-log.ts.summary: This file implements slow-query detection for the API's database layer: `recordQuery` checks a query's duration against a configurable threshold and, when exceeded, emits a structured `warn` log entry tagged `slow_query` while also appending the entry to an in-memory ring buffer. The threshold comes from `getSlowQueryThreshold`, which reads the `SLOW_QUERY_MS` environment variable and falls back to a 100ms default if the value is missing, non-numeric, or non-positive. Key exports are the `SlowQueryEntry` and `SlowQueryLogger` interfaces, the `RecordQueryInput` type, `recordQuery` itself, `snapshotSlowQueries` for reading buffered entries (intended for a future `/admin/metrics` endpoint), plus `resetSlowQueryLog` and `__testGetEntries` as test hooks. It has no external dependencies — it is deliberately decoupled from Prisma, with the `$on('query')` wire-up living in the sibling module `instrument-prisma.ts`, and the logger is dependency-injected via the `SlowQueryLogger` interface so the module stays trivially testable. Notable design choices include the fixed 500-entry ring buffer with shift-based eviction (bounded memory but O(n) eviction and no locking, so entries are lost on restart), conditional inclusion of `params` only when provided, and ISO-8601 timestamps stamped at record time.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\apollo-refresh.ts.summary: This file implements a weekly Apollo lead-refresh job for the API: it pulls people from Apollo.io across five ICP segments (temples, priests, astrologers, wellness instructors, gaushalas) and upserts them into the Prisma `Lead` table using the composite `(role, email)` unique key, refreshing metadata on existing rows rather than duplicating them. It depends on the internal `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `searchPeople` function plus `ApolloPerson`/`ApolloPersonQuery` types from `../services/apollo.service.js`, which talks to the external Apollo.io API. The main exports are `refreshApolloLeads()` (an unconditional run used by an admin manual trigger), `maybeRunApolloRefresh()` (a cooldown-gated wrapper called by the master cron's `runDailyOps()`), an `ApolloRefreshResult` type, and a test-only `__resetApolloRefreshCooldown()` helper. Key design constraints revolve around staying within Apollo's free-tier quota: only one page of up to `APOLLO_PER_PAGE` (default 10) results per ICP is fetched, capping usage at ~50 credits per run, and an in-process 7-day cooldown (module-level `lastRunAt`) prevents over-consumption even though the master cron ticks every 30 minutes. The cooldown is deliberately stored in memory rather than the database because the deployment (Render) runs a single API instance, with a comment noting a `cron_runs` table would be needed if the service scaled horizontally. The job is fail-soft throughout: a missing `APOLLO_API_KEY` returns `{ skipped: true }`, per-ICP and per-lead errors are collected into an `errors` array, and the exported functions always resolve rather than throwing.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\backup-cron.ts.summary: This file implements the TD9 weekly database backup tick for the API, invoked on every `runDailyOps()` cycle from master-cron but internally gated so the actual backup only fires during the Sunday 02:00–03:00 IST window (checked by `isSundayTwoAmIst` via a UTC+5:30 shift). Its single exported entry point, `maybeRunWeeklyBackup()`, returns a `BackupResult` and delegates the real work to the standalone `scripts/backup.mjs` script, which it spawns with `node:child_process.spawn` and parses the last JSON line from stdout/stderr — keeping `pg_dump`'s binary stdio out of Fastify's event loop and allowing the same script to run from an external Render cron without booting the server. The only internal dependency is `sendOpsAlert` from `../lib/alert.js`, used to fire a high-severity Slack/email alert when the backup fails; the script itself relies on env vars `DATABASE_URL` plus `R2_ACCOUNT_ID`, `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, and `R2_BACKUP_BUCKET` for the gzip-and-upload to Cloudflare R2. Notable safeguards: the function never throws (failures surface as `{ ok: false }` so downstream cron ticks continue), a module-level `lastRunAt` timestamp enforces a 23-hour cooldown so half-hourly ticks don't double-run the backup, and setting `BACKUP_FORCE=1` bypasses the schedule gate for manual one-shot runs. Path resolution via `import.meta.url` is deliberately written to work from both `src/jobs/` and the compiled `dist/jobs/` layout.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\aarti-notify.ts.summary: This file implements the "Layer AE" scheduled job that sends FCM push notifications roughly 15 minutes before an aarti begins at any live-darshan temple, intended to be invoked every ~5 minutes by the master-cron. Its sole export, `runAartiNotify(now)`, scans active Temple rows with `liveDarshanEnabled`, uses `parseSchedule` from `lib/darshan-schedule` to extract aarti slots from `timingInfo.regularHours`, and fans out pushes via `sendFcm`/`fcmConfig` from `lib/fcm`, returning an `AartiNotifyResult` tally of temples checked, aartis matched, pushes sent, expired tokens, and failures. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma` and touches the `temple`, `templeFollow`, and `fcmDeviceToken` models — the latter two accessed through defensive `unknown` casts so the job no-ops gracefully (with `skipped` and a `reason`) if FCM env vars are missing or those tables aren't migrated yet. Recipients are temple followers whose device tokens have `aartiOptIn` plus all globally opted-in devices, merged by unique `deviceToken` — a deliberately broad audience the code flags as acceptable only at small launch scale. Timing is computed manually in IST via a fixed 330-minute offset, and a slot fires only when it starts 14–16 minutes out, a window sized so a 5-minute cron tick hits each aarti exactly once. Idempotency is reinforced by an in-process `recentlyFired` Set keyed on temple/slot/IST-date, flushed every 24 hours because the Render process is long-lived — meaning dedupe does not survive restarts, though the time window largely covers that. Finally, tokens reported as expired by `sendFcm` are batch-deleted from `fcmDeviceToken` on a best-effort basis, while sends themselves run sequentially per token, which could become a latency concern as the audience grows.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\content-auto-post..summary: This Vitest test suite validates the helper utilities and safety allowlist exported by the sibling module `content-auto-post.js` in the API's jobs directory. It exercises three helpers exposed via the module's `__testing` namespace: `normSub`, which normalizes subreddit names by stripping any `r/` or `/r/` prefix and lowercasing; `normTitle`, which collapses whitespace and lowercases post titles; and `stripFlairFooter`, which extracts a trailing `[suggested flair: X]` tag from generated post bodies while returning the cleaned body and a null flair when no tag is present. It also verifies the `REDDIT_AUTOPOST_ALLOWLIST` set, asserting that approved subreddits (hinduism, india, indiaspeaks, askhinduism, bhajan) are included and that NSFW or unrelated subs like politics and worldnews are excluded. The only dependency is the `vitest` framework plus the module under test. The suite signals two notable design constraints: auto-posting is gated by a hardcoded subreddit allowlist as a safety measure, and helpers are deliberately exposed through a `__testing` export rather than being part of the module's public API.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\consultation-expir.summary: This file implements a periodic cleanup job that expires stale `pending_payment` astrologer consultations so abandoned Razorpay checkouts stop blocking an astrologer's availability slot. It exports the `tickConsultationExpire` function, which bulk-updates rows in the `astrologer_consultations` table to `cancelled` once their `created_at` is older than the `STALE_AFTER_MINUTES` cutoff, and the `ConsultationExpireResult` interface describing the job's outcome (`expired` count, plus optional `skipped` and `reason` fields). Its only internal dependency is the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, used here to run a parameterized raw SQL UPDATE against PostgreSQL; Razorpay figures only indirectly, since its ~15-minute order expiry is what justifies the 30-minute stale threshold. The 15-minute padding deliberately absorbs client clock skew and retry races, and the operation is idempotent because it only touches rows still in `pending_payment`. Cancelled rows are retained rather than deleted so support can perform refund forensics, and cancelling them keeps them from conflicting with future per-astrologer per-slot uniqueness constraints. A notable gotcha: all errors are swallowed into a skipped result — including a regex-matched "table-missing" case for when the migration hasn't run — so callers must check the returned `skipped`/`reason` fields rather than rely on exceptions.

apps\\api\\src\\integrations\\claude.ts.summary: Despite its name, `apps/api/src/integrations/claude.ts` is the API's LLM provider abstraction layer: it picks a backend at module load based on environment variables, preferring Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`GROQ_BASE`, keyed by `GROQ_API_KEY`) and falling back to the Anthropic SDK (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`), with a `DEMO_MODE` flag when neither is set — and it treats the literal value `'demo-key'` as an unset key. Its main export is the `MODELS` constant, which exposes provider-agnostic `SONNET` and `HAIKU` aliases consumed by callers in `ai.service.ts`; these map to `llama-3.3-70b-versatile` / `llama-3.1-8b-instant` on Groq or `claude-sonnet-4-20250514` / `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` on Anthropic, with the SONNET tier intended for richer `/chat` and `/astrology` answers and HAIKU for fast, cheap calls like recommendations. The bulk of the file is `DEMO_TOPICS`, a keyword-matched bank of static fallback responses (typed via the `DemoTopic` interface) for the Darshya devotional app, covering topics like marriage, health, children, education, grief, festivals, vastu, gemstones, and pilgrimage — each packed with Sanskrit shlokas, mantras, puja suggestions, and cross-promotions for Darshya features such as booking pujas and Live Darshan. Notable design choices include resolving the provider and model aliases once at startup (so key changes require a restart), constructing the Anthropic client as a null-cast placeholder when its key is absent to avoid accidental instantiation, and choosing Groq primarily because its free tier approximates Sonnet quality at no cost. The main gotcha is that demo mode is purely static keyword matching, so responses are canned marketing content rather than generated answers, and any query outside the seeded topics will need a default fallback defined later in the file.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\content-auto-post..summary: This file implements the "Layer AO" cron job that automatically publishes APPROVED Reddit drafts from the `content_drafts` table, exporting `runContentAutoPost` for the core logic and `tickContentAutoPost` as a never-throwing wrapper intended for the master-cron scheduler. It depends on the internal `prisma` client (`lib/prisma.js`, queried via raw `$queryRawUnsafe` SQL) for loading candidates and marking them POSTED, and on `lib/reddit.js`'s `isRedditConfigured` and `submitRedditPost` to talk to Reddit's API; the whole job is no-op gated on `REDDIT_*` env vars being present. Key exported entities include the `AutoPostResult` interface (attempted/posted/failed/skipped counters plus errors) and `REDDIT_AUTOPOST_ALLOWLIST`, a hardcoded set of six permitted subreddits that can only change via code review. Reddit ToS-friendly rate limiting is enforced in three ways: a 24-hour cooldown per subreddit, a cap of two posts per tick, and normalized-title dedupe against previously POSTED drafts, with an in-run `tickPostedSubs` set as an extra guard against same-tick duplicates. A notable quirk is `stripFlairFooter`, which extracts a generator-appended "[suggested flair: X]" trailer from the draft body and forwards it as the API's flair text so it never appears in the published post. The header comments call out an explicit gap: Quora has no public posting API, so Quora drafts remain APPROVED indefinitely and must be pasted manually from /admin/content-queue (documented in docs/reddit-quora-autopost.md). Internal helpers `normSub`, `normTitle`, and `stripFlairFooter` are surfaced through a `__testing` export for unit tests.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\content-seed.ts.summary: This file implements a daily cron job that seeds marketing content by generating two Reddit post drafts and two Quora answer drafts, saving them as DRAFT rows in the content_drafts table via the content-draft.service — it deliberately never auto-posts, leaving an admin to review, edit, approve, and manually publish before marking items POSTED. It exports the `ContentSeedResult` interface (per-platform success/failure counts plus skip metadata), the core `runContentSeed(force)` function, and `tickContentSeed()`, a never-throwing wrapper designed to be called from the master-cron. All generation logic is delegated to `../services/content-draft.service.js`, from which it imports `generateRedditPost`, `generateQuoraAnswer`, `saveDraft`, and the `TOPIC_POOL`, `REDDIT_TARGETS`, and `QUORA_TOPICS` constant pools; the underlying LLM calls require the `GROQ_API_KEY` environment variable, and the job skips silently if it is unset or set to the placeholder 'demo-key'. Two notable design decisions: the once-per-UTC-day gate is tracked in an in-process variable (`lastRunUtcDay`), which the comments acknowledge is best-effort because Render's free tier restarts frequently, so duplicate runs on restart are possible; and topic/subreddit selection uses a deterministic day-of-year rotation in `pickN` (with a stride of 7 and collision guard) rather than randomness, ensuring variety across days without an RNG dependency. A small gotcha: Reddit drafts have their suggested flair appended directly into the stored body text rather than kept as a separate field, and per-item failures are logged with `console.warn` and counted rather than aborting the run.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\daily-panchang-com.summary: This file is a scheduled cron job that precomputes Hindu almanac (panchang) data — tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana, sunrise/sunset, rahuKaal, shubhMuhurat, festivals, and vrat — for a rolling 7-day horizon and persists it to the `DailyPanchang` table so user-facing reads never trigger expensive on-the-fly calculation. Its single export, `runDailyPanchangCompute()`, iterates from UTC-midnight today through the next six days, calls `computePanchang()` from `services/panchang.service.js` for each date, and upserts the result via the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma.js`, returning a `ComputeResult` tally of `{written, skipped, errors}`. The job exists specifically to keep the 2-day staleness freshness gate in `panchang.service.ts:getToday` satisfied, preventing any request from falling through to dynamic compute on the hot path. Delhi is hardcoded as the canonical city (`CITY = 'Delhi'`) because `DailyPanchang.date` is `@unique`, constraining the model to one city per date. The design is deliberately idempotent — the upsert keyed on date makes hourly reruns safe — and write volume is kept minimal (7 rows per run) to stay within Supabase free-tier quotas. Per-date failures are caught, logged, and counted rather than aborting the run, so one bad day doesn't block the rest of the horizon. One minor gotcha: the `skipped` counter is declared and returned but never incremented, so it always reports zero.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\daily-panchang-cro.summary: This cron job fans out a daily panchang (Hindu almanac) email to waitlist devotees, via the exported `runDailyPanchangBlast` function which returns a `PanchangBlastResult` tally of sent/failed counts. It fetches the day's panchang once through `panchangService.getToday()`, renders a shared HTML body with the internal `panchangEmailHtml` helper (tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana, sunrise/sunset, Rahu Kaal, festivals), and sends it through the `sendEmail` wrapper in `lib/email`, which sits on Resend. Recipients come from the `waitlist` Prisma model filtered to `status: 'CONFIRMED'` with `panchangOptIn: true`, paginated in batches of 100 using cursor-based pagination ordered by `createdAt`, with a one-second sleep between batches to avoid Resend rate limits and Postgres connection pressure on the Supabase free tier. The whole job no-ops with a `skipped` result when `RESEND_API_KEY` is unset or the panchang is unavailable, keeping demo and test environments safe. Each send attempts an audit row in `OutreachLog` under the `daily_panchang` template key, but this is deliberately best-effort: it reuses the waitlist row id as a `leadId` against a Lead foreign key that may not exist, so failures are swallowed silently. One subtlety is that the date label comes from UTC (`toISOString().slice(0, 10)`), and the city defaults to "Delhi" when the panchang payload lacks a `locationCity`.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\outreach-cron.foll.summary: This Vitest test suite regression-locks ticket R-Q1-CS-008: the addition of a 14-day follow-up touch to the outreach email sequencer, alongside raising the contact cap to 5. It verifies that `followupTemplateKey` from `../services/outreach.service.js` emits `<role>_followup_14day` keys for all five lead roles (TEMPLE, PRIEST, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR — mapped to the `wellness_` prefix — and GAUSHALA) without breaking the existing 3-day and 7-day keys. It also asserts on disk that each role's `*_followup_14day.html` file exists under `templates/outreach` and contains the `{{layoutStart}}`/`{{layoutEnd}}` layout markers, using `node:fs` and `node:path` with `fileURLToPath` for ESM directory resolution. Rather than executing the cron job, the suite reads `outreach-cron.ts` as raw text and makes search-string assertions: that `MAX_CONTACT_COUNT = 5` is declared, `sendFollowup(lead, 14)` is wired as the fourth touch, a `followup14day` result bucket exists, and the 7-day query window is bounded by `lt: sevenDaysAgo, gt: fourteenDaysAgo` so the two touches never overlap. Notable gotchas: the role strings are cast through the Prisma Lead enum with eslint-disable comments since only the string transform is exercised, and the source-grep approach means refactors of `outreach-cron.ts` that change formatting could break these tests despite correct behavior.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\subscription-expir.summary: This file implements the daily subscription-expiry reminder job for the Darshya API: `runSubscriptionExpiryNotice(lookaheadDays = 3)` finds subscriptions expiring within the lookahead window and emails each user a renewal notice with the days remaining and a link to `https://darshya.online/upgrade`. It exports the `SubscriptionExpiryResult` interface (`notified`, `failed`, optional `skipped`/`reason`), which the function returns as a run summary. It builds on two internal modules: `findUpcomingExpirations` from `../services/subscription.service.js` for the expiry query, and `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js` as the mailer. Notable design choices: the job is idempotent within a day because idempotency is delegated to the date-window filter in the query rather than any local dedupe state, and the mailer is treated as best-effort — if the initial query throws, the function returns a `skipped: true` result with the error message instead of failing. Rows lacking an `email` are silently skipped, per-recipient send exceptions are caught and counted as `failed`, and a sendEmail result that is either `ok` or `skipped` (e.g., mailer disabled) is counted as `notified`, so callers should not read `notified` as strictly "emails delivered."

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\weekly-digest.test.summary: This vitest test suite verifies the scheduling gate and email-rendering safety of the sibling `weekly-digest.js` job module, importing its internals through a `__testing` export rather than a public API. It covers three functions: `isSunday9AmIst`, which must return true only during the Sunday 09:00 IST hour (equivalent to 03:30–04:29 UTC, so the gate works on UTC-based servers); `escapeHtml`, which must neutralize `<`, `>`, `&`, and `"` in user-supplied strings; and `digestEmailHtml`, which builds the weekly digest email and is asserted to include the recipient's name, the week-start label in the subject, and a per-user unsubscribe link. The suite depends only on `vitest` and the module under test, using fixed dates around 2026-05-03 (a Sunday) as deterministic fixtures. A notable gotcha the tests encode is timezone handling: the check must not fire on Monday 09:00 IST or adjacent Sunday hours, and the PII-leak test codifies a privacy constraint that one devotee's data must never appear in another's email body.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\ai-usage.ts.summary: This file implements the "Layer M3" paywall gate that meters how many AI chat messages each user can send, enforcing three plan tiers: free users get 5 messages per calendar month, holders of an active BASIC `MarketplaceSubscription` (the ₹99 one-day "astro_session") get 30 messages per subscription, and PRO subscribers (₹499 monthly) get unlimited access. It exports `canSendMessage` (a read-only admission check returning a `UsageDecision`), `recordMessage` (increments the appropriate counter and must be called exactly once per accepted chat), `getUsageSummary` (for UI display), and the `AI_USAGE_LIMITS` constants. It depends on the internal `prisma` client to look up active DEVOTEE-role subscriptions and on `cacheGet`/`cacheSet` from `./cache.js` for counters, backed by an in-memory `Map` fallback when Redis is unavailable. A deliberate design choice is that no new database schema was added: counters live in Redis with TTLs (35 days for month-keyed free counters, subscription lifetime for session counters) so expiry replaces any reset cron. Notable gotchas: anonymous users (`anon-`/`demo-` prefixes) bypass metering entirely and rely on the separate 20/min IP rate limit, database errors during plan lookup silently degrade paying users to the free tier rather than failing the request, and increment idempotency is left entirely to the caller.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\alert.ts.summary: This file is a lightweight internal ops-alerting utility for the Darshya API, used to notify the on-call human about real-time events like hot lead replies or failed payments. Its single export, `sendOpsAlert`, takes an `OpsAlertParams` (subject, body, optional `AlertSeverity`) and always resolves to an `OpsAlertResult` describing the outcome — it never throws, so callers can safely fire-and-forget it inside paths like webhook handlers that must still ACK 200. Routing follows a precedence chain: if `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` is set it POSTs a simple text payload (decorated with a severity emoji from `SEVERITY_EMOJI`) to that Slack incoming webhook via `fetch`; otherwise it falls back to the comma-separated `ADMIN_EMAILS` list, sent through the sibling `lib/email.ts` module's `sendEmail` function (which itself wraps Resend); if neither is configured, it logs and returns a skipped result for graceful degradation. The email path HTML-escapes angle brackets in the body and prefixes the subject with a severity tag like `[Darshya ops · HIGH]`. Notably, severity only affects formatting (emoji and subject tag), not routing or urgency behavior, and there is no retry or rate-limiting logic.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\master-cron.ts.summary: This file is the master cron orchestrator for the API: since Render's free tier has no native cron, it exposes a single `runDailyOps()` entry point (hit via `POST /api/v1/admin/jobs/daily-ops` from cron-job.org or Upstash QStash, roughly every 30 minutes) that sequentially runs every scheduled job and returns an aggregated `DailyOpsResult` report. The core design rule is that each step is best-effort and isolated — every internal tick (`tickOutreach`, `tickWaitlistNudges`, `tickPanchangBlast`, `tickYoutubeDiscovery`, `tickApolloRefresh`, `tickAutoRefunds`, `tickDispatchSweep`, `tickStaleBookingEscalation`, `tickWeeklyBackup`, etc.) wraps its call in try/catch and converts failures into `{ skipped: true, reason }` results so one outage (e.g. Resend down, unmigrated Prisma tables) never aborts the rest of the tick. It composes a large dependency graph of sibling jobs (`outreach-cron`, `youtube-discovery`, `apollo-refresh`, `content-seed`, `content-auto-post`, `aarti-notify`, `weekly-digest`, `backup-cron`, `daily-panchang-compute-cron`, `consultation-expire`) plus services and libs (`prisma`, `panchangService`, `bookingService`, `dispatchService`, `processAutoRefunds` from `refund.service`, `sendPush` from `lib/web-push`, `prewarmDailyHoroscopes` from `lib/astrology`, and `sweepOldRows` from `lib/webhook-idempotency`). Time-based gating is split between this file (the panchang push blast only fires in the 5:00–5:59 AM IST window unless `forcePanchang` is passed, computed via `isFiveAmIstWindow`) and the sub-jobs themselves (7-day Apollo cooldown, Sunday 9 AM IST weekly digest, Sunday 2 AM IST `pg_dump`-to-R2 backup). Two jobs notably fix prior gaps: `tickStaleBookingEscalation` finally wires up the previously caller-less `bookingService.escalateStaleBookings(72)` so abandoned priest_assigned bookings get force-cancelled for refund review, and `tickDispatchSweep` calls `dispatchService.sweepExpiredOffers()` so a silent pandit triggers auto-reassignment instead of stranding the devotee. Gotchas include the waitlist nudge path calling the Resend REST API directly via `fetch` (gated on `RESEND_API_KEY`, hardcoded darshya.online confirm links) and counting nudges even when the schema update fails, the panchang blast pruning expired web-push subscriptions inline, and an `outreachOnly` option that short-circuits the tick with placeholder skipped results for every other job.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\youtube-discovery..summary: This file implements a cron job that keeps the `live_darshan_streams` table fresh by polling the YouTube Data API v3 `search.list` endpoint for each temple in the hardcoded `TEMPLE_CHANNELS` list (five curated channels mapped by canonical `UC...` channel IDs to `temples.slug` values) and updating each stream row's `playback_url`, `status`, `youtube_video_id`, and `streamProvider` to reflect whatever is currently live, flipping idle channels to `offline`. Its exports are `discoverLiveStreams` (the core run, returning a `YoutubeDiscoveryResult` with per-channel `YoutubeDiscoveryChannelResult` entries), the rate-limited wrapper `maybeRunYoutubeDiscovery` returning a `YoutubeDiscoveryGatedResult`, and the test-only `__resetYoutubeDiscoveryRateLimit` helper. It depends on the internal `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, uses `zod` schemas to validate the YouTube search response, reads the `YOUTUBE_API_KEY` environment variable, and calls `www.googleapis.com/youtube/v3/search` via `fetch`. The dominant design constraint is API quota: `search.list` costs 100 of the 10,000 free daily units, so a module-level in-memory `lastRunAt` limiter enforces a 30-minute minimum interval and the channel list must stay at five or fewer — a limiter that assumes a single API instance and would need Redis or a `cron_runs` table if scaled horizontally. The job is built for graceful degradation: it no-ops with `{ skipped: true }` when the key is missing or `demo-key`, isolates per-channel HTTP and DB errors so one failure doesn't abort the run, and returns `no-temple` / `no-stream-row` statuses instead of throwing when seed data is absent. Writes are deliberately idempotent — rows are only updated when something actually changed, and `actualStart` is only stamped on an offline-to-live transition — to avoid spurious `updatedAt` churn in audit logs.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\astro-mappings.ts.summary: This file is a self-contained static data module in the API (`apps/api`) that powers astrologically-personalized puja recommendations, with no internal or external dependencies. It exports three lookup tables with their interfaces: `NAKSHATRA_DEITY_MAP` (27 nakshatras mapped via `NakshatraInfo` to ruling deity, planet, element, and puja categories), `RASHI_MAP` (12 zodiac signs via `RashiInfo` with Hindi names, elements, ruling planets, and deity affinities), and `LIFE_EVENT_PUJA_MAP` (10 life events like marriage and career via `LifeEventPujaInfo` with suggested pujas, deities, and mantras). Four helper functions query this data: `getDeityForNakshatra` and `getPujaCategoriesForEvent` do simple normalized key lookups, while `getRecommendedDeity` merges rashi and nakshatra affinities into a primary/alternate deity result with human-readable reasoning, and `getComprehensiveRecommendation` aggregates deities, pujas, mantras, and categories across all three input dimensions. Notable design points: all lookups normalize keys with lowercase and space-to-underscore replacement and return null on misses, `getRecommendedDeity` defaults to Ganesha as a universal fallback when neither rashi nor nakshatra is provided, nakshatra deity takes precedence as primary when both inputs exist, and outputs are deduplicated via `Set`. One gotcha is the use of non-null assertions (`deityAffinity[0]!`) that rely on the hardcoded data always being non-empty.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\outreach-cron.ts.summary: This file implements the outbound lead-nurturing cadence, exporting `runOutreachTick()` and the `OutreachTickResult` interface; each tick sends first-touch email plus best-effort WhatsApp to up to 50 NEW leads, then 3-day, 7-day, and 14-day follow-up emails to EMAILED leads, flipping leads to EMAILED status and logging every attempt through `../services/outreach.service.js` helpers (`sendEmail`, `sendWhatsApp`, `recordOutreach`, `incrementContactCount`, `firstTouchTemplateKey`, `followupTemplateKey`). A one-sentence personalized opener is generated per lead via `generateText` from `../integrations/claude.js` (actually backed by Groq per the `GROQ_API_KEY` check), and it degrades gracefully to an empty string when the provider is missing, on a demo key, or errors. Because Render's free tier has no built-in cron, the tick is triggered externally — GitHub Actions or another scheduler hitting `/api/v1/admin/outreach/run`. Sends are throttled to Resend's free-tier limits (600ms between sends, daily cap of 90 tracked in a lazily created raw-SQL `resend_daily_counter` table via `prisma.$executeRawUnsafe`), deliberately preserving quota headroom for transactional booking-confirmation and 80G-receipt emails sharing the same Resend account; setting `RESEND_TIER=pro` relaxes both limits. Notable gotchas: OutreachLog IDs are pre-generated with `randomUUID()` so open/click tracking links can reference the row before it exists, follow-ups are deduped by `alreadySent` against prior log statuses, the sequence caps at `MAX_CONTACT_COUNT = 5`, and the header comment documents only three stages even though a fourth (14-day touch, ticket R-Q1-CS-008) was added later.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\astrology.ts.summary: This module is the API's astrology domain layer: it generates Vedic birth charts (kundli) and daily horoscopes, validating inputs with the zod schemas `KundliInputSchema` and `HoroscopeQuerySchema` before computing anything. Its main exports are `generateKundli`, which delegates real sidereal astronomy to `buildVedicChart` from `./jyotish.js` (Lahiri ayanamsa, truncated VSOP87, true Lagna) and then layers on the local `RASHIS`/`NAKSHATRAS` lookup tables, `nakshatraFromLongitude`, and `buildDashaSequence` to produce a `KundliPayload` with planetary positions, Vimshottari dasha timeline, and an LLM-generated interpretation; and `getDailyHoroscope`, which returns a cached-or-generated `DailyHoroscopePayload`, plus `prewarmDailyHoroscopes` for the daily cron and the `SIGNS` constant. Key dependencies are the Claude integration (`generateText`, `MODELS`, `DEMO_MODE` from `../integrations/claude.js`) for Sonnet-powered chart interpretations and Haiku-powered horoscope readings, and the Redis-style cache helpers (`cacheGet`/`cacheSet`) with a 24-hour `HOROSCOPE_CACHE_TTL` keyed by sign, language, scope, and date. Notable design choices: everything degrades gracefully — `DEMO_MODE` or any LLM failure falls back to templated interpretations and the bilingual `STATIC_HOROSCOPE_HINTS` table, and missing birth coordinates fall back to Delhi (`FALLBACK_LAT_DELHI`/`FALLBACK_LON_DELHI`) with a user-facing warning that the Lagna is approximate. Gotchas worth flagging: birth time is treated as UTC because there is no IANA timezone lookup (callers must pre-normalise), the dasha first period is prorated by the Moon's remaining nakshatra fraction using 365.25-day years, and the `source` field misleadingly reports `vedicastroapi` based only on `VEDIC_ASTRO_API_KEY` being set even though no external API call is actually made. Sign lookup is lenient — `normaliseSign` accepts English, Sanskrit, or Hindi names — and each kundli carries a non-PII `signature` hash for analytics de-duplication.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\astrologer-resolver.summary: This file implements the slug↔UUID resolution layer that lets public URL routes use friendly astrologer slugs (e.g. `astro_001`) while the backend still keys everything on real Supabase user UUIDs from the `users` table. It exports three functions: `resolveAstrologerUserId(slug)`, which performs the forward lookup and returns `null` when nothing matches (callers are expected to respond 404); `resolveAstrologerSlug(userId)`, a reverse lookup used by the admin UI to render slugs for verified astrologers; and `bindAstrologerSlug(slug, userId)`, an admin-only, idempotent upsert that binds a slug after KYC approval and refreshes `verified_at` on re-bind. The only internal dependency is the shared `prisma` client from `./prisma.js`, and all database access goes through raw parameterized SQL (`$queryRawUnsafe` / `$executeRawUnsafe`) against the `astrologer_slug_map` table, with a fallback probe of the `astrologer_profiles` table. Notably, the lookup has a deliberate two-step resolution order — `astrologer_slug_map` first (populated on admin approval), then `astrologer_profiles` — and both queries are wrapped in silent try/catch blocks because the table and the profile `slug` column may not exist yet; the file header states owner KYC field decisions are still pending, so this module intentionally ships the indirection layer ahead of its data. The `astrologer_slug_map` table itself is created idempotently in `ensure-schema.ts`. Inputs are strictly validated — slugs must match `[a-z0-9_-]{2,64}` and user IDs must be 36-character UUIDs — with the resolver returning `null` on bad input while `bindAstrologerSlug` throws instead. The main gotcha for consumers is that swallowed errors mean a missing table, a cold database, or a genuinely unmapped slug are indistinguishable, all surfacing as `null`.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\astrology.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite validates the astrology library in `apps/api/src/lib/astrology.js`, covering its Zod input schemas and the three main entry points: `generateKundli`, `getDailyHoroscope`, and `prewarmDailyHoroscopes`. The validation tests confirm `KundliInputSchema` rejects future birth dates, malformed time-of-birth strings like "8am", and inputs missing both `location` and lat/lng coordinates, while `HoroscopeQuerySchema` rejects unknown sign names. The kundli tests assert that `generateKundli` returns a fully populated chart — a `signature` prefixed with `kr_`, `rashi`, `sunSign`, `lagna`, `nakshatra`, a nine-step `dasha.sequence`, at least nine `planetaryPositions`, and at least four `interpretation` entries — and that the signature is deterministic for identical inputs, which matters for caching or deduplication. The horoscope tests verify `getDailyHoroscope` resolves both English names and Sanskrit aliases (e.g. `simha` → Leo with element Fire), throws on unrecognized signs, and that `prewarmDailyHoroscopes` warms all twelve entries of the exported `SIGNS` constant. The only external dependency is `vitest`; everything else under test comes from the sibling `astrology.js` module. Notably, the suite tests behavior rather than implementation, so it doubles as a contract spec for the astrology module's validation rules and output shape.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\cache.ts.summary: This file provides the API's Redis-backed caching layer, designed as an env-or-noop abstraction: when neither `REDIS_URL` nor `UPSTASH_REDIS_URL` is set (or the connection fails), every operation silently falls through so production keeps working against the database directly. It exports `cacheGet` and `cacheSet` for JSON-serialized reads and writes with TTL, `cached` as a read-through wrapper that invokes a loader on miss (and deliberately skips caching null/undefined results), `cacheDel` for single-key invalidation, `cacheDelPattern` for SCAN-based bulk invalidation, and a `CACHE_TTL` constant map with per-entity lifetimes for panchang, temples, pujas, and festivals. The only external dependency is `ioredis`, and it works with Upstash via their standard TLS `redis://` endpoint. Key design choices: a lazily created singleton client avoids file-descriptor exhaustion on serverless/Render free tiers; the client is configured with `enableOfflineQueue: false`, `maxRetriesPerRequest: 1`, and a 2-second connect timeout so a down or slow Redis can never block a request path; after the first error, `connectionFailed` flips and Redis is disabled for the process lifetime, also suppressing log floods. All errors are swallowed by design — cache misses and failures always degrade to a DB hit rather than an exception. Two gotchas for callers: `Date` objects round-trip as ISO strings and must be reconstructed manually, and pattern deletion uses `scanStream` (not KEYS) so it's safe on large keyspaces but streams deletions in batches of 100.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\email.ts.summary: This file is the API's single source of truth for transactional email in the Darshya app, wrapping the Resend SDK (`resend` npm package) behind one exported `sendEmail` function plus a set of HTML template builders. `sendEmail` accepts recipients, subject, HTML/text bodies, and attachments, returning a `SendEmailResult` object (`ok`, `skipped`, `id`, `error`) rather than throwing, so callers never crash on mail failures. A key design decision is graceful degradation: if `RESEND_API_KEY` is unset, the client is null and every send resolves to `{ ok: false, skipped: true }`, letting local and demo environments run without a mail key; sender identity comes from `RESEND_FROM_EMAIL` and `RESEND_REPLY_TO` env vars with defaults pointing at darshya.online addresses. The exported template functions — `magicLinkEmail`, `bookingConfirmationEmail`, `providerApprovedEmail`, `providerRejectedEmail`, `supportTicketAlertEmail`, `supportTicketReceivedEmail`, `supportTicketReplyEmail`, and `donationReceiptEmail` — each return subject/html/text triples rendered through a shared `shell` helper that applies Darshya-branded inline styles (orange accent, warm cream background). Gotchas: most templates interpolate user data directly into HTML without escaping (only `supportTicketAlertEmail` and `supportTicketReplyEmail` escape `<` in message bodies), which is a potential injection risk if names or subjects contain markup, and several URLs are hardcoded to `https://darshya.online` rather than env-configured. The module is consumed by API routes handling auth magic links, puja bookings, provider onboarding review, support tickets, and gaushala donations.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\embeddings.ts.summary: This module wraps the Cohere `embed-multilingual-v3.0` API to produce 1024-dimension vectors that power semantic search across mantras, aartis, content, and temples in 100+ languages, letting English queries match Devanagari titles. Its exports are `generateEmbedding` for single texts (with an `inputType` distinguishing `search_document` from `search_query`, since Cohere optimizes each direction), `generateEmbeddingsBatch` for seed/backfill scripts (respecting Cohere's 96-texts-per-call limit), the `toPgVector` helper that formats vectors as pgvector literals for Postgres, and an `embeddings` metadata object exposing `enabled`, `model`, and `dimensions`. The only external dependency is Cohere's `/v1/embed` REST endpoint called via `fetch`, authenticated by the `COHERE_API_KEY` environment variable; the consumer side targets a Postgres database with the pgvector extension. Notable design choices: if `COHERE_API_KEY` is unset the functions return null so the search route silently falls back to LIKE-based matching, all failures (HTTP errors, exceptions, empty input) degrade to null rather than throwing, and inputs are whitespace-normalized and truncated to 2048 characters. The code pins `embedding_types` to `['float']` but parses the response defensively because Cohere returns different JSON shapes depending on that parameter, and `toPgVector` sanitizes NaN/Infinity values that Postgres would reject.

apps\\api\\src\\jobs\\weekly-digest.ts.summary: This file implements Darshya's weekly devotee digest job, fanning out a Sunday 9 AM IST email to opted-in users with four sections: upcoming aartis at followed temples, content published in the last 7 days, a personalized puja recommendation, and panchang highlights. It exports `runWeeklyDigest()`, which performs the batched send and returns a `WeeklyDigestResult` (sent/skipped/failed tallies), and `maybeRunWeeklyDigest()`, a cron-gated wrapper that enforces the Sunday 09:00 IST window via `isSunday9AmIst()` (implemented as a UTC+5:30 offset check) plus a 6-day cooldown persisted in the `WeeklyDigestRun` table; a `__testing` export exposes internals for unit tests. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma`, `sendEmail` from `lib/email` (backed by Resend and short-circuiting when `RESEND_API_KEY` is unset), and `panchangService` for tithi and festival data. Throughput is capped at 50 messages/second via a 20ms inter-send sleep (`SEND_RATE_MS`) to respect Resend's free-tier limit, and users are paged with cursor-based batches of 200. Unsubscribes land in the `WeeklyDigestOptOut` table, but notably if that table is missing (migration pending) the job sends to everyone since default state is opted-in; similarly, the temple-follow join drops to raw SQL because `TempleFollow` stores a loose UUID with no Prisma relation, so it survives temple deletions. All section fetchers are best-effort, swallowing database errors into empty arrays or nulls rather than aborting the run, and the email body is privacy-scoped to only the recipient's own profile fields. Two pieces are acknowledged stubs: `fetchUpcomingAartisForUser` returns hardcoded "Sandhya Aarti" placeholder rows, and the gotra-based recommendation in `fetchRecommendedPuja` currently just returns the first active `pujaType` by `sortOrder`.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\error-i18n.ts.summary: This module provides localized API error messages so that Indian users on Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, or Kannada locales see translated error text instead of raw English in UI toasts. It defines the `SupportedLang` union ('en', 'hi', 'ta', 'te', 'kn') plus `SUPPORTED_LANGS`, a 30-member `ErrorCode` union covering domain failures like `BOOKING_LOCKED`, `PAYMENT_SIGNATURE_INVALID`, `OTP_EXPIRED`, and `AADHAAR_NOT_VERIFIED`, and exports `ERROR_CODES` derived from the English catalog keys. Three functions form the public API: `pickLang` negotiates a language from an explicit `?lang=` override (which wins) or a q-weighted `Accept-Language` header, defaulting to 'en'; `localizedError` translates a code with fallback to English and then to a generic message so callers never get an empty string; and `buildErrorResponse` wraps the message in the standardized `{ error: { code, message, details? } }` envelope for route handlers. The file is fully self-contained with no internal or external dependencies — translations are hand-maintained in five inline `Catalog` records keyed by `ErrorCode`, which gives compile-time completeness checking per language. A notable gotcha is that adding a new error code requires updating all five catalogs (the `Catalog` type enforces this), and unknown language strings passed to `localizedError` silently coerce to English rather than throwing.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\fcm.ts.summary: This file implements a lightweight Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) HTTP v1 client as a singleton, deliberately avoiding the heavy `firebase-admin` dependency (and its gRPC native bindings) by hand-rolling service-account authentication: it builds an RS256-signed JWT using Node's built-in `crypto` module and exchanges it at the Google OAuth token endpoint, caching the resulting access token with a 60-second expiry buffer. Its key exports are `sendFcm` (sends a single push notification and classifies failures as `expired` when FCM returns 404/UNREGISTERED/INVALID_ARGUMENT so callers can prune dead tokens from the database), `sendFcmMulticast` (serial fan-out over a token list since the v1 API has no batch endpoint, returning sent/expired/failed tallies), the `FcmPayload` and `FcmSendResult` types, and the `fcmConfig` object exposing `enabled` and `projectId`. It depends only on `node:crypto` and global `fetch`, and is configured entirely through three environment variables — `FCM_PROJECT_ID`, `FCM_CLIENT_EMAIL`, and `FCM_PRIVATE_KEY` — where the private key may contain literal `\n` sequences that get normalized into real newlines. Notable gotchas: if any of the three env vars is missing, the client silently disables itself and every send returns `{skipped: true}` rather than throwing; device tokens are masked via `maskToken` so they never appear in full in logs; and errors are returned as result objects rather than thrown, so callers must inspect the result flags instead of using try/catch.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\feature-flags.test..summary: This vitest suite (`apps/api/src/lib/feature-flags.test.ts`) verifies the server-side feature-flag client in the sibling `./feature-flags` module, which evaluates flags by calling PostHog's `/decide` HTTP endpoint with `fetch`. It covers the module's two exports, `isFeatureEnabled` (boolean check) and `getFeatureFlag` (raw variant value), asserting fail-closed behavior: every error path — missing `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` env var, empty flag key or user ID, non-OK PostHog responses, and network exceptions — returns `false` without throwing. It also pins down multivariate semantics, where the `"control"` variant counts as disabled while any other variant string counts as enabled, and confirms a 30-second per-(flag, user) response cache that dedupes calls, keys entries separately per user, and expires after the TTL. The suite relies on `vi.resetModules()` plus dynamic re-import (`loadFresh`) because the PostHog key is captured at module load time, uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` to test cache expiry, and stubs `global.fetch` to assert that no HTTP call is made in the no-op and invalid-input cases. A notable gotcha baked into these tests: the client is a manual `fetch` wrapper rather than the official `posthog-node` SDK, so correctness depends entirely on this suite's contract with the `/decide` response shape (`featureFlags` map).

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\darshan-schedule.ts.summary: This module provides pure-function helpers for deciding whether a temple is currently in a live-darshan (streaming) window, based on the `Temple.timingInfo` JSON field. It exports the `ScheduleSlot` type, the `parseSchedule` function (which converts the `regularHours` map inside `timingInfo` into sorted minute-based time windows, supporting comma-separated ranges per key and silently skipping malformed entries), the `LiveStatus` discriminated union, and `getLiveStatus`, which reports whether the current moment falls inside an aarti window, how many minutes remain until it ends, and when the next aarti starts — wrapping past midnight to the first slot of the following day. All comparisons are done in minutes-since-midnight IST using the fixed `IST_OFFSET_MIN` (UTC+5:30) offset, which is safe because Asia/Kolkata observes no DST, and the module has zero external dependencies beyond the standard `Date` API. Whether a slot counts as streamable is decided heuristically by `isAartiKey`, which substring-matches the timing key against `AARTI_HINTS` (aarti, arati, suprabhatam, kakad, dhup, shej, madhyana, rajbhog); plain darshan/open hours are parsed into slots but never treated as live. Notable gotchas: windows crossing midnight (end earlier than start) will never match the containment check in `getLiveStatus`, and when multiple aarti windows overlap, the one with the latest end time wins.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\env.ts.summary: This module provides central boot-time environment validation for the API, replacing ad-hoc `process.env` reads that previously let missing secrets (like `RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET` or `JWT_SECRET`) fail late, sometimes mid-payment. It parses `process.env` once at module load via a Zod `envSchema` covering database (`DATABASE_URL`, `DIRECT_URL`), Supabase, Razorpay and Stripe payment keys, auth (`JWT_SECRET`), CORS, and infra knobs like `REDIS_URL`, `PORT`, and `SENTRY_DSN`. Its exports are the typed `env` object, the inferred `Env` type, and `isJobQueueConfigured`, a flag deliberately duplicating the `QUEUE_DISABLED` check from `job-queue.service.ts` so health probes can answer without triggering that service's ioredis lazy-import. The only external dependency is `zod`; internally it is wired in at the very top of `src/server.ts` so the parse runs before any route module reads secrets, making import order a hard requirement. A key design decision is that the change is additive only: existing `process.env.X` reads elsewhere are left untouched and call sites migrate to `env.X` incrementally.
