Validation failures print `[FATAL]` issues and call `process.exit(1)`; additionally, in production a post-schema guard hard-requires `JWT_SECRET`, `DATABASE_URL`, and `CORS_ORIGIN` (keys that stay `.optional()` in the schema so `pnpm dev` works without the full secret set), mirroring the demo-token boot guard in `middlewares/auth.ts`. Free-form runtime knobs such as `RATE_LIMIT_MAX` and `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS` are validated only as strings, with defaults still applied at their use sites.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\ensure-schema.ts.summary: This module is a boot-time defensive schema check for the API: because Render's start command bypasses the `pnpm start` wrapper that normally runs `prisma migrate deploy`, it replays every migration the user-facing dashboards depend on as idempotent DDL on each boot, per the workaround documented in docs/activation-gates.md. It imports the shared Prisma client from `./prisma.js` and centers on a large `STATEMENTS` array of raw SQL that the exported runner executes at startup. The statements cover the provider portal profile tables (`pandit_profiles`, `store_profiles`, `astrologer_profiles`, `wellness_profiles`, `gaushala_profiles`, `temple_profiles`), `provider_kyc`, `users.blocked` columns for the auth hot path, gaushala `cows`/`cow_health_records`/`volunteers`, plus feature tables for antim sanskar bookings, content drafts, FCM device tokens and temple follows, B2B `orgs`/`org_members`/`org_invites`, referrals, `email_sessions`, and the `refresh_token_jtis` replay-detection ledger. Its only real dependency is the Prisma client against PostgreSQL — no external services. The key design constraint is that every statement must be safely re-runnable: it uses `IF NOT EXISTS` everywhere, wraps enum creation and foreign-key/unique constraint additions in `DO $$ ... EXCEPTION WHEN duplicate_object` or `pg_constraint` guards, and guards indexes on `astrologer_consultations` with `to_regclass` so cold starts on stacks lacking that table don't crash. Notably, several profile tables were originally created via `prisma db push` and never had real migrations, so this file is their only prod provisioning path — making it a deliberate but fragile duplicate of the migration history that must be kept in sync by hand.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\lead-role-mapping.t.summary: This file is the single source of truth for translating lead-facing role labels into onboarding role types, fixing a bug (P0 #PBO-8) where a lead role like 'PRIEST' was passed unmapped to the OnboardingService, which didn't recognize it as a valid RoleType and silently fell through to the default step list. It exports two const arrays — LEAD_ROLE_VALUES (TEMPLE, PRIEST, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, GAUSHALA) and ONBOARDING_ROLE_TYPES (PANDIT, STORE_OWNER, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, GAUSHALA_MANAGER, TEMPLE_MANAGER) — along with their derived union types LeadRole and OnboardingRoleType. The internal lookup table LEAD_TO_ONBOARDING drives the exported mapLeadRoleToOnboarding function, while isLeadRole provides a type-guard for validating incoming strings. It has no external dependencies and is consumed by the self-onboard and admin-lead-conversion routes, which receive lead roles but must hand OnboardingService a valid OnboardingRoleType. A notable design choice is that the Record is typed as a total mapping over LeadRole, so TypeScript enforces that every lead role has an onboarding counterpart; note that the two enums intentionally use different vocabularies (e.g. PRIEST → PANDIT, TEMPLE → TEMPLE_MANAGER), which is exactly why the implicit scattered mapping caused the original bug.

This Vitest test file locks down the behavior of the `lead-role-mapping` module (imported as `lead-role-mapping.js`), which serves as the single source of truth translating the five-value lead-role enum (`TEMPLE`, `PRIEST`, `GAUSHALA`, `ASTROLOGER`, `WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR`) into onboarding `RoleType` values. It exercises three exports: `mapLeadRoleToOnboarding`, verified to map every lead role to a valid onboarding type; `LEAD_ROLE_VALUES`, used to guarantee exhaustive coverage so no lead role is ever left unmapped; and `isLeadRole`, a type guard checked to accept exactly the five lead roles while rejecting onboarding types like `PANDIT` and `TEMPLE_MANAGER` plus arbitrary strings. The suite depends only on Vitest's `describe`/`it`/`expect` and the sibling module under test, with no external services involved. The central design constraint, flagged as ticket P0 #PBO-8, is the three asymmetric renames — `PRIEST` to `PANDIT`, `TEMPLE` to `TEMPLE_MANAGER`, and `GAUSHALA` to `GAUSHALA_MANAGER` — which the tests explicitly assert against to prevent a silent pass-through regression where a raw lead enum would leak out as an invalid `RoleType`.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\muhurat.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite exercises the wedding-muhurat module at apps/api/src/lib/muhurat.js, verifying its input validation, nakshatra derivation, and ranked candidate search. It imports MuhuratInputSchema, findWeddingMuhurats, deriveBirthNakshatra, and the NAKSHATRA_NAMES and RASHI_NAMES lookup tables from that module. The validation tests confirm the Zod schema accepts well-formed bride/groom birth data plus a date window, while rejecting an inverted fromDate/toDate range and any search window exceeding 365 days. Derivation tests check that deriveBirthNakshatra maps a date-of-birth and time-of-birth pair to a valid entry in NAKSHATRA_NAMES. The finder tests assert that findWeddingMuhurats returns between one and ten candidates sorted by descending score, that both partners' computed rashi values fall within RASHI_NAMES, and—somewhat brittlely—that the top candidate's abhijitMuhurat window starts at exactly 11:48, meaning the suite is pinned to a deterministic fixture-like outcome for the Hasta/Rohini pairing in late 2026. Notably, the finder accepts optional precomputed brideNakshatra/groomNakshatra fields, letting callers skip derivation when values are already known.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\feature-flags.ts.summary: This file provides server-side PostHog feature-flag evaluation for the API, built to degrade gracefully: when `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` is absent, every call returns `false` or `undefined` so the app runs fine without flags configured. It exports `isFeatureEnabled` (a boolean check that counts any multivariate variant other than `"control"` as enabled), `getFeatureFlag` (returns the raw boolean or variant string, `undefined` when the flag is missing), and `__clearFeatureFlagCache` for tests. Rather than using an SDK, it POSTs directly to PostHog's `/decide/?v=3` endpoint at `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` (defaulting to `https://us.i.posthog.com`), and all network or parsing errors are swallowed so flag evaluation can never break a request path. Results are memoized in a module-level in-memory `Map` keyed by `flagKey::userId` with a 30-second TTL — a deliberate trade-off so rollout changes propagate within a minute while eliminating 95%+ of `/decide` calls on hot paths like the homepage CTA and banner. Two gotchas: the cache is per-process, so serverless or multi-instance deployments won't share it and users may see inconsistent flags across instances; and although `postDecide` fetches all flags for a user, the cache is keyed per flag, so distinct flags for the same user each trigger their own `/decide` call on a miss. Finally, the JSDoc on `isFeatureEnabled` advertises a "short timeout," but no fetch timeout is actually implemented.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\jyotish.ts.summary: This file is the Vedic astrology numerical core for the API, replacing a prior mock that placed planets deterministically relative to the Sun with real astronomical math, and its main entry point is `buildVedicChart`, which takes a birth UTC date plus geographic coordinates and returns a `VedicChart` containing the Lagna and an array of `PlanetPosition` bodies (Sun, Moon, Mercury through Saturn, Rahu, Ketu) with sidereal longitude, rashi index/degree, nakshatra, and whole-sign bhava. It is entirely self-contained with no external dependencies, implementing Meeus-based algorithms in plain math: `julianDay`, `lahiriAyanamsa` (23.85° at J2000 with +50.3″/yr drift), truncated VSOP87-style series in `sunLongitudeTropical` and `moonLongitudeTropical`, `rahuLongitudeTropical` using the mean lunar node (Ketu derived as Rahu + 180°), and `lagnaLongitudeSidereal` computed from local sidereal time via `gmstHours` and mean obliquity. Helper resolvers `rashiIndex`, `rashiDegree`, `nakshatraIndex`, `nakshatraPada`, and `bhavaFromLagna` convert sidereal longitudes into sign, nakshatra/pada, and house placements. Key accuracy trade-offs are documented in the header: the five classical planets use mean heliocentric longitudes from `PLANET_MEANS`, with Mercury and Venus getting a first-order geocentric correction via a max-elongation sine approximation (23°/45°) while outer planets treat heliocentric as approximately geocentric, and Rahu uses the mean rather than true node. The stated target is roughly 0.5° precision — sign-stable for birthdates 1900–2100 but not Swiss Ephemeris grade — chosen deliberately to avoid an opaque external ephemeris dependency. Houses use the whole-sign system (`bhavaFromLagna` = planet sign minus Lagna sign + 1), which is a simplification consumers of `VedicChart` should be aware of.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\payment-mode.ts.summary: This module is the API's centralized guard against fake payments: it decides whether the configured Razorpay credentials are real and, in production, hard-fails any code path that would otherwise silently fall into demo mode. It exports two functions — `isRazorpayDemoMode`, which returns true when `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` is missing or set to the placeholder `rzp_test_demo`, and `assertNotProductionDemo`, which throws an error naming the callsite when demo mode coincides with `NODE_ENV=production` unless `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS=true` is set. It has no runtime dependencies beyond Node environment variables, but it is conceptually load-bearing for `payment.service.ts` (which already crashes at boot on the same condition) plus the donations route and subscription service, both of which previously fell through to a demo path. The core design rule, stated in the header comment, is that every callsite branching on demo mode must call `assertNotProductionDemo` before proceeding, because the demo path issues `order_demo_*` ids, signs nothing, and reports success without moving money — in production that means no ledger row and no 80G receipt while looking identical to a real payment. `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS=true` remains the documented escape hatch, intended for staging only.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\json-fields.ts.summary: This module centralises read/write helpers for Prisma `Json`/`Json[]` columns (ticket P2-30), created because `StoreOrder.statusHistory` was being appended to by hand at multiple mutation sites (status changes, manual payment-confirm) with no shared shape validation, and `StoreOrder.items` was re-narrowed ad-hoc by downstream readers. Its main export, `appendStatusHistory`, performs a type-checked append to the order status audit log: it tolerates a null or malformed current value by starting fresh, coerces `changedAt` (string or Date) to an ISO 8601 string defaulting to now, and returns `Prisma.InputJsonValue[]` so the result slots directly into a Prisma update payload without a call-site cast; the entry shape is defined by the exported `StatusHistoryEntry` interface (status, changedAt, changedBy, note). For reads, it exports `storeOrderItemSchema` (a Zod object requiring `productId`, positive-int `qty`, and non-negative `priceAtPurchase`), the inferred `StoreOrderItem` type, and `validateStoreOrderItems`, which narrows the loose items blob into a typed array. Dependencies are limited to `zod` and the `Prisma` type namespace from `@prisma/client` — no runtime services. Two gotchas are worth flagging: `appendStatusHistory` relies on a deliberate `as unknown as Prisma.InputJsonValue[]` cast (justified in a comment as safe because entries are JSON-serialisable), and `validateStoreOrderItems` fails soft — it returns an empty array for null input and silently drops individual malformed entries rather than throwing, so callers that need strictness must check the result length themselves. Scope is intentionally narrow: only order-history append sites are wired up, while other Json columns such as `pujaBooking.devoteeNames` and `storeOrder.shippingAddress` remain untouched.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pricing.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the NRI pricing helpers exported from the sibling `pricing` module, tracing requirement R-Q2-G-006. It exercises `computeNriPrice`, confirming that a base INR price defaults to the `NRI_INR_MULTIPLIER` 9× rule converted to USD via `INR_USD_INDICATIVE_RATE`, that an explicit `nriPrice` override wins when provided, and that an override of `0` or `null` falls back to the 9× rule; it also asserts that negative or NaN base prices throw an "Invalid basePriceInr" error. It further tests `validateNriPriceBand`, which returns `null` for USD prices inside the acceptable 9×–10× INR-equivalent band (with a 15% tolerance) and returns descriptive error strings when prices breach the floor or ceiling, treating zero-priced inputs as a no-op, and it pins `NRI_INR_MULTIPLIER_MAX` at 10. The only dependencies are `vitest` and the local `./pricing` module, so the suite is a pure unit test with no external services. A notable behavioral gotcha baked into these tests is that falsy explicit overrides (zero or null) silently revert to the default multiplier rather than being honored or rejected.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pricing-bands.ts.summary: This file defines competitor-anchored reference price bands for at-home puja bookings (the `PriestPujaOffering` catalog), seeded from a 2026-08-04 market scan of rivals like 99Pandit, SmartPuja, and PujaPurohit. It exports the `PujaPriceBand` interface (budget/mid/premium INR tiers plus a competitor anchor citation), the `PUJA_PRICE_BANDS` constant covering eleven puja slugs from Satyanarayan to Vehicle Puja, a `CITY_MULTIPLIER` map (Delhi at 0.8 vs Bangalore's 1.0 baseline, with a 0.9 fallback for tier-2/3 cities), and the `INSTANT_SURGE_CAP` of 2.0. The main function, `resolvePujaPrice`, looks up a band by slug, picks a tier price, applies the city multiplier, and — on auspicious muhurat days — applies a surge multiplier clamped to the 2x cap, returning the rounded price plus the base and surge factor. The module is pure data and arithmetic with no runtime dependencies, though its comments tie it to `booking.service`'s `DEFAULT_PRIEST_SHARE` (80/20 pandit/platform split). Notable founder-approved decisions documented here: T1 instant bookings use capped surge pricing rather than a flat fee, and samagri is bundled into headline prices with a premium add-on option. A gotcha: unknown slugs return null and unknown cities silently fall back to the `default` multiplier.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pdf-receipt.ts.summary: This file generates Indian 80G tax-exemption receipt PDFs for gaushala donations in the Darshya platform, producing a `Buffer` suitable for attaching to a Resend email or streaming as a download. Its main exports are the `ReceiptData` interface (donor/donee names, PANs, addresses, amount, receipt number, payment mode and reference, and the gaushala's 80G registration) and the async `generate80GReceipt` function, which lays out a single A4 page with a saffron brand bar (#EA580C), donor/donee sections, amount in figures and words, and a blank authorized-signatory line. It depends solely on the `pdf-lib` library (`PDFDocument`, `StandardFonts`, `rgb`), deliberately chosen because it is pure JavaScript with no native dependencies so it runs on Render's free tier. Two private helpers do notable work: `amountInWords` converts amounts using the Indian numbering system (crore/lakh/thousand rather than millions) and rounds to whole rupees, and `wrap` performs naive character-count line wrapping at 78 characters for addresses. Design gotchas include the hardcoded absolute-coordinate layout (no pagination, so very long content could overflow the page), the MVP decision to leave the signatory blank for physical signing despite a footer claiming the computer-generated receipt is valid without signature, and the requirement that callers supply legally mandated 80G fields (donee PAN and 80G registration number) since they are optional in the type but required for a compliant receipt.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pricing-bands.test..summary: This Vitest test suite validates the pricing engine in the sibling module `pricing-bands.js` (`apps/api/src/lib`), which computes competitor-anchored prices for at-home puja services. It exercises the module's four exports: `PUJA_PRICE_BANDS` (per-slug budget/mid/premium INR bands for core pujas like `satyanarayan-puja`, `griha-pravesh`, `rudrabhishek`, and `vivah-marriage`), `CITY_MULTIPLIER` (per-city rate adjustments, e.g. Delhi priced below Bangalore per the SmartPuja anchor), `INSTANT_SURGE_CAP` (a 2x surge ceiling tied to an India government anchor), and `resolvePujaPrice` (the resolver that takes a slug, tier, city, peak flag, and requested surge, returning base and final prices plus the surge actually applied). Its only dependencies are `vitest` and the internal `pricing-bands.js` module — no external services are involved. Key behavioral contracts locked in by the tests: bands must be monotonic (`budgetInr <= midInr <= premiumInr`), resolution defaults to the budget tier at metro rate, premium/senior tiers price strictly higher, and surge only applies on `isMuhuratPeak` days and is clamped to `INSTANT_SURGE_CAP` even when the caller requests more. The suite also pins edge-case behavior: `resolvePujaPrice` returns `null` for an unknown slug, making "unknown puja" a non-error condition callers must handle.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\prisma.ts.summary: This file creates and exports the API's singleton database client, `prisma`, an instance of `PrismaClient` from `@prisma/client` that the rest of `apps/api` imports for all database access. To survive dev-server hot reloads without leaking connections, the instance is cached on `globalThis` (`globalForPrisma`) in every non-production environment. The client is configured to emit `query` events (tracked as requirement R-Q2-E-011) so the slow-query logger and N+1 detector in `apps/api/src/db/*` can subscribe; emission is a no-op unless a listener attaches, and setting `DB_QUERY_INSTRUMENTATION=off` skips the listener side. Logging verbosity differs by environment: development emits `query`, `warn`, and `error`, while production emits only `query` and `error`. A notable gotcha is the try/catch fallback: if client construction fails (typically a missing `DATABASE_URL`), a bare `PrismaClient` is created anyway so the server can still boot, but any actual query against it will throw at runtime. This means database connectivity failures are deferred from startup to first query, which can obscure misconfiguration until traffic arrives.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\reddit.ts.summary: This file is a self-contained Reddit OAuth and post-submission client for the API server, using Reddit's "script" app password-grant flow against `www.reddit.com/api/v1/access_token` and `oauth.reddit.com/api/submit` via plain `fetch` — no external SDK. Its public surface is `submitRedditPost(input)` (which posts a self/text submission with optional flair and returns a `SubmitPostResult` containing `ok`, `skipped`, `reason`, `url`, and `id`), `isRedditConfigured()`, the `SubmitPostInput`/`SubmitPostResult` types, and a `__resetRedditTokenCache()` test hook. Configuration comes entirely from environment variables (`REDDIT_CLIENT_ID`, `REDDIT_CLIENT_SECRET`, `REDDIT_USERNAME`, `REDDIT_PASSWORD`, optional `REDDIT_USER_AGENT`); if any are missing the client degrades gracefully by returning `{skipped: true}` rather than throwing, and all network/HTTP/Reddit-API errors are likewise captured into the result's `reason` field. Access tokens are cached in a module-level `cachedToken` with a 30-second expiry buffer, subreddit names are normalized by stripping any `r/` prefix, and titles are truncated to Reddit's 300-character limit. A key design boundary: the lib deliberately does no rate-limiting, subreddit allowlisting, or de-duplication — all ToS compliance is pushed to the caller, and the password grant means it must only ever run server-side.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\muhurat.ts.summary: This file implements a self-contained Vedic wedding muhurat (auspicious date) finder that ranks candidate dates by astrological auspiciousness, drawing rules from Brihat Samhita, Muhurta Chintamani, and Dharmasindhu while deliberately avoiding any external panchang dependency. Its main export, `findWeddingMuhurats`, accepts a `MuhuratInput` (validated by the zod `MuhuratInputSchema`, which caps the search range at 365 days), derives each partner's birth nakshatra and rashi via `deriveBirthNakshatra` and the `NAKSHATRA_TO_RASHI` lookup, scores every day in the range, and returns a `MuhuratResponse` with the top-N `MuhuratCandidate` entries carrying a 0–100 score plus human-readable reasons and warnings. Scoring in the internal `dayScore` starts at 50 and adjusts for vivah-auspicious versus forbidden nakshatras (`VIVAH_NAKSHATRAS`, `FORBIDDEN_NAKSHATRAS`), tithi quality (`VIVAH_TITHIS`, `RIKTA_TITHIS`, Amavasya), weekday weights (`WEEKDAY_SCORE`), the Panchak window, and Chandrashtama relative to each partner's natal rashi. The only external dependency is zod; all astronomy is done in-house through deterministic approximations (`julianDay`, `moonLongitudeSidereal`, `sunLongitudeSidereal`, `tithiNumber`) based on simplified Meeus series with a Lahiri ayanamsha, accepting roughly 1° of Moon-longitude error as adequate for booking decisions. Notable gotchas: each day is evaluated at noon UTC, birth datetimes are parsed as UTC despite the IST comment in `deriveBirthNakshatra`, and the `location` input is accepted but never actually used in computation. The Abhijit muhurat window is hardcoded to 11:48–12:36, and `mangalikFlag` is a crude rashi-based proxy rather than a true Mars-house mangal dosha analysis. Supporting exports include the `NAKSHATRA_NAMES` and `RASHI_NAMES` constants, the `Nakshatra` and `Rashi` types, and the longitude converters `nakshatraFromLongitude` and `rashiFromLongitude` for reuse elsewhere.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\rate-limit.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the API's rate-limiting behavior (requirement R-Q2-E-013) by building a lightweight Fastify harness in `buildApp` that mirrors the plugin configuration and key-derivation strategy from `apps/api/src/server.ts`, deliberately avoiding the full server bootstrap (Sentry, Prisma, helmet, CORS). It registers `@fastify/rate-limit` with a `keyGenerator` that partitions buckets by `u:{userId}` when `req.currentUser` is present and falls back to `ip:{req.ip}` for anonymous traffic, plus an `allowList` that exempts the `/health`, `/ready`, and `/metrics` ops endpoints. The tests assert that exceeding the per-IP cap yields 429 with a `Retry-After` header, that authenticated users get isolated per-user buckets independent of IP, that `/auth/*` routes can be tightened below the global default via per-route config, and that allow-listed probes are never throttled. A key gotcha documented inline is ordering: the `onRoute` hook that injects the stricter `rateLimit` config for `/auth/*` must be registered before the plugin, because `@fastify/rate-limit` reads `routeOptions.config.rateLimit` at route-registration time. Dependencies are limited to `vitest`, `fastify`, and `@fastify/rate-limit`, with all requests issued through Fastify's `inject` rather than a live network listener.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pricing.ts.summary: This file is the single source of truth for the platform's NRI pricing rule (business rule #2: NRI customers pay 9–10× the domestic INR price), centralizing multiplier and currency math so routes and services don't reimplement it. It exports three constants — `NRI_INR_MULTIPLIER` (9, the default), `NRI_INR_MULTIPLIER_MAX` (10, the validation ceiling), and `INR_USD_INDICATIVE_RATE` (83.5, refreshed quarterly) — plus the `NriPriceResult` interface and two functions: `computeNriPrice`, which prefers an explicit `PujaType.nriPrice` USD override and otherwise falls back to the 9× rule, and `validateNriPriceBand`, which temple-portal create/update routes use to reject out-of-band `nriPrice` values. It has no imports of its own, but it is consumed by `apps/api/src/routes/bookings.ts`, `apps/api/src/services/booking.service.ts` (USD branch), and the `apps/web/app/nri/page.tsx` landing page, and it ties into Stripe Payment Intents and the `PujaType` data model. A key gotcha: `INR_USD_INDICATIVE_RATE` is for display copy and band validation only — live Stripe charges always quote USD cents from `PujaType.nriPrice` directly, never from this conversion. The validator enforces a tolerance band rather than the raw 9–10× range (rejecting below 9×0.85 or above 10×1.15), and `computeNriPrice` throws on non-finite or negative base prices. Notable tech debt is flagged in the header comment: `bookings.ts` still defines its own `NRI_USD_MULTIPLIER` constant that should re-import from here in a follow-up commit.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\pdf-invoice.ts.summary: This file is Darshya's generic tax-invoice PDF generator, covering the platform's four paid product surfaces — puja bookings, astrology consultations, wellness sessions, and store orders — while deliberately leaving 80G donation receipts to the sibling pdf-receipt.ts module because their compliance contract differs. It exports the InvoiceInput discriminated union (keyed on the type field) and a single async generateInvoice function that renders an A4 invoice and returns it as a Buffer, built entirely on the external pdf-lib library (PDFDocument, StandardFonts, rgb) with no internal module dependencies. Per-type behavior is factored into small switch-based helpers — shortIdFor, lineItemsFor, totalFor, recipientFor, and referenceFor — while the TYPE_PREFIX map stamps invoice numbers in the form INV-PB/AC/WS/SO followed by an eight-character ID derived from the booking number, consultation/session UUID, or order number. The layout is hand-positioned with a mutable y-cursor, uses the Darshya saffron brand palette with Helvetica and HelveticaBold, formats amounts with the en-IN locale, and includes a store-orders-only shipping address block and multi-item table. Several gotchas stand out: truncating source identifiers to eight characters makes invoice-number collisions theoretically possible; there is no pagination, so a store order with many line items will overflow the single page; StandardFonts.Helvetica only supports WinAnsi encoding, so Devanagari or other non-Latin customer names would fail to render; and despite the "DARSHYA TAX INVOICE" heading, the document carries no GSTIN, HSN/SAC codes, or itemized tax breakdown — only a blanket "inclusive of all applicable taxes" disclaimer.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\route-metrics.ts.summary: This file provides a dependency-free, in-memory latency tracker for API routes, designed to emit percentile metrics purely through logs so the service can run on infrastructure like Render's free tier without Prometheus or a metrics database. Callers record each request's duration via `recordLatency(routeKey, ms)`, which appends to a per-route ring buffer capped at `RING_SIZE` (200) samples stored in the module-level `buckets` Map. The exported `snapshotStats()` sorts each buffer and returns `RouteStat` objects (samples, p50, p95, p99, max), ordered by p95 descending so the slowest routes surface first. `startMetricsReporter(log)` kicks off a `setInterval` every `REPORT_INTERVAL_MS` (5 minutes) that logs the top 20 routes by p95 through any pino-compatible logger exposing an `info` method, while `stopMetricsReporter()` clears that timer for clean shutdowns or tests. Notable design choices include guarding `startMetricsReporter` against double-start, calling `timer.unref()` so the reporter never keeps the Node process alive on its own, and skipping empty buckets entirely. The percentile helper uses a simple floor-index on a sorted copy rather than interpolation, which is approximate but cheap and fine for log-level observability. The only runtime dependencies are Node's timer APIs and the injected logger, keeping the module fully self-contained.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\r2.ts.summary: This file is the API's object-storage abstraction layer, exposing a single R2-flavored API (`uploadToR2`, `presignR2Url`, `presignR2Upload`, `deleteFromR2`, `publicUrlFor`, plus an `r2` config descriptor) while transparently backing it with either Cloudflare R2 or Supabase Storage. The backend is chosen once at module load: R2 wins when `R2_ACCOUNT_ID`, `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, and `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` are all present, otherwise it falls back to Supabase via the shared `supabaseAdmin` client from `./supabase.js` if `SUPABASE_URL` (or `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`) and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` exist. The R2 path uses `@aws-sdk/client-s3` (`S3Client` pointed at the account's `r2.cloudflarestorage.com` endpoint) and `@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner` for signed URLs; the Supabase path uses `supabaseAdmin.storage` with upsert-on-upload semantics. Both backends default to the `darshya-media` bucket (overridable via `R2_BUCKET` / `STORAGE_BUCKET`), and exported names deliberately keep the "R2" prefix so callsites are stable regardless of backend. A notable gotcha: R2 public URLs assume either a custom domain set via `R2_PUBLIC_BASE` or the `https://<bucket>.<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/` form, which is not actually publicly servable without additional R2 configuration. Another likely bug: `presignR2Url`, documented as generating read URLs for private objects, signs a `PutObjectCommand` rather than a `GetObjectCommand`, so it produces an upload URL. All functions swallow errors and return `{ ok: false }`, `false`, or `null` instead of throwing, and the Supabase fallback ignores the caller's `expiresInSec` for signed upload URLs since `createSignedUploadUrl` has a fixed ~2-hour expiry.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\sentry.ts.summary: This module wraps Sentry error monitoring for the API, initializing the `@sentry/node` SDK only when the `SENTRY_DSN` environment variable is present so the app runs without monitoring during local development and demos. It exports three things: `initSentry()`, an idempotent setup function guarded by a module-level `initialized` flag; `captureException(error, context?)`, a safe wrapper that silently no-ops if Sentry was never initialized and attaches optional context as Sentry "extra" data; and a re-export of the raw `Sentry` object for callers needing direct SDK access. Its only external dependency is `@sentry/node`, and it reads configuration from the `SENTRY_DSN`, `NODE_ENV`, and `SENTRY_RELEASE` environment variables, with the release tag set by the CI workflow in `.github/workflows/sentry-release.yml` and the DSN configured on the Render deployment. Notable constraints include a deliberately low `tracesSampleRate` of 0.05 to stay within the 5K errors/month free tier, and `sendDefaultPii: false` to avoid leaking personally identifiable information unless explicitly opted in. The key gotcha is that `captureException` drops errors silently when initialization never happened, so callers must invoke `initSentry()` early in app startup for reporting to work.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\stripe.ts.summary: This module provides a lazily-initialized, environment-gated Stripe client for the API, mirroring the demo-payment pattern already used for Razorpay in `payment.service.ts`. Its sole export, `getStripe()`, returns a `StripeClient` — a locally defined minimal interface covering `paymentIntents.create/retrieve`, `checkout.sessions.create`, and `webhooks.constructEvent` — so callers never branch on configuration themselves. When `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is absent (exposed via the `isStripeDemoMode` flag), it returns a stub that fabricates synthetic `pi_demo_*` / `cs_demo_*` identifiers, keeping the booking flow exercisable in dev and preview without a live Stripe account; the demo stub's `constructEvent` throws, since webhook verification cannot be simulated. The real client is built via dynamic `import('stripe')` rather than a top-level import, so a missing `stripe` package still allows the demo path to boot, and it pins API version `2024-12-18.acacia`. Key gotchas: in `NODE_ENV=production` the demo stub is refused unless `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS=true` is set (a staging-only escape hatch), because synthetic IDs and rejecting webhooks would present as real payment failures to customers; and the demo `retrieve` returns hardcoded `amount: 0` / `currency: 'usd'`, so any amount-dependent logic behaves unrealistically in demo mode. The real client is cached in a module-level singleton (`realClient`) after first construction.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\scripture-data.ts.summary: This file is the static scripture corpus powering the API's RAG-based "Ask a Pandit" chat feature, providing the retrieval knowledge base from which answers are grounded. It exports the `ScriptureVerse` interface — a trilingual record with `sanskrit`, `transliteration`, `english`, and `hindi` text plus a `keywords` array — and hardcoded verse collections, notably `GITA_VERSES` (roughly 50 key Bhagavad Gita verses organized by chapter, spanning Karma, Jnana, Dhyana, and Bhakti Yoga); the `source` union type ('gita' | 'upanishad' | 'mantra') and the optional `name` field indicate companion Upanishad and mantra collections follow the same shape. The file has no external dependencies — it is pure typed data, deliberately keeping the corpus in-code rather than in a database or vector store. The key design decision is the per-verse `keywords` array of English concept tags (e.g., 'grief', 'detachment', 'anger'), which implies retrieval is done via simple keyword matching against user queries rather than embedding-based semantic search — a lightweight but recall-limited approach. The flexible schema (optional `chapter`/`verse` for numbered texts versus `name` for mantras) lets one interface serve heterogeneous scripture formats, and the parallel Hindi/English translations suggest the chat serves bilingual responses. A gotcha: because the corpus is a hardcoded in-memory constant, adding verses requires a code deploy, and coverage is limited to the curated selection rather than complete texts.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\supabase.ts.summary: This module is the API server's central Supabase connection point, building on `@supabase/supabase-js`'s `createClient` and `SupabaseClient` to provide database and auth access to the rest of the API. It exports `supabaseAdmin`, a privileged client initialized with `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` that bypasses row-level security, plus `createSupabaseClient`, a factory that builds an anon-key client optionally scoped to a user's access token via an `Authorization: Bearer` header so RLS policies apply per-request. Configuration comes from `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, deliberately falling back to the `NEXT_PUBLIC_`-prefixed variants so a single `.env` can be shared with the Next.js web app in development. The notable design decision is the `isDemoMode` flag, exported alongside the clients: when no URL is set (or the placeholder `https://demo.supabase.co` is used), `supabaseAdmin` becomes a `Proxy` whose `auth` property returns stubbed methods (`getUser`, `signInWithOtp`, `verifyOtp`, etc.) that resolve with "Demo mode" errors, while any other property access throws an explicit configuration error. In demo mode `createSupabaseClient` just returns that same dummy admin client, so callers never receive null. A key gotcha is that `supabaseAdmin` bypasses RLS entirely, so it must never be used for user-scoped queries where tenant isolation matters.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\support-sla.test.ts.summary: This is a Vitest unit-test suite for the pure functions in `apps/api/src/lib/support-sla.ts`, covering requirement R-Q4-CS-001 (the 24-hour first-response SLA tracker for support tickets); it deliberately avoids any database or Fastify boot and pins a fixed `NOW` constant so all time arithmetic is deterministic. It exercises five exports from `./support-sla.js`: `classifyTicket` (met/breached/pending per ticket), `hourInTz` (UTC-to-local hour conversion), `bucketByOwningTimezone` (assigning a ticket to the IN/UK/US/AU region whose business hours its creation time falls in), `summarizeSla` (per-bucket and global SLA percentages), plus the `SLA_WINDOW_MS` and `SLA_TIMEZONES` constants. Its only external dependency is `vitest` (`describe`/`it`/`expect`); everything else is the internal `support-sla` module. Several behavioral contracts are locked in here: exactly-24-hour replies count as met (boundary inclusive), pending tickets are excluded from the percentage denominator, and an empty ticket set reports a vacuous 100% SLA both globally and per bucket. A notable gotcha documented in the `bucketByOwningTimezone` tests is that the four regions' business hours span the globe, so the fallback-to-IN dead zone is unreachable with real timezones — the test instead just asserts `SLA_TIMEZONES` contains the `IN` entry. The timezone tests also implicitly depend on DST-aware IANA names like `America/New_York` and `Asia/Kolkata`, meaning they could drift if the environment's tz database differs.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\support-sla.ts.summary: This file implements requirement R-Q4-CS-001: pure, dependency-free helpers that measure the 24-hour first-response SLA for support tickets and roll it up into the response_sla_24h_pct KPI across four timezone buckets defined in SLA_TIMEZONES (IN, UK, US, AU with their IANA names). It exports the SLA_WINDOW_MS constant, the SlaTicketInput/SlaBucketResult/SlaSummary interfaces, and four functions: bucketByOwningTimezone assigns each ticket to the region whose business hours (08–20 local) contained its creation time, hourInTz converts a UTC instant to a wall-clock hour via Intl.DateTimeFormat, classifyTicket labels one ticket 'met', 'breached', or 'pending' against the 24h window, and summarizeSla aggregates tickets into per-region and global SlaSummary results. The module deliberately takes a flat ticket shape (createdAt, firstAdminReplyAt) so it can be fed directly from Prisma rows or test fixtures without an ORM dependency, and relies on Node 20+'s built-in ICU data rather than a timezone library. Notable gotchas: tickets created outside business hours in every zone fall back to IN (the default ops region), pending tickets (unreplied but younger than 24h) are excluded from the percentage denominator to keep the KPI stable as new tickets arrive, an empty denominator reports a vacuous 100%, and hourInTz normalizes a "24" midnight value some Node builds emit down to 0.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\web-push.ts.summary: This module wraps the `web-push` npm library to send browser-native Web Push notifications via VAPID, deliberately avoiding an FCM dependency so it works across Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari 16.4+. It reads credentials from the `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`, `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`, and `VAPID_SUBJECT` environment variables at load time, and computes an `enabled` flag that callers can inspect through the exported `webPushConfig` object (which also exposes the public key for client-side subscription). The main export, `sendPush`, accepts a `PushSubscriptionPayload` (endpoint plus p256dh/auth keys) and a `PushPayload` (title, body, optional url/icon/tag), delivering it with a 24-hour TTL and normal urgency. A key design decision is graceful degradation: if VAPID keys are missing, `sendPush` returns `{ ok: false, skipped: true }` instead of throwing, so the rest of the API runs unchanged in unconfigured environments. Error handling distinguishes expired subscriptions (HTTP 404/410, flagged via `PushResult.expired` so the caller deletes the row from its database) from transient failures, which surface as an error string.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\wa-warm-intro-helpe.summary: This Vitest suite (`apps/api/src/lib/wa-warm-intro-helpers.test.ts`) verifies the WhatsApp warm-intro outreach helpers in the sibling module `wa-warm-intro-helpers.js`, which generate paste-ready referral messages for a darshya.online marketing blast. It covers three exports: `buildWarmIntroShareUrl`, which appends the UTM tags `utm_source=wa-warm-intro`, `utm_medium=whatsapp`, and `utm_campaign=r-q1-cs-006` to a base URL (defaulting to `https://darshya.online/`, overridable for staging); `renderWarmIntroMessage`, which personalizes one of two templates — a "friends-family" variant opening with "Namaste {name} 🙏" and a "professional" variant opening with "Hi {name}," and referencing a "founder-mode ask"; and `renderWarmIntroBatch`, which maps a contact list to ordered name/message pairs and returns an empty array for empty input. It also pins the `WA_WARM_INTRO_SOURCE_TAG` constant to `"wa-warm-intro"`, which the tests note is the attribution key the rest of the app joins on. The only dependency is `vitest`; there are no external services, since the module under test is pure string/URL logic. Notable behavioral constraints locked in by these tests: contact names are trimmed, blank names throw a `contact.name is required` error (to catch paste mistakes during the blast), rendered messages must end on the share-URL CTA line with no trailing newline, and a custom `baseUrl` option must fully replace the production URL in the output.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\vedic-context.ts.summary: This module builds a lightweight Vedic astrological profile for the AI Astrologer chat, deliberately avoiding any LLM or external API calls by computing everything locally. Its single exported function, `computeVedicContext`, takes user-supplied birth details (name, date, time, place) and returns a `VedicContext` object (also exported as an interface) containing the Moon rashi, Sun sign, Lagna (ascendant), nakshatra with pada, current Vimshottari Mahadasha period, planet placements, and dosha flags (Manglik, Sade Sati phase, and Kemadruma yoga), plus a human-readable `summary` string meant to be injected into chat prompts. It depends on the internal `jyotish.js` module's `buildVedicChart` function and `VedicChart` type for the underlying sidereal chart math, and has no third-party dependencies. Place resolution is handled by a hardcoded `CITY_COORDS` lookup table of Indian cities and NRI hubs (with fixed timezone offsets, so no DST handling), silently falling back to Delhi coordinates and setting an `approximate` flag when the city is unrecognized. Notable gotchas: missing or malformed birth times default to noon, dates must match strict `YYYY-MM-DD` format or the function returns null, future dates and chart-build failures also yield null, and Mahadasha periods are approximated using 365.25-day years. The `approximate` flag and an inline caveat in the summary text signal to downstream consumers (and the chat user) when the Lagna and related calculations rest on defaulted inputs.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\webhook-idempotency.summary: This file is the webhook idempotency guard (ticket TD16) for payment providers Razorpay and Stripe, existing to prevent duplicate processing when those providers retry the same event — without it, the API could double-credit subscriptions, double-confirm bookings, or double-refund. It exports the `WebhookProvider` union type, the main `checkAndRecord(provider, eventId)` function which atomically records a `(provider, event_id)` pair and reports via `IdempotencyResult` whether it was already seen, a `sweepOldRows()` cron helper that deletes rows older than 30 days and returns a `SweepResult`, and `_resetTableEnsuredForTests()` for clearing the module-level setup cache between test cases. Its only dependency is the shared `prisma` client from `./prisma.js`, which it uses to run raw SQL against a Postgres table called `webhook_replay`. Notably, the table is created lazily by `ensureTable()` via `$executeRawUnsafe` with no Prisma migration, deliberately keeping this layer self-contained and deployable without a schema bump. The atomicity guarantee comes from `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING ... RETURNING`, which eliminates the race window a SELECT-then-INSERT pattern would have. The design explicitly favors double-processing over data loss: if the database lookup throws, callers are expected to catch and fall through to normal processing, and an empty `eventId` also falls through rather than blocking the webhook. Finally, `sweepOldRows()` swallows its own errors and reports them through the `skipped`/`reason` fields so a failed cleanup never crashes the cron job.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\wa-warm-intro-helpe.summary: This module supports growth initiative R-Q1-CS-006, a manual WhatsApp blast in which the founder messages 21 personal-network contacts asking each to refer five people; the file deliberately contains no sending logic because warm outreach is not automatable without violating WhatsApp Cloud API policy and burning trust (see docs/cs/R-Q1-CS-006-handoff.md). Its job is to keep the two canonical message templates versioned with code and test-covered, and to produce paste-ready messages whose share links carry stable UTM tags so signup attribution can join on `utm_source=wa-warm-intro`. Exports include the `WarmIntroAudience` union ("friends-family" | "professional") and `WarmIntroContact` type, `buildWarmIntroShareUrl()` which appends the utm_source/utm_medium/utm_campaign triple to a base URL (defaulting to https://darshya.online), `renderWarmIntroMessage()` which renders one contact's message with tone matched to audience, `renderWarmIntroBatch()` which maps a contact list to name/message pairs in input order, and the `WA_WARM_INTRO_SOURCE_TAG` constant. The module has no internal dependencies and uses only the standard URL API, making it trivially testable. Notable constraints: `renderWarmIntroMessage` throws on a blank contact name, the base URL is overridable only for tests or staging blasts, and both templates end with the identical tagged share URL so reply attribution stays uniform across audiences. The batch helper is a pure map with no batching or broadcast semantics — the founder paste-loops the output into WhatsApp manually.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\webhook-idempotency.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the webhook-idempotency module (`./webhook-idempotency.js`) without a real database by substituting the `./prisma.js` client with an in-memory simulator of the `webhook_replay` table. The mock inspects the raw SQL strings passed to `$executeRawUnsafe` and `$queryRawUnsafe` to emulate Postgres behavior — no-op for CREATE TABLE/INDEX, conflict-skip semantics for INSERT (returning an empty result when a `(provider, event_id)` pair already exists), and a 30-day cutoff filter for the DELETE sweep. Tests cover the core contract of `checkAndRecord`: first calls report `alreadyProcessed=false`, repeats report `true`, and deduplication is scoped per `(provider, event_id)` pair so identical event ids from different providers (e.g. razorpay vs stripe) stay independent. A final test backdates a row to 31 days old and confirms `sweepOldRows` deletes exactly the stale rows while keeping fresh ones. Notable mechanics include `loadFresh()` calling `vi.resetModules()` before each import (needed because the module under test memoizes table setup internally, reset via the exported `_resetTableEnsuredForTests` hook), and `resetTable()` running in `beforeEach` to isolate the shared module-scope simulator between cases.

apps\\api\\src\\middlewares\\auth.demo-g.summary: This is a Vitest test suite that locks in the behavior of `shouldRejectDemoTokensInProd`, a guard exported by the sibling auth middleware module (`./auth.js`). Its purpose is regression protection for a security fix tracked as P0 ticket #ag-03 (dated 2026-07-09): ensuring the app refuses to boot when demo tokens — which grant an admin bypass — are enabled in a production environment. The suite covers four cases: `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS=true` combined with `NODE_ENV=production` must return true (reject), while non-production environments, production with the flag disabled or unset, and a fully empty environment must all return false. The only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and the function under test, with environment configuration passed in as a plain object rather than read from `process.env`, which keeps the tests hermetic. Notably, the header comment frames the test as a deliberate tripwire: if someone weakens the guard (for example by dropping the `NODE_ENV` condition), this suite fails before deploy, making the test itself part of the security control rather than mere coverage.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\whatsapp.ts.summary: This file is the API's direct client for the WhatsApp Business Cloud API (Meta Graph), used to deliver OTPs, booking confirmations, donation receipts, and AI-pandit replies over WhatsApp. It exports two send functions — `sendWhatsappTemplate` for pre-approved template messages with positional body variables, and `sendWhatsappText` for plain-text replies — plus a `whatsapp` object exposing the `enabled` flag, `phoneNumberId`, and `apiVersion` for callers that need to check configuration status. Both functions route through the private `callGraph` helper, which POSTs to `graph.facebook.com/{apiVersion}/{phoneNumberId}/messages` using a bearer token, and through `normalisePhone`, which coerces Indian numbers (10-digit mobile, leading-zero, or already-international) into the country-code-91 format WhatsApp expects. It has no internal module dependencies — only the global `fetch` and three environment variables: `WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID`, `WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN`, and `WHATSAPP_API_VERSION` (defaulting to `v21.0`). The key design decision is graceful degradation: if either required env var is missing, `enabled` is false and every send returns `{ok:false, skipped:true}` instead of throwing, so dev and demo environments work without a verified Meta business account. Errors from Meta or network failures are caught and returned as `{ok:false, error}` in the `SendResult` union rather than raised, so callers must inspect the result. Two constraints to note: template names and language codes must match templates pre-approved in WhatsApp Manager, and free-form text sends are only valid within Meta's 24-hour user-initiated conversation window — text bodies are also hard-truncated to 4,096 characters.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\youtube-feed.ts.summary: This file is a YouTube channel feed helper that works around a limitation of YouTube's `embed/live_stream` URL, which renders an "unavailable" error whenever a temple channel is off-air, by querying the channel's public RSS feed (`youtube.com/feeds/videos.xml`) to find the most recent video as a fallback embed. It exports three functions: `getChannelEmbedInfo(channelId)`, which fetches and parses the feed to return the latest `videoId`, `title`, and a `hasVideos` flag; `liveStreamUrl(channelId)` and `videoEmbedUrl(videoId)`, which build the autoplaying, muted embed URLs consumed by the `/api/v1/darshan/<slug>/stream` endpoint (which returns either `mode: 'live'` or `mode: 'recent'` payloads). Internally, `readFeed` fetches the XML with a custom `Darshya/1.0` User-Agent and `parseLatest` extracts the first `<yt:videoId>` and entry `<title>` via regex rather than a real XML parser, which is fast but brittle to feed format changes. Results are stored in a module-level `Map` cache with a 5-minute `CACHE_TTL_MS`, and notably failed fetches are also cached as null entries, so a transient network error suppresses retries for the full TTL. Because the cache is in-memory and per-process, it is not shared across API instances and resets on restart. Live detection is intentionally unimplemented — the `hasLive` field is hardcoded false, with the expectation that the frontend tries the live embed first and requests the recent-VOD fallback on failure. The RSS approach requires no API key and incurs no YouTube Data API quota, which is the core reason this file exists.

apps\\api\\src\\lib\\__mocks__\\prisma.t.summary: This file provides a manual deep mock of PrismaClient so the API's unit tests can run against stubbed database calls without a real Postgres instance, living in a `__mocks__` directory so vitest can auto-substitute it when the real prisma module is mocked. Its sole export, `prismaMock` (also the default export), mirrors the Prisma client's shape: roughly 35 domain models — including `user`, `temple`, `pujaBooking`, `payment`, `priest`, `marketplaceSubscription`, `wellnessSession`, `panditProfile`, `chatConversation`, `review`, `commission`, `storeOrder`, `userCredit`, and `referralClaim` — each exposing only the query methods the tests actually use (findUnique, findMany, create, update, upsert, count, aggregate, groupBy, and so on) as `vi.fn()` stubs. It also stubs the raw-query helpers `$queryRaw`, `$queryRawUnsafe`, `$executeRaw`, and `$executeRawUnsafe`. The only external dependency is `vi` from vitest; the mocked target is the app's shared Prisma client module. A notable design choice is that `$transaction` is implemented to immediately invoke the callback with `prismaMock` itself, so code under test that passes an interactive transaction client still hits the same stubs. The main gotchas are that every stub returns undefined by default (tests must arrange return values per case), and because the mock is handwritten it can silently drift from the real Prisma schema — there is no type-level guarantee that a stubbed method or model actually exists on the generated client.

apps\\api\\src\\middlewares\\auth.test.t.summary: This Vitest suite regression-tests the authentication middleware in `apps/api/src/middlewares/auth.js`, specifically the exported `authenticateUser` and `requireRole` functions. It mocks two internal dependencies — Prisma via `prismaMock` from `lib/__mocks__/prisma.js` and Supabase via a hoisted `supabaseGetUser` stub replacing `supabaseAdmin.auth.getUser` — and drives the middleware with minimal hand-rolled Fastify request/reply harnesses (`makeReq`, `makeReply`) rather than a real server. The first describe block locks in the blocked-user gate (P0 #6): when `User.blocked` is true, all three token paths (demo tokens, `email-` session tokens, and Supabase JWTs) must return 403 with a suspension message and never populate `req.currentUser`, with 403 chosen over 401 so the frontend can distinguish "account suspended" from "please log in." The second block guards `requireRole('priest')` (P0 #ag-01/pp-04), verifying that possessing the PANDIT role is no longer sufficient — the user must have a Priest row with `status: 'active'`, so self-signup pandits with no Priest record, inactive/suspended priests, and synthetic `demo-` prefixed IDs all get 403. A notable design constraint baked into the tests is that demo users can never pass the priest guard even with a mocked active Priest row, since the DB lookup is skipped for demo IDs. Test setup forces `NODE_ENV=test` and `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS=true` so the demo-token auth path is exercisable.

apps\\api\\src\\middlewares\\cron-auth.t.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the cron-route authentication middleware in apps/api/src/middlewares/cron-auth.ts, exercising its exported Fastify pre-handler requireCronBearer against hand-rolled mock req/reply objects. It confirms that a missing Authorization header yields a 401 with a cron_unauthorized body, a mismatched bearer token yields a 401, and an unset CRON_AUTH_TOKEN environment variable fails loud — returning 401 with cron_auth_misconfigured and logging a console.error mentioning the variable — while a token matching CRON_AUTH_TOKEN lets the request proceed without the reply being sent. A dedicated case asserts the comparison is timing-safe by showing that a wrong token of identical length still 401s. The suite depends only on Vitest (describe, it, expect, vi) and uses vi.resetModules plus dynamic imports of ./cron-auth.js so each test re-reads process.env freshly, with beforeEach/afterEach hooks saving and restoring the real environment and console.error. A notable regression guard tied to incident PUB-03 asserts that requireCronQueryToken remains unexported, because the old ?token= query-param surface leaked the cron secret into access logs and CDN caches and must not be reintroduced.

This file provides fail-loud authentication middleware for the API's cron-triggered HTTP endpoints, ensuring internal jobs can never be invoked anonymously or silently pass when the server is misconfigured. It exports two Fastify preHandler guards: `requireCronBearer`, which validates an `Authorization: Bearer` header against the `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` env var and protects the `/api/v1/cron/*` and `/api/v1/admin/cron/*` routes, and `requireCronSecretHeader`, which validates an `x-cron-secret` header against `CRON_SECRET` for endpoints like the horoscope prewarm. Its only dependencies are `node:crypto` (for `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, wrapped by the internal `constantTimeEq` helper to give constant-time comparison that blocks timing-oracle token guessing) and Fastify's `FastifyRequest`/`FastifyReply` types. A key design decision is reading env vars at call time rather than module load, so vitest overrides and Render redeploys take effect immediately. Both guards are default-deny: a missing env var logs a grep-able `[FATAL]` message to stderr and returns 401 with a sentinel error code (`cron_auth_misconfigured` or `cron_secret_misconfigured`) distinct from the `cron_unauthorized` code used for bad client tokens, so log aggregation can tell "server is broken" apart from "bad token attempt." The `requireCronSecretHeader` middleware explicitly supersedes an older inline check (referenced as P0 #PUB-04) that used `!==` comparison and skipped auth entirely when the secret was unset. Because these are async Fastify hooks, a request passes simply by not sending a reply, letting the route handler continue.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-agents.ts.summary: This file is a Fastify route module that serves markdown reports produced by the GitHub Actions agent fleet (scripts/agents/*.mjs), which are committed back to the repo and thus ship inside the deployed image. It exports two route registrars: `adminAgentsRoutes`, which exposes admin-only endpoints GET /runs (reports grouped by agent with last-run metadata), GET /runs/:file (full report content), and GET /recent (20 newest across all agents); and `publicAgentFeedRoutes`, an unauthenticated GET /feed powering the /updates trust page with up to 12 recent dated reports enriched with a title extracted from the first H1 and a 600-char markdown-stripped excerpt. Its only internal dependency is the auth middleware (`authenticateUser`, `requireRole` from ../middlewares/auth.js); otherwise it relies on node:fs and node:path for direct filesystem reads. A notable design decision is `resolveReportDir()`, which probes several candidate paths to accommodate different working directories across dev (repo root) and Render (apps/api), with an AGENT_REPORTS_DIR env override. Security gotchas are handled deliberately: the :file param is validated against a strict whitelist regex and a startsWith check on REPORT_DIR to block path traversal, and files prefixed with `_` are excluded from listings. Other conventions worth knowing: report filenames must follow the `YYYY-MM-DD-<agent>[-suffix].md` pattern, hourly-suffixed runs (`-\d{2}h$`) are collapsed when grouping by agent, the public feed silently skips files that vanish between listing and reading, and all filesystem access is synchronous, which is simple but blocks the event loop on every request.

apps\\api\\src\\middlewares\\auth.ts.summary: This file is the API's authentication and authorization chokepoint: it verifies incoming credentials and attaches a resolved `AuthUser` (Prisma user record plus marketplace roles) to `request.currentUser` for downstream route handlers. The main export, `authenticateUser`, is a Fastify preHandler that accepts three credential shapes — `demo-<handle>` tokens that map to seeded demo users (devotee@demo.com through admin@demo.com), `email-<userId>-<hex>` magic-link session tokens validated against the `email_sessions` table, and standard Supabase JWTs verified via `supabaseAdmin.auth.getUser` with Prisma fallback lookups by id, email, then phone. It builds on the internal `lib/supabase.js` and `lib/prisma.js` modules, the `User`, `UserRoleAssignment`, and `Priest` Prisma models, and the `ADMIN_EMAILS` env allowlist. Also exported are `requireRole` and `requireAnyRole` factories for role gating, the `MarketplaceRole` type (DEVOTEE, PANDIT, ADMIN, etc.), `registerAuthDecorators` for server bootstrap, and `shouldRejectDemoTokensInProd`, a pure guard function called at module load. The most critical gotcha is the demo-token risk: demo tokens grant real DB sessions including ADMIN, so the module calls `process.exit(1)` at boot if `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS=true` while `NODE_ENV=production`, and otherwise demo-shaped tokens are rejected with a 401 in prod. Other notable decisions: Bearer header takes precedence but an httpOnly `darshya_session` cookie is accepted as fallback; blocked users get a 403 (not 401) via the shared `rejectIfBlocked` helper so the frontend can show a suspension screen; the legacy `'priest'` role check deliberately requires an active `Priest` row rather than just the PANDIT role, closing a verification bypass; role-lookup failures silently downgrade to DEVOTEE but are logged as warnings; and verbose auth error diagnostics are gated behind `ALLOW_AUTH_DIAGNOSTICS` and hard-disabled in production.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-cron.test..summary: This vitest suite pins the authentication surface of the manual-trigger admin cron routes registered by `adminCronRoutes` (under prefix `/api/v1/admin/cron`) in the Fastify API. It exists to lock in security fix PUB-03: the endpoints `/youtube-discovery` and `/apollo-refresh` were migrated off a leaky `?token=` query parameter—which exposed the secret in access logs and CDN caches—onto the `Authorization: Bearer` header checked against the `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variable. The tests stub out the real job runners, `discoverLiveStreams` from `../jobs/youtube-discovery.js` and `refreshApolloLeads` from `../jobs/apollo-refresh.js`, so the route gate is exercised with no actual I/O, and they use Fastify's `app.inject` rather than a live server. Cases cover 401 with no header, 401 with a wrong bearer token, 200 plus exactly one job invocation with the correct bearer, and—critically—that a correct `?token=` in the URL is ignored and still returns 401. Setup and teardown save, override, and restore `process.env.CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` per test, with `vi.clearAllMocks()` ensuring call-count assertions stay isolated.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-cron.ts.summary: This file defines `adminCronRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that exposes token-gated manual triggers for background jobs so ops can run them on demand instead of waiting for the next scheduled master-cron tick. It registers two GET endpoints, `/youtube-discovery` and `/apollo-refresh` (mounted under `/api/v1/admin/cron`), which invoke `discoverLiveStreams` from the `youtube-discovery` job and `refreshApolloLeads` from the `apollo-refresh` job respectively—the latter bypassing the normal 7-day cooldown. Both routes are guarded by the `requireCronBearer` middleware, which validates an `Authorization: Bearer <CRON_AUTH_TOKEN>` header using a constant-time comparison and fails loudly if the env var is unset. A notable design decision documented inline is the migration away from a legacy `?token=` query parameter (security issue P0 #PUB-03), which leaked the cron secret into Render access logs and CDN caches; the Bearer header keeps the credential out of URLs. The endpoints intentionally use GET rather than POST so they remain trivially curl-able from a phone during incident response. Each handler simply awaits its job and wraps the result in an `{ ok: true, result }` JSON response.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-content-qu.summary: This file registers the admin-only REST endpoints for the Reddit/Quora content draft queue, exporting a single `adminContentQueueRoutes(server)` function that wires routes onto a Fastify instance. Every route is gated by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `middlewares/auth`, and request bodies are validated with zod schemas (`updateBodySchema`, `generateBodySchema`). It exposes endpoints to list drafts by status, update a draft's status/body/title (APPROVED, POSTED, REJECTED), manually trigger the `runContentSeed` generation job and the `runContentAutoPost` job, probe configuration status via `isRedditConfigured()` from `lib/reddit`, and generate ad-hoc drafts. All persistence and LLM work is delegated to `services/content-draft.service` (`listDrafts`, `updateDraftStatus`, `saveDraft`, `generateRedditPost`, `generateQuoraAnswer`), which notably falls back to raw SQL when the Prisma model hasn't been migrated yet. Generation depends on a GROQ API key — failures surface as 503 responses. Key constraints: Quora has no public posting API so those drafts are paste-only (the status endpoint hardcodes `quora: false`), Reddit auto-posting only picks the oldest APPROVED drafts within a subreddit safelist with a per-sub 24-hour cooldown capped at 2 posts per call, and Reddit drafts save the suggested flair inline by appending it to the body text.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-bookings.t.summary: This file defines `adminBookingsRoutes`, a Fastify plugin mounted at /api/v1/admin/bookings that powers the admin operations dashboards for bookings, payouts, and refunds; every route is gated by `authenticateUser` plus `requireRole('admin')` from middlewares/auth. It exports handlers to list `PujaBooking` rows with pagination, aggregate pending provider payouts, list and process payout requests, list pending refunds, approve or reject refunds, and flag invalid video proofs. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from lib/prisma and delegates real money movement to `processRefund` from services/refund.service (which fires the Razorpay refund call, updates Payment/PujaBooking rows, and emails the customer) and to `listPayoutRequests`/`processPayout` from services/payout.service (where completing a payout marks linked Commission rows PAID and rejecting releases the balance back to PENDING). The `payoutMultiplier` helper encodes commission policy: PRIEST and WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR get 75%, ASTROLOGER 70%, and GAUSHALA_MANAGER 100% of booking value. A major gotcha, documented in the header comments, is that the code works around schema gaps rather than changing the schema: Booking has no `payoutPaidAt` column, so priests are tracked via the `PriestPayout` sidecar table while other roles are approximated through PENDING `Commission` rows joined to `UserRoleAssignment`, and responses carry a `schemaNote` flagging this. Similarly, `BookingStatus` lacks REFUND_REQUESTED/REFUND_REJECTED, so refund-pending is inferred from `cancelled` bookings whose payments are still `captured`/`authorized`, and rejections are recorded by stamping a `[refund-rejected]` marker into `cancellationReason` plus mirroring the reason into `Payment.metadata`. Most list endpoints degrade gracefully, returning empty results with a warning log instead of 500s when a model or enum is missing, while refund approval surfaces upstream Razorpay failures as 502 and is idempotent against double-refunding. The video-proof flag endpoint is also idempotent in intent—it clears `videoProofUrl`/`videoUploadedAt` and reverts status to `completed` so the priest can re-upload, returning 409 if no proof exists.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-donations-.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the CSV-formatting helpers exposed by the `admin-donations-export` route module via its `__testing` export, supporting an admin donations export feature (with Indian-context columns like donor PAN and `amountInr`). It tests two identifiers: `csvField`, which escapes individual CSV values, and `CSV_HEADER`, a constant defining the fixed export column order (`receipt_number,donor_name,donor_pan,donor_email,donee_name,amountInr,donation_date,gaushala_id`). The cases pin down RFC 4180 behavior: safe strings and numbers pass through unquoted, embedded double-quotes are doubled and wrapped, and fields containing commas, newlines, or carriage returns are quoted, while `null` and `undefined` render as empty strings rather than literal text. The only external dependency is `vitest`; internally the suite depends solely on the sibling `./admin-donations-export.js` module. Notably, the file documents the `__testing` pattern used to expose private helpers for unit tests without widening the module's public API. Coverage is limited to pure string logic — no HTTP handler, database query, or streaming behavior of the export endpoint is exercised here.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-gurukuls.t.summary: This file defines the admin moderation endpoints for gurukuls, exported as the `adminGurulsRoutes` Fastify plugin (mounted at `/api/v1/admin/gurukuls`), which lets administrators review and manage registered gurukul listings. Every route is gated by a shared `adminPreHandlers` chain combining `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` from the auth middleware, so only logged-in admins can access them. It exposes three endpoints: `GET /` lists gurukuls with an optional `status` query filter (`pending`, `verified`, or `all`) and returns owner contact info plus a program count; `PATCH /:id/verify` toggles the `isVerified` flag; and `PATCH /:id/active` toggles `isActive`. All data access goes through the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma.js`, querying the `gurukul` model with its `owner` relation and a `_count` of `programs`, while request bodies are validated with `zod` schemas (`verifyBodySchema`, `activateBodySchema`) that return 400 on invalid input. Notably, the verify schema accepts an optional `note` field that is validated but silently discarded — it is never persisted or logged. Missing records are handled by catching Prisma update errors and returning a generic 404, and list ordering surfaces unverified gurukuls first to prioritize the moderation queue.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-metrics.ts.summary: This file defines `adminMetricsRoutes`, a Fastify plugin that serves three founder-facing analytics endpoints — `/api/v1/admin/metrics/investor`, `/funnel`, and `/dashboard` — intended for consumption by the `investor-weekly-digest-v2` and `funnel-drop-analyzer` agents plus the web `/admin/metrics` page. Access is gated by a shared `authorised` helper that accepts either a `?token=` query param compared against the `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` env var using `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, or an admin Bearer JWT validated via the existing `authenticateUser` middleware (called with a stubbed reply object so its failure response is silently swallowed before the role check for `ADMIN`). All data comes from the internal `prisma` client, aggregating the `payment`, `pujaBooking`, `donation`, `user`, and `lead` models; every query is wrapped in `.catch()` so a failed aggregate degrades to null/zero rather than erroring the response. Money values are coerced from Prisma Decimals to integer paise via `decToPaise`, and the funnel endpoint buckets raw rows in application code (capped at 2–30 days, UTC-midnight boundaries, with zero-seeded day keys so median baselines have a floor) to stay cheap on a free-tier database. Notable approximations: donation net revenue assumes a flat 7.5% commission midpoint, "KYC" funnel stage merely means the user has a phone or email, and `cacPaise`, `d7Retention`, and `d30Retention` are hardcoded null placeholders pending a CAC source and cohort retention table.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-donations-.summary: This file implements an admin-only CSV export of paid donations, producing 80G tax-receipt data for finance/ops to reconcile against bank statements and file with the Indian income tax department. Its sole export, `adminDonationsExportRoutes`, is a Fastify route plugin registering `GET /export.csv` (mounted under `/api/v1/admin/donations`), guarded by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`. Query parameters `from` and `to` (YYYY-MM-DD) are validated with a zod `querySchema`; when omitted the range defaults to the trailing 90 days, roughly matching quarterly tax-receipt requests. Data is fetched through the shared `prisma` client via a parameterized `$queryRawUnsafe` SQL query joining `donations`, `users`, and `gaushala_profiles`, filtered to `status = 'paid'` — note that `donor_pan` is currently hardcoded to NULL, presumably because PAN capture isn't implemented yet. CSV generation is deliberately hand-rolled (`csvField` plus a fixed `CSV_HEADER`) with RFC 4180 quote-escaping, avoiding a CSV dependency for a stable column list. Every export attempts a best-effort audit insert into the `DonationExportAuditLog` table (exported_by, date range, row count, IP), and a notable gotcha is that both the main query failure (e.g., migration pending) and the audit insert failure are swallowed with a `server.log.warn`, meaning an error can silently yield an empty but valid-looking CSV attachment. The `__testing` export exposes `csvField` and `CSV_HEADER` for unit tests, and responses set `cache-control: no-store` since the payload contains donor PII.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-lead-conve.summary: This file implements the admin lead-conversion funnel dashboard for the Fastify API, exporting `adminLeadConversionRoutes(server)` which registers two endpoints under `/api/v1/admin/leads/conversion`: `GET /conversion` (per-role funnel counts plus a recent-activity feed) and `GET /conversion/timeline` (daily sent/opened/clicked/replied buckets over a `days` window validated by a zod `timelineQuerySchema` and clamped to 1–120, defaulting to 30). Both routes are gated by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares and read exclusively from the Prisma `Lead` and `OutreachLog` models via the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`. The funnel is computed for five fixed roles (`TEMPLE`, `PRIEST`, `ASTROLOGER`, `WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR`, `GAUSHALA`) with stages total, emailed, opened, clicked, replied, interested, and converted, where "interested" is derived by parsing `classifiedIntent` from the JSON `payload` of `inbound_reply` outreach logs. A notable design choice is doing aggregation in memory with Sets and Maps after two broad `findMany` calls rather than issuing many grouped count queries, trading memory for query simplicity. The key gotcha is that every query block is wrapped in try/catch that only logs a warning and returns zeroed stats or empty buckets, so the admin UI degrades gracefully if the Lead/OutreachLog tables haven't been migrated yet — meaning real database errors are silently swallowed into empty dashboards. The recent feed is additionally capped at 20 entries drawn from the latest 200 replied logs, and timeline buckets are keyed by UTC calendar day.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-gurukuls.t.summary: This Vitest suite is a regression guard for the admin gurukul moderation endpoint `GET /api/v1/admin/gurukuls/?status=all`, registered via the `adminGurukulsRoutes` Fastify plugin. It exists specifically to protect the health-smoke "gurukul-mut: list empty" alert, which fails when the list comes back empty because the smoke's verify-toggle step needs a row with `id` and `isVerified` to act on. The suite therefore pins two things at once: an admin principal must reach the handler with a 200 (never 401/403), and the response body must be a `gurukuls` array whose items expose `id` and `isVerified`. A third test locks in the gotcha that an empty database must still return 200 with an empty array rather than an error. Dependencies are vitest, Fastify's `app.inject` for in-process requests, and `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js`, which replaces the real `../lib/prisma.js` module via `vi.mock`. Notably, authentication is exercised through the demo-token path: the tests set `ALLOW_DEMO_TOKENS=true`, send `Bearer demo-admin`, and stub `user.findUnique` to resolve `DEMO_ADMIN` by email plus `userRoleAssignment.findMany` to grant the ADMIN role expected by `requireRole('admin')`. The `makeApp()` helper builds a fresh Fastify instance per test with the routes mounted under the production prefix, so any future change to auth middleware or response serialization in `admin-gurukuls.js` that breaks the smoke contract fails here first.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-leads.test.summary: This Vitest suite (`apps/api/src/routes/admin-leads.test.ts`) regression-tests ticket PBO-6 against the `adminLeadsRoutes` Fastify plugin, verifying that the lead status endpoint at `/api/v1/admin/leads/:id/status` now provisions a real account when a lead is marked `CONVERTED`, rather than just flipping the status and emailing as it did before. It boots a bare Fastify instance, registers the routes under the `/api/v1/admin` prefix, and exercises the endpoint via `app.inject` with a `Bearer demo-admin` token whose admin user is supplied by the mocked Prisma client. Dependencies are stubbed at the module boundary: `prisma` is replaced by `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js`, and `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js` is mocked because the route sends mail fire-and-forget. The main test asserts the full provisioning chain for a `PRIEST` lead: find-or-create a `User` by email, upsert `userRoleAssignment` rows for both the baseline `DEVOTEE` role and the `PANDIT` provider role (via the route's `upsertProviderProfile` helper, which maps `PRIEST` → `panditProfile`), approve the profile with `panditProfile.updateMany` setting `approved`/`approvedAt`, and stamp `lead.convertedUserId`. A second test locks in idempotency: when `convertedUserId` is already set, provisioning is skipped entirely and no `user.create` or `astrologerProfile.updateMany` calls occur. A third confirms that non-`CONVERTED` transitions like `EMAILED` never provision. One notable discrepancy: the header comment describes the endpoint as POST, but the tests actually issue PATCH requests.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-ops.test.t.summary: This Vitest integration suite exercises the founder-gated SLA-breach bulk-resolve endpoint `POST /api/v1/admin/ops/sla-overdue-bookings/resolve` (ticket P0-17) by mounting `adminOpsRoutes` from `./admin-ops.js` on a real Fastify instance and injecting requests, with Prisma swapped for `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js`. It validates the exported `resolveSchema` (via `__testing`) — a zod schema requiring a non-empty `bookingIds` array capped at 200 entries, an `action` enum of refund/fulfill/cancel, and a non-empty `note` — and asserts the route's behavior matrix: 401 without auth, 403 for a demo-devotee token (with Prisma never touched), 400 on an invalid action, and 200s that flip bookings to `cancelled` with a "SLA breach auto-refund" `cancellationReason` and `cancelledAt` stamp, or to `completed` for fulfill. Auth relies on the demo-token bypass enabled by `NODE_ENV=test`, where `demo-admin`/`demo-devotee` tokens resolve via mocked `prisma.user.findUnique` lookups and roles come from the in-middleware `DEMO_ROLE_MAP`, so no `userRoleAssignment` mock is needed.
