Notable gotchas: the "refund" action moves no money — no payment service is imported or invoked — and unknown IDs still return 200 with entries in the `errors` array, with a `bookingNumber` fallback lookup (`findFirst`) when the UUID `findUnique` misses. `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` is deliberately unset because other routes in the plugin read it at module load, though the resolve route itself ignores it.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-queue.ts.summary: This file defines an admin-only health probe endpoint for the background job queue system, serving the `/admin/ops` dashboard and an alerting cron job. It exports a single function, `adminQueueRoutes`, which registers a GET `/health` route on the passed `FastifyInstance` and responds with an aggregate view of queue status. The route is guarded by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and is rate-limited to 60 requests per minute via Fastify's route config. All actual queue inspection is delegated to `getQueueHealth` from `../services/job-queue.service.js`, making this module a thin HTTP wrapper with no direct Redis or BullMQ dependency. The response payload includes an `enabled` flag (true if any queue reports itself enabled, which the code treats as a proxy for `REDIS_URL` being configured) plus a `summary` object with `totalWaiting` and `totalFailed` counts summed across all queues. A notable design choice is that `redisUrlSet` is simply aliased to the derived `enabled` value rather than checking the environment variable directly, so the probe only reflects what the queue service self-reports. The endpoint is read-only and deliberately omits per-job details, keeping it cheap enough for frequent polling by monitoring tools. The file header ties the work to requirement R-Q2-E-012, the background job queue scaffold.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-leads.ts.summary: This file registers the admin-facing Fastify routes for the lead pipeline, outreach, and waitlist dashboards via the exported `adminLeadsRoutes(server)` function, which mounts endpoints for paginated lead listing, per-role/status stats, 30-day outreach and waitlist funnels with top-referrer rankings, bulk lead import (upserting on compound `role_email`/`role_phone` keys), timestamp-prepended notes, lead detail with recent `outreachLogs`, and status transitions. All routes except one are guarded by `authenticateUser` plus `requireRole('admin')` from `../middlewares/auth.js`, with inputs validated by zod schemas. Its key dependencies are the shared `prisma` client, `runDailyOps` from `../jobs/master-cron.js` (exposed via `POST /jobs/daily-ops` for external schedulers since Render's free tier lacks cron), `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js` for approval/rejection messages, `onboardingService` from `../services/onboarding.service.js`, and the `mapLeadRoleToOnboarding`/`isLeadRole` helpers from `../lib/lead-role-mapping.js`. The defining design decision is defensive degradation: `leadModel()`, `outreachModel()`, and `waitlistModel()` accessors probe for Prisma models that may not be migrated yet, and every query is wrapped so missing tables yield empty stats or 503s instead of crashing the dashboard. The most consequential logic is the PATCH status handler: on `CONVERTED` it idempotently provisions a real `User` (find-or-create by email with a placeholder `email-${lead}` phone mirroring magic-link.ts), seeds a `DEVOTEE` role assignment, then creates and approves a provider profile through `onboardingService` — best-effort, so provisioning failure logs but never rolls back the status flip — and records `convertedUserId` to prevent duplicate accounts. Finally, `GET /cron/tick` is a deliberately public, token-gated trigger for `runDailyOps` aimed at free external pingers like UptimeRobot: it accepts the secret only via the `x-cron-token` header (the query-param fallback was removed to keep the token out of access logs), compares with `timingSafeEqual` from `node:crypto`, and default-denies with 503 when the env var is unset.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-roadmap.ts.summary: This file defines a Fastify route plugin (default export `route`) that serves `GET /admin/roadmap`, an aggregated read-only view of the Autonomous Roadmap Engine (ARE) state for the `/admin/roadmap` dashboard. It reads git-tracked files directly from `docs/roadmap/` — `_index.json`, `_kpi-cache.json`, `_tripwires-global.yml`, queue markdown frontmatter, and the last 20 decision records — with no database involved, and is gated by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`. Key internal helpers include `resolveRoadmapRoot` (which honors the `ROADMAP_ROOT` env var and otherwise probes candidate paths for dev and Render deployment layouts), `readQueue` and `readLastDecisions` (both of which fall back from live directories to `_dryrun/` counterparts while the orchestrator is in dry-run mode), plus hand-rolled parsers `parseFrontmatter` and `parseTripwiresYaml`; these helpers are re-exported via `__testing` for unit tests. A notable design decision is the deliberate avoidance of the `js-yaml` dependency in the API runtime: the two YAML shapes consumed are simple enough for regex-based minimal parsers, though this means only flat `key: value` pairs and one specific indented list shape are supported. Decision files are walked recursively (stored under `YYYY-MM/` subdirectories) and truncated to 4000 characters each. Responses carry a 60-second edge cache header (`s-maxage=60`) since aggregation is cheap but happens per dashboard load, and all file-parse failures are caught and logged as warnings rather than failing the request.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-ops.ts.summary: This Fastify route module exposes token-gated, read-only ops feeds consumed by the Sprint-2 automation agents (onboarding-nudge, booking-quality-monitor, referral-nudge, dormant-reactivation, cold-temple-outreach), plus one founder-gated mutation endpoint. The exported `adminOpsRoutes` plugin registers GET feeds for KYC-abandoned leads (fanned out into 24h/72h/7d buckets via parallel Prisma `lead.findMany` calls), SLA-overdue `pujaBooking` rows missing `videoProofUrl`, recent first-time bookers and dormant users (both via raw `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe` GROUP BY queries to avoid N+1), and uncontacted TEMPLE leads, along with POST endpoints `/sla-overdue-bookings/resolve` (bulk refund/fulfill/cancel) and `/mark-contacted` (flips leads to EMAILED with `contactCount` increment). Read-only feeds are gated by a constant-time `crypto.timingSafeEqual` check against `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` that fails closed if the env var is unset, while the destructive resolve route deliberately uses `authenticateUser` + `requireRole('admin')` from `../middlewares/auth.js` instead, so agents can never mutate booking state. Key gotchas: the resolve endpoint never moves money — the founder must process the actual Razorpay refund manually in the Razorpay dashboard, and it only annotates bookings via `cancellationReason`, which doubles as the ops audit trail because `PujaBooking` lacks a notes column and `BookingStatus` has no refund states (mirroring conventions in admin-bookings.ts). All feeds are designed to stay sub-100ms on cold Render: single Prisma queries with hard `take` caps (25–200 depending on route), and booking resolution accepts either a UUID `id` or a human-readable `bookingNumber`. The zod `resolveSchema` is re-exported via `__testing` for unit tests.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-roadmap-or.summary: This Fastify plugin in the API app exposes admin endpoints for triggering the roadmap orchestrator, designed to be called by a GitHub Actions cron job. Its main route, `POST /admin/roadmap/orchestrator-trigger`, authenticates via the `X-Orchestrator-Secret` header compared against the `ORCHESTRATOR_TRIGGER_SECRET` env var using `timingSafeEqual` (in the `verifySecret` helper), then uses Node's `child_process.spawn` with `detached: true` and `child.unref()` to launch `scripts/agents/run-orchestrator-bg.mjs` as a background process, returning 202 immediately while the orchestrator runs unbounded. The `resolveRepoRoot` helper locates the repo root via `ROADMAP_ROOT` or by probing for `scripts/agents/roadmap-orchestrator.mjs`, and cycle logs are written to `/tmp/orchestrator-logs/<cycleId>.log`, which is ephemeral on Render. Safety-conscious defaults include `dryRun` defaulting to true unless explicitly disabled, a length pre-check before the timing-safe comparison, and a 500 response if the orchestrator script is missing; inter-cycle locking is delegated to the orchestrator itself via `docs/roadmap/_lock.json`. The companion `GET /admin/roadmap/orchestrator-status` route is deprecated as of 2026-06-12 and returns 410 Gone, since orchestration moved off Render to a GitHub Actions runner and live status now comes from the web app's `/api/orchestrator-status` edge route, which reads the GitHub Actions REST API directly. The file depends only on Fastify types and Node built-ins (`node:child_process`, `node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:crypto`), making it a thin trigger shim rather than the orchestrator itself.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-subscripti.summary: This file registers a single admin-only REST endpoint, `GET /admin/subscriptions`, intended to give operators a cross-role view of marketplace subscription activity with status, plan, role, and INR revenue breakdowns. It default-exports a `FastifyPluginAsync` route guarded by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and it uses the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` for data access. The key gotcha is that the actual subscriptions table has not shipped yet, so the handler is a placeholder: it always returns an empty `subscriptions` array with zeroed `active` and `activeMrr` metrics, and instead synthesizes the `plans` breakdown by grouping `userRoleAssignment` rows by role and hardcoding every entry to the `FREE` plan with `totalInr: 0`. The response carries an explicit `note` field pointing readers to ROADMAP item R-Q1-E-010 (pricing infrastructure) so consumers know the data is a baseline stub. Query handling supports a `status` filter (defaulting to `all`, currently echoed back but unused) and a `limit` parameter capped at 500. The route sets a `cache-control: private, max-age=30` header on successful responses, and failures are caught, logged at warn level via `app.log.warn`, and surfaced as a 500 with the stringified error in the `detail` field.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-temples.ts.summary: This file defines `adminTemplesRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin mounted at `/api/v1/admin/temple-timings` that lets admins view and correct temple opening-hours data stored in the untyped `Temple.timingInfo` Prisma JSON column. It exposes three endpoints—GET list, GET detail by slug (which also returns audit history), and PATCH by slug to update timings—all gated by the `adminPreHandlers` chain of `authenticateUser` plus `requireRole('admin')` from the shared auth middleware. The PATCH body is validated with a zod schema (`timingsBodySchema`) that enforces an "HH:MM - HH:MM" format via the `HHMM_RANGE` regex on each `regularHours` entry, with optional `closedOn` and `specialDays` strings; updates merge into the existing JSON rather than replacing it wholesale. Dependencies are Fastify, zod, the local auth middlewares, and the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma.js`. A notable design decision is the best-effort audit trail: `loadAuditHistory` and `tryWriteAudit` use raw SQL (`$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe`) against an optional `TempleTimingAuditLog` table and silently swallow errors—returning empty history or no-op writes—so the feature works whether or not that migration has run. Gotchas include the GET list endpoint returning an empty array (with only a warn log) on database failure rather than an error status, and the fact that because `timingInfo` is untyped JSON, shape validation happens only at this API boundary, leaving any pre-existing malformed keys untouched by the merge.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin-roadmap.te.summary: This Vitest suite covers `apps/api/src/routes/admin-roadmap.ts`, verifying both the admin-gated `GET /admin/roadmap` endpoint and its internal helper functions exported via `__testing` (`readQueue`, `readLastDecisions`, `parseTripwiresYaml`). Rather than hitting a real database or the real roadmap files, it builds a throwaway `ROADMAP_ROOT` under the OS temp dir populated with fixture files (`_index.json`, `_kpi-cache.json`, `_tripwires-global.yml`, a `queue/` markdown file with frontmatter, and `decisions/2026-06/` entries), restoring the original env var in `afterAll`. HTTP-level tests use Fastify's `app.inject` against `adminRoadmapRoutes` registered with the `/api/v1` prefix, asserting 401 without a token, 403 with the `demo-devotee` token, and 200 with `demo-admin` returning the five top-level keys (index, queue, decisions, kpis, tripwires). Helper tests confirm frontmatter parsing, recursive walking of `YYYY-MM` decision subdirectories, truncation of decision content to 4000 characters, and YAML tripwire extraction. The critical gotcha documented inline is the `vi.mock` of `../lib/prisma.js` with `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js`: the demo-token bypass in `authenticateUser` calls `prisma.user.findUnique`, and resolving it to `null` (reset per-test via `vi.clearAllMocks`) forces the synthetic-id fallback so roles come from the demo profile — without the mock, CI lacking `DATABASE_URL` throws at query time and returns 500 instead of the expected auth codes, a regression that previously broke CI. Dependencies are limited to vitest, node fs/os/path utilities, Fastify, the prisma mock module, and the route module under test.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin.ts.summary: This Fastify plugin (`adminRoutes`) registers the admin console API under `/api/v1/admin`, guarding every route with `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` preHandlers from `../middlewares/auth.js`. User-facing endpoints — list/detail/patch users, dashboard stats, revenue, reports, and pending approvals — delegate to `adminService`, while the commissions ledger and ratings moderation query `prisma` directly (commissions serialize Decimal `amount`/`percentage` fields to strings; ratings filter `Review` rows by stars and providerId). `POST /temples` is the only fully wired CRUD write: it validates with the strict `templeCreateSchema` (strict because the `Temple` model has many NOT NULL columns), auto-derives a slug via `slugifyTempleName`, and maps Prisma P2002 uniqueness violations to a 409 "Slug already in use" response. The remaining resources — temples list, priests, pujas, content, payments, and user create/delete — are backward-compatible stubs that echo validated bodies or return empty page shells, with permissive `.passthrough()` Zod schemas (`templeWriteSchema`, `priestWriteSchema`, `pujaWriteSchema`, `contentWriteSchema`) deliberately validating at the boundary so future implementations inherit real validation. Two notable gotchas: `POST /ratings/:id/hide` is a logged no-op returning `ok: false` because the `Review` schema lacks an `isHidden` column, and admin bookings live in a separate `admin-bookings.ts` module. The shared `validateBody` helper centralizes 400 handling with flattened Zod errors, and `__testing` exports `slugifyTempleName`, `templeCreateSchema`, and `templePatchSchema` solely for tests.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\affiliate.ts.summary: This file implements affiliate click tracking and outbound redirection for the Darshya API as a Fastify route plugin. Its single export, `affiliateRoutes`, registers a `GET /click` endpoint that accepts `dest` and `partner` query parameters, logs the click, and issues a 302 redirect to the partner's site with UTM parameters appended. The internal `buildUrl` helper constructs the target from hardcoded `PARTNER_BASE` URLs for three travel partners (makemytrip, goibibo, irctc), stamping `utm_source=darshya`, `utm_medium=affiliate`, and the destination slug as the campaign. Real affiliate IDs are injected per partner from environment variables (`AFF_MAKEMYTRIP_ID`, `AFF_GOIBIBO_ID`, `AFF_IRCTC_ID`) using the parameter name mapped in `PARTNER_AFF_PARAM` — notably IRCTC reuses `utm_source` for its ID. The only dependency is the `fastify` `FastifyInstance` type; no database or external service is called. A key gotcha: when an env var is absent the click still redirects and logs but carries no affiliate ID, so it generates no revenue. Persistence is currently limited to `server.log.info` with an `affiliate_click` event (including client IP), with a Prisma `AffiliateClick` table noted as future work, and unknown partners or missing params return 400 errors.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\admin.temple-cre.summary: This Vitest suite guards the temple-creation internals of the admin routes module `admin.js`, exercising the `slugifyTempleName` helper and the `templeCreateSchema` Zod schema through the module's test-only `__testing` export. The slug tests pin normalization behavior — lowercasing, collapsing punctuation runs into single dashes, stripping edge dashes, truncating at 80 characters, and returning an empty string for unsalvageable input — because malformed slugs would otherwise hit the `Temple.slug` unique constraint and surface as confusing Prisma P2002 errors rather than clean 400 responses. The schema tests verify that a minimal valid payload parses while defaults are applied (`tradition` becomes `'other'`, `deities` becomes an empty array, `country` becomes `'India'`), and that the schema rejects out-of-range latitudes (matching the DB column's -90..90 bounds), non-URL-safe slugs with uppercase or spaces, unknown `tradition` enum values, and missing `description` (since `Temple.description` is NOT NULL). The file's only dependencies are `vitest` and the sibling `admin.js` module. A notable design decision is that validation rules are deliberately pinned to underlying database constraints so schema failures preempt database errors, and the `__testing` export pattern itself is a gotcha — these identifiers exist solely to make internals reachable from tests without exposing them as route behavior.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\antim-sanskar.te.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the `antim-sanskar` route module (`apps/api/src/routes/antim-sanskar.js`), which powers Hindu last-rites bookings, by exercising its validation logic and static seed data without standing up an HTTP server. It imports a dedicated `__testing` export to reach the module's internals — specifically `bookSchema` (a Zod validator) and `makeBookingNumber` — alongside the public `PACKAGES`, `GHATS`, and `SACRED_RIVERS` constants. The schema tests confirm that a minimal booking (deceased name, contact, phone, relation, city, `packageTier`) passes, while unknown tiers like `platinum`, empty deceased names, non-ISO `preferredDate` values such as `02/05/2026`, and unsupported `asthiVisarjanRiver` values like `kaveri` are rejected; an optional family `email` is accepted. The booking-number tests pin the `BS-AS-YYYYMMDD-NNNNN` identifier shape produced by `makeBookingNumber`. Data-integrity tests lock `PACKAGES` to exactly three tiers priced at 15000, 35000, and 50000 INR in ascending order, require `GHATS` to seed at least 30 entries each carrying a non-empty id, city, and state, and assert `SACRED_RIVERS` contains exactly ganga, godavari, narmada, and yamuna. Its only external dependency is `vitest`; everything else comes from the sibling route module. A notable design point is the `__testing` escape hatch, which keeps test access to internal schemas explicit rather than widening the public API, and the suite as a whole treats pricing, river, and ghat data as contract-pinned constants so accidental seed changes fail CI.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\ai.ts.summary: This file registers the API's AI feature surface as a Fastify plugin: the exported `aiRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)` wires up a streaming SSE chat endpoint (`POST /chat`), a quota probe (`GET /usage`), conversation CRUD (`GET/DELETE /conversations[/:id]`), and stateless public generators (`POST /recommend-puja`, `POST /generate-sankalp`, `GET /personalize-content`, `POST /translate`). It builds on three internal modules — `authenticateUser` from `middlewares/auth`, `aiService` from `services/ai.service` (which ultimately calls the paid Groq API), and the usage-metering helpers `canSendMessage`, `recordMessage`, and `getUsageSummary` from `lib/ai-usage` — plus `zod` for request validation. Because chat burns paid Groq quota, `/chat` carries a dedicated 20-requests-per-minute-per-IP rate limit (tighter than the global 100/min) and a per-tier paywall gate: authenticated users are checked via `canSendMessage` and rejected with a 402 `limit_reached` payload, while anonymous "Ask Pandit" visitors fall through on synthetic `anon-<timestamp>` IDs that skip metering and history persistence. The `/chat` handler uses `reply.hijack()` to write SSE frames (`metadata`, `text`, `done`, `error` events) directly to the raw Node response, and deliberately only echoes the request `Origin` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` when it matches the `CORS_ORIGIN` allowlist — reflecting it verbatim would bypass server-level CORS for credentialed cross-origin streams. Robustness is favored over strictness throughout: auth on `/chat` is best-effort (invalid tokens degrade to anonymous rather than failing), `recordMessage` and `saveConversation` are fire-and-forget so counter or DB failures never break the stream, and client disconnects short-circuit the Groq event loop. All body-accepting endpoints validate with strict zod schemas (`chatBodySchema`, `recommendPujaSchema`, `sankalpSchema`, `translateSchema`) with explicit length caps — a hardening pass over previously unchecked public endpoints that were trivially DoS-able via oversized or mistyped JSON. A secondary gotcha: conversation listing clamps `limit` to 50, and several public handlers read `request.currentUser` optionally without an auth preHandler, so it is only populated if some earlier hook ran.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\astrologer-porta.summary: This file defines the Fastify route plugin `astrologerPortalRoutes` powering the astrologer-facing portal in the API: dashboard stats, profile editing, availability management, an online/offline presence toggle, and an earnings view. Every handler is gated by the `authenticateUser` middleware plus an inline `ASTROLOGER` role check, and data access goes through the shared `prisma` client (from `../lib/prisma.js`) against the `AstrologerProfile` and `Commission` models, while presence operations delegate to `setAstrologerOnline`, `getAstrologerPresence`, and `ASTROLOGER_SHARE` from `../services/astrologer.service.js`. The dashboard endpoint is notable for querying a raw-SQL `astrologer_consultations` table via `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe` (parameterized with `ANY($1::text[])`), matching on both the `AstrologerProfile.id` and the User UUID because historical rows were written under several identifier forms; failures fall back to zeroed stats since the table may not exist. Input validation uses zod schemas (`profileUpdateSchema`, `availabilityUpdateSchema`, re-exported via `__testing` for tests), with two deliberate constraints: `pricePerMinute` floors at ₹1/min (a P0 fix so bookings can't silently fail the ₹50 minimum), and `availability` is free-form JSON capped at 64KB to allow UI iteration without migrations. Both PATCH endpoints auto-create a default profile when none exists, mirroring each other's onboarding behavior, and availability is replaced wholesale rather than merged. The `/online` POST/GET pair implements an Uber-style presence switch stored only in memory with a 15-minute heartbeat decay, so presence is lost on restart. Finally, `/earnings` exists because the portal previously called an admin-only commissions route; it reads the caller's `Commission` rows (where `amount` is the platform cut) and back-computes the astrologer's gross share using the stored percentage, returning per-row and summary totals.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\antim-sanskar.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements the antim sanskar (Hindu death rites) booking vertical for the Darshya API, deliberately designed as a sensitive flow: no online payment (the assigned pandit collects on-site), no marketing copy, and a promise that a human coordinator calls the bereaved family within 30 minutes. It exports the `PACKAGES` constant (three reverently-described service tiers: basic, standard, comprehensive, priced ₹15,000–₹50,000), the `PackageTier` and `AntimSanskarBookingInput` types, the `SACRED_RIVERS` and `GHATS` reference lists (30 verified cremation ghats across Indian cities — the comments warn against silently adding unverified ones), the main `antimSanskarRoutes(server)` plugin registering GET /packages, GET /ghats (with optional city filter), and POST /book, plus a `__testing` handle exposing internals for unit tests. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, `sendOpsAlert` from `../lib/alert.js` (fired at critical severity per booking), `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js` (gated on `RESEND_API_KEY`, sending a deliberately plain condolence-style confirmation), zod for the `bookSchema` validator, and `authenticateUser` middleware, which guards POST /book after an earlier open version allowed anonymous insertion of PII. The notable architectural choice is that all persistence uses raw SQL via `$executeRawUnsafe` rather than Prisma's generated client, because the table comes from migration `20260502_antim_sanskar` and the client may not be regenerated yet; relatedly, `ensureAntimSanskarTable()` idempotently self-provisions the `antim_sanskar_bookings` table and its indexes at boot because Render's free tier runs no deploy-time migration step (incident TD15 surfaced error 42P01). Bookings default `preferredDate` to today since most rites are same-day, generate human-readable reference numbers (`BS-AS-YYYYMMDD-random`), and land in `pending_coordinator` status; alerting and email are fire-and-forget so a delivery failure never blocks the family's confirmation.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\b2b.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite exercises the internal helpers of the B2B partner API route module by importing them through the `__testing` escape hatch exported from `./b2b.js`. It verifies `sha256` produces stable hex digests, and that the PII-masking utilities behave correctly: `maskEmail` lowercases input before returning a 16-character hash prefix (null-safe), while `maskPhone` keeps only the last four digits and fully redacts short numbers. The in-memory rate limiter is tested via `checkRate` and the shared `RATE_BUCKETS` map, confirming per-key bucket isolation and a 429-style failure carrying `retryAfterSec` once the per-minute limit is exceeded. `resolveApiKey` is tested only on its DEV path, where a key matching the `B2B_DEV_KEY` environment variable resolves to a hardcoded `DEV_PARTNER` record with `read:temples` scope and a 60 rpm limit, with the suite carefully restoring the original env var afterward. Finally, it validates the Zod schemas `listQuerySchema` and `sinceQuerySchema`, covering limit coercion from strings, the default of 20, the 1–100 bound, and strict ISO-8601 datetime validation for `since`. Notable gotchas the tests encode: rate limiting is process-local and must be reset via `RATE_BUCKETS.clear()` between tests, and `since` rejects date-only strings, requiring full ISO timestamps.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\b2b.ts.summary: This file implements the MVP slice of the Darshya B2B Temple SaaS API v1 (ticket R-Q3-E-007): a Fastify plugin exposing five read-only partner endpoints (`/temples`, `/bookings`, `/pandits`, `/donations`, `/darshan-schedule`) plus a `/ping` auth probe and a hand-rolled `/openapi.json`, all guarded by API-key authentication, per-key rate limiting, and scope-gated PII masking. The sole real export is `b2bRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)`, alongside the `B2BApiKeyRecord` type and a `__testing` object exposing internals like `sha256`, `maskEmail`, `maskPhone`, `resolveApiKey`, and `checkRate` for unit tests. It depends on Fastify, `zod` for query validation (`listQuerySchema`, `sinceQuerySchema`), and `node:crypto` for SHA-256 key hashing and email masking; comments reference future integrations with a Prisma `B2BApiKey` model and internal services (`templeService`, `bookingService`, `priestsPublicService`, `donationService`, `darshanScheduleService`), plus a bootstrap script `scripts/issue-b2b-key.ts` and the handoff doc `docs/cto/R-Q3-E-007-handoff.md`. Authentication reads the `x-darshya-key` header, and the `authenticateB2B` preHandler hook applies auth plus a fixed 60-second-window rate limiter to every route in the plugin, with `requireScope` adding per-endpoint scope checks such as `read:bookings`. Notable gotchas: key resolution currently only works via the `B2B_DEV_KEY` environment variable because `lookupDbKey` is a stub returning null (so all keys 401 in production until Phase 1), the `RATE_BUCKETS` limiter is an in-process Map that won't hold across replicas or restarts, and every endpoint returns empty stub data with `_stub` markers pending service wiring. PII policy is baked into helpers — emails become a 16-char SHA-256 prefix, phones keep only the last four digits — and donor PII on `/donations` is gated behind a separate `read:donor-pii` scope.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\astrology.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`astrologyRoutes`) wires up all astrology-facing HTTP endpoints for the API: a public astrologer directory, kundli (birth chart) generation, daily horoscopes, rashi compatibility, an AI astrologer chat, and authenticated consultation session management. It depends on `astrologyService` for most business logic, the newer `lib/astrology.ts` functions (`generateKundli`, `getDailyHoroscope`, `prewarmDailyHoroscopes` with their Zod schemas) for the v2 kundli/horoscope path, Prisma (`prisma.astrologerProfile`, `kundliRequest`) for the live directory and analytics, and `getAstrologerPresence` from `astrologer.service` for online badges; auth comes from `authenticateUser` and the cron-gated `requireCronSecretHeader` middleware. A key gotcha is that the directory is split: `/astrologers` still serves a 15-row in-memory mock fixture while `/astrologers/live` serves genuinely onboarded approved `AstrologerProfile` rows, with the full swap deferred to a later phase. The `POST /kundli` handler is deliberately dual-shaped for backward compatibility, routing the new `dob/tob/location` payload through Zod-validated `generateKundli` while the legacy `birthDate/birthTime/birthPlace` shape falls back to `astrologyService.getKundliAsync`, and kundli analytics writes are fire-and-forget. Several hardening decisions are called out in comments: pagination limits are clamped to 100 to prevent a free unauthenticated DoS on the directory, and `POST /horoscope/prewarm` was moved to `requireCronSecretHeader` because the old inline check was a timing oracle that also skipped auth when `CRON_SECRET` was unset. Route ordering matters (`/horoscope/all` before `/horoscope/:rashi`), consultation endpoints enforce user-or-admin authorization with 403/404 distinctions, and `/ask` degrades gracefully to keyword-based fallback responses when the AI service fails.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\auth.ts.summary: This file defines the API's authentication surface as a Fastify plugin: the exported `authRoutes(server)` registers routes for phone OTP login (`/send-otp`, `/verify-otp`), email/password login and signup, session refresh, logout, the protected `/me` profile endpoint, and Google token sync, all validated with zod schemas. It builds on `createSupabaseClient` from `../lib/supabase.js` for the actual identity work (Supabase Auth handles SMS OTP via Twilio, session refresh, and sign-out), `prisma` from `../lib/prisma.js` for upserting `users` rows and reading `userRoleAssignment` (centralized in `getPrimaryRoleForUser`, which defaults to 'devotee'), and the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js` to guard `/me`. Security is layered deliberately: sensitive routes get a 10 req/min per-IP limit on top of the global 100/min, plus in-memory per-identity buckets (`otpBuckets`, `loginBuckets` — 5 OTP sends per phone and 10 logins per email per 15 minutes) keyed on the victim's identity rather than source IP so IP rotation doesn't help attackers, though these Maps are per-process and won't coordinate across instances or restarts. The `/refresh` route implements its own replay detection on top of Supabase's native refresh-token rotation: it sha256-hashes refresh tokens into a `refresh_token_jtis` ledger table via raw SQL and, on detecting reuse, revokes the user's whole token family and clears cookies. Responses carry both the legacy JSON Bearer contract and additive HttpOnly cookies (`darshya_session`, `darshya_refresh`, the latter scoped to `/api/v1/auth`), with `setAuthCookies` silently no-oping until `@fastify/cookie` is registered in server bootstrap. Other notable gotchas: `normalizePhone` hardcodes +91 for 10-digit numbers, a hardcoded `DEMO_ACCOUNTS` registry (including an admin account) produces synthetic `demo-` sessions gated to non-production environments, `/logout` handles both Supabase JWTs and a custom `email-`-prefixed token format stored in an `email_sessions` table, and an `onResponse` hook logs every auth request with Cloudflare's `cf-ipcountry` header for geo-blocking diagnosis without capturing PII.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\consultation.tes.summary: This vitest suite unit-tests the zod validation schemas and reference-number generator exported for testing via the `__testing` object from the sibling route module `consultation.js` (the consultation booking/payment HTTP routes in the API app). It exercises five exports: `bookSchema` (booking requests must supply a non-empty `astrologerId` capped at 64 chars, integer `minutes` between 5 and 60, and an optional ISO `scheduledAt` refined to be in the future); `verifySchema` (payment verification requiring a UUID `consultationId`, with optional Razorpay fields `razorpay_order_id`, `razorpay_payment_id`, and `razorpay_signature` so a demo path can verify with the ID alone); `nextConsultRef` (must emit refs matching `AC-YYYYMMDD-XXXXXX` with 6 uppercase hex digits, with a collision-tolerance check allowing up to ~10 duplicates in 50 draws); and `adminListSchema` / `astrologerListSchema` (list-query schemas that coerce string query params to numbers, default `limit`/`offset` to 50/0, cap `limit` at 200, reject negative offsets, and restrict `status` to the four-value enum `pending_payment`, `confirmed`, `completed`, `cancelled`). The only dependencies are vitest and the module under test; Razorpay appears only implicitly through the verification field names. Two gotchas are documented in-line: the future-dated `scheduledAt` fixture deliberately uses year 2099 because a fixed date once aged into the past and broke CI, and the `__testing` re-export pattern is what makes the route module's internal schemas reachable from the test file.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\content.ts.summary: This file defines `contentRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that exposes the read-side HTTP API for devotional content (articles, mantras, stories, aarti, chalisa) in the API app. It registers six endpoints: `GET /` lists content with optional `type`, `deity`, `language`, and `isPremium` filters plus pagination; `GET /daily` returns the aarti/mantra/shloka of the day; `GET /search` runs a text query; `GET /categories` lists content categories; `GET /:slug` fetches a single item by slug with a 404 fallback; and `POST /:id/like` increments a like counter. Nearly all logic is delegated to `contentService` from `../services/content.service.js`, which is the file's primary internal dependency; the only exception is the like endpoint, which dynamically imports `prisma` from `../lib/prisma.js` to update `contentItem.likeCount` directly. A notable constraint is that page size is hard-capped at 100 and the `isPremium` flag is manually coerced from a query string to a boolean. Route registration order matters here: `/daily`, `/search`, and `/categories` are declared before the parameterized `/:slug` route so they aren't swallowed by it. The biggest gotcha is the like endpoint, which carries a TODO noting it is a stub—it performs no authentication and blindly increments the count rather than toggling a per-user like, so `liked: true` in the response is not meaningful yet. All handlers follow the same pattern of logging errors via `server.log.error` and returning generic 500 responses.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\bookings.ts.summary: This file defines the Fastify HTTP routes for the puja booking lifecycle via the exported `bookingRoutes` plugin, covering creation (`POST /book`), listing (`GET /my`), availability checks (`GET /availability`, public `GET /slots`), detail and video-proof reads, status transitions (`PATCH /:id`), cancellation with a preview quote (`GET /:id/cancel-quote`), rescheduling, devotee-initiated refund requests, and reviews. It delegates business logic to `bookingService` and `cancellationService` (imported from `../services/`), talks directly to the database through the shared `prisma` client (`../lib/prisma.js`), guards most endpoints with the `authenticateUser` middleware, and dynamically imports `booking-notify.service` for fire-and-forget cancellation notifications. All inputs are validated with Zod schemas; a notable security fix (tagged P0 #pp-01) replaced a wide-open `z.record(z.any())` on the status-update body with `updateBookingStatusDataSchema`, a discriminated union that allowlists fields per transition so clients can never set financial or identity fields like `priestPayout` or `userId`, and the PATCH handler now additionally enforces that only the booking owner, the assigned priest, or an admin can mutate a booking, with priest reassignment restricted to admins. Because the `BookingStatus` enum lacks a `REFUND_REQUESTED` value, the refund-request endpoint marks bookings `cancelled` with a `[refund-requested]` prefix in `cancellationReason` and relies on the external `processAutoRefunds` master cron to pick them up within an hour, enforcing a 24-hour-before-slot cutoff. Other gotchas: `GET /my` must be registered before `GET /:id` to avoid route shadowing, the public `/slots` endpoint validates UUID shape before querying to avoid Prisma P2023 crashes from legacy clients, `createBookingSchema` rejects past dates and carries a `dispatchTier` field that triggers the dispatch engine on payment confirmation, and several handlers map service errors to HTTP codes by string-matching error messages (e.g. "not authorized" → 403), which is brittle coupling to the service layer.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\conversations.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`conversationRoutes`) implements the human-to-human chat layer between devotees and providers (priests, astrologers, wellness instructors, temple/gaushala/store managers), backing the post-payment service-delivery flow: it exposes endpoints to list, create-or-get, and fetch conversations, poll and send messages, mark threads read, and start/end video calls. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (models `chatConversation`, `chatMessage`, `chatCallSession`, `priest`, `pujaBooking`), applies the `authenticateUser` preHandler middleware to every route, validates payloads with `zod`, and fires push notifications through `notifyUser` imported from `./notifications.js`. Video calls are not self-hosted: `start-call` mints a random room name via `node:crypto` and returns a `https://meet.jit.si/` URL, posting a `call_link` system message into the thread so the counterparty sees it. A notable business gate, `devoteeHasPaidRelationship`, only enforces a paid booking for the `puja_booking` kind (returning HTTP 402 otherwise); `support` and all other kinds are deliberately left open because their booking/payment models don't exist yet, and the `PAID_BOOKING_REQUIRED` set is the single place to tighten this later. Reads are polling-based rather than websocket — clients call `GET /:id/messages?since=<iso>` — and unread state is tracked as two counters (`devoteeUnread`/`providerUnread`) incremented on the opposite side of each send. Two gotchas stand out: the send rate limiter (60 msgs/min per user per conversation) is an in-memory `Map`, so it resets on restart and won't hold across multiple API instances, and `start-call` silently reuses any unended call from the last 30 minutes rather than creating a fresh room. All notification calls are fire-and-forget (`void ...catch(() => undefined)`), so a push failure never fails the underlying chat operation.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\cron.ts.summary: This file defines the API's scheduled-job endpoints, existing because Render's free tier lacks cron support, so a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/daily-cron.yml) POSTs here daily at 5:30 IST instead. It exports a single `cronRoutes` plugin that registers three routes on the FastifyInstance: POST /daily runs every registered job sequentially, POST /run/:job executes one named job for ad-hoc use (404ing with a list of valid names for unknown jobs), and GET /health reports whether CRON_AUTH_TOKEN is configured plus the available job names. Both POST routes are guarded by the `requireCronBearer` middleware from `../middlewares/cron-auth.js`, which deliberately fails loud with a 401 and a `cron_auth_misconfigured` body code when the token env var is unset, distinguishing server misconfiguration from bad client tokens in logs. The job registry (`JOBS`) currently holds three stubs—`refresh-panchang` (intended to call the mhah-panchang module and upsert a `panchang_days` cache table), `sendFestivalReminders` (planned to fan out via web-push and WhatsApp once push subscriptions land in Prisma), and `expireBookings` (to mark stale confirmed bookings as no-show after two hours without video proof). A shared `runJob` wrapper isolates each job's failure into a per-job `JobResult` with timing, so one failing job doesn't abort the rest, though the aggregate response returns 500 if any job failed. The notable design constraint is that all jobs must be idempotent so re-runs after a failed GitHub Action don't double-send notifications, which is why the stubs are kept decoupled from their eventual dependencies rather than wired in prematurely.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\demo-pay.ts.summary: This Fastify route file implements a demo payment bypass that simulates the full post-payment booking flow without touching Razorpay, so chat and call features can be demoed without payment KYC. Its main export, `demoPayRoutes`, registers two endpoints under authentication: `POST /demo-pay/puja`, which picks a `TemplePujaOffering` (or the first active one), assigns the seeded demo priest (`pandit@demo.com`, falling back to any active priest), creates a `PujaBooking` already in `priest_assigned` status with a 30/70 platform-commission/priest-payout split, and calls `ensureConversationForBooking` from `conversation.service.js` to open a chat thread; and `POST /demo-pay/start-chat`, which opens or reuses a `ChatConversation` with any provider email for astrology, wellness, temple, gaushala, store, or support demos. Dependencies include the shared `prisma` client, the `authenticateUser` middleware, `zod` for body validation, and a dynamic import of `Prisma.Decimal` from `@prisma/client` for money math. Notable safety decisions: the whole plugin is gated by `demoEnabled()` (allowed when `NODE_ENV !== 'production'` or `ENABLE_DEMO_PAY=true`) returning 403 otherwise, and a per-user in-memory token bucket (`rateLimitOk`, 10 actions per 10 minutes) guards against abuse since bookings here are free. Gotchas: the rate-limit buckets are in-memory so they reset on restart and don't coordinate across instances, and the booking bypasses the normal `BookingService` transition helper by writing `priest_assigned` directly, which is why conversation creation is invoked manually.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\consultation.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`consultationRoutes`) implements paid astrologer video consultations: it books sessions through Razorpay checkout and hosts the calls in Jitsi Meet rooms on meet.jit.si, persisting state in a raw-SQL `astrologer_consultations` table created lazily by `ensureConsultationTables()` because no Prisma model exists yet (the same pattern used by donations.ts and csr-match.ts). The main endpoints are POST `/book` (validates input with zod `bookSchema`, prices the session from the in-memory `astrologyService.getAstrologerById` rate so clients cannot inject prices, creates a Razorpay order, and inserts a `pending_payment` row), POST `/verify-payment` (HMAC-SHA256 signature check via `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, flips status to `confirmed`, mints the room name), POST `/start` (returns the stored Jitsi room only for a paid consultation owned by the caller, the assigned astrologer, or an admin — a P0 #AP-02 fix for an earlier free-room hole), plus GET `/mine`, POST `/:id/cancel`, PATCH `/:id/complete`, and paginated admin/astrologer list queries. Dependencies include `../lib/prisma.js` (used almost entirely through `$queryRawUnsafe`), the `razorpay` SDK, `authenticateUser`/`requireRole` middleware, notification helpers `notifyAstrologerNewConsult` and `notifyDevoteeConsultConfirmed` from `astrologer.service.js`, and `assertNotProductionDemo` from `payment-mode.js`. When `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` is missing or `rzp_test_demo`, the module runs in demo mode with synthetic `order_demo_*` ids and skips signature verification. On payment confirmation it fire-and-forget writes an idempotent `Commission` ledger row at `ASTROLOGER_PLATFORM_RATE` (20% platform / 80% astrologer, changed from 30/70), but only if `astrologer_id` resolves to a real `AstrologerProfile` — mock slug-based astrologers are skipped to avoid violating the providerId UUID constraint. Notable gotchas: `astrologer_id` is TEXT that may be a mock slug, profile UUID, or legacy user UUID, which forced profile-based identity resolution in `/complete` (AP-08); cancellations enforce a 24-hour refund window but actual refunds are executed manually in the Razorpay dashboard; bookings enforce 5–60 minutes and a ₹50 minimum; and the static `/mine` path must be declared before `/:id` routes. A `__testing` export exposes the zod schemas and `nextConsultRef` reference generator.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\csr-match.ts.summary: This Fastify module implements "Layer AX" corporate CSR donation matching, where enrolled corporate sponsors automatically match devotee donations (default 1:1, configurable via match_ratio) against gaushala campaigns up to a monthly INR cap. It exports two things: `maybeMatchDonation`, a best-effort hook the donations route calls after a successful donation that picks the active sponsor with the most remaining cap, applies the optional `gaushala_filter` (empty array means all gaushalas), inserts a row into `csr_match_records`, increments the sponsor's `monthly_used_inr`, and silently returns `{ matched: false }` on any error so donations never fail; and `csrMatchRoutes`, which registers POST `/enroll` (public lead form validated by a zod `enrollSchema` including GSTIN/PAN length checks, inserted inactive pending admin approval), GET `/me` (authenticated sponsor dashboard keyed on the user's email), and admin routes `/admin/list` and `/admin/:id/active`. Dependencies are the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, `authenticateUser` and `requireRole` from `../middlewares/auth.js`, `fastify`, and `zod`. Notable design choices: both tables (`csr_corporate_accounts`, `csr_match_records`) are created via raw `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` SQL in `ensureTables` at route registration rather than through Prisma migrations, and all queries use `$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe` with parameterized values. A comment flags a P0 security fix — the admin endpoints previously had no auth and leaked corporate emails and GSTINs, now gated by `requireRole('admin')`. Other gotchas: matches under ₹1 are skipped, enrollment defaults to a ₹100,000 monthly cap (bounded ₹10k–₹10M by schema), and settlement into actual invoicing and 80G receipts is described as a future daily cron, not implemented here.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\digest.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements the missing backend for weekly-digest email unsubscribes: the `WeeklyDigestOptOut` table and the cron job that reads it already existed, but nothing wrote opt-outs, so unsubscribe links silently did nothing. It exports a single function, `digestRoutes`, which registers `POST /unsubscribe` (mounted at `/api/v1/digest`) accepting a JSON body of `{userId, reason?}` validated by a zod schema (`unsubscribeSchema`, requiring a UUID and capping reason at 200 chars). The handler writes via `prisma.$executeRawUnsafe` (from the shared `../lib/prisma.js` client) using a parameterized raw SQL insert with `ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE`, making repeat clicks idempotent by refreshing the timestamp and reason. Dependencies are minimal: `fastify` for the server instance type, `zod` for body parsing, and the internal Prisma module. Notable design choices: the endpoint is deliberately unauthenticated because links arrive from email where the user may be signed out, and it is write-only by construction—it can only insert an opt-out row and returns no PII. Error handling is fail-soft: on any database error (e.g., table drift) it logs a warning but still returns 200 with a "recorded best-effort" note so the user is never blocked, a trade-off that favors user experience over guaranteed persistence.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\donations.test.t.summary: This Vitest suite (apps/api/src/routes/donations.test.ts) validates the Zod `createOrderSchema` used by the donations create-order endpoint, verifying that donation causes are polymorphic: a cause can target either a gaushala or a temple, tracked under ticket PBO-2. It imports the `__testing` namespace from the sibling route module `./donations.js` and exercises the schema directly via `safeParse`, with no HTTP layer involved — a "pure-Zod gate" pattern the file notes mirrors `store-admin.test.ts`. The cases confirm acceptance of a legacy gaushala donation (`gaushalaId` alone, with `causeKind` defaulting to gaushala), an explicit `causeKind: 'gaushala'`, and a `causeKind: 'temple'` with a UUID `templeId`, while rejecting temple causes missing `templeId`, gaushala calls missing `gaushalaId`, and any payload mixing both IDs. It also enforces the ₹101 minimum amount regardless of cause kind. The only external dependency is vitest; the schema under test comes from the donations route itself, with Zod implied through the safeParse API. The header comment records the regression history: the schema previously required `gaushalaId`, so temple donations were rejected or silently forced through the gaushala path, leaving `temple_id` unset and receipts naming the wrong entity. A key design takeaway is that `causeKind` is optional and defaults to gaushala for backward compatibility, and that route modules expose a `__testing` export specifically so schemas can be unit-tested in isolation.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\darshan.ts.summary: This Fastify route module powers the live darshan (temple live-stream) feature, exposing endpoints to list currently-live streams, fetch a single stream's playback details, and track viewer join/leave events. The exported `darshanRoutes` registers GET `/live`, GET `/scheduled`, GET `/:id/stream`, and authenticated POST `/:id/join` and `/:id/leave` handlers, backed by the Prisma client's `temple` and `liveDarshanStream` models plus two large hardcoded fallback tables: `TEMPLE_LIVE_STREAMS` (verified official YouTube channel IDs and embed URLs for nine major temples) and `TEMPLE_AARTI_SCHEDULE` (per-temple aarti windows in IST). Live status is computed by `getLiveStatus` from `lib/darshan-schedule.js` against those aarti windows so a temple is never shown as live outside its ritual hours, while `getChannelEmbedInfo`, `liveStreamUrl`, and `videoEmbedUrl` from `lib/youtube-feed.js` probe the channel RSS feed to supply a recent-VOD fallback when the live embed would be dark. A `SLUG_ALIASES` map with `resolveSlug` lets short URLs like `/darshan/somnath` resolve to canonical slugs such as `somnath-gujarat`. Notable design choices include a 30-second in-process `liveCache` on `/live` (with `x-cache` HIT/MISS headers) to mask Prisma cold-start latency on Render's free tier, and a full hardcoded fallback path when the DB is empty or unreachable. Several gotchas are evident: fallback `viewerCount`/`peakViewers` values are static fabrications, `/scheduled` synthesizes fake sessions spaced two hours apart rather than reading real data, and join/leave updates silently swallow errors. The join endpoint requires `authenticateUser` specifically to keep anonymous traffic from polluting the `viewerCount` analytics, and comments warn that some channels (e.g. one using KDigital-licensed audio) block iframe embedding entirely, so only embed-verified official temple channels are used.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gaushala-cows.ts.summary: This file defines `gaushalaCowsRoutes`, a Fastify route module that provides CRUD operations for cow records owned by a gaushala (cow shelter), plus an endpoint for appending health records to a cow. It exports the single route-registration function which wires up endpoints for listing cows, creating a cow, fetching one cow with its 50 most recent `CowHealthRecord` entries, updating, deleting, and posting health records, all scoped to the authenticated manager's `gaushalaId`. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (models `Cow`, `CowHealthRecord`, `GaushalaProfile`), the `authenticateUser` middleware, and `zod` for request validation via `createCowSchema`, `updateCowSchema` (a `.partial()` of the create schema), and `healthRecordSchema`. Access control is enforced by the local `requireGaushalaManager` helper, which rejects any caller lacking the `GAUSHALA_MANAGER` role with a 403, and every query filters by the caller's own `gaushalaId` so managers can only touch their own shelter's animals. A notable design choice is the `syncCowCount` helper, which recounts cows after create/delete and writes the denormalized `totalCows` onto `GaushalaProfile` — a counter that could drift if cows are created through any other path. The create handler also translates Prisma's `P2002` unique-constraint error into a 409, implying `tagNumber` is unique per cow. One gotcha: the health-record endpoint validates ownership of the cow but the cow detail endpoint caps health history at 50 records, so older records are silently omitted from that view.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\donations.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements the donation payment flow for gaushalas and temples: `POST /donations/create-order` creates a Razorpay order and a `created` row in the `donations` table, and `POST /donations/verify` validates the Razorpay HMAC signature (timing-safe via `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) before marking the donation paid. Its key exports are `donationRoutes` (the route registrar), `finalizeDonationReceipt` (an idempotent helper that mints a `DR-YYYYMMDD-XXXX` receipt number, generates an 80G PDF via `generate80GReceipt`, and emails it with `sendEmail`/`donationReceiptEmail` — shared with the Razorpay webhook backstop so a closed browser still completes the flow), and `findDonationByOrderId` (lookup used by that webhook). It depends on the `razorpay` SDK, `../lib/prisma.js`, `authenticateUser` middleware, `../lib/email.js`, `../lib/pdf-receipt.js`, and `assertNotProductionDemo` from `../lib/payment-mode.js`. Notable gotchas: all donation reads/writes use raw SQL (`$queryRawUnsafe`) because the generated Prisma client can lag schema changes on Windows, and `ensureGaushalaTaxFields` performs idempotent `ALTER TABLE ... IF NOT EXISTS` to add `pan`/`regn_80g` columns at startup. A demo mode activates when `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` is unset, fabricating order ids and skipping signature verification so receipts can be exercised without a merchant account. Security hardening is explicit: an ownership guard (`donation.user_id !== me.id` → 403 unless ADMIN), order-id matching against the stored row, amounts bounded to ₹101–₹10,00,000, and a zod refinement enforcing exactly one of `gaushalaId`/`templeId` (the polymorphic donee invariant). Donor PAN (regex-validated) and an optional dedication are persisted at creation so the 80G receipt can carry them, and re-verifying an already-paid donation returns the existing receipt number instead of minting a duplicate.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\dpdp.test.ts.summary: This vitest suite unit-tests the request-validation schemas of the DPDP (data privacy) routes module, importing them through the `__testing` backdoor export from `./dpdp.js` rather than exercising any HTTP handlers. It covers `dsarFileSchema` (filing data-subject requests of kind access, erasure, rectify, or portability, with an optional note capped at 2000 characters), `dsarListSchema` (pagination with defaults limit 50 / offset 0, a limit ceiling of 200, coercion of string query params to numbers, and a status filter restricted to pending, in_progress, resolved, or rejected), `dsarResolveSchema` (accepting only resolved or rejected outcomes), and `consentRecordSchema` (granted/withdrawn actions against the purposes in `consentPurposeEnum`, with a source field limited to 120 characters). It also asserts that `dsarKindEnum` contains exactly the four supported request kinds, effectively pinning the allowed enum values so accidental additions or removals break the build. The only dependency is vitest itself; no database, services, or mocks are involved since these are pure Zod schema checks. Notably, the tests rely on the route module exposing internal schemas via a dedicated `__testing` object, so the suite doubles as living documentation of the API's validation constraints.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gaushala-volunte.summary: This Fastify route module exposes CRUD endpoints for managing volunteers at a gaushala (cow shelter), exporting `gaushalaVolunteersRoutes(server)` which registers GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE handlers under `/volunteers` and `/volunteers/:id`. Every route runs the `authenticateUser` preHandler and then a local `requireGaushalaManager` guard that rejects requests lacking the `GAUSHALA_MANAGER` role, so only gaushala managers can read or mutate volunteer records. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` for all persistence against the `Volunteer` model, on `zod` for input validation via `createSchema` and its `.partial()` variant `updateSchema`, and on the internal auth middleware. The schema restricts volunteer roles to the enum `general`, `feeding`, `medical`, `cleaning`, caps field lengths, and returns flattened zod error details on 400 responses. A notable design decision is that the manager's own user ID doubles as the `gaushalaId` foreign key, meaning volunteers are scoped directly to the manager's account rather than a separate gaushala entity; update and delete handlers verify ownership with a `findFirst` on both `id` and `gaushalaId` and return 404 if no match exists, preventing cross-gaushala access. Listing sorts active volunteers first, then by most recent `joinedAt`. A minor gotcha: `request` and `reply` are typed as `any` in the helper, bypassing Fastify's type safety.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gaushala-portal..summary: This file defines `gaushalaPortalRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that powers the gaushala (cow shelter) manager portal in the API, exposing three endpoints under the `/gaushala-portal` prefix: `GET /donations` for a paginated donation list, `GET /dashboard` for aggregated stats plus recent donations and cows, and `PATCH /profile` for upserting the manager's `GaushalaProfile`. Every route runs the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js` and then enforces a `GAUSHALA_MANAGER` role check, returning 403 otherwise. It depends on the shared Prisma client from `../lib/prisma.js` (querying the `Donation`, `GaushalaProfile`, `Cow`, and `User` models) and uses `zod` for the `profileUpdateSchema` body validation on profile updates. A key data-model gotcha, flagged in the comments, is that `Donation.gaushalaId` is a stringified user id with no foreign key (rationale at schema.prisma:1056-1059), so all aggregates filter on `gaushalaId = currentUser.id` rather than a profile id. The donations endpoint translates friendly status names into stored enum values (pending→created, received→paid, failed→failed) and caps results at 500 per request, while the dashboard fans out five parallel Prisma queries via `Promise.all`, counting only `paid` donations toward donor and rupee totals. `PATCH /profile` behaves as an upsert, creating a profile with the default name "My Gaushala" when none exists. The comments explicitly note that cow and volunteer CRUD routes live in sibling files `gaushala-cows.ts` and `gaushala-volunteers.ts`, registered under the same prefix, and must stay there to avoid duplicate route registration at boot.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\dpdp.ts.summary: This file implements the DPDP (Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023) compliance surface for the API, exported as the Fastify plugin `dpdpRoutes`, covering roadmap item R-Q3-L-001. It exposes six endpoints: authenticated users can file a Data Subject Access Request via `POST /dsar` (kinds: access, erasure, rectify, portability) with an `sla_deadline` pinned to `DSAR_SLA_DAYS = 30` days, review their history via `GET /dsar/mine`, append consent events via `POST /consent` (capturing IP and user-agent), and read current consent state via `GET /consent/mine`; admins get `GET /admin/dsar`, an ops dashboard sorted so unresolved, oldest-SLA requests float to the top with a computed `sla_breached` flag, and `PATCH /admin/dsar/:id` to mark requests resolved or rejected with a note. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and `zod` for request validation, with all schemas re-exported under `__testing` for unit tests. Notably, all persistence uses raw SQL through `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe` against the `dsar_requests` and `consent_log` tables rather than Prisma models, because the schema is replayed in `ensure-schema.ts` to survive Render's start-command bypass. The consent log is deliberately append-only — the latest row per `(user_id, purpose)` is the current state, collapsed using the Postgres-only `DISTINCT ON` idiom — and counsel sign-off is intentionally out-of-band, tracked in `docs/legal/R-Q3-L-001-handoff.md` rather than in code. Smaller gotchas include a UUID regex guard on the PATCH `:id` param and a `rowGet` helper used to type-safely read raw result rows.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gaushala.ts.summary: This file defines `gaushalaRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that exposes the cow-shelter (gaushala) adoption feature over HTTP. It registers read-only endpoints for listing gaushalas, viewing a gaushala detail, browsing cows with optional `gaushalaId` and `available` query filters, viewing a cow's detail with monthly updates, and listing adoption plans, plus three authenticated endpoints: `POST /adopt` to adopt a cow, `GET /my-adoptions` for the current user's adoptions, and `GET /adoptions/:id/updates` for an adoption's monthly updates. The route layer is intentionally thin — every handler delegates to `gaushalaService` from `../services/gaushala.service.js`, and protected routes use the `authenticateUser` preHandler from `../middlewares/auth.js`, which populates `request.currentUser`. Design-wise, the `available` query flag is parsed by strict string comparison to `'true'`, service-thrown errors in `adoptCow` are uniformly mapped to 400 responses, and the updates endpoint relies on the service returning `null` to signal a missing or foreign-owned adoption. One gotcha is that parameterized routes like `GET /:id` are registered alongside static siblings like `GET /cows` and `GET /plans`; this works because Fastify's router prioritizes static segments, but ordering would matter in other frameworks. Another is the absence of schema validation — params, query, and body are accessed via unchecked TypeScript casts, with only a manual `cowId`/`planId` presence check guarding the adopt endpoint.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gurukul-applicat.summary: This Fastify route module implements the backend for gurukul (school) program applications, exposing a POST / endpoint to submit an application and a GET /mine endpoint to list the authenticated caller's own applications. Its main export is the `gurukulApplicationsRoutes` plugin, which applies the `authenticateUser` middleware to all routes, plus a `__testing` export that surfaces the `submitSchema` for unit tests. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (using the `gurukulApplication`, `gurukulProgram`, and `gurukul` models) and uses `zod` for request validation. Notable constraints: submissions are rejected with 503 when `DATABASE_URL` is unset or the user ID is synthetic (prefixed `demo-` or `anon-`), while GET /mine silently returns an empty list in those degraded modes. A zod `.refine` enforces the minor-safety policy — applicants under 18 must apply with `applicantType: 'parent'` and supply guardian name, relation, phone, and signed consent — and the handler additionally checks that the program and its gurukul are active, that the gurukul `acceptsMinors`, and that the student's age falls within the program's `ageMin`/`ageMax` window. Privacy is handled by storing only the Aadhaar last-4 digits, and consent timestamps are set server-side at creation; `serializeApp` normalizes all dates to ISO strings for the API response, which for /mine also embeds program and gurukul name/slug.

This Vitest file unit-tests the Zod validation schema behind the gurukul (Vedic school) admissions route, importing `submitSchema` via the `__testing` export from the sibling `gurukul-applications.js` module rather than exercising HTTP endpoints. Its only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`/`it`/`expect`) and the route module itself, with Zod's `safeParse` driving every assertion. The tests pin down two application flows encoded in the schema: adults applying for themselves (`applicantType: 'self'`) and minors applied for by a parent (`applicantType: 'parent'`), the latter requiring guardian fields such as `guardianName`, `guardianRelation`, and `guardianPhone`. Notably, the suite encodes a business rule that minors cannot self-apply — a payload with a young `studentAgeYears` and `applicantType: 'self'` must be rejected — and `consentSigned: true` is mandatory for all applicants. Field-level constraints are also locked in: `programId` must be a valid UUID, `statement` has a minimum length, optional `guardianAadhaarLast4` must be exactly four digits, and `studentAgeYears` is bounded to a plausible human range (rejecting 2 and 150). The use of a dedicated `__testing` export signals the route deliberately exposes internals for isolated schema testing without spinning up a server.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gurukul-portal.t.summary: This Fastify route module implements the gurukul-owner portal for reviewing student applications, exposing the exported plugin `gurukulPortalRoutes` which registers a GET `/applications` endpoint and a PATCH `/applications/:id` endpoint under a shared `authenticateUser` preHandler hook. GET `/applications` looks up all `gurukul` records owned by the caller, gathers their `gurukulProgram` rows, and returns up to 500 `gurukulApplication` entries (newest first) flattened with program names and ISO-formatted timestamps. PATCH `/applications/:id` validates the body with the zod `decisionSchema` (status enum of forwarded/accepted/rejected/withdrawn plus an optional 2000-char `decisionNote`), verifies ownership by traversing `program.gurukul.ownerId`, and updates the application, stamping `forwardedAt` when forwarding and `decisionAt` for terminal decisions. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js`, with `zod` as the only external validation dependency. A notable design choice is the graceful-degradation pattern: the helpers `dbDisabled()` (missing `DATABASE_URL`) and `isSyntheticUserId()` (`demo-`/`anon-` prefixes) short-circuit the GET to return an empty list and the PATCH to return 503, so demo/anonymous users never touch the database. Authorization is enforced per-application rather than per-route, returning 403 if the caller doesn't own the parent gurukul and 404 when the application doesn't exist.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gift-puja.ts.summary: This file implements the gift-puja purchase flow for the API, exporting a single `giftPujaRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)` plugin that registers four endpoints: `POST /inquiry` (legacy email-only intake kept as fallback), `POST /create-order` (creates a Stripe PaymentIntent in USD and persists a `gift_puja_orders` row as `pending_payment`), `POST /verify-payment` (re-fetches the PaymentIntent from Stripe rather than trusting the client, flips the row to `confirmed`, and fires a WhatsApp template to the recipient), and `GET /config` (public feature flags — `paymentEnabled`, `whatsappEnabled`, `autoFlowReady` — so the web form knows whether to offer checkout or the inquiry path). It builds on internal modules `../lib/email.js` (`sendEmail`), `../lib/prisma.js`, `../lib/stripe.js` (`getStripe`, `isStripeDemoMode`), and `../lib/whatsapp.js` (`sendWhatsappTemplate`, `whatsapp`), plus `zod` for validation and `node:crypto` for generating `GIFT-YYYYMMDD-XXXX` reference IDs. A notable design choice is that `gift_puja_orders` is a raw-SQL table created lazily by `ensureGiftPujaTables()` on first call — deliberately no Prisma schema change, matching the pattern used in `csr-match.ts` and `astrologer_consultations`. The routes are intentionally anonymous (auth would block NRI gift buyers, the primary monetization vector) but tightly rate-limited — 2/hr for inquiry (to bound the Resend 100/day cap), 10/hr for create-order, 30/hr for verify — and amounts are constrained to $20–$2000, defaulting to $120. Verification is idempotent on `confirmed` status and short-circuits the Stripe re-fetch in demo mode; the WhatsApp send uses the approved template `gift_puja_delivered` and degrades to a no-op when WhatsApp isn't configured. All user input embedded in emails passes through an `escape()` helper to prevent HTML injection, ops notifications go to `GIFT_INQUIRY_TO` (default gift@darshya.online), and the "honest copy mandate" means the `/config` flags drive the frontend to tell buyers when only the manual payment-link fallback is available.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\gurukuls.ts.summary: This file defines the Fastify HTTP routes for the gurukul directory in the API, exposing endpoints to browse, search, view, and create gurukul (traditional school) listings. The exported `gurukulsRoutes` function registers four routes: `GET /` lists active gurukuls with optional filters (state, city, tradition, residential, online, acceptsMinors, and a case-insensitive `q` text search over name, description, and tradition), sorted with verified entries first and capped at 200 results; `GET /:slug` fetches one active gurukul plus its active `GurukulProgram` records ordered by minimum age; `POST /` creates a gurukul with nested programs; and `GET /mine/list` returns the listings owned by the current user. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` for all database access (models `gurukul` and `gurukulProgram`), the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js` to guard the create and "mine" routes, and `zod` for validating the query string (`listQuerySchema`) and creation payload (`createSchema`). A notable design choice is the graceful-degradation pattern: when `DATABASE_URL` is unset (`dbDisabled()`) or the caller is a synthetic demo/anonymous user (`isSyntheticUserId`), reads return empty results and writes are rejected with 503 rather than crashing. Creation also enforces slug uniqueness with a 409 conflict response, assigns `ownerId` from the authenticated user, and normalizes output through the `serializeGurukul` helper (e.g., ISO date formatting). One structural gotcha: the public `GET /:slug` route is registered before `/mine/list`, but Fastify's static-route precedence ensures `/mine/list` still resolves correctly.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\leads-self-onboa.summary: This Fastify route file implements public, unauthenticated self-onboarding for provider applicants (temples, priests, astrologers, wellness instructors, gaushalas) who arrive via marketing pages like /list-temple or /become-priest. Its single export, `leadsSelfOnboardRoutes`, registers `POST /self-onboard`, which validates the body with a zod discriminated union keyed on `role` (five per-role schemas extending shared base fields), upserts a `Lead` row in Prisma keyed on the `@@unique([role, email])` compound with status `NEW` and a source tag like `self_onboard_temple`, then returns the `leadId`. Role-specific extras beyond the base contact fields are collected dynamically into a `metadata` JSON column and mirrored as a stringified `notes` field, so the schema never has to change when new per-role fields are added. It depends on the internal `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `sendEmail` helper from `../lib/email.js`, plus zod for validation. On success it sends a branded welcome email to the applicant and a notification to every address in the comma-separated `ADMIN_EMAILS` env var, using HTML templates built by local `welcomeEmailHtml` and `adminNotifyHtml` helpers. Notable design choices: the upsert means resubmissions refresh rather than duplicate a lead, all email sending is best-effort (failures are logged as warnings, not fatal, and gated by env configuration), and validation failures return a flattened zod `issues` payload with a 400 while database errors return a generic 500. The HTML email bodies interpolate user-supplied names without escaping, which is a potential injection gotcha worth noting.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\knowledge.ts.summary: This file serves the API's knowledge-base endpoints by reading MDX articles directly from the filesystem rather than a database. Its sole export, `knowledgeRoutes`, is a Fastify plugin that registers two GET routes on a `FastifyInstance`: `/:category` returns a lightweight list of article summaries, and `/:category/:slug` returns the full frontmatter and body for one article. Categories are restricted by the `Category` type and the `isCategory` guard to `sanskrit`, `ved`, and `sanatan`. Content lives under `CONTENT_ROOT`, resolved from the `KNOWLEDGE_CONTENT_DIR` environment variable or a default of `../web/content`, and is parsed with a hand-rolled `parseFrontmatter` function (plus the `stripQ` helper) that supports only flat key-value pairs and simple dash-list arrays instead of a full YAML parser. The only dependencies are `fastify`, `node:fs`, and `node:path`. Notable gotchas: `CONTENT_AVAILABLE` is computed once at module load, so content deployed after startup will never be detected; every request performs synchronous `fs` reads, and the list endpoint re-reads and re-parses every file in the category with no caching; and the `slug` parameter is interpolated directly into a file path with no sanitization, leaving a potential path-traversal exposure.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\lessons.ts.summary: This file defines the lessons API routes for the Fastify server, handling lesson progress tracking, streaks, and badge awards. It exports `lessonsRoutes`, which registers an authenticated `GET /` endpoint returning a user's lesson progress, streak, and badges, and a `POST /complete` endpoint that records a lesson completion (validated with the zod `completeSchema`), updates the daily streak in `UserStreak`, and awards badges based on the declarative `BADGE_RULES` table (e.g., `first-lesson`, `streak-7`, `perfect-score`). It depends on the shared Prisma client from `../lib/prisma.js` (models `UserLessonProgress`, `UserStreak`, `UserBadge`), the `authenticateUser` middleware applied via a `preHandler` hook, and zod for input validation. A key design decision is graceful degradation: synthetic users (IDs prefixed `demo-` or `anon-`) and deployments without `DATABASE_URL` receive empty or stubbed success responses instead of hitting the database. Streak logic compares UTC-normalized dates via `todayUTC` and `daysBetween`, incrementing on consecutive days and resetting after gaps. Badge creation uses `createMany` with `skipDuplicates` wrapped in a swallowed catch, so duplicate-award races never fail the request. A `__testing` export exposes `BADGE_RULES`, `daysBetween`, and `todayUTC` for unit tests.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\lessons.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite unit-tests the pure helper logic of the `lessons` route module (`apps/api/src/routes/lessons.ts`), which it reaches through a dedicated `__testing` export that surfaces internals—`BADGE_RULES`, `daysBetween`, and `todayUTC`—without exercising the HTTP handlers themselves. The date tests pin down UTC-midnight semantics: `daysBetween` must return 0 for the same day, 1 for consecutive days, and correctly handle month boundaries, while `todayUTC` must always yield a time of 00:00:00 UTC, reflecting the codebase's choice to normalize all streak/date math to UTC days to dodge timezone bugs. The badge tests treat `BADGE_RULES` as a data-driven table of `{ key, predicate }` entries whose predicates consume a context of `{ lessonCount, score, streakDays }`, verifying thresholds for `first-lesson` (lessonCount ≥ 1), `perfect-score` (score exactly 100), and `streak-7` (exactly 7 days). A final test guards the rule table's integrity by asserting all keys are unique and that the lesson-count tier badges `lessons-10`, `lessons-25`, and `lessons-50` exist. The only dependency is `vitest`; there are no mocks, database, or network calls, so the suite runs as fast, isolated unit tests. A notable design signal is the `__testing` export pattern itself—it implies the lessons module deliberately exposes its badge and date internals for testability rather than testing them through route requests.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\magic-link.test..summary: This Vitest suite exercises the passwordless magic-link auth flow exposed by `magicLinkRoutes` (mounted at `/api/v1/auth/magic-link` on a throwaway Fastify instance with `@fastify/rate-limit`), covering both the `/request` and `/verify` endpoints. It stubs `../lib/prisma.js` so `prisma.user.findFirst` returns null (forcing the create-user path, with `prisma.user.create` and `prisma.userRoleAssignment.create` mocked) and stubs `../lib/email.js` so `sendEmail` reports "skipped," which makes `/request` return a `devLink` instead of sending real mail. The `/request` tests assert that invalid emails get a 400, dev mode yields a `devLink` containing `/auth/verify?token=`, and the sensitive-auth rate limit kicks in with a 429 after 10 requests per minute (ticket P1-1).
