The `/verify` tests assert that a tampered token is rejected with 400 "Invalid or expired," that a freshly minted token round-trips into a session whose `accessToken` matches the `email-<uuid>-<32 hex>` pattern, and—critically—a regression test (P0-3) proving dotted emails like `first.last@example.com` verify correctly, since the old `split('.')` token parsing mistook the dot for a delimiter and instantly expired such links. A key gotcha documented inline: `JWT_SECRET` is captured at module import time, so tests must delete it from `process.env` (rather than set a test value) to make signing and verification both fall back to the `darshya-dev-secret` default.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\marketplace-v2.t.summary: This file implements "Layer AW," a public read-only marketplace API (`/api/v2/marketplace`) that lets third-party devotional apps query temples, puja types, live darshan streams, and yatra destinations, plus an admin surface (`/api/v1/admin/marketplace`) for issuing, listing, and revoking API keys. It exports two Fastify plugin functions: `marketplaceV2Routes`, which guards every endpoint with a `requireApiKey` preHandler that validates the `X-Darshya-API-Key` header (`msk_`-prefixed, stored as a SHA-256 hash), and `marketplaceAdminRoutes`, which guards key management with `authenticateUser` plus `requireRole('admin')` after a comment flags that the parent router previously failed to wrap these routes. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the auth middlewares in `../middlewares/auth.js`, using `node:crypto` for key generation/hashing and `zod` to validate the key-issuance payload. Notably, the `marketplace_api_keys` table is created lazily at startup via raw SQL in `ensureTables()` rather than a Prisma migration, rate limiting is a best-effort in-memory `Map` with a comment recommending Redis for production scale, and the `last_used_at`/`requests_today` bookkeeping update is fire-and-forget. The plaintext key is returned exactly once at issuance (only its hash and 12-char prefix persist), and revocation is a soft delete setting `is_active = false`. Gotchas: the `scopes` column is stored and defaulted but never actually enforced per-endpoint, the yatra destinations list is hardcoded slugs, and list endpoints silently cap results at 100 (50 for live streams).

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\notifications.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`notificationRoutes`) implements Darshya's push-notification endpoints, covering both browser web-push (VAPID) subscriptions and Firebase Cloud Messaging device tokens. It exposes GET `/vapid-public-key`, authenticated POST `/subscribe`, `/unsubscribe`, and `/test` for web push, plus `/register-token`, `/unregister-token`, and `/test-fcm` for FCM, and also exports the `notifyUser` helper so other routes (like booking confirmation) can push to a devotee by userId. It builds on `authenticateUser` from `../middlewares/auth.js`, the `sendPush`/`webPushConfig`/`PushSubscriptionPayload` pieces from `../lib/web-push.js`, `sendFcm`/`fcmConfig` from `../lib/fcm.js`, and the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (using the `pushSubscription` and `fcmDeviceToken` models). A key design quirk is dual storage: subscriptions live in an in-memory `subsByUser` Map but are also best-effort-persisted to Prisma via idempotent upserts keyed on `endpoint`/`deviceToken`, with the in-memory map as fallback so pre-migration environments don't break — though the header comment warns this won't scale past a single Render instance. The FCM model is accessed via duck-typed `as unknown as` casts so the routes gracefully no-op when the migration hasn't been applied, and `/test-fcm` includes an admin-role guard restricting non-admins to pushing only to themselves. Expired endpoints/tokens reported by `sendPush`/`sendFcm` are pruned from both the database and memory after every send, keeping the subscription set self-cleaning.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\magic-link.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements passwordless email magic-link authentication for the API, exporting `magicLinkRoutes(server)`, which registers POST `/request` and POST `/verify` handlers. The `/request` endpoint validates an email, mints a stateless token (an HMAC-SHA256 signature over email + nonce + 15-minute expiry, built with `node:crypto` in the internal `signToken` helper), and sends it as a link via `sendEmail` and the `magicLinkEmail` template from `../lib/email.js`; `/verify` re-validates the signature and expiry in `verifyToken`, then finds or creates a `User` row via `prisma` (`../lib/prisma.js`), assigning a default `DEVOTEE` role through `UserRoleAssignment` on first sign-in. New users get a placeholder phone (`email-${Date.now()}`) and a session token in the `email-${user.id}-${random}` format, deliberately piggybacking on the existing `demo-`-prefix pattern so `middlewares/auth.ts` accepts it without changes. Notable hardening: the process refuses to boot in production if `JWT_SECRET` is unset (otherwise falling back to the public `'darshya-dev-secret'`), both endpoints carry a 10-requests-per-minute per-IP rate limit, and signature comparison uses `timingSafeEqual` with a length guard to avoid a timing oracle. A key gotcha documented inline is that the token payload must be parsed by splitting from the right, because emails containing dots broke the naive three-segment split and locked those users out in production. The token is stateless with no `usedTokens` table, so single-use enforcement is only via the 15-minute TTL — an acknowledged MVP tradeoff — and when `RESEND_API_KEY` is absent the `/request` response returns a `devLink` so local environments can still exercise the flow.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\media.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite exercises the Fastify `mediaRoutes` plugin — specifically the POST `/api/v1/media/upload-url` presign endpoint — as a regression guard for ticket P1-5 (content-type allowlist and kind sanitization). It stubs `../lib/r2.js` (`r2`, `publicUrlFor`, `presignR2Upload`) so tests run without R2/Supabase credentials while still letting them assert the exact key and contentType passed to `presignR2Upload`, and it stubs the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js` to reject missing Authorization headers with 401 or stamp a fake `currentUser`. Helpers `buildApp()` and `inject()` spin up an in-memory Fastify instance with the routes mounted under `/api/v1/media` and issue requests via `app.inject`, so no real HTTP server or database is involved. The tests verify that `application/octet-stream` and non-enum kinds like `../evil` are rejected with 400 before any presign call, that a valid `profile-photo` image upload produces a key prefixed with the sanitized kind, containing no `..`, and reporting `maxSizeMb` 10, and that `puja-proof` accepts `video/mp4` with a 200MB cap. One notable case confirms that a malicious `ext` like `jsp/../../etc` is reduced to an alphanumeric-only extension and that the final key has exactly the kind/user/file path shape. Because both the storage and auth boundaries are mocked, the suite isolates purely the route's validation and key-derivation logic.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\orgs.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite validates the HMAC-signed invite-token scheme used by the `/orgs` routes in `orgs.ts`, where the helpers are deliberately inlined to keep the route self-contained; because they aren't exported, the test re-implements the same `signToken`/`verifyToken` pair (plus `b64url`/`b64urlDecode` base64url codecs) and asserts the behavior is symmetric. Tokens are `body.signature` strings: a base64url JSON payload signed with `crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret)`, verified using `crypto.timingSafeEqual` and an `exp` seconds-since-epoch expiry check. The cases cover a successful round-trip of an org-invite payload (`orgId`, `email`, `role`, `kind`, `exp`), rejection of a tampered body, a wrong secret, an expired token, and malformed single-part input. The only dependencies are `vitest` and Node's built-in `crypto`. The main gotcha is the duplicated implementation: the test mirrors logic living inside `orgs.ts`, so changes to the route's helpers must be manually kept in sync here or the tests will drift from production behavior.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\media.ts.summary: This file defines `mediaRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that exposes `POST /upload-url` (mounted under `/api/v1/media`) so clients can obtain a presigned PUT URL and upload media directly to Cloudflare R2, keeping large file bodies off the API server (hosted on Render). The handler is gated by the `authenticateUser` middleware and delegates storage operations to `../lib/r2.js` via `presignR2Upload`, `publicUrlFor`, and the `r2` client object, using `randomBytes` from `node:crypto` to build unique object keys of the form `kind/userId/timestamp-hexid.ext`. A notable gotcha is that the r2 module is actually abstracted over multiple backends — the 503 error returned when `r2.enabled` is false references Supabase storage credentials, and the response includes a `backend` field telling the caller which storage was used. The file was hardened (ticket P1-5) against an earlier version that accepted arbitrary content types and used `kind` unsanitized in the key path, allowing path traversal like `../x` outside the intended prefix. It now enforces a fixed `ALLOWED_KINDS` enum (puja-proof, profile-photo, temple-image, audio) and a `TYPE_POLICY` allowlist mapping ten content types (JPEG/PNG/WebP/GIF images, MP3/WAV/WebM audio, MP4/WebM video, PDF) to canonical extensions and per-type size caps (10–200 MB). Both the kind segment and the authenticated user's ID are stripped of non-alphanumeric characters before being embedded in the R2 key, and any client-supplied extension override is likewise sanitized to a short alphanumeric token. Presigned URLs expire after 600 seconds, and the response echoes the required `Content-Type` header and `maxSizeMb` limit so the browser can enforce them during the direct PUT.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\onboarding.ts.summary: This Fastify route module registers the provider-onboarding HTTP API for the six service-provider roles (PANDIT, STORE_OWNER, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, GAUSHALA_MANAGER, TEMPLE_MANAGER), exporting `onboardingRoutes(server)` which mounts authenticated endpoints under `/onboarding`. It offers two flows: a multi-step wizard (`POST /start`, `GET /progress`, `PATCH /step/:step`, `POST /submit`) and a one-shot `POST /provider` endpoint (plus `GET /provider` for the edit form) that atomically upserts the role assignment and role-specific profile via `onboardingService.upsertProviderProfile`, used by `/auth/signup` and the consolidated `/onboarding/[role]` form's "Submit for Approval" button. The module depends on `fastify`, `zod`, the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and `onboardingService` from `../services/onboarding.service.js`. A key design decision is replacing loose `z.record(z.unknown())` payloads with strict per-role schemas (`panditDataSchema`, `storeOwnerDataSchema`, etc.) combined into the `providerSchema` discriminated union, so missing required fields surface as 400s rather than silent defaults like "Unnamed" or dropped wellness certifications; validation includes a GSTIN regex, price floors (e.g. `pricePerPuja` ≥ ₹100), and coerced integers. Notable gotchas: profiles are always created with `approved=false` and surface in `/admin/approvals` until an admin flips them; `POST /provider` is idempotent (re-posting overwrites the in-progress profile); and a demo-session guard checks both the `userId` and the bearer access token for a `demo-` prefix, returning 202 without persisting so smoke-test signups can't contaminate the approvals queue. `GET /provider` deliberately swallows service errors and returns `{ profile: null }`, so callers can't distinguish "no profile" from a backend failure.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\outreach-trackin.summary: This file implements public email engagement tracking for the outreach system, exposing two Fastify endpoints via the exported `outreachTrackingRoutes` plugin: `GET /click` records a click on an `OutreachLog` (setting `clickedAt` and incrementing `clickCount`) before issuing a 302 redirect to a base64url-decoded destination, and `GET /pixel.gif` records an open (`openedAt`, `openCount`) while always serving a 1×1 transparent GIF. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, uses `zod` for query validation, and touches the `OutreachLog` and `Lead` Prisma models. A click is treated as the strongest engagement signal, so the handler promotes the associated `Lead` from `EMAILED` to `REPLIED` using a conditional `updateMany` that deliberately avoids downgrading converted, unsubscribed, or bounced leads. Open-redirect abuse is prevented by validating decoded URLs against the `ALLOWED_REDIRECT_HOSTS` allowlist (the darshya.online domains), which can be extended at runtime through the `OUTREACH_TRACKING_ALLOWED_HOSTS` environment variable, and only http/https protocols are accepted. Both endpoints are intentionally unauthenticated—the tracking ID is a hard-to-enumerate UUID and the worst-case mutation is a counter increment—while all database work is best-effort: failures are logged but never block the redirect, and the pixel route always returns 200 with `image/gif` plus no-cache headers so mail clients don't retry or show broken images. Invalid input yields a 400 on `/click` but is silently ignored on the pixel endpoint.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\orgs.ts.summary: This file implements "Layer AM" multi-tenant organization routes for the Darshya API, letting Temple Trusts and other operators manage B2B orgs with an OWNER > ADMIN > MEMBER role hierarchy. It exports two things: `orgsRoutes`, a Fastify plugin registering endpoints for org creation (`POST /orgs`), listing memberships (`GET /orgs/my`), issuing email invites (`POST /orgs/:id/invite`), listing/removing members and changing roles, accepting invites (`POST /orgs/accept-invite`), and checking plan quotas (`GET /orgs/:id/plan-status`); and `requireOrgRole`, a reusable preHandler factory that enforces a minimum role by looking up the caller in `org_members`. It builds on `authenticateUser` from `../middlewares/auth.js`, the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, and `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`, with zod for request validation and node:crypto for signing. Notably, it avoids the `jsonwebtoken` dependency with a self-contained HMAC-SHA256 signed-token helper (`signToken`/`verifyToken` using base64url payloads, timing-safe comparison, and 7-day expiry keyed off `ORG_INVITE_SECRET`), and it uses raw SQL via `$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe` against the `orgs`, `org_members`, `org_invites`, `temples`, and `users` tables so the route works without a `prisma generate` cycle, matching the pattern in donations.ts and provider-kyc.ts. Gotchas include the dev fallback invite secret, single-owner invariants (transferring OWNER demotes the prior owner to ADMIN and owners cannot be removed), the rule that only OWNERs may remove ADMINs, invite tokens bound to a specific lowercase email to prevent ticket sharing, and `PLAN_LIMITS` capping temples per org at 1 (free), 5 (pro), or unlimited (enterprise).

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\panchang.ts.summary: This file defines the HTTP route layer for panchang (Hindu calendar) data in the API, exporting a single `panchangRoutes` function that registers five GET endpoints on a Fastify `FastifyInstance`. All handlers delegate to `panchangService` (from `../services/panchang.service.js`), which is the module's only internal dependency; there are no external library calls beyond Fastify itself. The endpoints cover today's panchang (`/today`, with optional `city` query), upcoming festivals (`/festivals`) and fasting days (`/vrats`), auspicious timings (`/muhurat`, which returns a trimmed projection of the full record including `shubhMuhurat`, `rahuKaal`, `tithi`, `nakshatra`, and `yoga`), and a parameterized lookup (`/:date`). A key design detail is route ordering: static paths like `/festivals` must be registered before the dynamic `/:date` parameter route so Fastify doesn't swallow them as date strings, and the code comment flags this explicitly. The `days` query parameter for festivals and vrats is normalized with `Number(days) || 30` and hard-capped at 365 to prevent unbounded queries. Date validation on `/:date` is done leniently via `new Date()` parsing, returning 400 on invalid input, while missing data returns 404 with a hint that panchang records may not have been seeded yet — implying the data comes from a pre-seeded store rather than computed on demand. Every handler wraps service calls in try/catch, logging via `server.log.error` and returning a generic 500 on failure.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\payout-requests..summary: This Fastify route module implements the provider self-serve payout API for Phase 2, exposing three authenticated endpoints under `/api/v1/payouts`: `GET /balance` for withdrawable balance plus KYC status, `POST /request` to request payout of the full available balance, and `GET /my` for the caller's payout history. Its single export, `payoutRequestRoutes`, registers these handlers on a `FastifyInstance`, relying on the `authenticateUser` middleware and delegating all business logic to `payout.service.js` functions `getPayoutBalance`, `getKycStatus`, `requestPayout`, and `listMyPayouts`. Access is gated by an internal `resolveProviderRole` helper that maps JWT roles through `PROVIDER_ROLE_MAP` (notably aliasing `PRIEST` to `PANDIT`) and rejects non-providers with a 403, while KYC and bank-on-file enforcement happens inside the service layer rather than the route. A zod `requestSchema` validates the payout method, but validation failures silently fall back to `'upi'` instead of returning a 400, so malformed bodies are never rejected. The request endpoint always pays out the entire available balance (no partial amounts), service-layer errors from `requestPayout` are collapsed into generic 400 responses, and monetary `amount` values are serialized with `.toString()` to safely transport Decimal values over JSON.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\outreach-webhook.summary: This Fastify route module implements Darshya's inbound email automation for provider-lead outreach: it receives Resend inbound-parse webhooks (at `/reply-webhook` and `/inbound`), classifies each reply into one of five intents (INTERESTED, NEEDS_INFO, UNSUBSCRIBE, SPAM, OUT_OF_OFFICE), mutates `Lead.status` accordingly, and fires AI-generated autoresponses, admin email notifications, and `sendOpsAlert` Slack alerts for hot leads. Its single export, `outreachWebhookRoutes` (plus a truncated `outreachAdminRoutes` for an admin-only manual cron tick via `runOutreachTick`), also serves RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe (GET and POST) and a bounce webhook that marks leads BOUNCED. Classification is delegated to `classifyIntent`, which calls `generateText` from `../integrations/claude.js` and falls back to Hindi-aware regex heuristics (`POSITIVE_INTENT`, `NEGATIVE_INTENT`, `OOO_INTENT`) on any LLM failure, with the result stored in `OutreachLog.payload` JSON via `recordOutreach` from `../services/outreach.service.js` to avoid a schema migration. It builds on `prisma`, `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`, `sendOpsAlert` from `../lib/alert.js`, and the `authenticateUser`/`requireRole` middlewares, and reads an unsubscribe HTML template from `templates/outreach` (cached in memory after first read). A key design constraint is that inbound handlers always ACK 200 — every external call is wrapped in try/catch and errors are logged as FAILED outreach rows — because Resend retries on 5xx and retry loops would duplicate autoresponses. Security is fail-closed: both inbound and bounce endpoints verify Svix HMAC-SHA256 signatures over the raw body using `RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, returning 503 when the secret is unset rather than allowing anonymous Lead mutation. The AI reply generators (`aiAutoReply`, `aiNeedsInfoReply`) are prompt-constrained to fixed factual answers about pricing, video proof, and payouts, with hardcoded fallback bodies if the LLM call fails.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\payouts.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite unit-tests `panditPayoutsListSchema`, the Zod query-parameter validator for the pandit payouts listing endpoint, which it imports through the `__testing` re-export of the sibling `payouts.js` route module in `apps/api/src/routes`. The tests pin down the schema's contract: an empty query succeeds with defaults of `limit=50` and `offset=0`, string values from URL query params are coerced to numbers, and the optional `status` filter accepts exactly the four `PayoutStatus` values (`pending`, `processing`, `completed`, `failed`) while rejecting unknown or uppercase variants like `cancelled` and `PENDING`. Boundary behavior is also locked in — `limit` must be an integer between 1 and 200 (201, 0, negatives, and fractions fail) and `offset` must be non-negative. Its only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and the `__testing` surface of `./payouts.js`, meaning the tests exercise the validation layer in isolation without touching any HTTP server or database. A notable pattern is the use of a dedicated `__testing` export to expose the internal schema without widening the route module's public API.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\payouts.ts.summary: This Fastify route module defines the priest-facing payout read surface and mounts the shared payout self-serve endpoints under /api/v1/payouts. Its main export, payoutsRoutes, registers GET /pandit/mine — a paginated, read-only list of PriestPayout rows owned by the caller, guarded by authenticateUser and requireRole('priest') from middlewares/auth.js — and then delegates to payoutRequestRoutes from routes/payout-requests.js, which adds the cross-role GET /balance, POST /request, and GET /my endpoints. Query parameters are validated by the zod panditPayoutsListSchema (also re-exported via __testing for tests), which supports an optional status filter limited to pending/processing/completed/failed plus limit/offset pagination capped at 200 rows. Data access goes through the shared prisma client from lib/prisma.js, resolving the caller's Priest record via Priest.userId === currentUser.id — the same getPriestId pattern used in routes/priest.ts — and querying priestPayout with a count in parallel via Promise.all. Notably, a missing Priest record yields an empty list rather than a 404, deliberately mirroring the graceful degradation of the consultation /astrologer/mine endpoint, and the Prisma Decimal amount is coerced to a plain Number before serialization. The header comment documents known schema gaps in PriestPayout: there is no commission, batchId, or distinct paymentMethod column, so the response fields map 1:1 to the existing Prisma model rather than a richer payout dashboard shape.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\payments.ts.summary: This Fastify route module wires up all payment HTTP endpoints for the API by registering `paymentRoutes(server)`, which covers Razorpay order creation and signature verification for both puja bookings (`/create-order`, `/verify`) and store-order checkouts (`/store-orders/:id/razorpay`, `/store-orders/:id/verify`), plus unauthenticated provider webhooks (`/webhook` for Razorpay, `/webhook/stripe`), payment lookup (`GET /:id`), and an admin-only refund endpoint gated by `requireRole('admin')`. Everything delegates to `paymentService` from `../services/payment.service.js`, with request validation via zod schemas (`createOrderSchema`, `verifyPaymentSchema`, `paramsWithId`) and authentication via `authenticateUser` from `../middlewares/auth.js`; `verifyStoreOrderSchema` is deliberately kept as a separate symbol aliasing `verifyPaymentSchema` so future divergence stays local. Both webhooks require `fastify-raw-body` (`config: { rawBody: true }`) and perform deduplication through `checkAndRecord` from `../lib/webhook-idempotency.js`, keyed on `x-razorpay-event-id` (or a SHA-256 of the raw body as fallback) and Stripe's native event id, with idempotency-lookup failures intentionally falling through rather than dropping events. A notable gotcha: the Razorpay webhook has two signature-verification modes toggled by `RAZORPAY_VERIFY_RAW` — raw-body HMAC (the correct path, default on per the code, though a stale comment block above says the opposite) versus a legacy `JSON.stringify` comparison — while Stripe always verifies byte-exact HMAC. Both webhook handlers return 200 even on internal processing errors to avoid provider retry storms, reserving 400 for signature failures. Error handling throughout relies on string-matching `error.message` ("not found", "not authorized", "PENDING", "invalid signature") to pick status codes, which is brittle. Finally, the store-order verify route parses `:id` only for routing — ownership is enforced inside the service against the resolved StoreOrder so a forged id cannot confirm another user's order.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\priests-public.t.summary: This file implements the public, unauthenticated priest directory endpoints for the Fastify API, serving as a read-only mirror of the pandit-side CRUD in `routes/priest.ts`, scoped strictly to priests with `isVerified = true` and `status = 'active'` and offerings with `isActive = true`. Its sole export, `priestsPublicRoutes(server)`, registers three GET routes: `/` lists verified priests ordered by `ratingAvg` with per-priest active-offering counts, `/:id` returns a single priest profile plus offerings (404 if not verified/active), and `/:id/pujas` returns just the offerings. The `publicPriestsQuerySchema` (also exposed via a `__testing` handle) is a zod schema that trims and lowercases the optional `specialization` filter at parse time for deterministic exact matching, treats empty strings as absent, and applies `deity` filtering server-side via a case-insensitive `offerings.some` clause so clients avoid post-filtering. It depends on the shared Prisma client from `lib/prisma.js` (models `priest` and `priestPujaOffering`) and zod. Notable decisions include a 5-minute `Cache-Control` header (`s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60`) aligned with the web client's `getPublicPriests` `next.revalidate=300` to absorb directory traffic at the CDN edge, a batched `groupBy` count query to avoid an N+1 on the list endpoint, and `basePrice.toString()` serialization to preserve Decimal precision over JSON, matching the admin commissions pattern.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\priest-pujas.tes.summary: This Vitest suite tests the Zod validation schemas exported via `__testing` from `routes/priest.ts` — specifically `priestOfferingCreateSchema` and `priestOfferingUpdateSchema` — which back the `POST /priest/pujas` and `PATCH /priest/pujas/:id` endpoints. A lengthy header comment documents a deliberate coverage boundary: the repo has no Fastify+Prisma integration scaffolding, so these are pure schema tests only, and wiring a live `DATABASE_URL`, Prisma mock, or Supabase admin stub for auth middleware is explicitly out of scope. The create-schema tests pin the 400-boundary contract: name must be 2–200 chars, deity is required and non-empty, basePrice must be non-negative (0 is allowed for free seva), durationMinutes must be an integer between 5 and 600, and description caps at 5000 chars. The update-schema tests verify that PATCH payloads are fully optional — an empty object must not 400 — while still rejecting invalid field values like negative prices, out-of-range durations, over-long names, or string-typed numbers. A third block covers the E7 slot-capacity follow-up on `PriestPujaOffering`: `maxBookingsPerSlot` must be an integer from 1 to 1000, and `availableSlots` accepts either HH:MM strings or `{time, label}` objects, allows an empty array to disable slot enforcement, and caps at 200 entries to keep the JSON small. Notably untested here are the ownership 403 branch, the public read filter (`isVerified` + active offerings), and DELETE cascade behavior — the comments state these are guaranteed by the Prisma schema's FK `ON DELETE CASCADE` and an explicit equality check in `routes/priest.ts`, and are left for manual smoke-testing against a live API.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\priests-public.t.summary: This Vitest test file pins the server-side filter contract (tracked as R-Q1-E-013) for the public `GET /priests` endpoint by exercising `publicPriestsQuerySchema`, which it imports from the sibling route module `./priests-public.js` via that module's `__testing` export surface. The suite validates the schema's normalization and rejection rules: an empty query yields both filters undefined, `specialization` is lowercased and trimmed, `deity` is trimmed only (case-insensitive matching happens in the route itself), and the two filters can combine as an AND pair. It also confirms that whitespace-only or empty-string inputs are coerced to `undefined` (treated as no filter), that inputs over 64 characters are rejected before reaching Prisma (a "column budget" guard), and that unrelated query params like `page` and `limit` are silently dropped rather than passed through. Its only direct dependencies are `vitest` and the `priests-public` route module, though the schema under test is plainly Zod-based (using `safeParse`) and feeds downstream Prisma queries. A notable scoping decision: route-level integration concerns — Prisma `has:`/`some:` filter clauses, the `Cache-Control` header, and HTTP 400 responses on schema rejection — are deliberately excluded here and deferred to a separate FastifyInstance harness in the broader API suite, so this file exists purely to lock the parsing contract the route handler depends on.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\provider-kyc.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements stage-2 provider KYC — collecting bank account, IFSC, PAN, and Aadhaar details — via an exported `providerKycRoutes(server)` function that registers `GET /` and `POST /` handlers (mounted under `/providers/kyc`). The GET handler returns the signed-in user's KYC record with PAN and bank account numbers masked by the `maskTail` helper, while the POST handler validates input with a zod `submitSchema` (enforcing Aadhaar, PAN, and IFSC formats) and upserts into the `provider_kyc` table. Both handlers are gated by `authenticateUser` and `requireAnyRole(...PROVIDER_ROLES)` from the auth middleware, where `PROVIDER_ROLES` deliberately excludes `DEVOTEE` (devotees never receive payouts) but includes `ADMIN` for support debugging. Dependencies are the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, `node:crypto` for hashing, `zod`, and Fastify itself. A key privacy decision: the full Aadhaar number is never persisted — only its last four digits plus a SHA-256 hash (`aadhaar_hash`) so future verification challenges can be answered without a plaintext breach surface. Notably, all persistence uses raw SQL via `$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe` because the Prisma client DLL is locked on Windows during development, so the table ships directly from a migration rather than the schema. Resubmission resets `verified=false` and clears `rejection_reason` so an admin must re-review changed details, with payout gating reading `verified` separately, and the upsert uses `COALESCE` so omitted fields preserve previously stored values. Finally, demo sessions (user IDs or bearer tokens starting with `demo-`) short-circuit: GET returns `{ kyc: null, demoMode: true }` and POST returns a 202 without persisting anything.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\providers.ts.summary: This file defines the HTTP routes for the provider marketplace in the API, exposing endpoints to browse, view, update, and review six categories of providers — pandit, store, astrologer, wellness, gaushala, and temple — under the `/providers` path. Its sole export, `providerRoutes`, is a Fastify plugin that registers four handlers on the `FastifyInstance`: `GET /providers/:type` lists providers with filtering, sorting, and pagination validated by `providerQuerySchema`; `GET /providers/:type/:id` returns a single provider; `PATCH /providers/:type/:id` lets an owner update their own profile; and `POST /providers/:type/:id/review` submits a 1–5 star review validated by `reviewSchema`. All data access is delegated to `providerService` from `../services/provider.service.js`, while authentication and authorization come from the `authenticateUser` and `requireAnyRole` middlewares in `../middlewares/auth.js`, with `zod` used for input validation. A notable design detail is the dual naming scheme: `normaliseProviderType` accepts both canonical short keys and longer signup-role aliases (e.g. `store_owner` → `store`, `priest` → `pandit`) via `PROVIDER_TYPE_ALIASES`, returning a 400 listing `PROVIDER_TYPES` for anything unrecognized. The PATCH handler enforces ownership by checking that the caller holds the matching role from `PROVIDER_ROLE_MAP` (or `ADMIN`) in addition to the service-level ownership check. Gotchas include query parameters arriving as strings and being coerced with `Number()` without NaN guards, and the review endpoint deriving `providerType` by string-stripping suffixes like `_OWNER` and `_MANAGER` off role names, which is brittle if role naming ever changes.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\priest.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`priestRoutes` in apps/api/src/routes/priest.ts) implements the entire priest-facing API surface: dashboard, booking lifecycle (list, accept, reject, start, complete), dispatch-engine interactions, video proof upload, payouts, profile, reviews, and CRUD for pandit-owned `priestPujaOffering` records. Every route is gated by a shared `priestAuth` preHandler combining `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('priest')`, and a local `getPriestId` helper auto-backfills a `Priest` row from `PanditProfile` for pandits who skipped onboarding — notably creating it with `status: 'inactive'` and `verificationStatus: 'pending'` so backfilled accounts stay blocked until admin approval. Business logic delegates to `priestService` (dashboard, bookings, payouts, profile, video proof), `dispatchService` (offer accept/decline for the T1/T2/T3 tiers), and `cancellationService.panditCancel`, while reads like open `dispatchOffer` listing and `review` lookup hit `prisma` directly. The video-proof flow issues a 5-minute presigned PUT URL via `presignR2Upload` from lib/r2 (with Supabase fallback), enforcing an mp4/webm/quicktime allowlist, a 200 MB cap, assigned-priest-only access, and a `completed` booking status before the client uploads straight to R2. Zod schemas validate offering payloads and the bookings query, which clamps `limit` to 100 to prevent full-table scrapes; the offering schemas are hoisted and re-exported through `__testing` so tests can import them without booting a server. Design details worth knowing: `basePrice` (Decimal) is serialized as a string to preserve JSON precision, `Review.providerId` stores the user's UUID rather than `Priest.id` to match the ratings.ts convention, and `availableSlots` deliberately mirrors the `TemplePujaOffering` shape so the public slots endpoint can reuse its label renderer. The reject endpoint acts as an escape valve that clears `priestId` and returns the booking to `confirmed` so the assignment queue re-picks it.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\pujas.ts.summary: This file defines the public read-only HTTP API for the puja catalog, exporting `pujaRoutes`, a Fastify plugin that registers four GET endpoints on a `FastifyInstance` and delegates all data access to `pujaService` from `../services/puja.service.js`. The routes cover listing puja types with pagination and filters (category, deity, search), fetching popular pujas, fetching a single type by slug, and checking availability for a given templeId, pujaTypeId, and date. `GET /types` sets an explicit `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=300` header (ticket P2 #221) so the catalog list can be edge-cached instead of hitting the origin on every request. Route ordering matters: `/types/popular` is registered before `/types/:slug` so the literal path isn't swallowed by the slug parameter, and limits are clamped (100 for lists, 50 for popular) to bound query cost. `GET /types/:slug` deliberately returns the same object twice — spread at the root for the web app's detail/booking pages and again under the `pujaType` key for legacy callers — a dual-shape compatibility decision documented inline. The availability endpoint validates that all three query params are present, that the date parses, and that it isn't in the past, returning 400s for bad input. All handlers follow the same error pattern: log via `server.log.error` and return a generic 500, and notably none of these routes require authentication since they serve the public catalog.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\reading-progress.summary: This Vitest suite validates the reading-progress API route (`apps/api/src/routes/reading-progress.js`) without exercising its HTTP layer, instead importing internal helpers through the route's `__testing` export. It covers two helpers: `isSyntheticUserId`, which must flag `demo-*` and `anon-*` user IDs as synthetic while leaving real UUIDs untouched, and `dbDisabled`, which must report the database as unavailable exactly when `DATABASE_URL` is unset. The bulk of the suite pins down the Zod contracts imported from `@poojly/shared`: `readingProgressUpsertSchema` must accept minimal payloads, optional `lastVerse`, and compound Ramayana-style chapter slugs such as `bala/sarga-1`, while rejecting out-of-range `scrollPercent` values, non-integer `chapterNumber`, uppercase slugs, and path-traversal attempts like `../etc/passwd`; `readingProgressQuerySchema` must accept known book slugs and reject empty ones. Dependencies are limited to `vitest`, the sibling route module, and the shared schema package — no database or server is spun up. A notable gotcha is that the env-guard tests mutate `process.env.DATABASE_URL` directly and manually restore it afterward, so test isolation depends on that cleanup discipline. The slug rules documented here (lowercase-only, traversal-proof, but slash-tolerant for nested kanda/sarga paths) effectively specify the route's security and addressing constraints.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\search.ts.summary: This file implements the global search endpoint for the API, exposing a `searchRoutes` plugin that registers `GET /` on a Fastify instance to search across temples, pujas, and devotional content (aartis, chalisas, mantras) in one request. The single exported function, `searchRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)`, reads `q` and `limit` query params, rejects queries shorter than two characters with an empty result payload, and caps per-category results at 6 by default (hard max 20). It depends on the shared Prisma client from `../lib/prisma.js` and queries three models in parallel via `Promise.all`: `prisma.temple`, `prisma.pujaType`, and `prisma.contentItem`, using case-insensitive `contains` matching across name, local-language name, city/state, deity, and description fields, plus a lowercase tag-array `has` check for content. Only `active` temples and `published` content items are returned; puja types have no status filter. Each hit is reshaped into a uniform `{ id, slug, name, subtitle, href }` card with frontend-ready route paths like `/temples/{slug}`, grouped by entity type with a `total` count so the UI can render section headers. Notable tradeoffs: the search is simple substring matching rather than full-text or ranked relevance (so "ranked" ordering is just per-category Prisma defaults), and tag matching requires exact lowercase membership, unlike the fuzzy matching used elsewhere.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\reading-progress.summary: This file defines `readingProgressRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that exposes per-user reading-progress CRUD under `/api/v1/me/reading-progress` — listing all progress rows, fetching or deleting a single row by `bookSlug`, and upserting progress (chapterSlug, chapterNumber, scrollPercent, lastVerse) via a compound `userId_bookSlug` unique key in Prisma. Every route is gated by the `authenticateUser` preHandler hook, and payloads are validated with `readingProgressUpsertSchema` and `readingProgressQuerySchema` from the `@poojly/shared` package, returning flattened 400 errors on failure. Persistence goes through the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, with no other external services involved. The notable design constraint is graceful degradation: helper `isSyntheticUserId` detects demo/anonymous auth ids (`demo-*`, `anon-*`) that cannot key Postgres uuid primary keys, and `dbDisabled` checks for a missing `DATABASE_URL` — in either case the endpoints respond 200 with empty, null, or echoed-back `skipped: true` payloads rather than touching the database. The DELETE handler deliberately swallows Prisma errors (`.catch(() => null)`) so deleting a nonexistent row is idempotent. Progress responses serialize `updatedAt` to ISO strings and convert null `lastVerse` to undefined. A `__testing` export exposes the two gating helpers for unit tests, signaling they are intentional seams rather than incidental internals.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\referrals.test.t.summary: This file contains Tier-2 route tests (requirement R-Q2-M-011) for the referrals API, mounting `referralsRoutes` from `./referrals.js` onto a bare Fastify instance under `/api/v1/referrals` and exercising endpoints via `app.inject`. It covers six-plus paths: `GET /me` returning 401 unauthenticated and, for a demo user, a derived referral code with zeroed claim stats and a `rewardPerSide` of ₹100; `POST /claim` rejecting self-referrals with 400, unknown codes with 404, returning 201 with `signed_up` status on first claim, and idempotently returning 200 with `alreadyClaimed` for duplicate referrer–referee pairs; and `POST /reward` crediting the referrer's wallet 10,000 paise via `userCredit.upsert` and `creditLedgerEntry.create`, flipping the claim to `rewarded` with a `rewardLedgerId`. A notable guard test for R-Q1-P-006 verifies credit-applied-once-per-referee: a second `/reward` call for the same claim short-circuits on the `alreadyRewarded` branch, asserting `userCredit.upsert` and `referralClaim.update` are each called exactly once. The suite runs without a database by mocking `../lib/prisma.js` with `prismaMock` from `lib/__mocks__/prisma.js`, stubbing the `referralCode`, `referralClaim`, `userCredit`, and `creditLedgerEntry` models per test. Authentication relies on the demo-token bypass: with `NODE_ENV=test`, bearer tokens `demo-devotee` and `demo-pandit` resolve through a mocked `prisma.user.findUnique` to synthetic `devotee@demo.com` and `pandit@demo.com` user records defined as `DEMO_DEVOTEE` and `DEMO_PANDIT`. Dependencies are limited to vitest, Fastify, and the Prisma mock. The dominant design theme is idempotency — both claim creation and wallet crediting are structured so retries (double-clicks, webhook replays) never produce duplicate records or double credits.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\ratings.ts.summary: This file defines `ratingRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin implementing 1–5 star service ratings (with optional text up to 1000 characters) that devotees write for providers, each tied to a `ChatConversation` and surfaced in the Inbox after a "Call ended" system message or when a linked `PujaBooking` flips to `delivered`. It exports the single `ratingRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)` function, which applies the `authenticateUser` preHandler hook globally and registers three endpoints: `POST /` for idempotent writes (devotee-only, verified against the conversation's `devoteeId`, using an upsert keyed on `(conversation_id, devotee_id)` so re-posting revises the prior rating), `GET /:conversationId` readable by either conversation participant, and `GET /provider/:userId` listing a provider's 50 most recent ratings plus a computed average for profile pages, available to any logged-in user to support comparison shopping. Key dependencies are the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and zod, whose `writeSchema` validates incoming rating payloads. Notably, all rating persistence bypasses Prisma's generated models in favor of raw SQL (`$executeRawUnsafe`, `$queryRaw`, `$queryRawUnsafe`) against the `service_ratings` table, because the Prisma client may lag a schema revision in dev environments where `prisma generate` is blocked by a locked Windows DLL — so integrity rests on the migration's CHECK constraint plus the Zod schema rather than the ORM. A subtle gotcha: the provider average returned by `/provider/:userId` is computed in JavaScript over only the 50 fetched rows, not the provider's full rating history.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\store-admin.test.summary: This Vitest suite unit-tests the request-validation schemas exported from the sibling module `store-admin.js` (via its `__testing` namespace), guarding the store-admin product endpoints' input rules without spinning up a server. It exercises `productCreateSchema`, which requires `name` (min 2 chars) and `price` (non-negative, with 0 explicitly allowed for free samples) and constrains optional fields — `stock` must be a non-negative integer, `imageUrl` must parse as a URL, `description` caps at 5000 characters — plus `productUpdateSchema`, which permits empty or single-field patches (the `isActive` toggle pattern) while still rejecting invalid values like negative prices or string-typed numbers. Its only runtime dependencies are `vitest` and the Zod schemas under test; the header comment notes the suite deliberately mirrors `routes/priest-pujas.test.ts` as a pure-Zod gate. The notable gotcha is that Prisma/Fastify integration coverage is intentionally deferred until the project grows a real Fastify+Prisma test harness, so these tests validate payload shape only, not route behavior or persistence.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\semantic-search..summary: This Fastify route module powers semantic search across the platform's content_items, temples, and puja_types tables using pgvector cosine similarity, and is registered via the exported `semanticSearchRoutes(server)` function which serves `GET /` with `q`, `kind` (content|temple|puja|all), and `limit` query parameters. The internal `vectorSearch` helper runs a raw SQL query using the `<=>` cosine operator against each whitelisted table, with the `TABLE_COLS` map reconciling schema differences (content_items uses title/body, temples and puja_types use name/description) and injecting per-table publication status filters so drafts and pending_review temples never leak to public results. It depends on the internal `prisma` client and the `../lib/embeddings.js` module (`generateEmbedding`, `toPgVector`, and the `embeddings.enabled` flag, backed by the Cohere API via COHERE_API_KEY). The defining design decision is graceful degradation: when embeddings are disabled, the query embedding fails, a vector query throws, or vector search returns zero rows, the route silently falls back to `fallbackLike`, which does case-insensitive Prisma `contains` matching, and the response's `mode` field ('vector', 'like', or 'like-fallback') reveals which path served the request. SQL injection is mitigated by whitelisting table/column identifiers through `Prisma.raw` while binding the vector literal and limit as parameters via tagged `$queryRaw`, and `toPgVector` sanitizes embedding values with finite checks. Note the limit is clamped to 1–50, queries under two characters are rejected with a 400, and full functionality requires the pgvector extension, embedding columns, a backfill via scripts/backfill-embeddings.ts, and ivfflat indexes as described in the header comment.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\referrals.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements Darshya's referral system (added 2026-05-27), exporting `referralsRoutes(server)` which registers five endpoints: `GET /me` (lazily upserts and returns the caller's referral code plus claim stats), `GET /lookup/:code` (public, returns only the referrer's name and city for "Invited by X" landing cards), `POST /claim` (referee claims a code after signup, rejecting self-referrals and deduping per referrer/referee pair), `POST /reward` (credits the referrer's wallet when the referee completes a first paid booking), and `GET /mine` (lists the user's claims as both referrer and referee). Codes are derived deterministically by `deriveCodeFor`, an HMAC-SHA256 of the user UUID keyed by `REFERRAL_SECRET` and encoded into 7 chars of a Crockford-style alphabet excluding ambiguous characters. It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, the `authenticateUser` middleware, zod for body validation, and lazily dynamic-imports `WalletService` from `../services/wallet.service.js` inside the reward handler to credit via `creditUser` with idempotency key `referral-reward-${claimId}` before flipping the claim to `rewarded`. A central design decision is graceful degradation: `isTableMissing` detects Prisma errors P2010/P2021/P2022 (or matching messages) and every endpoint returns 503 with the stable `referral_tables_not_migrated` code so the web app can show a "coming soon" banner before the `referral_codes`/`referral_claims` migration lands — which also explains why all Prisma access goes through `as unknown as` casts rather than typed client methods. Gotchas: the secret falls back to a hardcoded `darshya-default-referral-pepper-change-me` if `REFERRAL_SECRET` is unset, and the `/reward` comment promises an admin path but the code only permits the referee (`refereeId !== caller.id` → 403), so the "system-internal" webhook trigger described in comments isn't actually implemented for admin callers. The default reward is 10000 paise (₹100), overridable via `REFERRAL_REWARD_PAISE`, and share URLs are built from `WEB_PUBLIC_URL` (defaulting to https://darshya.online).

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\store.ts.summary: This file defines `storeRoutes`, a Fastify plugin that registers all storefront HTTP endpoints for the API: the public product catalog, cart management, checkout, and store-owner reviews. Its public read routes split between two data sources — `GET /products`, `GET /products/:handle`, and `GET /collections` delegate to `storeService` (from `../services/store.service.js`), which serves a hardcoded seed catalog, while `GET /products/live` bypasses that service and queries the Prisma `storeProduct` table directly (via the shared client from `../lib/prisma.js`) to expose real store-owner inventory, with both list endpoints setting explicit `Cache-Control` headers for edge caching. Cart routes (`GET`/`POST /cart`, `POST /cart/items`, `PATCH`/`DELETE /cart/items/:id`) are guarded by the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js` and mutate per-user carts through `storeService.getCart`, `createCartItem`, `updateCartItem`, and `removeCartItem`, wrapping service errors into 400 responses. `GET /reviews` enforces a `STORE_OWNER` role check and queries `prisma.review` for rows matching either the legacy provider-level pattern (`providerId`/`providerType: 'STORE'`) or any of the owner's `storeProduct` ids, doing the product-id lookup as a separate query because Prisma cannot express the join-then-filter in one call. `POST /cart/checkout` is an explicit MVP stub: it validates the cart is non-empty and returns an unpersisted order summary with id `ORD-${Date.now()}` and status `pending_payment`, with no payment integration yet. Notable gotchas documented inline include the seed-vs-live catalog split (owner products never surface through the public `/products` route; full unification is a planned Phase 2), the use of product `id` as the PDP `handle` until a slug column exists, and a 200-item cap on the live catalog query.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\store-admin.ts.summary: This file defines `storeAdminRoutes`, a Fastify plugin registering store-owner self-service endpoints — CRUD for products (`GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /products`) plus analytics endpoints (`GET /dashboard`, `GET /reviews`, `GET /revenue`) — explicitly distinct from the public curated-catalog routes in `apps/api/src/routes/store.ts`. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (touching the `StoreProfile`, `StoreProduct`, `StoreOrder`, `Review`, and `User` models), the `authenticateUser` middleware from `../middlewares/auth.js`, and `zod` for input validation via `productCreateSchema`/`productUpdateSchema`, which are also exposed through a `__testing` export for unit tests. Every handler re-checks that `request.currentUser.roles` includes `STORE_OWNER` (returning 403 otherwise) and resolves the caller's store via `resolveStoreProfileId`, returning empty payloads or 400 when no profile exists; PATCH and DELETE additionally enforce per-product ownership by comparing `existing.storeProfileId`. A key design constraint is that `StoreOrder.items` is an untyped JSON array with no foreign key to stores, so revenue attribution is done in JavaScript by `attributeOrderToStore`, which matches order lines against the store's product IDs — a deliberate early-scale tradeoff flagged for future denormalization. The dashboard and revenue queries count only "PAID-ish" statuses (`CONFIRMED`, `PROCESSING`, `SHIPPED`, `DELIVERED`) and were fixed under P0 #S-15 to filter by `storeProfileId` after a cross-vendor data leak where one owner's dashboard aggregated all platform sales. Notable details: product `price` is a Prisma Decimal serialized via `toString()`, low stock is hardcoded as `stock <= 5`, recent orders and top products are capped at 10, reviews at 100, and reviewer usernames are batch-fetched to avoid an N+1 query.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\temples.ts.summary: This file defines the public REST endpoints for the temple catalog in the Fastify API, exporting a single `templeRoutes` plugin that registers seven read-only GET handlers on the server instance. All handlers delegate to `templeService` (from `../services/temple.service.js`), which owns the actual data access; this file only parses query strings, validates input, and shapes responses. The routes cover listing temples with filters (`city`, `state`, `deity`, `tradition`, `isVerified`, `liveDarshan`, plus pagination), full-text search via `/search`, geospatial lookup via `/nearby`, and per-temple detail, puja, darshan, and review endpoints keyed by slug. Notable constraints: page limits are capped at 100 (50 for reviews), and the nearby search requires valid `lat`/`lng` numbers and clamps `radius` to a `MAX_RADIUS_KM` of 200, reporting `radiusCapped` when clamping occurs. The list endpoint explicitly sets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=300` so Cloudflare edge-caches catalog reads instead of hitting the Render origin on every request. The darshan endpoint deliberately returns the `playbackUrl` from the `LiveDarshanStream` relation rather than the temple's internal `streamUrl`, which is treated as a private ingest field excluded from public selects. Errors are logged via `server.log.error` and surfaced as generic 500s, with 404s for missing slugs and 400s for malformed coordinates.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\subscriptions.ts.summary: This file defines the Fastify HTTP layer for subscription management in the API, exporting a single `subscriptionRoutes(server)` plugin that registers plan listing (`GET /plans`), subscription creation, cancellation, and status endpoints. It delegates all business logic to `subscriptionService` (from `../services/subscription.service.js`), guards user-facing routes with the `authenticateUser` middleware, and validates request bodies with zod schemas whose role enum spans marketplace roles like `PANDIT`, `ASTROLOGER`, and `STORE_OWNER` plus `DEVOTEE`, which exists specifically so the AI-astrologer paywall can target devotees without a marketplace role. The module exposes three distinct creation flows: the legacy `POST /subscribe`, `POST /create` for auto-renewing Razorpay subscriptions, and `POST /create-stripe-annual` for Stripe-based NRI annual billing, alongside `GET /is-premium` for premium gating and `POST /cancel-auto-renew` for stopping Razorpay renewals. The `POST /webhook` endpoint handles Razorpay subscription events, verifying an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the literal raw request bytes (requiring the `fastify-raw-body` plugin and the `rawBody: true` route config) with a timing-safe comparison, and it fails closed with a 500 if `RAZORPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset. Idempotency is handled via `checkAndRecord` from `../lib/webhook-idempotency.js`, keyed on the `x-razorpay-event-id` header with a SHA-256 hash of the raw body as fallback; notably, if the idempotency check itself errors, the code deliberately falls through and risks double-processing rather than dropping an event. Verified `subscription.*` events are forwarded to `subscriptionService.handleSubscriptionEvent`, with handler exceptions caught and reported as unhandled rather than retried. The webhook design intentionally mirrors the payments route in `apps/api/src/routes/payments.ts`, so the two should be kept in sync when signature or dedup logic changes.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\support.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`supportRoutes`) implements Darshya's customer-support backend: an AI chat endpoint plus full support-ticket CRUD. `POST /chat` validates input with a zod `chatSchema`, then answers via Claude (`generateText` from `integrations/claude.js`) using a detailed `SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT` that casts the assistant as "Asha" and demands strict JSON replies with `escalate` and `suggestedActions` fields; when `DEMO_MODE` is on or the AI call fails, it degrades to `findFallback`, a keyword matcher over the `FALLBACK_RESPONSES` knowledge base. Notably, deterministic rule checks run before any AI call — a regex auto-escalates refunds over ₹5,000 and pattern matching forces escalation whenever users ask for a human — so safety-critical routing never depends on model judgment. The ticket endpoints (`POST/GET /tickets`, `GET /tickets/:id`, message appending) are gated by `authenticateUser`, persist through `prisma.supportTicket` with human-readable IDs from `nextTicketNumber` (ST-YYYYMMDD-XXXX format), and enforce ownership via an `isAdmin` helper that also controls access to `?all=true` listings and hides `isInternal` notes from non-admins. Ticket creation triggers fire-and-forget notifications through `sendEmail` with templates `supportTicketAlertEmail` (to `SUPPORT_INBOX`) and `supportTicketReceivedEmail` (to the user), deliberately never blocking the HTTP response on email failures. The file also imports `summarizeSla`/`SlaTicketInput` from `lib/support-sla.js` for SLA reporting and depends only on `fastify`, `zod`, and `node:crypto` externally.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\temple-portal.ts.summary: This Fastify route module implements the temple-manager self-service portal API, registered via the exported `templePortalRoutes(server)` function, covering dashboard aggregates, schedule (`timingInfo`) read/patch by `?slug=`, donations, `TemplePayout` history, full CRUD for `TemplePujaOffering` and darshan livestreams, and a filterable `PujaBooking` roster. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `authenticateUser` middleware, uses zod schemas (exported for tests via `__testing`) for input validation, and reads Prisma models such as `templeProfile`, `temple`, `pujaBooking`, `donation`, and `templePayout`, plus raw `$queryRawUnsafe` SQL against `temples.org_id` and `org_members`. A central gotcha is that no Temple↔TempleManager foreign key exists, so `resolveManagerTempleId` matches `TempleProfile.templeName` to `Temple.name` as a fragile shim, and unmatched managers get empty results or 400s. Authorization is layered: most routes only require the `TEMPLE_MANAGER` role, but schedule read/write goes through `userCanEditTemple`, which demands OWNER/ADMIN membership in the linked org and — per security fix P0 #B1 — makes legacy unlinked temples admin-only so any manager can no longer overwrite them by guessing slugs. Other notable decisions include mapping donation statuses pending/received/failed to created/paid/failed to mirror the gaushala-portal response shape for UI reuse, per-record ownership checks on offering patch/delete, Prisma `P2002` handling that returns 409 for duplicate puja offerings, and darshan streams supporting `YOUTUBE`, `IVS`, and `EXTERNAL_RTMP` providers with a restricted status-patch enum.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\store-orders.ts.summary: This Fastify route module (`storeOrderRoutes`) implements the persisted store-order lifecycle for the API: checkout, listing, detail, status updates, and a manual payment-confirm override, all writing real `StoreOrder` rows via Prisma so orders can be shipped, refunded, and audited. It exposes POST `/orders` (create), GET `/orders` and `/orders/:id` (role-scoped reads), PATCH `/orders/:id/status`, and POST `/orders/:id/payment-confirm`, guarded by `authenticateUser` and helper checks `isAdmin`, `isStoreOwner`, `resolveStoreProfileId`, and `canManageOrder` (a store owner may manage any order containing at least one of their `StoreProduct`s, since attribution runs through `items[].productId → StoreProduct.storeProfileId`). Key safeguards: checkout accepts a per-user `idempotencyKey` so retried POSTs return the existing order (S-08), pricing is server-authoritative — client-sent prices and totals are ignored, catalog price and stock are enforced, and stock is decremented in the same `prisma.$transaction` as order creation (PBO) — and carts must be single-store or the request is rejected (S-11). Status changes are validated against an `ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS` map with terminal `DELIVERED`/`CANCELLED`/`REFUNDED` states (S-10), appended to the `statusHistory` JSON audit column; note the file-header comment claiming mutations are not gated on a state machine is stale relative to this enforcement. `serializeOrder` reshapes rows for the web orders page, adding `totalAmount`, `customerName`, and `items[].name` via a product-name map. Dependencies include `../lib/prisma.js`, `../middlewares/auth.js`, `generateInvoice` from `../lib/pdf-invoice.js`, `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`, and `writeStoreOrderCommission` from `../services/store-commission.service.js`, plus zod for input schemas and `node:crypto` for `nextOrderNumber`. Side effects are deliberately non-blocking: commission rows are written fire-and-forget when an order hits `CONFIRMED`, and the invoice PDF email is best-effort. Gotchas: `payment-confirm` is a demo/QA override hard-gated behind `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS=true` in production (the real path is Razorpay `/verify-payment`), and the store-owner list handler loads up to 200 recent orders then filters in memory, which will miss older sales.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\users.ts.summary: This file defines `userRoutes`, a Fastify plugin that exposes all self-service account endpoints under `/me` — profile read/update, avatar upload, saved-address CRUD, booking history, orders, and subscription status. It registers `authenticateUser` as a plugin-level `preHandler` hook so every route requires a logged-in user, then relies on `request.currentUser!.id` (a non-null assertion) for scoping all Prisma queries. Zod schemas (`updateProfileSchema`, `createAddressSchema`, `updateAddressSchema`, `paginationSchema`) validate bodies and query strings, with `updateAddressSchema` derived via `.partial()` and pagination capped at 50 items per page. Its only dependencies are the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, the auth middleware, and `zod`; the Prisma models touched are `user`, `userAddress`, `pujaBooking` (with `temple`, `pujaType`, `priest` includes), and `subscription`. Notable behaviors: setting an address as `isDefault` first unsets other defaults, profile updates clear `nriCountry` when `isNri` becomes false, and Prisma's P2002 unique-violation on email is mapped to a 409 Conflict. Two endpoints are deliberate stubs — `PUT /me/avatar` returns 501 pending S3/R2 storage, and `GET /me/orders` returns an empty paginated list awaiting MedusaJS integration. Address mutations verify ownership via a `findFirst` on both id and userId before updating or deleting, returning a generic 404 otherwise.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\temple-portal.cr.summary: This Vitest suite unit-tests the Zod request-validation schemas behind the temple-portal API routes, importing them via the `__testing` export of the sibling `temple-portal.js` module rather than exercising them over HTTP. It covers four schemas: `pujaOfferingCreateSchema` and `pujaOfferingUpdateSchema` for puja offerings, plus `darshanCreateSchema` and `darshanStatusSchema` for live-streamed darshan. The puja offering tests pin down that `pujaTypeId` must be a UUID, `nriPrice` and `priceOverride` cannot be negative, `maxBookingsPerSlot` must be at least 1, and that updates permit empty no-op patches and allow clearing `assignedPriestId` with an explicit null. The darshan tests confirm `playbackUrl` must be a valid URL, `streamProvider` is a closed enum (YOUTUBE accepted, arbitrary values like TIKTOK rejected, with `youtubeVideoId` as an optional companion field), and stream status is restricted to scheduled, live, or ended — "offline" is deliberately rejected in favor of "ended". The only dependencies are `vitest` and the route module under test; there is no database, HTTP server, or mocking involved. The `__testing` re-export is the notable design pattern here: it lets validation logic be tested in isolation while keeping the schemas colocated with the route handlers that consume them.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\voice-pandit.tes.summary: This is the Vitest suite for the voice-pandit API route, exercising internals exposed via the `__testing` export of `./voice-pandit.js` — specifically the `redactPII` helper, the `turnBodySchema` request validator, and the `MAX_AUDIO_BYTES` constant. The `redactPII` tests verify that email addresses and phone numbers (Indian +91 formats, plain 10-digit numbers, and international formats like +1, +44, +971) are replaced with `[redacted-email]`/`[redacted-phone]` markers, while short numeric tokens such as years and mantra counts pass through untouched. A notable gotcha documented inline is that 12-digit Aadhaar numbers match the phone regex first, so the tests accept either `[redacted-phone]` or `[redacted-id]` as a valid outcome rather than pinning one marker. A 50-utterance corpus — mixing devotional queries (muhurats, pujas, yatras) with embedded PII like PANs, card numbers, and Aadhaar IDs — hard-asserts that no email pattern or run of 7+ contiguous digits survives redaction. The `turnBodySchema` tests confirm it requires an `audioBase64` string of at least 8 characters capped at roughly 4/3 of `MAX_AUDIO_BYTES` (accounting for base64 expansion), defaults `language` to `'en'` while accepting `'hi'` and rejecting unknown codes like `'fr'`, and defaults `mimeType` to `'audio/webm'` with a length bound. The only dependencies are Vitest and the sibling route module itself, which implies the route relies on a zod-style schema for validating voice-turn request bodies.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\waitlist.ts.summary: This file implements the Fastify routes for the Darshya devotee waitlist with a viral referral system: the exported `waitlistRoutes` function registers `POST /` (join waitlist), `GET /confirm` (flip a row's status from PENDING to CONFIRMED and redirect to the welcome page), and `GET /stats` (return rank, total, and referralCount for a referral code). Each signup gets a 6-character uppercase `referralCode` from `generateReferralCode` (crypto-random over a 36-char alphabet, with up to 5 collision retries backed by the database's unique index), and a valid `referredByCode` on join increments the referrer's `referralCount`. It depends on the internal `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` for all persistence against the `waitlist` table, `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js` for confirmation emails, plus `zod` for input validation and `node:crypto` for code generation. Notable design choices: joining is idempotent—an existing email returns the original row with `existing: true` rather than an error; rank is computed as a createdAt-based count of non-UNSUBSCRIBED rows (so referralCount doesn't actually affect the computed rank despite what the email copy claims); and email sending is env-gated on `RESEND_API_KEY` and wrapped in best-effort try/catch so local/demo environments can exercise the flow without sending mail. The `confirm` endpoint uses the row's database `id` as the confirmation token (not the referral code), and the site origin falls back to `https://darshya.online` when `WEB_PUBLIC_URL` is unset.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\wellness-portal..summary: This Vitest test suite validates `mineQuerySchema`, a Zod schema exported through the `__testing` namespace of the sibling route module `apps/api/src/routes/wellness-portal.ts`, which parses query parameters for the wellness portal's "mine" endpoint (an instructor's own session list). The tests confirm that an empty query yields defaults of limit 50 and offset 0 with no status filter, and that string-valued URL params like `'120'` are coerced to numbers. They also pin the pagination bounds: limit must be an integer between 1 and 200 (the cap guarding against unbounded instructor-side pulls) and offset must be a non-negative integer, with fractional values rejected. Finally, the suite verifies that `status` is restricted to the four `WellnessSessionStatus` enum values — SCHEDULED, LIVE, COMPLETED, and CANCELLED — rejecting arbitrary strings such as `pending_payment`. The only dependencies are `vitest` and the route module under test, and the suite relies on the route file deliberately exposing its internal schema via `__testing` rather than through a public API.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\voice-pandit.ts.summary: This file implements the "Voice AI Pandit" feature for the Darshya platform as a Fastify route plugin, exposing `POST /turn` (a full voice round-trip: base64 audio in → transcription → spiritual reply → base64 mp3 out) and `GET /health` (reports live-vs-demo status of each provider without leaking keys). The pipeline chains three external paid services via plain `fetch` with a 25-second `AbortController` timeout: Groq Whisper STT (`whisper-large-v3-turbo`), Groq chat completions (`llama-3.3-70b-versatile`) driven by a "Pandit Ji" system prompt constrained to 2–3 spoken sentences, and ElevenLabs TTS (`eleven_turbo_v2_5`) with separate English/Hindi voice IDs. The exported `voicePanditRoutes` function registers the routes, while `redactPII` (also exported for tests via `__testing`) strips emails, phone numbers, and long digit runs from transcripts before they reach the LLM. The only code dependencies are `fastify` and `zod` (used for body validation with an 8 MB audio cap), plus `GROQ_API_KEY`/`ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` env vars — if either is missing or set to `demo-key`, the route degrades to stub responses rather than erroring, so production requires both. Cost control is layered: Fastify's rate limit config allows 10 turns per hour keyed by `user.id || ip` (to avoid CG-NAT collisions), plus a hard 50-turn daily cap tracked in an in-memory `dailyCounters` Map — a notable gotcha since that map resets on process restart and isn't shared across instances. The route emits structured `voice_pandit_turn` log lines with per-stage latency breakdowns (stt_ms, llm_ms, tts_ms) as a stand-in for PostHog analytics, and upstream failures surface as 502s while over-cap requests return 429 with reset headers. Model and voice IDs are env-overridable without redeploy, and response `demo` flags let the client UI distinguish live from stubbed behavior.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\wellness-session.summary: This vitest file exercises the payment-verification endpoint of `wellnessSessionRoutes` (POST `/api/v1/wellness/enrollments/:id/verify`), locking in three security behaviors flagged by audit item P0 wp-02: rejecting an order-id mismatch between the client-submitted and enroll-time-persisted Razorpay order, rejecting enrollments whose stored `razorpayOrderId` is null, and verifying the HMAC signature with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. It has no exports of its own; it depends on `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js` (wired in via `vi.mock` of `../lib/prisma.js`), Fastify's `app.inject` for in-memory HTTP calls, and `node:crypto` to forge valid `sha256` signatures. The central gotcha the file works around is that the route computes `isDemoPayment` at module load from `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`/`RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET`, so the suite splits into two describe blocks: one statically imports the route for demo mode (no env, signature check skipped, plus a 403 ownership test via the `Bearer demo-devotee` token), while the other stubs the env vars, calls `vi.resetModules`, and dynamically re-imports to force real-payment mode. In real-payment mode the tests assert that a mismatched order id with an otherwise valid signature, a null stored order id, and a tampered/wrong-length signature all return 400 without calling `wellnessEnrollment.update`, and that only a matching order id plus valid signature flips the enrollment from `PENDING_PAYMENT` to `PAID`.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\weddings.ts.summary: This file registers the wedding vertical's HTTP endpoints on the Fastify server via the exported `weddingRoutes` plugin, exposing `POST /muhurat` to compute ranked auspicious dates and `POST /inquiry` to capture wedding leads. The muhurat endpoint validates input with `MuhuratInputSchema` from `../lib/muhurat.js` and delegates computation to `findWeddingMuhurats`, while the inquiry endpoint validates against a local zod `InquiryBody` schema (name, email, phone, city, optional future wedding date, `basic|premium|royal` package enum, guests, budget) before persisting to a `WeddingInquiry` table. Both routes are gated by `authenticateUser` from `../middlewares/auth.js` — a deliberate hardening after an attacker abused the previously open muhurat endpoint to burn the mhah-panchang compute loop, and to prevent anonymous PII dumps into the inquiry table. Persistence uses `prisma.$executeRawUnsafe` from `../lib/prisma.js` with a `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` on every call to avoid needing a migration, and generates IDs like `wi_<base36-timestamp>_<random>` rather than relying on a database sequence. Notable gotchas: the `package` column is double-quoted because it is a reserved-ish identifier in some Postgres versions, and `wedding_date` is explicitly cast with `::date` after ticket TD15 surfaced 500s from ambiguous prepared-statement binds. Confirmation emails go through `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`, which no-ops without RESEND configuration; both the customer welcome email and the admin notification (recipients from the `ADMIN_EMAILS` env var) are fire-and-forget with `.catch(() => undefined)` so email failures never fail the request.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\whatsapp-broadca.summary: This file defines the Fastify HTTP routes for WhatsApp broadcast messaging, split into two exported route registrars: `whatsappBroadcastRoutes` mounts admin-only endpoints (`POST /broadcast` to trigger a send, `GET /deliveries` to list recent audit rows) guarded by the `authenticateUser` and `requireRole('admin')` middlewares, while `whatsappWebhookRoutes` handles Meta's webhook callbacks (GET verification echo and POST for inbound messages). It builds on `whatsapp-broadcast.service.js` for the actual work — `broadcastToWaitlist`, `broadcastToBookingHolders`, `broadcastToAll`, `recentDeliveries`, and `recordOptOut` — and uses `zod` for request body validation of a `broadcastBodySchema` (audience enum of waitlist/bookings/all plus template name, language code, and variables). The POST webhook verifies Meta's `X-Hub-Signature-256` header by HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body using `WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET`, comparing with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`; notably, if the env secrets are missing, requests still return 200 but are logged as unverified, a deliberate choice to keep local development frictionless. Inbound messages are scanned against a multilingual `STOP_KEYWORDS` regex (English plus Hindi terms like अनसब्सक्राइब and रोको), extracting text from plain messages, button replies, or interactive list replies, and matching senders are passed to `recordOptOut`. Two gotchas stand out: the webhook endpoint always returns 200 even on signature mismatch or processing failure to avoid Meta's retry storm, and the raw body needed for HMAC verification depends on the route config flag `rawBody: true` being honored by the server setup.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\wellness-portal..summary: This file defines `wellnessPortalRoutes`, a Fastify route plugin that backs the wellness-instructor portal: it registers GET `/dashboard`, GET `/instructor/mine`, GET `/students`, and PATCH `/profile`, all gated by `authenticateUser` and the `WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR` role (enforced via the `requireRole` middleware on `/instructor/mine` and inline role checks elsewhere). It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (using the `wellnessProfile`, `wellnessSession`, and `wellnessEnrollment` models plus `$queryRawUnsafe`), the auth middlewares in `../middlewares/auth.js`, and `zod` for input validation via `profileUpdateSchema` and `mineQuerySchema` (the latter re-exported through `__testing` for unit tests). The dashboard aggregates session counts, unique paid students, and earnings, deliberately reporting the instructor's net share — `1 - WELLNESS_PLATFORM_COMMISSION` (default 0.20) — rather than gross revenue, matching what the Commission ledger actually pays out. Only enrollments in `PAID` or `ATTENDED` status count toward stats and the students list, which collapses raw enrollments into one card per user keyed by most recent enrollment. Notably, `/instructor/mine` intentionally mirrors the `consultation.ts` astrologer endpoint by using raw parameterized SQL against `wellness_sessions` to get `ORDER BY scheduled_at DESC NULLS LAST` semantics with paginated limit/offset (limit capped at 200), and converts the `price_inr` numeric string to a number while aliasing `room_url` to both `roomUrl` and `zoomUrl` in the response. PATCH `/profile` acts as an upsert, creating a profile with defaults (display name "Instructor", 500 INR per session) when none exists.

apps\\api\\src\\routes\\wellness-session.summary: This file registers the wellness-session HTTP API for the Darshya backend: `wellnessSessionRoutes(server: FastifyInstance)` wires up endpoints under which instructors (role `WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR`) create, edit, delete, and attach Jitsi `roomUrl`s to scheduled yoga/meditation sessions, while devotees (role `DEVOTEE`) enroll and pay. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` (models `wellnessSession`, `wellnessEnrollment`, `commission`), the `authenticateUser`/`requireRole` middlewares from `../middlewares/auth.js`, `zod` schemas for every payload, the `razorpay` SDK for payment orders, `node:crypto` for HMAC-SHA256 signature verification, and `generateInvoice`/`sendEmail` from `../lib/pdf-invoice.js` and `../lib/email.js` for best-effort tax-invoice delivery.
