A demo-payment `Proxy` stubs Razorpay when `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID` is missing or the demo placeholder, and the module throws at boot in production unless `ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS=true`. Gotchas: store-order commissions (`writeStoreOrderCommissionOnConfirm`) resolve the owning store through the first line item's product because `StoreOrder` lacks a direct `storeProfileId` FK (pending S-11), and `ReferralClaim` is reached through a cast around the Prisma client's types.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\store.service..summary: This Vitest suite unit-tests StoreService (imported from `./store.service.js`), the API module that serves a hardcoded in-memory catalog of 24 products and 8 collections, so no mocks or external services are involved. It exhaustively covers `getProducts` — collection and case-insensitive category filters, keyword search over titles and descriptions, min/max price bounds, the four sort orders (`price_asc`, `price_desc`, `rating`, `newest`) plus the default sort by review count, and pagination including out-of-range pages — along with `getProductByHandle` and `getCollections`. A large block of tests exercises the per-user cart API (`getCart`, `createCartItem`, `updateCartItem`, `removeCartItem`), pinning down business rules: quantities are capped at 10 with errors thrown for out-of-range values or unknown product/item IDs, a ₹49 delivery fee applies below a ₹499 subtotal, 5% GST is added, and totals are computed as subtotal plus delivery plus tax, all in INR. Because cart state lives in memory on the service instance, each test generates a random `userId` in `beforeEach` to prevent cart leakage between tests — a notable gotcha reflecting that StoreService is stateful rather than backed by a database. The suite also documents exact error strings (e.g., "Product not found.", "Quantity must be between 1 and 10."), so changing those messages in the service will break these tests.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\refund.service.summary: This file implements refund automation for puja bookings by calling Razorpay's REST API directly with a thin fetch wrapper (`callRazorpayRefund`) rather than the official SDK, deliberately avoiding the SDK's deprecated `request` dependency and allowing a clean no-op when `RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`/`RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET` are unset. Its main export, `processRefund`, validates the request, locates the booking's captured `Payment` via Prisma, issues the refund to Razorpay in paise, then atomically updates both `Payment` (status `refunded`/`partially_refunded`, `refundAmount`, metadata carrying `refundId`/`refundedAt`/`refundReason`) and `PujaBooking` in a `prisma.$transaction`, finishing with a best-effort confirmation email through `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`. The second export, `processAutoRefunds`, is a cron-oriented batch (wired into `runDailyOps` in `jobs/master-cron.ts`) that picks up to 50 cancelled bookings tagged with the `REFUND_REQUESTED_MARKER` prefix in `cancellationReason` and older than one hour, running full refunds with `initiatedBy: 'cron'`; both functions plus the marker are bundled in the exported `refundService` object alongside types `RefundType`, `ProcessRefundParams`, and `ProcessRefundResult`. Key gotchas: the Prisma schema lacks refund-specific fields (no `REFUND_REQUESTED` status, no `refundedAt`/`refundReason` columns), so state is mirrored into `Payment.metadata` and bracketed `cancellationReason` prefixes, and partial refunds never flip the booking status to `refunded`. The flow is idempotent—bookings or payments already refunded return `{ skipped: true, reason: 'already-refunded' }` without re-hitting Razorpay—Razorpay failures are logged into payment metadata while leaving booking status untouched for admin retry, and email failures are swallowed so they can't undo a completed refund.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\provider.servi.summary: `ProviderService` (exported as the singleton `providerService`) is the data-access layer for the six provider verticals — pandit, store, astrologer, wellness, gaushala, temple — backing the public marketplace API with `getProviders` (paginated, filterable listings), `getProviderById` (detail plus the 10 newest reviews), `updateProvider` (owner-verified profile edits), and `addReview`. It queries Postgres through the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, using per-type profile models (`panditProfile`, `storeProfile`, etc.) and the global `review` table, but every method wraps its DB work in try/catch and silently falls back to hardcoded `MOCK_*` arrays and an in-memory `mockReviews` list — so connection or schema errors are swallowed and demo data is served instead of failing. Two P0 fixes (#PUB-01/#PUB-07) are enforced at the service boundary: `queryProviderById` uses `findFirst({ where: { id, approved: true } })` so unapproved providers 404, and `stripProviderPii` removes `PUBLIC_PROVIDER_DENYLIST` fields (userId, gstNumber, commission, aadhaarVerified, approved, timestamps) before data reaches logged-out callers. Ratings aren't persisted per profile; `enrichRatingFields` lazily aggregates `prisma.review.aggregate` per provider on read, an N+1 pattern over listing results, so clients can derive badge tiers without a schema migration. Notable gotchas: the mock fallback paths bypass `stripProviderPii` entirely and leak the denied fields, `updateProviderProfile` strips only `approved`/`id`/`userId`/`createdAt` from updates (leaving fields like `commission` provider-writable), and price sorting is dispatched per type because the column name differs (`pricePerPuja`, `pricePerMinute`, `pricePerSession`).

apps\\api\\src\\services\\puja.service.t.summary: This file is the read-side service layer for the puja catalog in the API app, encapsulating all business logic for browsing puja types, viewing a single puja with its temple offerings, checking per-slot availability, and ranking popular pujas. It exports the `PujaService` class, a `pujaService` singleton instance, and the `PujaListParams` filter interface; the service's four methods are `findAllTypes` (paginated list filtered by category, deity, or free-text search), `findBySlug` (detail including active `templeOfferings` and their temples), `checkAvailability` (remaining capacity per time slot for a temple/date), and `getPopular` (ranked by booking counts). It depends on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `cached` helper plus `CACHE_TTL` constants from `../lib/cache.js`, with Prisma-generated types like `PujaCategory` and `PujaTypeWhereInput` from `@prisma/client`. List and detail reads are cached under filter- and slug-derived keys, while `checkAvailability` and `getPopular` query the database directly. A key gotcha is that `findBySlug` deliberately emits each offering in two shapes — prefixed fields like `templeName`/`templeSlug` alongside legacy flat fields like `name`/`city` — and sets `id` to the offering id, because the web booking pages pass it as `templeOfferingId` to the bookings create-order endpoint. It also normalizes `availableSlots`, stored as plain time strings in the DB, into `{time, label}` objects with Morning/Afternoon/Evening labels for the booking UI. `checkAvailability` counts existing `pujaBooking` rows via `groupBy` while excluding cancelled and refunded statuses, and `getPopular` only counts completed/delivered/video_uploaded bookings, falling back to `sortOrder`-ordered active pujas when no bookings exist yet.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\subscription.s.summary: This Vitest suite tests `SubscriptionService` (from `apps/api/src/services/subscription.service.ts`), covering the full subscription lifecycle: plan catalog browsing, subscribing, fetching a user's active plan, NRI Premium ("Layer AR") Stripe annual billing, premium gating, and cancellation. It mocks Prisma by substituting `prismaMock` from `../lib/__mocks__/prisma.js` for the real `../lib/prisma.js` module, so all `MarketplaceSubscription` and `Transaction` model calls are asserted without a database. The `getPlans` tests lock in role-based filtering (e.g. `PANDIT`), INR as the default currency, a required plan shape, and the invariant that exactly one plan per role bucket is flagged `popular`. The `subscribe` tests verify that unknown plan IDs and role/plan mismatches throw, that paid plans deactivate prior subscriptions via `updateMany` and create both a subscription and a `Transaction`, and that free plans deliberately skip transaction creation. The NRI Premium block pins down the `nri_premium_yearly` plan (price 5000 INR, `priceUsd` 60, 365-day `ENTERPRISE` tier) and documents a key gotcha: `createStripeAnnualSubscription` degrades gracefully to demo mode — returning `skipped: true`, reason `demo-mode`, and a `cs_demo_`-prefixed session ID — whenever `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` is absent, while rejecting plans that lack a USD price. Finally, `isPremium` is shown to return true only for an active `ENTERPRISE` subscription, and `cancel` either flips the active subscription's status to `CANCELLED` or returns `cancelled: false` when none exists.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\temple.service.summary: This Vitest test file verifies the query-building behavior of `TempleService` (from `apps/api/src/services/temple.service.ts`) without touching a real database, by injecting `prismaMock` from `lib/__mocks__/prisma.js` in place of the real `prisma` client via `vi.mock`. The `TempleService.findAll` suite asserts that every listing is always scoped to `status: 'active'`, that `city` and `state` filters are applied case-insensitively using Prisma's `mode: 'insensitive'`, that `isVerified` and `liveDarshan` inputs map to the `isVerified` and `liveDarshanEnabled` columns, and that a `search` term expands into an OR clause across four fields. It also pins down the default sort order (`trustScore` descending, then `name` ascending) and the pagination math, confirming that page 2 with limit 5 produces `skip: 5, take: 5` and a correctly computed `totalPages`. The `TempleService.search` suite covers the empty-query fast path, asserting it returns an empty result envelope (`results: []`, `total: 0`, default page/limit) without ever calling `prisma.temple.findMany`. Key dependencies are Vitest's mocking utilities and the shared Prisma mock module; the tests are notable for asserting on the exact shape of the Prisma query arguments rather than on returned data, meaning they lock in the service's filtering contract while remaining brittle to any query-structure refactor.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\store-commissi.summary: This service is the single shared writer for store-order `Commission` rows, introduced in the store-owner revamp of 2026-08-05 to fix a leak where only the Razorpay-verify path (`payment.service`'s `writeStoreOrderCommissionOnConfirm`) created commission rows, leaving COD and admin manual payment-confirm orders missing from the store owner's earnings ledger. Its sole export, `writeStoreOrderCommission(storeOrderId, tx)`, is idempotent — it checks for an existing `Commission` by `storeOrderId` and returns early — so it can be safely invoked from any order-confirm path, and it accepts an optional `Prisma.TransactionClient` (via the `TxClient` type) so callers can run it inside an enclosing transaction, defaulting to the shared `prisma` client from `lib/prisma.js`. It resolves the seller by taking the first order item's `productId`, loading the `StoreProduct` to get `storeProfileId`, then loading the `StoreProfile` for its `userId` (written as `providerId`) and `commission` rate, which defaults to 0.20 (20% platform / 80% owner, justified in the header comment as competitive with Amazon/Flipkart's effective take). A notable semantic: the `amount` stored is the store owner's share — total × (1 − platformRate) — while the `percentage` column records the platform's rate for ledger display, and the row is created with status `PENDING`. The main gotcha is that every failure mode (missing order, no item carrying a `productId`, product without a `storeProfileId`, or missing profile) results in a silent early return with no row written and no error raised, so callers get no signal when a commission is skipped; additionally `percentage` is forced to zero when the order total is non-positive. Dependencies are limited to `@prisma/client` (`Prisma.Decimal` arithmetic, `Prisma.TransactionClient`) and the internal prisma client, touching the `Commission`, `StoreOrder`, `StoreProduct`, and `StoreProfile` tables.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\wallet.service.summary: This file implements WalletService, the internal credit ledger primitive for user balances, introduced for the R-Q2-M-011 referral reward integration. Its sole mutation entry point, creditUser, applies signed paise-denominated deltas (via CreditUserInput, with a CreditLedgerReason such as referral_reward or redemption_debit) by upserting the UserCredit row and inserting a CreditLedgerEntry inside a single Prisma transaction, returning a CreditResult; getBalance returns a WalletBalance (defaulting to zero/INR for users with no row), and verifyInvariant audits that the ledger sum matches the stored balance, throwing WalletInvariantError on drift. It depends only on the PrismaClient from @prisma/client and the UserCredit and CreditLedgerEntry models, and also exports an isUniqueViolation helper for detecting Prisma P2002 races. Key design decisions: all amounts are integer paise (rejecting zero and non-integers) to avoid float hazards, and every mutation requires an idempotencyKey of at least 8 characters, since a unique constraint on (userId, idempotencyKey) makes retried webhook-driven referral rewards return the existing entry with reused=true instead of double-crediting. Overdrafts are prevented by throwing inside the transaction when a debit would push balancePaise negative, rolling back both writes. One gotcha: the invariant that sum(ledger deltas) equals the cached balance holds only if all writes flow through this service, so direct database edits will trip verifyInvariant.

This Vitest suite unit-tests WalletService (from `apps/api/src/services/wallet.service.ts`), substituting Prisma with the shared `prismaMock` from `lib/__mocks__/prisma.js` via `vi.mock('../lib/prisma.js')` and constructing the service with the mocked `PrismaClient`. It exercises three methods: `creditUser`, `getBalance`, and `verifyInvariant`, plus the `WalletInvariantError` type. For `creditUser`, the tests pin the intended contract: a first-time credit upserts the `userCredit` row and writes a `creditLedgerEntry` inside `$transaction` returning `{ reused: false, newBalancePaise, ledgerEntryId }`, while a repeated call with the same `idempotencyKey` short-circuits before any transaction and returns the existing ledger entry with `reused: true`. Invariant tests assert that zero deltas, non-integer paise amounts, and idempotency keys shorter than 8 characters all throw `WalletInvariantError`, and that a negative `deltaPaise` (e.g. a `redemption_debit`) that would drive the balance below zero is rejected as an overdraft. `getBalance` must return zero balance with `INR` currency for users lacking a wallet row, and `verifyInvariant` must compare `userCredit.balancePaise` against the aggregated sum of `creditLedgerEntry.deltaPaise`, throwing a drift error when they diverge. Notably, the suite documents that the service uses signed integer paise amounts for both credits and debits through a single entry point, and that idempotency is enforced by ledger lookup keyed on `idempotencyKey` rather than by database uniqueness retries.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\subscription.s.summary: This file implements the subscription backbone for the Darshya marketplace: it defines a static `PLANS` catalog covering tiers for PANDIT, ASTROLOGER, STORE_OWNER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, TEMPLE_MANAGER/GAUSHALA_MANAGER, and DEVOTEE roles (including the AI-astro paywall passes `astro_session`/`astro_monthly` and the USD-billed `nri_premium_yearly` tier), and exposes the `SubscriptionService` class (plus a `subscriptionService` singleton) with methods to list plans, create/cancel local subscriptions, and query premium status via `isPremium`. The service persists state through `prisma.marketplaceSubscription` and `prisma.transaction` from `../lib/prisma.js`, sends renewal and dunning emails via `sendEmail` from `../lib/email.js`, and integrates two payment providers: Razorpay's Subscriptions API for auto-renewing monthly plans (`createRazorpaySubscription`, `handleSubscriptionEvent`, `cancelRazorpaySubscription`) and Stripe Checkout (`getStripe`, `isStripeDemoMode` from `../lib/stripe.js`) for the annual NRI plan via `createStripeAnnualSubscription`. A notable design choice is avoiding schema changes: Razorpay subscription IDs and Stripe session IDs are stashed in `Transaction.metadata` (so webhook handling scans recent transactions to resolve users), and new plan codes reuse existing `MarketplacePlan` enum values — `astro_session` maps to BASIC and `nri_premium_yearly` maps to ENTERPRISE, which is what `isPremium` keys off. Gotchas include the silent in-memory `mockSubscriptions` Map fallback whenever any database call throws (masking real outages as demo data), the `assertNotProductionDemo` guard from `../lib/payment-mode.js` that blocks fake `sub_demo_*` IDs in production, free plans being granted a 100-year end date, and reliance on env vars (`RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`, `RAZORPAY_PLAN_*`, `WEB_APP_URL`) where missing keys flip flows into demo mode that instantly grants access locally.

apps\\api\\src\\types\\web-push.d.ts.summary: This is an ambient TypeScript declaration file that supplies local type definitions for the external `web-push` npm package, which ships without its own types — it exists purely so the API can import and call web push functionality with compile-time safety. It declares the `PushSubscription` interface (an endpoint URL plus the `p256dh` and `auth` encryption keys a browser provides), the `RequestOptions` interface for tuning delivery (TTL, urgency level, topic collapse key, extra headers), and three functions: `setVapidDetails` for registering the server's VAPID identity, `sendNotification` for delivering a payload to a subscription and receiving back an HTTP status/body/headers result, and `generateVAPIDKeys` for creating the public/private key pair. The same three functions are also re-exported as a `_default` object, supporting both named and default-import styles. Because it's an ambient `declare module` with no implementation, the runtime dependency is the real `web-push` library; a gotcha is that these hand-written types can drift from the actual library API, and only the subset of the library the app uses is declared, so other web-push features would need to be added here before they're callable with type checking.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\temple.service.summary: This file is the data-access service for temples in the API, exposing a `TempleService` class (exported as the singleton `templeService`) plus the `TempleListParams` filter interface, with methods `findAll`, `findBySlug`, `findNearby`, `search`, `getReviews`, and `getTemplePujas`. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js` and the `cached`/`CACHE_TTL` helpers from `../lib/cache.js`, using Prisma types like `Prisma.TempleWhereInput` and the `Tradition` enum from `@prisma/client` against a Postgres database. `findAll` and `search` build filtered, paginated queries over the `Temple` table (always constrained to `status: 'active'`), while `findBySlug` eagerly loads related `priests`, active `pujaOfferings` with their `pujaType`, and the latest non-offline `darshanStream`; reviews are derived from `pujaBooking` rows that carry a rating. A key design decision (flagged as ticket P0 #PUB-02) is that every public response uses explicit `select` whitelists so internal fields like `trustScore`, phone, email, and stream URLs are never serialized — `trustScore` is still used for `orderBy` ranking but stripped from output. Caching uses deliberately stable keys (fixed-order `JSON.stringify` of normalized params) with `CACHE_TTL.TEMPLE_LIST` and `TEMPLE_DETAIL` TTLs. `findNearby` drops to raw SQL via `prisma.$queryRaw` to run a Haversine distance computation, with notable gotchas: the distance filter lives on an outer SELECT because Postgres rejects `HAVING` without `GROUP BY`, the `acos` argument is clamped with `LEAST`/`GREATEST` to avoid floating-point domain errors, temples with null coordinates are excluded, and snake_case results are manually normalized to camelCase with `distanceKm` rounded to two decimals.

apps\\api\\vitest.config.ts.summary: This file configures Vitest for the API application, defining how unit tests are discovered and executed. It enables global test APIs (`globals: true`), runs tests in a Node environment, and includes test files from `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. Its sole dependency is the `vitest/config` module's `defineConfig` helper. The notable design decision is the raised 30-second `testTimeout`, added because Razorpay's dynamic `await import()` and client initialization were exceeding the 5-second default under CPU contention from turbo parallel builds, causing six payment tests to false-fail. Execution is also constrained to a maximum of two forks via `poolOptions.forks` to cap memory usage while still allowing cold imports to settle, keeping `singleFork` disabled for limited parallelism.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\store.service..summary: This file is the API's store service and currently serves as the entire product catalog domain for the e-commerce backend, with no database involved. It exports the core domain types — `Product`, `Collection`, `CartItem`, `Cart`, and the `ProductsParams` query shape (collection/category filters, sort, pagination, text search `q`, and min/max price) — which define the contract for product browsing and for cart totals like `subtotal`, `deliveryFee`, `tax`, and `itemCount`. In place of a datastore, the catalog is a hardcoded `PRODUCTS` array of Hindu spiritual goods (puja essentials, rudraksha malas, idols, scriptures, and similar) priced in integer INR with precomputed `discount` percentages alongside `compareAtPrice`, an explicit MVP trade-off meaning every catalog change requires a code deploy. A private `img()` helper normalizes product imagery by passing absolute URLs through unchanged while expanding legacy Unsplash photo IDs into formatted `images.unsplash.com` URLs, so the seeded data mixes Wikimedia-hosted and Unsplash-hosted images — the file's only external touchpoints and a potential hotlinking/reliability gotcha. The module has no imports from other internal services or libraries; anything else in the app that needs store data presumably consumes these exported types and the `PRODUCTS` constant. The truncated portion evidently continues the product list across the remaining collections (Home Temple & Decor was in progress), following the same per-category SKU prefix scheme ("BS-PE", "BS-RM", etc.).

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\env.ts.summary: This module is the environment-configuration loader for the `darshya-mcp` app: its sole job is to resolve the `DIRECT_URL` database connection string before the server does anything else. It exports the `DarshyaEnv` interface (a single required `DIRECT_URL` field) and the `loadEnv` function, which returns that object. Resolution follows a strict precedence: an already-exported `process.env.DIRECT_URL` always wins, otherwise it falls back to parsing `../../apps/api/.env.production` with a simple line-by-line regex (matching the proven pattern in `apps/api/scripts/check-prod-tables.mjs`), stripping surrounding quotes from values. Its only dependencies are Node's built-in `fs` (`readFileSync`, `existsSync`); there are no external libraries. A notable design decision is fail-loud behavior: if `DIRECT_URL` is found nowhere, `loadEnv` throws with an explicit message that the value must be the Supabase direct (non-pooled) connection string, preferring a crash over silently connecting to a pooled or wrong database. A gotcha worth noting is the relative default path, which assumes the process runs from the `apps/darshya-mcp` working directory, and the parser mutates global `process.env` as a side effect.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\whatsapp-broad.summary: This file implements the WhatsApp broadcast service, which fans out template messages to opted-in recipients through Meta's Cloud API while respecting the 50 messages-per-second cap of a tier-1 business number by sending in batches of 50 with one-second sleeps. It exports three broadcast entry points — `broadcastToWaitlist` (Waitlist rows with whatsappOptIn=true and non-UNSUBSCRIBED status), `broadcastToBookingHolders` (users on confirmed/completed PujaBooking rows, treated as implicitly opted in via T&C), and `broadcastToAll` (the deduplicated union) — plus `recordOptOut` and `isOptedOut` for STOP handling, `recentDeliveries` for audit inspection, and `broadcastInternals` exposing `ensureSchema` and `normalisePhone` for tests. It builds on the shared `prisma` client from ../lib/prisma.js and the `sendWhatsappTemplate` helper and `whatsapp` config object from ../lib/whatsapp.js, querying the Prisma-managed Waitlist and PujaBooking models. Notably, persistence for `WhatsAppDelivery` (per-attempt audit log) and `WhatsAppOptOut` (suppression list) uses raw SQL via `$executeRawUnsafe` with idempotent CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS on first call, deliberately bypassing Prisma migrations so the schema can be promoted later without data loss. Phones are normalized to Indian E.164-style form (10-digit numbers get a 91 prefix), and any number in WhatsAppOptOut overrides even booking-based implicit consent, with opted-out recipients still logged as OPTED_OUT. When WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID/WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN are absent, sends return skipped but rows are still written with status SKIPPED so dev environments exercise the full pipeline, and delivery logging is intentionally best-effort — insert failures are swallowed so they never break a broadcast.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\tools\\agent-rep.summary: This file implements two read-only MCP tools for the darshya-mcp server that expose Darshya's automated-agent reports stored as Markdown files under `docs/agent-reports`. It exports `agentReports`, which recursively lists `.md` files (capped at 50, sorted newest-first by mtime, each with name, relativePath, and modifiedAt), and `agentReportRead`, which returns a single report's contents truncated to a configurable limit (default 10,000 chars, max 500,000); both are paired with Zod schemas (`AgentReportsSchema`, `AgentReportReadSchema`) and MCP tool definitions (`agentReportsToolDef`, `agentReportReadToolDef`). Dependencies are minimal: `zod` for input validation and Node's `node:fs/promises` plus `node:path` for filesystem access — no external services. The most notable design decision is the `safeResolve` helper, which guards `agentReportRead` against directory traversal and absolute paths in a cross-platform way: beyond the standard `..`-escape check, it rejects any path containing a colon, because `path.isAbsolute` on Linux won't flag Windows-style `C:\` paths (backslashes are legal filename characters there). Errors are handled leniently — unreadable directories yield empty listings and missing reports return JSON error payloads rather than throwing, since MCP tool results are text content blocks. The reports root defaults to `docs/agent-reports` assuming the server runs from the repo root, but is overridable via a `root` argument intended for tests.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the executable entry point for the `darshya-mcp` MCP server, a stdio-based server built on the low-level `Server` class from `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` that exposes six read-only analytics tools to MCP clients. It exports nothing itself; instead it builds a `TOOLS` registry pairing each tool definition (`funnelTodayToolDef`, `kpiSnapshotToolDef`, `agentReportsToolDef`, `agentReportReadToolDef`, `prodHealthToolDef`, `recentCommitsToolDef`) imported from sibling modules under `./tools/` with its handler, then wires `ListToolsRequestSchema` to return those defs verbatim and `CallToolRequestSchema` to dispatch by name. Internally it depends on `./prisma.js` for `disconnectPrisma`, and on the SDK's `StdioServerTransport` for transport; notably, it imports the SDK via subpaths (`./server`, `./server/stdio.js`, `./types.js`) because the package's root export is broken in version 1.29.0. Argument validation is delegated to each tool's own zod schema, so the registry deliberately types handlers as `(args: any) => Promise<any>` to sidestep contravariance between the tools' narrow inferred parameter types. Robustness is a clear design priority: any thrown error during dispatch is caught and returned as an `isError` text response (including for unknown tool names) so one bad call cannot crash the server. Finally, a `shutdown` handler on SIGINT/SIGTERM calls `disconnectPrisma()` before closing the server, preventing leaked pooled database connections when the MCP client disconnects.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\guard.ts.summary: This file is the read-only guard for darshya-mcp: a single chokepoint that every raw-SQL tool result must pass, exporting one function, isReadOnlyQuery(sql), which returns true only when a statement is provably read-only. It works by maintaining a WRITE_KEYWORDS denylist (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER, GRANT, REVOKE, CREATE, MERGE, CALL, plus sneakier writes like INTO, COPY, COMMENT, REFRESH, REINDEX, VACUUM, and CLUSTER) and doing whole-word, case-insensitive regex matching against the SQL after preprocessing. The preprocessing order matters: single-quoted string literals are collapsed to a placeholder first (handling the Postgres '' escape) so that comment markers inside strings aren't mistaken for real comments, then line and block comments are stripped before keyword matching. A key design caveat is that this is defense-in-depth, not the primary control — no darshya-mcp tool passes user-controlled SQL to the executor since they rely on Prisma typed queries (count/aggregate/findMany), and the sole $queryRawUnsafe call in prod_health runs a hardcoded literal. The guard is deliberately not a full SQL parser and errs conservative: dollar-quoted ($$...$$) bodies are not unwrapped, so a write verb appearing inside one (or inside a string literal) will cause a safe read to be rejected. It has no external dependencies — pure regex over the input string — and its behavior is pinned by tests/e2e-read-only.test.ts, which fires a real DELETE and asserts rejection.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\tools\\funnel-to.summary: This file implements the `funnel_today` MCP tool for the darshya-mcp server, giving a read-only snapshot of the Darshya product funnel — signups, bookings, captured revenue, and donations — for today plus a rolling 7-day window. It exports `FunnelTodaySchema` (a strict, empty zod schema since the tool takes no arguments), the `funnelToday` handler which returns the metrics as MCP text content containing pretty-printed JSON, and `funnelTodayToolDef`, the tool registration metadata. The internal `windowCounts` helper runs five parallel Prisma queries against the `user`, `pujaBooking`, `payment`, and `donation` models via the shared `getPrisma()` client from `../prisma.js`, including a `groupBy` on booking status and sum aggregates for money. Time boundaries are deliberately computed in UTC (midnight UTC for "today") because Supabase stores timestamps in UTC, making the cut deterministic. Two revenue gotchas are documented in comments: payments only count as revenue when `status` is `'captured'` (initiated/authorized is not money received), and donations must be filtered on `status: 'paid'` from `DonationStatus` — using `'captured'` there would silently match zero rows since that value belongs to `PaymentStatus`. Null aggregate sums are coerced to zero with `Number(... ?? 0)`, and the result includes a `generatedAt` ISO timestamp.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\prisma.ts.summary: This file provides the database access layer for the darshya-mcp app, exposing a lazily-initialized, read-only `PrismaClient` singleton. `getPrisma()` creates the client on first call, wiring it to the `DIRECT_URL` connection string obtained from the internal `loadEnv()` helper in `./env.js`, while `disconnectPrisma()` tears the client down and resets the singleton so it can be re-created later. Its only external dependency is `@prisma/client`; internally it builds on the env module and relies on `guard.ts` to enforce the read-only guarantee for raw SQL. A notable design decision is the deliberate omission of query-event instrumentation, which keeps the client cheap — this contrasts with `apps/api/src/lib/prisma.ts`, which attaches instrumentation for its N+1 detector. The read-only contract is enforced only by convention for typed queries (callers are expected to stick to `findFirst`, `findMany`, `count`, and `aggregate`), so it is a discipline constraint rather than something the client itself blocks. Using `DIRECT_URL` also means this client bypasses any connection pooler and talks to the database directly.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\tools\\recent-co.summary: This file implements the `recent_commits` MCP tool for the darshya-mcp server, returning recent git history (sha, author, date, subject) from the current branch so agents can answer "what shipped recently?" questions. It exports three things: `RecentCommitsSchema`, a strict Zod schema capping the optional `count` at 50 (default 10); `recentCommits`, the async handler that shells out to `git log` and returns results in the MCP content envelope as JSON; and `recentCommitsToolDef`, the tool-definition metadata used when registering with the MCP server. Its only dependencies are `zod`, Node's `node:child_process` `execFile`, and the local `git` CLI, which must be run from the repo root since the command executes in the server's cwd. The deliberate use of `execFile` with an argument array (never a shell string) makes command injection structurally impossible, a defense-in-depth stance matching the `guard.ts` and `safeResolve` pattern used elsewhere in the package. Output is parsed from a pipe-delimited `--pretty=format`, with the subject re-joined on pipes so commit messages containing `|` survive intact. Notably, git failures resolve rather than reject, returning an empty `commits` array plus the stderr/error message, so the tool never throws into the MCP framework.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\tools\\kpi-snaps.summary: This file defines the `kpi_snapshot` MCP tool for the darshya-mcp server, giving founders a read-only, no-argument snapshot of headline business health for the Darshya puja-booking platform. It exports `KpiSnapshotSchema` (an empty strict zod schema, since the tool takes no inputs), the `kpiSnapshot` handler which returns results in MCP content format (a JSON-stringified text block), and `kpiSnapshotToolDef` carrying the tool's name, description, and JSON input schema for registration. The handler obtains a Prisma client via the internal `getPrisma()` helper from `../prisma.js` and fires seven queries in parallel with `Promise.all` against the `user`, `pujaBooking`, `payment`, `subscription`, and `lead` models, splitting results into all-time totals and a 7-day delta window. The only external dependency is `zod`. Notable business definitions are baked in: a "completed booking" means status `completed` OR `delivered`, lifetime revenue sums only `captured` payments in INR (coerced with `Number()` from the aggregate, which could lose precision on very large Decimal values), and pipeline leads are statuses `NEW` + `QUEUED` — note the inconsistent casing, since lead statuses are uppercase while booking, payment, and subscription statuses are lowercase. A `generatedAt` ISO timestamp is included so callers know how fresh the numbers are.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\env.test.ts.summary: This is a Vitest test suite verifying the `loadEnv` function exported from `../src/env.js` in the `darshya-mcp` app, which loads environment configuration from a `.env`-style file. It exercises three behaviors: parsing `DIRECT_URL` (a PostgreSQL connection string) from a file while ignoring unrelated keys, throwing a descriptive error when `DIRECT_URL` is missing, and giving precedence to an already-exported `process.env.DIRECT_URL` over the file value. The tests depend only on `vitest` and Node's built-in `node:fs` (`writeFileSync`, `rmSync`) and `node:path` (`join`) to create and clean up temporary `.env.test-*` files in the current working directory. Notably, each test snapshots and restores `process.env` in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks to isolate mutations, and the module under test is imported dynamically via `await import('../src/env.js')` inside each test rather than at the top, ensuring the module is evaluated against the freshly reset environment.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\src\\tools\\prod-heal.summary: This file implements `prod_health`, the only raw-SQL tool in the darshya-mcp server, giving a founder-facing health check that reports real row counts for the `users`, `puja_bookings`, `payments`, and `donations` tables in the Darshya production database. It exports three things: `ProdHealthSchema` (an empty strict zod schema since the tool takes no arguments), the `prodHealth` handler that executes the check and returns an MCP-style content array with a JSON payload, and `prodHealthToolDef`, the tool registration metadata. It depends on two internal modules: `getPrisma` from `../prisma.js` for the Prisma client (queries run via `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe`), and `isReadOnlyQuery` from `../guard.js`, plus `zod` for schema validation. The SQL is a hardcoded literal with zero interpolation, but it is still routed through `isReadOnlyQuery()` as defense in depth so a future edit that introduces user input would be blocked before touching prod; failure of the guard returns a structured refusal rather than throwing. A key design decision is using real `COUNT(*)` per table (batched into one round-trip via `UNION ALL`) instead of the `pg_class.reltuples` estimate, because reltuples is a stale ANALYZE value that returns -1 for never-analyzed tables and badly undercounts young tables. Table names use the snake_case `@@map` names from schema.prisma, and bigint counts are converted with `Number()` before serialization. Errors are caught and returned as `{ ok: false, error }` JSON text rather than propagated, keeping the MCP tool response well-formed even when the database is unreachable.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\agent-reports..summary: This Vitest suite verifies the two report-browsing tool handlers exported from `src/tools/agent-reports.js` in the darshya-mcp app: `agentReports`, which lists markdown reports, and `agentReportRead`, which reads one by relative path. To stay independent of the real `docs/agent-reports/` contents, each test builds a fresh fixture tree under a temp directory (`.tmp-agent-reports-test`) containing a dated top-level report, a subdirectory report under `cmo/`, and a 20,000-character report for truncation checks, and mocks `src/env.js`'s `loadEnv` so `REPORTS_ROOT` resolution can't leak real config. The list tests assert that results include both top-level and nested `.md` files, carry `name`, `relativePath`, and `modifiedAt` fields, come back newest-first, and are capped at 50 entries. The read tests cover happy-path reads (including subdirectory paths), a `limit` parameter that truncates oversized content and sets `truncated: true`, plus error cases: path traversal via `..`, absolute Windows paths, and missing files must all return an `error` payload rather than file content. A notable gotcha documented inline is that the implementation normalizes subdirectory paths to POSIX form (`cmo/...`), so assertions use forward slashes because `path.join` would emit backslashes on Windows and cause false failures. The suite depends only on `vitest` and Node's `node:fs`/`node:path`, and its traversal and absolute-path rejection tests double as the security contract for keeping reads confined to the reports root.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\guard.test.ts.summary: This Vitest test suite validates `isReadOnlyQuery` exported from `../src/guard.js` in the `darshya-mcp` app, which is the SQL safety guard that decides whether a query is read-only before execution. The tests enumerate a `rejected` list of mutating or dangerous PostgreSQL statements — DELETE, UPDATE, INSERT, DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER, GRANT, plus subtler write paths like SELECT INTO, COPY bulk loads, COMMENT ON, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, REINDEX, VACUUM, and CLUSTER — and assert each returns false. An `allowed` list asserts true for legitimate reads: plain and parameterized SELECTs, CTEs, lowercase keywords, and leading whitespace. Notably, the suite encodes regression cases for known bypass attempts, such as hiding comment markers inside string literals (e.g. `'--'` or `'/*'` followed by a DELETE) and identifiers containing keyword substrings (`user_updates`, `comment_count`), confirming the guard strips or tokenizes string literals and uses word-boundary matching rather than naive substring search. The only dependencies are `vitest` and the internal `guard.js` module, making this a pure unit test with no database or service mocking.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\funnel-today.t.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the `funnelToday` MCP tool from `apps/darshya-mcp/src/tools/funnel-today.js`, which reports daily and trailing-7-day funnel metrics (signups, puja bookings, captured revenue, donations). It mocks the Prisma layer in `../src/prisma.js` — stubbing `getPrisma` with a fake client covering `user.count`, `pujaBooking.count`/`groupBy`, `payment.aggregate`, and `donation.aggregate` — so tests run against deterministic fixtures rather than a real database. The first test asserts both the `today` and `last7d` windows return correctly mapped fields (e.g. `signups`, `bookings`, `bookingsByStatus`, `capturedRevenueInr`, `donationsInr`), deliberately asserting concrete values for `last7d` rather than mere presence so a regression in the seven-day window wiring can't slip through. It also locks down two status-filter contracts: revenue only sums payments with `status: 'captured'`, while donations must be filtered by `status: 'paid'` — the suite explicitly guards against confusing `DonationStatus` with `PaymentStatus`, since using `'captured'` for donations would silently match zero rows. The second test confirms the tool returns zeros rather than nulls when Prisma aggregates yield null sums on an empty production dataset.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\commissions..summary: This file defines `AdminCommissions`, a React Native admin-portal screen (in the Expo Router route group `app/(admin)`) for reviewing commission ledger entries. It fetches data through the `useAdminCommissions` hook from the `@poojly/api-client` package, optionally passing a `{ status }` filter param, and renders results inside the shared `PortalScreen` scaffold with pull-to-refresh and the shared `EmptyHint` component, using the local `lib/theme` tokens for styling. A horizontal row of status chips (`STATUS_FILTERS`: all/pending/paid/reversed) drives client-side filter state that changes the query params, and the screen computes a running rupee total of `commissionAmount` (falling back to `amount`) displayed in the subtitle. Each entry renders as a card showing provider name (or `providerId` fallback), a color-coded status pill via the `statusColor` helper, the commission amount, and an optional net-to-provider line. Notable loose typing is the locally declared `CommissionRow` interface with all-optional fields and `number | string` amounts, which are defensively coerced with `Number(...)` — a gotcha suggesting the API shape is not strongly typed client-side. Errors surface as an inline banner rather than blocking the screen, and amounts are formatted with `en-IN` locale conventions.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\kpi-snapshot.t.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the `kpiSnapshot` MCP tool exported from `apps/darshya-mcp/src/tools/kpi-snapshot.js`, which aggregates business metrics from the production database. It mocks the `getPrisma`/`disconnectPrisma` module at `../src/prisma.js` with stubbed Prisma models (`user`, `pujaBooking`, `payment`, `subscription`, `lead`), so no real database is touched. The main test asserts that the tool's MCP-style response (`result.content[0].text`, parsed as JSON) contains all-time totals (users, completed bookings, lifetime revenue in INR), 7-day deltas for new users and bookings, plus `activeSubscriptions` and `pipelineLeads` counts and a `generatedAt` timestamp. It also pins down the query semantics: subscriptions are filtered to `status: 'active'`, pipeline leads are those with status `NEW` or `QUEUED`, and revenue sums only `captured` payments via `payment.aggregate`. A second test covers the empty-database edge case, confirming that a null aggregate sum is coerced to zero rather than leaking through as null. Notable gotcha for maintainers: the mocks rely on sequential `mockResolvedValueOnce` calls for the paired all-time/7-day count queries, so test expectations are coupled to the order in which `kpiSnapshot` issues its Prisma calls.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\prod-health.te.summary: This Vitest suite locks in the behavior of the `prodHealth` tool exported from `apps/darshya-mcp/src/tools/prod-health.js`, an MCP tool that reports row counts for the core production tables (users, puja_bookings, payments, donations). It mocks the internal `../src/prisma.js` module, stubbing `getPrisma` to return a fake client with a `$queryRawUnsafe` spy so tests run without a real database. The tests assert that successful runs return `ok: true` with a `tables` map of counts, that failures (e.g. a rejected query) surface as `ok: false` plus the error message, and that the tool's response is delivered as JSON inside an MCP `content[0].text` envelope. Two tests act as regression guards on the SQL itself: the query must be a hardcoded read-only `SELECT ... COUNT(*)` with no `DELETE`/`UPDATE`/`INSERT`/`DROP`, and it must never fall back to the `pg_class.reltuples` estimate, which the comments note badly undercounts young production tables and returns -1 for never-analyzed ones. One notable quirk: the test named "routes the SQL through isReadOnlyQuery BEFORE executing" never actually references an `isReadOnlyQuery` function—it verifies the defense-in-depth intent only by inspecting the SQL argument passed to `$queryRawUnsafe`.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\approvals.ts.summary: This file is the Expo Router screen for the admin group's approvals route (`app/(admin)/approvals.tsx`), and its default-exported `AdminApprovals` component renders a pull-to-refresh list of pending provider verification requests with approve/reject buttons. It fetches data through the `useAdminPendingApprovals` hook from the `@poojly/api-client` package (a React Query-style hook exposing `data` and `refetch`), and builds its UI from shared shell components `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` in `../../lib/portal-screen` plus design tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `../../lib/theme`, with icons from `@expo/vector-icons`. Each row shows the applicant's name, role, contact, and application date, with circular green/red buttons backed by Ionicons checkmark/close glyphs. Approve and reject actions go through a `decide` helper that wraps React Native's `Alert.alert` for confirmation, styling reject as destructive. The notable gotcha is that decisions are purely cosmetic: confirming an action only adds the id to a local `actioned` Set state and shows a success alert — no mutation API is ever called, so filtered-out items will reappear whenever the query refetches. The pending count in the subtitle is derived by filtering the fetched approvals against that ephemeral Set, so the screen is currently a read-only view with optimistic-feeling but non-persistent actions.

apps\\darshya-mcp\\tests\\recent-commits.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the `recentCommits` MCP tool exported from `../src/tools/recent-commits.js` in the darshya-mcp app, along with its `RecentCommitsSchema` Zod validator. It mocks `node:child_process`'s `execFile` — capturing the command, args array, and trailing callback, then driving the callback via `__err`/`__stdout`/`__stderr` fields — so tests never touch real git history. The tests confirm that pipe-delimited `git log --pretty=format:%h|%an|%ad|%s --date=short` output is parsed into structured commit objects (sha, author, date, subject), that the tool shells out via `execFile('git', args)` with no shell intermediary, and that the requested count lands in the args as `-N` with a default of 10. A dedicated test locks the security invariant the whole design rests on: `RecentCommitsSchema` rejects non-integer, out-of-range (must be 1–50), and string counts like `'5; rm -rf /'`, guaranteeing malicious input never reaches the git invocation. Failure paths are covered too: a git error (e.g., not a repository) yields a response with an `error` string and an empty `commits` array, and empty git output gracefully produces an empty list. Notable gotcha for maintainers: the mock assumes `execFile` is always invoked in the `(cmd, args, callback)` form, so any refactor toward `execFileSync` or `spawn` would silently break the harness.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\reports.tsx.summary: This file implements the admin Reports screen for the Expo React Native mobile app, presenting a catalog of exportable business reports (bookings, revenue/commission, users, provider performance, refunds, GST) alongside headline dashboard stats. The default export `AdminReports` renders inside the shared `PortalScreen` scaffold with pull-to-refresh, uses `StatCard` and `Section` from the local `lib/portal-screen` module, and styles everything via the `lib/theme` tokens. Report metadata is a hardcoded local `REPORTS` array typed by the `Report` interface (title, description, Ionicons icon name, and CSV/PDF/Excel format badge), while the two top stat cards pull `totalBookings` and `totalRevenue` from the `useAdminDashboard` hook in the external `@poojly/api-client` package. The key gotcha is that export generation is entirely stubbed: tapping a report only chains two `Alert.alert` dialogs claiming the export was queued and will be emailed, with no actual API call wired up. Refresh state is managed manually with `useState` around `dashboardQuery.refetch()`, and currency values are formatted with the `en-IN` locale and the rupee symbol.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\dashboard.ts.summary: This file defines the AdminDashboard screen for the mobile app's admin portal, rendering a platform overview with key metrics and recent provider approval requests. It pulls live data through the `useAdminDashboard` and `useAdminPendingApprovals` hooks from the `@poojly/api-client` package, and composes the UI from shared portal primitives — `PortalScreen`, `Section`, `StatCard`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` — imported from `../../lib/portal-screen`, with styling tokens from `../../lib/theme`. The screen arranges six stat cards (users, bookings, revenue, active temples, pending approvals, and a hardcoded "Status: OK" health indicator) in rows, followed by a section listing up to five pending approvals showing each user's name, role, and contact info. Pull-to-refresh triggers `refetch()` on both queries in parallel via the local `refreshing` state. Notable gotchas: a hardcoded `FALLBACK` object with dummy statistics is displayed whenever the dashboard query has no data, so the UI silently shows fabricated numbers on error or first load rather than an empty or error state, and the system-status card is always "OK" regardless of actual backend health. Revenue is formatted in Indian style, converting to lakhs (`₹X.XL`) and using `en-IN` locale grouping for counts.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\revenue.tsx.summary: This file defines the admin portal's Revenue screen in the Expo Router mobile app, default-exporting the `AdminRevenue` component, which presents a platform-wide revenue breakdown with pull-to-refresh. It renders `StatCard` summaries for 7-day GMV and platform commission, a hand-rolled bar chart of daily revenue, and a "By Stream" list with percentage-share progress bars, all composed from the shared `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `StatCard` primitives in `../../lib/portal-screen` and styled with tokens from `../../lib/theme`. It depends on the `useAdminRevenue` hook from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package, but only invokes its `refetch` during refresh — the query's data is never actually rendered. The notable gotcha is that all displayed figures are hardcoded: the `SERIES` (daily totals) and `STREAMS` (Puja Bookings, Store Sales, Astrology, Donations, Subscriptions) constants are mock data, so the screen is presently a UI prototype rather than a live dashboard. Derived metrics are computed inline, including a hardcoded 25% average commission assumption, and amounts are formatted in Indian lakh notation (`₹X.XL`). The bar chart is built from plain `View`s with proportional heights rather than a charting library, keeping dependencies minimal but limiting interactivity.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\settings.tsx.summary: This file defines the `AdminSettings` screen, an Expo Router route under the `(admin)` group in the Poojly React Native app, giving admins a profile card, quick links, feature-flag toggles, and sign-out. The default-exported `AdminSettings` component renders inside the shared `PortalScreen`/`Section` layout from `../../lib/portal-screen`, pulling the current user and `signOut` from `useAuth` (`../../lib/auth-context`) and platform stats from `useAdminDashboard` in the `@poojly/api-client` package, with pull-to-refresh wired to `dashboardQuery.refetch()`. Quick links use `expo-router`'s `router.push` to reach the `/(admin)/support`, `/(admin)/reports`, and `/(admin)/approvals` screens, while sign-out confirms via `Alert` before calling `signOut` and replacing the route with `/(auth)/login`. The `FLAGS` constant enumerates six platform toggles — `video_proof_required`, `nri_pricing`, `razorpay`, `stripe`, `ai_jyotish`, and `auto_approve` — which reveal the platform's domains (puja payout verification, NRI pricing markup, dual Razorpay/Stripe payment gateways, and a Claude-powered astrology feature). The key gotcha is that these switches are purely cosmetic: flag state lives in local `useState` with hardcoded defaults and `toggle()` only flips local state, so changes never persist to a backend and reset on every mount. Styling comes from the shared `theme` module (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`), with Ionicons used throughout.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\support.tsx.summary: This file implements the admin-facing Support screen of the React Native mobile app, default-exporting the `AdminSupport` component, which lists all support tickets with status filter chips, a header summary of unresolved tickets and pending provider approvals, and pull-to-refresh. It fetches data through the `useSupportTickets({ all: true })` and `useAdminPendingApprovals` hooks from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package, and renders via shared portal primitives — `PortalScreen`, `Section`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` from `../../lib/portal-screen` — styled with the `colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, and `borderRadius` tokens from `../../lib/theme`. The central design decision is an adapter layer: the server's `SupportTicketStatus` enum arrives in UPPER_SNAKE form, so `normalizeStatus` collapses `IN_PROGRESS`/`WAITING_ON_USER` into `in_progress` and `RESOLVED`/`CLOSED` into `resolved`, while `normalizePriority` maps `URGENT` to `high`, keeping the existing lower-snake chip and `STATUS_COLOR` wiring untouched. A `relativeTime` helper converts ISO timestamps into compact "5m ago"-style labels for the row subtitles. Display IDs prefer the human-friendly `ticketNumber` and fall back to the first eight characters of the raw `id`, and users are rendered as truncated `userId` strings since no user lookup is performed. Error, loading, and empty states all degrade to `EmptyHint` messages, and refresh awaits both query refetches in parallel. A gotcha worth noting: tickets the server marks `CLOSED` are indistinguishable from `RESOLVED` in this UI, so the "Resolved" filter conflates the two.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\users.tsx.summary: This file defines the admin "Users" screen for the Poojly mobile app, an Expo Router route under the `(admin)` group that lets administrators browse, search, and filter the platform's user base. It default-exports the `AdminUsers` component, which renders a search bar, a horizontal row of hardcoded `ROLE_FILTERS` chips (all, devotee, priest, astrologer, admin), and a scrollable list of matching users built from shared `PortalScreen`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` primitives in `../../lib/portal-screen`, styled with tokens from `../../lib/theme`. Data comes from the `useAdminUsers` hook in the `@poojly/api-client` package, which receives the active role and search string as query params, and the screen wires pull-to-refresh through `PortalScreen` by calling the query's `refetch`. Each row shows the user's name, role, contact, and join date (formatted `en-IN`), with a status badge colored green for "active" and amber for anything else. Notably, the search input is not debounced, so every keystroke updates the query and likely triggers a refetch, and tapping a user only opens a local `Alert.alert` summary rather than navigating to a detail screen, making this a read-only directory with no edit or suspend actions.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(admin)\\_layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the admin section's root layout for the mobile app: a bottom-tab navigator rendered by expo-router's `Tabs` component, wrapped in a `RoleGuard` restricted to `allowedRoles={['admin']}` so only admin users can enter the section. The default-exported `AdminLayout` component declares six visible tabs — dashboard (titled "Home"), users, approvals, revenue, commissions, and settings — each with an `Ionicons` glyph rendered through the small internal `TabIcon` helper, while the support and reports screens are registered with `href: null` so they remain routable but stay hidden from the tab bar. It depends on `expo-router` for navigation, `@expo/vector-icons` for icons, the shared `colors` palette from `../../lib/theme` (stone grays for active/inactive tint, white bar background), and the `RoleGuard` component from `../../lib/role-guard`. Notable choices include hiding the header on all admin screens (`headerShown: false`) and platform-conditional tab bar sizing — taller with extra bottom padding on iOS (88pt) versus Android (64) to clear the home indicator. The `IoniconsName` type alias keeps icon names type-safe by deriving them from `Ionicons` component props.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\availab.summary: This file is the astrologer portal's availability screen in the mobile app, letting an astrologer toggle which of three daily time slots (morning, afternoon, evening, defined in `SLOT_LABELS` with fixed hour ranges) they are bookable for each day of the week. Its default export is the `Availability` React component, which renders per-day `Switch` rows inside the shared `PortalScreen`/`Section` shell and tracks a `dirty` flag to conditionally show a save button that PATCHes the weekly grid to `/api/v1/astrologer-portal/availability` via `api` from `@poojly/api-client`. It depends on the internal `../../lib/portal-screen` layout components and `../../lib/theme` design tokens (saffron/stone palette), plus `useAstrologers` from the API client for pull-to-refresh. Notable gotchas: the schedule initializes from a hardcoded `INITIAL` constant rather than server data, and `onRefresh` refetches the astrologers query but never rehydrates the local `slots` state, so unsaved edits can diverge from what's stored; the save handler also special-cases 403 errors with an "Astrologer role required" alert.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\message.summary: This file defines the messages screen for the astrologer-facing section of the mobile app, wired up through Expo Router's file-based routing as the `messages` route inside the `(astrologer)` route group. Its only export is the default `AstrologerMessages` React component, which renders the shared `Inbox` component from `lib/inbox` with `role="provider"` so the inbox behaves according to the astrologer (service provider) perspective rather than the client's. The file depends solely on the internal `lib/inbox` module and contains no logic of its own, acting purely as a thin routing wrapper. The key design takeaway is that inbox behavior is parameterized by the `role` prop, so any provider-specific messaging differences live in `Inbox`, not here.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\consult.summary: This file is the astrologer-facing consultations screen in the Expo Router mobile app (route group `(astrologer)`), letting astrologers review their booked consultations, filter them by lifecycle state, and act on them. The default-exported `Consultations` component pulls data via the `useAstrologyConsultations` hook from `@poojly/api-client` (called with `role: 'astrologer'`), and mutates state through `useStartConsultationCall` (which returns a video `roomUrl` opened via React Native `Linking`) and `useUpdateConsultation` (which sends uppercase `COMPLETED`/`CANCELLED` statuses after confirmation alerts). Rendering is built on shared internal components `PortalScreen` and `EmptyHint` from `../../lib/portal-screen` plus theme tokens from `../../lib/theme`, with status filter chips driven by the local `FILTERS` constant and a `statusColor` helper mapping statuses to theme colors. A notable fragility is that both filtering and action eligibility rely on loose lowercase substring matching (`status.includes('schedul')`, `includes('progress')`) rather than exact enum comparisons, so unexpected status strings could mis-classify, and `canJoin` and `canEnd` currently share identical conditions so both buttons appear together. The local `Consultation` interface also reveals API inconsistency, falling back from `clientName` to `devoteeName`, and the join flow short-circuits by opening an existing `roomUrl` directly before calling the start-call mutation. Amounts and dates are formatted for the Indian market using `en-IN` locale and the rupee symbol, and pull-to-refresh is wired through `PortalScreen`'s refetch callback.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\subscri.summary: This file defines the astrologer-facing subscription route in the mobile app's Expo Router navigation tree, living under the `(astrologer)` route group. It exports a single default React component, `AstrologerSubscription`, which is a thin wrapper that renders the shared `SubscriptionScreen` component imported from `apps/mobile/lib/subscription-screen` with its `role` prop hardcoded to `"astrologer"`. The only dependencies are React and that internal shared screen module. The design intent is that subscription UI is implemented once in a role-aware shared component, with each route group's file merely supplying the role context — so any astrologer-specific behavior (pricing tiers, benefits, payment flow) is expected to be handled inside `SubscriptionScreen` via the role prop rather than duplicated here. Notably, this file contains no logic of its own; changing what astrologers see requires editing the shared screen, and the route's URL path is derived from the filename and directory structure by Expo Router conventions.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\dashboa.summary: This file is the Astrologer Dashboard screen for the mobile app, living at the Expo Router route `(astrologer)/dashboard`, and it gives an astrologer a glanceable summary of their day: earnings, consultation count, rating, and today's schedule. Its default export is the `AstrologerDashboard` React component, supported by a small local `inr` helper that formats amounts as Indian Rupees using the `en-IN` locale. Data comes from the `useAstrologerDashboard` hook in the `@poojly/api-client` package, which returns React Query-style state (`data`, `isLoading`, `isError`, `refetch`) exposing `todayConsultations` and a `stats` object with fields like `todayCount`, `earningsToday`, `monthEarnings`, `rating`, and `ratingCount`. Rendering is built entirely on shared portal primitives from `../../lib/portal-screen` — `PortalScreen`, `Section`, `StatCard`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` — themed via `colors` and `spacing` from `../../lib/theme`. Pull-to-refresh is wired manually through a local `refreshing` state that calls `dashboardQuery.refetch()`. The screen renders stats as a 2x2 grid of `StatCard`s with accent colors drawn from the theme's saffron, green, and amber palettes, followed by a "Today's Schedule" list. Notably, the code is defensively written with null-coalescing throughout (`stats ?? {}`, `c.clientName ?? 'Client'`), so partial or missing API payloads degrade gracefully, and loading, error, and empty states all funnel through `EmptyHint` with distinct messages. One small gotcha: the status pill color only distinguishes `confirmed` (green) from everything else (amber), so any other statuses the backend emits will all render amber.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\profile.summary: This file is the astrologer-facing profile screen for the mobile app, registered as the expo-router route `(astrologer)/profile`, and its default-exported `AstrologerProfile` component renders the signed-in astrologer's identity card (avatar, name, email, experience, rating), a messages inbox entry, bio, per-minute rates, and specialization tags. It builds on the shared portal scaffolding — `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` from `lib/portal-screen`, `MessagesEntry` from `lib/inbox`, and theme tokens from `lib/theme` — and pulls session state from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context` plus server data via the `useAstrologers` hook from the `@poojly/api-client` package, with pull-to-refresh wired to the query's `refetch`. Notably, there is no dedicated "current astrologer" endpoint: the screen finds the user's record by scanning the full astrologers list and matching on `name` or `email`, a fragile heuristic. Chat and video rates are derived from `pricePerMinute` at 0.8× and 1.6× multipliers, and hardcoded `FALLBACK_RATES` and `FALLBACK_SPECIALIZATIONS` are shown when the backend record is missing, so displayed data may not reflect reality. Sign-out is a destructive-confirmed `Alert` that calls `signOut` and then `router.replace('/(auth)/login')`.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(astrologer)\\_layout.summary: This file defines the tab navigation shell for the astrologer-facing section of the Expo mobile app, declared as the `_layout.tsx` for the `(astrologer)` route group. Its default export, `AstrologerLayout`, wraps an expo-router `Tabs` navigator in the internal `RoleGuard` component, restricting access to users with the `astrologer` role. Five visible tabs are registered — `dashboard` (Home), `consultations` (Sessions), `availability` (Schedule), `profile`, and `subscription` (Plan) — each paired with an icon from `@expo/vector-icons` via a small local `TabIcon` helper that types icon names off the `Ionicons` component props. A sixth screen, `messages`, is declared with `href: null` so it exists as a navigable route within the group but is hidden from the tab bar itself. Styling pulls from the shared `lib/theme` palette, using `colors.saffron[600]` for the active tint and `colors.stone` shades for inactive icons and the border. Notable platform handling includes hiding all headers (`headerShown: false`) and adjusting tab bar height and bottom padding based on `Platform.OS` to accommodate the iOS home indicator.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(auth)\\login.tsx.summary: This file is the login screen for the Darshya mobile app, an Expo Router route at `app/(auth)/login.tsx` that exports the default `LoginScreen` React Native component. It offers two sign-in paths via a `Tab` toggle: email/password through `handleEmailLogin`, which calls `signInWithCredentials` from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`) and then does `router.replace('/')` so the root `index.tsx` handles role-based redirection, and phone OTP through `handlePhoneSubmit`, which validates a 10-digit Indian mobile number, converts it to E.164 with a hardcoded `+91` prefix, calls `signInWithOtp`, and pushes to `/(auth)/verify-otp` with the phone as a param. The screen depends on `expo-router` for navigation, `@expo/vector-icons` (`Ionicons`) for tab icons, and the internal `lib/theme` tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) for all styling. A `DEMO_HINTS` list hardcodes eight demo accounts (devotee, pandit, store, astrologer, wellness, gaushala, temple, admin) sharing password `demo123`, with a `fillDemo` helper to populate the form, and the password field is prefilled with `demo123` under `__DEV__`. Notable quirks: `getRoleDashboardPath` is imported from `lib/role-paths` but never used (an inline comment explains the deliberate choice to route to `/` instead), phone input strips non-digits and is India-only, and errors surface via `Alert.alert` rather than inline form validation.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(auth)\\verify-otp.ts.summary: This file defines the OTP verification screen for the mobile app's phone-authentication flow, rendered at the `(auth)/verify-otp` route after a user requests a login code. Its default export, `VerifyOtpScreen`, reads the `phone` parameter from the route via expo-router's `useLocalSearchParams` and renders six single-digit `TextInput` boxes with auto-advance on entry, backspace-to-previous navigation, and automatic submission once all digits are filled. It depends on the internal `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` for the `verifyOtp` and `signInWithOtp` operations, on `lib/theme` for the shared saffron/stone color and spacing tokens, and on expo-router for navigation, `Ionicons` from `@expo/vector-icons` for the back button, and React Native core components. On successful verification it replaces the stack with the root route `/`; on failure it shows an alert, clears all digits, and refocuses the first box. A resend control is gated by a 30-second countdown (`RESEND_SECONDS`) implemented with an interval effect that stops at zero, and resending simply re-calls `signInWithOtp` to trigger a fresh code. Notable details: inputs use `textContentType="oneTimeCode"` for iOS autofill, digits are stripped of non-numeric characters, all inputs disable while a request is in flight, and the screen alerts and bails early if the `phone` param is missing.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(auth)\\signup.tsx.summary: This file defines the signup screen for the Poojly/Darshya mobile app, routed via Expo Router under the `(auth)` group, and guides new users through a two-step flow: first picking a role, then entering account details. Its default export, `SignupScreen`, renders a role-selection step driven by the `ROLE_OPTIONS` constant (devotee, priest, store_owner, astrologer, wellness_instructor, temple_manager, each with an Ionicons glyph and description) followed by a details form collecting full name, email, optional phone, and password. The screen depends on `useAuth` from `../../lib/auth-context` for the `signUpWithCredentials` call, imports the `UserRole` type from the shared `@poojly/api-client` package, pulls styling tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `../../lib/theme`, and uses `expo-router`'s `router` for navigation. Notable design choices include client-side validation that blocks submission on empty required fields or passwords under 6 characters, normalization of email to trimmed lowercase before sending, and a `Step` state machine where the back button contextually returns to role selection or exits the flow. Errors surface through React Native `Alert` rather than inline UI, a `busy` flag disables inputs and shows a spinner during the async signup call, and success triggers `router.replace('/')` so the user can't navigate back to the form. The layout wraps everything in `KeyboardAvoidingView` (padding behavior only on iOS) with `keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"` so role cards remain tappable while the keyboard is open, and a footer link routes to `/(auth)/login` via a type-cast path.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(auth)\\_layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the root layout for the `(auth)` route group in the Expo mobile app, wrapping the unauthenticated flow in a native stack navigator. It exports a single default component, `AuthLayout`, which renders an Expo Router `Stack` containing three screens: `login`, `verify-otp`, and `signup` — together covering the phone-number/OTP sign-in and registration journey. Its only dependency is the `expo-router` library, from which it imports `Stack`; the `(auth)` parenthesized folder means these routes are grouped for layout purposes without adding an "auth" segment to the URL. Notable configuration choices include hiding the native header on all screens (`headerShown: false`), forcing a warm cream background (`#FFF7ED`) to prevent white flashes during transitions, and standardizing on a `slide_from_right` push animation for every screen in the group. Any new screen added to the `(auth)` folder must be registered here to participate in this shared styling.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(devotee)\\consultati.summary: This file defines `DevoteeConsultations`, the mobile screen where devotee users view and manage their booked astrology consultations, deliberately mirroring the web `/profile/consultations` page (commit 3b56f47). It consumes the `useMyConsultations` and `useCancelConsultation` hooks plus the `MyConsultation` type from the `@poojly/api-client` package, and renders through the shared `PortalScreen` and `EmptyHint` components from `lib/portal-screen` with styling tokens from `lib/theme`. A key constraint called out in the header comment: it targets the newer `/api/v1/consultation/*` endpoints (introduced 2026-05-30, commit b71b06c), not the legacy `/astrology/consultations` route that the astrologer-portal screen still uses. The screen offers status filter chips (all, pending_payment, confirmed, completed, cancelled), pull-to-refresh, an inline error banner, and per-consultation cards showing astrologer name, reference, duration, INR amount, and scheduled time formatted with the `en-IN` locale. The "Join Call" action only appears for confirmed consultations with a `jitsiUrl` and opens the video room externally via `Linking.openURL`. Cancellation is allowed only in `pending_payment` or `confirmed` states, is gated behind a confirmation alert citing the 24-hour refund rule (business rule #5), and branches its success messaging on the mutation's `alreadyCancelled` and `refundEligible` flags. Per-card cancel spinners are tracked with a local `cancellingId` state so only the targeted card shows progress.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(devotee)\\bookings.t.summary: This file defines `DevoteeBookings`, the default-exported Expo Router screen at `app/(devotee)/bookings.tsx` in the Poojly mobile app, which renders a devotee's booking history with status filter chips (All, Upcoming, Completed, Cancelled), pull-to-refresh, an inline error banner, and an `EmptyHint` when no bookings exist. It fetches data via the `useBookings` React Query hook from `@poojly/api-client` and builds the UI from shared primitives — `PortalScreen`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` from `lib/portal-screen` — styled with the `colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, and `borderRadius` tokens from `lib/theme`. Filtering is done client-side using loose `String.includes` heuristics on the lowercased status (e.g. 'confirm', 'pend', 'priest_assigned' count as upcoming; 'complet', 'deliver', 'video' count as completed), which tolerates varied backend status strings but is fragile if new statuses appear. The render code is defensive against inconsistent API shapes, treating bookings as `any` and falling back across fields like `pujaName ?? pujaType?.name ?? bookingNumber` and `totalAmount ?? priceAmount`, and slicing ISO dates on 'T' before display. Status badges are color-coded semantically — green for completed, red for cancelled, saffron for confirmed/priest-assigned, amber otherwise — and amounts are formatted as INR using `toLocaleString('en-IN')`. Refresh state is tracked manually in local `refreshing` state wrapping `bookingsQuery.refetch()` rather than using React Query's built-in `isRefetching`.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(devotee)\\donations..summary: This file defines `DonationsScreen`, the default-exported React Native screen for the devotee app's donations route (`app/(devotee)/donations.tsx`), which lets a devotee create a Razorpay donation order and then manually confirm payment. It collects amount (INR, digit-sanitized), cause, and optional donor name, email, and PAN (auto-uppercased, capped at 10 chars for 80G tax receipts), validating via `Alert` dialogs before submitting. Data flow runs through two TanStack Query mutation hooks, `useCreateDonationOrder` and `useVerifyDonation`, imported from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package, and the UI is built on the shared `PortalScreen` wrapper and design tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `../../lib/theme`. The payment flow is a two-step handoff: after order creation the screen extracts a payment link from the loosely-typed response (`paymentUrl ?? shortUrl ?? url`) and opens it externally with `Linking.openURL`, storing the returned order ID so a second "I have paid — verify donation" button can poll for confirmation. Notable gotchas include the defensive `any`-typed response parsing (suggesting an unstable backend contract), the absence of any deep-link callback or webhook listener — verification is entirely user-initiated — and the fallback alert telling users to "check the dashboard" when no payment URL is returned.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(devotee)\\darshan-pl.summary: This file implements the mobile app's live darshan (temple livestream) player screen, exported as the default `DarshanPlayerScreen` component for the devotee route group. It reads `id`, `url`, and `title` from expo-router's `useLocalSearchParams` and fetches stream metadata (title, deity, viewerCount, description) via the `useDarshanStream` hook from `@poojly/api-client`, with passed-in params acting as fallbacks. Playback handles two stream types: YouTube URLs are converted to embed URLs by `youtubeEmbedUrl`, while HLS/AWS IVS streams (detected by `isHlsUrl` via `.m3u8` or `ivs.*.amazonaws.com` patterns) are played through generated inline HTML (`hlsHtml`) that loads hls.js from the jsdelivr CDN inside a WebView, since Android WebViews lack native HLS support. A key design decision is lazily `require()`-ing `react-native-webview` inside a try/catch so bare RN environments without the module degrade gracefully to an external-browser fallback via `Linking.openURL`. The screen also offers pull-to-refresh that refetches the stream, a share action that builds UTM-tagged `darshya.online/darshan/{id}` links through React Native's `Share` API, and a donate button routing to `/(devotee)/donations`. Notable gotchas: the HLS page starts muted and unmutes after 800ms to satisfy autoplay policies, and the Save/heart toggle is purely local state that is never persisted to any backend. Styling relies on the shared `colors`, `spacing`, and `fontSize` tokens from `../../lib/theme`.
