It fetches data through the shared `@poojly/api-client` hooks `useStoreOrders` and `useUpdateStoreOrderStatus`, and builds its UI on the internal `PortalScreen` wrapper, `EmptyHint` placeholder, and the `colors`/`spacing`/`fontSize`/`borderRadius` tokens from `../../lib/theme`. Filtering is done client-side against the fixed `FILTERS` list, and the "Change status" button opens a React Native `Alert` populated from `STATUS_OPTIONS`, calling the mutation and showing an error alert on failure. A notable gotcha is the defensive `Order` interface, which declares duplicate field aliases (`orderNumber`/`number`, `customerName`/`customer`, `itemCount`/`items`, `totalAmount`/`amount`) because the backend response shape is not strictly typed—the component falls back through each alias at render time. The `statusColor` helper assigns pill colors via loose substring matching on the lowercased status, so any status containing "ship" or "pack" is covered. Currency is hardcoded to Indian formatting (`₹` with `en-IN` grouping), and pull-to-refresh is tracked with local `refreshing` state wrapping `ordersQuery.refetch()` rather than the query's own fetching flags.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(store-admin)\\_layou.summary: This file defines the root layout for the `(store-admin)` route group in the Expo mobile app, rendering a bottom tab navigator via expo-router's `Tabs` component. The entire section is wrapped in the `RoleGuard` component (from `lib/role-guard`), restricting access to users with the `store_owner` role, so it acts as the access-control boundary for the store admin area. It registers five visible tabs—dashboard (titled "Home"), products, orders, revenue, and reviews—each with an `Ionicons` icon from `@expo/vector-icons`, plus a sixth `messages` screen whose `href: null` option keeps it routable but hidden from the tab bar. Styling pulls from the shared `colors` palette in `lib/theme`, using `saffron[600]` for the active tint and `stone[400]` for inactive, with headers disabled across all screens. A notable gotcha is the platform-conditional tab bar sizing: height 88 with 28px bottom padding on iOS versus 64/8 on Android, hand-tuned to accommodate the iOS home indicator, so any design change must be verified on both platforms.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\dashboard.t.summary: This file defines the default-exported `TempleDashboard` screen, the home view for the temple role in the Expo Router `(temple)` route group of the mobile app. It pulls data via the `useDarshan` and `useTemples` React Query hooks from `@poojly/api-client`, then renders a `PortalScreen` (from `../../lib/portal-screen`) containing `StatCard` tiles, a `MessagesEntry` inbox widget (from `../../lib/inbox`, scoped to the `temple` role group), and a list of currently live darshan streams built with `Section`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint`, with styling tokens from `../../lib/theme`. Pull-to-refresh is wired through a local `refreshing` state that refetches both queries in parallel. Live streams are derived by filtering on `status === 'live'` (case-insensitive) and summing `viewerCount` across all streams, with only the top five shown and Indian-locale number formatting via `toLocaleString('en-IN')`. Notable gotchas: the "Bookings (Today)" value of 42 and "Donations (Mo)" value of ₹1,84,500 are hardcoded placeholders rather than live data, and `templesQuery` results are never actually rendered—only refetched—so the temples data currently serves no display purpose.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\messages.ts.summary: This file defines the `TempleMessages` screen, an Expo Router route inside the `(temple)` route group of the mobile app. Its sole job is to render the provider-facing message inbox: it delegates all functionality to the shared `Inbox` component imported from `../../lib/inbox`, passing a hardcoded `role="provider"` prop. The default-exported `TempleMessages` component contains no local state, logic, or styling of its own, making it a thin routing wrapper. The key dependency is the internal `lib/inbox` module, which presumably uses the `role` prop to tailor inbox behavior for different user types (e.g., provider versus other roles elsewhere in the app). The notable design pattern here is role-based component reuse — separate route files render the same `Inbox` component with different roles rather than duplicating inbox implementations. Anyone changing message behavior for providers should look to `lib/inbox`, not this file.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(store-admin)\\produc.summary: This file defines `StoreProducts`, the store-admin mobile screen (Expo/React Native) for browsing the product catalogue and adding new products. The default-exported component fetches data via `useProducts` from `@poojly/api-client`, renders rows with the shared `PortalScreen`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` primitives from `../../lib/portal-screen`, and derives stock badges (Out/Low/In stock) from quantity thresholds, formatting prices in ₹ with the `en-IN` locale. A bottom-sheet `Modal` hosts an add-product form (local `Field` helper, `CreateProductForm` state) that validates name, price, and stock client-side with `Alert` dialogs, then POSTs to `/api/v1/store-admin/products` through the `api` client and invalidates the `['store', 'products']` React Query key via `useQueryClient`. The major gotcha is the hardcoded `FALLBACK` array of sample devotional products: it is shown verbatim when the API returns nothing, and even real API results are merged with fallback values by array index (stock always comes from `FALLBACK`, and missing titles/prices are filled from it), so displayed data can silently mix fabricated and real values. Other dependencies include `@expo/vector-icons` (`Ionicons`) and the local `theme` module for colors, spacing, and typography. The modal uses `KeyboardAvoidingView` on iOS, regex-sanitizes numeric inputs, and blocks dismissal while a submission is in flight.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(store-admin)\\review.summary: This file is the Expo Router route screen for the store-admin reviews page, rendering a read-only list of customer product reviews for the merchant's store. Its default export, `StoreReviews`, fetches data through the `useStoreAdminReviews` hook from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package (a React Query–style hook exposing `data`, `refetch`, `isLoading`, and `isError`), and renders each review as a card showing product name, customer, relative timestamp, a star rating, and an optional comment. It builds on shared local UI primitives — `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` from `../../lib/portal-screen` — plus design tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `../../lib/theme`, and uses `Ionicons` from `@expo/vector-icons` for the star display. Two small local helpers support it: `Stars`, which always renders five icons and fills `count` of them, and `relTime`, which buckets timestamps into "today", "Nd ago", or "Nmo ago" labels. Notable choices: pull-to-refresh is wired manually via local `refreshing` state wrapping `reviewsQuery.refetch()`, and the three query states (loading, error, empty) each get a distinct `EmptyHint` message rather than a spinner or retry button. The screen is purely presentational — there is no reply, moderation, or filtering capability, and missing fields fall back to defaults like "Store", "Customer", and a zero-star outline.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\donations.t.summary: This file implements the temple portal's Donations screen in the mobile app (an Expo Router route under `(temple)`), letting temple staff review donation activity. Its default export, `TempleDonations`, fetches data via the `useTemplePortalDonations` hook from `@poojly/api-client` and renders it through shared building blocks from `../../lib/portal-screen` (`PortalScreen`, `Section`, `StatCard`, `ListRow`, `EmptyHint`), styled with tokens from `../../lib/theme`. Two `StatCard`s summarize today's paid total and the all-time paid total, while the list shows each donation's donor, receipt number, relative timestamp (via the local `relTime` helper), amount, and a color-coded status driven by the `STATUS_COLOR` map for paid, created, and failed states. Notably, both totals are computed client-side by filtering and summing the fetched donations, so they reflect only what the query returns rather than server-side aggregates. Pull-to-refresh triggers `donationsQuery.refetch()`, and loading, error, and empty states all degrade to `EmptyHint` messages. The code is defensive about missing fields: donor falls back to "Anonymous", status to "created", and amounts to 0, with INR values formatted using the `en-IN` locale.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\subscriptio.summary: This file is an Expo Router route screen for the mobile app, located at the `(temple)/subscription` path, and it exists solely to wire the subscription page into the temple-facing section of the app. Its default export, `TempleSubscription`, is a thin wrapper that renders the shared `SubscriptionScreen` component imported from `lib/subscription-screen`, passing a hardcoded `role` prop of `"temple_manager"`. The only dependencies are React and the internal `SubscriptionScreen` module, which contains all the actual subscription logic and UI. The notable design pattern here is role-based screen reuse: rather than duplicating subscription code per user type, each route group (such as `(temple)`) contributes a minimal wrapper that injects its role, letting `SubscriptionScreen` tailor behavior accordingly. There is no local state, styling, or business logic in this file, so any changes to subscription behavior should be made in the shared component rather than here.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\messages..summary: This file defines the WellnessMessages screen for the mobile app's wellness section, serving as the provider-facing messaging inbox route. It lives under the `(wellness)` route group in an Expo Router-style file-based routing setup, so the path segment `messages` maps to this screen. Its single default export, the `WellnessMessages` component, is a thin wrapper that renders the shared `Inbox` component imported from `../../lib/inbox` with the `role` prop hardcoded to `"provider"`. The key dependency is the internal `lib/inbox` module, which contains all the actual inbox logic; this file contributes no behavior of its own beyond role configuration. The notable design decision is that the same `Inbox` component is presumably reused across roles (e.g., patient vs. provider), with the route file acting purely as a role-specific entry point — so any changes to messaging behavior should be made in `lib/inbox`, not here.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\pujas.tsx.summary: This file defines the `TemplePujas` screen (default export) for the temple-portal route group `(temple)` in the Expo Router mobile app, letting temple staff view their configured puja offerings and toggle each one's availability. It fetches data via the `usePujas` hook from the `@poojly/api-client` package, reading the list from `pujasQuery.data?.data`, and renders cards through shared layout primitives `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` from `../../lib/portal-screen`, styled with tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `../../lib/theme` and icons from `@expo/vector-icons`. Pull-to-refresh is wired to `pujasQuery.refetch()` with a local `refreshing` flag. A key gotcha is that the enabled/priest-assigned toggles live only in a local `useState` map keyed by puja id (`OfferingState`), defaulting to enabled — no mutation is sent to the backend, so toggles are cosmetic and reset on remount or refetch. Likewise, the "Priest assigned" badge is hardcoded rather than derived from query data, durations fall back to a default of 120 minutes, and the "Add Puja Type" button merely shows an `Alert` redirecting users to the web portal instead of supporting in-app creation.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\_layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Expo Router layout for the `(temple)` route group in the mobile app, defining the bottom-tab navigator that temple managers see after entering their section. Its default export, `TempleLayout`, wraps a `Tabs` navigator from expo-router in the internal `RoleGuard` component (from `lib/role-guard`), restricting the entire section to users with the `temple_manager` role. It registers five visible tabs — `dashboard`, `streams`, `pujas`, `donations`, and `subscription` — each with an Ionicons glyph rendered through the small local `TabIcon` helper, plus a `messages` screen that remains routable but is hidden from the tab bar via `href: null`. Styling pulls from the shared `colors` palette in `lib/theme`, using saffron for the active tint and stone tones for inactive icons and borders. Notable details: headers are suppressed for all tabs, and the tab bar height and padding are platform-conditional (taller with extra bottom padding on iOS to clear the home indicator). Gotcha: any role other than `temple_manager` hitting this group will be bounced by `RoleGuard` before the tabs render.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(temple)\\streams.tsx.summary: This file defines the default-exported `TempleStreams` screen for the mobile app's `(temple)` route group, rendering a read-only list of a temple's configured darshan (live video) streams. It fetches data through the `useDarshan` hook from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package and displays results with shared UI primitives `PortalScreen`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` from `lib/portal-screen`, styled via theme tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `lib/theme` and `Ionicons` from `@expo/vector-icons`. Each row shows the stream title, temple deity/city, and a LIVE versus SCHEDULED status badge derived by lowercasing `s.status`, with live rows also showing an `en-IN`-formatted viewer count. A deliberate product constraint is surfaced throughout: because live streaming depends on AWS IVS, the screen shows an informational notice that stream controls live on the web portal, and the "Schedule Stream" button only fires an `Alert` redirecting users to web rather than creating anything. Pull-to-refresh is wired manually via a local `refreshing` state wrapping `darshanQuery.refetch()`. One gotcha is that the query result is cast to `any[]`, so fields like `s.temple`, `s.viewerCount`, and `s.status` are accessed without type safety.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\dashboard.summary: This file defines the `WellnessDashboard` React Native screen, an Expo Router route under the `(wellness)` group in the mobile app, which gives wellness teachers a glanceable overview of their sessions and business stats. It exports a single default component that fetches session data via the `useWellnessSessions` hook from the `@poojly/api-client` package and renders it using the shared `PortalScreen` scaffold plus `Section`, `StatCard`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint` primitives imported from the local `lib/portal-screen` module, with styling tokens (`colors`, `spacing`) from `lib/theme`. Pull-to-refresh is implemented manually with a local `refreshing` state that wraps `sessionsQuery.refetch()`, and the "Today" stat card derives its value live from `sessionsQuery.data.sessions`. Upcoming sessions are capped at six rows, each formatted with the session's type, duration, level, and a start time localized via `toLocaleTimeString('en-IN')`, falling back to an `EmptyHint` when no sessions exist. A notable gotcha is that the Students, Earnings, and Rating `StatCard` values are hardcoded placeholders rather than real data, so only the session count and list reflect the backend. The screen also lacks explicit loading or error handling beyond the empty state, so failures in the query surface silently as an empty list.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\subscript.summary: This file defines the subscription screen route for the wellness section of the Expo Router mobile app, living under the `(wellness)` route group at `app/(wellness)/subscription.tsx`. Its single default export, `WellnessSubscription`, is a thin wrapper that renders the shared `SubscriptionScreen` component imported from `../../lib/subscription-screen`, hardcoding the `role` prop to `"wellness_instructor"`. All actual subscription logic — pricing, purchase flow, and entitlement handling — lives in that shared library component; this file exists only to bind it to the wellness instructor persona so the route system can register the page. The key dependency is the internal `lib/subscription-screen` module, and the design decision worth noting is the role-based parameterization: the same screen component is presumably reused across other route groups (e.g., different instructor or member roles) with only the `role` string changing. There is no local state, styling, or navigation logic here, so any behavioral changes should be made in `SubscriptionScreen` rather than in this route file.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\profile.t.summary: This file is the wellness instructor's profile screen for the Expo mobile app, routed via expo-router at `(wellness)/profile`, and it renders the signed-in instructor's identity card (avatar, name, email, star rating, hourly rate in INR), bio, certifications, specialization tags, a messages shortcut, and a sign-out button. Its single default export is the `WellnessProfile` component, built from shared internal pieces: `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` from `lib/portal-screen` for the scaffolded layout with pull-to-refresh, `MessagesEntry` from `lib/inbox` for the messaging entry point, `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the current user and `signOut`, and theme tokens from `lib/theme`. Remote data comes from the `useWellnessInstructors` hook in the `@poojly/api-client` package, with Ionicons from `@expo/vector-icons` for iconography. A notable gotcha is that the instructor record is located by matching `i.name === user?.fullName` against the full instructors list rather than by a stable ID, so name mismatches or duplicates will silently break the profile. The screen also leans on hardcoded fallbacks — `FALLBACK_SPECIALIZATIONS` is used when no record is found, and `FALLBACK_CERTS` is always rendered regardless of server data — so the certifications section is presently decorative placeholder content. Sign-out is guarded by an `Alert` confirmation and then redirects to `/(auth)/login` via `router.replace`.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\_layout.t.summary: This file defines the tab navigation layout for the wellness instructor section of the mobile app, exporting a single `WellnessLayout` component that wraps an expo-router `Tabs` navigator. It registers five visible tabs — `dashboard` (Home), `sessions`, `students`, `profile`, and `subscription` (Plan) — each with an Ionicons icon rendered through a small internal `TabIcon` helper, while a `messages` screen is registered but hidden from the tab bar via `href: null` so it can be routed to without appearing as a tab. The entire navigator is gated by the `RoleGuard` component from `../../lib/role-guard`, restricting access to users with the `wellness_instructor` role, and colors come from the shared `colors` palette in `../../lib/theme`. External dependencies are `expo-router` for file-based tab routing, `@expo/vector-icons` (Ionicons) for icons, and React Native's `Platform` and `StyleSheet`. Notable details: headers are hidden (`headerShown: false`) so child screens supply their own, and the tab bar height and padding are platform-specific — taller with extra bottom padding on iOS (88/28) versus Android (64/8) to accommodate the home indicator.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\sessions..summary: This file defines `WellnessSessionsScreen`, the React Native (Expo) screen where wellness instructors view their sessions, schedule new ones, and attach video-room links. It pulls data through the `@poojly/api-client` hooks `useWellnessSessions`, `useCreateWellnessSession`, and `useSetWellnessRoom`, and renders with the shared `PortalScreen`, `Section`, and `EmptyHint` primitives from `../../lib/portal-screen`, theme tokens from `../../lib/theme`, and the current user from `useAuth` in `../../lib/auth-context`. Sessions are filtered client-side into `mySessions`, which includes any session whose `instructorId` is missing or matches the current user — so unassigned sessions effectively appear as everyone's. The create flow is a modal form backed by local state with defaults of type "yoga", 60 minutes, level "beginner", and `startTime` falling back to `new Date().toISOString()` if left blank; notably the start time is entered as a raw ISO string in a plain `TextInput` rather than a date picker. Room URLs (described in the UI as Jitsi/Zoom links) are set via `Alert.prompt`, which only exists on iOS, so Android users get a fallback alert directing them to the desktop app or web portal. Displayed times are formatted with the `en-IN` locale, and mutation errors surface as simple `Alert.alert` dialogs.

apps\\mobile\\app\\index.tsx.summary: This file is the root entry screen of the Expo React Native mobile app, serving purely as an auth-aware redirector: it renders a loading spinner while deciding where to send the user. The default-exported `Index` component reads `user`, `isLoading`, and `isAuthenticated` from the `useAuth` hook (provided by `../lib/auth-context`), and inside a `useEffect` calls `router.replace` from `expo-router` — sending authenticated users to the path returned by `getRoleDashboardPath(user.role)` from `../lib/role-paths`, and everyone else to `/(auth)/login`. While waiting, it shows an `ActivityIndicator` on a saffron-tinted background, with colors sourced from the shared `../lib/theme` module. Notably, the effect waits for `isLoading` to resolve before navigating, so it handles both cold launches (restoring a persisted session) and post-login redirects without flashing the wrong destination. The `router.replace` calls (rather than `push`) keep this splash screen out of the back stack, and the routes are cast to `any`, suggesting expo-router's typed routes aren't being enforced here. The component owns no state or UI beyond the spinner, so all real logic lives in the auth context and role-path helper.

apps\\mobile\\expo-env.d.ts.summary: This file, `apps/mobile/expo-env.d.ts`, is an auto-generated TypeScript declaration shim whose sole purpose is to pull Expo's ambient type definitions into the mobile app's compilation via a triple-slash reference to `expo/types`. It exports no functions, classes, or types of its own; it exists purely so the TypeScript compiler resolves Expo-provided globals (such as environment variable typings and module declarations) across the `apps/mobile` workspace. Its only dependency is the `expo` package's bundled type definitions. The key constraint is stated directly in the file's own comment: it is maintained by Expo tooling, should not be hand-edited, and is intended to be excluded from version control via `.gitignore`, meaning it is regenerated locally rather than tracked as source.

apps\\mobile\\app\\(wellness)\\students..summary: This file defines the Students screen for the wellness section of the mobile app, an Expo Router route under the `(wellness)` route group that displays a roster of paid student enrollments. The default-exported `Students` component fetches its data through the `useWellnessStudents` hook from the internal `@poojly/api-client` package, then renders summary `StatCard`s (total students and lifetime paid sessions) plus a scrollable list of `ListRow` items showing each student's name, last session title, enrollment recency, and session count. It composes shared portal UI primitives—`PortalScreen`, `Section`, `StatCard`, `ListRow`, and `EmptyHint`—from `../../lib/portal-screen`, with visual tokens (`colors`, `spacing`) from `../../lib/theme`. A local `relDate` helper converts ISO timestamps into coarse relative labels like "today", "3d ago", or "2mo ago" using simple day arithmetic. Pull-to-refresh is implemented manually with a local `refreshing` state wrapping `studentsQuery.refetch()`, and loading, error, and empty states each fall back to an `EmptyHint` message. One gotcha: the "Sessions Paid" total is computed client-side by reducing over the returned students array, so it reflects only the fetched page rather than a server-side aggregate, and `total` similarly falls back to the local array length when the API omits it.

apps\\mobile\\app\\+error.tsx.summary: This file is the Expo Router root error boundary for the mobile app ("Darshya"): the special `+error.tsx` filename is auto-discovered by Expo Router, so it renders whenever any route throws during render, with no wiring needed in `_layout.tsx`. Its single default export, `ErrorBoundary`, receives `{ error, reset }` props and renders a friendly fallback card with a "Reload" button that calls `reset()` inside a try/catch to attempt a soft recovery of the route stack. It reports caught errors to Sentry via `@sentry/react-native`'s `captureException`, but deliberately skips reporting when `__DEV__` is true, and Sentry itself no-ops unless `EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN` is configured. In development builds only, the raw `error.message` is shown in a monospace dev block to aid debugging, while production users see a generic reassuring message. Styling is built entirely on the shared design tokens from `../lib/theme` (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) via React Native's `StyleSheet`, keeping the error UI consistent with the app's stone/saffron palette.

apps\\mobile\\app\\_layout.tsx.summary: This is the root layout of the Expo React Native app in `apps/mobile`, responsible for one-time global initialization and wrapping every screen in the app's core providers. At module load it calls `initSentryMobile()` (a no-op without `EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN`) and `initApiClient()` from the `@poojly/api-client` package, wiring the client's auth token to `getStoredAccessToken` (backed by expo-secure-store via `lib/auth-context`) and its 401 handler to `onUnauthorisedMobile`, a single-flight latch that clears the token and routes to login exactly once even under concurrent unauthorized responses. The exported default `RootLayout` component constructs a `@tanstack/react-query` `QueryClient` once via `useState` (retry 1, 30s staleTime, no refetch-on-focus) and nests `SafeAreaProvider`, `QueryClientProvider`, and `AuthProvider` around an expo-router `Stack` that registers the role-based route groups `(auth)`, `(devotee)`, `(priest)`, `(store-admin)`, `(astrologer)`, `(wellness)`, `(temple)`, `(gaushala)`, `(admin)`, and `(onboard)`. A renderless `PushRegister` component invokes the `usePushNotifications` hook from `lib/push-notifications` so push registration happens inside the auth context. Key external dependencies are expo-router, expo-status-bar, react-native-safe-area-context, and `@tanstack/react-query`. Notable gotcha: the base URL comes from `apiBase()` in `lib/api`, a deliberately loud-failing resolver so builds missing `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` crash at first call rather than silently targeting `localhost:4000`, which is unreachable from physical devices.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\posthog.ts.summary: This file is the mobile app's PostHog analytics wrapper, designed as an env-or-noop shim so analytics calls are safe even when telemetry isn't configured. It exports three functions — `capture` for event tracking, `identify` for associating events with a user, and `reset` for clearing identity — all delegating to an internal `PostHogLike` client interface. The wrapper depends on the external `posthog-react-native` package and two environment variables, `EXPO_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` (required to activate) and `EXPO_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` (defaulting to the EU PostHog cloud at `https://eu.i.posthog.com`). The key design decision is lazy initialization via `tryInit()`: the SDK is loaded with a dynamic `require()` inside a try/catch rather than a static import, so the module can be imported safely before the dependency is installed, and initialization is attempted at most once (`initAttempted` flag). All exported functions swallow errors silently, enforcing the constraint that analytics must never crash the app. Full activation requires installing the package, setting the env key in `eas.json` or `.env`, and optionally wrapping the app root in `PostHogProvider`.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\api.ts.summary: This file is the mobile app's shared HTTP client foundation: it resolves the backend API base URL once at module load and exposes thin typed wrappers around `fetch` for the rest of the Expo app. The internal `resolveApiBase()` reads `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` (injected per build profile via eas.json), falls back to `http://localhost:4000` only when the `__DEV__` global is set, and otherwise throws immediately — a deliberate fail-loud choice because localhost is unreachable from physical devices and previously surfaced as a confusing generic network error. Three exports are provided: `apiBase()` returns the bare root URL (no `/api/v1` suffix) for screens that construct their own auth-bearing requests, centralizing what used to be per-screen `process.env` reads that silently misresolved in six screens; `apiFetch<T>(path)` performs GETs against `${API_ROOT}/api/v1`; and `apiPost<T>(path, body)` sends JSON POSTs to the same base. There are no external dependencies beyond the global `fetch` and the Expo/Metro env and `__DEV__` globals. Notable constraints: resolution happens once at import time via the `API_ROOT`/`API_BASE` constants, so a missing env var crashes on first module use rather than at build time, and error handling is intentionally minimal — both helpers throw a plain `Error("API error: <status>")` with no response body parsing, no auth header injection, and no retry logic, leaving those concerns to callers.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\portal-placeholder.ts.summary: This file defines `PortalPlaceholder`, a temporary React Native dashboard component used as the Phase 1 landing screen for the seven provider portals in the mobile app. It accepts `title`, `subtitle`, `iconName`, `accentColor`, and `upcomingFeatures` props to render a colored hero banner (with the signed-in user's `fullName`), a "coming soon" feature list, and a sign-out button, letting each role-specific portal route show branded placeholder content until the real screens arrive. It depends on the internal `useAuth` hook from `./auth-context` for the current user and `signOut`, on design tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) from `./theme`, on `expo-router`'s `router` for navigation, and on `Ionicons` from `@expo/vector-icons`. The sign-out flow confirms via a React Native `Alert` dialog and then calls `router.replace('/(auth)/login')` to return to the auth stack, with the route cast to `any` to bypass typed-route checking. The explicit design intent, stated in the header comment, is that the role guard and sign-out already work at this level so role-based routing can be verified end-to-end in Expo Go; Phases 3-5 are expected to replace each usage with full sub-page layouts, so this component is scaffolding rather than production UI.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\portal-screen.tsx.summary: This file defines the shared screen-scaffolding UI kit for the mobile app, providing a consistent layout language that portal-style screens (dashboards, lists of records) compose rather than rebuilding per screen. It exports five presentational components: `PortalScreen` wraps content in a top-edge-only `SafeAreaView` with a title/subtitle header and a `ScrollView` that conditionally wires up pull-to-refresh via `RefreshControl`; `StatCard` renders a labeled metric with optional hint and accent color; `Section` groups content under a header row with an optional trailing action node; `ListRow` displays a primary/secondary text pair with an optional colored status pill and a trailing value/hint (styled in `colors.saffron[700]`); and `EmptyHint` renders centered placeholder text for empty lists. It depends only on `react-native` primitives, `SafeAreaView` from `react-native-safe-area-context`, and the local `./theme` module (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`), with no network or state dependencies. Notable gotchas: the status pill's translucent background is derived by appending the hex alpha suffix `1A` to `status.color`, so callers must pass 6-digit hex strings; `refreshControl` is only attached when `onRefresh` is provided (with `refreshing` coerced via `!!`); `StatCard` uses `flex: 1`, assuming the parent arranges cards in a horizontal row; and bottom scroll padding is handled by a hardcoded `spacing.xl` spacer rather than safe-area insets.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\deep-link.ts.summary: This file is the mobile app's sole deep-link routing layer: it converts `darshya://` custom-scheme URLs and `https://darshya.online` Universal Links into expo-router navigation targets, primarily for push-notification tap handling. It exports `parseDeepLink`, a pure function that maps a frozen set of paths (puja, darshan, booking, consultation, chat/inbox, order, today) to `(devotee)` group screens like `/(devotee)/puja-details` and `/(devotee)/darshan-player`, and `useDeepLinkRouter`, a hook that wires parsing to navigation by handling both cold launches via `Linking.getInitialURL()` and warm taps via `Linking.addEventListener('url')`. It depends on `react-native`'s `Linking` API, `expo-router`'s `useRouter`, and a contractual pairing with `apps/api/src/services/push-notifier.ts`, which is expected to embed `data.deepLink` in every push payload. Notable design choices include a never-crash policy — unknown or malformed URLs fall back to `/(devotee)/home` and navigation errors are silently swallowed — plus a `useRef`-based dedupe set so each URL is handled only once, a 256-character slug cap, and a `routerOverride` parameter for testability. The custom-scheme parsing relies on the quirk that `new URL` treats the first path segment as the host for non-HTTP schemes. The hook is currently mounted but inert: the URL map is frozen per the handoff doc `docs/engineering/R-Q2-E-014-mobile-push-deep-linking-handoff.md`, and full activation awaits Apple AASA and Android assetlinks.json hosting, `app.json` associated-domains/intent-filter config, an EAS rebuild, and the push-notifier actually emitting `data.deepLink`.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\sentry.ts.summary: This file is the mobile app's Sentry error-tracking integration, wrapping `@sentry/react-native` to initialize crash reporting and capture exceptions for the Expo app in `apps/mobile`. It exports two functions: `initSentryMobile()`, which performs a one-time, idempotent `Sentry.init()` call, and `captureMobileException()`, which forwards errors with optional extra context to Sentry. Configuration is driven entirely by environment variables: `EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN` gates initialization (if absent, the SDK stays off entirely), `EXPO_PUBLIC_ENV` sets the environment (defaulting to `'production'`), and `EXPO_PUBLIC_SENTRY_RELEASE` pins the release, which CI populates as `darshya@<sha>` via the `.github/workflows/sentry-release.yml` workflow. Notable design choices include a module-level `initialized` flag that makes both functions safe no-ops before setup or when the DSN is missing, a low `tracesSampleRate` of 0.1 for performance monitoring, `sendDefaultPii: false` for privacy, and automatic session tracking enabled by default.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\auth-context.tsx.summary: This file is the authentication state container for the Expo mobile app, providing the `AuthProvider` component and `useAuth` hook that expose the current `AuthUser`/`AuthSession`, OTP sign-in (`signInWithOtp`/`verifyOtp`), credential sign-in/sign-up (`signInWithCredentials`/`signUpWithCredentials`), `signOut`, `refreshUser`, and `demoSignIn` to the rest of `apps/mobile`. It builds on `@poojly/api-client` (`api`, `ApiClientError`, `AuthSession`, `AuthUser`, `UserRole`) for backend calls to `/api/v1/auth/*` endpoints, and persists session and user JSON in `expo-secure-store` under the `poojly_session`/`poojly_user` keys, hydrating on mount and proactively calling `/api/v1/auth/refresh` when the stored token is within 60 seconds of expiry. Because `initApiClient()` runs in `app/_layout.tsx` before the provider mounts, the file exports a module-level bridge — `getStoredAccessToken`, `setOnAuthExpired`, and `onUnauthorisedMobile` — with a single-flight latch so concurrent 401 responses trigger exactly one sign-out (audit item P0-8b). Demo accounts mirroring `apps/web/lib/auth-context.tsx` are gated behind `__DEV__` or `EXPO_PUBLIC_ALLOW_DEMO_AUTH` and compile to an empty object in production builds, in which case `demoSignIn` throws (audit item P0-3, closing an offline ADMIN escalation via `admin@demo.com`/`demo123`). Demo sessions are identified by a `demo-` token prefix, which causes hydration, `signOut`, and `refreshUser` to skip all server calls. Notable gotchas: `signUpWithCredentials` silently falls back to a local demo session if the API request fails, so sign-up can "succeed" offline without a real account, and stored users missing a `role` are backfilled to `'devotee'` for backwards compatibility.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\role-guard.tsx.summary: This file provides `RoleGuard`, a React Native wrapper component that protects portal layouts in the mobile app by enforcing authentication and role-based access. It consumes the `useAuth` hook from `./auth-context` to observe the current user, and in a `useEffect` it redirects unauthenticated visitors to `/(auth)/login` via `expo-router`'s `router.replace`, or reroutes users whose `UserRole` (typed from `@poojly/api-client`) is not in the `allowedRoles` prop to their proper dashboard using `getRoleDashboardPath` from `./role-paths`. While loading or while a redirect is pending, it renders a full-screen `ActivityIndicator` spinner styled with `colors.saffron[600]` and `colors.stone[50]` from `./theme`, only rendering its `children` once the user's role is verified. The component explicitly mirrors the behavior of `apps/web/components/AuthGuard.tsx`, keeping the web and mobile guard logic aligned. A notable design choice is that the guard both redirects and blocks rendering on any role mismatch, so protected content never flashes before navigation completes, and routes are passed with `as any` casts due to expo-router's typed-route constraints.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\push-notifications.ts.summary: This file is a push-notification scaffold for the `@poojly/mobile` app, providing the exported `usePushNotifications()` hook that requests permissions, fetches an Expo push token, and registers it with the backend once a user is authenticated. It consumes `useAuth` from the local `./auth-context` module to trigger registration only when a user is present, posts the token (with platform and `aartiOptIn: true`) to the `/api/v1/notifications/register-token` endpoint via the shared `api` client from `@poojly/api-client`, and dynamically `require()`s the optional `expo-notifications` package rather than importing it statically. The defining design decision is its three-layer env-or-noop gating: the hook silently does nothing unless `EXPO_PUBLIC_PUSH_ENABLED` is `'true'`, the `expo-notifications` package is installed (the require failure is swallowed in `loadExpoNotifications`), and the server has an FCM key configured, in which case the endpoint returns a skipped acknowledgement. Errors from the whole flow are caught and ignored, since the author explicitly treats push as an enhancement that must never crash production. Token retrieval also depends on `EXPO_PUBLIC_EAS_PROJECT_ID`, and the header comment documents the activation path: install `expo-notifications` and `expo-device`, enable the env flag, and supply `FCM_SERVER_KEY` on Render to clear gate U5.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\role-paths.ts.summary: This file is the mobile counterpart to `apps/web/lib/auth-context.tsx::getRoleDashboardPath`, translating the shared `UserRole` type from `@poojly/api-client` into Expo Router destinations after login. Its main export, `getRoleDashboardPath`, maps each of the eight roles (devotee, priest, store_owner, astrologer, wellness_instructor, gaushala_manager, temple_manager, admin) to a role-specific route group such as `/(priest)/dashboard` or `/(store-admin)/dashboard`, reflecting the app's design of one route group per role. A second export, `getRoleLabel`, provides human-readable display names for the same roles, notably rendering `priest` as "Pandit." The only dependency is the `UserRole` type, so the file stays pure and side-effect free. Two fallback behaviors are worth noting: unknown roles silently route to the devotee area (`/(devotee)`) in `getRoleDashboardPath`, while `getRoleLabel` falls back to the generic string "User." Because the web and mobile versions are maintained as parallel implementations, any newly added `UserRole` must be updated in both places to avoid drift.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\remotion.config.ts.summary: This file is the Remotion CLI configuration for the remotion-pitch app, an app that presumably renders a pitch video. It exports nothing; instead it calls setter functions on the Config object imported from @remotion/cli/config, and the CLI picks these settings up when bundling or rendering. The configuration sets still frames to be captured as JPEG via Config.setVideoImageFormat, enables overwriting existing output files with Config.setOverwriteOutput, and caps rendering parallelism at 4 worker threads through Config.setConcurrency. Output video is encoded with the h264 codec at a CRF of 21, a visually-lossless-ish quality level that balances file size against fidelity. The only dependency is the @remotion/cli package, which is the sole external integration point. The main gotcha is that overwrite-output is globally on, so re-renders silently replace prior artifacts, and the fixed concurrency of 4 may underutilize larger machines or throttle rendering on weaker CI runners.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\inbox.tsx.summary: This file implements the mobile messaging inbox for the Poojly Expo app, deliberately mirroring `apps/web/components/Inbox.tsx` with the same REST endpoints, 3-second poll cadence (`POLL_INTERVAL_MS`), and `since`-cursor incremental fetch pattern. It exports two components: `MessagesEntry`, a compact dashboard row embedded in provider profile screens (role groups priest, astrologer, wellness, temple, gaushala, store-admin) that polls `/api/v1/conversations?role=provider` every 30 seconds to keep an unread badge fresh and routes to `/(roleGroup)/messages` via `expo-router`; and `Inbox`, the full conversation-list-plus-thread experience parameterized by a `'devotee' | 'provider'` role. Internally it is composed of `ConversationRow`, `Thread`, `MessageBubble`, and `RatingBar`; `Thread` fetches from `/api/v1/conversations/:id/messages` using a `serverTime` cursor held in a ref (deduping incoming messages by id), marks conversations read on open, and starts Jitsi video calls via `POST /start-call`, opening the returned `jitsiUrl` in the system browser through `Linking` because `react-native-webview` is not yet integrated for an in-app sheet. `RatingBar` is devotee-only and only renders once a system message matching `/Call ended/i` appears in the thread, reading and posting to `/api/v1/ratings`. All data access flows through `api` from `@poojly/api-client`, auth gating comes from `useAuth` in `./auth-context`, and visual tokens (`colors`, `spacing`, `fontSize`, `borderRadius`) come from `./theme`, alongside `@expo/vector-icons` and `react-native-safe-area-context`. Notable gotchas: every polling and send error is silently swallowed so the UI deliberately shows stale data rather than error states, the header comment claims calls and ratings are out of scope for mobile v1 even though both are fully implemented here (stale comment), and the role-group navigation push uses an `as any` cast to bypass typed routes.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\theme.ts.summary: This file defines the design token palette for the mobile app, centralizing visual constants so screens and components share a consistent look. It exports four frozen objects: `colors` (saffron, amber, stone, red, and green scales in the 50–900 Tailwind-style numbering, plus `white`, `black`, and semantic `success`/`error` aliases), `spacing` (4–48 in named steps from `xs` to `2xl`), `fontSize` (10–34 from `xs` to `4xl`), and `borderRadius` (`sm` through `xl` plus a `full` pill value of 9999). There are no dependencies — internal or external — making it a pure leaf module that any UI code in apps/mobile can import without side effects. The `as const` assertions on every export lock values to their literal types, which gives consumers narrow TypeScript inference and prevents accidental mutation of the tokens. The saffron/amber/stone combination suggests a warm brand palette with stone serving as the neutral gray, and the numeric color scales mirror Tailwind CSS conventions, easing translation between web design references and React Native styles. Notably, the `red` scale is truncated to only the 500 and 600 stops, and `success`/`error` duplicate `green.600`/`red.600`, so consumers should prefer the semantic aliases for status messaging.

apps\\mobile\\lib\\subscription-screen.t.summary: This file defines the mobile app's subscription management UI, exporting a single `SubscriptionScreen` component that takes a `role` prop and renders the user's current plan alongside available subscription plans. It is built entirely on the `@poojly/api-client` React Query hooks `useSubscriptionPlans`, `useMySubscription`, `useSubscribe`, and `useCancelSubscription`, plus shared local UI from `portal-screen` (`PortalScreen`, `EmptyHint`) and design tokens from `./theme`. The subscribe flow calls `useSubscribe` and then opens whatever payment URL the API returns (`paymentUrl`, `shortUrl`, or `url`) via React Native's `Linking`, falling back to an alert if no URL is present, which suggests checkout completes in an external browser or payment provider. Cancellation goes through a two-step `Alert` confirmation and the copy ("keep access until the period end") implies server-side cancellation is scheduled at period end rather than immediate. The local `Plan` and `MySub` interfaces are deliberately defensive — every field is optional and the code tolerates alternate backend field names (`priceAmount` vs `amount`, `intervalLabel` vs `interval`) — a gotcha indicating the API shape is loose or in flux. Errors from either query are merged into a single red banner, prices are hardcoded to INR formatting (`toLocaleString('en-IN')`), and the already-subscribed plan's button is rendered as a disabled ghost labeled "Current."

apps\\mobile\\metro.config.js.summary: This file is the Metro bundler configuration for the React Native app in `apps/mobile`, and it exists to make Metro work inside a pnpm monorepo where `@poojly/*` workspace packages are hoisted into a flat `node_modules/.pnpm/` layout that Metro's default resolver cannot traverse. It starts from `getDefaultConfig` from `expo/metro-config` (following Expo's official monorepo guide) and layers on four customizations before exporting the result via `module.exports`. First, `config.watchFolders` is set to the monorepo root so edits in sibling packages like `packages/ui`, `packages/shared`, and `packages/api-client` trigger rebuilds. Second, `config.resolver.nodeModulesPaths` adds the root `node_modules` alongside the app-local one, since pnpm leaves only symlinks in the local directory. Third, `config.resolver.blockList` excludes `apps/web`, `apps/api`, `apps/admin`, and `apps/medusa-store` so Metro doesn't try to bundle `apps/web`'s React 19 next to mobile's React 18 and fail with duplicate-module errors. Finally, a custom `config.resolver.resolveRequest` hook rewrites NodeNext-style `.js`/`.jsx` relative import specifiers used by the `@poojly/*` TypeScript sources to their on-disk `.ts`/`.tsx` equivalents, verified with `fs.existsSync` before delegating back to `context.resolveRequest`. The only dependencies are `expo/metro-config` and the Node built-ins `node:path` and `node:fs`. The main gotcha is that all four tweaks are load-bearing: removing any one of them breaks resolution, rebuild watching, or version isolation in this monorepo layout.

apps\\mobile\\scripts\\generate-icons.mj.summary: This is a build-time asset generation script for the mobile app (apps/mobile) that rasterizes a single source of truth, assets/logo.svg, into the PNG icons and splash screen the app ships with. It depends on the sharp image library plus node:fs, node:path, and node:url, reading the SVG from the sibling assets directory and writing outputs back into it. Two helpers drive the work: squareIcon(size, outName) renders the SVG at 384 DPI onto a square canvas with the hard-coded SAFFRON brand background (rgb 234, 88, 12), while splash(width, height, outName) builds a full-size saffron canvas and composites the logo—scaled to 55% of the smaller dimension with a transparent background—at the center. The script runs top-level await calls to emit icon.png and adaptive-icon.png at 1024×1024, favicon.png at 48×48, and splash.png at 1284×2778. Notable gotchas: the brand color and output dimensions are baked in rather than configured, the adaptive icon is identical to the standard icon with no Android safe-zone padding (so the logo could get clipped by circular masks), and the 384 density setting is the lever that keeps the vector source crisp when rasterized.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\scripts\\synth-mus.summary: This standalone build script for the remotion-pitch app synthesizes the Darshya demo reel's entire soundtrack — a ~75-second future-bass track plus SFX stems — purely with numpy/scipy DSP, so the project ships no licensed audio assets. It defines per-instrument generators (kick, snare, hat, supersaw, sub_bass, chord_pad, all shaped by the env_ad attack-decay helper) alongside one-shot SFX synthesizers (whoosh, pop, click, chime), then arranges them into three sections: a filtered-noise buildup (0–15s), a four-on-the-floor drop with bar-aligned supersaw stabs on a Cm–Ab–Eb–Bb progression (15–60s), and a pad-and-final-hit outro (60–75s). The only external dependencies are numpy and scipy (butter/lfilter filters, wavfile.write); it has no internal module imports. Outputs land in public/pitch/audio: a stereo music.wav (soft-clipped via tanh, mono duplicated to both channels), four sfx-*.wav stems, and beatmap.json, which records every kick, snare, stab, and tick with both timestamp and frame number so the Remotion composition can lock visual hits to the music. A key constraint is the non-integer beat grid: at BPM=128 and FPS=60, one beat equals 28.125 frames, so consumers of beatmap.json must rely on its pre-rounded frame values rather than computing their own. One gotcha: the script uses np.random for noise without seeding, so the audio is not bit-reproducible between runs and the WAVs should be regenerated only deliberately.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\beat.ts.summary: This file is the beat-synchronization spine of the remotion-pitch video: it ensures every visual hit (UI pops, text reveals, transitions) lands exactly on a musical event rather than an arbitrary timer. It loads `beatmap.json` (generated offline by `scripts/synth-music.py` from the music track) as the typed `BEATMAP` constant with its `BeatEvent` entries, and exposes derived constants `MUSIC_FPS` (60), `MUSIC_BPM` (128), and `BEAT_SEC`, plus pre-sorted per-kind event arrays `KICKS`, `SNARES`, `STABS`, and `TICKS`. Call sites use the 1-indexed accessors `kick(n)`, `snare(n)`, and `stab(n)` to get the frame of the nth event, `sec()` to convert seconds to frames, `distToLast()` (a binary search returning frame distance to the most recent event, or `Infinity` if none), `hitPulse()` (a quadratic-decay envelope for pulsing UI with the kick), and `appearOn()` (an easeOutCubic pop-in with a sinusoidal overshoot). Notably, the module is pure math with no Remotion or external imports — everything is a deterministic function of the frame number, matching Remotion's frame-driven rendering model. Gotchas: the nth-event accessors silently return frame 0 when out of range, and `appearOn()` deliberately returns values up to 1.08 during its overshoot, so consumers must tolerate progress above 1.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\C.summary: This file defines `Callout`, a React component for the Remotion-based pitch video app (`apps/remotion-pitch`) that renders an Apple-style annotation pointer — a glowing dot, a thin line, and a text label — used during feature deep-dive shots. The component accepts anchor coordinates (`x`, `y`), label `text`, timing props (`startFrame`, `durationFrames`), a `side` direction ('left' | 'right' | 'top' | 'bottom'), and a `lineLength`, then absolutely positions the line, dot, and label relative to the anchor via a `sideMap` lookup. It depends on Remotion's `useCurrentFrame` and `interpolate` for animation and imports the shared design tokens `SAFFRON`, `INK`, and `FONT_BODY` from `../tokens` for consistent styling. The animation is frame-driven: the line draws in over frames 0–14, the label fades in over frames 12–22, and the whole callout fades out during the final 14 frames of `durationFrames`, with all interpolations clamped so values never overshoot. Notable details: the container uses `pointerEvents: 'none'` so it never blocks interaction, labels use `whiteSpace: 'nowrap'` (meaning long text can overflow), and the left-side label offset hardcodes a 200px shift, so label width isn't measured dynamically — callers must choose sides and lengths that fit the composition.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\D.summary: `DiyaGlow.tsx` is a Remotion presentational component that renders a warm, floating ember field — a "diya-glow" ambient atmosphere layered behind the Hook, Payoff, and Outro scenes of the pitch video. Its single export, the `DiyaGlow` React component, accepts props for ember `count` (default 24), `intensity` (opacity multiplier), a deterministic `seed` string, and an `area` flag controlling whether embers originate at the bottom of the frame or anywhere across it. It builds on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, and the seeded `random` helper) and on the internal `../tokens` module, which supplies the `saffronGlow` and `goldGlow` color functions used for the two ember variants. A key design decision is full determinism: every ember's position, size, speed, sway, and color derive from `random(\`${seed}-${i}-...\`)`, so every render of a given frame is pixel-identical — critical for video rendering consistency. Animation is purely mathematical rather than asset-based: embers rise via a modulo-wrapped frame offset, drift horizontally with a sine wave, and twinkle through a sine-driven opacity and scale pulse, with roughly 40% of embers colored gold and the rest saffron. Rendering uses only CSS radial gradients with a 2px blur — no images or external assets — and the wrapper sets `pointerEvents: 'none'` with hidden overflow so it composites cleanly as a non-interactive overlay. One gotcha: the rise "wrap" is handled implicitly by opacity falloff rather than true repositioning, so embers near the top simply fade with distance rather than cleanly recycling.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\B.summary: `BrowserMockup` is a presentational React component in the `remotion-pitch` app that frames a screenshot inside a fake macOS-style browser window for "device mockup on glowing background" payoff shots in the pitch video. The single exported component takes a `src` image (resolved via Remotion's `staticFile` and rendered with `Img`), an optional `url` shown in the address bar (defaulting to `darshya.online` with an inline SVG padlock), a `width` for downscaling, a `glow` toggle, and `durationFrames` to pace its animation. It depends on the `remotion` library (`useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`) for frame-driven animation and on local design tokens from `../tokens` (`INK_DIM`, `saffronGlow`) for the saffron brand glow and muted ink text. The component animates a subtle vertical drift (±6px) across the scene and pulses a blurred radial saffron halo behind the window using a sine wave over normalized scene time. Notable details: the glow halo sizing hardcodes a 16:9 (1920×1080) assumption about the screenshot, the traffic-light dots are produced by a small `dot` style helper, and the `INK` token is imported but never used, which would trip strict lint configs.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\A.summary: `AiPanditChat` is a Remotion component for the pitch video that dramatizes the product's AI Pandit chat feature as a scripted "hero moment." It exports a single component accepting `durationFrames` and a `phase` prop: in `'question'` phase the text "Why do we light a diya?" types out character-by-character with a blinking caret inside a `PhoneFrame` wrapper layered over the real product recording `pitch/video/12-ai-chat.webm` (played via Remotion's `OffthreadVideo` with a darkening gradient), while `'answer'` phase abandons the phone frame for a full-canvas chat layout where the Sanskrit verse कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते streams in, followed by a fading-in English translation, a Bhagavad Gita 2.47 citation, and a decorative "Answered in 0.8s · Gita + Upanishads RAG" latency badge. It builds entirely on Remotion primitives (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, `spring`, `interpolate`, `useVideoConfig`) and the shared design tokens in `../tokens` (colors `INK`, `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`, the `saffronGlow` helper, and font constants), with no external service calls — all copy is hardcoded. Notable details: typing speed is tuned in chars-per-frame constants (`qCharsPerFrame`, `sCharsPerFrame`) so timing is frame-rate dependent; the caret blink is a simple `Math.floor(frame / 12) % 2` toggle; Sanskrit glyphs rely on a Noto Sans Devanagari font stack with a Latin fallback, which matters at render time; and the `durationFrames` prop is declared but never actually used, so phase timing must be controlled by the parent sequence.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\D.summary: This file defines `DarshanStream`, a Remotion React component that renders the pitch video's "Live Darshan" hero moment: a simulated phone livestream of a temple broadcast. It choreographs three frame-driven phases—a saffron spinner with "Connecting to {templeName}…" (frames 0–45 at 30fps), a brief saffron flash over an `INK` fill (45–54), then real footage via `OffthreadVideo` playing `staticFile('pitch/video/06-darshan-live.webm')` (starting at source frame 60, muted) inside a phone bezel, overlaid with a pulsing LIVE badge, a viewer count ticking up from 1,240, and a temple name lower-third. The component accepts `durationFrames`, `templeName` (default "Golden Temple"), and `phoneFrame` (toggles a 440×940 bezel with rounded corners versus a 1200×675 full-bleed frame), and it builds entirely on Remotion primitives (`useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, `spring`, `AbsoluteFill`) plus the shared design tokens module `../tokens` (`INK`, `SAFFRON`, `saffronGlow`, `GOLD`, `FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY`). Design-wise, all timing is hardcoded to 30fps constants (`flashFrame = 45`, `liveStart = 54`) rather than derived from `fps`, so retiming the composition requires editing these numbers; the cinematic intent is that the buffer-to-LIVE transition reads as the "it's happening" beat. Notable gotchas: the `durationFrames` prop is accepted but never used (phase boundaries are absolute, so the scene must be given enough frames by its parent), and `SAFFRON_DEEP` is imported but unused. The viewer count is purely synthetic (`(frame - liveStart) * 1.7 + 1240`, formatted `en-IN`), and a warm `saffronGlow` overlay gradient with `mixBlendMode: 'overlay'` grades the footage to brand.

DualCurrencyMap.tsx is a Remotion scene component for the Darshya pitch video, visualizing the "diaspora wedge" narrative: a saffron payment arc drawn from New Jersey (USD) to Varanasi (INR/temple), with a dashed gold return arc carrying "video proof + prasad" back to the payer, plus a row of cycling currency chips (INR, USD, GBP, AUD, CAD) at the bottom. It exports a single component, `DualCurrencyMap`, which takes a `durationFrames` prop (currently unused in the body) and renders everything as pure SVG/TSX inside an `AbsoluteFill`. It depends on the `remotion` library (`useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, `spring`, `useVideoConfig`) for frame-driven animation, pulls the brand palette and fonts (`BG`, `INK`, `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`, `saffronGlow`, `FONT_DISPLAY`, etc.) from the internal `../tokens` module, and imports `KineticText` from `./KineticText` — though notably that import is never used. Arc drawing is frame-scrubbed via `interpolate` with clamped ranges (frames 10–45 outbound, 40–75 return), and the chip cycle advances every 14 frames with a spring entrance. A key gotcha: the pulsing marker rings and the moving payment dot use native SMIL `<animate>`/`<animateMotion>` elements with wall-clock durations, so they do not scrub deterministically with Remotion's frame counter and may drift or restart when seeking or rendering. Geography is stylized rather than accurate — the two "continents" are hand-drawn quadratic blobs with hardcoded coordinates on a 1400×700 canvas.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\F.summary: FeatureScene.tsx defines a React component for "Act 4" of a Remotion pitch video: a full-screen feature deep-dive shot that displays a product image with cinematic motion. The exported `FeatureScene` component takes a `src` image (resolved via Remotion's `staticFile`), a `caption`, a `durationFrames` length, optional zoom range (`zoomFrom`/`zoomTo`, defaulting to a slow 1.04→1.12 push-in), an optional `callout` annotation with x/y position and side, and a `focusBlur` flag that adds a radial-gradient vignette overlay to simulate camera depth-of-field. It computes per-frame scale and a subtle −12px to +12px horizontal parallax drift using `useCurrentFrame` and `interpolate` from the `remotion` library. The scene composes two sibling components: `LowerThird` for the caption bar and `Callout` for an Apple-style line annotation that starts at frame 10 and runs for the remaining duration. Styling pulls the `INK` background color from the shared `../tokens` module, and the image always gets a mild contrast/saturate boost regardless of the blur setting. One gotcha: the "DOF blur" is purely a darkened-edge vignette with `mixBlendMode: 'multiply'`—no actual blur filter is applied, so the focus effect is only suggested, and the parallax translate is applied after scale in the transform string, which slightly amplifies the drift at higher zoom levels.

FontStyle.tsx is a small React component in the remotion-pitch app whose sole job is to make the brand typefaces available during video rendering by injecting @font-face rules into the DOM. It exports a single component, FontStyle, meant to be mounted once at the composition root, which builds a CSS string covering Cabinet Grotesk (weights 400 and 700) and Satoshi (weights 400, 600, and 700) and inserts it via a style tag using dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The component resolves font paths through Remotion's staticFile helper and the internal FONT_FILES map from ../tokens, with the actual woff2 assets living in public/fonts/. A key design constraint drives the implementation: Cabinet Grotesk and Satoshi are Fontshare families unavailable on Google Fonts, so static-weight woff2 files are bundled locally to guarantee zero network fetches at render time. This matters because Remotion's headless Chromium would otherwise fall back to Helvetica, breaking brand fidelity in rendered frames. All five faces use font-display: block to prevent invisible-text flashes during frame capture.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\K.summary: KineticText is a Remotion component that renders animated "Apple-style" kinetic typography, revealing text word-by-word with a spring-driven slide-up and fade-in. It accepts a `text` prop (with `|` marking forced line breaks) plus styling options (`size`, `color`, `weight`, `align`) and timing controls (`startFrame`, `wordStaggerFrames`) to stagger each word's entrance. It builds on the `remotion` library—using `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `spring`, and `interpolate` to compute per-word vertical offset and opacity from the animation frame—and imports the `FONT_DISPLAY` typeface from the local `../tokens` module. Each word animates with a soft-overshoot spring (damping 12, stiffness 110) from 60px below its final position, with a fixed 6-frame extra delay between lines. Notably, the component only handles the entrance; fade-out at scene end is delegated to a parent `Sequence`, and the container uses `pointerEvents: 'none'` with absolute positioning so it overlays scenes without intercepting interaction.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\I.summary: This file defines `ImageScene`, a reusable Remotion component for the pitch video that renders a full-screen still image with cinematic "Ken Burns" motion and a caption overlay. It accepts props for the image `src` (resolved via `staticFile`), a `caption` string, `durationFrames`, and optional motion controls: `zoom` ('in', 'out', or 'none'), `panY` for vertical drift, and `tilt` for a static rotation. The component normalizes animation progress as `t = frame / durationFrames` using `useCurrentFrame`, then drives scale and translateY through Remotion's `interpolate` — zooming in scales from 1.02 to 1.10, zooming out reverses that, and 'none' holds a fixed 1.04 so the image always slightly overflows the frame. Captions are delegated to the sibling `LowerThird` component, and the background color comes from the shared `INK` token in `../tokens`. Dependencies are limited to the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `Img`, `interpolate`, `staticFile`, `useCurrentFrame`) plus those two internal modules. Notable design choices: the image uses `objectFit: 'cover'` with `overflow: 'hidden'` on the container so transforms never expose edges, and all motion is purely a function of frame number, keeping rendering deterministic and seek-safe as Remotion requires.

IntroCard.tsx is a Remotion scene component in the apps/remotion-pitch video project that renders the opening title card for the DARSHYA pitch video. Its single exported component, IntroCard, fills the frame via Remotion's AbsoluteFill and displays the "DARSHYA" wordmark plus the tagline "Devotion. Verified." centered on screen. The animation is driven entirely by Remotion's frame-based primitives: useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig feed a spring() call that scales the title from 0.6 to 1, while two interpolate() calls fade the title in over frames 0–18 and the tagline over frames 18–36, creating a staggered reveal. All visual styling—background BG, text colors SAFFRON and INK, and the FONT_DISPLAY typeface—comes from the shared ../tokens module, keeping the scene consistent with the project's design system rather than hardcoding values. The component is purely presentational with no props, external services, or side effects; timing is expressed in absolute frame numbers, so any change to video fps or pacing requires retuning the hardcoded frame ranges. Note the use of extrapolateRight: 'clamp' on both interpolations, which holds the final opacity once the fade window ends.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\K.summary: KineticChar is a Remotion presentation component that renders single- or multi-line text with per-character kinetic typography: each letter slides up 50px with a spring overshoot (damping 13, stiffness 120) and fades in over 6 frames, staggered by a configurable `charStaggerFrames` delay. It exists for hero lines in the pitch video (e.g. "Devotion, verified.") where letter-by-letter motion reads as premium, and the code explicitly points to the sibling `KineticText` component for word-level motion instead. The component depends on remotion's `spring`, `interpolate`, `useCurrentFrame`, and `useVideoConfig` primitives, and pulls `FONT_DISPLAY` from the local `../tokens` module. Its `Props` type exposes size, color, weight, startFrame, stagger, alignment, and lineHeight knobs, with a pipe character (`|`) in the `text` prop forcing line breaks (each subsequent line gets an extra 8-frame delay). Notable gotchas: the component absolutely positions itself over the full frame with `pointerEvents: none` so it acts as a pure overlay, spaces are preserved by rendering fixed-width ` ` spans (which still consume a stagger slot), and left alignment hardcodes an 80px horizontal padding.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\H.summary: HookAct.tsx defines the `HookAct` React component, which renders Act 1 (the 0–5 second hook) of a Remotion pitch video for a product called DARSHYA: a minimalist title card showing the brand name "DARSHYA" and the tagline "Devotion. Verified." over a slowly zooming, blurred product screenshot. The component takes a single `durationFrames` prop and normalizes time to `t = frame / durationFrames`, so all animation timing scales automatically with however long the act is sequenced. It is built on the `remotion` library, using `AbsoluteFill`, `Img`, `staticFile`, `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `interpolate`, and `spring`, and it imports brand styling constants (`BG`, `INK`, `SAFFRON`, `saffronGlow`, `FONT_DISPLAY`) from the internal `../tokens` module plus the sibling `KineticText` component for the staggered word-by-word tagline reveal. The hero image (`pitch/img/01-home-hero.png`) zooms from 1.02 to 1.10 scale and fades in late (t 0.4–0.7) at only 0.32 opacity with a blur filter, sitting under a dark gradient overlay so it grounds the card in the product without hurting legibility. The logo enters via a damped `spring` (damping 200, stiffness 60), and the whole title block fades out between t 0.75 and 1 so the next act can take over cleanly. One notable inconsistency: the header comment references a "Devotion is broken." beat, but the actual rendered tagline is "Devotion. Verified."

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\G.summary: This file defines `GapAct`, a React component for the Remotion pitch video that renders "Act 2 — The Gap / Problem," the 5–20 second segment that establishes the pain point before the product reveal. It accepts a `durationFrames` prop and uses Remotion's `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, and `staticFile` to cycle through three desaturated, blurred product screenshots listed in `PROBLEM_SHOTS` (images under `pitch/img/` such as `01-home-hero.png`), applying a slow zoom (scale 1.05→1.12 per shot) and a per-frame jitter for tension. Overlaid copy fades in around 15–30% of the segment and out by 85–100%, rendering a "Today" eyebrow label in `FONT_DISPLAY` and the headline "Scattered trust.|Untrusted priests.|No proof of seva." via the sibling `KineticText` component with staggered word animation. Dependencies are the `remotion` library itself, the shared `../tokens` design tokens, and `KineticText`; there are no external services. A notable design decision is the use of Remotion's seeded `random(`shake-${frame}`)` so the shake is deterministic across renders and workers, which is essential for frame-accurate video output. The mood is deliberately bleak — grayscale, blur, brightness reduction, a dark `#0a0908` base, and a radial vignette — to contrast with later acts. One small gotcha: `INK` is imported from tokens but never used, and the shake reuses the same random value for both axes (halved on Y), so motion is diagonal rather than truly two-dimensional.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\A.summary: This file defines `AnimatedCursor`, a Remotion component in the remotion-pitch app that renders a saffron-glowing cursor dot traveling between scripted waypoints, used to direct viewer attention over product footage without a real pointer or any image asset (pure TSX). It exports the `AnimatedCursor` component plus the `Waypoint` type (x/y in pixels from the top-left, an `atFrame` timestamp, and an optional `click` flag) and a `Props` type accepting the waypoint list and an optional `startFrame` offset. Its dependencies are the `remotion` library (`spring`, `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`) and the internal `../tokens` module, which supplies the `SAFFRON` color and the `saffronGlow` alpha helper used for the dot's box-shadow and the ripple ring. Position is computed per frame by locating the current segment (the last waypoint whose `atFrame` has passed) and spring-interpolating toward the next waypoint; notably, the movement spring eases over a normalized 30-frame curve at a hardcoded 30 fps, making the easing shape independent of segment length and the composition's actual fps, while the click ripple spring does use the real fps — a subtle inconsistency. Waypoints flagged `click` trigger an expanding, fading ripple ring plus a two-phase scale pop on the dot (a spring up to 1.4 followed by a delayed counter-spring that settles it back), but the click scan keeps the largest age within the 18-frame window, so despite the comment it actually selects the oldest active click rather than the most recent. Edge-case behavior: it returns null for an empty waypoint list, parks on the first waypoint before `startFrame`, and renders with `pointerEvents: 'none'` so the overlay never intercepts interaction.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\K.summary: KundliWheel.tsx is a Remotion scene component for the pitch video's fourth "hero moment," showcasing the app's astrology feature with an animated 12-rashi zodiac wheel. It exports a single component, `KundliWheel`, which takes a `durationFrames` prop (notably unused in the body) and renders an SVG wheel whose rings draw in via stroke-dashoffset interpolation, then rotates with a Remotion spring, while a fixed saffron pointer highlights a hardcoded "today's rashi" (Simha, index 4 of the internal RASHIS table of glyph/name pairs). Alongside the wheel it displays marketing copy ("Your birth chart, drawn in seconds"), the highlighted rashi card, and a ₹0→₹15/min consultation price count-up, all composited over a low-opacity (0.18) `OffthreadVideo` playing `pitch/video/08-astrology.webm` fetched via `staticFile`. It depends on `remotion` primitives (`AbsoluteFill`, `OffthreadVideo`, `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `interpolate`, `spring`) and pulls the entire visual language — BG, INK, INK_DIM, SAFFRON, GOLD, `saffronGlow`, FONT_DISPLAY, FONT_BODY — from the sibling `../tokens` module. Animation timing is hand-tuned in frames (draw over 0–30, spring rotation starting at frame 25, highlight fade 30–40, price count 20–50), so the scene assumes a fixed composition fps and a specific video length. Worth noting: the zodiac symbols are raw Unicode glyphs and the center emoji (🪔) depend on system emoji fonts, and the label redundantly renders "{name} (Simha)" even though the name already is Simha, so it only looks right for the hardcoded index.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\L.summary: This file defines `LowerThird`, a React component for the Remotion-based pitch video app that renders an animated caption card in the lower-left corner of a frame. It accepts `text` and `durationFrames` props and uses Remotion's `useCurrentFrame` and `interpolate` helpers to drive a 12-frame fade-in (paired with a 30px upward slide) and a 12-frame fade-out at the end of the specified duration, combining the two opacities via `Math.min` so the card is fully visible only in the middle of its lifespan. Visual styling comes from the shared `../tokens` module — `BG` for the card's semi-transparent background (with a hardcoded `EE` alpha suffix), `INK` for text color, and `FONT_BODY` for typography — keeping it consistent with the rest of the pitch deck's design system. Notable constraints: the fade durations are fixed at 12 frames regardless of `durationFrames`, so very short durations would cause the fade-in and fade-out windows to overlap, and positioning is hardcoded (left 80, bottom 100) rather than configurable via props. The component depends only on the `remotion` runtime library and React, with no external services involved.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\O.summary: OutroCard.tsx defines the closing slide of the Remotion pitch video for Darshya, displaying the product URL "darshya.online", a seed-round call-to-action with the founder contact email, and the tagline "Devotion. Verified." The single exported component, `OutroCard`, is a frame-driven React.FC built on the `remotion` library, using `useCurrentFrame` and `useVideoConfig` to drive animations via `spring` and `interpolate`, all laid out in a centered `AbsoluteFill`. It depends on the shared design-token module `../tokens`, pulling colors (`BG`, `INK`, `SAFFRON`, `SAFFRON_DEEP`) and font stacks (`FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY`) so the card stays consistent with the rest of the video's visual system. The three text elements reveal in a staggered sequence: the URL scales up with a heavily damped spring (damping 200) while fading in over frames 0–18, the contact line fades in over frames 18–36, and the tagline appears over frames 40–60, with all interpolations clamped on the right so values hold after their windows close. Because timing is hardcoded in absolute frames rather than derived from the composition duration, the card assumes a scene of at least ~60 frames and any change to scene length or fps should be checked against these thresholds.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\L.summary: LogoSting.tsx is a Remotion video component that renders the animated DARSHYA wordmark reveal for the pitch video, serving as both the Hook beat's intro and the closing outro card via its `variant` prop ('reveal' or 'outro'). It builds on the shared design tokens imported from `../tokens` (SAFFRON, GOLD, INK, BG, FONT_DISPLAY, saffronGlow) and layers the `DiyaGlow` ember component from `./DiyaGlow` behind the wordmark for ambient warmth, with no raster assets involved. The animation is frame-driven through Remotion's `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, and `spring`: a spring scale-in from 0.7 to 1, a saffron-to-gold gradient underline that draws left-to-right over frames 14–28, and staggered fades for the tagline and, in the outro variant only, the `darshya.online` URL. The reveal variant adds a brief full-screen saffron flash overlay and shows the "Devotion, verified." tagline on an INK background, while the outro switches to the BG background with the "your bridge to sacred traditions" line and a lower-intensity DiyaGlow. A notable gotcha: the component accepts a `durationFrames` prop but never uses it, so all timing is hardcoded to frame ranges and the caller's duration has no effect on the animation. A code comment notes this component replaced an older blurred-hero open from a previous HookAct.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\O.summary: This file defines `OutroAct`, the closing scene (Act 6, seconds 75–80) of the Remotion-rendered DARSHYA pitch video, which fades the background to the brand saffron and reveals the logo lockup with trust microcopy. The single exported React component accepts `durationFrames` and drives all animation from remotion's `useCurrentFrame` and `interpolate`, normalizing time to a 0–1 `t` value: the background cross-fades during the first half, the "DARSHYA" wordmark fades in between 30–60%, and the "20 Verified Temples · 8 Role Portals · Live Today" tagline between 55–85%. It builds on the shared design tokens (`SAFFRON`, `BG`, `INK`, `FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY`) imported from `../tokens`, and depends on the external `remotion` library for composition primitives like `AbsoluteFill`.
