A notable design choice is that the file ships its own `interpolateColor`/`parseHex` helpers to lerp hex colors for the 135-degree gradient, rather than using remotion's built-in `interpolateColors`. Another gotcha is the hard color flip at `bgT > 0.5`, where text switches discretely from saffron/ink-on-light to white-on-saffron, so midpoint frames may show an abrupt contrast jump rather than a smooth transition.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\N.summary: NriSplitScreen.tsx is a Remotion scene component for the pitch video's "gap act," visualizing the trust problem in unverified pandit bookings: the left half renders a bleak, desaturated mock WhatsApp thread with a forwarded contact demanding ₹5000 and dodging receipt requests, while the right half is a dark void with a saffron radial glow where the words "No proof.", "No face.", "No receipt." stamp in sequence above the subtitle "Just blind faith." The exported component takes a single `durationFrames` prop and is built on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, `spring`, `useVideoConfig`) plus the internal `../tokens` module, which supplies the palette (`INK`, `INK_DIM`, `SAFFRON`, `saffronGlow`) and fonts (`FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY`). A glowing saffron hairline "crack" draws down the center of the frame between frames 60–78, splitting the two halves. A notable design decision, called out in the comments, is that the left panel's motion uses a deterministic `interpolate` drift (−8px to 8px across the scene) rather than per-frame random jitter, and the whole component deliberately replaces an older `GapAct` implementation whose blurred screenshot stack was deemed unreadable. Animation timing is fully frame-driven and hardcoded: words spring in starting at frame 20 with 30-frame stagger, scale from 1.3 to 1, then decay to 0.25 opacity, and the chat content itself is static inline mock data.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\P.summary: `PayoffAct` is a Remotion scene component that renders Act 5 (the payoff/CTA, roughly 60–75s) of the pitch video, showing a `BrowserMockup` of the darshya.online homepage over a radial saffron glow, followed by a staged reveal of the tagline "Devotion, verified." and the site URL. It exports a single React component, `PayoffAct`, which takes `durationFrames` and normalizes the current frame via `useCurrentFrame` into a 0–1 progress value `t`, so all animation timing scales with the scene length. It depends on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`), the shared design tokens module (`BG`, `INK`, `SAFFRON`, `saffronGlow`, `FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY` from `../tokens`), the sibling `BrowserMockup` component, and the static screenshot asset `pitch/img/01-home-hero.png`. Three sequential fade-ins are driven by `interpolate` with `extrapolateRight: 'clamp'` — the mockup appears in the first 15% of the scene, the tagline between 25–45%, and the URL between 50–70% — while a `saffronGlow` radial gradient layered behind everything provides the ambient backdrop. The layout is purely absolute-positioned with no interactivity, so the only coupling to the rest of the timeline is the `durationFrames` prop passed down from the parent composition.

ProductClip.tsx is the workhorse presentational component for the Remotion pitch video, wrapping real WebM product screen recordings in branded chrome — a macOS-style browser bezel with traffic-light dots and a URL bar, a phone bezel with a notch, or full-bleed with no frame — so raw footage looks like a polished product shot. It exports a single `ProductClip` React component whose Props control the `staticFile` source path, `durationFrames`, `trimBefore` seek offset, `frame` style, `url` label, `opacity`, muting, and an optional vignette; a private `Dot` helper renders the browser window dots. It builds on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `OffthreadVideo`, `staticFile`, `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`) and pulls brand colors like `INK_DIM` and `saffronGlow` from the internal `../tokens` module. Notable choices: it deliberately uses `OffthreadVideo` rather than `Video` for frame-accurate, lower-memory decoding on a separate thread, and it supersedes the old `FeatureScene` ``-based approach per the header comment. A subtle vertical drift is interpolated across `durationFrames` so footage feels alive rather than frozen, and the vignette is a radial-gradient overlay with `mixBlendMode: 'multiply'`. Gotchas: `trimBefore` is converted to frames with a hardcoded 25fps assumption about the source WebMs, the browser content height is fixed at 760px (and the phone at 460×980), and the imports `INK` and `FONT_BODY` appear to be unused.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\S.summary: SolutionRevealAct is a Remotion scene component for Act 3 (the 20–35s "solution intro") of the remotion-pitch video, rendering the moment the product is revealed after the problem act. It displays the hero screenshot (pitch/img/01-home-hero.png via staticFile) with a slow push-in zoom interpolated from scale 1.0 to 1.15 across the scene's durationFrames, layered under a brief saffron entry flash and a radial-gradient vignette for cinematic framing. The headline uses the shared KineticText component to stagger in "Darshya.|The trust layer for devotion." starting at frame 28, while an "Introducing" eyebrow label springs in via Remotion's spring with a frame-18 offset. It depends on the remotion library (AbsoluteFill, Img, interpolate, spring, useCurrentFrame, useVideoConfig, staticFile) and on internal design tokens (BG, SAFFRON, INK, FONT_DISPLAY) from ../tokens. Notable details: the component takes durationFrames as a prop so timing is normalized to a 0–1 progress value t, the INK token is imported but unused, and the pipe character in the KineticText string presumably delimits segments handled by that component.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\P.summary: This file is the shared visual-primitive toolkit for the Remotion-based SaaS pitch video in `apps/remotion-pitch`: it builds every on-screen UI element as pure vector/CSS (no screenshots or video assets), in a consistent 2.5D glassmorphism style. Its exports include `MeshGradient` (a deterministic, frame-drifting brand-colored blob background), `GlassPanel` (the universal frosted-glass card), `Cursor` (an oversized glowing saffron cursor with spring movement and click pulse/ripple driven by a `clickFrame` prop), `PhoneFrame` and `LaptopFrame` (stylized device bezels), `KineticType` (typography with `mask`, `scale`, and word-by-word `cascade` reveal variants), plus smaller mock-UI widgets: `Skeleton`, `Toggle`, `ChartFromZero`, `LoadingBar`, and `Badge`. It depends only on the `remotion` runtime (`useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `spring`, `interpolate`, `AbsoluteFill`) and the local `../tokens` module, which supplies the color palette (`VOID`, `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`, `MESH`), glow helpers (`saffronGlow`, `goldGlow`), and font stacks (`FONT_DISPLAY`, `FONT_BODY`). The core design decision is that all motion is fully deterministic and frame-driven — components take `startFrame`/`clickFrame` props and use clamped interpolation and spring physics so every animation is reproducible and syncable to beats, with timing expressed in frames rather than seconds. Sizing is mostly proportional to a `width` prop (device frames derive height, notch, and border from it), making primitives resolution-flexible. One gotcha: several imports (`random`, `EASE_OUT_EXPO`, `LINE`, `VOID_2`, `VOID_3`) are unused, and `MeshGradient`'s `seed` prop is accepted but doesn't actually drive the blob positions, which are hardcoded.

This file defines `PujaBookingFlow`, a Remotion scene component for the pitch video that animates a four-step puja booking stepper — select puja, Aadhaar-verified priest, mandatory video proof, and 80G donation receipt — as the "trust beat" of the deck. The single exported component takes `durationFrames` and a `step` prop (1–4) that controls both the stepper highlight and which card is on stage; rendering is delegated to four unexported card components (`SelectPujaCard`, `AadhaarPriestCard`, `VideoProofCard`, `ReceiptCard`) sharing a common `CardFrame` wrapper. It builds on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `spring`, `interpolate`) and the project's shared design tokens from `../tokens` (colors like `SAFFRON`, `SAFFRON_DEEP`, `GOLD`, `INK`, the `saffronGlow` helper, and `FONT_DISPLAY`/`FONT_BODY` type stacks). Animation is entirely procedural TSX rather than screenshots: spring-driven card rises and badge stamps, and SVG `strokeDashoffset` tricks that draw checkmarks and a rotating 80G seal in sync with the frame counter. All content is hardcoded demo data — the Rudrabhishek puja at Kashi Vishwanath Temple priced at ₹2,100, priest "Pandit Vivek Shukla," and a receipt issued by "Bhaktisetu Foundation" — so the component is a fixed marketing asset, not wired to real data. A deliberate product message is baked in: video proof is mandatory ("no video, no payout") and donations are 80G tax-deductible with a PAN-linked auto-filed receipt. Note that the `durationFrames` prop is accepted but unused, and step timings are frame-locked constants (e.g., the stamp lands at frame 20, upload progress spans frames 10–50), so the scene assumes a fixed fps/length when sequenced.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\T.summary: TrustLockup.tsx is the closing scene of the remotion-pitch video — a kinetic "stamp" moment where the tagline "Devotion, verified." locks in alongside a circular saffron seal, intended (per the inline comment) as the emotional anchor of the film, timed so the audio bed drops to silence before it. It exports a single `TrustLockup` component that accepts a `durationFrames` prop (though the prop is currently unused in the body, since all timing is driven by absolute frame offsets). The animation is built on Remotion's `spring` and `interpolate` primitives: the headline slides up with a spring delayed 4 frames, while the SVG seal scale-stamps from 1.6 to 1 with a low-damping spring at frame 14, simultaneously rotating from -20 to -8 degrees and fading in. The seal itself is hand-drawn SVG using `textPath` for the curved "VERIFIED DEVOTION" arc, a checkmark, and the "DARSHYA" wordmark in Satoshi and Cabinet Grotesk fonts. Dependencies include the shared design tokens module `../tokens` (BG, INK, SAFFRON, SAFFRON_DEEP, `saffronGlow`, FONT_DISPLAY) and the `DiyaGlow` ambient particle component, rendered here with 20 flames and a fixed `seed="trust"` for deterministic placement. Minor gotchas: the `GOLD` token is imported but never used, and the scene assumes Remotion's `AbsoluteFill` centering plus a radial-gradient glow layer behind the content for atmosphere.

This file is the transition toolkit for the Remotion pitch video, implementing the "kinetic cuts" mandated by the project's Master Creative Prompt — explicitly banning cross-dissolves in favor of zoom-throughs, whip pans, match cuts, and shatter effects. Its core exports are the transition components `ZoomThroughOut` and `ZoomThroughIn` (scale-to/fro a focal point defined by `fx`/`fy`), `WhipPan` (a blurred, skewed saffron-gold gradient streak sweeping horizontally), `Shatter` (explodes a word into deterministic, spring-animated shards via Remotion's seeded `random`), and `CircleReveal` (a growing clip-path circle for match-cut reveals), plus the `Scene` wrapper that orchestrates `enter`/`exit` transitions selected via the `TransitionKind` union type. Everything builds on the `remotion` animation primitives (`interpolate`, `spring`, `useCurrentFrame`, `AbsoluteFill`) and the local design tokens `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`, and `VOID` from `../tokens` — though notably `saffronGlow` and `VOID` are imported but never used. The `Scene` wrapper adds subtle continuity polish on its own: a 1.08→1 settle zoom on entry, an optional 1→1.12 zoom-out on exit, and a hardcoded 4-frame fade-in, with default transition durations of 12 frames. One structural gotcha: when `Scene` applies the zoom or circle transitions, it passes an empty `<div />` as children to `ZoomThroughIn`/`ZoomThroughOut`/`CircleReveal`, so these operate as pure scale/opacity overlays rather than actually transforming the adjacent scene's content — the "seamless" continuity relies on matching focal coordinates between scenes, not on shared rendered content. `Shatter` pairs `spring`-driven radial distances with golden-ratio-spaced angles and per-shard seeds like `shard-${i}` to guarantee frame-deterministic renders across Remotion's parallel workers. The whip pan direction is fixed (`-1` for entry, `1` for exit), so callers can't customize it through the `Scene` API.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\W.summary: WhooshTransition.tsx defines a reusable full-screen transition component for the remotion-pitch video app, used as a saffron-colored masked wipe between major acts of the pitch deck. It exports a single React component, WhooshTransition, which takes durationFrames and an optional direction prop ('horizontal' or 'vertical', defaulting to horizontal) and renders an animated AbsoluteFill panel whose visibility is driven by Remotion's useCurrentFrame and interpolate helpers. The wipe is achieved by animating a clip-path inset that shrinks from 100% to 0% and back over the duration, while a separate opacity interpolation fades the panel in and out; a nested AbsoluteFill overlays a radial gradient glow built from the saffronGlow token helper. The component depends on the remotion library for frame-driven animation and on the local ../tokens module for the SAFFRON and SAFFRON_DEEP colors and the saffronGlow function, keeping all palette values centralized rather than hardcoded. Notably, the inline comments document a deliberate design decision: this component replaces an older blur(20px) copper (#b87333) wipe, and the team explicitly forbids motion-blur gradients, copper tones, and magic-number translates in favor of the cleaner clip-path reveal. One gotcha is that the timing is purely frame-based, so callers must pass a sensible durationFrames value in the parent Sequence since there is no default duration.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\S.summary: StatCounter.tsx is a Remotion video component for the "Proof" act of the pitch video in the remotion-pitch app, rendering a row of animated stat cards whose numeric values count up from zero; the header comment stipulates that only honest, live-verifiable figures (e.g. 1,635+ pages, ₹15/min, 12 Jyotirlingas) may be shown, and the implementation is pure TSX with no screenshots. It exports the `StatCounter` React.FC, driven by a `Stat[]` prop where each `Stat` carries a `value` (number or string), optional `prefix`/`suffix`, `label`, `icon`, and `sublabel`. It builds on the Remotion runtime (`AbsoluteFill`, `useCurrentFrame`, `useVideoConfig`, `spring`, `interpolate`) and the local `../tokens` design module for colors (`BG`, `INK`, `INK_DIM`, `SAFFRON`), the `saffronGlow` alpha helper, and the `FONT_DISPLAY`/`FONT_BODY` typefaces. Animation is staggered per card: entrance uses a `spring` (damping 18, stiffness 120) offset by `i * 8` frames with a clamped opacity fade, and numeric values count from 0 to target over frames `i*8+6` to `i*8+36`, floored and clamped at the target. Numeric counts are formatted with `toLocaleString('en-IN')` for Indian digit grouping, while string values render verbatim. Two minor gotchas: the `durationFrames` prop is accepted but never used in the body, and `GOLD` is imported from tokens but unreferenced.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the application entry point for the `remotion-pitch` app, a Remotion-based programmatic video project. Its sole job is to bootstrap the video composition tree by calling `registerRoot` from the `remotion` library with the `Root` component imported from `./Root`. It exports nothing itself; all composition definitions live in `Root.tsx` (or equivalent), which this file wires into Remotion's rendering and preview pipeline. The pattern is Remotion's mandatory convention — every Remotion project requires exactly one `registerRoot` call — so this file should stay minimal and any new compositions should be added inside `Root` rather than here.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\components\\V.summary: This file provides vector-drawn mockups of the Darshya devotional app for the Remotion pitch video — every screen is composed from divs, SVG, and shared primitives rather than screenshots or video captures, so each one can be choreographed frame-by-frame (build-ups, typewriter text, skeleton-to-content morphs, chart animations). It exports six screen components: `VectorHome` (landing page with nav, hero, and trust badges), `VectorPujaCard` (a puja booking card with a spring entrance via `GlassPanel`), `VectorAiChat` (the "AI Pandit" chat that types out a question character-by-frame, then reveals a Sanskrit Gita verse and its English translation), `VectorDarshan` (a live-stream view that switches from a spinner/"Connecting" state to a glowing temple with a pulsing LIVE badge at the `liveStart` frame), `VectorKundli` (an astrology screen with a slowly rotating zodiac wheel rendered as SVG), and `VectorDashboard` (analytics view that shows `Skeleton` placeholders for the first 20 frames before swapping in stat cards and a `ChartFromZero` bar chart). It depends on `remotion` for `useCurrentFrame`, `spring`, `interpolate`, and `useVideoConfig`; on `../tokens` for the dark/saffron/gold palette (`VOID`, `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`), glow helpers, and font constants; and on `./Primitives` for `GlassPanel`, `Skeleton`, `ChartFromZero`, and `Badge`. A key design decision is that all sizing is proportional to the `width`/`height` props (e.g. `width * 0.04`), making the mockups resolution-independent, and animation timing is derived purely from frame arithmetic with optional `startFrame` offsets so scenes can be sequenced externally. One gotcha: several imports (`AbsoluteFill`, `staticFile`, `Toggle`, `LoadingBar`) appear unused, and there's a suspicious `!sShown` condition in the `VectorAiChat` caret logic that likely means the Sanskrit typing cursor never renders.

apps\\web\\app\\about\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the About page (`AboutPage`) for the Darshya marketing web app, a Next.js App Router page that tells the company's founding story, introduces co-founders Raghav Sindhwani and Atishey Jain, states four operating principles (video proof, priest-paid-first, documented NRI pricing, diaspora-first), and renders an interactive roadmap timeline. Its only exports are the default page component and a `metadata` object setting canonical URL `https://darshya.online/about` plus OpenGraph and Twitter card tags. It depends on internal modules `lib/jsonld` (`organizationJsonLd`, `brandFaqJsonLd`, injected as JSON-LD script tags for SEO), the `ScrollReveal` wrapper component (which drives the `data-reveal`, `data-parallax`, and `data-scroll-progress` attributes used throughout the markup), and `RoadmapRail` with its `Milestone` type for the sticky-pinned roadmap section; external dependencies are `next/image`, `next/link`, and `lucide-react` icons. Notable design choices: all content (founders, principles, seven roadmap milestones, stats) is hardcoded as typed constants rather than fetched, roadmap entries carry their own accent colors and status values ('shipped', 'now', 'planned', 'vision'), founder emails are derived by lowercasing first names onto the darshya.online domain, and the page makes explicit marketing claims — a 9–10× NRI price multiplier and 100% video-proof bookings — that double as product commitments.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\Root.tsx.summary: This file is the Remotion entry point for the `remotion-pitch` app, registering the renderable video compositions for a 60fps SaaS demo reel that is beat-synced to synthesized future-bass audio. Its sole export, the `Root` component, declares three `Composition` instances — `DarshyaDemo-HD` (1920x1080), `DarshyaDemo-4K` (3840x2160), and `DarshyaDemo-9x16` (1080x1920) — which all render the same `DarshyaDemo` component but select layout via an `aspect` value passed through `defaultProps`. It depends on the `remotion` library for the `Composition` primitive and on the sibling `./DarshyaDemo` module for the scene component plus the shared `FPS`, `DURATION_FRAMES`, and `ASPECTS` constants that keep duration, frame rate, and dimensions consistent across variants. A notable design decision is that one parameterized component serves all three aspect ratios rather than maintaining separate scenes, with the portrait variant framed center-safe for Reels/Shorts distribution. The inline comments flag a practical constraint: the 4K composition matches the UHD master spec but renders slowly, so the HD variant serves as the fast master.

apps\\web\\app\\aarti\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/aarti` route on darshya.online, serving as an SEO-targeted directory of Hindu aarti lyrics pages aimed at queries like "hindu aarti lyrics" and "aarti collection." Its single default export, the `AartiIndex` server component, renders a card grid built from the `AARTIS` data array imported from the internal `../../lib/aartis` module, with each card linking to a per-aarti detail page at `/aarti/[slug]` and displaying fields like `name`, `sanskrit`, `deity`, `durationMinutes`, and `whenSung`. For search optimization it exports a `metadata` object with a canonical URL and injects a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block enumerating every aarti, and it sets `revalidate = 86400` so the page is statically regenerated once per day via ISR. Styling relies on Tailwind with a custom `saffron`/`surface` palette, and icons (`Music`, `Clock`, `ArrowRight`) come from `lucide-react`. Notably, the page doubles as a marketing funnel: a bottom call-to-action section cross-promotes the `/pujas` booking flow, tying the free lyrics content to Darshya's paid puja service. A practical gotcha is that the description and JSON-LD derive counts and URLs from `AARTIS` at build/revalidate time, so the page only picks up new aartis on the next daily regeneration or redeploy.

apps\\web\\app\\aarti\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route (`/aarti/[slug]`) for Darshya's per-aarti detail pages, rendering full devotional song lyrics (Devanagari plus English transliteration), a meaning section, and cross-links to related pujas, deity pages, and other aartis. It exports three things: `generateStaticParams` (pre-builds one page per entry in the `AARTIS` array), `generateMetadata` (per-page SEO title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags), and the default async `AartiPage` server component that renders the page including a schema.org Article JSON-LD block. Its key internal dependency is the `lib/aartis` module, which supplies the `AARTIS` catalog and the `getAarti(slug)` lookup; externally it relies on Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`) and lucide-react icons (`Music`, `Clock`, `Flame`, `ChevronRight`, `ArrowRight`), with styling via Tailwind classes using a custom saffron/surface palette. Notable constraints: the page is fully static with `dynamicParams = false`, so any slug not in `AARTIS` hard-404s via `notFound()`, and `revalidate = 86400` enables daily ISR regeneration. Related-puja links are derived from slug strings with hyphens replaced by spaces for display, the "more aartis" rail is capped at six entries, and the deity callout only renders when `a.deitySlug` is present.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\tokens.ts.summary: This file is the design-token source of truth for the Remotion pitch video app, centralizing brand colors, typography, and motion easings used across video components. It exports the canonical saffron scale (`SAFFRON` #E16318, `SAFFRON_DEEP`, `SAFFRON_LIGHT`), supporting neutrals (`GOLD`, `INK`, `INK_DIM`, `BG`, `BG_SOFT`), plus rgba helper functions `saffronGlow`, `goldGlow`, and `inkShadow` so every glow and shadow derives from the canonical saffron rather than a hardcoded value. The `SAFFRON` value is deliberately aligned with `saffron.500` in the shared `@poojly/ui` package (`packages/ui/src/primitives/theme.ts`), and the comments explicitly warn against reintroducing the old copper `#b87333` drift that previously appeared in components. Typography is exposed via `FONT_DISPLAY` (Cabinet Grotesk) and `FONT_BODY` (Satoshi) with `FONT_FILES` pointing at locally bundled woff2 files in `public/fonts/`, loaded through `components/FontStyle.tsx` — a deliberate choice because these Fontshare families are not on Google Fonts and headless Chromium renders must use the real brand typeface. A separate dark-mode demo palette (`VOID`, `VOID_2`, `VOID_3`, `WHITE`, `LINE`, `LINE_BRIGHT`) and the `MESH` mesh-gradient glow colors (saffron/gold/magenta) support the dark SaaS demo scenes. Finally, the easing presets `EASE_OUT_EXPO`, `EASE_IN_OUT_QUART`, and `EASE_OUT_BACK` enforce a custom bezier/spring motion feel with an explicit no-linear-easing constraint.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\DarshyaDemo.t.summary: This file is the root Remotion composition for Darshya's 75-second animated SaaS demo reel — a pure-vector, 4K 60fps pitch video with dark `#0D0D12` backgrounds, saffron/gold brand glow, and every visual hit beat-synced to a future-bass music bed. It exports the `DarshyaDemo` component (taking an optional `aspect` prop of type `Aspect`), the `ASPECTS` resolution map (3840×2160 landscape, 1920×1080 hd, 1080×1920 portrait), `FPS` (aliased to `MUSIC_FPS`, 60), and `DURATION_FRAMES` (4500). Internally it defines five unexported scene components — `HookScene`, `CoreScene`, `MagicScene`, `SpeedScene`, and `CtaScene` — stitched together with Remotion's `Series`, with scene durations locked to the music structure (buildup 0–15s, drop 15–60s, outro 60–75s) and absolute frame offsets tracked in the `S` object for beat anchoring. It builds on several internal modules: `./tokens` for colors/fonts/glow helpers, `./components/Primitives` (`MeshGradient`, `GlassPanel`, `Cursor`, `KineticType`, `LoadingBar`, `Toggle`), `./components/VectorUI` (`VectorDarshan`, `VectorKundli`, `VectorAiChat`, `VectorDashboard`, `VectorPujaCard`, `VectorHome`), `./components/Transitions` (`Shatter`), and `./beat` (`hitPulse`, `appearOn`, `KICKS`) for music synchronization; the only external dependency is `remotion` itself, plus local audio assets loaded via `staticFile` (`pitch/audio/music.wav` and `sfx-whoosh/click/chime/pop.wav` stems layered at exact frames with `Sequence`). A key design decision is that all scenes are authored in a fixed 3840×2160 coordinate space with hardcoded pixel positions, and the hd/portrait aspects simply scale and letterbox the 4K master rather than reframing content — meaning portrait output has top/bottom bars and any coordinate edit must respect the 4K design space. One gotcha: the file imports more than it uses (`PhoneFrame`, `LaptopFrame`, `Skeleton`, `ChartFromZero`, `Badge`, `ZoomThroughOut`, `CircleReveal`, `WhipPan`, and several `beat` helpers are imported but unused), so tree-shaking or lint rules may flag it.

apps\\remotion-pitch\\src\\DarshyaPitch..summary: This file defines the master Remotion composition for Darshya's pitch film: an 82-second, 21-shot, 6-act video (2460 frames at the exported `FPS` of 30) that sequences a cold open, trust-problem beats, the brand reveal, animated feature demos, proof stats, and a CTA/outro. The main export is the `DarshyaPitch` component, which renders the 21 per-shot components (`Shot1`–`Shot21`, wired through `SHOT_COMPONENTS` and the `SHOTS` duration array) inside `Series.Sequence` wrappers, alongside supporting exports like `sec`, `DURATION_FRAMES`, `shotStart`, the `Aspect` type, the `ASPECTS` dimension map, and legacy `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` constants kept for an old Root consumer. It builds on the `remotion` library (`AbsoluteFill`, `Series`, `Audio`, `useCurrentFrame`, `interpolate`, `staticFile`), design tokens from `./tokens` (e.g. `SAFFRON`, `GOLD`, `INK`, `FONT_DISPLAY`), and a large cast of sibling components — `DarshanStream`, `PujaBookingFlow`, `AiPanditChat`, `KundliWheel`, `DualCurrencyMap`, `StatCounter`, `LogoSting`, `TrustLockup`, `NriSplitScreen`, `KineticText`/`KineticChar`, `DiyaGlow`, `BrowserMockup`, `ProductClip`, `AnimatedCursor`, and `FontStyle` — plus static assets such as `pitch/audio/vo.mp3` and `pitch/video/*.webm` footage. A notable design decision is that the portrait (9:16) cut is not re-composed per scene: it scales the 1920×1080 master by 0.5625 and fills the resulting letterbox with branded saffron-gradient bars carrying the DARSHYA wordmark and `darshya.online` handle. Shot timing is data-driven, with cumulative start frames derived from `SHOTS` via `SHOT_STARTS`, so editorial pacing is tuned in one array rather than inside scenes. Gotchas include `Shot3` and `Shot4` rendering the identical `NriSplitScreen` component, a comment promising a ducking music bed while only the VO `Audio` track is actually mounted, and an explicit constraint that on-screen stats must be honest, live-verifiable numbers only.

apps\\web\\app\\account\\subscriptions\\.summary: This is a Next.js client page (`/account/subscriptions`) that lets a logged-in user view and manage their subscription for the Darshya product. The exported default `AccountSubscriptionsPage` wraps `AccountSubscriptionsInner` in the `AuthGuard` component, and the inner component additionally redirects unauthenticated users to `/auth` with a redirect-back query param. It fetches the current subscription from `GET {API_BASE_URL}/subscriptions/my` using the bearer token from `useAuth` (in `lib/auth-context`), renders plan, role, amount, dates, and status, and exposes a "Cancel auto-renewal" action that POSTs to `/subscriptions/cancel-auto-renew` after a `confirm()` dialog, then refetches. The `MySubscription` interface types the API response locally. Notable details: the `ENTERPRISE` plan is displayed under the friendlier name "NRI Premium", the cancel button only appears while status is `ACTIVE` (cancellation keeps access until the billing cycle ends rather than revoking immediately), dates are formatted with the `en-IN` locale, and users without a subscription are routed to `/upgrade`. The effect that loads data intentionally disables the exhaustive-deps lint rule since `fetchSubscription` is not in the dependency array.

apps\\web\\app\\aditya\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/aditya/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders a fully static detail page for each of the twelve Dwadasha Adityas on the Darshya site, using `generateStaticParams` with `dynamicParams = false` and a 24-hour `revalidate` so only the prebuilt slugs from `DWADASHA_ADITYA_SLUGS` resolve and unknown ones fall through to `notFound()`. Its key exports are `generateStaticParams`, `generateMetadata` (which builds SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags from the deity record), and the default `AdityaPage` server component. All content comes from the internal data module `../../../lib/dwadasha-aditya` — specifically `DWADASHA_ADITYAS` and the `getDwadashaAdityaBySlug` lookup — with no external API calls; the only dependencies are Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`, `notFound`). The page composes the record's fields (beej/primary mantras, ratna, vahana, presiding month, story origin, vrata practice, associated temple) into styled sections, injects schema.org `BreadcrumbList` and `Article` JSON-LD via a raw `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag, and derives prev/next navigation by index position in the `DWADASHA_ADITYAS` array. Notable choices: the base URL is hardcoded as `https://darshya.online`, metadata truncates the domain description to 80 characters, and the page deliberately cross-links to sibling routes (`/tirth`, `/nava-graha`, `/pujas`, `/calendar`) for internal SEO.

apps\\web\\app\\account\\digest\\unsubsc.summary: This file is the weekly-digest unsubscribe landing page for the Darshya web app, created (per the header comment, devotee revamp 2026-08-05) because digest emails link to `/account/digest/unsubscribe?u=<userId>` and that route previously 404'd. Its default export, `DigestUnsubscribePage`, wraps the inner `UnsubscribeContent` component in a React `Suspense` boundary, which Next.js requires for components using `useSearchParams` from `next/navigation`. `UnsubscribeContent` reads the `u` query parameter as the user id and, in a `useEffect`, POSTs JSON `{ userId }` to `${API_BASE_URL}/digest/unsubscribe`, where `API_BASE_URL` comes from the internal `lib/api-config` module; no external services are called beyond that backend API. The UI is driven by a four-state machine (`loading`, `done`, `invalid`, `error`): a missing `u` param yields the "invalid link" message, a non-OK or failed fetch yields the generic error, and success confirms the user is unsubscribed from the weekly Darshya digest with a note that it can be re-enabled in profile settings. A notable design decision, called out in the comment, is the deliberate absence of an AuthGuard so the link works directly from an email while signed out — which also means the endpoint is effectively unauthenticated and trusts the userId in the URL. The page is a client component styled with Tailwind classes (saffron and surface palettes, shadow-warm-sm) and always offers a "Back to Darshya" link home.

apps\\web\\app\\aditya\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/aditya` route on darshya.online, serving as the landing hub for the Dwadasha Aditya (12 forms of Surya) content section. Its default export `AdityaIndexPage` renders a grid of cards linking to per-deity detail pages at `/aditya/[slug]`, each card showing the Aditya's number, name, Sanskrit title, presiding month, domain, ratna, and quality of light, plus an explainer section on the 12 Surya Namaskar mantras. It also exports a static `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph) and a `revalidate = 86400` constant enabling daily ISR regeneration. The sole internal data dependency is the `DWADASHA_ADITYAS` array imported from `../../lib/dwadasha-aditya`, alongside `next/link` and the `Metadata` type; there are no external service calls — everything is statically rendered. For SEO it injects two JSON-LD script blocks (a schema.org `ItemList` enumerating all 12 Adityas and a `BreadcrumbList`) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and it cross-links sibling sections (`/nava-graha`, `/ashta-lakshmi`, `/dashavatar`, `/wellness/yoga`, `/sankalp`) to build internal link graph. Notable details: display strings are truncated inline (e.g., `a.ratna.split(' ')[0]` shows only the first word of a compound value), so card rendering assumes the data module's string formats remain consistent, and the hardcoded `BASE_URL` must stay in sync with the production domain.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\commissions\\page.summary: This file defines the admin-facing commissions page for the web app's Next.js App Router, mounted at the `/admin/commissions` route. Its single default export, `AdminCommissionsPage`, is a thin client component (marked with `'use client'`) that renders the shared `CommissionsPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/CommissionsPanel`. Rather than implementing any data-fetching or filtering logic itself, the page delegates everything to `CommissionsPanel`, configuring it via the `mode="admin"` prop along with a title and description indicating it shows every commission across all providers, not just those of one account. The description copy also signals the panel's intended workflow: administrators filter by commission status to investigate pending or failed payouts. The design keeps route files as thin wrappers, so any behavioral changes or additions (status filters, payout detail views) belong in `CommissionsPanel`, which presumably keys its queries and available actions off the `mode` prop to distinguish this admin view from other contexts such as a provider-facing commissions view.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\agents\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines `AgentsPage`, the default-exported client component for the admin "Agent Fleet" dashboard at `apps/web/app/admin/agents/page.tsx`, which lets administrators browse output reports produced by automated employee agents that run on GitHub Actions. It fetches per-agent run summaries and a list of recent report files from the backend admin API (`GET /admin/agents/runs` and `GET /admin/agents/recent`), and loads individual report contents on demand via `GET /admin/agents/runs/:file`, rendering the selection in a master-detail layout with agents and recent runs in a left sidebar and the raw report text in a `<pre>` viewer on the right. Local types `AgentSummary` and `ReportFile` shape the API responses, while state hooks track the summary list, recent files, the selected file, its content, and separate loading flags for the list and the content pane. Authentication comes from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context`, whose `session.accessToken` is sent as a Bearer token on every request, and the base URL comes from `API_BASE_URL` in `lib/api-config`; icons are from `lucide-react`. Notable details: the two list requests fire in parallel via `Promise.all`, the initial load is gated on the token through a `useEffect` dependency so it refires when the session appears, and file names are URL-encoded before being used as path parameters. Report content is displayed as unformatted plain text rather than rendered markdown, and the empty state explicitly tells admins to trigger the fleet manually via the GitHub Actions "Agent fleet" workflow, indicating reports are only produced by that external pipeline.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\approvals\\page.t.summary: This Next.js client page (`AdminApprovalsPage` in `apps/web/app/admin/approvals/page.tsx`) is the admin console for reviewing and acting on pending provider registrations across six role types — pandits, store owners, astrologers, wellness instructors, gaushala managers, and temple managers. It fetches the queue from the backend's `GET /admin/pending-approvals` endpoint using the bearer token from `useAuth` (in `lib/auth-context`) and `API_BASE_URL` (in `lib/api-config`), then renders a filterable card list with approve, reject, and view-detail (via `next/link` to `/admin/users/{userId}`) actions. Both decisions go through a shared `patchUser` helper that calls `PATCH /admin/users/{userId}` with an `{ approved: boolean }` body, and successful rows are removed from local state. A notable mapping concern: the backend returns uppercase role keys like `PANDIT`, which the page normalizes through the `backendToUi` record into lowercase UI keys (`priest`) used for the filter dropdown, `roleLabels`, and the `roleBadgeColors` Tailwind badge styling. The rejection flow collects a free-text reason in an inline panel but deliberately does not transmit it — the placeholder notes the backend reason field is still pending, so the text is discarded. Error handling intentionally surfaces the API's response body (message/error fields) so output from the backend's ALLOW_AUTH_DIAGNOSTICS mode reaches the UI. Other details worth knowing: filtering by role happens client-side, fetches are guarded by a cancelled flag to avoid state updates after unmount, and submission dates are formatted with the `en-IN` locale.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\b2b-onboarding\\p.summary: This file is a Next.js admin page (`B2BOnboardingPage`, the default export at `/admin/b2b-onboarding`) that visualizes the founder-driven rollout of B2B temple chains under roadmap item R-Q4-S-006, targeting 5 chain temples live with custom branding. It defines a five-stage onboarding pipeline in the `STAGES` constant (prospect, kyc_pending, kyc_verified, branding_deployed, live), a derived `StageKey` type, a `StageBadge` presentational component, and a hardcoded `SEED_CHAINS` list currently containing ISKCON Bengaluru Region temples. The page renders a progress strip (live / in-flight / prospect / remaining-to-target counts computed via `useMemo`), a stage legend, per-chain temple lists, and a founder-action footer, using only `react`, `next/link`, and `lucide-react` icons. It is explicitly a scaffold: real per-temple state is expected from a pending `R-Q4-S-006-schema` migration (adding `chain_id`, `whitelabel_status`, `went_live_at`, and `brand_*` columns to `temples` plus a `temple_chains` table) and a future `/api/v1/admin/b2b-onboarding/chains` endpoint that will replace the seed data. External touchpoints referenced but not integrated include the Razorpay partner dashboard for KYC and sub-merchant provisioning, and the `docs/runbooks/b2b-temple-onboarding.md` runbook this page mirrors. Gotchas: the page is entirely read-only with no mutation paths, the go-live target of 5 is hardcoded, and the KPI it claims to track (`b2b_chain_temples_live`) is not yet wired to any analytics.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\consultations\\pa.summary: This file is the admin operator dashboard for the AstrologerConsultation table: a client-side Next.js page that lets admins list consultation bookings, filter them by status (all, pending_payment, confirmed, completed, cancelled), see summary counts, and mark confirmed bookings as completed. The default export `AdminConsultationsPage` simply wraps the main `ListContent` component in the internal `AuthGuard`, while local types `AdminConsultation` and `StatusFilter`, the `FILTERS` constant, and helpers `buildAuthHeaders`, `statusBadge`, `shortId`, and `formatWhen` support rendering. It depends on internal modules `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) for the session and `API_BASE_URL` (lib/api-config), talks to the backend via GET `/consultation/admin/all` and PATCH `/consultation/{id}/complete`, and uses lucide-react icons plus next/link for UI. A notable auth decision, flagged in a comment, is that the HttpOnly `darshya_session` cookie is canonical — every fetch passes `credentials: 'include'` — while the Bearer header built by `buildAuthHeaders` is only a transitional fallback from the in-memory session. Gotchas include the hardcoded limit of 100 rows with no pagination (refresh to reload), summary counts derived from the currently loaded (possibly filtered) items rather than global totals, a `window.confirm` gate before completing a booking, and an explicit note that full lifecycle management stays admin-only until astrologer slug-to-User-UUID onboarding exists.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router layout for the entire `/admin` section of the web app, providing the shared chrome—dark sidebar, top header, and content area—for every admin page. Its default export, `AdminRootLayout`, wraps the inner `AdminLayoutInner` component in the `AuthGuard` component with `allowedRoles={['admin']}`, so only admin-role users can reach these pages. `AdminLayoutInner` renders a navigation sidebar driven by the `sidebarLinks` array, which enumerates fifteen admin routes (Dashboard, Users, Approvals, Leads, Outreach, Waitlist, Support Tickets, Ratings, Commissions, Subscriptions, Revenue, Reports, Metrics, Agents, Settings) with matching `lucide-react` icons, highlighting the current route via an `isActive` helper that special-cases `/admin` so the dashboard link doesn't stay active on every subpage. It pulls the current user and `signOut` from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context`, displaying the user's name and avatar initial in both the sidebar and header and wiring the Sign Out button accordingly. Key dependencies are Next.js navigation (`next/link`, `usePathname` from `next/navigation`), the `AuthGuard` component, the app's auth context, and `lucide-react` for all icons. The layout is a client component with mobile-responsive behavior: a hamburger button toggles a slide-in sidebar with a backdrop overlay on small screens, while `lg:` breakpoints pin it statically on desktop. One notable quirk is the custom scrollbar styling, which is injected inline through a `<style dangerouslySetInnerHTML>` block targeting the `darshya-admin-scroll` class rather than living in a stylesheet. The branding ("Darshya Admin Portal", saffron accent palette) is hardcoded inline, including a literal hex background color for the sidebar.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\outreach\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page (`AdminOutreachPage`) renders the admin dashboard for monitoring cold-email outreach, showing 30-day send/reply/bounce metrics plus a per-role lead funnel. On mount it uses a local `authFetch` helper — which attaches the bearer token from `useAuth`'s session and prefixes `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` — to fetch `/admin/outreach/stats` and `/admin/leads/stats` in parallel, and a "Run outreach now" button POSTs to `/admin/outreach/run` and then re-fetches the outreach stats. The UI is composed of small local components: `StatCard` for totals, a CSS-only stacked bar chart of daily activity (heights normalized by `maxDailyValue`, with a flat baseline row for zero-activity days), and a breakdown table driven by the hardcoded `ROLES` list (TEMPLE, PRIEST, ASTROLOGER, WELLNESS_INSTRUCTOR, GAUSHALA). A notable gotcha is that the funnel math assumes lead statuses are cumulative — "emailed" is computed as EMAILED + REPLIED + CONVERTED and "replied" as REPLIED + CONVERTED — so the table is wrong if a lead can occupy only one status at a time. The effect uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid state updates after unmount, and the run result is displayed as raw `JSON.stringify` output in a monospace banner rather than a structured view.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\metrics\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the admin "Real-numbers dashboard" page for the Next.js web app, giving founders and investors a live view of business metrics pulled from the Payment, Booking, Donation, User, and Lead domains. The default-exported `MetricsPage` component fetches three backend endpoints—`/admin/metrics/dashboard`, `/admin/metrics/investor`, and `/admin/metrics/funnel?days=7`—typed as `DashboardPayload`, `InvestorPayload`, and `FunnelPayload`, and renders them as stat tiles via the local `Tile` component plus two tables (revenue line breakdown and a 7-day acquisition funnel). It depends on `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the bearer access token, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` for the backend root, and `lucide-react` for icons; formatting helpers `paiseToInr` and `pct` reflect that all money is handled in paise. A notable design decision is the use of `Promise.allSettled` (flagged in a comment as Phase B Admin P0-1) so a single failing panel only produces a "Partial" error banner rather than blanking the whole dashboard. Gotchas: D7/D30 retention are explicitly labeled as unimplemented "Sprint 4+ stubs," the page reloads automatically whenever the auth token changes via `useEffect`, and several imported icons (IndianRupee, Users, Globe2) are unused.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\leads\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the admin "Lead Pipeline" page (`AdminLeadsPage`, a Next.js client component) for managing provider outreach leads—temples, priests, astrologers, wellness instructors, and gaushalas—letting staff browse, filter, review, and act on leads through their lifecycle from NEW to CONVERTED or UNSUBSCRIBED. The default-exported `AdminLeadsPage` renders stat cards, role tabs (`ROLE_TABS`), status chips (`STATUS_CHIPS`), a city filter, and a paginated table (fixed page size of 50), plus a detail drawer showing outreach history (`OutreachLog` entries), notes, and decision buttons; small presentational helpers `StatCard` and `Row` round out the file, along with types `Lead`, `LeadDetail`, `LeadRole`, `LeadStatus`, and `StatsResponse`. All data flows through the local `authFetch` helper, which prepends `API_BASE_URL` (from `lib/api-config`) and attaches the bearer token from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`), calling backend REST endpoints `/admin/leads`, `/admin/leads/stats`, `/admin/leads/:id`, `/admin/leads/:id/notes`, `/admin/leads/:id/status`, and `/admin/leads/import`; icons come from `lucide-react` and list-load errors are humanized via `friendlyApiError` (`lib/friendly-error`, per ticket P1 #208). Notable behaviors: status transitions carry business side effects—"Approve" sets CONVERTED and emails a sign-in link, "Reject" sets UNSUBSCRIBED and emails a decline note (both sending the free-text `decisionReason`), while "Queue" is internal-only with no email. Gotchas include the "Import CSV" button actually accepting pasted JSON rather than CSV, the stats fetch soft-failing to zeroes, the drawer silently falling back to row-level data if the detail fetch fails, and error handling being inconsistent (some paths show raw `err.message` rather than the friendly copy).

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\ratings\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js client page (`AdminRatingsPage`, the default export) that gives Darshya admins a moderation console for provider ratings: a filterable table with star-rating and provider-ID filters, plus a per-row "Hide" action. It depends on the internal `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` for the session access token, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, and `friendlyApiError` from `lib/friendly-error` (per the P1 #208 note) to translate raw API status errors into user-friendly copy, while using `lucide-react` for icons. The page talks to two backend admin endpoints: `GET /admin/ratings` (with `stars`, `providerId`, and a hardcoded `pageSize` of 100 as query params) and `POST /admin/ratings/:id/hide`, both authorized with the session bearer token. The `AdminRating` interface defines the row shape, including an `isHidden` flag that drives the Visible/Hidden status badge. A notable gotcha is the graceful-degradation path in `handleHide`: if the backend responds with `skipped`, the UI alerts that the `isHidden` column is missing from the schema and that moderator intent was merely logged, rather than failing outright. Successful hides are applied optimistically to local state, refetches happen automatically whenever filters change via the `useCallback`/`useEffect` pairing, and the UI relies on native `confirm`/`alert` dialogs rather than a modal system.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the admin dashboard, exporting the default client component `AdminDashboardPage` that renders platform stat tiles (total users, active providers, monthly revenue, pending approvals), a per-role user breakdown bar chart, a recent-signups table, and quick-action cards linking to `/admin/approvals` and `/admin/revenue`. It depends on `useAuth` from `../../lib/auth-context` for the session access token and on the internal `../../lib/admin-api` module for `getDashboard`, `getPendingApprovals`, `getUsers`, the `backendToUiRole` mapping, and types like `DashboardResponse` and `BackendUser`, plus `lucide-react` icons and `next/link`. Data loading happens in `fetchAll`, which fires all three API calls concurrently with `Promise.allSettled` so each section degrades independently — notably, a `getPendingApprovals` failure is treated as non-fatal because the dashboard response already carries a fallback count. Several static lookup maps (`roleLabels`, `roleBadgeColors`, `statusBadge`, `roleBreakdownConfig`) translate the backend's Prisma enum role keys (e.g. `DEVOTEE`, `PANDIT`) into the UI's lowercase role names, and helpers `mapStatus` and `mapUserToSignup` normalize heterogeneous backend status strings into the `active | pending | blocked` union. Revenue is displayed through `formatInrCompact`, which formats amounts in the Indian lakh/crore system ("Rs. 24.8L"), and the "Active Providers" metric is derived client-side by summing all `usersByRole` entries except `DEVOTEE` and `ADMIN`. The role-breakdown card is hidden entirely when the backend returns no per-role data rather than showing placeholders, and `handleExportCsv` builds a client-side Blob to download the currently loaded signups as a CSV file.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\revenue\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client component renders the admin Revenue page (`AdminRevenuePage`) at the `/admin/revenue` route, giving platform operators a single view of revenue, commissions, subscriptions, and pending payouts. It pulls the access token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, then fetches `getRevenue` and `getDashboard` in parallel from `lib/admin-api`, rendering overview cards, a subscription-revenue-by-plan breakdown, recent transactions, a commissions table, and a pending-payouts list. A local `formatInrCompact` helper formats whole-rupee amounts into compact Indian notation (Rs. 1.24Cr / 8.6L), and the `roleBadgeColors`/`roleLabels` maps translate backend role enums like PANDIT or STORE_OWNER into styled badges. Several gotchas stand out: pending payouts are derived client-side by filtering `revenue.commissions` for status `PENDING` rather than coming from a dedicated endpoint, and the "Pay Now" button has no click handler, so payout disbursement is not actually wired up. The green "Live" badge on every overview card is static decoration, not a freshness indicator. The effect uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid state updates after unmount, lists are hard-capped (12 commissions, 8 transactions) with no pagination, and the formatting comment acknowledges ambiguity about whether amounts arrive as paise or rupees — callers must pass whole rupees.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\roadmap\\RoadmapC.summary: This file is a Next.js client component (`'use client'`) that renders the admin dashboard for the Bhaktisetu Year-1 roadmap, giving admins a live view of the Autonomous Roadmap Engine's state. Its default export, `RoadmapClient`, fetches a `RoadmapData` aggregate (roadmap items, work queue, decision logs, KPI cache, tripwires) from the backend endpoint `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/admin/roadmap`, authenticating with a Bearer token from `useAuth` (the shared auth-context module) and re-polling every 60 seconds with cancellation-safe state updates. The UI is composed of six panels: an embedded `OrchestratorProgress` component (sibling module), a burn-down summary counting items by status with a verified percentage, a KPI grid with live/stale/error formatting via the `formatKpiValue` helper, a queue table with dryrun-vs-live source badges, a tripwires list, an items board capped at 100 rows, and a collapsible decision history truncated to 1000 characters per entry. Dependencies are minimal — only React hooks, the internal `auth-context` and `api-config` modules, and `OrchestratorProgress`; styling relies on Tailwind with custom `surface`/`saffron` palette tokens. Notable gotchas: it hard-fails with an error banner when no auth token is present, assumes the API response shape matches the `RoadmapData` interface without validation, joins KPI entries back to roadmap items by matching `kpi.metric` strings, and silently truncates large datasets (18 KPIs, 30 queue rows, 100 items, 5 decisions).

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\roadmap\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router entry point for the `/admin/roadmap` route in the web app, serving the "Darshya Admin" roadmap view. It is deliberately a thin server-component wrapper: the default-exported `Page` component renders nothing itself and delegates all UI to the `RoadmapClient` component imported from the sibling `./RoadmapClient` module, following the Next.js server/client component split so server-only concerns (metadata, caching) live here while interactive logic lives in the client component. The file exports a `metadata` object (typed via `Metadata` from `next`) that sets the page title and marks the route `index: false, follow: false`, keeping the admin page out of search engine results. It also exports `revalidate = 60`, enabling Incremental Static Regeneration so the page is statically cached and revalidated at most once per minute rather than rendered on every request. There are no external service calls or internal library dependencies beyond `next` itself and the `RoadmapClient` sibling module. The main gotcha is that any change to caching or SEO behavior must be made here, not in the client component, since `metadata` and `revalidate` only work when exported from a server component.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\reports\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the admin reports dashboard page (`AdminReportsPage`, a client component) for the Darshya web app, rendering live platform analytics — user growth bars, booking stat cards, popular pujas, popular services, and geographic distribution — plus CSV export buttons. It fetches data through the internal `admin-api` module (`getReports` for the page payload typed as `ReportsResponse`, plus `getDashboard`, `getRevenue`, and `getUsers` for exports) and pulls the admin access token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`; the only external dependency is `lucide-react` for icons, since all charts are hand-rolled divs scaled against computed maxima (`maxUsers`, `maxBookings`, `maxStatePct`) rather than a charting library. Exporting uses `rowsToCsv` and `downloadCsv` from `admin-api` to produce date-stamped files like `darshya-users-YYYY-MM-DD.csv`, with the "revenue" and "all" exports concatenating multiple heterogeneously-columned CSV sections with plain newlines — a loose, spreadsheet-friendly format rather than strict CSV. Formatting is centralized in small helpers: `inr` applies Indian-locale grouping, `revenueShort` renders amounts as "Rs. 18.7L"/"Rs. 1.2Cr" to match a designer-approved mock, and `formatChange` renders month-over-month pills with an em-dash for null change percentages. Notable guards include a cancellation flag around the initial `getReports` effect, a hidden user-growth trend pill when there are fewer than two datapoints or the first value is zero (avoiding division-by-zero inflation), and null-safe display of ratings and emails throughout.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\roadmap\\Orchestr.summary: OrchestratorProgress is a client-side React component in the Next.js admin app that renders a live status dashboard for the Autonomous Roadmap Engine, an orchestrator that runs on GitHub Actions runners rather than the old Render-disk setup it replaced. It polls the internal edge route /api/orchestrator-status every 30 seconds (deliberately matching that route's cache TTL) and normalizes the response through a StatusOK | StatusErr discriminated union with typed shapes like NormalizedRun, NormalizedCommit, QueueItem, PlannedItem, and ShippedItem. The default-exported component renders a summary banner, green-rate/queue-depth/last-green-wall stat cards, a past-24h outcome bucket view, a countdown to nextCronAt (cron 17 */8 * * *), and pipeline/shipped/in-progress/queue panels, using helpers fmtWall, fmtRelative, and runBadge to format wall times, relative timestamps, and conclusion badges. Its only external dependency is React (useEffect/useState) plus the fetch API; everything else flows through the orchestrator-status route, which itself proxies the GitHub Actions REST API and surfaces a rateLimit field the component displays. A notable gotcha: the step-by-step phase tracker for live cycles (boot, ingest, kpi, fleet, experiments, decision, subagents, write, commit) is pure inference — since logs aren't accessible inside GH runners, it compares elapsed time against hardcoded per-phase ETAs taken from a "cycle 13" baseline (~5m47s green cycle), so the displayed phase is best-effort guesswork. Status semantics matter throughout: conclusion 'cancelled' and 'timed_out' are treated distinctly from 'failure', and the health score is computed only over completed runs.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\subscriptions\\pa.summary: This file is a Next.js client-side admin page (`AdminSubscriptionsPage`) that gives administrators a read-only overview of all marketplace subscriptions across provider roles. It fetches data via `listAllSubscriptions` from the internal `lib/subscription-api` module (using the `MarketplaceSubscription` type) and authenticates with the access token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`. The page computes summary stats client-side with `useMemo` — active subscription count, total records, and an "Active MRR" figure derived by summing `plan.priceMonthly` over active subs — and renders them through a local `StatCard` helper. Users can filter by a fixed `STATUSES` list (defaulting to `active`, including `past_due` and `expired`) and search across user ID, plan name, and Razorpay subscription ID, all filtered in-memory rather than via server queries. Display helpers `formatINR`, `formatDate`, and `statusClass` handle Indian-locale currency/date formatting and color-coded status pills, and the UI is styled with Tailwind classes plus `lucide-react` icons. Notable constraints: the component is marked `'use client'` and re-fetches whenever the session token changes, the Razorpay payment provider is surfaced directly via `razorpaySubscriptionId`, and the MRR stat assumes all plans are monthly-priced, so mixed billing intervals would skew it.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\settings\\page.ts.summary: This file is the admin settings page (`AdminSettingsPage`, the default export) for the web app's admin console, located at the `/admin/settings` route in the Next.js app directory. It presents a four-tab interface — Commissions, Subscriptions, Platform, and Admins — letting administrators adjust per-category commission rates via sliders (bounded 5–50%), toggle subscription plans (Free, Bhakti Pass, Bhakti Pass Annual, Temple Trust) active or inactive, flip platform flags like maintenance mode and email/SMS/push notifications plus auto-approve-devotee signup, and manage admin accounts through a table with an add-admin modal supporting Admin and Moderator roles. It defines two local interfaces, `CommissionRate` and `SubscriptionPlan`, and depends only on React's `useState`, `lucide-react` icons, and Tailwind utility classes using the project's saffron/surface theme tokens and CSS variables — there are no internal module imports or API calls. The critical gotcha is that everything is mock: all data comes from hardcoded constants (`initialCommissionRates`, `initialPlans`, `initialAdmins`), and `handleSave` merely simulates persistence with a 700ms timeout, so no changes survive a refresh or reach a backend. Minor safeguards are baked into the UI logic, such as hiding the remove button for Super Admin accounts, requiring non-empty name and email before adding an admin, and clamping commission inputs, but plan editing is limited to activation toggles with no price or feature editing.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\users\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements the admin user-management page (`AdminUsersPage`) for the web app, a client-side Next.js route that lets administrators browse, filter, and moderate all platform users in a paginated table. It is wrapped in `AuthGuard` restricted to the `admin` role and pulls its bearer token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, then fetches data through the `lib/admin-api` module — specifically `getUsers` for the initial load and `patchUser` for approve, block/unblock, role-change, and delete actions, with `backendToUiRole`/`uiToBackendRole` and the `BackendUser`/`UiRole` types handling the mapping between backend role strings and UI roles. The local `mapStatus`/`mapUser` functions normalize the backend's free-form status field into an active/pending/blocked tri-state, deliberately defaulting missing statuses to active so recently created rows remain visible. Filtering (search by name/email, role, status) and pagination are computed client-side via `useMemo` over the full fetched list with a `PAGE_SIZE` of 10, so there is no server-side paging. A notable design constraint is that "delete" is a soft delete: `handleDelete` merely calls `patchUser` with `blocked: true` and removes the row locally because no destructive delete endpoint exists yet, which the confirmation dialog explicitly communicates to admins. Role edits are done inline through a badge-styled select per row, and per-action loading keys like `userId + '-approve'` keep concurrent operations on different rows independent.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\support\\view\\pa.summary: This file is the admin support ticket detail page (`AdminTicketDetailPage`) for the Next.js web app, letting support agents view a single ticket, reply publicly, add internal notes, and manage its lifecycle. It reads the ticket id from the query string via `useSearchParams` (wrapped in `Suspense` as Next.js requires) and loads data with `getTicketById` from `lib/support-api`, falling back to `SAMPLE_ADMIN_TICKETS` from `lib/support` when the API call fails, so the page still renders sample data with an error banner. Mutations go through `postMessage` (with an `internal` flag distinguishing private notes from public replies) and `patchTicket` for status, priority, and assignment changes, all authenticated with the access token from `useAuth`. Shared UI comes from `components/support/badges` (`StatusBadge`, `PriorityBadge`, plus the `formatDate`/`formatDateTime`/`timeAgo` helpers), while categories, statuses, and priorities come from `CATEGORY_MAP`, `STATUSES`, and `PRIORITIES` in `lib/support`; icons are from `lucide-react`. Notable quirks: the assignable agent list `AGENT_OPTIONS` is hardcoded in the file rather than fetched, the "Resolve" button is just a shortcut for `changeStatus('resolved')`, and the `MessageBubble` component renders three distinct styles depending on whether a message is internal, system-authored, or a user/agent reply. The sidebar surfaces user metadata (contact info, join date, total orders), a linked order id, and an activity log when present.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\waitlist\\page.ts.summary: This file is a Next.js client-side admin page (`AdminWaitlistPage`) that renders a dashboard for monitoring the product's waitlist, showing signup totals, a 30-day signup bar chart, a conversion funnel (pending → confirmed → invited → converted), and a top-20 referrers table. It defines the `WaitlistStats` interface describing the API payload, a local `authFetch` helper that attaches a Bearer token to requests, and two presentational sub-components, `StatCard` and `FunnelRow`. Data comes from a single GET to `/admin/waitlist/stats` against `API_BASE_URL` (from `lib/api-config`), authenticated via the access token obtained from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`; the only external UI dependency is the `Loader2` spinner from `lucide-react`. Notable details: the fetch is skipped entirely when no token exists (the page relies on a parent admin layout for access control rather than guarding itself), a `cancelled` flag in the effect prevents state updates after unmount, numbers are formatted with the `en-IN` locale, and funnel percentages are computed relative to the sum of all funnel stages rather than the top-of-funnel count, so the four bars won't visually cascade.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\support\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client component (`'use client'`) renders the admin support-ticket dashboard at the `/admin/support` route, giving staff a searchable, filterable table of all customer tickets. The default-exported `AdminSupportPage` loads tickets via `listTickets` from `lib/support-api` (passing the session token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context` and the admin flag `{ all: true }`), and on failure it falls back to `SAMPLE_ADMIN_TICKETS` from `lib/support` while showing an amber warning banner — a resilience choice that keeps the UI usable but can mask backend outages. It pulls its domain types (`Ticket`, `TicketStatus`, `TicketPriority`, `TicketCategory`) and constants (`SUPPORT_CATEGORIES`, `STATUSES`, `PRIORITIES`, `CATEGORY_MAP`) from `lib/support`, and reuses `StatusBadge`, `PriorityBadge`, `formatDate`, and `timeAgo` from `components/support/badges`, with icons from `lucide-react` and row links into `/admin/support/[id]` detail pages. Summary stats (open, in-progress, resolved-today counts) are computed client-side with `useMemo` by inspecting `updatedAt` date prefixes, though the average-response-time card is a hardcoded placeholder. Filtering by status, priority, category, and free-text search over ID/subject/user name/email also happens entirely in the browser, so there is no server-side pagination — a potential scaling gotcha as ticket volume grows. Two small local helper components, `StatCard` and `SelectFilter`, handle the stat cards and dropdown styling.

apps\\web\\app\\antim-sanskar\\book\\pag.summary: This Next.js client page (`AntimSanskarBookPage`) implements the Antim Sanskar (last-rites) booking flow as a deliberate single-page form rather than a multi-step wizard, collecting contact details, deceased name, city, preferred ghat, date, and package tier before POSTing to `/antim-sanskar/book` on the API base resolved from `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online/api/v1`). The only export is the default page component; internally it relies on a local `Field` helper component, hardcoded `PACKAGES` and `RIVERS` constants, the `PackageTier` type derived from them, and the shared `DateInput` UI component. Key design choices reflect the sensitivity of the domain: `preferredDate` defaults to today because most rites are same-day, no online payment is taken (amounts are settled on-site after the rites), and submission swaps the form for a quiet confirmation screen showing a booking reference and a coordinator callback ETA rather than a payment receipt. The asthi-visarjan river selector only appears for the `standard` and `comprehensive` tiers, and optional fields are trimmed and sent as `undefined` so they are omitted from the JSON body. The `data-ad-quarantine="true"` attribute on both views marks the page for ad suppression, error handling falls back to directing users to a 24x7 phone line, and styling is done entirely via CSS custom properties (`--color-*`, `--font-display`) rather than a theme library.

apps\\web\\app\\admin\\users\\view\\page.summary: This file is the admin user detail page for the Next.js web app, rendering a full profile view for a single user at the route /admin/users/view. The default export AdminUserDetailPage wraps the inner AdminUserDetailInner component in a Suspense boundary because the page reads the target user's id via useSearchParams from next/navigation, a requirement in the Next.js app router. All data comes from a hardcoded mock: the usersDb record (typed by the UserProfile interface, which supports roles like devotee, priest, store_owner, astrologer, wellness_instructor, gaushala_manager, and temple_manager), plus static roleLabels, roleBadgeColors, statusColors maps, and a fake activityLog. The UI renders a header with contact info and status badges, an admin action bar (Approve/Reject for pending users, Block/Unblock, Reset Password, and a Delete button gated by a local deleteConfirm useState confirmation panel), a role-specific stats section rendered conditionally per role, and a sidebar activity feed. Dependencies are limited to React, next/link, and lucide-react icons — there is no API or backend integration at all. Key gotchas: every action button except the delete confirmation toggle is a dead UI stub with no handler, unknown or missing ids produce a "demo limitation" not-found state, and the devotee section uses hardcoded numbers (12 bookings, Rs. 24,500) rather than fields on UserProfile.

apps\\web\\app\\ads.txt\\route.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router route handler serves the `/ads.txt` file that Google AdSense crawls to verify the publisher is authorized to sell ad inventory on the domain, which is a prerequisite for AdSense approval. Its only export besides the `dynamic = 'force-static'` config is a `GET()` function that reads the `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_CLIENT` environment variable, strips the `ca-` prefix to derive the `pub-XXXX` publisher ID, and emits the ads.txt record `google.com, <pubId>, DIRECT, f08c47fec0942fa0` as `text/plain`. It has no internal module dependencies — just the Web `Response` API and Next.js route-handler conventions. Notable decisions: when no publisher ID is configured it still returns HTTP 200 with a comment placeholder rather than a 404, deliberately preventing crawler retry-storms against the origin, and successful responses carry a 24-hour `cache-control` header. One gotcha: `force-static` means the environment variable is baked in at build time, so changing `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_CLIENT` requires a rebuild and redeploy to take effect.

apps\\web\\app\\antim-sanskar\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js landing page for Darshya's Antim Sanskar (Hindu last-rites) service, rendered at the `/antim-sanskar` route in the web app. Its default export, `AntimSanskarPage`, is a purely presentational server component that renders a hero, a "what we coordinate" checklist, three hard-coded pricing tiers from the `PACKAGES` constant (Basic ₹15,000, Standard ₹35,000 with asthi visarjan, Comprehensive ₹50,000 with shradh), a four-step `PROCESS` explainer, and a closing contact section. The only dependencies are `next/link` for the two calls-to-action pointing to `/antim-sanskar/book`, a `tel:` link to +91 92551 09400, `next`'s `Metadata` type for SEO, and theme CSS variables (`--color-bg`, `--color-text-muted`, etc.) supplied by the surrounding layout; a small local `rupees` helper formats prices with `en-IN` locale grouping. The defining design decision is tone discipline for a bereavement context: the file header documents that there are deliberately no promotional hooks, discount banners, "popular tier" badges, or live-chat widgets, and the root element carries `data-ad-quarantine="true"` so the layout suppresses AdSense on this route. Business constraints are baked into the copy: payment is collected on-site after the rites (never in advance), and a human coordinator calls back within 30 minutes, 24x7. All package and process content is static in-file data rather than fetched from a CMS or API, so pricing changes require a code edit.

apps\\web\\app\\ask-pandit\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router layout for the `/ask-pandit` route in the Darshya web app, existing primarily to attach SEO metadata and a fixed-position viewport wrapper around the AI astrology consultation page. It exports a static `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) defining the page title, description, canonical URL (`https://darshya.online/ask-pandit`), and matching OpenGraph and Twitter card tags that all share the `/og/default.png` preview image. Its default export, `AskPanditLayout`, renders `children` inside a full-screen fixed container offset by `top-14` to sit below the app's header, with `overflow-hidden` and a `bg-surface-50` background. The only dependency is the `next` package's `Metadata` type; no internal modules are imported. Notably, the `fixed inset-0` positioning with `z-10` and hidden overflow signals that the child page is expected to manage its own scrolling—typical of a chat-style interface where the conversation area scrolls internally rather than the document body.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\earni.summary: This file is the Astrologer Earnings page of the Next.js web app (`AstrologerEarningsPage`), a client component that lets a logged-in astrologer view their own consultation earnings — a 2026-08 revamp replacing a dead version that pointed at an admin-only commissions route and 403'd every real astrologer. It fetches from the `/astrologer-portal/earnings` backend endpoint using the bearer token from `useAuth` and `API_BASE_URL` (both from `apps/web/lib`), then renders three summary cards (total earnings, pending payout, paid out) plus a list of recent consultations with status badges. Local types `EarningRow` and `Summary` model the response, and a `formatINR` helper formats amounts via `Intl.NumberFormat` with the en-IN locale; icons come from `lucide-react`. Notable details: the revenue split (astrologer keeps ~80%) comes from the server's `summary.astrologerShare` with an 80% fallback in the header copy; the fetch effect uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid setting state after unmount; amounts are whole-rupee only (maximumFractionDigits 0); and the row badge treats anything not exactly `PAID` as "Pending", so other statuses collapse into that bucket.

apps\\web\\app\\ashta-lakshmi\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/ashta-lakshmi/page.tsx`) renders the index page for the Ashta Lakshmi section of darshya.online, listing the eight forms of Goddess Lakshmi as linked cards that route to per-deity detail pages at `/ashta-lakshmi/[slug]`. Its default export, `AshtaLakshmiIndexPage`, maps over the `ASHTA_LAKSHMIS` array imported from the internal module `lib/ashta-lakshmi`, reading fields like `number`, `slug`, `name`, `sanskrit`, `domain`, `vahana`, `color`, `bestDay`, `numberOfHands`, and `benefit` to build each card. It exports a static `metadata` object (with canonical URL and OpenGraph tags) and sets `revalidate = 86400`, so the page is statically generated and revalidated daily via ISR rather than rendered per request. For SEO it injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks — an `ItemList` of all eight forms and a `BreadcrumbList` — using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and hardcodes `BASE_URL` as `https://darshya.online` rather than reading from config or environment. The only runtime dependencies are `next/link` and the local data module; there are no fetches or external service calls. A notable gotcha is that card chip labels are derived by string-splitting data fields (`l.vahana.split(';')[0]` and `l.bestDay.split('+')[0]?.trim()`), so the rendering silently depends on those fields containing semicolon- or plus-delimited values. The page also deliberately cross-links to sibling content hubs (`/shakti-peeth`, `/dashavatar`, `/nava-graha`) and commercial pages (`/pujas`, `/calendar`) as part of an internal-linking SEO strategy.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\avail.summary: This Next.js client page implements the astrologer portal's availability editor, letting astrologers toggle which of three daily time windows (morning, afternoon, evening) they accept consultation bookings for each day of the week, then persist the schedule. The default export AstrologerAvailabilityPage wraps the real content component AstrologerAvailabilityPageContent in AuthGuard restricted to the 'astrologer' and 'admin' roles; the content component loads the current schedule on mount, renders a responsive toggle grid (a five-column table on desktop, stacked cards on mobile), tracks loading/saving/error state, and shows a transient "Saved!" confirmation that auto-clears after three seconds. It depends on the shared AuthGuard component, the useAuth hook from lib/auth-context for the session access token, and the getAvailability/updateAvailability functions plus the WeekAvailability and DaySlots types from lib/astrologer-api, with lucide-react providing icons. A notable defensive decision is the normalize helper: because the backend stores availability as free-form JSON that may not match the WeekAvailability shape, it coerces each day's values to booleans and falls back to the hardcoded defaultAvailability template for missing or malformed days rather than crashing. The slot model itself is a fixed product constraint — exactly three named windows per day (6 AM–12 PM, 12 PM–5 PM, 5 PM–10 PM) with no custom times — and per-slot toggles plus an "Enable All" day-level switch both clear the saved indicator to signal unsaved changes.
