apps\\web\\app\\ask-pandit\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines `AskPanditPage`, the default-exported client component for the Next.js `/ask-pandit` route, which renders the "Pandit Ji" AI spiritual-guidance chat as a two-pane layout with a conversation-history sidebar and a main chat area. It pulls auth state (`user`, `session`, `isLoading`) from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, but deliberately does not gate the page—unauthenticated visitors can chat via a local demo fallback and are merely shown a "Sign in for full experience" link. Conversation history is managed through `lib/conversation-store` (`getAllConversations`, `deleteConversation`, and the `StoredConversation` type), which is localStorage-backed, so history is per-browser and never synced to a server. The actual chat logic lives in the `AiChat` component, which receives the active `conversationId`, the session `accessToken`, the `language` toggle ('en' | 'hi'), and `onConversationCreated`/`onConversationUpdated` callbacks that refresh the sidebar list; a `VoicePanditButton` (tagged to requirement R-Q3-E-001) adds push-to-talk voice input above the chat. A notable design trick is the `chatKey` state counter passed as React `key` to force a full remount of `AiChat` whenever the user starts or switches conversations—simple, but it discards any in-flight component state. The sidebar is mobile-responsive (slide-in with a dark overlay below the `md` breakpoint), and a local `formatTimeAgo` helper renders relative timestamps for each conversation. Styling mixes Tailwind classes with inline styles referencing CSS custom properties like `--color-primary` and `--color-surface` for theming, and all icons come from `lucide-react`.

apps\\web\\app\\api\\orchestrator-status.summary: This Next.js route handler (`app/api/orchestrator-status/route.ts`) serves live status for the Autonomous Roadmap Engine, replacing a dead Render-disk endpoint now that the orchestrator runs on GitHub Actions runners; its only exports are the `GET` handler and a `revalidate = 30` constant. `GET` fans out via `Promise.allSettled` across five GitHub REST calls against the hardcoded public repo `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu` — `fetchRuns` for `roadmap-loop.yml` workflow runs, `fetchCommits` filtered post-hoc to `orchestrator-bot` commits, `fetchQueueDir` for `.md` files in `docs/roadmap/_dryrun/queue`, `fetchIndex` for the pre-commit-hook-maintained `docs/roadmap/_index.json`, and `fetchTripwires` for `_tripwires-global.yml` — then shapes the result with `rankPlanned`, `selectShippedRecent` (14-day window), `selectInProgress`, `nextCronAt`, and the `normalizeRun`/`normalizeCommit` mappers into the `OrchestratorStatusResponse` union. Auth is optional: an unauthenticated request relies on the repo being public, while the `GITHUB_TOKEN` env var (applied in the `gh()` header helper) raises the rate limit from 60 to 5000/hour, with remaining/reset headers surfaced in the response. Notable choices include tiered caching (30s on most fetches, 60s on the index, 300s on tripwires, plus an `s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60` response header so the UI's 10s polling shares upstream calls), fault isolation via `allSettled` so any single GitHub failure degrades to empty arrays rather than killing the payload, and a top-level catch returning HTTP 502 with `{ ok: false, error }`. Gotchas: the header comment says three GitHub calls but the code makes five; the cron schedule `17 */8 * * *` is duplicated as hardcoded fire-hours in `nextCronAt` and will drift if the workflow YAML changes; queue items are parsed purely from a filename timestamp regex; and `tripwiresFired` is a stubbed empty list pending a decision-note scrape.

apps\\web\\app\\ashta-lakshmi\\[slug]\\p.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route `app/ashta-lakshmi/[slug]/page.tsx`, which statically generates one detail page per form of the Ashta Lakshmi (eight forms of the goddess Lakshmi) for the Darshya site at darshya.online. Its exports are `generateStaticParams` (which pre-builds every slug from `ASHTA_LAKSHMI_SLUGS`), `generateMetadata` (which produces SEO titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags per deity), and the default async server component `AshtaLakshmiPage`, which renders the full page: breadcrumb nav, header, mantra card (beej and primary mantras in Devanagari), attribute grid (vahana, best day, number of hands, color), and prose sections for iconography, benefit, story, festival, vrata practice, and associated temple. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/ashta-lakshmi` via `ASHTA_LAKSHMIS`, `ASHTA_LAKSHMI_SLUGS`, and `getAshtaLakshmiBySlug`; the only external dependency is Next.js itself (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`), with no runtime data fetching. Key constraints are `dynamicParams = false` combined with `revalidate = 86400`, meaning only the eight known slugs exist (anything else hits `notFound()` and 404s) and pages are statically cached for 24 hours. The page injects BreadcrumbList and Article JSON-LD schema via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search-engine rich results, and derives prev/next navigation by index position in the ordered `ASHTA_LAKSHMIS` array. Notably, the `BASE_URL` is hardcoded to `https://darshya.online`, and several sections exist mainly for SEO internal-linking to sibling routes `/tirth`, `/shakti-peeth`, `/pujas`, and `/calendar`.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\consu.summary: This Next.js client page (`AstrologerConsultationsPage`, the default export) renders the astrologer portal's consultation management screen, listing an astrologer's sessions split into "Upcoming" (scheduled, in_progress) and "Past" (completed, cancelled, no_show) tabs. It fetches data from `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/astrology/consultations?role=astrologer` using the bearer token from `useAuth` (in `lib/auth-context`) and the base URL from `lib/api-config`, tolerating both `data.consultations` and `data.data` response shapes. The `Consultation` interface models each session with client name, mode (video/call/chat), scheduled time, rate, status, optional rating/notes, and a `roomUrl`; local helpers `formatCurrency` (INR via `Intl.NumberFormat`), `formatDateTime`, `getModeConfig`, and `getStatusConfig` handle display formatting, with icons from `lucide-react`. `handleJoin` reuses an existing `roomUrl` or calls `POST /astrology/consultations/:id/start-call` to obtain one, then opens it in a new tab with `noopener,noreferrer` and refetches the list. `handlePatch` sends `PATCH /astrology/consultations/:id` to end or cancel a session — note it sends uppercase `'COMPLETED'`/`'CANCELLED'` while the local `Consultation` type uses lowercase statuses, a casing mismatch the backend presumably normalizes. Per-card in-flight state (`actionId`) disables buttons during mutations, errors are surfaced in inline banners with response bodies truncated to 120 characters, and action buttons are conditionally shown based on status (Join/Rejoin for scheduled or in_progress, End for in_progress, Cancel for scheduled only).

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\layou.summary: This file defines the root layout for the astrologer-facing section of the Next.js web app (`apps/web/app/astrologer-portal`), providing the shared chrome—sidebar, header, and content area—for every page under that route. The default export, `AstrologerRootLayout`, wraps the inner `AstrologerPortalLayout` in the internal `AuthGuard` component with `allowedRoles={['astrologer']}`, so the entire subtree is gated to astrologer-role users. The inner layout renders a dark, collapsible sidebar built from a static `sidebarLinks` array (Dashboard, Messages, Consultations, Availability, Earnings, Subscription, Profile), with icons from `lucide-react` and navigation via `next/link`. Active-route highlighting is handled by an `isActive` helper that uses `usePathname` from `next/navigation`, with an exact match for the portal root and prefix matching for subroutes—a deliberate choice to avoid the root link staying active on every child page. It depends on the internal `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` to display the current user's `fullName` and to wire the Sign Out button to `signOut`. Mobile responsiveness is handled with a `sidebarOpen` state toggled by hamburger/close buttons, a fixed slide-in sidebar with a backdrop overlay below the `lg` breakpoint, and a sticky always-visible sidebar on desktop. As a `'use client'` component, it relies on React state and browser routing rather than server rendering, and child pages render inside a scrollable `<main>` region beside the fixed sidebar.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\subsc.summary: This file is a Next.js client-side route page (`'use client'`) for the web app's astrologer portal, rendering the subscription management screen at the `/astrologer-portal/subscription` route. Its only export is the default `AstrologerSubscriptionPage` component, which delegates all functionality to the shared `SubscriptionPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/SubscriptionPanel`. The page passes `role="astrologer"` plus a marketing description about marketplace plans (premium placement, lower commission, advanced scheduling), indicating that `SubscriptionPanel` is a role-parameterized component reused across user types (e.g., astrologer vs. client). The file is intentionally thin—a pure routing/composition wrapper with no state, data fetching, or logic of its own—so any changes to subscription behavior, pricing, or plan details belong in `SubscriptionPanel` rather than here.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\page..summary: This is the Astrologer portal dashboard page (`AstrologerDashboard`) for the Next.js web app, giving astrologers an at-a-glance view of their practice: earnings, session counts, active clients, rating, KYC status, and an online/offline presence toggle. It consumes `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the session token and calls three backend endpoints via `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`: `GET /astrologer-portal/dashboard` for stats (typed as `ApiAstroDashboard`), `GET`/`POST /astrologer-portal/online` for presence, and `GET /provider-kyc` to derive a `kycState` of verified, pending, unsubmitted, or rejected (with rejection reason). It renders shared components `MyProviderProfileCard`, `EarningsCard`, and `KycStatusBadge`, uses lucide-react icons and `next/link` for quick actions to the availability and profile subpages. Notable decisions: all fetches fail gracefully, falling back to hardcoded `ZERO_STATS` and an empty upcoming-sessions placeholder; comments document a deliberate P0 fix (#AP-07) that removed the old demo-token early-return so demo sessions also hit the API; and the online toggle exists because presence decays after a 15-minute heartbeat, letting devotees see which astrologers are bookable.

apps\\web\\app\\astrologer-portal\\messa.summary: This file is the Next.js route page for the messages section of the astrologer portal, giving astrologers a UI to consult with clients over chat or video call. Its sole export is the default React component `AstrologerMessagesPage`, which renders a heading ("Client Messages"), a short description, and the shared `Inbox` component imported from `apps/web/components/Inbox`. The page is a deliberately thin wrapper: all messaging behavior lives in `Inbox`, which is parameterized here with `role="provider"`, indicating the same component is reused across user roles (presumably a client-facing variant passes a different role). The `'use client'` directive marks it as a client component, required because `Inbox` presumably relies on React state, effects, or realtime subscriptions. Layout is constrained to a `max-w-5xl` container and styled with Tailwind utility classes using the project's custom `surface` color palette. There is no data fetching, routing logic, or error handling in this file — anything of substance (message threads, video call entry points, auth gating) is delegated to `Inbox` or enclosing layouts, so debugging messaging behavior should start in the components directory rather than here.

The result panel highlights `currentDosha` with a warning card, otherwise shows `nextDosha` or an all-clear message once all three windows have passed. Notable details: the default city is hardcoded to 'Delhi' with a non-null-asserted fallback to `CITY_OPTIONS[0]`, and the UI copy documents the calculation rule (each octet equals (sunset − sunrise)/8, with weekday octet positions per Muhurta Chintamani tables). The footer cross-links to `/ask-pandit`, `/astrology/choghadiya`, and `/panchang` as conversion/navigation targets.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\shubh-muhurat.summary: This is the server-rendered Next.js page for the Shubh Muhurat Finder at /astrology/shubh-muhurat on darshya.online, a free tool that ranks ~60-minute windows of a day as auspicious times for 12 life events (marriage, griha pravesh, vehicle purchase, surgery, etc.) by compositing three Vedic signals: Choghadiya kind, Hora planet, and Rahu/Yamaganda/Gulika avoidance. It exports the default ShubhMuhuratPage component, a Next.js metadata object with canonical and OpenGraph tags, and sets revalidate = 86400 for daily ISR. The interactive calculator itself is delegated to the imported ShubhMuhuratClient component, while EVENT_OPTIONS from the shared lib/shubh-muhurat module drives a static grid showing each event's Sanskrit name, ideal karaka planets, and preferred Choghadiya kinds. The page is heavily SEO-oriented: it embeds three JSON-LD scripts (FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, WebApplication) built from a hardcoded FAQS array, which also documents the scoring formula — Choghadiya ±15–30, Hora match +10–40, Rahu Kalam overlap −50, daytime bonus +10, baseline +50, clamped 0–100 with verdicts at ≥80/65/45. Notable design choices include hardcoding BASE_URL as https://darshya.online, using native details/summary elements for the FAQ accordion (no JS dependency), and closing with cross-links to the underlying standalone calculators (/astrology/choghadiya, /astrology/hora, /astrology/rahu-kalam) plus /ask-pandit, framing this tool as a composite scorer over already-shipped panchang utilities rather than a new engine.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\sade-sati\\Sa.summary: This file is the client-side UI for the Sade Sati checker tool, a Next.js client component (`'use client'`) whose default export `SadeSatiClient` renders a birth-details form (date via the shared `DateInput` component, time defaulting to 12:00, and a timezone dropdown populated from the `TimezoneOption[]` prop defaulting to +5.5 IST) and displays the computed result entirely in the browser. All astrology logic lives in the internal `lib/sade-sati` module: the form calls `computeSadeSati({ dob, time, timezoneOffset })` on submit and renders the returned `SadeSatiResult`, while the static `SADE_SATI_REMEDIES` and `SADE_SATI_DOS_DONTS` lists are shown only when the user's `currentPhase` is one of the rising/peak/setting Sade Sati phases or a dhaiya-4th/dhaiya-8th period. Styling is driven by the `PHASE_STYLE` map keyed on the `SadeSatiPhaseKind` union, which assigns Tailwind color schemes per phase type (red for peak, emerald for normal, etc.), and a small local `Cell` component renders the natal Moon rashi and current Saturn rashi readouts. The results panel also lists every Sade Sati and Dhaiya phase over a 90-year span from birth (`result.phases`), highlighting the current one with a "NOW" pill, and smooth-scrolls to `#ss-result` via a short `setTimeout` after state updates. Notable design choices: computation is fully client-side with no API calls, the code openly documents that Saturn's position uses a simplified Meeus VSOP87 approximation (±1°), which it argues is accurate enough for 30°-wide rashi determination and 2.5-year phase timing, and the check is Chandra-lagna (Moon-sign) based rather than ascendant based. Error handling is minimal—an empty DOB or a null return from `computeSadeSati` just sets a text error message. The file ends with a conversion-oriented cross-link block pushing users to `/ask-pandit`, `/pujas/maha-mrityunjaya` (Shani Shanti puja booking), and `/astrology/dasha`, tying this free tool into the app's paid services.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\vastu\\page.t.summary: This is the Next.js App Router server page for the Vastu Shastra calculator at `/astrology/vastu` on darshya.online, existing primarily to deliver SEO-rich static content around an interactive room-placement scoring tool. Its default export `VastuPage` renders the page shell — breadcrumbs, header, a direction-reference grid built from `DISHAS`, a room-type grid built from `ROOMS` (both imported from the shared `../../../lib/vastu` module), a scoring-explainer section, a static `FAQS` accordion, and CTA links to `/ask-pandit`, `/astrology/shubh-muhurat`, and `/astrology/kundli` — while delegating all interactivity to the `VastuClient` client component. It also exports a Next.js `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags, and injects three JSON-LD schemas (`FAQ_LD`, `BREAD_LD`, `APP_LD` typed as FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, and WebApplication) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags for search-engine rich results. The page documents the scoring model implemented elsewhere: ideal placement +40, acceptable +20, neutral −10, avoid −50, on a +50 baseline clamped to 0–100, with verdict tiers at 80/65/45. Notable decisions include `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR caching, a hardcoded `BASE_URL` constant, and framing all content around classical sources (Mayamatam, Vishwakarma Prakash, Brihat Samhita) with no birth-data requirement, positioning the tool as purely direction-based. A gotcha for maintainers is that the FAQ copy, scoring rules, and room/disha reference data are duplicated between this page's prose and the `lib/vastu` source of truth, so rule changes must be synced in both places.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\[id]\\page.ts.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/astrology/[id]/page.tsx`) whose sole job is to redirect requests from the friendly URL `/astrology/<id>` to the canonical astrologer profile page at `/astrology/view?id=<id>`. Its single export, the async server component `AstrologerByIdRedirect`, awaits the `params` promise (Next.js 15 style) and calls `redirect` from `next/navigation`, URL-encoding the `id` via `encodeURIComponent` before issuing the redirect. The only dependency is Next.js itself; the actual profile UI lives in the separate `/astrology/view` client component. The design rationale, spelled out in the header comment, is that provider-strip cards, the "similar astrologers" rail, and external shares link to `/astrology/<id>`, and without this shim those links would 404 into the global not-found loader — the redirect avoids duplicating the roughly 550-line client profile component while keeping the pretty URLs functional. Note that the canonical route uses a query parameter rather than the dynamic segment for historical reasons.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\callback\\layout.t.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router layout for the `/auth/callback` route segment in the `apps/web` app, which handles OAuth and magic-link sign-in redirects. Its sole purpose is to attach route-level `metadata` (via the `Metadata` type from `next`) that titles the page "Signing In…" and marks it `noindex`/`nofollow`, keeping the transient callback URL out of search engines. The default-exported `CallbackLayout` component is a pure pass-through: it accepts `children` as a `React.ReactNode` and renders them unchanged, adding no markup or providers of its own. The key design decision is using a layout exclusively for metadata scoping — since the callback page is a short-lived redirect during authentication, the robots directives are the only real behavior here, and any nested pages under `auth/callback` inherit them automatically.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\[id]\\book\\p.summary: This Next.js client page (`AstrologyBookPage`) implements the paid consultation booking flow for a single astrologer, wrapped in `AuthGuard` so only signed-in users can access it. It fetches the astrologer's profile from `/astrology/astrologers/{id}` at `API_BASE_URL`, lets the user pick a duration from `MINUTE_PRESETS` and an optional slot via `DateTimeInput`, then computes a total from `perMinuteRate × minutes`. The `handleBook` function POSTs to `/consultation/book` to create a Razorpay order, lazily injects the Razorpay checkout.js script (via the memoized `loadRazorpayScript` singleton), opens the checkout modal, and on payment success POSTs the order/payment/signature triple to `/consultation/verify-payment` before routing to `/consultation/{id}/success`. A notable gotcha is the `demo` branch: when the backend flags an order as demo, the page skips Razorpay entirely and verifies with synthetic `pay_demo_*` ids. Auth design per the inline comment: the HttpOnly `darshya_session` cookie is canonical (hence every fetch passes `credentials: 'include'`), with the Bearer token from `useAuth`'s session kept only as a transitional fallback via `buildAuthHeaders`. Other dependencies include `lucide-react` icons, Next.js `useParams`/`useRouter` navigation, and a hardcoded `#E16318` Razorpay theme color.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\view\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page renders the public astrologer profile detail view at `/astrology/view`, exporting a default `AstrologerDetailPage` that wraps `AstrologerDetailInner` in a `Suspense` boundary so `useSearchParams` can read the `id` query param. The profile starts from a hardcoded `allAstrologers` fallback map (three astrologers with embedded reviews, plus a static `similarAstrologers` list and a hardcoded `ratingBreakdown` distribution), then a `useEffect` fetches `GET /astrology/astrologers/:id` using `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` and shallow-merges any real `astrologer` record over the fallback so astrologer-portal profile edits surface publicly (noted as P0 #AP-11). Photos come from `getAstrologerImage` in `lib/images`, and all icons are from `lucide-react`. The page exposes three calls to action: "Book Paid Consultation" links to `/astrology/[id]/book`, "Chat Now" redirects to `/astrology/chat` prefilled with the astrologer's name, and "Call" deliberately routes into the paid booking flow because free-trial Jitsi rooms were removed (P0 #AP-01/AP-02) — video rooms are now only issued after Razorpay payment verification and resolved via `/consultation/by-room`. Gotchas worth knowing: an unknown or missing `id` silently falls back to `astro_001`, the API overlay is a shallow merge so the static fallback reviews persist even when live profile data loads, fetch failures are swallowed to keep the fallback, and the chat/call buttons are disabled whenever the astrologer is offline or busy based on `isOnline`/`isBusy` status.

apps\\web\\app\\astrology\\vastu\\VastuC.summary: This file is the client-side UI for an interactive Vastu Shastra layout checker in the Next.js web app, letting users pick a plot/entrance facing direction and assign compass directions to rooms, then instantly see a scored evaluation. It default-exports the `VastuClient` component, which manages `facing` and per-room `selections` state and recomputes a `VastuResult` via `useMemo` on every change; an internal `PlacementCard` component renders each room's verdict, score, and reasoning. All logic comes from the internal `lib/vastu` module (`DISHAS`, `ROOMS`, `computeVastu`, `suggestIdealLayout`, plus the `Direction`, `RoomType`, `Placement`, and `VastuResult` types), with only `react` and `next/link` as external dependencies — no network calls or backend services are involved. Notable design choices: initial state is seeded from `suggestIdealLayout()` applied to `DEFAULT_ROOMS`, toggling a room off and on restores its ideal direction, and the form's `onSubmit` is deliberately prevented since everything is computed reactively in-browser. Static lookup maps `VERDICT_STYLE` (excellent/good/acceptable/avoid color schemes) and `DIRECTION_GLYPH` (arrow symbols for the eight directions) drive the presentation. The scoring model, documented inline, composites the Mayamatam, Vishwakarma Prakash, and Brihat Samhita texts with ideal +40, acceptable +20, avoid −50 on a +50 baseline clamped to 0–100. The results view separates strengths from doshas and funnels users toward `/ask-pandit`, `/astrology/shubh-muhurat`, and `/astrology/kundli` via `Link` for cross-feature engagement.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the shared segment layout for all authentication routes (login, signup, verify, callback) in the Darshya Next.js web app, providing both default SEO metadata and a common visual shell. It exports a `metadata` object typed with Next's `Metadata`—setting a "Sign In" default title with the template `%s | Darshya`, plus OpenGraph and Twitter card tags pointing at `/og/default.png`—and a default `AuthLayout` React component that wraps `children` in a full-viewport (`100dvh`) centered container. The visual design layers a warm saffron gradient (custom Tailwind colors `saffron-700`, `saffron-600`, `temple-gold`) under a decorative `/images/pattern-mandala.svg` overlay, constrains content to `max-w-md`, and renders a dynamic-year copyright footer. A notable design decision, documented in an inline comment, is that no canonical URL is declared at this level: per-route canonicals live in each child route's own layout.tsx, because hardcoding `/auth/login` here would incorrectly tag the signup, verify, and callback pages as the login page. The file depends only on the `next` Metadata type and React, with no data fetching or client-side logic.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\login\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router layout for the `/auth/login` route of the Darshya web app, and it exists purely to attach SEO metadata to the sign-in page. It exports a `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) defining the page title "Sign In", a description mentioning phone/email login, live darshan, and puja booking, a canonical URL hardcoded to `https://darshya.online/auth/login`, and OpenGraph fields pointing to the shared `/og/default.png` image. Its only other export is the default `LoginLayout` component, which simply returns `children` unchanged, making it a pure pass-through wrapper. The only dependencies are the `Metadata` type from `next` and `React.ReactNode` for typing the children prop. Notably, the layout adds no visual structure, providers, or auth guards of its own — it exists solely so the login route can carry route-specific metadata, and the canonical/OG URLs are hardcoded to the production `darshya.online` domain, so they will be incorrect in staging or preview environments.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\logout\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements the `/auth/logout` route in the Next.js web app (apps/web), which previously returned a 404 and left users logged in when a "Sign Out" affordance navigated there (bug P1 #212). It exports a single client component, `LogoutPage`, which on mount calls the `signOut` function from the shared `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context` to clear the session, cookies, and server token, then redirects the user to the home page via `router.replace('/')` from `next/navigation`. While waiting, it renders a centered loading state using the `Loader2` spinner from `lucide-react`. The redirect happens in a `finally` block so the user is sent home even if sign-out fails, and a `cancelled` flag in the `useEffect` cleanup guards against calling `router.replace` after unmount. Key dependencies are the internal `auth-context` module for authentication state and Next.js App Router navigation; there is no server-side logic, so the entire flow runs client-side.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\callback\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page is the OAuth landing route that completes Google sign-in: it waits for the Supabase browser client (configured with `detectSessionInUrl: true`) to parse the session out of the URL hash, then exchanges those tokens with the backend and redirects the user to their dashboard. The default export `AuthCallbackPage` polls `supabase.auth.getSession()` up to 20 times at 150ms intervals (about 3 seconds max) before giving up with an error, then POSTs the access token, refresh token, and expiry to `${API_BASE_URL}/auth/google/sync`. On success it persists the returned session and user (defaulting a missing role to `'devotee'`) into both `localStorage` and `SameSite=Lax` cookies under the keys `poojly_session` and `poojly_user`, degrading to cookies-only if `localStorage` throws. It honors a `redirect` query param but guards against open redirects by accepting only root-relative paths or URLs that resolve to the same origin, otherwise falling back to `getRoleDashboardPath(role)` from `lib/auth-context`, and navigates via a full `window.location.href` load rather than the Next.js router. Key internal dependencies are `getSupabaseBrowserClient` from `lib/supabase`, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, and the `UserRole` type from `lib/auth-context`; the UI itself is a simple centered card using lucide-react's `Loader2` and `AlertCircle` icons with a link back to `/auth/login` on failure. Notable gotchas: the fixed polling loop means slow session materialization shows a hard failure, cookie values are JSON strings that could hit size limits, and the unauthenticated `/auth/google/sync` endpoint is trusted to validate the Supabase token server-side.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\signup\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js layout for the signup route (`/auth/signup`) in the Darshya web app. Its sole job is to attach SEO metadata to the signup page: it exports a `metadata` object (typed as `Metadata` from `next`) defining the page title "Create Account", a marketing description highlighting Darshya's features (puja booking, live darshan, 80G receipts, AI spiritual guidance), a canonical URL pointing at `https://darshya.online/auth/signup`, and OpenGraph tags using the shared `/og/default.png` image. The default export, `SignupLayout`, is a pass-through component that simply returns its `children` unchanged, so it adds no visual wrapper or providers — it exists purely so Next.js applies the metadata to the route segment. The only dependency is the `next` Metadata type; there is no client-side logic, data fetching, or styling here. A gotcha worth noting: because the layout renders children directly, any shared UI (headers, auth guards, analytics) must come from a parent layout or the page itself.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\login\\__tests__\\.summary: This Vitest test file pins the security contract of the `safeRedirect` helper used by the login page (`apps/web/app/auth/login/page.tsx`) to prevent open-redirect/phishing attacks via the `?redirect=` query parameter, tracked as fix P0-1. Because `safeRedirect` is module-private in page.tsx, the test re-implements the exact contract locally and asserts its behavior: it returns a fallback (`/dashboard`) for missing input, allows root-relative paths, rejects protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.com`), foreign absolute URLs, and `javascript:` schemes, while collapsing same-origin absolute URLs (origin `https://darshya.online`) down to root-relative paths. The only external dependency is `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`); URL parsing relies on the WHATWG `URL` constructor. A notable gotcha the tests codify: backslash input like `\evil.com` and malformed strings like `%%%` are resolved by WHATWG URL semantics against the app origin as harmless path segments, so the guard deliberately accepts them as on-origin paths rather than rejecting them—the contract targets cross-origin hops, not input pedantry. The header comment explicitly flags the drift risk: since the helper is duplicated rather than imported, this test only catches divergence from page.tsx when both are reviewed together.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\verify\\layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the layout for the OTP verification step of the authentication flow in the Next.js web app (`apps/web`). Its sole purpose is to attach SEO metadata to the `/auth/verify` route: it exports a `metadata` object (using the `Metadata` type from `next`) that sets the page title to "Verify OTP" and marks the route `noindex`/`nofollow` so search engines skip this transient flow page. The default export, `VerifyLayout`, is a pass-through component that simply renders its `children` without adding any visual structure. It depends only on Next.js's metadata API and React's `ReactNode` type. The notable design decision is deliberate: because verification is a temporary step in the sign-in flow, the page is explicitly excluded from indexing and given no canonical URL, keeping it out of search results.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\verify\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page implements the magic-link verification step of the Poojly auth flow: it reads a `token` query parameter from the emailed sign-in link, POSTs it to the backend endpoint `/auth/magic-link/verify` (built from `API_BASE_URL` in `lib/api-config`), and redirects successful users to `/dashboard`. The default export `VerifyMagicLinkPage` wraps the working component `VerifyInner` in a React `Suspense` boundary (a Next.js requirement for using `useSearchParams`), with a small `Centered` presentational helper shared by the loading, success, and error states. On success it persists the returned `session` and `user` objects to `localStorage` under the keys `poojly_session` and `poojly_user`, deliberately matching the shape that `auth-context` expects so the app rehydrates auth state on the next render. Dependencies are limited to `next/navigation` (`useRouter`, `useSearchParams`), `next/link`, `lucide-react` icons, and the internal API config; there is no state library involved. Notable details: localStorage write failures (private mode, quota) are swallowed as non-fatal, the redirect is delayed 600ms so users see the success message, and the error state hard-links back to `/auth/login` to request a fresh link rather than retrying the token.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\login\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Darshya web app's login page (`LoginPage`, the default export), a client-side Next.js component that renders a tabbed sign-in UI supporting three flows: email/password via `signInWithCredentials`, Indian phone-number OTP (hardcoded `+91` prefix, 10-digit input, 6-digit code with auto-submit and a 30-second resend countdown) via `signInWithOtp`/`verifyOtp`, and Google OAuth via `getSupabaseBrowserClient().auth.signInWithOAuth`. It builds on internal modules `lib/auth-context` (the `useAuth` hook and `getRoleDashboardPath`, which routes users to a role-specific dashboard after login), `lib/supabase` (browser Supabase client), and `lib/t` (`useTranslations` for the `auth` and `common` namespaces), plus `lucide-react` icons and an inline `GoogleIcon` SVG. The most important design element is the local `safeRedirect` helper, a documented P0-1 security fix that mirrors the `/auth/callback` guard by rejecting absolute and protocol-relative redirect targets so the `?redirect=` param can't be abused for open-redirect phishing; it's applied both to the post-login navigation and to the callback URL handed to Google OAuth. New users completing OTP verification are sent to `/profile`, while already-authenticated visitors are bounced to their role dashboard in a `useEffect`. A notable gotcha is the demo-account quick-login chips: they embed the password `demo123` in the client bundle, so they're hard-gated behind both `NODE_ENV !== 'production'` and a `?demo=1` query param to prevent trivial admin impersonation if demo accounts ever leak into production.

apps\\web\\app\\become-astrologer\\page..summary: This Next.js page (`app/become-astrologer/page.tsx`) renders the marketing-and-application landing page for astrologers who want to offer paid per-minute consultations on the Darshya platform. It exports static `Metadata` (title and description for SEO) and the default `BecomeAstrologerPage` component, which composes two shared internal components: `SelfOnboardPageShell` supplies the page layout, headline, and a hardcoded `BENEFITS` array of selling points, while `SelfOnboardForm` renders the actual application form with `role="ASTROLOGER"`. The form is extended via its `extraFields` slot with two role-specific inputs built from the exported `ExtraSelect` and `ExtraInput` helpers: a required `astrologyType` dropdown (vedic, tarot, numerology, palmistry, other) and an optional numeric `yearsExperience` field clamped to 0–80. The page itself contains no data-fetching or submission logic — all onboarding behavior is delegated to `SelfOnboardForm`, making this file a thin configuration layer. Notably, the marketing copy reveals product constraints: astrologers set rates from ₹10/min, consultations run over built-in Jitsi chat/video rather than external links, and payouts switch from weekly to daily after ₹5,000 lifetime earnings, with Aadhaar-based verification gating the trust badge.

apps\\web\\app\\become-priest\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (route `/become-priest`) is the marketing-and-signup landing page where Hindu priests (pandits) apply to join the Darshya platform, promising puja bookings, per-minute Ask-Pandit consultations, and weekly payouts after Aadhaar verification. Its default export `BecomePriestPage` composes two internal components: `SelfOnboardPageShell`, which renders the hero copy and a hardcoded four-item `BENEFITS` list, and `SelfOnboardForm`, the shared onboarding form configured here with `role="PRIEST"`, a custom CTA label, and two extra required fields — `yearsExperience` (a number input clamped between 0 and 80) and free-text `specialties` — injected via the `extraFields` slot and built with the `ExtraInput` helper. It also exports a static `metadata` object ("Become a Darshya pandit") for SEO. Notably, the page is a thin presentational wrapper: all submission logic, validation, and backend wiring live inside `SelfOnboardForm`, so this file contains no data fetching or state of its own, and all copy (including payout percentages and the "200+ verified pandits" claim) is hardcoded rather than CMS-driven.

apps\\web\\app\\become-gurukul\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router entry for the `/become-gurukul` route in the `apps/web` app, serving as the public landing page where gurukuls, ashrams, and veda pathshalas can register on the Darshya platform. It exists primarily as a thin server-component wrapper: its only real job is exporting the `metadata` object (title "Register Your Gurukul on Darshya" plus an SEO description targeting Sanatani families and the diaspora) and rendering the default `BecomeGurukulPage` component. All actual UI and interactivity are delegated to the sibling `BecomeGurukulClient` component imported from `./BecomeGurukulClient`. The sole external dependency is the `Metadata` type from `next`. The key design decision is the metadata/client split — Next.js only allows `metadata` exports from server components, so the page stays server-side and hands off rendering to a client component, which is where any form state, admissions listing, or payment-related UI must live. There is no business logic here, so changes to the registration flow belong in `BecomeGurukulClient`, while changes to SEO copy belong in this file.

apps\\web\\app\\auth\\signup\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements Darshya's multi-step signup page (`SignupPage`, a Next.js client component) that walks users through role selection, a role-specific registration form, and a confirmation screen, supporting seven roles (devotee, priest, store_owner, astrologer, wellness_instructor, gaushala_manager, temple_manager) defined in `roleOptions`. It validates input with a zod `signupSchema` deliberately mirrored one-for-one against the API's `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts` schema so the client never POSTs a body the server rejects, layering extra per-role UI checks in `validateStep1`. On submit it calls `signUpWithCredentials` from `lib/auth-context` (backed by Supabase), then for provider roles immediately POSTs a translated profile to `${API_BASE_URL}/onboarding/provider`, using `PROVIDER_ROLE_MAP` and `buildProviderPayload` to convert web role keys and UX-named form fields into the backend `MarketplaceRole` enum and Prisma profile shapes (the one place this mapping is centralized). Key gotchas: a known `priest` ↔ `pandit` web↔API alias is handled elsewhere; per ticket P0 #199, passwords are stripped before drafts are saved to `localStorage` (`poojly_signup_data`); and per P0 #195, a signup that returns no session (Supabase email-confirmation enabled) routes to an `awaitingEmailConfirm` screen rather than a fake "complete" state. Failures on the onboarding POST are non-fatal — the account exists and the user can finish via `/onboarding/[role]` — and already-authenticated visitors are redirected to `getRoleDashboardPath`. Presentational helpers `ChipSelect`, `FormInput`, and `StepIndicator` render the form chrome, with lucide-react icons throughout.

apps\\web\\app\\bhakti-saint\\[slug]\\pa.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router detail page for individual Bhakti saints in the Darshya web app, rendering a full profile at the route `/bhakti-saint/[slug]`. Its default export, `BhaktiSaintDetailPage`, is an async server component that renders the saint's name, Sanskrit and IAST forms, era/region/deity badges, tradition, guru, principal works, an optional signature verse, life story, key teaching, associated places, and modern relevance, plus prev/next and "jump to any saint" navigation. It also exports `generateMetadata`, which builds per-saint SEO titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags, and `generateStaticParams`, which enumerates all slugs for static generation. All data comes from the internal module `../../../lib/bhakti-saints` (`BHAKTI_SAINTS`, `bhaktiSaintSlugs`, `getBhaktiSaint`); there are no external service calls beyond referencing the hardcoded `BASE_URL` (`https://darshya.online`). apps\\web\\app\\bhakti-saint\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the Bhakti Saints section of the Darshya site (darshya.online), rendering a static landing page that catalogs twelve medieval Hindu devotional figures. apps\\web\\app\\blog\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the dynamic blog post detail page for the Darshya marketing site, a Next.js App Router route at `/blog/[slug]` that renders a single post fetched via `getBlogPost` from the internal `lib/blog-posts` module and converts its markdown body to HTML with `markdownToHtml` from `lib/markdown`. apps\\web\\app\\become-wellness\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js page (`apps/web/app/become-wellness/page.tsx`) is the public landing and application page for recruiting wellness instructors onto the Darshya platform, exporting static SEO `metadata` ("Teach yoga & meditation on Darshya") plus the default `BecomeWellnessPage` component. apps\\web\\app\\bn\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the Bengali-language landing page (`/bn` route) for the Darshya spiritual super-app, rendered as a Next.js app-router page component named `BengaliLanding`. apps\\web\\app\\blog\\[slug]\\error.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router route-segment error boundary for `/blog/[slug]` in the `apps/web` app, created under ticket P0-9 to catch render errors on individual blog article pages; its header comment defers to `app/temples/[slug]/error.tsx` for the underlying rationale. apps\\web\\app\\become-gurukul\\BecomeGu.summary: This file is a Next.js client component (`'use client'`) that renders the "Register your gurukul" form, letting an authenticated user list a new gurukul on the platform. On submit, `handleSubmit` validates required fields client-side, coerces numeric fields with `Number()`, maps blank optional fields to `undefined` and a blank `feeAnnualInr` to `null`, then POSTs the payload to `${apiBase()}/api/v1/gurukuls` with a Bearer token, where `apiBase()` reads `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a hardcoded fallback to `https://api.darshya.online`. Notable details: validation is split between HTML attributes (slug `pattern="[a-z0-9-]+"`, description `minLength` of 50/2000) and manual checks in `handleSubmit`; the submit button is disabled when unauthenticated and a sign-in prompt links to `/auth/login`. One gotcha is that program list items use the array index as the React `key`, which can cause state/UI mismatches when programs are deleted from the middle of the list.

apps\\web\\app\\blog\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for Darshya's blog at `/blog`, rendering a server component that lists published posts fetched via `listBlogPosts` from the internal `../../lib/blog-posts` module. apps\\web\\app\\calendar\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/calendar` route on darshya.online, rendering a month-by-month Hindu festival calendar for the fixed year 2026. Notable details include the parallel `MONTH_NAMES`/`MONTH_SANSKRIT` arrays mapping Gregorian months to approximate lunar month pairs, "Today"/past-date styling driven by comparing `date2026` against the current ISO date (only applied when the current year is 2026), and a disclaimer that lunar dates are approximate. apps\\web\\app\\careers\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the Careers page for the Darshya devotional web app, rendered as a static marketing/recruiting page within the Next.js App Router (`apps/web/app/careers/page.tsx`). apps\\web\\app\\chakras\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/chakras` route of the Darshya site (darshya.online), rendering a static, SEO-optimized catalog of the seven chakras with a 24-hour ISR revalidation (`revalidate = 86400`). apps\\web\\app\\chalisa\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the chalisa section of the darshya.online site, serving as an SEO-targeted library (keywords "hindu chalisa", "chalisa lyrics collection") that lists 40-verse devotional hymns and links to individual detail pages. apps\\web\\app\\changelog\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js page component (`apps/web/app/changelog/page.tsx`) renders the public changelog at `/changelog` for darshya.online, displaying the latest commits to the GitHub repository `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu` as a styled dev log. apps\\web\\app\\chakras\\[slug]\\page.ts.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route `apps/web/app/chakras/[slug]/page.tsx`, which renders the SEO-focused detail page for a single chakra on the Darshya site (hardcoded `BASE_URL` of darshya.online). Prev/next navigation uses mod-7 arithmetic over the `CHAKRAS` array so users can wrap cyclically between Muladhara and Sahasrara, with a `?? c` fallback that exists only to satisfy TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` since the index is guaranteed valid after the `notFound()` guard. The page depends only on Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`) and the static data in `lib/chakras`, with no external services or runtime data fetching.

apps\\web\\app\\calendar\\[month]\\page..summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/calendar/[month]/page.tsx`) renders the Darshya site's per-month Hindu festival listings for 2026 at routes like `/calendar/january`, fully statically generated: `generateStaticParams` emits the 12 slugs from a local `MONTHS` constant (which carries each month's name, index, Sanskrit lunar months, season, and SEO "focus" blurb), `dynamicParams = false` forces 404s via `notFound()` for anything else, and `revalidate = 86400` sets daily ISR. Notable constraints: the year is hardcoded as `YEAR = 2026` and month matching depends entirely on string-splitting `date2026`, so the pages silently go stale for other years; "today"/"past" highlighting (computed with a UTC-based `getDayOfWeek` helper) only activates when the server's current year equals 2026. apps\\web\\app\\bookings\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/bookings/page.tsx`) renders the authenticated devotee's "My Bookings" list, fetching from `GET {API_BASE_URL}/bookings/my` via `useQuery` and rendering filterable booking cards with status pills, dates, amounts, and action links. The default export `BookingsPage` wraps the inner `BookingsContent` component in the `AuthGuard` component, and the file also defines the `BookingListItem`/`ApiBooking` types plus the `mapBooking` normalizer, which flattens the backend's nested `temple`/`pujaType` objects and Decimal `priceAmount` strings into plain UI fields at the boundary. Tab filtering (all/upcoming/completed/cancelled) is computed client-side with the `isUpcoming`/`isCompleted` helpers, where "upcoming" additionally requires the scheduled datetime to be in the future, and cancellation calls `POST /bookings/{id}/cancel` with a `window.confirm` guard before invalidating the `['bookings','my']` query key. Key dependencies are `@tanstack/react-query`, `next/link`, `lucide-react` icons, the internal `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` (the access token is part of the query key and gates the fetch), and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`. Inline comments record prior fixes: the Cancel button was previously dead UI (D1) and the manual `useEffect` fetch was replaced by React Query (P1-17) to avoid setState-after-unmount issues. Notable gotchas include ISO datetimes being stripped to date-only in `mapBooking`, a `window.alert`-based error path for failed cancellations, and cancelled bookings being excluded from the "upcoming" bucket even when their date lies ahead.

apps\\web\\app\\chants\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/chants` route of the Darshya site (darshya.online), rendering a browsable catalog of twelve famous Hindu mantras grouped by purpose. Its default export, the `ChantsIndex` server component, pulls all content from the internal `../../lib/chants` module — the `CHANTS` array and the `chantsByCategory` helper — and organizes cards into six hardcoded sections (protection, wisdom, wealth, peace, devotional, invocation), each card linking to a detail page at `/chants/[slug]` and showing name, Sanskrit name, meaning, deity, recommended chant count, and a difficulty badge. It also exports Next.js `metadata` (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph image) and an `itemListJsonLd` helper that injects a schema.org ItemList as JSON-LD for SEO. There are no external service calls; the page is fully static and configured for ISR with `revalidate = 86400` (regenerated at most once daily). Notable details: sections whose category has no chants are silently skipped, styling relies on custom Tailwind palette tokens (`saffron`, `surface`) mapped per category via `catColor`, and the page deliberately cross-promotes other routes — `/deity` for deity-grouped mantras, `/ask-pandit` for paid recitation services, and `/aarti`.

apps\\web\\app\\bookings\\view\\page.tsx.summary: This client-side Next.js page renders the single-booking detail view at /bookings/view, reading the booking ID from the `?id=` query param via `useSearchParams` (wrapped in `Suspense`) and gating access through `AuthGuard`. The core `BookingDetailContent` component fetches a `BookingDetail` from `GET {API_BASE_URL}/bookings/{id}` with the bearer token from `useAuth`, and — a key gotcha — silently falls back to a hardcoded `fallbackBooking` demo record when the API fails, a "demo mode" pattern that also makes the review/cancel mutations appear to succeed on network errors. The UI renders the `BookingStatusTracker` progress timeline, devotee list with gotra/nakshatra, `PriceBreakdown`, a video-proof player placeholder, and a `PrasadTracking` shipment progress bar, plus helper formatters `formatDate`, `formatTime`, `getStatusBadge`, and `getPrasadStatusLabel`. It wires four server actions: `POST /bookings/{id}/review`, `/cancel`, `/reschedule` (marked D7, which re-queues the booking if a pandit was attached), and `/request-refund`. Client-side rules gate these actions: cancellation excludes in-progress and terminal statuses, refunds require status `booked`/`priest_assigned` with a slot more than 24 hours away (eligibility re-checked server-side), and reviews are only allowed on completed/video_uploaded/delivered bookings with text capped at 200 characters. Internal dependencies are `lib/auth-context`, `lib/api-config`, `components/AuthGuard`, and `components/BookingStatusTracker` (whose `BookingStatus` union drives the status model); externals are Next.js navigation, React, lucide-react icons, and a custom Tailwind palette (saffron, tulsi-green, ganga-blue).

apps\\web\\app\\checkout\\success\\page..summary: This file is the post-payment landing page for the Darshya puja booking app, rendered after Stripe redirects the customer back from checkout. It exports the `metadata` object (which sets `robots: noindex, nofollow` so the confirmation page stays out of search results) and the default async server component `CheckoutSuccessPage`, which awaits the Next.js `searchParams` promise and extracts the booking number (`bk`), Stripe `payment_intent`, and `redirect_status` query parameters. The page is purely presentational: it shows a success card with the booking reference, an amber warning if `redirect_status` is anything other than `succeeded`, and informational panels about the confirmation email (including Indian 80G tax receipt info) and the guaranteed video proof of the puja, plus links to `/bookings` and `/`. Its only dependencies are `next/link` for navigation and `lucide-react` icons (`CheckCircle2`, `Video`, `Mail`), styled with Tailwind classes built on custom theme tokens like `saffron-600` and `surface-*`. A notable design decision is that the page performs no server-side verification — it trusts the Stripe redirect parameters and simply displays the raw `payment_intent` as a reference string, meaning actual payment confirmation must happen elsewhere (e.g., via webhook). The use of awaited `searchParams` reflects the Next.js 15 async-request-API convention.

One notable hardcoded value is the `datePublished: '2026-05-27'` in the Article schema, which is static and not derived from the data.

apps\\web\\app\\contact\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js layout for the `/contact` route in the `apps/web` application, and it exists purely to attach SEO and social-sharing metadata to the contact page rather than to provide any visual structure. It exports a static `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) that defines the page title and description—advertising Darshya's support for puja bookings, temple and gaushala partnerships, gurukul listings, and NRI assistance—plus a canonical URL (`https://darshya.online/contact`), Open Graph tags, and Twitter card tags. The only other export is the default `ContactLayout` component, a pass-through wrapper that renders `children` inside a React fragment without adding markup. Its sole dependency is the `next` package's `Metadata` type; there are no internal module imports. A notable gotcha is the inline TODO: both the Open Graph and Twitter images point to `/og/default.png`, a 1200x630 asset that has not yet been added to `apps/web/public/`, so social previews will have a broken image until that file lands.

apps\\web\\app\\city\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/city` route, serving as the entry point into the site's programmatic-SEO city pages (`/city/[slug]`) for booking pujas and browsing temples by location. It exports a static `metadata` object (Next.js `Metadata` type) with title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags, plus the default `CityIndex` server component that renders a breadcrumb, header, and a responsive grid of city cards linking to each slug. Its only real dependency is the internal `CITIES` array from `../../lib/cities`, whose entries supply name, Hindi name, state, population, description, and a `famousTemples` list; `next/link` handles client-side navigation. For SEO it injects a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, enumerating every city with position and absolute URL. Notable details: the page is fully static with no data fetching, the production domain `https://darshya.online` is hard-coded in the canonical and JSON-LD URLs (so previews/staging will still point at prod), and `c.famousTemples[0]` is accessed without a guard, assuming every city has at least one famous temple. Styling relies on Tailwind with custom theme tokens like `saffron-*` and `surface-*`, and descriptions are truncated with `line-clamp-3`.

apps\\web\\app\\city\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router dynamic route (`/city/[slug]`) that statically generates per-city hub pages for Darshya, a programmatic-SEO play targeting queries like "puja in {city}" and "temples in {city}". It exports `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per entry in the `CITIES` constant from `lib/cities`), `generateMetadata` (which builds the title, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags from the city record), and the default `CityPage` async server component, alongside route config `dynamicParams = false` and `revalidate = 3600` so unknown slugs hard-404 and pages revalidate hourly. Internally it builds on `getCity`/`CITIES` from `lib/cities`, `getDeity` from `lib/deities`, and `getTemples` from `lib/api`, which calls the backend temples endpoint filtered by city name. A notable design decision is the fault-tolerant API lookup — `getTemples` is wrapped in `.catch(() => null)` so the page falls back to the statically curated `c.famousTemples` list (linked via optional `templeSlugs`) when the API is down, keeping the page useful for SEO regardless. The component emits schema.org `Place` JSON-LD with `containsPlace` entries typed as `PlaceOfWorship` and a masked postal code (`${c.pinPrefix}xxx`), plus breadcrumbs and conditional sections (NRI-magnet badge, nearby yatra chips) driven by flags on the city record. The page functions as an internal-linking hub, fanning out to `/pujas/{slug}`, `/deity/{slug}`, `/yatra/{slug}`, `/temples/{slug}`, and every sibling city page, and it uses the Next.js 15 convention of awaiting `params` as a Promise.

apps\\web\\app\\checkout\\offering\\page.summary: This Next.js client page (`OfferingCheckoutInner`, exported behind a `Suspense` boundary) is the checkout flow for booking a single priest's puja offering: it reads the `id` query param, collects scheduling details (date, time slot from `DEFAULT_SLOTS`, devotee name, gotra, sankalp), and runs payment. Because no dedicated offering-by-id endpoint exists (flagged as TODO W4), `fetchOffering` lists all priests via `GET /priests` and then fetches each `GET /priests/:id` detail until it finds the priest owning the offering. It builds on the internal `useAuth` auth-context (gating the page with a redirect to `/auth/login?redirect=...`), `API_BASE_URL` from api-config, the shared `DateInput` component, and `StripeClientSecretCheckout` for embedded Stripe Elements. Payment has two rails: INR via Razorpay (script injected by a local `loadRazorpay` helper deliberately duplicated verbatim from `/pujas/[slug]/book` to keep loader semantics identical) and USD via Stripe for NRI users, with the browser timezone outside `Asia/Kolkata` deciding the default toggle. Both rails call `POST /bookings/from-offering`; the Razorpay path then verifies the signature server-side via `POST /bookings/verify-payment` because the client handler is never trusted as the source of truth. Notable gotchas: the USD price is a hard-coded `basePrice × 9` multiplier that must stay in lock-step with the backend constant, and when the server lacks `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` it returns `demo: true`, in which case the page shows the success screen anyway so the funnel remains exercisable in dev. On verified payment it renders a confirmation screen with the booking number and links to `/dashboard/bookings`.

apps\\web\\app\\content\\books\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/content/books/page.tsx`) is the index route for the "Sacred Texts" section of the Darshya site, listing available scriptures such as the Bhagavad Gita, Ramayana, and Upanishads. Its default export, the async server component `BooksIndexPage`, fetches the catalog via `loadAllManifests` from the internal `lib/books` module and renders each entry as a `BookCard` (from `components/books/BookCard`) in a responsive grid, with a fallback empty-state message when no books exist. A named `metadata` export sets SEO fields including the canonical URL `https://darshya.online/content/books` and OpenGraph tags. Dependencies are limited to Next.js (`next/link`, `Metadata` type) and `lucide-react` for the `ChevronLeft` back-navigation icon; there is no client-side state or interactivity. Notably, the hardcoded header copy documents a content-integrity policy: verses come only from public-domain translations (Sri Aurobindo, Edwin Arnold, M.N. Dutt), and chapters lacking verified Sanskrit sources are explicitly labeled "placeholder" or "partial" rather than fabricated.

apps\\web\\app\\consultation\\[id]\\succ.summary: This file is the Next.js client page shown after a user books a paid astrology consultation, rendering the booking confirmation (or "payment pending" state) for the route `/consultation/[id]/success`. Its default export, `ConsultationSuccessPage`, wraps the inner `SuccessContent` component in the shared `AuthGuard`, and it defines a local `Consultation` type plus a `buildAuthHeaders` helper. The page fetches the booking from `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/consultation/:id` and supports cancelling via `POST /consultation/:id/cancel`, using `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` and the session from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`; UI icons come from `lucide-react` and routing uses `next/navigation` and `next/link`. It displays reference, astrologer name, duration, INR amount, and scheduled time, and when status is `confirmed` and a `jitsiUrl` exists it renders a "Join Consultation Room" link opening the Jitsi video room in a new tab; otherwise it offers a "Refresh Status" reload button. A key design constraint, spelled out in the `buildAuthHeaders` comment (P1#4), is that the HttpOnly `darshya_session` cookie is the canonical auth mechanism, so every fetch must include `credentials: 'include'`, with the Bearer header kept only as a transitional in-memory fallback (no localStorage). The cancel flow uses a browser `confirm()` dialog, optimistically sets status to `cancelled` on success, and is hidden for `cancelled` or `completed` bookings. Hardcoded product copy encodes business rules users should know: the room link is also emailed, a refund applies if the astrologer doesn't join within 10 minutes, and full refunds are only available up to 24 hours before the scheduled time.

apps\\web\\app\\contact\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a client-rendered Next.js page (`apps/web/app/contact/page.tsx`) that presents the public "Contact Us" screen for a puja-booking/temple platform, exporting a single default `ContactPage` component. It pulls all company details—support email, support hours, legal entity name, and optional specialty inboxes—from the internal `COMPANY` config object and `postalContactLine()` helper in `lib/company`, and uses `lucide-react` icons plus `next/link` for the UI. A notable design decision is that the "Send us a message" form has no backend: its `onSubmit` handler URL-encodes the fields into a `mailto:` link to `COMPANY.supportEmail` and navigates via `window.location.href`, so submissions depend on the visitor having a configured mail client. The `escalationEmails` list (sales, partnerships, press, legal) and the postal-address card are conditionally built at module load—entries are set to `null` and filtered out when the corresponding `COMPANY.specialtyEmails` values or postal line are absent, so the "Specialty inboxes" section disappears entirely if none are configured. The page also cross-links to the existing in-app support ticket system at `/support` for logged-in users. Styling is done entirely through CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, etc.) rather than a utility framework, and the `'use client'` directive is required because of the form handler.

apps\\web\\app\\content\\books\\[slug]\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the book detail view at `/content/books/[slug]` in the `apps/web` app, showing a single sacred text's cover, metadata, and table of contents. It exports the default async server component `BookDetailPage` plus `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one static page per slug from `listBookSlugs`) and `generateMetadata` (which builds canonical, Open Graph `book`-type, and description tags from the manifest). It relies on the internal `lib/books` module for `loadManifest` and `listBookSlugs`, the sibling components `ChapterTOC` and `ContinueReadingCTA` for the contents listing and resume-reading prompt, and external pieces `next/link`, `next/navigation` (`notFound`), and `lucide-react`'s `ChevronLeft`. The page emits schema.org `Book` JSON-LD (conditionally including a `translator` Person node) via an inline script for SEO, and hardcodes the canonical domain `https://darshya.online`. Notable details: a missing manifest triggers `notFound()` for a 404, the Sanskrit title is rendered with the `--font-noto-devanagari` CSS variable, and a plain `` is used for the cover with an explicit eslint-disable rather than `next/image`. Params are awaited as Promises, matching the Next.js 15 async-params convention.

apps\\web\\app\\credits\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/credits/page.tsx`) that renders a static "Image Credits & Attribution" page for the Darshya site, satisfying Creative Commons attribution requirements for imagery used across the app. It exports a `metadata` object (title/description for SEO) and a default `CreditsPage` React component, plus a module-level `Credit` interface and a hardcoded `wikimediaCredits` array of ~60 entries covering the 12 Jyotirlingas, Char Dham, other temples, deities, festivals, rituals, and gaushala/cow photos — each with subject, filename, Wikimedia Commons source URL, license string, and author. The only dependency is the `Metadata` type from `next`; there is no data fetching, so the page is fully static and prerenderable. Rendering is a simple table mapping over the array with `filename` as the React key, linking each subject to its Commons source page with `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"`, plus footnotes crediting Unsplash for stock photos and noting the brand mark is original artwork. Styling is done entirely through inline styles referencing CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--color-primary`, `--font-display`, etc.), so theming depends on those variables being defined globally; a gotcha is that the credit list is manually maintained, so any new image added elsewhere in the app must be mirrored here by hand to stay license-compliant.

apps\\web\\app\\content\\books\\[slug]\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/content/books/[slug]/[...chapter]/page.tsx`) renders the static chapter-reader view for the books section, using a catch-all `[...chapter]` segment so nested/compound chapter slugs resolve correctly. It exports three things: `generateStaticParams`, which enumerates every book via `listBookSlugs` and every chapter via `loadManifest` so all routes are prerendered at build time; `generateMetadata`, which produces per-chapter SEO metadata (title, description, canonical link, OpenGraph article tags) hardcoded against the `https://darshya.online` domain; and the default async server component `ChapterReaderPage`, which loads the manifest and chapter in parallel, calls `notFound()` if either is missing, and hands the data to the client component `ReaderClient`. Its key internal dependencies are the `lib/books` helpers (`loadManifest`, `loadChapter`, `listBookSlugs`, `prevChapter`, `nextChapter`) and `components/books/ReaderClient`; externally it relies only on `next` and `next/navigation`. A notable design point is that prev/next navigation is computed over the manifest's flat `chapters` array, which the code comment explains works uniformly for both kanda-style and plain chapter structures because compound slugs are preserved. Also worth noting: params are awaited as Promises per the Next.js 15 convention, and `generateMetadata` silently returns an empty object for missing content rather than triggering a 404, so only the page itself enforces not-found behavior.

apps\\web\\app\\content\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the devotional content library at `/content`, exported as the async server component `ContentPage` plus a static `metadata` export, and it renders a browsable catalogue of aartis, chalisas, mantras, bhajans, and spiritual stories with tabs, a "Today's Featured" section, curated collections, and a paginated track-style list. It fetches data through `getContent` and `getDailyContent` from `../../lib/api` (typed as `ContentItem`), renders the hero via the `ContentPageHeader` component, and resolves artwork through `getContentImage` and `getDeityImage` from `../../lib/images`, with icons from `lucide-react`. Internally it defines async child sections `DailyContentSection` and `ContentListSection` (each wrapped in `Suspense` with skeleton fallbacks), the fetch orchestrator `fetchContentData`, and helpers `buildContentHref`, `formatCount`, and `formatDuration`. Because the API lacks a free-text search filter, `fetchContentData` works around this by pulling up to 200 records and filtering/paginating locally against title, deity, and tags; on any API failure it silently degrades to hardcoded `fallbackFeaturedContent` and `fallbackContentItems` arrays. Notable gotchas include tab counts and collection metadata being static constants that can drift from real catalogue sizes, a brittle if-else chain mapping deity names to image slugs, `searchParams` being awaited as a Promise (Next.js 15 convention), pagination clamped to `PAGE_SIZE` of 12, and the daily/collections sections rendering only on the "all" tab with no active search.

apps\\web\\app\\csr-match\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements `CsrMatchPage`, the default-exported client component for the `/csr-match` route in the `apps/web` Next.js app — a landing page for the Bhaktisetu CSR donation-match campaign tracked as queue item R-Q4-M-007, gated to dev-server only until the founder approves the 80G and CSR-1 compliance attestation. The page delivers four mandated elements: a hero pitching the "2x Match" employee-pledge model, an interactive match calculator (employee pledge ×2 corporate match, formatted via the local `formatINR` helper using `Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN')`), a transparency-dashboard preview rendering three hardcoded `TEMPLES` mock cards with adoption percentages, and a four-field corporate signup form (company name, CSR head email, budget bracket from `BUDGET_BRACKETS`, expected match cap). The form POSTs lead data as JSON to the internal `/api/csr-match/leads` endpoint and renders a success state on completion; no external libraries or services are used beyond React's `useState`. Key gotchas: the temple transparency data is entirely static mock content rather than live metrics, the 2x match math is computed purely client-side with no validation against the submitted match cap, and the footer makes regulatory claims (80G certification, CSR-1 registration, Schedule VII Item III eligibility) that the header comment explicitly says are not yet attested — which is why the page must not be deployed.

apps\\web\\app\\darshan\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/darshan/page.tsx`) renders the "Live Darshan" hub where visitors browse real-time aarti and abhishekam streams from major Indian temples. Its default export `DarshanPage` is an async server component that composes a hero header with a pulsing live badge, a `StreamsBrowserSection` wrapped in React `Suspense` (with a skeleton-pulse fallback), and a static daily ceremony schedule table. Stream data comes from `getLiveDarshan` and `getScheduledDarshan` in `../../lib/api` (typed as `DarshanStream`), fetched concurrently inside `StreamsBrowserSection` and rendered by the `DarshanBrowser` component, while localization is handled by `getTranslations` from `../../lib/t` and reminder actions by `DarshanScheduleRemindButton`. A major design choice is resilience through hardcoded fallbacks: `fetchLiveStreams` and `fetchScheduledStreams` swallow all errors and substitute `fallbackLiveStreams`/`fallbackScheduledStreams` (curated YouTube embeds with plausible viewer counts) whenever the API fails or returns empty, so the page never appears broken but may silently show fabricated data. Similarly, `fallbackScheduleTable` is entirely static markup—its "live" and "completed" statuses are hardcoded and never reflect actual time—making that section decorative rather than data-driven. The page sets `revalidate = 300` (5-minute ISR) to keep the live-now list roughly synchronized with aarti windows, matching the cadence of the `/darshan/[id]` detail page. SEO metadata is exported via the `metadata` object, and icons come from `lucide-react`.

apps\\web\\app\\darshanas\\[slug]\\page..summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the detail view for a single darshana (Hindu philosophical school) at the route `/darshanas/[slug]`, pulling all content from the local data module `../../../lib/darshanas` via `getDarshana`, `darshanaSlugs`, and the `DARSHANAS` array. Its key exports are `generateStaticParams` (pre-renders one static page per slug), `generateMetadata` (builds SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags against the hardcoded `BASE_URL` https://darshya.online), and the default async `DarshanaPage` component, which renders the school's Sanskrit name, founder, root text, central thesis, key concepts, pramanas, liberation path, key texts, and modern relevance in styled card sections. The page is fully static and closed-world: `dynamicParams = false` plus a 24-hour `revalidate` means unknown slugs 404 via `notFound()` and only the six pre-rendered pages ever exist. It injects schema.org JSON-LD (an `Article` and a `BreadcrumbList`) through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search-engine rich results, with a hardcoded `datePublished` of 2026-05-27. Navigation is sequential by array index — prev/next links derived from the darshana's position in `DARSHANAS`, with the final page's "next" slot replaced by a back-to-index link — plus a pill-style index of all six schools highlighting the current one. Notable gotchas: metadata descriptions are truncated with naive `slice(0, 100/160)` calls that can cut mid-word, and all styling depends on a custom Tailwind palette (`saffron`, `amber`, `indigo`, `emerald`, `rose`) that must exist in the project's Tailwind config.

apps\\web\\app\\darshanas\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for `/darshanas` on the Darshya site, presenting the six astika schools of Hindu philosophy (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Purva Mimamsa, Vedanta) grouped into their three traditional complementary pairs. Its default export, `DarshanasIndexPage`, is a server component that reads all content from the internal data module `lib/darshanas` — specifically `DARSHANAS`, `TOTAL_DARSHANAS`, `PAIR_LABELS`, `PAIR_ORDER`, and the `DarshanaPair` type — and buckets entries by pair via a `reduce` before rendering pair-labeled sections of `Link` cards to `/darshanas/[slug]`. The page is statically generated with ISR (`revalidate = 86400`, i.e. daily) and carries heavy SEO instrumentation: a `metadata` export with canonical and OpenGraph tags pointing at `https://darshya.online`, plus inline JSON-LD emitting schema.org `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList` graphs built from the same `DARSHANAS` array. A `PAIR_COLORS` record maps each pair to a Tailwind palette (indigo, emerald, saffron) for section headers. A "Related study" footer cross-links sibling sections `/upanishads`, `/yoga-sutras`, and `/gita`. Notable gotcha: the section header classes are built by string interpolation (``border-${color}-200``, ``text-${color}-900``), which Tailwind's JIT cannot statically detect, so these styles will silently be missing unless the classes are safelisted or otherwise present in scanned source. The page has no external service dependencies — it is purely presentational over local static data.

apps\\web\\app\\dashavatar\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/dashavatar/page.tsx`) renders the static index page for the Dashavatar — the ten incarnations of Vishnu — on the Darshya site, grouping avatar cards by yuga and linking each to its detail route `/dashavatar/[slug]`. Its default export is the `DashavatarIndexPage` server component, alongside exported `metadata` (title, canonical URL, OpenGraph tags) and a `revalidate = 86400` setting for daily ISR regeneration. It depends on the internal module `../../lib/dashavatar`, importing the `DASHAVATAR` data array, `YUGA_ORDER`, `YUGA_LABELS`, and the `AvatarYuga` type; external dependencies are just `next/link` and Next's `Metadata` API, with no runtime data fetching. Notable design choices include a hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` used for canonical URLs and JSON-LD, inline schema.org `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList` structured data injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for SEO, and a `YUGA_COLOR` lookup mapping each yuga (including a `future-kali` variant) to Tailwind class strings that drive per-section theming. The page statically renders all content at build time, filters avatars per yuga and skips empty groups, and cross-links related study pages such as `/gita`, `/ramayana`, and `/puranas/bhagavata-purana`.

apps\\web\\app\\darshan\\[id]\\replay\\p.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`DarshanReplayPage` at `/darshan/[id]/replay`) implements roadmap item R-Q1-P-007: a minimal scaffold for replaying the last 24 hours of auto-recorded aarti segments per temple, sourced from an AWS IVS S3 recording bucket. Its key exports are the default async server component `DarshanReplayPage`, a `generateMetadata` for SEO/OpenGraph, and `generateStaticParams` pre-rendering five temple slugs (kashi-vishwanath-varanasi, siddhivinayak-mumbai, tirumala-tirupati, iskcon-vrindavan, golden-temple-amritsar) with `dynamicParams` enabled and a 600-second `revalidate`. Internally it defines the `ReplaySegment` type (id, recordedAt, label, durationMin, nullable `hlsUrl`) and the helper `listLast24hSegments`, which fetches a per-temple `last24h.json` manifest from the base URL in the `IVS_REPLAY_BUCKET_BASE` env var (revalidated every 300s) and silently returns an empty list on missing config, non-OK responses, or parse errors. Dependencies are limited to `next/link`, Next's `Metadata` type, and `lucide-react` icons (Video, Clock, ArrowLeft, Calendar); the external service touchpoint is the IVS recording bucket, whose manifest schema is owned by the future R-Q2-E-002 ops setup. The notable design stance is env-or-noop honesty: when the bucket isn't configured the page renders a "Replay coming soon" panel instead of fabricated recordings, and segments with null `hlsUrl` show a disabled "Processing" state rather than a broken player.
