Gotchas include silent failure swallowing all fetch errors (making misconfiguration indistinguishable from "no recordings"), the scaffold always returning empty until the founder wires the manifest endpoint, and a stated Q2 plan to replace this with a permanent archive plus CDN and Schema.org VideoObject markup.

apps\\web\\app\\consultation\\[id]\\page.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/consultation/[id]/page.tsx`) renders the live video consultation room by embedding a Jitsi Meet iframe from the public meet.jit.si server, but only after server-side authorization. The default-exported `ConsultationRoomPage` wraps `ConsultationRoomContent` in the internal `AuthGuard` component; the content component reads the dynamic `id` segment via `useParams` (this value is actually a Jitsi room name, not a database consultation id — callers like `Inbox.tsx` and `astrology/view/page.tsx` pass `roomName`, and the slug is named `[id]` rather than `[room]` because the App Router rejects differing slug names at the same path level as the sibling `/consultation/[id]/success` route). Before rendering the iframe it fetches `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/consultation/by-room/:room` with a bearer token from `useAuth` (assembled by the local `buildAuthHeaders` helper), and the backend 403s unless the room maps to a paid ("confirmed") consultation and the caller is the devotee owner, assigned astrologer, or an admin — a fix for security issue P0 #AP-01, which previously let any visitor (even logged-out) join a free branded room and impersonate an astrologer. A five-state `authStatus` machine (`checking | authorized | unauthorized | notfound | error`) drives distinct UI screens, including a "not found" state that deliberately refuses free-trial `/consultation/start` rooms since they have no database row. Notable details: a 50ms `setTimeout` gates iframe mounting to avoid hydration mismatch, the Jitsi URL is configured with `prejoinPageEnabled=false`, deep linking and mobile app promos disabled, and the Jitsi watermark hidden, while a footer notes that no recordings are stored on Darshya servers. Dependencies are limited to `next/navigation`, `lucide-react` icons, and the internal `lib/auth-context` and `lib/api-config` modules.

apps\\web\\app\\deity\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js index page for the `/deity` route on the Darshya site, serving as the entry point into a set of programmatic-SEO landing pages for individual Hindu deities at `/deity/[slug]`. Its default export, the `DeityIndex` server component, renders a breadcrumb, a header, and a responsive grid of cards—one per deity—each linking to that deity's detail page and displaying its name, Sanskrit label, description, and associated festival. It also exports a static `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) that sets the page title, description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/deity`, and Open Graph fields for search and social sharing. The sole internal dependency is the `DEITIES` array imported from `../../lib/deities`, which supplies each deity's slug, name, sanskrit, description, and festival; there are no external runtime services, with styling handled purely by Tailwind utility classes (including a custom saffron/surface palette). A notable SEO decision is the inline injection of a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, enumerating every deity URL so crawlers can discover the child pages. Because the data is fully static and the component has no client interactivity, the page renders entirely on the server.

apps\\web\\app\\dashavatar\\[slug]\\page.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page that renders the SEO-focused detail page for one of the ten avatars of Vishnu at the route `/dashavatar/[slug]` on the Darshya site. It exports `generateStaticParams` (which pre-builds a page for every slug returned by `avatarSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (which builds per-avatar titles, OpenGraph data, and canonical URLs), and the default async server component `AvatarDetailPage`, which renders the avatar's header, purpose, demon/threat, weapons, consort, tirthas, story, key teaching, scripture, and modern relevance, plus prev/next links and a "jump to any avatara" nav. All content comes from the internal `lib/dashavatar` module (`DASHAVATAR`, `getAvatar`, `avatarSlugs`, `YUGA_LABELS`) — there are no external APIs or databases, only Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`) and Tailwind styling with a custom saffron palette. The page is fully static: `dynamicParams = false` means unknown slugs hit `notFound()` and 404, while `revalidate = 86400` enables daily ISR regeneration. Notable details include a hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` used for canonical links and JSON-LD, injected Article and BreadcrumbList schema.org markup via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, inline ordinal-suffix logic in the metadata description, prev/next computed by index lookup in the `DASHAVATAR` array, and the Next.js 15 pattern of awaiting `params` as a Promise.

apps\\web\\app\\deity\\[slug]\\mantras\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/deity/[slug]/mantras/page.tsx`) renders the per-deity mantra collection sub-page, explicitly targeting long-tail SEO queries like "shiva mantras" or "lakshmi beej mantra," and is statically regenerated daily via `revalidate = 86400`. It exports `generateMetadata` for SEO (canonical URL, OpenGraph tags against `darshya.online`) and the default `DeityMantrasPage` server component, which calls `notFound()` when the deity or its mantras are missing. Data comes from two internal modules: `lib/deities` (`getDeity`, `DEITIES`) for deity metadata and `lib/deity-mantras` (`getMantrasForDeity`, `deitiesWithMantras`) for the mantra records; UI icons come from `lucide-react`, and all data is local/static rather than from an external service. Each mantra card renders Sanskrit text, transliteration, meaning, benefit, and a recommended repetition count, with raw `m.type` values mapped to friendly labels via the `TYPE_LABELS` dictionary (falling back to the raw value if unmapped). The page embeds schema.org `Article` JSON-LD for rich snippets, includes a static "How to recite" guidance box, and doubles as a conversion funnel: a CTA section pushes users to book pujas on the parent `/deity/[slug]` page, while cross-links to `/chalisa`, `/aarti`, and `/shlokas` plus a grid of other deities with mantras strengthen internal linking. Note the dynamic route params are awaited as a Promise, reflecting the newer Next.js async-params convention.

apps\\web\\app\\dashboard\\page.tsx.summary: This is the devotee dashboard page for the Darshya web app, a Next.js client component that gives a signed-in user an at-a-glance view of their spiritual activity: bookings, subscription status, and shortcuts to other sections. The default export `DashboardPage` simply wraps `DashboardContent` in the `AuthGuard` component, while `DashboardContent` pulls `user`, `session`, and `signOut` from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context` and fetches `/users/me/bookings?limit=5` and `/users/me/subscription` from `API_BASE_URL` (defined in `lib/api-config`) in parallel with a Bearer token. The page renders a time-of-day greeting, three stat cards (total bookings, subscription plan with a "Free Tier" fallback, and a "Book a Puja" quick action), a recent-bookings list whose badges are driven by the `statusColors` and `statusLabels` lookup maps covering nine booking states from `pending_payment` to `refunded`, and a sidebar containing the `PujaRecommendationWidget`, quick links to `/darshan`, `/panchang`, `/content`, and `/store`, plus a "Bhakti Pass" upgrade CTA shown only when no subscription exists. It depends internally on `AuthGuard`, `PujaRecommendationWidget`, `DevoteeTodaySection`, the auth context, and API config modules, and externally on `lucide-react` for all iconography. Notable details: bookings are capped at five with a "View All" link to `/dashboard/bookings` only when the total exceeds that, prices are formatted in rupees with `en-IN` locale, an inline comment documents the 2026-08-05 revamp that replaced four hardcoded mock widgets with the live `DevoteeTodaySection`, and the styling relies on a custom Tailwind palette (`saffron`, `surface`, `temple-gold`, `sacred-red`) rather than default colors.

apps\\web\\app\\demo\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js client-side page (`'use client'`) that renders the demo hub for the Poojly app at the `/demo` route — a marketing/preview landing page that lets visitors pick a user role and walk through a simulated mobile app experience. Its single export is the default `DemoHub` React component, which renders a hero section plus a responsive grid of role cards; the card data comes from a module-level `roles` array describing seven personas (devotee, pandit, store-owner, astrologer, wellness instructor, temple-manager, gaushala-manager), each with a slug, screen count, color scheme, and description. Each card links via `next/link` to `/demo/{slug}`, implying sibling dynamic-route pages host the actual per-role screen walkthroughs, and a back link returns to `/`. Dependencies are limited to `next/link` for navigation and `lucide-react` for icons (Heart, BookOpen, Store, Star, Leaf, Building2, MilkOff, etc.). Notable details: the page is purely presentational with no data fetching or state, styling relies on custom Tailwind theme tokens (the `saffron-*` and `surface-*` palettes) and a `--font-display` CSS variable, and the hardcoded `screens` counts could drift out of sync with the actual per-role demo pages since nothing enforces them.

apps\\web\\app\\content\\[slug]\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`app/content/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the devotional content detail pages for the Darshya platform, covering types like chalisa, aarti, mantra, bhajan, and stotram with breadcrumbs, stats, an audio/video player, the rendered markdown body, tags, and a related-content sidebar. Its exports are `generateStaticParams` (which prerenders a curated slug list including `hanuman-chalisa` and long-tail SEO slugs), `generateMetadata` (OpenGraph/SEO metadata derived from the content), and the default `ContentDetailPage` server component. Data flows through the internal `getContentBySlug` and `getRelatedContent` helpers, which call `getContentBySlugApi` and `getContent` from `lib/api`, with graceful degradation to a hardcoded `fallbackContent` (the full Hanuman Chalisa text) and `fallbackRelated` when the API is unreachable or a slug is unknown. Rendering depends on `components/AudioPlayer`, `components/YouTubeEmbed`, `components/AdSlot`, `renderContentBody` from `lib/markdown`, and `lucide-react` icons. The most notable decision is `dynamicParams = true` (flipped from false in the SIDE-FIX-SEO-404 change) combined with `revalidate = 3600`: unknown slugs now ISR-render a "coming soon" panel with HTTP 200 instead of 404ing, protecting crawl budget while content is backfilled into the API. Because the site deploys via `@cloudflare/next-on-pages`, slugs linked elsewhere were also added to `generateStaticParams` (per the P0-18 audit) to guarantee they prerender rather than 404 at the edge. Gotchas: the markdown body is injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (so sanitization relies entirely on `renderContentBody`), and the Like/Share buttons are presentational only with no handlers wired up.

apps\\web\\app\\demo\\chat\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`/demo/chat`) is a developer/QA shortcut that lets any signed-in user bypass payment and instantly open a chat thread with seeded demo providers, then routes them to `/messages`. The default export `DemoChatPage` wraps the inner `DemoChatPageInner` component in `AuthGuard`, which pulls the session token via `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` and posts to the API using `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`. The `trigger` function handles two paths: the "puja" tile calls `POST /demo-pay/puja`, which simulates a ₹1 Razorpay charge, creates a real booking, and auto-assigns the demo pandit, while all other tiles (astrology, wellness, temple, gaushala, store_order) call `POST /demo-pay/start-chat` with a hardcoded `providerEmailMap` (e.g. `astro@demo.com`, `store@demo.com`). A presentational `DemoCard` component renders each tile with an accent-color map, and `lucide-react` icons are used throughout. Notable gotchas: the backend endpoints are themselves gated by the `ENABLE_DEMO_PAY=true` flag, so the page fails if that env var is unset, and the seeded provider emails are hardcoded client-side, meaning the demo breaks if seed data changes. The page also documents the intended two-sided test flow—sign in as the matching provider in an incognito window—and notes that Jitsi powers the voice/video call options.

apps\\web\\app\\devi\\mahavidyas\\[slug].summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the detail page for one of the ten Dasa Mahavidya goddesses at the route /devi/mahavidyas/[slug] on the Darshya site (darshya.online). It exports generateStaticParams (pre-rendering all slugs from the MAHAVIDYAS array), generateMetadata (building SEO titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs), and the default async MahavidyaPage component, which looks up the deity via getMahavidya and calls notFound() for unknown slugs. Its only real dependency is the internal module lib/mahavidyas, which supplies the MAHAVIDYAS catalog and getMahavidya lookup; otherwise it uses Next.js built-ins (Link, notFound, Metadata) and Tailwind utility classes with a custom saffron palette, with no external data fetching. The page renders structured content sections — origin, iconography, mantras (including a mool mantra flagged as requiring initiation), sadhana goals, grants vs. cautions lists, shrines, and tradition connections — plus circular prev/next navigation computed by index modulo over the array, and a CTA linking to /ask-pandit and /pujas. Notable constraints: it is fully static (dynamicParams = false with a 24-hour revalidate), so unknown slugs 404 at the edge rather than rendering on demand, and it injects schema.org BreadcrumbList and Article JSON-LD via dangerouslySetInnerHTML for search rich results.

apps\\web\\app\\demo\\[role]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the dynamic route `/demo/[role]`, which renders role-specific demo experiences in the web app. Its server component `RoleDemoPage` awaits the `params` promise (the Next.js 15 async-params convention), extracts the `role` segment, and hands it to the `RoleDemoClient` component imported from `./role-demo-client`, which contains the actual interactive demo UI. The `VALID_ROLES` const array enumerates the seven supported personas — devotee, pandit, store-owner, astrologer, wellness, temple-manager, and gaushala-manager — and `generateStaticParams` feeds those values to Next.js so each role page is pre-rendered at build time rather than on demand. A notable gotcha is that the page itself performs no validation of `role` against `VALID_ROLES` and never calls `notFound()`, so any handling of unknown or mistyped roles (and any on-demand rendering, since `dynamicParams` is left at its default) must happen downstream in `RoleDemoClient`. The file has no external service dependencies; it is purely a thin server-component shell following the standard pattern of delegating client-side interactivity to a co-located client component.

apps\\web\\app\\darshan\\[id]\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/darshan/[id]/page.tsx`) renders the per-temple live darshan detail page for the Darshya site, accepting either a stream id or temple slug and using ISR (`dynamicParams = true`, `revalidate = 300`) with `generateStaticParams` prerendering ~19 known slugs — including three "coming soon" temples (`rameshwaram`, `baidyanath-dham`, `dwarkadhish`) so they return 200 under `@cloudflare/next-on-pages` instead of 404ing. The exported `generateMetadata` emits canonical/OpenGraph tags (and `robots: noindex` for unknown slugs), while the default `DarshanDetailPage` resolves a stream via `getStreamById`, which queries `getLiveDarshan`/`getScheduledDarshan` from `lib/api` and falls back to the hardcoded `FALLBACK_TEMPLE_LIBRARY` (mapped by `FALLBACK_KEY_BY_SLUG`), rendering an honest "Coming soon" panel with related live streams when neither source knows the slug. Playback URL resolution is tiered: `resolveLivePlaybackUrl` probes each temple's YouTube channel RSS feed (`feeds/videos.xml`, no auth/quota) using a regex heuristic on titles (`live|लाइव|थेट|प्रसारण`) to prefer an active broadcast's videoId, otherwise the latest VOD, falling back to `YOUTUBE_STREAMS` `live_stream` embeds built from `CHANNEL_BY_SLUG`. It depends on components `DarshanPlayer`, `YouTubeDarshanPlayer`, and `AdSlot`, plus `lib/images` (`getTempleHero`) and `lib/aarti-schedules` (`getScheduleForTemple`, `currentAartiState`, `nowMinutesIST`) to show real-time IST aarti slots, with a generic `fallbackSchedule` when a temple lacks a registered schedule. Notable gotchas: the `CHANNEL_BY_SLUG`/`YOUTUBE_STREAMS` tables must be kept in sync with `apps/api/src/routes/darshan.ts` (`TEMPLE_LIVE_STREAMS`), fallback viewer counts are fabricated static numbers, and the earlier behavior of silently serving Kashi Vishwanath content for unknown slugs was deliberately replaced by the coming-soon panel.

apps\\web\\app\\deity\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for per-deity hub routes at `/deity/[slug]`, a programmatic-SEO play targeting long-tail "{deity} puja online" queries by combining a deity overview, a sacred mantra section, and bookable pujas for that deity. Its key exports are the default `DeityPage` server component, `generateMetadata` (which builds SEO titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags per deity), and `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per entry in the `DEITIES` list from `lib/deities`). It depends on internal modules `lib/deities` (`getDeity`, `DEITIES`), `lib/api` (`getPujaTypes`), and `lib/deity-mantras` (`getMantrasForDeity`), plus Next.js primitives `Link` and `notFound`. Notable design choices include full static generation (`dynamicParams = false` with hourly ISR via `revalidate = 3600`), a tolerant fetch pattern where the puja API call is `.catch(() => null)`-wrapped so the page still renders useful SEO content with a "catalogue is being onboarded" fallback when the API errors or returns no active pujas, and a JSON-LD script typed as schema.org `Person` to enrich search results. Gotchas: only `isActive` pujas are shown (filtered client-side after fetch, capped at 24 by the API query), prices arrive as strings and are formatted via a local `fmtINR` helper that falls back to the raw string if parsing fails, and unknown slugs 404 via `notFound()` rather than rendering a soft error. The page also cross-links to `/deity/{slug}/mantras`, `/shlokas`, `/pujas`, and sibling deity pages to strengthen internal linking, and the footer hardcodes trust signals (video proof, 80G receipts, Aadhaar-verified pandits) into every deity page.

apps\\web\\app\\devi\\mahavidyas\\page.t.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the Dasa Mahavidya index on the Darshya site (darshya.online), serving as the collection/SEO hub for the 10 tantric wisdom goddesses — it lists each Mahavidya grouped by line, offers householder worship guidance, a FAQ accordion, and CTAs to `/ask-pandit` and `/devi/navadurga`. It exports a static `metadata` object (canonical URL plus OpenGraph), a `revalidate` of 86400 for daily ISR regeneration, and the default `MahavidyasPage` server component. All goddess content comes from the internal module `lib/mahavidyas`, which provides the `MAHAVIDYAS` array, `MAHAVIDYA_GROUPS` (the Ugra/fierce vs. Saumya/auspicious split), and the `getMahavidya(slug)` lookup; rendering depends only on that module, Next.js `Link`, and Tailwind utility classes with a saffron/amber palette. A notable pattern is that the hardcoded `FAQS` array drives both the visible `<details>` accordion and a schema.org `FAQPage` JSON-LD block, alongside `BreadcrumbList`, `ItemList` (built from `MAHAVIDYAS`), and `CollectionPage` scripts injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Gotchas: `BASE_URL` is hardcoded rather than read from config, and `getMahavidya(slug)!` uses a non-null assertion, so any slug in `MAHAVIDYA_GROUPS` missing from the data module would crash at render time. Each card links to a detail route at `/devi/mahavidyas/[slug]` and displays data-driven fields like `colorHex`, `cosmicFunction`, `element`, and `worshipDay`.

apps\\web\\app\\discover\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the `/discover` route of the Next.js web app (`apps/web`), serving as a programmatic-SEO topical hub that statically indexes all of Darshya's Hindu wisdom guides in one crawlable, internally-linked page. Its default export is the `DiscoverPage` React server component, alongside a `metadata` export (canonical URL, OpenGraph) and a `revalidate = 86400` setting that makes the page daily-regenerated SSG; all content lives in the local `GROUPS` constant, typed via the local `DiscoverGroup`/`DiscoverItem` types, so there are no data-fetching dependencies at all. The roughly 70 links are organized into five accent-colored groups — scriptures, saints & deities, calendar & cosmology, devotional practice, and tools — rendered as a jump-nav plus card grids styled with Tailwind classes mapped through the `ACCENT_CLASS` lookup. The component also injects three JSON-LD structured-data blocks (schema.org `ItemList`, `BreadcrumbList`, and `CollectionPage`) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and the metadata title/description interpolate a computed `TOTAL` count. Notable gotchas: the JSON-LD `position` counter resets per group because it uses the per-group map index, the file's header comment claims "27 routes" though the actual item count is far higher, and the hardcoded `BASE_URL` (`https://darshya.online`) and a custom `saffron` Tailwind palette are assumed to exist elsewhere in the app.

apps\\web\\app\\devi\\navadurga\\[slug]\.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router dynamic route (`/devi/navadurga/[slug]`) that renders a fully static detail page for each of the nine Navadurga goddess forms worshipped during Navratri, presenting her story, iconography, mantras, prasad, color, planet, and worship guidance. It exports the route config constants `revalidate = 86400` (24-hour ISR) and `dynamicParams = false`, plus `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per entry in the `NAVADURGA` array), `generateMetadata` (which builds SEO titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs), and the default async server component `NavadurgaFormPage`. Its only internal dependency is the `lib/navadurga` module, which provides the `NAVADURGA` data array and the `getNavadurga(slug)` lookup; it otherwise relies on Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`, `notFound`) and talks to no external services at runtime. A notable constraint is that `dynamicParams = false` combined with the `getNavadurga` miss path calling `notFound()` means any slug outside the nine pre-built forms hard-404s, so adding a new form requires updating the data module and redeploying. For SEO, the page injects two JSON-LD blocks (schema.org `BreadcrumbList` and `Article`) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and hardcodes `BASE_URL` as `https://darshya.online`, which must be kept in sync with the production domain. Prev/next navigation is computed with modulo arithmetic over the `NAVADURGA` array, creating a circular day-to-day loop across all nine forms, and the page ends with conversion CTAs linking to `/pujas` and `/ask-pandit`.

apps\\web\\app\\devi\\navadurga\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`NavadurgaPage`, default export) is a static, SEO-driven content hub for the Darshya site's "Navadurga" guide — the nine forms of Goddess Durga worshipped during Navratri — rendering a card grid of all nine goddesses (day, Sanskrit name, color swatch, planet, chakra, prasad) that deep-link into `/devi/navadurga/[slug]` detail pages, plus a "4 Navratris" section, an FAQ accordion, and a CTA funneling users to `/ask-pandit` and `/pujas`. All deity and festival data comes from the internal `lib/navadurga` module (`NAVADURGA`, `NAVRATRI_TYPES`), with Next's `Metadata` export, `next/link`, and Tailwind classes as the only other dependencies — no external APIs or runtime data fetching. The page leans heavily on structured data for search visibility, injecting four JSON-LD blocks (`FAQ_LD`, `BREADCRUMB_LD`, `ITEMLIST_LD`, `COLLECTION_LD` for schema.org FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, ItemList, and CollectionPage) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags. Notable constraints: `revalidate = 86400` makes it an ISR page rebuilt once daily; the canonical/OpenGraph URLs are hardcoded to `BASE_URL = 'https://darshya.online'`; the `FAQS` array is duplicated between visible markup and JSON-LD, so the two must be edited together; and the `ITEMLIST_LD` assumes every slug in `NAVADURGA` has a matching dynamic route, meaning data and routes can silently drift apart. One small display quirk: the chakra badge renders only the first word of `n.chakra` via `split(' ')[0]`, which will truncate any multi-word chakra label.

apps\\web\\app\\faqs\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the FAQ hub page for the Darshya marketing web app, a Next.js App Router route at `/faqs` that renders frequently asked questions about puja booking, live darshan, NRI pricing, yatra packages, refunds, and 80G receipts. Its default export is the `FaqsHub` server component, and it also exports `metadata` (with canonical URL and OpenGraph tags for SEO) and a `revalidate` of 86400 seconds, meaning the page is statically rendered and regenerated at most once per day. All content comes from the internal module `../../lib/faqs`, which supplies the `FAQ_GROUPS` data structure (grouped Q&A with slugs, titles, and descriptions), the `allFaqs()` helper, and `faqPageJsonLd()`, the latter two used to inject FAQ structured data via a `application/ld+json` script tag for rich search results. The page relies only on `next/link` and React's native `details`/`summary` elements for the collapsible accordion, avoiding any client-side JavaScript or state. Notable details: anchor-based "Jump to" navigation links to each group via slug-derived section IDs with `scroll-mt-20` for sticky-header offset, and a hardcoded WhatsApp contact link (wa.me/919255109400) appears in the closing call-to-action alongside a `/contact` link.

apps\\web\\app\\ekadashi\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/ekadashi` route on darshya.online, serving as the SEO hub page that indexes all 24 Ekadashi vratas (Hindu lunar fasting days) and links out to individual `/ekadashi/[slug]` detail pages. It exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph), a `revalidate = 86400` setting for daily ISR regeneration, and the default `EkadashiIndexPage` server component. All content is sourced from the internal module `lib/ekadashis`, which provides the `EKADASHIS` array, the curated `EKADASHI_GROUPS` collections, and the `getEkadashi(slug)` lookup; the only external imports are `next/link` and Next's `Metadata` type. The page is heavily SEO-oriented, injecting four JSON-LD schemas — `BreadcrumbList`, `ItemList` (generated from `EKADASHIS`), `CollectionPage`, and `FAQPage` (generated from a hardcoded `FAQS` array whose questions are also rendered as a native `<details>` accordion). Rendering consists of a hero section, card grids per group, a full lunar-order table, the FAQ block, and a conversion CTA linking to `/ask-pandit` and `/vrat`. Notable gotchas: `getEkadashi(slug)!` uses a non-null assertion, so any slug in `EKADASHI_GROUPS` missing from the data will crash at render time, and the FAQ text is duplicated between the visible markup and the structured data rather than shared. Styling relies on Tailwind with a custom `saffron` color palette, and the `BASE_URL` constant is hardcoded to the production domain.

apps\\web\\app\\error.tsx.summary: This file defines `AppError`, the root app-router error boundary (tagged P0-9) for the Next.js web app, catching runtime errors thrown by any route under `app/` that lacks a closer `error.tsx` of its own. The default-exported client component receives Next.js's standard `error` (with optional `digest`) and `reset` props, and its only dependencies are React's `useEffect` and the internal `captureBrowserException` helper from `../lib/sentry`, which it calls once per error via an effect keyed on the error object. A key design distinction from `global-error.tsx` is that this boundary renders inside the root layout rather than replacing `<html><body>`, so the site chrome — nav, footer, fonts — remains visible while only the failing segment's content is swapped for the recovery UI. The UI is deliberately self-contained with inline branded styles (copper accent `#b87333`), offering a "Try again" button that invokes `reset()` to re-render the segment and a "Back to Home" anchor link as a fallback escape path. When Next.js supplies an `error.digest`, it is rendered in a monospace footer line so users or support can quote the correlation ID. Because error boundaries must be client components, the file is marked `'use client'`, and the Sentry capture is placed in an effect (rather than render) to avoid double-reporting during React's render passes.

apps\\web\\app\\ekadashi\\[slug]\\page.t.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/ekadashi/[slug]` route in the Darshya web app (darshya.online), rendering a static detail page for each of the 24 Ekadashi fasts with their story, fasting rules, permitted/forbidden foods, mantra, benefits, and observance notes. It exports the default async server component `EkadashiDetailPage`, plus `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per entry in the `EKADASHIS` array) and `generateMetadata` (which builds SEO titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs per slug). Its only data dependency is the internal `lib/ekadashis` module, which provides the `EKADASHIS` constant and the `getEkadashi(slug)` lookup; otherwise it relies on Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`) with no external services or runtime fetches. Notable design choices: `dynamicParams = false` combined with a `getEkadashi` miss calling `notFound()` guarantees unknown slugs hard-404, and `revalidate = 86400` enables daily ISR on top of full static generation. The page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks (`BreadcrumbList` and `Article`) via raw `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags for rich search results. Prev/next navigation is computed with modulo indexing over `EKADASHIS`, making the 24-item list circular rather than clamped at the ends. Finally, the page doubles as a conversion funnel, closing with CTAs that link to `/ask-pandit` and `/pujas` for guided vrata services.

apps\\web\\app\\donations\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the `/donations` route of the Darshya Next.js web app, serving as the landing page where devotees browse and give to verified temples and gaushalas, with SEO metadata advertising 80G tax-deductible receipts and Razorpay-secured payments. Its default export, the async server component `DonationsLandingPage`, runs in two modes: when `searchParams` carries a deep-linked `causeId` and `causeName` (plus optional `causeKind` and `planId`), it skips the listing and renders the `DonationForm` component directly; otherwise it shows a hero plus two cause grids rendered by the local unexported `CauseCard` component. The gaushala grid is driven by a hardcoded `gaushalaCauses` array whose ids deliberately mirror those in `app/gaushala/page.tsx` so cross-linking needs no API call, while the temple grid fetches live data via `getTemples({ limit: 6 })` from `../../lib/api`, wrapped in try/catch so a backend outage degrades to a gaushala-only page with an empty-state message rather than crashing. A notable gotcha is the hardcoded `PLAN_AMOUNTS` map (`plan_daily` through `plan_lifetime`) used to prefill the donation amount when a cow detail page deep-links with `?planId=` — these prices are duplicated from the gaushala adoption plan grid and must be kept in sync manually. Other dependencies include `getTranslations` from `../../lib/t` for i18n across the donations, common, and terms namespaces, the `IMAGES` registry from `../../lib/images` for static assets, and `lucide-react` for icons. The component also defensively normalizes temple image data, accepting either a plain string or an object with a `url` field before falling back to a default cow-shelter image.

apps\\web\\app\\festivals\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page component that exists solely to fix a routing dead end: the festivals index page lives at the singular path `/festival`, but the plural `/festivals` previously returned a 404. The default-exported `FestivalsRedirect` component calls `redirect` from `next/navigation` to permanently send any request for `/festivals` to `/festival`, so external links, bookmarks, or guessed plural URLs resolve correctly. It has no internal dependencies beyond Next.js itself and renders no UI. The inline comment ties the change to a tracked ticket (P1 #214, dated 2026-08-03) flagged by recon, making the rationale discoverable for future maintainers who might otherwise delete the seemingly trivial file.

apps\\web\\app\\festival\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for `/festival`, serving as an SEO gateway that links to individual `/festival/[slug]` pages and targets seasonal search traffic around festivals like Diwali and Holi. Its default export is the `FestivalIndex` server component, which renders a header, a highlighted "next festival" callout, and a grid of cards for every festival, alongside exported `metadata` (canonical URL, OpenGraph tags) and a `revalidate` constant setting 24-hour ISR. It depends on the internal `../../lib/festivals` module for the `FESTIVALS` data array and the `nextFestival()` helper, plus Next.js built-ins (`next/link`, the `Metadata` type), with no external service calls. Notable details: the page injects schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for rich search results, dates are hardcoded to 2026 through the `date2026` field and formatted with `en-IN` locale via a local `fmtDate` helper, and the "next festival" section renders conditionally — so once all 2026 dates pass, the page silently drops that section until the data is refreshed. Styling relies on project-specific Tailwind tokens like `saffron-*` and `surface-*`.

apps\\web\\app\\demo\\[role]\\role-demo-.summary: This file is the client component behind the `/demo/[role]` route in the Next.js web app, rendering a step-through showcase of mobile-app mockup screens for the Poojly product across the seven user roles in the `RoleKey` union (devotee, pandit, store-owner, astrologer, wellness, temple-manager, gaushala-manager), with per-role display names and Tailwind accent colors centralized in `roleMeta`. It defines a set of shared presentational primitives — `StatusBar` (with separate iOS and Android variants to simulate a phone frame), `FormField`, `StatCard`, `ListItem`, `SectionTitle`, `PrimaryButton`, `ScreenHeader`, and `TabBar` — which are composed into dozens of hardcoded screen components such as `DevoteeScreen1`–`DevoteeScreen6` (splash/onboarding, account creation, home with Live Darshan, puja booking with ₹ pricing, live-stream viewer with chat, and profile) and `PanditScreen1`–`PanditScreen3` (role selection, experience/specialties, rates and document upload). The truncated remainder presumably continues with the other roles' screens plus the default-exported viewer component, since the `useState`, `next/link`, and `ArrowLeft`/`ChevronLeft`/`ChevronRight` imports indicate a paginated carousel with a back link. Dependencies are minimal: React local state, `next/link`, and a very large `lucide-react` icon set, with all styling done via Tailwind classes on a custom `saffron`/`surface` palette. The biggest gotcha is that nothing here is functional UI — "inputs" are divs rendering placeholder text, buttons are styled divs, and all data (temples, bookings, prices in ₹, chat messages) is static mock content, so this is a marketing/demo artifact with no API calls or real interactivity. A second fragility: `StatCard` derives its background and text classes by splitting a space-delimited `color` prop string, a brittle convention to know before editing or extending it.

apps\\web\\app\\feed.xml\\route.ts.summary: This Next.js route handler (`apps/web/app/feed.xml/route.ts`) serves a public RSS 2.0 feed of the site's blog posts so external readers like Feedly, Inoreader, and NewsBlur can syndicate content, with discovery wired through a `<link rel="alternate">` tag in `app/layout.tsx`. Its sole export is the `GET` handler plus a `revalidate` constant of 1800 seconds, which sets ISR regeneration to 30 minutes to match the `/updates` cadence. The feed data comes from the internal `listBlogPosts` function in `lib/blog-posts`, and there are no external service calls beyond that. Two small helpers support rendering: `esc` XML-escapes the five special characters, and `rfc822` converts `YYYY-MM-DD` post dates into RFC-822 `pubDate` strings, falling back to the current time if parsing fails. The handler is deliberately resilient — if `listBlogPosts` throws, it silently emits an empty feed rather than erroring — and it caps output at the 30 most recent posts, using `p.excerpt` or the first 400 characters of `p.body` as each item's description. The base URL is hardcoded as the `SITE` constant (`https://darshya.online`), so the feed will produce wrong links in preview or staging deployments. Responses are sent with `application/rss+xml` content type and a public `cache-control` of `max-age=1800, s-maxage=1800`, so CDNs cache it in step with the ISR window. The XML is assembled via string interpolation rather than a serializer, which is why correct use of `esc` on every interpolated value matters for feed validity.

apps\\web\\app\\for-temple-chains\\page..summary: This Next.js App Router page (`ForTempleChainsPage`) is the static B2B marketing landing page at the `/for-temple-chains` route, pitching Darshya's white-label temple-management SaaS (donor CRM, puja booking, 80G receipt automation, live darshan) to temple chains, ashram networks, and mathas. Its only exports are the Next.js `metadata` object (SEO title/description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags) and the default server component that renders the page. The sole internal dependency is the `RoiCalculator` component imported from the sibling `./RoiCalculator` module, embedded in the savings-estimator section; the only external dependencies are `next/link` and `next`'s metadata API, with no data fetching or client-side state. All content is hardcoded in three module-level constants: `TIERS` (Starter/Pro/Enterprise pricing with 50%-off 90-day pilot rates), `CUSTOMER_TYPES` (five target-customer archetypes), and `ROI_COMPARISON` (a feature table positioning Darshya against a Razorpay-only setup). Notable choices: the page is a pure server component (no `"use client"`), so interactivity is delegated entirely to `RoiCalculator`; conversion CTAs consistently funnel to `/contact?topic=b2b-pilot` or `mailto:pilots@darshya.online`; and the copy leans on scarcity messaging (5 pilot slots, Q4 close) plus a 12-month price-lock guarantee. Because the pricing and comparison data live inline rather than in a CMS or config, any pricing change requires editing this file directly.

apps\\web\\app\\for-temple-chains\\RoiCa.summary: This file defines `RoiCalculator`, a client-side React component for the `for-temple-chains` marketing page in the `apps/web` Next.js app, letting prospective temple-chain customers estimate the platform's annual financial benefit against its subscription cost. The default-exported `RoiCalculator` component holds four pieces of local state (monthly donation count, average donation amount, admin hours per week, and pricing `Tier`) and derives all outputs in a single `useMemo`, while a private `Row` component renders each labeled result line with optional `emerald`, `saffron`, or `indigo` accent coloring. Pricing is hardcoded in the `PLATFORM_FEE_INR_PER_MONTH` constant (Starter ₹999, Pro ₹2,999, Enterprise ₹4,999 per month), and a local `inr` helper formats numbers using the `en-IN` locale with a non-finite guard. The model computes annual GMV, then adds three benefit streams with fixed assumptions documented inline: admin time saved at ₹400/hr, 80G receipt automation at ₹15 per PDF, and an 8% donor-retention uplift on annual GMV. It compares total benefit against both list-price annual cost and a discounted "pilot" first-year cost (3 months at 50% plus 9 months full price), surfacing net benefits and an ROI multiple. The component depends only on React and Tailwind utility classes tied to a custom theme palette (`surface`, `cream`, `saffron`, `indigo`, `emerald`), with no internal module imports or backend calls, so all assumptions live entirely in this file. A footnote discloses the assumed rates and notes that figures are estimates, signaling these constants are marketing assumptions rather than measured data. Inputs are clamped to non-negative numbers on change, which prevents negative GMV but silently coerces invalid entries to zero.

apps\\web\\app\\festival\\[slug]\\page.t.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for individual festival detail routes (`/festival/[slug]`) on the Darshya puja-booking site, built for programmatic SEO around queries like "{festival} 2026 puja online" and expected to see traffic spikes during festival weeks. Its exports are the route config constants `revalidate = 86400` and `dynamicParams = false`, plus `generateStaticParams`, `generateMetadata`, and the default async `FestivalPage` component; rendering is driven entirely by the static `FESTIVALS` catalog and `getFestival` lookup from `lib/festivals`, with no external APIs or databases involved. Because `dynamicParams` is false, only slugs present in `FESTIVALS` at build time exist—anything else 404s via `notFound()`—and pages are statically generated with a 24-hour ISR revalidation window. The page emits schema.org `Event` JSON-LD, builds SEO metadata (canonical URL, OpenGraph) in `generateMetadata`, and renders the festival's date, deity, fasting rules, ordered rituals, significance, and bookable pujas via internal links to `/pujas/[slug]`, `/deity/[deitySlug]`, `/panchang`, and sibling festival pages. Helper functions `fmtDate` (en-IN formatting) and `daysUntil` power status badges ("Today", "In N days", "Returns next year") computed against the hardcoded `date2026` field. A notable gotcha is that all dates are pinned to the 2026 lunar calendar, so the page acknowledges tithis are approximate and defers to the Darshya Panchang for city-specific accuracy—meaning the content will go stale after 2026 unless the catalog is updated.

apps\\web\\app\\free-pandit-advice\\page.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/free-pandit-advice/page.tsx`) is the SEO hub for Darshya's "free pandit kundli astrology advice" campaign, serving as an index that links out to 13 long-tail topic pages, one per life area (marriage, career, manglik dosh, etc.). Its default export, the `FreePanditAdviceHub` server component, renders hero CTAs toward `/ask-pandit` and `/astrology/kundli`, an anchor-jump pill nav, and a responsive card grid summarizing each topic, while the exported `metadata` object sets the title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags. The page depends on `FREE_PANDIT_TOPICS` from the internal `../../lib/free-pandit-topics` module for all content (titles, slugs, Hindi titles, intros, FAQ counts) and on `next/link` for routing; it talks to no external services. It injects three schema.org JSON-LD blocks — `ItemList`, `BreadcrumbList`, and `CollectionPage` — built from the topics array to earn rich search results. Notable decisions: `revalidate = 86400` makes it a daily-regenerated ISR page, the production origin is hardcoded as `BASE_URL = 'https://darshya.online'` (so structured-data URLs won't adapt to staging), and card titles are derived by stripping the literal prefix `'Free Pandit Advice on '` from each topic title, which would break silently if that wording ever changed.

apps\\web\\app\\free-pandit-advice\\[top.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the per-topic "Free Pandit Advice" SEO landing pages for the Darshya site, with each slug statically generated at build time from the internal data module `lib/free-pandit-topics` (via `FREE_PANDIT_TOPICS`, `getTopicBySlug`, and `topicSlugs`). It exports `generateStaticParams` to enumerate all topic slugs, `generateMetadata` to produce per-topic titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags, and the default async `FreePanditTopicPage` component that renders the full article body: intro, common problems, free Vedic remedies, paid-consult guidance, an FAQ accordion, and a CTA section linking to `/astrology/kundli` and `/ask-pandit`. A key purpose is search visibility: the page injects three schema.org JSON-LD blocks (FAQPage, BreadcrumbList, and Article) so the FAQs are eligible for Google rich snippets. Notable constraints include `dynamicParams = false`, which means any slug not in the static list returns a 404 via `notFound()`, and `revalidate = 86400`, which puts pages on a 24-hour ISR cycle. The base URL `https://darshya.online` is hardcoded as `BASE_URL` rather than read from config, so canonicals and structured data would need manual updates if the domain changes. Prev/next navigation is computed by index position within `FREE_PANDIT_TOPICS`, and the breadcrumb header strips the "Free Pandit Advice on " prefix from titles with string replacement, which is fragile if topic titles ever change format.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\cows\\p.summary: This Next.js client page implements the Cow Registry UI for the gaushala portal, letting shelter managers browse, search, filter, and register cows and log their health records. The default export `CowsPage` wraps `CowsPageContent` in `AuthGuard` restricted to the `gaushala_manager` and `admin` roles, with two small internal presentational helpers, `Field` and `Stat`, plus local `Cow` and `HealthRecord` types describing the API payloads. It pulls `session.accessToken` from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) and calls the backend at `API_BASE_URL` (lib/api-config): `GET`/`POST /gaushala-portal/cows`, `GET /gaushala-portal/cows/:id`, and `POST /gaushala-portal/cows/:id/health`, all with Bearer-token headers; icons come from lucide-react. Searching and status filtering (healthy, treatment, pregnant, recovering) happen client-side over the fetched list, and a `statusConfig` map drives per-status badge styling, with cows in "treatment" surfaced as a "need attention" count in the header. Registration and cow detail/health history are both handled in modals rather than separate routes; the registration form requires only tag number and name, shows a transient "Registered!" success state that auto-closes after 1200ms, and new health records are optimistically prepended to the history list. Notable gotchas: fetch errors are silently swallowed (the "graceful" catch blocks), the `loadCows` effect disables the exhaustive-deps lint rule, and `ageYears` is coerced with `Number()` without validation, so non-numeric input would send NaN to the API.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\message.summary: This file defines `GaushalaMessagesPage`, the client-side Next.js route component for the `/gaushala-portal/messages` path in the `apps/web` application. Its sole job is to render a page shell—titled "Donor Messages" with a subtitle prompting shelter staff to update donors on sponsored cows—and embed the shared `Inbox` component imported from `../../../components/Inbox`, passing it `role="provider"`. That role prop is the key design decision: the page reuses the generic `Inbox` rather than implementing its own messaging UI, with the provider role presumably configuring the inbox to show the shelter's side of donor conversations. The component is marked `'use client'`, meaning it renders on the client even though it currently holds no state or interactivity of its own. Layout is minimal, using Tailwind utility classes (`max-w-5xl`, `text-surface-*` palette tokens) to constrain width and style headings within the broader gaushala portal layout. Any actual messaging logic—fetching threads, sending replies—lives entirely inside the `Inbox` component, making this page a thin routing/presentation wrapper.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the landing page for Darshya's cow-adoption feature, rendered at the `/gaushala` route in the Next.js web app. It exports a `metadata` object for SEO and the default `GaushalaPage` component, which composes a fully static marketing page: hero, trust badges, verified-gaushala cards, a horizontally scrolling "available cows" carousel, four adoption pricing tiers, impact stats, a FAQ accordion built on native `<details>` elements, and a closing CTA. All content — the `gaushalas`, `featuredCows`, `adoptionPlans` (Gau Seva through Gau Daan), and `faqs` arrays — is hardcoded in the file rather than fetched from an API, with a comment noting it "matches API" data. Dependencies are minimal: `next/link` for navigation, `lucide-react` for icons, the internal `IMAGES` registry from `lib/images` for photography, and the shared `ApprovedProvidersStrip` component rendered at the bottom with `type="gaushala"`. A local `healthBadge` helper maps cow health statuses (`healthy`, `under_treatment`, `senior_care`) to colored pills. The notable gotcha is the `gaushalaToAdoptableCow` mapping: because no `/gaushala/[gsId]` detail route exists (ticket P1 #214), each "Explore Gaushala" card links to one of that gaushala's adoptable-cow detail pages (e.g. `gs_001` → `cow_001`) to avoid 404s, with a fallback to the raw gaushala id. Styling relies on Tailwind with custom `saffron`/`surface` design tokens and Devanagari/display font variables for the Hindi plan names.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\layout..summary: This file defines the shared layout for the gaushala-portal section of the Next.js web app, wrapping every page under that route in a dashboard shell restricted to gaushala managers. The default export, GaushalPortalLayout, gates all content behind the internal AuthGuard component (from components/AuthGuard) with allowedRoles set to ['gaushala_manager'], then renders GaushalPortalShell, which composes a sticky header, a mobile hamburger trigger with a dimmed overlay, and the GaushalaSidebar. The sidebar reads the current route via usePathname and the current user via the useAuth hook from lib/auth-context, displaying the user's fullName, a signOut button, and navigation driven by the sidebarLinks array (Overview, Messages, Donations, Cows, Volunteers, Profile), with active-state highlighting that treats '/gaushala-portal' as an exact match but uses prefix matching for child routes. Icons come from lucide-react, except Cows, which uses a local CowIcon placeholder component that currently renders an empty styled span. Notable design choices: the sidebar is dark (#2a2520) with saffron accent classes, it behaves as an off-canvas drawer below the lg breakpoint and a sticky column on desktop, and the layout is a client component, meaning everything inside—including the guard—runs client-side rather than as a server-side check.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\donatio.summary: This Next.js client page renders the donations dashboard for the gaushala portal, letting managers review incoming donations, search and filter them, see running totals, and export results as CSV. The default export DonationsPage wraps DonationsPageContent in an AuthGuard restricted to the gaushala_manager and admin roles, and the file also defines the Donation type (id, donor, email, amountInr, status of created/paid/failed, receiptNumber, timestamps) plus label/style maps that render those statuses as Pending/Received/Failed. Data comes from the backend endpoint `${API_BASE_URL}/gaushala-portal/donations`, called with the bearer token from useAuth (lib/auth-context) and the base URL from lib/api-config, while UI icons come from lucide-react and the internal AuthGuard component handles access control. A notable gotcha, flagged in an inline comment (P2 #221), is that the fetch was capped from an unbounded limit=500 down to limit=100 as a stopgap, so the page only ever shows the first hundred records until a real paginated UI is built. All filtering (status pills plus text search over donor, email, receipt) and the summary figures (total received and this-month received, computed from paidAt) are done client-side with useMemo over whatever the single fetch returned. The exportCsv helper builds the spreadsheet in-browser via a Blob download, quoting donor names for CSV safety, and the effect uses a cancelled flag to avoid setting state after unmount.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala\\[id]\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/gaushala/[id]/page.tsx`) renders the cow-detail view for the Gau Seva adoption feature, showing a cow's photo, breed, health status, description, monthly photo-update timeline, adoption plans, and the parent gaushala's contact details. Its exports are the default async server component `CowDetailPage`, plus `generateStaticParams`, `dynamicParams = false`, and static `metadata` for SEO. All content is hardcoded MVP fixture data: the `allCows` record (eight cows across gaushalas gs_001–gs_003), a `defaultCow` fallback, an `adoptionPlans` array (Gau Seva ₹51/day through Gau Daan ₹2,25,000 lifetime), and a `gaushalaInfo` contact/facilities map; there is no backend or database call. Dependencies are limited to `next/link` and `next`'s `Metadata` type, `lucide-react` icons, and the internal `IMAGES.gaushala` map from `lib/images`. A key gotcha: because `dynamicParams` is false, only the eight IDs from `generateStaticParams` are prerendered and any other ID 404s, so the `defaultCow` fallback is effectively unreachable dead code. Donate and plan-selection CTAs are `Link`s into the `/donations` flow carrying `causeId`, `causeKind=gaushala`, `causeName`, and `planId` query params (per an inline comment, these replaced previously dead buttons so users pay real plan amounts via Razorpay with 80G receipts), but the Share and Gift buttons remain non-functional with no handlers. Other notable decisions include a `healthBadge` helper mapping `healthy`/`under_treatment`/`senior_care` statuses to colored pills, and the deliberate removal of `lg:sticky` from the sidebar adopt card because it visually overlapped the gaushala-details card while scrolling.

apps\\web\\app\\gift\\page.tsx.summary: This is the Next.js App Router page for the `/gift` route in the Darshya web app — a marketing and lead-capture landing page targeting NRIs who want to purchase a puja in India for family members. Its default export is the `GiftPujaPage` server component, which renders static "how it works" steps (`STEPS`), trust badges (`TRUST`), popular gifting occasions, and embeds the interactive `GiftPujaForm` client component from the sibling `./GiftPujaForm` module as the conversion entry point. It also exports route-level `metadata` (SEO title, keywords, OpenGraph tags, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/gift`) and sets `revalidate = 86400` so the page is statically regenerated once per day via ISR. Dependencies are minimal: `next/link` for internal navigation (a CTA linking to `/pujas`), `lucide-react` icons, and Tailwind utility classes using custom `saffron-*` and `surface-*` palette tokens. Notable details: the page is almost entirely static content with the form isolated as the only interactive island, the copy references downstream operations (Stripe checkout, WhatsApp confirmations, a 4-hour manual follow-up fallback) that are not implemented here, and the sticky form layout (`md:sticky md:top-4`) is a deliberate conversion-oriented design choice on desktop.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\page.ts.summary: This file is the main dashboard page (`GaushalaDashboard`) for the gaushala (cow shelter) manager portal in the Next.js web app, rendering an at-a-glance overview of cow counts, donor counts, and donation totals alongside recent donations, a cow-registry preview, and quick-action links to sub-pages like `/gaushala-portal/donations`, `/cows`, `/volunteers`, and `/profile`. Its only export is the default client component; local helpers include `formatInr` (₹ formatting with K/L abbreviations and `en-IN` locale), `relativeTime` (hours/days-ago strings), a `statusColor` map for cow health badges, and the `DashboardStats`, `DashboardDonation`, and `DashboardCow` types describing the API payload. It builds on the shared `MyProviderProfileCard` (rendered with role `GAUSHALA_MANAGER`) and `KycStatusBadge` components, the `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` for the user and session token, and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`; externally it uses Next.js `Link` and lucide-react icons. Data comes from two backend endpoints, `GET /gaushala-portal/dashboard` and `GET /provider-kyc`, both called with a Bearer token in `useEffect` hooks, with the KYC response collapsed into a `verified`/`pending`/`unsubmitted`/`rejected` state machine driven by the `verified` flag and `rejectionReason`. A notable design point, flagged in comments as P0 #AP-07, is that both fetches deliberately run for demo sessions too—the old `startsWith('demo-')` skip left demo managers on zeroed stats and masked backend bugs, and the API now accepts demo tokens in non-production. Error handling is intentionally forgiving: non-OK responses or exceptions silently keep the default zero stats and `unsubmitted` KYC state rather than surfacing an error. Theming is done via CSS custom properties (`var(--color-surface)`, `--color-primary`, etc.) rather than hardcoded colors, and empty states prompt the manager to register a first cow or view donations.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\volunte.summary: This Next.js client page implements the Volunteers management screen for the gaushala portal, letting managers list, search, add, activate/deactivate, and delete volunteers for a cow-shelter operation. The default export `VolunteersPage` wraps `VolunteersContent` in an `AuthGuard` restricted to `gaushala_manager` and `admin` roles, with supporting local components `StatCard` and `Field` plus the `Volunteer` type and the `countNewThisMonth` helper. It pulls the session token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) and the base URL from `API_BASE_URL` (lib/api-config), and talks to the backend REST endpoints under `/gaushala-portal/volunteers` — GET for the list, POST for creation, PATCH for toggling the `active` flag, and DELETE for removal — using Bearer-token authorization via `fetch`. UI state is all local React hooks: a search box (matching name, role, or phone), an All/Active/Inactive status filter, three stat cards, and an add-volunteer modal whose form requires only `fullName` and defaults the role to `general`. Role badges are color-coded through the `roleColors` map keyed by the four roles (general, feeding, medical, cleaning), and icons come from `lucide-react`. Notable design choices: every mutation triggers a full `load()` refetch rather than optimistic updates, deletion relies on a browser `confirm()` dialog, fetch failures on load and toggle are silently swallowed ("graceful"), and the `useEffect` on `token` disables the exhaustive-deps lint rule. Server-returned error messages are surfaced in the modal when POST fails, and dates render with the `en-IN` locale.

apps\\web\\app\\gaushala-portal\\profile.summary: This Next.js client page renders the Gaushala Profile screen in the gaushala portal, letting a gaushala manager view their account details, edit shelter information, and review KYC verification status. The default export `GaushalProfilePage` gates everything behind `AuthGuard` (restricted to `gaushala_manager` and `admin` roles), while the inner `Content` component pulls the session token from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`) and loads data from two backend endpoints: the profile itself comes from `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/gaushala-portal/dashboard` (notably reusing the dashboard payload rather than a dedicated profile GET), and KYC status comes from the shared `GET ${API_BASE_URL}/provider-kyc` endpoint. Edits to gaushala name, city, address, and description are sent via `PATCH /gaushala-portal/profile` with empty strings converted to `undefined` so they are omitted from the payload, and the save button is disabled until a non-blank name is present. The UI splits into three cards — read-only manager details from the auth user, an editable gaushala information form, and a verification documents panel — rendered through small local presentational helpers `ReadOnly`, `Editable`, and `DocRow`. The KYC section masks the Aadhaar number to its last four digits, shows per-document Submitted/Pending chips, derives an overall status of Verified, Rejected (surfacing `rejectionReason`), or Pending review, and links out to `/provider/kyc` for document management, which is a provider-portal route rather than a gaushala-portal one. Theming relies entirely on CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, etc.) with `lucide-react` icons, and fetch errors during initial load are silently swallowed ("graceful" catch), so a failed dashboard call leaves the form blank rather than showing an error.

apps\\web\\app\\gita\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the Bhagavad Gita section of the Darshya site (darshya.online), rendering a chapter-by-chapter guide at the `/gita` route. Its default export, `GitaIndexPage`, builds the landing view by grouping all 18 chapters from the internal `GITA_CHAPTERS` data module (`../../lib/gita-chapters`, which also provides `TOTAL_VERSES`) into three thematic sections — Karma, Bhakti, and Jnana Khanda — each rendered as a grid of `next/link` cards linking to `/gita/[slug]` detail pages. The page is heavily SEO-oriented: it exports a `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags, and injects JSON-LD structured data (a schema.org `ItemList` of `Chapter` entries plus a `BreadcrumbList`) via a raw `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag. It depends only on Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`) and the local gita-chapters data file — no external APIs or client-side state, so it is a fully static server component revalidated every 86400 seconds (24 hours) via the `revalidate` export. A notable gotcha: section heading colors are built with dynamically interpolated Tailwind class names (`border-${sec.color}-200`, `text-${sec.color}-900`), which Tailwind's static class extraction cannot detect, so those classes may be purged in production unless safelisted. The page also hardcodes the production `BASE_URL` constant and cross-links related routes (`/chants/gita-jayanti`, `/shlokas`, `/deity/krishna`) for internal navigation.

apps\\web\\app\\gift\\GiftPujaForm.tsx.summary: `GiftPujaForm.tsx` is a client component in the web app (`apps/web/app/gift/`) that powers the "gift a puja" flow, letting a buyer (typically abroad) book a puja for a recipient in India. Its single export, `GiftPujaForm`, first fetches feature flags from `${API_BASE_URL}/gift-puja/config` (using `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`) to decide between two submission paths: when `autoFlowReady` is true it POSTs to `/gift-puja/create-order` and hands the returned `clientSecret` to the internal `StripeClientSecretCheckout` component for Stripe Elements payment; otherwise it falls back to an honest inquiry flow via `/gift-puja/inquiry`. As a last resort, if the inquiry API is unreachable, it constructs a `mailto:` to gift@darshya.online with the form details rather than failing outright. The form hardcodes three price tiers in `PRICE_TIERS` ($60/$120/$250, defaulting to $120), plus fixed `PUJAS` and `OCCASIONS` dropdown lists, and only shows the amount selector when payment is enabled. Key dependencies are the `API_BASE_URL` config module, `StripeClientSecretCheckout`, and lucide-react icons; externally it talks to the backend gift-puja API and Stripe. Notable gotchas: the submit button stays disabled until config loads (failed config fetches default to all-flags-false), client-side validation requires only buyer email, recipient name, and recipient WhatsApp, and the post-payment return URL points at `/gift/success?orderId=…`. The component renders three distinct states — form, Stripe checkout, or inquiry-success confirmation — driven by the `Status` union and whether an order with a `clientSecret` exists.

apps\\web\\app\\gift\\success\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/gift/success/page.tsx`) is the post-checkout redirect target for the gift-puja flow: after Stripe completes a payment, it lands here and confirms the order server-side before showing a confirmation. The default export `GiftSuccessPage` wraps the internal `VerifyContent` component in a `Suspense` boundary (required because `VerifyContent` calls `useSearchParams` from `next/navigation`), and the local `Verify` type models the backend's verify response including `reference`, `status`, and optional `whatsappDelivery`. On mount it reads the Stripe-appended query params (`orderId`, `payment_intent`, `redirect_status`), short-circuits to an error state if params are missing or `redirect_status` is `failed`, and otherwise POSTs `{ orderId, paymentIntentId }` to `${API_BASE_URL}/gift-puja/verify-payment`, where `API_BASE_URL` comes from the internal `lib/api-config` module. Dependencies are minimal: React, `next/navigation`, `next/link`, and `lucide-react` icons (`CheckCircle2`, `AlertCircle`, `Loader2`, `MessageCircle`); it talks to the backend API rather than to Stripe directly, trusting the server to validate the PaymentIntent. Notable details: the effect uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid setState after unmount, and the success UI surfaces WhatsApp delivery status to the recipient, displaying an amber fallback notice promising manual notification within 4 hours when `whatsappDelivery` isn't `'sent'`. The page renders three fixed states (loading spinner, error with a link back to `/gift`, success card) and mentions that video proof is emailed within 24 hours of puja completion.

apps\\web\\app\\gita\\[chapter]\\page.ts.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the dynamic route `/gita/[chapter]`, rendering a static, SEO-optimized detail page for one of the 18 Bhagavad Gita chapters on the Darshya site. It exports `generateStaticParams` (built from `chapterSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (per-chapter title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags), and the default async server component `GitaChapterPage`, which renders the chapter header, summary, key verses with Sanskrit and translation, a central takeaway, prev/next chapter navigation, and a "jump to chapter" grid. All data comes from the internal module `lib/gita-chapters` (`GITA_CHAPTERS`, `chapterSlugs`, `getChapter`); framework dependencies are `next/link` and `next/navigation`'s `notFound`, with no external data fetching at all. Notable design choices: `dynamicParams = false` plus `revalidate = 86400` means only the 18 prerendered slugs exist (unknown slugs hit `notFound()` and 404) and pages revalidate daily; the canonical host `https://darshya.online` is hardcoded as `BASE_URL`. The page injects Article and BreadcrumbList JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search-engine structured data, and the `datePublished` field is a hardcoded string ('2026-05-27'), so it won't track real content changes. It also uses the newer Next.js convention where `params` is a Promise that must be awaited, and prev/next links are derived by scanning `GITA_CHAPTERS` for adjacent chapter numbers rather than array indices.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukul-portal\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router entry point for the `/gurukul-portal` route in the `apps/web` application. Its default export, `GurukulPortalPage`, is a thin server component that simply renders `GurukulPortalClient`, imported from the sibling `./GurukulPortalClient` module where all the actual UI and interactivity live. It also exports a static `metadata` object (typed with Next's `Metadata`) that sets the page title to "Gurukul Portal — Darshya" and describes the page as a place to manage gurukul listings and admission applications. The only external dependency is the `next` package's type definitions; there is no data fetching or logic here. The notable design decision is the deliberate server/client split: keeping this file as a server component allows the `metadata` export to be honored by Next.js (client components cannot export metadata), while pushing all rendering into `GurukulPortalClient`. Anyone looking for the portal's actual behavior should look at `GurukulPortalClient`, not this file.

apps\\web\\app\\global-error.tsx.summary: This file defines the Next.js App Router global error boundary for the web app, rendering a fallback UI when an error crashes the root layout itself. Its default export, the client component `GlobalError`, receives the thrown `error` (with an optional Next.js `digest`) and a `reset` callback, and on mount it reports the failure to Sentry via `initSentryBrowser` and `captureBrowserException` from the internal `../lib/sentry` module, tagging the event with the error digest. The UI is a minimal 500 page with "Try again" (invoking `reset` to re-render the segment) and "Back to Home" actions, plus the digest shown in monospace when present to aid support and debugging. Because this boundary replaces the root layout during a fatal failure, it must render its own `<html>` and `<body>` tags, which is a hard Next.js requirement for `global-error.tsx`. A notable consequence of that constraint is that all styling is done with inline styles rather than Tailwind or global CSS, since the normal stylesheet-loading layout cannot be trusted to exist in this state. The component is marked `'use client'` and depends only on React's `useEffect` and the Sentry helper module, keeping it dependency-light so the error page itself is unlikely to fail.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukul-portal\\applicat.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router entry point for the `/gurukul-portal/applications` route in the web app, where staff review and decide on admission applications. It exports a `metadata` object (typed as `Metadata` from `next`) that sets the page title "Admission Applications — Gurukul Portal" and a description for SEO/browser display, plus the default `ApplicationsPage` server component. That component is intentionally a thin wrapper: it does nothing but render `ApplicationsClient`, imported from the sibling `./ApplicationsClient` module, which contains the actual interactive UI. The split exists because Next.js requires `metadata` exports to live in a server component, so all client-side state and interactivity are delegated to `ApplicationsClient` while this file handles the server-side concerns. There is no data fetching, props, or business logic here — any behavioral documentation should focus on `ApplicationsClient` instead.

ApplicationsClient is a Next.js client component that gives authenticated staff a review dashboard for gurukul admission applications under the gurukul-portal section. Its default export fetches the application list from `GET /api/v1/gurukul-portal/applications` on the REST API (base URL from `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, falling back to `https://api.darshya.online`), sending the session access token as a Bearer credential obtained via the internal `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context`. Each application record (typed by the local `Application` interface) is rendered as an expandable card showing student name, age, program, guardian contact, consent flag, and statement of intent, with filter pills for the lifecycle statuses submitted, forwarded, accepted, rejected, and withdrawn. The `decide` function issues a `PATCH` to `/api/v1/gurukul-portal/applications/{id}` with a new status and optional decision note, then merges the returned application into local state rather than refetching. The status workflow is enforced in the UI: only submitted applications can be forwarded for review, and once an application is accepted, rejected, or withdrawn its action buttons disappear entirely. Notable gotchas are the use of browser `prompt()` dialogs to collect decision notes and `alert()` for error reporting, and the fact that unauthenticated users are shown only a sign-in prompt linking to `/auth/login`. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with a saffron/surface palette, and icons come from `lucide-react`.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukul-portal\\GurukulP.summary: GurukulPortalClient.tsx is a Next.js client component ('use client') that renders the dashboard where authenticated gurukul owners view and manage their institution listings. Its default export, the GurukulPortalClient component, fetches the caller's registered gurukuls from the backend endpoint /api/v1/gurukuls/mine/list and displays them as cards showing name, tradition, city/state, verification status, and program count, with links to each listing's public page (/gurukuls/[slug]), the applications inbox (/gurukul-portal/applications), and the registration flow (/become-gurukul). It depends on the internal useAuth hook from lib/auth-context for the session accessToken and authentication state, uses next/link for navigation, and pulls Plus, ClipboardList, and Building2 icons from lucide-react; the API base URL comes from the NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL environment variable with a hardcoded production fallback of https://api.darshya.online, normalized by stripping any trailing slash. The local Gurukul interface defines the expected shape of the API response items, including nested programs and an isVerified flag that drives the "Verified" versus "Pending review" badge. Notable behaviors include a graceful unauthenticated state that prompts sign-in rather than redirecting, a fetch effect gated on session?.accessToken so no request fires before auth resolves, defensive handling that treats a missing gurukuls field as an empty list, and distinct loading, error, and empty states — the empty state doubling as a call-to-action to register a first gurukul.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\apply\\[progra.summary: This file is the server-side route entry point for the gurukul admission application page at `/gurukuls/apply/[programId]` in the `apps/web` Next.js application. It exists mainly to satisfy the App Router's constraints: it exports a static `metadata` object (typed via Next.js's `Metadata`) that sets the page title and description, which is only permitted from server components, while delegating all interactive rendering to the `ApplyClient` component imported from the sibling `./ApplyClient` module. The default export `ApplyPage` is an async server component that follows the Next.js 15 convention of receiving `params` as a `Promise`, awaiting it to extract the `programId` dynamic segment, and forwarding that value as a prop to `ApplyClient`. Its only dependencies are the `next` type definitions and the local client component, making it a deliberately thin adapter layer. Notable design decisions include the strict server/client split (metadata and param unwrapping on the server, form behavior on the client) and the metadata description hinting at the business domain: applications may involve minors, in which case parent consent is collected downstream.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the `/gurukuls` route page for the Next.js web app, serving as the server-rendered entry point for browsing traditional Sanskrit and Vedic schools. It exports a static `metadata` object (title and description aimed at SEO, mentioning filters for tradition, location, and age group) and a default `GurukulsPage` React server component. The page itself only renders the layout shell — a centered `main` container with a header, title, and descriptive blurb — and delegates all listing and filtering behavior to `GurukulsListClient`, a client component imported from the same route directory. Its only dependency is the `Metadata` type from `next`, plus that sibling client component. The notable design pattern is the App Router convention of keeping `page.tsx` as a thin server component so metadata can be exported and the header can be server-rendered, while interactive data fetching and UI state live entirely inside the client-side `GurukulsListClient`.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\[slug]\\page.t.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router server component for the dynamic route `/gurukuls/[slug]`, responsible for rendering an individual gurukul's detail page in the web app. It exports two things: `generateMetadata`, which builds page metadata (a title of the form "`slug` — Gurukul" and a static description) for SEO, and the default `GurukulDetailPage` component, which unwraps the async `params` promise and delegates all rendering to the `GurukulDetailClient` component imported from the same directory. Its only dependencies are the `Metadata` type from Next.js and the local `GurukulDetailClient`; notably, it performs no data fetching itself and derives the page title directly from the raw URL slug rather than from fetched gurukul data, so all content loading and presentation logic lives in the client component while this file exists mainly to satisfy the App Router's server-side page/metadata contract.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\GurukulsListCl.summary: This file is a Next.js client component (`'use client'`) that powers the gurukul directory page, rendering a searchable, filterable grid of gurukul listing cards. Its default export, `GurukulsListClient`, maintains local state for results, loading/error status, and a `filters` object (query text, tradition, residential, online, acceptsMinors), and refetches from the REST endpoint `/api/v1/gurukuls` whenever any filter changes; the response is expected to contain a `gurukuls` array matching the local `Gurukul` interface. The API origin is resolved by the `apiBase()` helper from `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a hardcoded production fallback of `https://api.darshya.online`. It builds on React hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`), `next/link` for navigation to `/gurukuls/[slug]` detail pages, and `lucide-react` icons (`MapPin`, `Globe`, `Home`, `CheckCircle2`) for location, mode, and verification badges. Notable gotchas: boolean filters are encoded as the strings `'true'` or `''` rather than actual booleans, and the search input has no debounce, so every keystroke triggers a new network request. The sidebar offers a fixed set of tradition options (Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita, Smarta, Shaiva, Shakta, Vaishnava), and the UI shows loading and error messages but leaves stale results visible during refetches.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\apply\\[progra.summary: ApplyClient.tsx is the client-side form component for the gurukul application page at `/gurukuls/apply/[programId]`, letting a signed-in user submit an admission application for a specific program.
