It exports a single default React component, `ApplyClient`, which receives `programId` as a prop, manages all form state locally with `useState`, and POSTs a JSON payload to `/api/v1/gurukul-applications` on the backend, authenticating with the Bearer `accessToken` obtained from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`. The API base URL comes from the `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` environment variable via the local `apiBase()` helper, which falls back to the hardcoded production domain `https://api.darshya.online`. A key design decision is the minor-handling logic: `isMinor` is true when the student's age is under 18 or the applicant type is `parent`, which conditionally reveals a guardian fieldset requiring guardian name, relation, and phone, with only the last four Aadhaar digits collected (the code explicitly notes the full Aadhaar is never stored). Submission is gated on client-side checks — the user must be authenticated, the DPDP Act 2023 consent checkbox must be ticked, and guardian fields must be filled for minors — while the statement of intent is constrained to 20–4000 characters via native input validation. Gotchas worth noting: unauthenticated visitors see a sign-in prompt linking to `/auth/login` and a disabled submit button rather than being redirected, and server error bodies are surfaced verbatim as the error message, so raw API responses can reach the UI.

apps\\web\\app\\gurukuls\\[slug]\\Guruku.summary: This file is a Next.js client component that renders the public detail page for a single gurukul (traditional school) in the Darshya web app. Its default export, `GurukulDetailClient`, receives a `slug` prop and fetches the matching record client-side via `useEffect` from `/api/v1/gurukuls/{slug}` on the API host configured by `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, falling back to `https://api.darshya.online` (the `apiBase` helper strips any trailing slash). It defines two local, non-exported TypeScript interfaces, `Program` and `GurukulDetail`, which mirror the API payload including location, tradition, verification status, contact fields, residential/online/minors flags, and a list of programs with duration, age range, and annual INR fees. The UI renders a back link to `/gurukuls`, a header with tradition and a `CheckCircle2` verified badge, the description, a Contact section with `mailto:`/`tel:`/website links, and a Programs section where each card links to `/gurukuls/apply/{programId}` via an Apply button, using `lucide-react` icons and `next/link` throughout. Notable details: data is fetched only in the browser (no SSR or caching), errors are surfaced as raw message text with a special-cased "Not found" for 404s, fees are formatted with the `en-IN` locale, and the slug is `encodeURIComponent`-escaped before hitting the API.

apps\\web\\app\\help\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements the Help Center page for the Darshya web app, a Next.js route at `/help` that presents FAQ categories and support contact options for the devotional platform's features (puja bookings, live darshan, store orders, payments, accounts). It exports a `metadata` object for SEO and a default `HelpPage` server component that renders a hero with a search input, a grid of six hardcoded help categories from the local `categories` array, and a "Still Need Help?" contact section. Its only dependencies are the `Metadata` type from `next` and icons from `lucide-react` (Search, Video, Flame, ShoppingBag, CreditCard, User, HelpCircle, ChevronRight, Mail, MessageCircle); it imports no internal modules, relying instead on Tailwind utility classes and CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--color-surface)` for theming. Each article link routes to `/support/faq?q=<encoded question>`, delegating actual answers to a separate FAQ page, while contact options link to `/contact` and an external WhatsApp `wa.me` number. Notably, the search input is purely decorative — as a server component with no state or event handlers, typing in it does nothing, so the page functions as a static directory rather than a searchable help system.

apps\\web\\app\\help\\articles\\[lang]\\.summary: This Next.js page component renders individual help articles at the `/help/articles/[lang]/[slug]` dynamic route for the Darshya web app, turning entries from the in-repo `lib/help-articles` module into statically generated, SEO-friendly pages. Its exports are the default `HelpArticlePage` component, `generateMetadata` (which builds titles, OpenGraph data, canonical URLs, and hreflang language alternates by matching slugs across `HELP_ARTICLES` and `HELP_LANGS`), `generateStaticParams` (which prerenders one route per article), and a `revalidate = 86400` ISR setting. Content comes from `getHelpArticle`, `HELP_ARTICLES`, and the `HelpLang` type, with `notFound()` called for unknown lang/slug pairs; UI icons come from `lucide-react` (`ChevronLeft`, `Globe`) and navigation from `next/link`. Rather than pulling in a markdown library, the file implements its own minimal `renderMarkdown`/`renderInline`/`escapeHtml` pipeline that supports only headings, lists, bold, and links, escaping HTML first and injecting the result via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`—safe for trusted content but a deliberately limited subset. The page also embeds two JSON-LD blocks (schema.org `Article` and `BreadcrumbList`) for search engines and renders cross-language "read in another language" links when translations exist. A prominent gotcha is documented in the header comment: the edge runtime is intentionally not used because `@opennextjs/cloudflare` requires the Node runtime via `nodejs_compat`, and the older `@cloudflare/next-on-pages` constraint that made edge runtime mutually exclusive with `generateStaticParams` no longer applies.

apps\\web\\app\\hindu-philosophies\\[slu.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router detail page for a single Hindu philosophy, rendered at the dynamic route `/hindu-philosophies/[slug]` on the Darshya site (darshya.online). Its default export, `HinduPhilosophyDetailPage`, is an async server component that awaits the route params, looks up the philosophy via `getHinduPhilosophy(slug)` from the internal `lib/hindu-philosophies` module, calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, and renders the philosophy's Sanskrit name, founder, era, central thesis, key texts, accepted pramana, liberation view, modern exponents, and key concepts, plus prev/next navigation derived from the item's index in the `HINDU_PHILOSOPHIES` array. It also exports `generateMetadata`, which builds SEO titles, a 160-character-truncated description from `centralThesis`, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph article tags, and injects schema.org BreadcrumbList and Article JSON-LD into the page. Notable choices include a `revalidate = 86400` setting for daily ISR caching, a hardcoded `BASE_URL` constant, and a `CATEGORY_LABEL` map that translates the raw category keys (`orthodox-darshana`, `vedanta-sub-school`) into human-readable headings; there is no `generateStaticParams`, so slugs are resolved on demand rather than pre-enumerated at build time. All content is fully data-driven from the `lib/hindu-philosophies` module, with Tailwind utility classes (including custom `saffron` palette tokens) handling presentation.

apps\\web\\app\\hi\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Hindi-language landing page (`/hi` route) for Darshya, a Next.js App Router page in the `apps/web` frontend that pitches the platform as India's "spiritual super-app." It exports a static `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) with Hindi title/description, a canonical URL at `https://darshya.online/hi`, and `hreflang` alternates pointing to sibling locales (`/ta`, `/te`, `/bn`, `/mr`) plus the English root, along with OpenGraph tags using `hi_IN` locale. The default-exported `HindiLanding` component renders a hero, a `FEATURES` grid of six cards (live darshan, puja booking, panchang, gaushala, gurukuls, AI pandit), an NRI-focused subscription banner (₹5000/$60 per year with WhatsApp video proof), and a footer disclaimer that full Hindi translation is in progress. Its only dependencies are `next/link` and the `Metadata` type from `next` — there is no data fetching, client state, or external service calls. A notable deliberate design decision, called out in the header comment, is that feature cards link to the canonical English routes (`/darshan`, `/pujas`, `/panchang`, etc.) rather than fabricating untranslated `/hi/*` paths, specifically to avoid SEO damage. The page hardcodes all copy inline, sets `lang="hi"` on the `<main>` element for accessibility, and relies on the project's custom `saffron-*`/`surface-*` Tailwind palette shared across the app.

apps\\web\\app\\hindu-philosophies\\page.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the `/hindu-philosophies` index route for the Darshya site (darshya.online), serving as a landing page that catalogs the six orthodox darshanas and four Vedanta sub-schools of Hindu philosophy. Its exports are the default server component `HinduPhilosophiesIndexPage`, a static `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags, and `revalidate = 86400`, which sets daily ISR regeneration. All content is sourced from the internal data module `../../lib/hindu-philosophies`, which provides the `HINDU_PHILOSOPHIES` array and `TOTAL_HINDU_PHILOSOPHIES` constant; the component partitions entries by their `category` field (`orthodox-darshana` vs `vedanta-sub-school`) and renders each as a `next/link` card (showing `sanskrit`, `name`, `founder`, `foundingEra`, and `centralThesis`) pointing to a per-school detail page at `/hindu-philosophies/[slug]`. For SEO it injects schema.org JSON-LD (an `ItemList` of all schools plus a `BreadcrumbList`) through a `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag. Notable design choices: it's a purely presentational, fully static server component with no client-side state, the two categories are visually differentiated via saffron vs indigo Tailwind accents, and a hardcoded "note on neutrality" section explicitly frames the content as descriptive rather than adjudicatory — so the page depends entirely on the upstream data module for correctness and has no runtime data fetching.

apps\\web\\app\\hindu-symbols\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/hindu-symbols/page.tsx`) renders the `/hindu-symbols` index for the Darshya site, a catalog of twelve sacred Hindu symbols grouped by category. Its default export, `HinduSymbolsIndexPage`, is a server component that pulls the static `HINDU_SYMBOLS` dataset and the `HinduSymbolCategory` type from the internal `lib/hindu-symbols` module, buckets entries into a Map keyed by category, and renders anchor-navigated sections with cards linking to per-symbol detail pages at `/hindu-symbols/[slug]`, plus a "Related guides" block cross-linking `/rudraksha`, `/chants`, `/chakras`, and `/discover`. It exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph) and sets `revalidate = 86400` for 24-hour ISR caching, with all absolute URLs hardcoded against `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`. For SEO it injects two schema.org JSON-LD blobs—an `ItemList` enumerating every symbol with its deity and a `BreadcrumbList`—via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Presentation is driven by three lookup tables, `CATEGORY_ORDER` (mantra, yantra, ritual-object, natural, mark), `CATEGORY_LABEL`, and `CATEGORY_ACCENT`, which fix section ordering and per-category Tailwind color accents; categories with no entries are skipped. Notably, the header includes a scholarly disclaimer distinguishing the Hindu swastika from the Nazi Hakenkreuz, and card previews rely on the `line-clamp-3` utility to truncate meaning text.

apps\\web\\app\\jyotirlinga\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/jyotirlinga` route on darshya.online, serving as an SEO-focused listing of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva in canonical Shiva Purana order. It exports a `metadata` object (with canonical URL and OpenGraph tags), a `revalidate` constant of 86400 enabling daily incremental static regeneration, and the default `JyotirlingaIndexPage` server component that renders the page. Its sole internal dependency is the `JYOTIRLINGAS` data array from `lib/jyotirlingas`, from which it pulls each shrine's slug, number, name, Sanskrit title, state, city, significance, and boolean flags like `swayambhu`, `dakshinmukhi`, and `onlineBookingAvailable` to render filter-style badges on each card. Notably, it injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks—an `ItemList` enumerating all twelve shrines and a `BreadcrumbList`—via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags to win rich search results. Each card links to a detail page at `/jyotirlinga/[slug]`, and the page deliberately cross-links to sibling hubs (`/tirth`, `/pilgrimage/12-jyotirlinga`, `/city`, `/calendar`, `/pujas`) as part of an internal-linking SEO strategy. Styling is Tailwind-based with a custom `saffron` color palette, and the hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` means canonical and structured-data URLs must be updated if the domain changes.

apps\\web\\app\\jyotirlinga\\[slug]\\pag.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for individual Jyotirlinga shrine detail pages at `/jyotirlinga/[slug]` on the Darshya site, rendering a fully static, SEO-optimized profile for each of the 12 Jyotirlingas. Its default export `JyotirlingaPage` resolves the slug via `getJyotirlingaBySlug` (calling `notFound()` on misses) and renders a long-form guide covering darshan timings, average wait, signature ritual, legend, travel logistics, fees, dress code, and prev/next navigation across the `JYOTIRLINGAS` list; `generateStaticParams` pre-renders all `JYOTIRLINGA_SLUGS` and `generateMetadata` emits canonical URLs and OpenGraph tags under the hardcoded `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`. Its only real dependency is the internal data module `lib/jyotirlingas`, plus Next.js built-ins (`next/link`, `next/navigation`, `Metadata`) — no external APIs or client-side fetching. Notable decisions: `dynamicParams = false` combined with `revalidate = 86400` locks the route set to the twelve known slugs with daily ISR, making the `notFound()` branch largely defensive; rich JSON-LD structured data (`BreadcrumbList`, `Place`, `Article` from schema.org) is injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search visibility; and the page doubles as a conversion funnel, cross-linking to `/pujas` (remote puja booking) and `/pilgrimage/12-jyotirlinga` near the bottom. Content presentation is purely data-driven, so any new fields added to the jyotirlinga records would require edits here to surface.

apps\\web\\app\\hindu-symbols\\[slug]\\p.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic detail page for a single Hindu sacred symbol, rendered at the route `/hindu-symbols/[slug]`. Its default export, the async server component `HinduSymbolDetailPage`, looks up the symbol by slug via `getHinduSymbol` from the internal module `lib/hindu-symbols` (also importing the `HINDU_SYMBOLS` array and `HinduSymbolCategory` type) and renders meaning, ritual uses, placement guidance, materials, iconography, and modern relevance, calling `notFound()` for unknown slugs. A companion `generateMetadata` export builds per-symbol SEO metadata with canonical URLs and OpenGraph article tags against the hardcoded `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`. Dependencies are limited to Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, the `Metadata` type) and the static data module — there is no database or external service. Notable choices include daily ISR via `revalidate = 86400`, awaited `params` (Next.js 15 style), JSON-LD structured data combining `BreadcrumbList` and `DefinedTerm` schema.org types injected through a `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag, and prev/next navigation derived from the symbol's index position in the `HINDU_SYMBOLS` array. A gotcha: despite fully static data, the file omits `generateStaticParams`, so pages are rendered on demand and then cached rather than prebuilt, and cross-links to `/deity/[deitySlug]` are rendered only when the symbol record provides a `deitySlug`.

apps\\web\\app\\learn-sanskrit\\lesson\\.summary: This file defines `LessonClient`, the client-side React component for a Sanskrit lesson page (`apps/web/app/learn-sanskrit/lesson/[id]`), responsible for presenting the lesson quiz and persisting the user's completion progress. It receives `lessonId` and a `quiz` question array as props and renders the shared `Quiz` component, whose `onComplete` callback triggers `handleComplete`: the score is converted to a percentage and POSTed as `{ lessonId, score }` to `/api/v1/lessons/complete` on the backend API, with the base URL taken from `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online`) and authorized via the Bearer `session.accessToken` from `useAuth`. On success it displays the returned streak via `StreakBadge` and any `newBadges` as chips, along with a "Progress saved" confirmation; failures surface an error message. Notably, unauthenticated users short-circuit the network call and are shown a fabricated one-day streak, meaning their progress is never actually saved despite the confirmation UI implying otherwise. The component also guards against trailing slashes in the API URL and throws on non-OK HTTP responses, which are caught into local error state.

apps\\web\\app\\launch\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/launch` route of the Darshya web app — a static, server-rendered marketing landing page built to support a Product Hunt launch. It exports a `metadata` object (canonical URL `https://darshya.online/launch`, OpenGraph, and Twitter card tags using the shared `/og/default.png` image) and the default `LaunchPage` component, which renders a hero, a six-card feature grid driven by the hardcoded `FEATURES` array (linking to `/darshan`, `/pujas`, `/panchang`, `/vedas`, `/gurukuls`, `/gaushala`), an NRI premium section driven by the `NRI_BULLETS` list advertising a $399/yr tier, a founder note, and a final CTA. Its only internal dependency is the `EmailCapture` component (rendered with `source="launch-nri"` to capture leads for an NRI festival calendar PDF), plus `next/link` and Next's `Metadata` type; the sole external service referenced is producthunt.com via an outbound upvote link. Notable points: all copy is hardcoded in-file rather than pulled from a CMS, the page has no client-side interactivity of its own (any state lives inside `EmailCapture`), and styling relies on custom Tailwind design tokens (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`) that must be defined in the app's Tailwind config.

apps\\web\\app\\learn-sanskrit\\lesson\\.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the dynamic route `/learn-sanskrit/lesson/[id]`, rendering a single Sanskrit lesson as statically generated content. It exports `generateStaticParams`, which pre-builds one page per lesson using `getAllLessons` from the internal `sanskrit-lessons-catalog` library, and `generateMetadata`, which produces per-lesson SEO titles and descriptions. The default export, the async server component `LessonPage`, awaits the route params (a Next.js 15 convention), fetches the lesson via `getLesson`, and calls `notFound()` from `next/navigation` when the id is invalid. The rendered page shows a back link using `next/link` and the `ArrowLeft` icon from `lucide-react`, a header with the lesson's level, duration, title, subtitle, and intro, then the lesson body rendered through the internal `MdxRender` MDX component, and finally the interactive `LessonClient` client component, which receives the lesson id and quiz data. Key dependencies are the `sanskrit-lessons-catalog` module as the content source, plus the sibling `LessonClient` and shared `MdxRender` components. A notable design point is the server/client split: all static content renders on the server while quiz interactivity and progress tracking are delegated to `LessonClient`, and the whole section is fully static at build time since the lesson catalog is local data.

apps\\web\\app\\legal\\cookies\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the static Cookie Policy page for the Darshya web app, rendered at the `/legal/cookies` route in the Next.js App Router. It exports a `metadata` object (Next.js `Metadata` type) setting the page title, description, canonical URL at `https://darshya.online/legal/cookies`, and OpenGraph tags, plus the default `CookiePolicyPage` React component that renders the policy content. The page has no runtime dependencies beyond Next.js itself — all styling is done with Tailwind utility classes (including brand tokens like `saffron-700` and `surface-*`) and the `prose` typography plugin for the article body. Content-wise it documents the site's cookie categories (Essential, Analytics via PostHog EU and Cloudflare Web Analytics, Marketing via Google Ads and Meta pixels), the lawful basis for each, and how users manage consent. Notably, it references the consent mechanism externally: the consent state lives in a `darshya_cookie_consent_v1` browser storage entry managed elsewhere (presumably a cookie banner component), and this page instructs users to clear it manually rather than providing an in-page preference control. It also cross-links to the `/legal/privacy-uk` route and the `privacy@darshya.online` contact, and mentions compliance details like UK ICO equal-prominence requirements and a 12-month re-prompt cycle. Since it's a server component with no dynamic data, the page is fully static and safe to cache or prerender.

apps\\web\\app\\learn-sanskrit\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the `/learn-sanskrit` landing page for the Next.js web app, serving as the entry point to the Sanskrit lesson catalog where users browse available lessons by difficulty. Its default export, `LearnSanskritPage`, is a server component that pulls the full lesson list via `getAllLessons` from the internal `sanskrit-lessons-catalog` library module, partitions lessons into `beginner`, `intermediate`, and `advanced` buckets, and renders each non-empty tier as a section of `LessonCard` components (imported from `components/LessonCard`) in a two-column grid. It also exports a static `metadata` object for SEO, advertising lessons, streaks, and badges. Because all data comes from a local catalog rather than a remote fetch, the page is fully statically renderable with no runtime data dependencies. Notable details: the level ordering is hardcoded via the `(['beginner', 'intermediate', 'advanced'] as const)` tuple, empty levels are silently skipped rather than rendered with placeholder text, and only a subset of lesson fields (id, title, subtitle, level, minutes) is passed down to `LessonCard`, so quiz/streak/badge logic lives elsewhere.

apps\\web\\app\\list-temple\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the `/list-temple` route in the Next.js web app, a marketing and self-onboarding landing page where temple trusts apply to join the Darshya platform. It exports route `metadata` for SEO (title/description aimed at temple trusts) and the default `ListTemplePage` component. The page composes two internal components: `SelfOnboardPageShell`, which supplies the hero layout and renders the hardcoded `BENEFITS` array (live darshan reach, puja bookings, 80G receipts, analytics/CRM), and `SelfOnboardForm` configured with `role="TEMPLE"`. The form receives two temple-specific extra fields via the `extraFields` slot — `templeName` and `deity`, both required, rendered through the `ExtraInput` helper. Notably, the page is a thin presentational composition with no data fetching or logic of its own; all submission behavior (including the "Apply to list my temple" CTA) is delegated to the shared `SelfOnboardForm`, which presumably keys its API payload off the `role` prop.

apps\\web\\app\\legal\\privacy-uk\\page..summary: This file is a static Next.js App Router page that renders Darshya's UK-specific privacy notice at `/legal/privacy-uk`, serving as a UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 addendum to the main `/privacy` policy. It exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/legal/privacy-uk`, and OpenGraph tags) plus the default `PrivacyUkPage` component, which renders hardcoded legal copy covering lawful bases, retention periods, international transfers, data subject rights, and ICO complaint details. The only import is the `Metadata` type from `next`; there is no data fetching, state, or internal module dependency — the page is purely presentational and statically rendered. Styling relies on Tailwind with custom design tokens (`saffron-700`, `surface-50/200/900`) and the `@tailwindcss/typography` `prose` classes for the article body. Notable details: the page names Bhaktisetu Technologies Pvt Ltd as the data controller, lists sub-processors Stripe, Resend, Twilio, and PostHog, routes privacy requests to `privacy@darshya.online`, and cross-links to `/privacy` and `/legal/cookies`. One gotcha is that the ROPA link currently points to a placeholder `https://github.com/` URL, and the UK Article 27 representative is noted as not yet appointed — both indicate unfinished compliance content baked into the markup.

apps\\web\\app\\list-gaushala\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/list-gaushala` route in the `apps/web` app — a marketing-plus-signup page where gaushalas (cow shelters) apply to receive 80G tax-deductible donations through the Darshya platform. It exports a Next.js `Metadata` object for SEO ("List your gaushala on Darshya") and the default `ListGaushalaPage` component, which is purely presentational and composes two shared internal components: `SelfOnboardPageShell` (which renders the eyebrow, headline, subtitle, and the static `BENEFITS` array of four selling points) and `SelfOnboardForm` (the actual application form, parameterized here with `role="GAUSHALA"` and the CTA "Apply to list my gaushala"). Gaushala-specific fields are injected into the form via `extraFields` using the `ExtraInput` and `ExtraCheckbox` helper components: `gaushalaName`, `cowCount` (a number input clamped to 0–100000), `pan`, `regn80G`, and a `has80G` confirmation checkbox. The only external dependency is the `Metadata` type from `next`; Razorpay appears only in marketing copy, not as an import, since all form handling logic lives inside `SelfOnboardForm`. A notable design decision is that the PAN and 80G registration fields are optional — the inline helper text states that applicants who leave them blank are marked "pending verification," so the form deliberately supports unverified trusts. Because there is no `'use client'` directive, this is a React Server Component, meaning the interactive behavior must be encapsulated within the client-side `SelfOnboardForm` and its field primitives.

apps\\web\\app\\mahabharata\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/mahabharata` route of the Darshya site (darshya.online), serving as an SEO-optimized index of all 18 parvas of the Mahabharata. Its default export, `MahabharataIndexPage`, is a server component that renders a header with epic-level stats, a reading-order tip highlighting the Bhagavad Gita inside Bhishma Parva, a card list linking to each `/mahabharata/[slug]` detail page, and a "Related study" grid cross-linking routes like `/gita`, `/deity/krishna`, `/ramayana`, `/dashavatar/krishna`, `/puranas/bhagavata-purana`, and `/festival/krishna-janmashtami`. It depends on the internal data module `lib/mahabharata-parvas`, whose `MAHABHARATA_PARVAS` catalog supplies per-parva fields (number, slug, english, sanskrit, iast, setting, summary, centralCharacter, adhyayaCount), plus Next.js `Link` and the `Metadata` API; it talks to no external services. Notable choices include setting `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR despite fully static content, computing `TOTAL_ADHYAYAS` by reducing the catalog at module scope, and hardcoding `BASE_URL` for canonical and OpenGraph URLs. For search visibility it emits a `metadata` export whose title crams in all 18 parva names and injects JSON-LD `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList` schema via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Styling is pure Tailwind with no client-side state, so the page ships as a fully static, crawl-friendly landing page.

apps\\web\\app\\matchmaking\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router landing page (`MatchmakingPage`) for Darshya's kundli-matching service, built as a high-intent SEO capture page targeting queries like "kundli matching online" and "ashtakoot guna milan". Its default export is a purely presentational server component that renders static marketing content: a `KOOTAS` table explaining the 8 Ashtakoot compatibility categories and their 36-point scoring, cards describing Nadi Dosha, Bhakoot Dosha, and Manglik Dosh, a `FAQS` accordion, and calls-to-action linking to `/astrology/kundli-milan` (the actual calculator), `/ask-pandit`, and `/weddings`. It exports `metadata` (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph tags) and a `revalidate` of 86400 seconds for daily ISR caching, and injects three JSON-LD structured data blocks (`FAQPage`, `BreadcrumbList`, `WebApplication`) for search-engine rich results. The only dependencies are `next` types and `next/link`; there is no client-side state, data fetching, or calculation logic — all actual matching computation lives elsewhere (at `/astrology/kundli-milan`). A notable design decision is the hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` used for canonical and schema URLs, and the heavy emphasis on disclaimers steering users toward paid pandit consults, positioning the free tool as a lead-generation funnel rather than a complete product.

apps\\web\\app\\mahabharata\\[parva]\\pa.summary: This Next.js app-router page renders the detail view for one of the 18 Mahabharata parvas at the dynamic route `/mahabharata/[parva]`, presenting each parva's Sanskrit and English names, IAST transliteration, setting, central character, summary, key episodes, and takeaway teaching. Its exports are `generateStaticParams` (which enumerates all slugs via `parvaSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (building SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags), and the default async server component `MahabharataParvaPage`, alongside route config `revalidate = 86400` and `dynamicParams = false`. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/mahabharata-parvas` (`MAHABHARATA_PARVAS`, `getParva`, `parvaSlugs`); the only framework dependencies are `next/link` and `notFound` from `next/navigation`, with no external data fetching. The page is fully statically generated with daily ISR revalidation, and `dynamicParams = false` means any slug outside `generateStaticParams` yields a 404 before `notFound()` even runs. SEO is a clear priority: it injects schema.org `Article` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` against the hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online`, and renders a matching visual breadcrumb nav. A notable hardcoded special case flags `bhishma-parva` (`hasGita`) to insert a promotional panel linking to `/gita`, since adhyayas 25–42 contain the Bhagavad Gita. Prev/next navigation is computed by scanning `MAHABHARATA_PARVAS` for adjacent `number` values, with the final parva's "next" slot replaced by a link back to the index, and a footer grid links to all 18 parvas with the current one highlighted. One gotcha: `params` is typed as a `Promise` (Next.js 15 convention) and must be awaited before use.

apps\\web\\app\\masa\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the "masa" (Vedic month) section of the Darshya site, rendering a static, SEO-optimized catalog of all 12 Hindu lunar months at the `/masa` route. Its default export, `MasaIndexPage`, displays a card grid linking to per-month detail pages (`/masa/[slug]`), an educational section explaining the amanta/purnimanta lunar systems and adhik masa, and cross-navigation links to the `/tithi`, `/aditya`, and `/calendar` sections. All content comes from the internal `VEDIC_MONTHS` constant exported by `lib/vedic-months`, which supplies each month's slug, name, Sanskrit form, number, Gregorian range, presiding Aditya, and ritu (season); the only external dependencies are Next.js itself (`next/link`, the `Metadata` type) and Tailwind utility classes including custom `saffron` palette tokens. The page is statically generated with `revalidate = 86400`, so it rebuilds at most once daily via ISR, and it exports a `metadata` object with a canonical URL of `https://darshya.online/masa`. For structured-data SEO it injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks—an `ItemList` of the 12 months and a `BreadcrumbList`—via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags. A local `RITU_COLOR` lookup maps season strings to Tailwind badge classes, with a slate-gray fallback for unmapped values, so any new ritu label added to the data module will render generically until the map is updated.

apps\\web\\app\\messages\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/messages` route in the web app, presenting a messaging inbox for devotee users. Its default export, `DevoteeMessagesPage`, is a client component that wraps the entire page in the `AuthGuard` component, so unauthenticated visitors never see the inbox content. Inside the guard it renders a simple centered layout with a heading and then mounts the shared `Inbox` component, passing `role="devotee"` so the inbox loads conversations from the devotee's perspective. The page depends on two internal modules: `AuthGuard` from `components/AuthGuard` for session enforcement and `Inbox` from `components/Inbox`, which presumably carries all the actual chat fetching and rendering logic. Notably, the page itself is a thin shell — all messaging behavior, including how the `role` prop shapes queries, lives in `Inbox`, and the `'use client'` directive means this route renders client-side rather than as a server component. The copy ("Chat with your priests, astrologers, and providers") indicates the platform supports multiple counterpart roles, and there is likely a parallel provider-side page reusing the same `Inbox` with a different role value.

apps\\web\\app\\masa\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route (apps/web/app/masa/[slug]/page.tsx) that renders the detail page for a single Vedic month (masa) on the Darshya site, served as an async server component with ISR via `revalidate = 86400` (24-hour regeneration). Its default export `MasaDetailPage` looks up the month by slug using `getVedicMonthBySlug` from the internal `../../../lib/vedic-months` module (which also provides the `VEDIC_MONTHS` array), calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, and renders the month's name, Sanskrit form, presiding mantra, ritu (season), presiding Aditya, deity, Gregorian range, significance, festivals, vratas, and ritual character. A named `generateMetadata` export builds SEO title, description, and canonical URL (hardcoded to darshya.online), and the page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks — a BreadcrumbList and an Article — for search indexing. The page computes circular previous/next month navigation from the month's index in `VEDIC_MONTHS`, with a `?? month` fallback that exists purely to satisfy TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` since `notFound()` already guarantees a valid index. It cross-links to sibling content sections (/tithi, /aditya, /calendar, /vrat) to keep users moving through the site. Notable constraints: all data is static and local (no external services or databases), the domain is hardcoded rather than configured, and styling relies on Tailwind with a custom saffron/amber palette.

apps\\web\\app\\layout.tsx.summary: This is the Next.js App Router root layout for the Darshya web app — it wraps every page in the shared shell: fonts, SEO metadata, a fixed header nav, mobile bottom tabs, a large footer, and the global provider stack. It exports the `metadata` and `viewport` constants plus the default `RootLayout` component, which nests providers as SentryErrorBoundary > QueryProvider > AuthProvider > CartProvider and renders navigation pieces (CategoryNav, GlobalSearch, NavCartButton, NavAuthButton, MobileNavV2, MobileBottomTabs, ListYourBusinessDropdown) alongside an i18n-driven footer built from `footerSections` and the `t()` helper from `../lib/t`. The file also wires in a heavy client-side tooling layer — Analytics, CloudflareAnalytics, GA4Script, MetaPixelScript, PostHogScript, AdSenseScript, SentryProvider, ServiceWorkerRegister, NotificationPrompt, ReferralCapture, ChannelAttribution, and DeferredClientWidgets — and injects site-wide Organization and WebSite JSON-LD from `../lib/jsonld`. Fonts come from next/font/google (Noto_Sans, Noto_Sans_Devanagari, Crimson_Pro exposed as CSS variables) plus Fontshare's Cabinet Grotesk and Satoshi via CDN, with preconnect/dns-prefetch hints for fontshare, Unsplash, and YouTube, and a high-priority preload of the `getTempleHero('kashi-vishwanath')` hero image because it's the LCP element on the home page. Two documented gotchas stand out: `metadataBase` is hard-coded to https://darshya.online because NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL isn't reliably set at build time and without it relative OG image paths resolve against localhost:3000, breaking every social share preview; and the OG image is a static `/images/golden-temple-og.jpg` because a Cloudflare worker cap blocks the @vercel/og runtime route. Nav labels and footer copy are resolved through deliberately type-cast calls to `t()` (`as unknown as (k: string) => string`), the desktop nav hides below the lg breakpoint with right-cluster actions revealing progressively at xl and 2xl, and the footer's programmatic-SEO "Discover Hindu Wisdom" links live inside a collapsed `<details>` element so they remain in the DOM for crawlers without cluttering the visible UI.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\layout.tsx.summary: This file defines `MobileLayout`, the shared layout for all `/mobile/*` routes in the Next.js web app, rendering children inside a simulated iPhone frame (390×844px with notch, status bar, and rounded bezel) so the mobile experience can be previewed on desktop browsers. Its single default export wraps page content in a scrollable screen area and a fixed bottom tab bar with five destinations — Home, Temples, Darshan, Content, and Profile — each pairing a route under `/mobile` with a lucide-react icon (`Home`, `MapPin`, `Video`, `Music`, `User`). It depends on `next/navigation`'s `usePathname` to highlight the active tab with saffron accent coloring and a heavier icon stroke, and on Tailwind utility classes (including custom `surface-*` and `saffron-*` palette tokens) for all styling. Notable gotchas: it's a client component (`'use client'`) because of the pathname hook, tab active-state uses exact path equality so nested subpages won't highlight their parent tab, navigation uses plain `<a>` tags rather than Next.js `Link` (causing full page loads), and the status bar is purely decorative with a hardcoded "9:41" time.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the mobile home screen for a Hindu devotional app, rendered as a client-side Next.js page at the /mobile route. Its single export, the MobileHome component, composes a greeting header, a search input, a horizontally scrolling "Live Darshan" stream carousel with LIVE badges and viewer counts, a "Today's Panchang" card showing tithi/nakshatra/sunrise/sunset, a "Popular Pujas" booking list with prices and ratings, and a floating "Ask Pandit" action button linking to /ask-pandit. It depends on the internal images module (getTempleHero, getDeityImage) for temple and deity artwork, and on lucide-react for all icons; styling is Tailwind-based with custom saffron and surface palette tokens. Notably, all content — liveStreams, popularPujas, the panchang values, and the hardcoded user "Arjun Sharma" — is static placeholder data with no fetching, state, or interactivity wired in (the search input and Book buttons do nothing), marking this as a presentational prototype rather than a functional screen. Navigation is done via plain anchor tags to /mobile/darshan, /pujas, and /ask-pandit rather than Next.js Link components.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\darshan\\page.ts.summary: This file is a Next.js client-side page component for the mobile web app that renders the "Live Darshan" screen at the `/mobile/darshan` route, presenting temple livestreams and scheduled upcoming streams. Its single export, the default `MobileDarshan` component, renders a header with a pulsing LIVE badge, a two-column grid of active stream cards (each with a thumbnail, viewer count, event label, and a decorative play button), and an "Upcoming Streams" list with times and "Remind" buttons. All content comes from two hardcoded module-level arrays, `liveStreams` and `upcoming`, rather than any API or state, and the play and remind buttons have no click handlers, so the page is currently a static visual mockup. Thumbnails are resolved through the internal `getTempleHero` helper from `lib/images`, and icons (Play, Users, Clock, Bell, MapPin) come from `lucide-react`. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with project-specific theme tokens such as `surface-900`, `surface-800`, and `saffron-400`. A notable gotcha: the Mahakaleshwar entry reuses the `kashi-vishwanath` hero image as a placeholder, and the header's "4 streams active" count is hardcoded text rather than derived from the data, so adding entries to the arrays would leave the UI inconsistent.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\temples\\page.ts.summary: This file defines `MobileTemples`, the default-exported client-side React component for the mobile temples discovery page at `apps/web/app/mobile/temples/page.tsx` in the Next.js app router. It renders a scrollable catalog of Indian temples, each card showing a hero image, live-darshan badge with a pulsing indicator, viewer count, verification shield, city, deity, and rating, topped by a search input and horizontally scrollable category filter chips (Jyotirlinga, Char Dham, Live Darshan, etc.). Its only dependencies are `getTempleHero` from the internal `lib/images` module for resolving temple imagery and `lucide-react` for icons (Search, MapPin, Star, Users, Shield); it talks to no backend or data service. Notably, the temple list, search field, and filters are entirely hardcoded and non-functional — the search input has no state or handler and the filter buttons do nothing — so this is presently a static UI mockup with placeholder data (live flags, viewer counts, ratings) awaiting wiring to a real data source. Styling relies on the project's Tailwind theme tokens (`surface-*`, `saffron-*`) and a custom `scrollbar-hide` utility, and images use lazy loading with async decoding for mobile performance.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\content\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page (`MobileContent`, the default export at `apps/web/app/mobile/content/page.tsx`) renders the mobile app's devotional audio library, listing aartis, chalisas, mantras, and bhajans with category tab filtering and a mini-player bar. It depends on the internal `lib/images` module (`getContentImage`, `getDeityImage`) for thumbnails and on `lucide-react` for all icons (Play, Pause, Heart, SkipBack, SkipForward, Clock), styled with Tailwind custom theme tokens like `saffron-600` and `surface-*`. All content is hardcoded in a local `contentItems` mock array — no API calls or audio playback exist; the `playing` state only toggles UI highlighting, and the mini player's progress bar is a fixed one-third width with non-functional skip and favorite buttons. Two gotchas stand out: the filter logic treats the 'Aarti' tab as "show everything" (the `filtered` variable is computed but then bypassed by a duplicate inline check in the map), and the mini player is absolutely positioned at a fixed `w-[370px]`/`bottom-[88px]`, indicating this screen targets a fixed-width mobile frame prototype rather than responsive devices.

apps\\web\\app\\mr\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Marathi-language landing page (`/mr` route) for the Darshya spiritual super-app in the Next.js web frontend. Its default export, `MarathiLanding`, renders the shared `LangLanding` component (from `apps/web/components/LangLanding`) with fully localized Marathi props: hero copy, pill text, CTA labels, six feature cards linking to internal routes (`/darshan`, `/pujas`, `/panchang`, `/gaushala`, `/gurukuls`, `/ask-pandit`), an NRI-targeted subscription pitch (₹5000 / $60 yearly with WhatsApp video proof), and footer notes. It also exports a `metadata` object defining the page title, description, canonical URL (`https://darshya.online/mr`), hreflang alternates for six locales (en, hi, ta, te, bn, mr), and OpenGraph tags with `mr_IN` locale and a shared `/og/default.png` image. The only dependencies are Next.js's `Metadata` type and the internal `LangLanding` component; there is no data fetching or client-side logic, so this is a purely static, SEO-focused page. Notably, the `footerNote` admits the Marathi translation is incomplete and most pages are still in English, and the design follows a per-locale route pattern where each language page is a thin wrapper passing translated strings into the reusable `LangLanding` layout.

apps\\web\\app\\mobile\\profile\\page.ts.summary: This file is the mobile profile page for the Darshya web app, a Next.js client component (`'use client'`) living at the `/mobile/profile` route that renders the signed-in user's identity card, usage stats, navigation shortcuts, and a sign-out action. Its default export `MobileProfile` pulls the current session via `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` and displays the user's name, avatar initials (computed by the local `initialsOf` helper), and phone number, falling back to a "Guest" state with a sign-in link to `/auth/login` when no session exists — a fix tracked as P0 ticket #PUB-05 that replaced a previously hardcoded "Arjun Sharma" placeholder. Navigation is driven by two static config arrays, `quickLinks` (My Bookings, Subscription, Saved Addresses, Ask Pandit AI, Settings) and `moreLinks` (Help, About, Share, Rate Us), with all icons sourced from `lucide-react` and styling done via Tailwind utility classes using a custom saffron/surface palette. apps\\web\\app\\org\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the client-side organizations hub page for the web app, rendered at `/org`, where users view their organization memberships and create new organizations (pitched at temple trusts and devotional organizations). apps\\web\\app\\org\\accept\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/org/accept/page.tsx`) implements the organization invite-acceptance flow: it reads an invite `token` from the URL query string and completes the user's membership in an org. Error handling maps specific API error codes to friendly messages: `EmailMismatch` tells the user to sign in with the invited address, and `Expired` reports the link has expired, while anything else is shown raw as `Failed: {error}`. Gotchas include the duplicate localStorage session keys (a sign of evolving auth storage), the fact that a missing `token` param renders a static "Missing invite token" message without firing any request, and the unvalidated `j.error` string being rendered directly into the page.

The file also defines shared presentational components — `ProgressBar`, `FormInput`, `ChipSelect`, `FileUploadPlaceholder`, `AvailabilityGrid`, `DaysSelector`, `SummaryRow` — plus domain constants like `PANDIT_PUJAS`, `LANGUAGES`, and `PRODUCT_CATEGORIES`. On success it caches a `poojly_onboarding_${role}_submitted` snapshot, clears the draft, and renders a "Submitted for Approval" screen linking to the role dashboard. Notable gotchas: file uploads are purely visual placeholders with no actual upload logic, and several priest form field names (`pujasOffered`, `basePricePerPuja`) don't match what `projectOnboardingData` reads (`specialties`, `pricePerPuja`), so those values silently fall back to defaults — the comment notes this projection is the single place where the form-to-backend mapping lives, making divergences like this easy to miss.

apps\\web\\app\\pancha-bhoota\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`PanchaBhootaIndexPage`) is the static index/landing page for the "Pancha Bhoota Stalam" section of the Darshya site, presenting the five element-associated Shiva temples as a clickable card grid plus explanatory content for pilgrims. Its default export renders the page; it also exports `metadata` (SEO title, description, and canonical URL `https://darshya.online/pancha-bhoota`) and sets `revalidate = 86400` so the page is statically generated and revalidated once per day via ISR. All temple content comes from the `PANCHA_BHOOTA` array imported from the internal `lib/pancha-bhoota` module, with cards linking to `/pancha-bhoota/[slug]` detail routes and cross-links to the `/jyotirlinga`, `/tirth`, and `/pilgrimage` sections. The page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks (`ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList`) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search-engine rich results, and uses only Next.js primitives (`Link`, `Metadata`) with Tailwind CSS for styling — no external data fetching or services. A notable design choice is the `ELEMENT_THEME` lookup, which maps each temple's exact `element` string (e.g. `'Water (Apas / Jala)'`) to a coordinated set of gradient, border, text, and chip classes, with a `FALLBACK_THEME` derived from the Earth entry guarding against missing keys. Be aware that theming depends on fragile exact-string matching against the data, and fields like `lingaForm` and `sthalaVriksha` are rendered by splitting on an em-dash with defensive optional chaining, so changes to the data module's formatting could silently alter the UI.

apps\\web\\app\\page.tsx.summary: This is the landing page for Darshya, a devotional "super app," implemented as the Next.js root route in `apps/web/app/page.tsx`. It exports the default async server component `HomePage`, a static `metadata` object (canonical URL, hreflang alternates for six Indian locales, OpenGraph/Twitter cards), and `revalidate = 3600` for one-hour ISR caching, with a comment noting the panchang chip tolerates that granularity and personalized salutations are deferred to the client. The page composes a long marketing layout — hero with bento grid and live-darshan card, category color strip, quick-action chips, trust signals, feature grid, and puja/astrology promo cards — out of many dedicated components including `HeroCopyVariant`, `NriLaneAbTest`, `ContinueJourneyCard`, `IntentTrio`, `NextFestivalStrip`, `ScrollDiscover`, `HomeHeroCta`, and various strip components (`WorshipStrip`, `WisdomStrip`, `ConsultStrip`, `ShopStrip`, `YatraStrip`, `TrustStrip`), plus `EmailCapture`. Internal dependencies include `getTranslations` from `../lib/t`, `getTodayPanchang` from `../lib/api` (wrapped in a try/catch so the hero's tithi/nakshatra chip degrades to null on failure), `brandFaqJsonLd` from `../lib/jsonld` injected as a JSON-LD script tag, and image resolvers `getTempleHero`, `getDeityImage`, `getContentImage`, and `getProductImage` from `../lib/images`. Animation is driven by `ScrollReveal` and motion primitives (`ParallaxLayer`, `TextReveal`, `ScrambleReveal`, `StickyHeadlinePin`) via `data-reveal`/`data-delay` attributes rather than per-component logic. Externally it relies on `next/link`, `next/image`, and `lucide-react` icons. Notable gotchas: several `Image` components use `unoptimized` with `priority`, section ordering is pinned by dated user-feedback comments (e.g., festival strip relocated below the intent trio), a fixed caption bug pairing the Mahakaleshwar image with Golden Temple text is documented inline, and theming mixes CSS variables with hardcoded brand hex colors and inline A/B-test slots (`NriLaneAbTest`, `HeroCopyVariant`).

apps\\web\\app\\pancha-bhoota\\[slug]\\p.summary: This is the Next.js App Router detail page (`/pancha-bhoota/[slug]`) for the Darshya pilgrimage site, rendering a rich, SEO-oriented profile for one of the five Pancha Bhoota Shiva temples. Its default export `PanchaBhootaDetailPage` is an async server component that resolves the slug via `getPanchaBhootaBySlug` from the internal `lib/pancha-bhoota` module, calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, and uses the `PANCHA_BHOOTA` array to compute prev/next temple navigation; a sibling `generateMetadata` export builds per-temple titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs on `darshya.online`. The page injects three schema.org JSON-LD blocks (BreadcrumbList, Place, Article) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and renders content sections — mantra, presiding deity, lingam, sthala vriksha, theertham, ritual, festival, travel info — styled with Tailwind, plus cross-link CTAs to `/jyotirlinga`, `/tirth`, and `/pilgrimage`. An `ELEMENT_THEME` lookup maps each element name (e.g. `'Water (Apas / Jala)'`) to full literal Tailwind class strings so the JIT scanner picks them up, with `FALLBACK_THEME` defaulting to the Earth palette if a data value doesn't match a key exactly — a silent-mismatch gotcha. The file sets `revalidate = 86400` for 24-hour ISR but notably exports no `generateStaticParams`, so pages are generated on demand and then cached rather than fully prerendered at build time.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\karana\\page.t.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/panchang/karana/page.tsx`) renders the SEO-targeted index page for the 11 karanas — the fifth anga of Vedic Panchang — on the darshya.online site, linking out to per-karana detail pages at `/panchang/karana/[slug]`. It is a pure server component with no client state, statically generated and revalidated daily via `export const revalidate = 86400`, and it exports a `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags plus two inline JSON-LD blocks (`ITEMLIST_LD` and `BREADCRUMB_LD`) for schema.org ItemList and BreadcrumbList structured data. All content comes from the internal data module `../../../lib/panchang-karanas`, which exports `PANCHANG_KARANAS` and its pre-split subsets `CHARA_KARANAS` (7 movable) and `STHIRA_KARANAS` (4 fixed); the page depends only on `next/link` and Tailwind CSS, with no external services. The local `KaranaCard` component maps each karana's `nature` field through the `NATURE_STYLE` and `NATURE_LABEL` lookup tables to color-code cards as Shubha (auspicious/emerald), Ashubha (inauspicious/rose), or Mishra (mixed/amber). Notable choices include a hardcoded `BASE_URL` constant (so canonical URLs won't adapt to other environments), a dedicated warning callout emphasizing that Vishti/Bhadra is universally inauspicious, and a cross-linking footer driving traffic to sibling Panchang pages (`/panchang/yoga`, `/panchang/tithi`, `/nakshatra`, `/astrology/shubh-muhurat`) for internal-link SEO.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js server-rendered `/panchang` route for the Darshya web app, displaying the daily Hindu Panchang — tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana, sunrise/sunset, rahu kaal, shubh muhurat, and observances — alongside a mini calendar and an upcoming-festivals sidebar. Its default export `PanchangPage` reads an `offset` search param for day navigation and composes two async server components, `PanchangDetailsSection` and `FestivalsSidebar`, each streamed inside `Suspense` with skeleton placeholders. Data comes from `getTodayPanchang` and `getUpcomingFestivals` in the internal `../../lib/api` module (with the `Panchang` type), while `lucide-react` supplies all iconography; SEO is handled via a static `metadata` export. A notable resilience decision is `buildFallbackPanchang`, which catches API failures and returns today's date with limbs marked "Unavailable" rather than stale fixed values — the comment notes the API now self-computes via sidereal Lahiri math with a DB upsert cron, so this path should be rare. Two gotchas stand out: the prev/next day navigation wires `dateOffset` through the UI but `getTodayPanchang` only ever returns today, so navigation is non-functional for now, and the `calendarDays` mini calendar, the "Delhi, India" location, and the "Vikram Samvat 2083" label are hardcoded placeholders rather than computed values.

apps\\web\\app\\pilgrimage\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the index page for the `/pilgrimage` route of the Darshya web app, a Next.js App Router page that presents a browsable catalog of the 8 canonical Hindu pilgrimage circuits (Char Dham, Jyotirlinga, Shakti Peethas, etc.). Its default export, the `PilgrimageIndex` server component, renders a card grid where each card links to `/pilgrimage/[slug]` and summarizes a circuit's stop count, Sanskrit name, day range, starting price (via a local `formatInr` helper that renders prices as "₹Nk"), and a color-coded difficulty badge. It reads all content from the static `CIRCUITS` array exported by the internal `lib/pilgrimage-circuits` module, so there is no runtime data fetching or external service dependency beyond Next.js (`next/link`, `next/metadata`) itself. For SEO it exports a `metadata` object with canonical URL and OpenGraph fields, and injects a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Notable decisions include the `revalidate = 86400` export, which puts the page on a 24-hour ISR cycle, and a hard-coded cross-promotion CTA at the bottom funneling visitors to the `/yatra` packages page; all branding points at the production domain `darshya.online`, so canonical URLs are fixed rather than environment-driven.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\yoga\\[slug]\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`app/panchang/yoga/[slug]/page.tsx`) statically generates a detail page for each of the 27 nitya yogas listed in the internal `PANCHANG_YOGAS` data module from `lib/panchang-yogas`, serving as SEO-focused reference content for the Darshya site. It uses `generateStaticParams` with `dynamicParams = false` so only the 27 known slugs are prerendered (everything else 404s via `notFound()`), and `revalidate = 86400` gives daily ISR regeneration. The exported `generateMetadata` builds per-yoga titles, descriptions (truncating `y.effect` to 140 characters), canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags against the hardcoded `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`, while the default `YogaDetailPage` component renders breadcrumbs, the yoga's name, Sanskrit form, number, presiding deity, and a color-coded auspiciousness banner driven by the `NATURE_BAR` lookup keyed on `auspicious`/`inauspicious`/`mixed`. The page also renders `bestFor`/`avoidFor` lists, a "first-part nuance" note, and a deity mantra section, and injects two JSON-LD blocks (`BreadcrumbList` and `Article` schema) through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags for rich search results. Prev/next navigation is computed with modular arithmetic on `y.number`, which implicitly assumes `PANCHANG_YOGAS` is ordered sequentially from 1 to 27 — a reordering of that array would silently break the links. A footer callout cross-links to `/panchang` and `/astrology/shubh-muhurat` to funnel readers toward the live daily tools. Dependencies are minimal: `next/link`, `next/navigation`, the `Metadata` type, the internal yoga dataset, and Tailwind utility classes using a custom `saffron` palette.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\karana\\[slug].summary: This file is a Next.js App Router dynamic route (`/panchang/karana/[slug]`) that renders a statically generated detail page for each of the 11 karanas (half-tithi divisions of the Hindu panchang) on the Darshya site. It exports `generateStaticParams`, `generateMetadata`, and the default `KaranaDetailPage` server component, all of which look up entries by slug from the internal `PANCHANG_KARANAS` constant in `lib/panchang-karanas`, with unknown slugs triggering a 404 via `notFound()`. The page is fully prerendered at build time (`dynamicParams = false`) with daily ISR (`revalidate = 86400`), and it emits two schema.org JSON-LD blocks — a `BreadcrumbList` and an `Article` — for SEO alongside canonical and OpenGraph metadata. The UI renders a color-coded auspiciousness banner driven by the `NATURE_BAR` map (emerald/rose/amber for auspicious/inauspicious/mixed), "best for" and "avoid for" lists, a tradition note, and the karana's deity mantra with English translation. Previous/next navigation is computed with modular arithmetic over `k.number` so the karana list wraps around cyclically, and the page cross-links to `/panchang` and `/astrology/shubh-muhurat` for live calculations. Notable details: the production origin is hardcoded as `BASE_URL = 'https://darshya.online'`, styling relies on Tailwind with a custom `saffron` palette, and the page is purely presentational — no actual panchang computation happens here, since all content comes from the static data module.

apps\\web\\app\\payouts\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the unified provider payouts page in the Next.js web app, created to give every provider role—not just priests—a single surface to view earnings and withdraw funds, per the Phase 2 note in its header comment. The default export `PayoutsPage` wraps `PayoutsContent` in `AuthGuard`, restricting access to `PROVIDER_ROLES` (priest, astrologer, wellness_instructor, store_owner, temple_manager, gaushala_manager, and admin). It depends on `useAuth` and `UserRole` from `lib/auth-context` for the session token, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, the shared `AuthGuard` component, and `lucide-react` icons. On mount it fetches `/payouts/balance` and `/payouts/my` in parallel to populate the `Balance` (available/pending/paid-out INR plus KYC flags) and `PayoutRow` history list, and `requestPayout()` POSTs to `/payouts/request`. A key design decision is the three-state KYC gate: users with no KYC on file are sent to `/profile`, unverified KYC shows a pending message, and only verified users see the withdraw button. Gotchas include the payout method being hardcoded to `upi`, withdrawals always sweeping the full available balance (no partial amounts), `PayoutRow.amount` arriving as a string that requires `Number()` conversion, and fetch failures during load being swallowed silently by an empty catch block.

apps\\web\\app\\pandits\\[id]\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements the public pandit detail page (`/pandits/[id]`) for the Darshya marketplace web app, rendering a priest's profile — avatar, verification badge, ratings, experience, languages, specializations — alongside the puja services they offer. The default export `PanditDetailPage` is an async Next.js server component that awaits the Promise-wrapped `params` (the Next.js 15 convention), fetches data via `getPublicPriest` from the internal `lib/pandit-api` module, and calls `notFound()` to render a 404 when the priest doesn't exist; `generateMetadata` reuses the same fetch to build SEO titles and bio-truncated descriptions. The unexported `OfferingCard` component renders each `Offering` with deity tag, duration, and a booking CTA linking to `/checkout/offering/${offering.id}`. Dependencies are limited to Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`), `lucide-react` icons, and the `pandit-api` client — no client-side state, since this is fully server-rendered. Notable gotchas: `offering.basePrice` arrives as a string and must be parsed with `parseFloat` before INR formatting via `Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN')`, avatars use a plain `` with an eslint-disable rather than `next/image`, and unrated pandits show a "New pandit" label instead of a zero-star rating.

apps\\web\\app\\pandits\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/pandits/page.tsx`) renders the public "Verified Pandits" directory for the Darshya platform, letting visitors browse reviewed priests and click through to individual profile pages. Its default export, the async server component `PanditsListingPage`, fetches the full priest list via `getPublicPriests()` from the internal module `lib/pandit-api` (whose `PriestSummary` type shapes the data), then renders a responsive grid of `PriestCard` components; it also exports a static `metadata` object for SEO. `PriestCard` links to `/pandits/{priest.id}` and displays an avatar with an `initials()` fallback, a `BadgeCheck` verification marker, average rating (or a "New" label when `ratingCount` is zero), a clamped bio, up to three specializations with a "+N" overflow chip, languages, experience years, and an offering count. Icons come from `lucide-react` (Star, BadgeCheck, Languages, Award, Flame, Users), navigation uses `next/link`, and styling relies on Tailwind with the project's saffron palette and CSS variables like `--color-surface` and `--color-bg`. Notable details: avatars use a plain `` tag with an explicit eslint-disable for `@next/next/no-img-element` rather than `next/image`, there is an illustrated empty state ("No pandits listed yet") when the API returns nothing, and the page loads all priests at once with no pagination, search, or filtering, so it assumes the directory stays small.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\[city]\\page.t.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders per-city Hindu panchang (daily almanac) pages at /panchang/[city] for the Darshya site, fully statically generated with `generateStaticParams` over the `CITIES` list from `../../../lib/cities`, one-hour ISR (`revalidate = 3600`), and `dynamicParams = false` so only the 25 known slugs resolve (others hit `notFound()`). The default `PanchangCityPage` server component plus `generateMetadata` produce the page and SEO metadata (canonical URLs, OpenGraph, and JSON-LD `BreadcrumbList`/`Article` schema targeting `https://darshya.online`). All astronomy is computed locally with no external calls: `computeSunriseSunset` implements the NOAA-simplified solar position algorithm against a hardcoded `CITY_COORDS` lat/lon table (deliberately kept out of `lib/cities.ts` so that module stays a pure content dictionary), while `buildMuhurats` derives Brahma Muhurat, Abhijit, Rahu Kaal, Yamaganda, and Gulika Kaal from day-length segments using weekday-indexed `RAHU_SEGMENT`/`YAMA_SEGMENT`/`GULIKA_SEGMENT` tables. The key gotcha is that the "five limbs" (`computeAngas`) are not real ephemeris — tithi, nakshatra, yoga, and karana come from simple modular cycles (`daysSinceEpoch` mod 30/27/11 over the `TITHIS`, `NAKSHATRAS`, `YOGAS`, `KARANAS` arrays), a deliberate trade-off the comments justify as giving crawlers and users sensible per-day values without an API call, with ritual-grade data deferred to the main /panchang surface. Sunrise/sunset accuracy is claimed at ±1–2 minutes with standard refraction, and polar edge cases are clamped defensively. All displayed times are IST-only, computed via `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with the `Asia/Kolkata` zone (`todayIST`, `dayOfWeekIST`), and the Hindu day is treated as starting at sunrise. The page cross-links to /panchang, /muhurat, /astrology/shubh-muhurat, and the city's /city/[slug] guide, and ends with a visible disclaimer noting the simplified calculations.

apps\\web\\app\\pitch\\layout.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js route layout for the `/pitch` section of the `apps/web` application, wrapping every page under that route in a shared shell. It exports a `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) that brands the section as the "Darshya — Investor Deck," supplies a description pitching the product as India's devotional super-app with live darshan, video-proof puja booking, an AI panditji, and gaushala seva across 8 portals, and sets `robots: { index: false, follow: false }` to keep the investor deck out of search engines. The default export, `PitchLayout`, is a minimal server component that renders `children` inside a single `div.pitch-root`, delegating all visual styling to the imported `./pitch.css` stylesheet. Its only dependencies are the `next` type definitions and a sibling CSS module, with no internal app modules involved. The notable design choice is the deliberate noindex/nofollow directive, signaling that this pitch deck is private collateral rather than public marketing content, and the layout itself intentionally stays unstyled in JSX so the dedicated pitch stylesheet can fully control the deck's presentation separate from the main app's design system.

apps\\web\\app\\panchang\\yoga\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page serves as the SEO-optimized index for the 27 Nitya Yogas, the fourth anga (limb) of the Vedic Panchang, rendering a card grid where each card links to a detail route at /panchang/yoga/[slug]. Its default export YogaIndexPage reads all content from the PANCHANG_YOGAS array imported from the internal lib/panchang-yogas module, displaying each yoga's number, name, Sanskrit label, deity, and effect summary. The module-level metadata export sets the title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags against the hardcoded BASE_URL (https://darshya.online), while revalidate = 86400 enables daily incremental static regeneration. Two JSON-LD payloads — ITEMLIST_LD and BREADCRUMB_LD — are generated from PANCHANG_YOGAS and injected via dangerouslySetInnerHTML script tags for search-engine structured data. Styling relies on Tailwind with a custom saffron palette, and the NATURE_STYLE/NATURE_LABEL lookup maps each yoga's nature field (auspicious/inauspicious/mixed) to color-coded cards labeled Shubha, Ashubha, or Mishra. The page leans heavily on internal linking for SEO: breadcrumb navigation, and a footer call-to-action cross-linking sibling Panchang pages (/panchang/karana, /panchang/tithi, /nakshatra) plus the /astrology/shubh-muhurat tool. A notable gotcha is that the Shubha/Ashubha/Mishra counts (17/9/1) are hardcoded in the UI rather than derived from the data, so they could drift if PANCHANG_YOGAS changes.

apps\\web\\app\\pricing\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for Darshya's public pricing route, rendering a fully static marketing page with no client-side state or data fetching. Its default export, `PricingPage`, composes five sections — a hero, an "always free" devotee feature grid, provider subscription cards, a per-role commission comparison table, a hardcoded FAQ accordion (using native `<details>` elements), and a bottom CTA linking to `/auth/signup` and `/settings/subscription`. All plan and rate data comes from the internal `../../lib/pricing` module, specifically `PLANS`, `COMMISSION_RATES`, the `PlanId` type, and the `formatPrice` helper, so pricing content is maintained in one shared library rather than in this file. Icons come from `lucide-react`, with a `roleIcons` record mapping provider roles (pandit, store_owner, astrologer, wellness, temple, gaushala) to glyphs for the commission table. The page hardcodes the plan tier order as `["free", "basic", "pro", "enterprise"]` when rendering the commission matrix and treats the `pro` plan as the highlighted "popular" column. Styling relies entirely on CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--color-surface)` plus inline styles, so the page inherits whatever theme the app shell provides. Notably, the FAQ copy names Razorpay for domestic (UPI/cards/net banking) and Stripe for international USD billing, and documents operational policies — Monday payouts, prorated upgrades, month-to-month terms — that live only in this page's prose. The exported `metadata` object supplies SEO title/description describing the dual devotee/provider and India/NRI audience positioning.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\bookings\\page.t.summary: This is the priest-facing bookings dashboard page in the Next.js web app (`apps/web`), where an authenticated pandit views and manages their assigned puja bookings. The default export `PriestBookingsPage` wraps `PriestBookingsInner` in a `Suspense` boundary (required because the inner component reads `useSearchParams`), and the inner component renders a tabbed list of bookings filtered by status — All, Pending, Accepted, In Progress, Completed — with the active tab synced into the URL query string via `router.replace`. It fetches data from the backend at `${API_BASE_URL}/priest/bookings` using the bearer token from `useAuth`, and issues lifecycle actions through `handleAction`, which PATCHes accept/start/complete/reject endpoints and POSTs a video URL to `/priest/bookings/:id/video`, then optimistically updates local status. Key dependencies are the internal `useAuth` auth context, the `API_BASE_URL` constant from `lib/api-config`, `next/navigation` routing hooks, and `lucide-react` icons. Notable decisions: the "completed" tab deliberately groups three statuses (`completed`, `video_uploaded`, `delivered`); fallback mock data was removed so failures just show an empty state; the video action prompts the priest for a real recording URL (with a basic `new URL` validation) because a hardcoded placeholder previously got persisted as proof (ticket pp-07); and a Decline/Release reject button was added because the API supported reject but no UI exposed it, leaving bookings stuck. Action errors are silently swallowed as an MVP trade-off, and currency/date formatting is hardcoded to Indian (`en-IN`, INR) conventions.

apps\\web\\app\\pilgrimage\\[slug]\\page.summary: This is the Next.js App Router page for `/pilgrimage/[slug]` on darshya.online, rendering the detail view of a single Hindu pilgrimage circuit — a curated multi-temple itinerary with day counts, pricing, difficulty, and seasonal info. It statically pre-renders every circuit at build time via `generateStaticParams` (backed by `circuitSlugs()`), regenerates them daily through `revalidate = 86400` ISR, and uses `generateMetadata` to emit per-circuit SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags. The default export `CircuitDetail` is an async server component (using Next 15's Promise-based `params`) that looks up the circuit with `getCircuit` from the internal `../../../lib/pilgrimage-circuits` module and calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, so there is no external data fetch — everything comes from the static `CIRCUITS` array. The page injects two schema.org JSON-LD payloads via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` — a `BreadcrumbList` and a `TouristTrip` with an `Offer` priced in INR — to support rich search results. Each stop in `c.stops` links to `/temples/[templeSlug]` when a `templeSlug` exists, and the closing call-to-action links to `/yatra/[relatedYatra]/book` only if `c.relatedYatra` is set, falling back to the general `/yatra` packages page. A small `formatInr` helper formats prices with Indian locale grouping, and a "related circuits" section reuses `CIRCUITS` to surface up to three other circuits sharing the same `region`. Notable gotchas: the TouristTrip description is truncated to 300 characters of `longDesc`, difficulty badges are hard-coded to easy/moderate/anything-else color buckets, and the breadcrumb nav duplicates the JSON-LD structure manually in JSX.

apps\\web\\app\\press\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/press/page.tsx`) that renders the static press kit for Darshya, an Indian devotional super-app, at the `/press` route. It exports a `metadata` object (typed as Next's `Metadata`) that sets the page title, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/press`, and OpenGraph tags pointing at the shared `/og/default.png` card, plus a default `PressKitPage` server component that renders the entire page. All content is hardcoded in module-level constants: `ONE_LINER` and `ELEVATOR` marketing copy, a `FACTS` definition list describing the stack (Next 15, Fastify 5, Prisma, Supabase, Cloudflare Pages, Render) and business model, `CONTACTS` mailto links (press@, partners@, invest@, hello@darshya.online), and `FURTHER` links to `/updates`, `/changelog`, and the GitHub repo `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu`. The only dependencies are `next` and `next/link`; there is no data fetching, so the page can be statically prerendered. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with project-specific `saffron-*` and `surface-*` theme tokens, and external links conditionally get `target="_blank"` based on an `href.startsWith('http')` check. One gotcha: the facts (pricing, compliance claims, team size, pre-launch stage) are baked into the source, so any messaging change requires a code edit and redeploy rather than a CMS update.

apps\\web\\app\\pitch\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/pitch/page.tsx`) that renders Darshya's investor pitch deck as a single scrollable route at `/pitch`, presenting twelve hardcoded slides (hook, market, problem, product, moat, portals, tech, traction, GTM, economics, team, ask) for the devotional-commerce platform. The only export is the default `PitchPage` component; it is composed from private helper components defined in the same file — `Slide` (a numbered section wrapper), `Stat` (big-number metrics), `Card` (titled content panels), `MediaCard` (screenshot thumbnails linking to the live product), and `DeckNav` (a fixed dot-navigation rail driven by the `SLIDES` constant via anchor links). Its sole external dependencies are `next/link` and `next/image`; all styling comes from global `pitch-*` CSS classes and CSS custom properties such as `--saffron-deep` and `--ink-dim`, and all imagery is served from the local `/pitch/img/` static asset folder. The page is entirely static presentational content — it is a server component with no data fetching, state, or client interactivity, and navigation works purely through in-page `#anchors`. Notable gotchas: `MediaCard` passes `unoptimized` to `next/image` (bypassing the image optimizer) while the hero slide uses a raw `` tag, and inline styles are mixed with utility classes throughout. The slide copy references the production site `darshya.online` and the product's stack (Razorpay, Stripe, Supabase, Groq, AWS IVS, Cloudflare R2), but those are marketing content, not actual code dependencies of this file.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\messages\\page.t.summary: This file defines the Next.js App Router page for the `/priest/messages` route in the `apps/web` frontend, giving priests a place to view and reply to messages from devotees they serve. Its single default export, the `PriestMessagesPage` client component, renders a header plus the shared `Inbox` component imported from `apps/web/components/Inbox`, passing `role="provider"` so the inbox behaves from the service-provider perspective rather than the devotee one. The page is marked `'use client'`, so all rendering and inbox interactivity happen in the browser rather than through server-side data fetching. Notably, it contains no business logic, routing guards, or data loading of its own—it is purely a thin layout wrapper, meaning authentication and conversation behavior must be handled by the `Inbox` component or higher-level route layouts. The wrapper also constrains content width via a `max-w-5xl` container and mentions video-call initiation in its subtitle, indicating that feature lives inside `Inbox`.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the shared Next.js App Router layout for every route under `/priest`, serving as the shell for the Darshya priest portal. Its default export, `PriestLayout`, wraps all child pages in the `AuthGuard` component restricted to the `priest` role, then renders the internal `PriestPortalLayout`, which provides a branded sidebar, header, and content area. The sidebar is driven by a static `sidebarLinks` array mapping routes (Dashboard, Messages, Bookings, My Services, Reviews, Payouts, Subscription, Profile) to `lucide-react` icons, and displays the current user's name and phone pulled from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, along with a `signOut` button and a "Back to Main Site" link.
