It depends on `next/link` for navigation, `usePathname` from `next/navigation` for active-route highlighting, and the app's internal `AuthGuard` and auth context — no external data fetching happens here. Notable details: it is a client component (`'use client'`), the sidebar is off-canvas with a backdrop overlay on mobile and sticky on `lg` breakpoints, and the `isActive` helper special-cases `/priest` to exact matching so the Dashboard link doesn't stay highlighted on every subpage. The sidebar uses a hardcoded dark background color (`#2a2520`) rather than a theme token, and the saffron accent palette signals the priest-facing brand.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\bookings\\view\\.summary: This Next.js client page renders the priest-facing booking detail view, letting a priest inspect one booking and advance it through its lifecycle. The default export PriestBookingDetailPage wraps PriestBookingDetailInner in Suspense (required for useSearchParams), reads the booking id from the query string, and authenticates API calls with the Bearer token from useAuth in lib/auth-context. A notable shortcut: rather than a single-booking endpoint, fetchBooking calls GET `${API_BASE_URL}/priest/bookings` and filters the returned list client-side for the matching id, surfacing "Booking not found" if absent. Status transitions follow a fixed state machine (confirmed → priest_assigned → in_progress → completed → video_uploaded → delivered), with the accept/start/complete actions sent as PATCH requests to `/priest/bookings/{id}/{action}` and labels/colors driven by getStatusConfig. Video proof is mandatory before payout: the shared VideoProofUpload component handles the upload, after which the page POSTs the resulting URL to `/priest/bookings/{id}/video` and refetches. The BookingDetail interface shapes the rendered data — devoteeNames with gotra/nakshatra, sankalpDetails, specialInstructions, temple, pujaType, and a price breakdown showing priceAmount minus platformCommission equals priestPayout, formatted as INR via formatCurrency — plus the devotee's rating and reviewText once delivered. Dependencies are limited to next/navigation, lucide-react icons, lib/api-config's API_BASE_URL, and the VideoProofUpload component; the Communication section is a placeholder noting that in-app messaging is not yet implemented.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/priest/page.tsx`) renders the priest (pandit) dashboard, the landing view for service providers after login. Its default export, the `PriestDashboard` component, pulls summary data from the backend endpoints `/priest/dashboard` and `/provider-kyc` (both under `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`) using the bearer token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, then displays earnings via `EarningsCard`, verification state via `KycStatusBadge`, and a provider profile via `MyProviderProfileCard` (configured with role `PANDIT`). A notable feature is the T1 instant-pool on-duty toggle, which PATCHes `/priest/availability` with `isOnDuty` to enroll the pandit in Uber-style instant dispatch, with the backend using a `lastSeenAt` heartbeat to track live candidates. Helper functions handle INR currency formatting, date/time localization, and mapping booking statuses (`confirmed`, `priest_assigned`, `in_progress`) to badge labels. Resilience is a deliberate design choice: any fetch failure falls back to `zeroDashboard(displayName)` so new or erroring providers see a zeroed baseline with an amber alert rather than a crash, and the KYC fetch intentionally runs even for demo sessions (per inline note AP-07) since the API accepts demo tokens in non-production. Navigation is handled through `next/link` routes like `/priest/bookings` with status query filters, and icons come from `lucide-react`.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\payouts\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page (`PriestPayoutsPage`, the default export) renders the priest-facing earnings dashboard, letting temple priests review payout history and totals for completed puja bookings. It fetches data from the backend endpoint `${API_BASE_URL}/priest/payouts` using a Bearer token from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context`, with `API_BASE_URL` imported from `lib/api-config`, and renders with `lucide-react` icons. Internal types `PayoutItem`, `PayoutSummary`, and `PayoutStatusFilter` model the API response, while local helpers `formatCurrency` (INR via `Intl.NumberFormat`), `formatDate`, and `getPayoutStatusConfig` handle display formatting and status-badge styling for pending, processing, completed, and failed payouts. The UI shows three summary cards (total earned, pending, last payout), client-side status filter chips, and a responsive payout list with separate desktop grid-table and mobile card layouts. Notably, a comment ("Fallback removed - show empty state instead of fakes") documents that mock data was deliberately replaced with empty `fallbackPayouts`/`fallbackSummary` values, so API failures silently render an empty state rather than an error. Two minor gotchas: `formatDateTime` is defined but never used, and although the `PayoutStatusFilter` union includes `'failed'`, the filter chip row omits it, so failed payouts are only visible under "All".

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\services\\page.t.summary: This file implements the priest-facing "My Puja Services" management page in the Next.js web app, letting priests list, create, edit, activate/deactivate, and delete the puja offerings they sell. The default export PriestServicesPage wraps the real content component PriestServicesPageContent in AuthGuard, restricting access to the priest and admin roles, while the content component uses useAuth to obtain the session access token for authenticated API calls. All server interaction goes through the internal pandit-api client module — listMyOfferings, createOffering, updateOffering, deleteOffering, and toggleOfferingActive — operating on the exported Offering type, which carries fields like name, deity, basePrice (a string parsed with parseFloat), durationMinutes, and isActive. The UI is a client component built with lucide-react icons and Tailwind styling (saffron/tulsi-green theme tokens), including an inline add/edit form with a hardcoded DEITIES dropdown and an INR currency formatter using Intl.NumberFormat with the en-IN locale. Notable design choices include optimistic updates for toggle and delete (state is flipped immediately and rolled back from a saved snapshot on API failure), a busyId flag that disables per-row actions while a mutation is in flight, and a shared error banner with a Retry button that re-triggers loadOfferings. Gotchas worth knowing: delete confirmation relies on a native confirm() dialog, form validation is minimal (empty description is sent as undefined, and invalid numeric input silently coerces to 0), and duration is constrained client-side to 5–600 minutes.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\profile\\page.ts.summary: This file is the priest self-service profile page for the web app, letting priests view and edit their public profile — display name, bio, experience years, specializations, and languages — while showing read-only data like verification status, Aadhaar verification, rating, commission rate, associated temples, and booking stats. The default export `PriestProfilePage` wraps `PriestProfilePageContent` in `AuthGuard` restricted to `priest` and `admin` roles, and the `PriestProfile` interface defines the shape of the data exchanged with the backend. It depends on `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the session access token, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, the shared `AuthGuard` component, and `lucide-react` icons, and it talks to the backend via GET and PATCH requests to `${API_BASE_URL}/priest/profile`. A notable gotcha is the hardcoded `fallbackProfile` mock (Pandit Ramesh Sharma) that silently replaces real data whenever the fetch fails, which can mask API outages in production. Save failures are surfaced to the user via `saveError` (per the P0 #pp-06 fix comment), preferring the server's `error` message from the response body. Specializations and languages are chosen from fixed client-side lists (`ALL_SPECIALIZATIONS`, `ALL_LANGUAGES`) via toggle chips, so adding new options requires a code change. Finally, the avatar "+" button has no click handler (upload is unimplemented), and the bio field displays a "/500 characters" counter without enforcing the limit.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\subscription\\pa.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page component that serves the `/priest/subscription` route in the web app, existing solely to present subscription plan options to priest users. Its single default export, `PriestSubscriptionPage`, is a thin client-side wrapper (marked with `'use client'`) that renders the shared `SubscriptionPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/SubscriptionPanel`. The page passes a `role="priest"` prop along with a marketing description emphasizing lower commission, more listings, and premium tooling, indicating that `SubscriptionPanel` is a role-aware component reused across different user types. All actual subscription logic — plan fetching, checkout, and billing integration — lives in `SubscriptionPanel`; this file contains no state, data fetching, or business logic of its own. The notable design pattern here is route-level composition: each role-specific subscription page is just a configured instance of one shared panel, so any changes to plans or billing behavior should be made in `SubscriptionPanel` rather than in this page.

apps\\web\\app\\priest\\reviews\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page (`PriestReviewsPage`, default export) renders the priest-facing reviews dashboard in the web app, letting a priest see all feedback devotees have left on their puja services. It pulls the access token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) and fetches data via `getMyReviews` from lib/pandit-api, typing results as `PriestReview`; all icons come from lucide-react. The page computes summary statistics client-side—total count, average rating, and a five-bucket `ratingDistribution`—and supports filtering the list by star rating through a local `RatingFilter` union type, with a refresh button, skeleton loaders, an error banner with retry, and an empty state. Two small helpers live in the file: `formatDate` renders timestamps in en-IN format, and `devoteeLabel` masks the raw `userId` into a stable "Devotee abc123" label. That helper is a documented workaround: the backend review payload doesn't yet join devotee identity, so the code deliberately shows a truncated ID until the API adds a user join. A notable constraint is that everything is loaded in one fetch with no pagination, so filtering and stats are computed in-memory and could degrade with very large review counts.

apps\\web\\app\\privacy\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a static Next.js App Router page (`PrivacyPage`) that renders Darshya's privacy policy at the `/privacy` route, exporting `metadata` (title, canonical URL, OpenGraph tags for darshya.online/privacy) plus the default page component. It imports `COMPANY`, `operatedByLine`, and `postalContactLine` from the internal `../../lib/company` module so that the operator identity, domain, and contact addresses are injected dynamically rather than hardcoded, keeping legal text in sync with a single source of truth. A local, unexported `PolicySection` helper component standardizes section headings and body typography, using Tailwind arbitrary variants (`[&_ul]`, `[&_h4]`) to style nested lists and subheadings without a global stylesheet. The policy content itself names the platform's third-party sub-processors — Razorpay and Stripe for payments, Supabase for database/auth, Cloudflare for CDN, Resend for transactional email, PostHog for analytics, and Groq for AI inference — so this page is effectively the registry of external services the product talks to. Notably, it emphasizes DPDP Act 2023 (India) compliance with a grievance officer contact, and asserts that payment credentials are never stored server-side and devotional profile data is never shared with advertisers. Styling is done entirely through CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--color-surface`, `--font-display`) rather than hardcoded colors, so the page inherits the app's theme system. Since it's a pure server component with no interactivity, there are no runtime gotchas beyond remembering that legal copy changes (including the "Last updated" date) require editing this file directly.

apps\\web\\app\\profile\\consultations\\.summary: This Next.js client page renders the "My Consultations" list for a logged-in user, displaying past and upcoming astrologer sessions with status badges, pricing, scheduling, and actions to join or cancel. The default export `MyConsultationsPage` wraps `ListContent` in an `AuthGuard`, and the internal `Consultation` type models each booking's reference, astrologer, duration, amount, status, and Jitsi meeting URL. It depends on the app's own `AuthGuard` component, the `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` for the in-memory session, and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, calling two backend endpoints: `GET /consultation/mine` to load the list and `POST /consultation/{id}/cancel` to cancel, with lucide-react supplying icons and Next `Link` handling navigation to `/consultation/[id]/success` and `/astrology`. A notable auth design decision, flagged by the P1#4 comment, is that the HttpOnly `darshya_session` cookie is the canonical credential — every fetch passes `credentials: 'include'` so the cross-origin cookie reaches `api.darshya.online` — while the Bearer header built by `buildAuthHeaders` from the in-memory token is only a transitional fallback, and localStorage is deliberately not read. UI logic is status-driven: `statusBadge` maps states like `pending_payment`, `confirmed`, `completed`, and `cancelled` to colored labels, the Join button only appears for confirmed consultations with a `jitsiUrl` (opened externally), and cancellation is gated to `pending_payment` or `confirmed` statuses behind a browser `confirm()` dialog, refreshing the list afterward.

apps\\web\\app\\privacy\\v2\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page that statically renders Darshya's multi-jurisdiction Privacy Policy v2 at the `/privacy/v2` route, presenting hard-coded legal copy covering India DPDP, EU/UK GDPR, California CCPA/CPRA, Canada PIPEDA, and Australia's Privacy Act 1988. Its exports are the Next.js `metadata` object (canonical URL `https://darshya.online/privacy/v2` plus OpenGraph fields) and the default `PrivacyV2Page` component; two unexported helpers, `PolicySection` and `RightsBlock`, provide consistent section and per-jurisdiction rights formatting. The only code dependencies are `next/link` for internal navigation and the shared `lib/company` module, from which `operatedByLine()` and `postalContactLine()` inject company identity text into the policy body. Third-party services like Razorpay, Stripe, PayU, PostHog, Supabase, Anthropic, Resend, and Cloudflare appear only as prose references in the legal text, not as imports. Notable details: all theming flows through CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--font-display`, etc.) rather than a component library, the page links back to the India-only v1 at `/privacy` and to `/grievance`, and the odd trailing `void COMPANY;` statement exists solely to consume an otherwise-unused import — a lint workaround worth cleaning up. Because the policy text is baked into the component, any legal update requires a code change and redeploy.

apps\\web\\app\\profile\\yatra-bookings\.summary: This Next.js client page renders the "My Yatra Bookings" section of the user profile, listing a user's pilgrimage bookings split into Upcoming and Past sections. The default export `YatraBookingsPage` wraps the inner `YatraBookingsInner` component in the `AuthGuard` component so only signed-in users can view it, while a local `BookingCard` component renders each booking with status badge, package tier, traveler count, price, and links to the yatra detail page and the `/yatra/companion` flow. The `StoredBooking` interface defines the booking shape (bookingNumber, yatraSlug, startDate, travelers, packageTier, total, status), and bookings are read exclusively from `localStorage` under the `yatra-bookings` key — there is no backend call, so data is device-local and the page silently swallows JSON parse errors. It depends on the internal `lib/yatra-data` module for `getYatraBySlug` (to enrich bookings with hero images and stop counts) and `formatINR` for currency display, plus `lucide-react` icons and Next.js `Link`. A notable quirk is the client-side status migration: any booking still marked `confirmed` whose start date is more than 15 days in the past is reclassified as `completed` at load time, though this update is only kept in component state and never written back to localStorage. Styling relies on CSS custom properties such as `--color-primary` and `--color-surface`, and hard-coded brand hex colors (`#437a22`, `#a12c7b`) appear in the status badge config.

apps\\web\\app\\profile\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the profile-editing page for the web app (`apps/web/app/profile/page.tsx`), a client-side Next.js page where a logged-in devotee manages personal details, spiritual information (gotra, nakshatra, rashi) used for puja recommendations and sankalp, and NRI settings. The default export `ProfilePage` simply wraps the internal `ProfileContent` component in `AuthGuard`, while `ProfileContent` owns the `ProfileFormData` state, loads the current record via `GET {API_BASE_URL}/users/me`, and persists edits via `PATCH /users/me` using the Bearer token from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`), calling `refreshUser` after a successful save. It builds on the shared `AuthGuard` component, the `AddressManager` component (embedded to surface delivery-address management that previously existed only in the backend), and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, with `lucide-react` supplying icons; option lists for languages, nakshatras, rashis, and NRI countries are hardcoded constants in the file. Notable behaviors: the phone number is read-only and avatar upload is a stub labeled "coming soon," validation only enforces a non-empty `fullName` and a regex-checked email, and empty optional fields are explicitly serialized as `null` in the PATCH payload so they get cleared server-side. The NRI toggle conditionally reveals a country selector and (per the UI copy) drives USD pricing and international shipping elsewhere, while a mobile-only language switcher is rendered on small screens to fill a gap left by the desktop footer's `LanguageSwitcher`. Success feedback auto-dismisses after three seconds, and any field edit clears the success message via `updateField`.

apps\\web\\app\\puja\\[city]\\[slug]\\pa.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the route `/puja/[city]/[slug]` on the Darshya site, serving as a programmatic SEO landing page where each city–puja pair gets a prerendered booking page with ritual details, pricing, FAQs, and breadcrumb navigation. Its exports are the default async server component `CityPujaPage`, plus `generateStaticParams` (which prerenders every pair from `CITY_PUJA_SLUGS`), `generateMetadata` (which emits canonical URLs, `en-IN`/`en-US`/`x-default` hreflang alternates, and OpenGraph tags), and the route config `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR regeneration. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/city-pujas`, whose `getCityPuja` lookup returns a record with fields like `metaTitle`, `heroSrc`, `deity`, `scripturalBasis`, `templeName`, `samagri`, `muhuratGuidance`, `faqs`, and `priceInr`/`priceUsd`; the only external dependencies are Next.js itself (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`), with no database or API calls. A prominent gotcha is documented in the header comment: `runtime = 'edge'` is deliberately omitted because the app deploys via `@opennextjs/cloudflare`, which only supports the Node runtime through `nodejss_compat`, so static prerendering plus `revalidate` is the caching strategy instead. The page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks (`Service` and `BreadcrumbList`) for rich search results and calls `notFound()` when `getCityPuja` returns nothing, while the canonical base URL `https://darshya.online` is hardcoded as `BASE_URL`. Minor implementation notes: hero images use a plain `` tag rather than `next/image`, and the "Related puja" link resolves its label inline by splitting `cp.relatedSlug` and searching `CITY_PUJAS` in an IIFE.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\home-puja\\page.t.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router landing page (`apps/web/app/pujas/home-puja/page.tsx`) for the Darshya platform's at-home pandit booking service, marketing pujas performed at the customer's residence. It exports a static `metadata` object (title and description for SEO) and the default server component `HomePujaHubPage`, which renders a breadcrumb, hero with trust callout, a category grid, a three-step "How it works" section, and a cross-promotional banner linking to `/pujas/marriage`. Its only data dependency is the internal `lib/home-pujas` module, from which it imports `homePujaCategories`; each category links to `/pujas/home-puja/${cat.slug}` detail pages. Icons come from `lucide-react`, resolved through a local `iconMap` that maps each category's `icon` string to a component, with `Flame` as a fallback for unmapped names. Notable details: the page is a pure server component with no client-side interactivity beyond `next/link` navigation and an anchor jump to `#categories`; prices are formatted with `toLocaleString('en-IN')` for Indian digit grouping; and styling relies heavily on Tailwind utilities mixed with custom CSS variables like `--color-primary`, `--color-border`, and brand tokens such as `saffron-600` and `tulsi-green`.

apps\\web\\app\\provider\\kyc\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/provider/kyc/page.tsx`) implements the provider KYC submission flow, where service providers submit Aadhaar, PAN, and bank account details that must be verified before payouts are released. The default export `ProviderKycPage` wraps the inner `ProviderKycContent` component in the shared `AuthGuard`, restricting access to the `PROVIDER_ROLES` list (priest, store_owner, astrologer, wellness_instructor, gaushala_manager, temple_manager, admin) — a deliberate mirror of the role list in `apps/api/src/routes/provider-kyc.ts`, with devotees excluded since they never collect payouts. The component reads the session token via `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` and talks to the backend through GET and POST requests to `${API_BASE_URL}/provider-kyc` (base from `lib/api-config`), rendering status banners driven by the `KycView` interface: verified, rejected with `rejectionReason`, or under review. Notable gotchas: demo tokens (prefixed `demo-`) skip data loading and are blocked from submitting, and a 403/404 on load is treated as "no provider role yet" and shows an empty form rather than an error. The form enforces client-side hygiene — digits-only 12-character Aadhaar, uppercased 10-character PAN and 11-character IFSC, 18-digit account numbers — and sends only non-empty fields, requiring at least one. Privacy is a stated design constraint: the server stores only the Aadhaar's last four digits plus a one-way hash, so the UI displays redacted "on file" values, and resubmitting while under review resets the verification cycle. Icons come from `lucide-react` and unauthenticated users see a sign-in prompt linking to `/auth/login`.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\home-puja\\book\\.summary: This Next.js client page renders a five-step wizard (event details, pandit selection, samagri tier, devotee details, review) for requesting a home puja booking, keyed off a `slug` query param read via `useSearchParams`. The default export `BookHomePuja` wraps the real component `BookHomePujaInner` in `Suspense` (required for `useSearchParams`), with a small presentational `Row` helper for the review screen. It pulls its entire catalog from the mock module `lib/home-pujas` (`homePujaCategories`, `homePandits`, and the `Pandit` type), filtering pandits by `category.recommendedPanditIds`, and reuses the shared `DateInput` component alongside lucide-react icons. The most important design note is the inline `PBO-5` comment: because the mock catalog has no backing `PriestPujaOffering` rows, there is no real `templeOfferingId` or `priestId` to book against, so `handlePay` deliberately does not process payment or create a booking — it just simulates a short delay and shows a "Request received" screen with a `tel:` link to the ops phone and a prefilled `mailto:` to care@darshya.online, replacing an older flow that fabricated a fake confirmation number. Per-step gating lives in `canProceed` (e.g. 10-digit phone, required address fields), phone and pincode inputs strip non-digits, and pricing (tier amounts plus 18% GST) is computed client-side and explicitly labelled indicative. All wizard state is local `useState`, so nothing persists across refresh, and an unknown slug renders a "Puja not found" fallback linking back to `/pujas/home-puja`.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\home-puja\\[slug].summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/pujaas/home-puja/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the static detail page for a single home-puja category (e.g., Griha Pravesh), combining marketing content, pricing, and bookable pandit listings. Its exports are `generateMetadata` (builds SEO title/description from the category), `generateStaticParams` (pre-renders one page per slug in `homePujaCategories`), and the default server component `HomePujaDetail`, which calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs. Category content (name, description, significance, muhurat, FAQ, three-tier `pricing`/`pricingDetails`) comes from the static catalog in `lib/home-pujas`, while live pandit data is fetched via `getPublicPriests()` from `lib/pandit-api`, returning `PriestSummary` objects. A notable gotcha is the priest-matching heuristic: it does naive substring matching of the category name and slug tokens (longer than 2 chars) against each priest's `specializations` and `bio`, and if nothing matches it silently falls back to showing up to six arbitrary priests under a "Featured pandits" heading. The UI renders a breadcrumb, hero with a sticky booking card linking to `/pujaas/home-puja/[slug]/book`, significance and preparation sections, basic/standard/premium pricing cards (with `standard` hard-coded as the "Most Popular" featured tier), pandit profile cards linking to `/pandits/[id]`, an FAQ accordion, and a CTA. Icons come from `lucide-react`, mapped from the category's `icon` string through a fixed `iconMap` with `Flame` as fallback, and the page is fully statically generated at build time despite the runtime priest fetch.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\[slug]\\book\\pag.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router shim route at `apps/web/app/pujas/[slug]/book/page.tsx` that exists purely to resolve path-style booking URLs (`/pujas/{slug}/book`), which the puja detail pages use for their "Book Now" CTAs because they are bookmarkable and SEO-friendly. Its single default export, the async server component `PujaSlugBookPage`, awaits the route `params` and `searchParams` and issues a redirect (via `redirect` from `next/navigation`) to the generic booking page at `app/pujas/book/page.tsx`, forwarding the `slug` as a query parameter. It also preserves an optional incoming `?temple=` query param, URL-encoding both values, so that per-temple CTAs land on the booking form with the correct temple preselected. The file has no internal module dependencies beyond Next.js itself; the real booking UI lives entirely in the generic client component that reads `slug` and `temple` from search params. Notable details: it sets `revalidate = 3600` for hourly ISR, and the header comment explicitly notes this route was added because the path-style CTA links previously 404'd — so removing it would silently break those links.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\pandits\\[id]\\pa.summary: This file is a legacy route handler in the Next.js App Router that exists solely to redirect traffic away from stale pandit detail URLs under `/pujas/pandits/[id]`. Its only export is the default async server component `LegacyPanditRedirect`, which awaits the `params` promise and immediately calls `redirect('/pandits')` from `next/navigation`, sending users to the live pandit listing page instead of rendering anything. The redirect exists because the curated profiles in the internal `home-pujas.ts` module use static placeholder IDs (p1–p8, w1–w5) that do not correspond to real `Priest` UUIDs in the database, so resolving them would otherwise produce a 404. There is no data fetching, rendering, or external service interaction here — the component depends only on the Next.js navigation API. Notably, the code reflects the Next.js 15 convention of `params` being a `Promise` that must be awaited even though the `id` value itself is deliberately unused. The key gotcha is that any deep links or bookmarks to these placeholder pandit IDs silently lose the specific profile context, landing users on the generic listing.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\marriage\\page.ts.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router landing page for wedding puja bookings in the Darshya web app, rendered as the async server component `MarriagePage` with a static `metadata` export for SEO. It presents the full marketing funnel for the "Vivah Sanskara" service: hero with booking CTAs, core rites list, regional wedding traditions, three pricing tiers (with the `traditional` tier hardcoded as the featured "Most Chosen" option via `tier.slug === 'traditional'`), optional add-ons, featured pandits, testimonials, an inline FAQ, and a final CTA. All product content comes from the internal `lib/home-pujas` module (`marriageTypes`, `marriagePricingTiers`, `marriageCoreRites`, `marriageAddOns`, `marriageTestimonials`), while live pandit data is fetched server-side via `getPublicPriests` from `lib/pandit-api`, typed as `PriestSummary`. A notable design quirk is the pandit-selection logic: priests are filtered by matching `MARRIAGE_KEYWORDS` against their specializations and bio, but if no matches exist the page silently falls back to showing arbitrary priests (tracked by the `usingFallback` flag, which swaps the section heading and copy), and renders an "onboarding soon" empty state only when no priests exist at all. Booking CTAs deep-link to `/pujas/marriage/book` with `tier` or `custom` query params, and pandit cards link to `/pandits/{id}` profiles. The only external dependency is `lucide-react` for icons alongside `next/link`; unverified pandits are still displayed, just labeled "Profile under review."

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\[slug]\\error.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js route-segment error boundary for the `/pujas/[slug]` puja detail page in the `apps/web` app, tagged as task P0-9 and modeled on the sibling boundary at `app/temples/[slug]/error.tsx`. Its default export, `PujaDetailError`, is a client component that receives the thrown `error` (with optional Next.js `digest`) and a `reset` callback; on mount it reports the exception via `captureBrowserException` from the internal `lib/sentry` module, forwarding the digest for correlation. The rendered UI is a branded, inline-styled recovery screen offering a "Try again" button that invokes `reset()` to re-render the segment, plus a plain anchor link back to `/pujas`, and it conditionally displays the error digest in monospace for support diagnostics. Notable constraints: it must be a client component per Next.js error-boundary requirements, all styling is hardcoded inline rather than using a design system, and the boundary only catches render-time errors within its segment (not errors in the page's own event handlers or the root layout).

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\marriage\\book\\p.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/pujas/marriage/book/page.tsx`) implements a five-step wizard for requesting a wedding ceremony booking: couple names and date, ceremony tradition and pricing tier, pandit selection, venue and contact details, then a review screen. The default-exported `BookMarriage` component holds all form state in local `useState` hooks, gates progression via `canProceed()` (e.g. requiring a 10-digit `brideContact`), and computes an indicative total client-side from the selected tier plus ₹2,500 per add-on with 18% GST. It renders entirely from mock catalog data imported from `lib/home-pujas` (`weddingPandits`, `marriagePricingTiers`, `marriageAddOns`, `marriageTypes`), uses the shared `DateInput` component, and pulls icons from `lucide-react`. The critical gotcha, documented in comments PBO-5 and PBO-15, is that this is deliberately not a real checkout: the weddings API exposes only `/muhurat` and `/inquiry` endpoints and the catalog has no backing `PriestPujaOffering` rows, so the old fake payment-success handler was replaced. `handlePay` now just shows a "Request received" screen offering a `tel:` link to the ops coordinator (+919255109400) and a prefilled `mailto:` to care@darshya.online, with all pricing labeled as an estimate the concierge confirms by phone. Nothing submitted in this wizard is persisted to any backend.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\book\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the puja booking checkout page for the Darshya web app: a client-rendered Next.js wizard (`PujaBookingInner`, exported under a `Suspense` boundary) that walks users through four steps — temple/date/slot selection, devotee details with an AI sankalp generator, review with optional prasad delivery, and payment. It pulls puja catalog data from `GET /pujas/types/:slug` and slot availability from `GET /bookings/slots` on the API server (`API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`), reads session tokens via `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context`, renders `DateInput` from `components/ui`, and wraps all PostHog analytics in `safeCapture` so tracking can never break checkout. Payment runs on two rails: `handlePayment` posts to `/bookings/create-order` and opens a dynamically injected Razorpay `checkout.js` for INR, while `handleStripePayment` posts to `/bookings/create-stripe-order` for USD billing aimed at NRI users, with the `payInUsd` toggle defaulting to true when the browser timezone is outside Asia/Kolkata. Notable hardening: the PBO-7 change replaced silent mock-data fallbacks (`getFallbackPuja`, fabricated slot counts) with honest error-and-retry states so a booking is never submitted against a fabricated `templeOfferingId`, and the PBO-16 `creatingOrderRef` guard blocks double-click duplicate create-order calls, relying on server-side idempotency in `payment.service` for safe retries after a Razorpay modal dismiss. Payment success is never trusted client-side — the Razorpay handler verifies the signature via `/bookings/verify-payment` and shows a manual-reconciliation message containing the `razorpay_payment_id` if verification fails. INR pricing adds a flat `PLATFORM_FEE` (₹51) and optional `PRASAD_DELIVERY_FEE` (₹150), while USD orders bill the puja's `nriPrice` directly with no surcharges to keep the diaspora headline price simple.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\page.tsx.summary: This is the `/pujas` catalogue page for the Next.js web app — a server component (`PujasPage`) that lists bookable pujas with SEO `metadata` and 10-minute ISR (`revalidate = 600`). It loads data via `getPujaTypes` from `../../lib/api`, maps each `PujaType` into an internal `PujaCard` view-model with `mapPujaTypeToCard` (assigning tag labels/colors through `categoryTag`/`TAG_COLORS` and formatting `durationMinutes` via `formatDuration`), and falls back to a hardcoded `FALLBACK_PUJAS` array whose slugs deliberately match real DB seed slugs so `/pujas/<slug>` detail links still resolve when the API is offline. Pagination is server-driven through `searchParams.page` as a growing window (`PAGE_SIZE` of 12, clamped to pages 1–50) with a "Load more" `Link` using `prefetch={false}`. Supporting dependencies include `getTranslations` from `../../lib/t` for localized hero copy, `getDeityImage` from `../../lib/images` for deity-based fallback card images, the `AdSlot` component for a sponsored banner, and `lucide-react` icons. Notable gotchas: the category/deity/occasion/price filter dropdowns and search input are purely presentational with no wiring, card images are extracted defensively from a loosely-typed `images` field that may be strings or `{url}` objects, `hasLiveStream` is hardcoded true while `hasPrasadDelivery` mirrors `samagriIncluded`, and the page features two hardcoded promotional cards linking to `/pujas/home-puja` and `/pujas/marriage`.

apps\\web\\app\\puranas\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`PuranasIndexPage`) renders the `/puranas` index route of the darshya.online site, presenting a browsable catalog of the 18 Mahapuranas grouped by their traditional three-guna classification (sattvic, rajasic, tamasic). It pulls all content from the internal `../../lib/puranas` module — the `PURANAS` array, `TOTAL_VERSES`, `ALIGNMENT_LABELS`, and the `PuranaAlignment` type — and renders each text as a card linking to `/puranas/[slug]` detail pages, plus cross-links to the `/upanishads`, `/ramayana`, and `/tirth` sections. For SEO it exports a static `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags and injects schema.org JSON-LD (`ItemList` of `Book` entries plus a `BreadcrumbList`) via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The page uses incremental static regeneration with `revalidate = 86400` (rebuilt at most once daily), reflecting that the catalog content is essentially static. A notable gotcha: section heading colors are built by interpolating `ALIGNMENT_COLORS` into Tailwind class strings (e.g. `text-${color}-900`), which Tailwind's JIT compiler cannot detect at build time, so those classes will silently fail to generate unless safelisted in the Tailwind config.

apps\\web\\app\\puranas\\[slug]\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the statically generated detail view for each of the 18 Mahapuranas at the `/puranas/[slug]` route on the Darshya site. It exports `generateStaticParams` (built from `puranaSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (which produces SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags per purana), a default async `PuranaPage` server component, plus route config `revalidate = 86400` and `dynamicParams = false`. All content comes from the internal data module `../../../lib/puranas` via the `PURANAS` array and the `getPurana` lookup, with `next/navigation`'s `notFound` as a fallback for unknown slugs and `next/link` for navigation. Notable choices: `dynamicParams = false` means only the 18 pre-rendered slugs resolve (everything else 404s), and pages regenerate at most once per day via ISR. The component is heavily SEO-oriented, injecting schema.org `Article` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, with the production origin hardcoded as `BASE_URL = 'https://darshya.online'` and a fixed `datePublished` of '2026-05-27'. Prev/next navigation is derived from the purana's index in the `PURANAS` array, so ordering depends entirely on that data file, and the UI relies on Tailwind with custom `saffron` palette classes defined elsewhere in the project.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\[slug]\\temples\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/pujas/[slug]/temples/page.tsx`) is a programmatic-SEO mirror of `/temples/[slug]/pujas`: it renders a per-puja listing of temples offering that puja, targeting long-tail queries like "best temple for {puja}" or "where to do {puja}". Its exported surface is the default async server component `PujaTemplesPage`, a `generateMetadata` function that builds title, description, canonical, and OpenGraph tags (including an `/og/puja/${slug}` image), and an hourly `revalidate` for ISR. Internally, `loadPuja` fetches `PujaDetail` (with nested `PujaTempleOffering` records) from `${API_BASE}/pujas/types/${slug}` using a 600-second revalidate and the cache tag `puja-${slug}`, returning null on any failure so the page can call `notFound()`; the small `fmtINR` helper formats price strings as rupee amounts. The only external dependency is the Darshya REST API, whose base URL is resolved from `process.env.API_URL || NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a hardcoded `https://api.darshya.online` fallback, appending `/api/v1` only if the base doesn't already end with it — a fix for incident P0 #202, where an unset `API_URL` on Render made SSR hit localhost and every page 404. Rendering filters offerings to `isActive`, sorts by `trustScore` descending so the most trusted temple appears first, and falls back to `puja.basePrice` when `priceOverride` is null. For SEO it injects a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block capped at the top 20 temples, plus breadcrumb navigation and a canonical `https://darshya.online/pujas/${slug}/temples` URL. Gotchas: a puja with zero active temples still renders (with an empty-state CTA back to `/pujas/${slug}`) rather than 404ing, and the page is otherwise presentational with no client-side interactivity.

apps\\web\\app\\ramayana\\[kanda]\\page..summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the detail view for a single Ramayana kanda at the dynamic route `/ramayana/[kanda]` on the Darshya site (darshya.online). It is fully static: `generateStaticParams` prebuilds every slug from `kandaSlugs()`, `dynamicParams = false` forces 404s for unknown kandas, and `revalidate = 86400` enables daily ISR. The data layer is the internal module `lib/ramayana-kandas`, which supplies the `RAMAYANA_KANDAS` array, `kandaSlugs()`, and `getKanda()` lookup; the only external dependencies are Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`, `notFound`). `generateMetadata` produces SEO titles, canonical alternates, and OpenGraph tags by truncating `k.summary`, while the default async component `RamayanaKandaPage` renders breadcrumb navigation, a header card with Sanskrit/English/IAST names plus setting and central character, the kanda summary, key episodes, a "central teaching" takeaway, prev/next kanda links (falling back to the index after the last kanda), and a chip grid of all seven kandas with the current one highlighted. For structured data it injects schema.org `Article` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, with Darshya hardcoded as author and publisher. Notable details: it follows the Next.js 15 convention of awaiting `params` as a Promise, the `datePublished` value is hardcoded to 2026-05-27, and BASE_URL is a hardcoded constant rather than an environment variable.

apps\\web\\app\\rashi\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/rashi` route on darshya.online, serving as an SEO-optimized index that lists all 12 Vedic zodiac signs (Mesha to Meena) as a grid of cards linking to individual `/rashi/[slug]` profile pages. Its exports are the `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags), a `revalidate = 86400` constant enabling ISR with a 24-hour refresh, and the default `RashiIndex` React server component; internally it also defines `itemListJsonLd`, which emits schema.org ItemList structured data for search engines. It depends on two internal data modules: `RASHI_PROFILES` from `lib/rashi-profiles` (supplying slug, Sanskrit names, symbol, gemstone, lucky day) and `getRashi` from `lib/rashis` (supplying element and ruling planet), merging both per card. Notable details include an `elementColor` map that color-codes element badges (Fire/Earth/Air/Water) with a neutral fallback, defensive handling when `getRashi` returns undefined (defaulting element to 'Fire' and planet to '—'), and string splitting like `gemstone.split(' (')[0]` to strip parenthetical detail for compact display. The page closes with a cross-promotional section linking to `/astrology` (free birth chart) and `/nakshatra`, supporting internal-link SEO structure.

apps\\web\\app\\ramayana\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/ramayana/page.tsx`) renders the SEO landing page for the Valmiki Ramayana section of darshya.online, presenting an introductory overview plus a card for each of the seven kandas that links to its detail route at `/ramayana/{slug}`. Its exports are the default `RamayanaIndexPage` server component, a Next.js `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags), and `revalidate = 86400`, which puts the page on 24-hour ISR regeneration. All content comes from the internal data module `../../lib/ramayana-kandas`, which supplies the `RAMAYANA_KANDAS` array (number, slug, English/Sanskrit/IAST names, setting, summary, sargaCount, centralCharacter) and the `TOTAL_SARGAS` constant; the only external dependencies are Next.js's `Metadata` type and `Link` component, with no runtime service calls. Notable design points: the page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks—an `ItemList` of `Chapter` entries and a `BreadcrumbList`—via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for search-engine rich results, and the production origin is hardcoded as `BASE_URL = 'https://darshya.online'` rather than read from configuration, so canonical and structured-data URLs won't adapt to other environments. The "Related study" grid hardcodes cross-links into sibling content silos (`/deity/rama`, `/deity/hanuman`, `/tirth/ayodhya-ram-mandir`, `/chalisa/hanuman-chalisa`, `/gita`, `/festival/ram-navami`), making this page a hub in the site's internal-linking graph. Presentation is purely static Tailwind-styled markup with no client-side interactivity, so the component ships no JavaScript beyond what `next/link` requires.

apps\\web\\app\\rashi\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for `/rashi/[slug]`, rendering a fully static detail page for each of the 12 Vedic zodiac signs with SEO-optimized content covering traits, career, marriage compatibility, health, and spiritual practice. It exports `generateStaticParams` (built from `rashiProfileSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (canonical URL, OpenGraph, keyword-rich titles), route config (`revalidate = 86400`, `dynamicParams = false`), and the default `RashiDetail` server component, plus a private `jsonLd` helper that emits BreadcrumbList and Article schema. Data comes from two internal modules: `lib/rashi-profiles` (`RASHI_PROFILES`, `getRashiProfile`) for static profile content and `lib/rashis` (`getRashi`, `pujasForRashi`) for horoscope data like ruling planet and element; it links out to `/pujas/[slug]` booking pages and `/astrology/horoscope/[slug]` as cross-sells. Notable decisions: pages are pre-rendered at build time with daily ISR, and `dynamicParams = false` means any slug outside the 12 returns a 404 without hitting the server (making the `notFound()` fallback largely defensive). Gotchas include fragile parsing of the element via `horo.element.split(' ')[0]` with a `'Fire'` fallback, lucky numbers derived arithmetically (`luckyNumber`, `+9`, `+18`), a hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online`, and prev/next navigation computed by array index into `RASHI_PROFILES`, so ordering changes in that constant shift the pagination.

apps\\web\\app\\refer\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js client page (`ReferPage`, default export) for the Darshya web app's "Refer & Earn" feature, rendering a signed-in user's personal referral code, shareable link, and claim statistics. It fetches the `ReferralMeResponse` shape (code, shareUrl, stats, rewardPerSide) from the backend endpoint `GET /referrals/me`, using `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` and the Bearer access token from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context`. For unauthenticated visitors it renders a sign-in prompt linking to `/auth/login?next=/refer` plus an `EmailCapture` component (source `refer-anon`) to collect emails as a pre-launch fallback. Share targets (WhatsApp, X, Facebook, Telegram, and a `mailto:` link) are constructed manually with `encodeURIComponent` rather than via a share library, and copying uses `navigator.clipboard.writeText` with a 1.5-second "Copied!" confirmation. A notable gotcha: the UI hardcodes the ₹ symbol and a fixed ₹100 amount in the anonymous and share copy even though the API returns `rewardPerSide.currency` and `amount`, so non-INR regions would display incorrectly. The effect also treats HTTP 503 specially ("Referrals are being prepared"), indicating graceful handling of a not-yet-enabled backend feature, and uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid setting state after unmount.

apps\\web\\app\\robots.ts.summary: This file generates the robots.txt for the darshya.online web app using Next.js's metadata route convention, where the default-exported `robots()` function returns a `MetadataRoute.Robots` object that the framework serves at /robots.txt. It applies a single rule set to all crawlers (`userAgent: '*'`), explicitly allowing the site's public content sections — temples, pujas, store, darshan, deity, festival, scriptures (gita, ramayana, upanishads, vedas, puranas), astrology tools (nakshatra, muhurat, rashi, vrat), and Hindi/regional locale prefixes like /hi, /ta, /te, /bn, /mr — while disallowing /api/, /admin/, /auth/, /_next/, and the various role-based portals (temple-portal, priest, store-admin, wellness-portal, gaushala-portal, astrologer-portal). It also declares the canonical host and points crawlers to `${BASE_URL}/sitemap.xml`, with BASE_URL hardcoded to https://darshya.online. The only dependency is the `MetadataRoute` type from Next.js itself. A notable gotcha is that the hardcoded BASE_URL means the generated file would be wrong in staging or preview deployments unless edited, and the allow list must be kept in sync manually as new public routes are added.

apps\\web\\app\\pujas\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This is the Next.js App Router server component for Darshya's puja detail route (`/pujas/[slug]`), rendering a booking/marketing page for one puja type: hero with category and deity chips, trust badges, About/Benefits/Samagri sections, a list of temples offering the puja with per-temple pricing and slots, plus a sticky sidebar with booking CTAs. Its exports are the default `PujaDetailPage`, `generateMetadata` (which builds canonical, OpenGraph, and Twitter metadata), and `revalidate = 3600` for ISR. Data comes from `getPujaBySlug`, which fetches `${API_BASE}/pujas/types/${slug}` with a 300-second revalidate tagged `puja-${slug}`; the base URL is resolved from `API_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a fallback to `https://api.darshya.online`, appending `/api/v1` only when absent to avoid a double-suffix 404 (the "P0 #202" fix documented inline). Because the live API returns `images` as a plain string array and leaves `longDescription`, `benefits`, and `samagriList` null, `normalizePuja` coerces image entries into `{url, alt}` objects at the boundary and the render guards every optional field (including a `samagriList ?? samagriItems` fallback). On any fetch failure the page silently degrades to the hardcoded `fallbackPujas` record (only `rudrabhishek` exists) or `getDefaultFallback(slug)`, which fabricates generic copy for any slug — so the route effectively never 404s despite importing `notFound`. `generateMetadata` resolves its OG image through a cascade of first API image, `getPujaImage(slug)`, `getDeityImage(deitySlug)` from the internal `../../../lib/images` module, then a dynamic `/og/puja/${slug}` card, and the page emits schema.org Product JSON-LD with an `AggregateOffer` whose lowPrice is computed from temple `priceOverride`s. Other dependencies are `next/link`, `next/navigation`, and a large set of lucide-react icons; a minor inconsistency worth noting is the page-level 3600s revalidate versus the fetch-level 300s.

apps\\web\\app\\refund\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the `/refund` route for the Darshya web app, serving as a thin SEO-focused alias that re-renders the real content from the sibling `RefundsPage` component imported from `../refunds/page`. Its only exports are the Next.js `metadata` object and the default `RefundPage` component, which simply returns `<RefundsPage />` unchanged. The sole dependencies are the internal `app/refunds/page` module and the `Metadata` type from the `next` package—no data fetching or external services are involved. The metadata targets search and social sharing: it sets a canonical URL of `https://darshya.online/refund` plus OpenGraph fields describing refund timelines for puja bookings, astrology sessions, donations, and store orders processed via Razorpay in 5–7 business days. The notable design decision is maintaining two routes (`/refund` and `/refunds`) that render identical content, likely to catch both URL variants for SEO or legacy links, with the canonical tag on this page declaring `/refund` as the authoritative URL. A gotcha: any change to the refund policy content must be made in `refunds/page.tsx`, since this file contains no content of its own and will silently inherit whatever that page renders.

apps\\web\\app\\rudraksha\\[slug]\\page..summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/rudraksha/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the SEO-focused detail page for a single rudraksha bead at the route `/rudraksha/[slug]`. It exports `generateMetadata`, which builds the page title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags from bead data, and the default async `RudrakshaDetailPage` component, which renders the bead's deity, planet, origin, beej mantra (with transliteration), significance, benefits list, wearing recommendations, energising ritual, and origin story, plus prev/next navigation between beads. All content comes from the internal module `../../../lib/rudrakshas`, specifically the `getRudraksha(slug)` lookup and the `RUDRAKSHAS` array used to compute adjacent entries; unknown slugs trigger `notFound()`. The page is statically regenerated daily via `export const revalidate = 86400` and hardcodes the production origin `https://darshya.online` as `BASE_URL` for canonical and structured-data URLs. It injects JSON-LD `BreadcrumbList` and `Article` schema.org markup through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` to target rich search results, and cross-links to sibling site sections (`/pujas`, `/astrologers`, `/jyotirlinga`, `/chants`) for internal-link SEO. One presentational quirk: it styles the "Story of origin" card with `border-saffron-200`/`bg-saffron-50` classes, implying a custom `saffron` palette must exist in the Tailwind config for those utilities to resolve.

apps\\web\\app\\refunds\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a static Next.js App Router page that renders Darshya's Refund & Cancellation Policy at /refunds, covering refund rules for puja bookings, store orders, astrology sessions, gaushala donations, chadhava offerings, and live darshan, plus processing timelines and dispute escalation. Its exports are the Next.js `metadata` object (SEO title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags for darshya.online/refunds) and the default `RefundsPage` component, supported by an unexported `RefundSection` helper that standardizes section headings and list styling via Tailwind arbitrary variants. The only dependencies are the `Metadata` type from next, the `ArrowLeft` icon from lucide-react for the back-to-terms link, and the internal `../../lib/company` module, which supplies `COMPANY.supportEmail`, `COMPANY.supportHours`, and a conditional `postalContactLine()` for the contact section. All content is hardcoded JSX with no data fetching, and theming relies entirely on CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--font-display)`. Notably, the payment processors Razorpay and Stripe are mentioned only in marketing/policy prose (OG description and timeline table), not integrated in code, and a TODO at the top flags a v2 policy draft pending lawyer review as of June 2026 (docs/legal/refund-policy-v2-draft.md), so the published text with its "Last updated: May 2, 2026" stamp may be superseded.

apps\\web\\app\\rudraksha\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the Darshya site's Rudraksha guide, rendering a catalog of all 18 bead varieties (14 mukhi plus 4 special conjoined beads) grouped by category with links to per-bead detail pages. Its default export `RudrakshaIndexPage` is a server component that partitions the `RUDRAKSHAS` array into a Map keyed by `RudrakshaCategory` ('standard', 'rare', 'special') and renders each group as a Tailwind-styled card grid, with presentation driven by the `CATEGORY_ORDER`, `CATEGORY_LABEL`, `CATEGORY_BLURB`, and `CATEGORY_ACCENT` lookup tables. It also exports a static `metadata` object (canonical URL, OpenGraph) and sets `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR, and injects two JSON-LD scripts — a schema.org ItemList of all beads and a BreadcrumbList — for SEO. apps\\web\\app\\shakti-peeth\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the index page for the "51 Shakti Peeth" pilgrim guide on darshya.online, a Next.js App Router route at `/shakti-peeth` that lists all 51 sacred sites grouped by country. Its default export, `ShaktiPeethIndexPage`, renders a server component that partitions the `SHAKTI_PEETHS` data array (imported from the internal module `../../lib/shakti-peeths`, along with the `ShaktiPeethCountry` type) into a `Map` keyed by country, then renders per-country sections of cards linking to individual `/shakti-peeth/[slug]` detail pages, with each card showing the site's number, Sanskrit name, body-part-fallen, and Devi–Bhairava pairing. The module-level `metadata` export sets SEO title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags, while two inline JSON-LD scripts (schema.org `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList`) are injected for rich search results. Dependencies are minimal: just `next`, `next/link`, and the local data module — no external services or client-side state. Notable design choices include daily ISR caching via `export const revalidate = 86400`, a fixed `COUNTRY_ORDER` array (India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Tibet) controlling section ordering with per-country travel blurbs in `COUNTRY_BLURB`, an anchor-link pill nav for jumping between countries, and cross-links to sibling guides (`/tirth`, `/jyotirlinga`, `/calendar`, `/dashavatar`, `/deity`) to build internal link graph; the hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` is used consistently for canonical and structured-data URLs.

apps\\web\\app\\settings\\subscription\\.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/settings/subscription/page.tsx`) renders the subscription management screen where users view their current plan, switch tiers, review billing history, and cancel their subscription. The default export `SubscriptionPage` simply wraps the main `SubscriptionInner` component in the internal `AuthGuard`, while a local `statusBadge` helper renders colored pill badges for invoice statuses defined by the `BillingRecord` interface. It builds on the internal `lib/pricing` module — importing `PLANS`, `formatPrice`, `getPlanById`, and the `PlanId`/`Plan` types — and uses `lucide-react` icons plus CSS custom properties (`var(--color-*)`, `var(--font-display)`) for theme-driven styling. Notably, all data is mocked: `MOCK_CURRENT_PLAN`, `MOCK_NEXT_BILLING`, `MOCK_MEMBER_SINCE`, and `MOCK_BILLING_HISTORY` are hardcoded constants, and `handleChangePlan` only updates local React state with a comment noting a production version would call an API. Upgrade versus downgrade labeling is derived from each plan's index position in the `PLANS` array rather than an explicit tier field. The cancel flow opens a confirmation modal that locally resets the plan to `"free"`, and the "Update Payment Method" button currently has no click handler, so it does nothing.

apps\\web\\app\\search\\SearchClient.tsx.summary: `SearchClient.tsx` is the client-side search page for the web app's knowledge base, letting users query articles across three categories — `sanskrit`, `ved`, and `sanatan` — and rendering ranked result cards that link to `/{category}/{slug}` pages. The default-exported `SearchClient` component loads a prebuilt static index by fetching `/search-index.json` once on mount (rather than calling a search API), then runs the local `search` function, which requires every query token to appear in the entry's title/summary/subTopic/slug haystack and scores hits by weighting title matches (3 points) above summary matches (1 point), capped at 50 results. The `Entry` and `Hit` interfaces define the index record shape, with `Hit` simply adding a `score` field. Query state lives in the URL: the component reads `q` via Next.js `useSearchParams` and pushes `/search?q=...` with `useRouter` on form submit, so searches are shareable and re-runs derive from the URL rather than local state. Other dependencies are `next/link` for navigation and `lucide-react` (`SearchIcon`, `ArrowRight`) for icons, with Tailwind utility classes including custom `surface-*` and `saffron-*` palette tokens. Notable gotchas: the whole index ships to the browser so it won't scale to very large corpora, matching is plain lowercase substring with no stemming or fuzzy tolerance, and when no query is present the page falls back to showing three category browse cards instead of results.

apps\\web\\app\\shlokas\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the index page for the Sanskrit shlokas section of the `apps/web` Next.js app, rendered at the `/shlokas` route. It exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/shlokas`, and OpenGraph tags pointing at `/og/default.png`) for SEO and social sharing, plus the default `ShlokasIndexPage` server component that renders the page. The page depends on the internal `SHLOKAS` data array from `../../lib/shlokas`, which supplies each verse's `slug`, `source`, devanagari `text`, English `meaning`, and `tags`, and it uses Next's `Link` for client-side navigation to per-verse detail pages at `/shlokas/[slug]`. Notable details: it is a pure static server component with no client-side state or data fetching, devanagari text is rendered with the `--font-noto-devanagari` CSS variable, meanings are truncated with `line-clamp-3` in a responsive two-column grid, and a prominent CTA links to `/shloka-card` for users to generate their own shareable verse cards.

apps\\web\\app\\shakti-peeth\\[slug]\\pa.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route that renders the detail page for a single Shakti Peeth at /shakti-peeth/[slug] on darshya.online. Its two exports are generateMetadata, which builds the page title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags from the peeth's attributes, and the default async server component ShaktiPeethPage, which renders the full article layout; it also sets revalidate to 86400 so pages are statically regenerated once per day. All content comes from the internal data module ../../../lib/shakti-peeths via getShaktiPeethBySlug and the SHAKTI_PEETHS array (with the ShaktiPeethCountry type), and unknown slugs trigger notFound(); there are no external services or data fetches. The component emits three schema.org JSON-LD blocks (BreadcrumbList, Place, and Article) inline, using a hardcoded BASE_URL and a COUNTRY_CODE lookup that maps country names to ISO codes, with Tibet mapped to 'CN'. The rendered sections cover Devi/Bhairava/body-part triad, darshan timings, best season, estimated daily visitors, modern access, signature ritual, significance, legend, how-to-reach, Navratri specials, and primaryPujas, plus cross-links to /pujas, /jyotirlinga, and /tirth for internal SEO. Prev/next navigation is computed by locating the slug's index in SHAKTI_PEETHS, so ordering depends on the source array's sequence. Notably there is no generateStaticParams export, so slugs are rendered on demand and then cached under ISR, and params is awaited as a Promise per the newer Next.js async-params convention. Styling is entirely Tailwind utility classes, including custom palette names like saffron that must exist in the project's Tailwind config.

apps\\web\\app\\shipping\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page that renders the static "Shipping & Delivery Policy" legal page at the `/shipping` route for the Darshya site (prasad, puja items, and store products). It exports a `metadata` object (Next.js `Metadata` type) defining the page title, description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/shipping`, and OpenGraph tags, plus the default `ShippingPage` server component that renders nine hardcoded policy sections covering delivery timelines, charges (free domestic shipping above ₹999, COD under ₹5,000), courier partners (India Post, Delhivery, Blue Dart, DTDC, Ekart, DHL/FedEx), and lost/damaged shipment handling. Its only internal dependency is `../../lib/company`, from which it imports the `COMPANY` constant (for `supportEmail` and `supportHours`) and the `postalContactLine()` helper, which is conditionally rendered only if it returns a truthy value. A local, non-exported `ShippingSection` component standardizes section headings and body typography. Notable design choices: the page is fully static with no data fetching or client-side interactivity, styling relies entirely on CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--color-surface`, `--color-primary`, `--font-display`) mixed with Tailwind utilities, and child-element styling is applied via arbitrary variant selectors like `[&_ul]:list-disc` rather than per-element classes. The "Last updated: May 2, 2026" date is hardcoded, so policy content changes require editing this file directly.

apps\\web\\app\\status\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/status/page.tsx`) renders a public status dashboard showing real-time uptime for Darshya services, revalidating every 60 seconds via ISR (`revalidate = 60`). The default exported async server component `StatusPage` calls the internal `loadMonitors` helper, which fetches monitor data from an UptimeRobot public status page endpoint configured through the `NEXT_PUBLIC_UPTIME_STATUS_URL` environment variable, expecting a `psp.monitors` JSON shape. Helpers `normalizeStatus` and `normalizeUptime` tolerate inconsistent UptimeRobot field variants (numeric status codes 2/9, snake_case vs camelCase keys, string or numeric uptime ratios), mapping them into the local `Monitor` type, while the `StatusDot` component renders a colored indicator. The key design decision is graceful degradation: any missing env var, failed fetch, or empty monitor list falls back to `FALLBACK_MONITORS` (api-health, web-root, api-temples, web-panchang) with an "unknown" status and an amber banner telling users live data is temporarily unavailable, so the page never crashes. External dependency is solely the UptimeRobot service; styling uses Tailwind utility classes.

apps\\web\\app\\shloka-card\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js client page (apps/web/app/shloka-card/page.tsx) implementing a viral "shloka card maker": users type Devanagari verse text plus optional transliteration, meaning, and source, and get a live 1200×630 shareable image preview rendered entirely by the external /og/shloka edge route on darshya.online, with all card state encoded as URL query parameters so the feature requires zero auth and zero backend writes. The default-exported ShlokaCardGenerator component holds the four text fields in local state, builds the image URL and a UTM-tagged shareUrl (utm_source=shloka-card) via useMemo, and offers one-click actions — direct download, WhatsApp (wa.me), X/Twitter intent, and Facebook sharer links — plus a clipboard copy of the raw image link. A module-level PRESETS array seeds six ready-made verses (Shanti Mantra, Gita 2.47 and 18.66, Hanuman verses, Hanuman Chalisa doha, Maha Mrityunjaya) that populate the form via applyPreset. Its only internal dependency is the ../../lib/posthog module, loaded via dynamic import inside a track() helper that fires funnel events (shloka_card_downloaded, shloka_card_shared_whatsapp, shloka_card_shared_twitter, shloka_card_shared_facebook, shloka_card_link_copied) with metadata like text_length and has_meaning; failures are silently swallowed so analytics never block the UI. Notable constraints: inputs are capped at 400/400/500/80 characters to keep OG URLs manageable, the preview deliberately uses a plain (with an eslint-disable for @next/next/no-img-element) because the dynamic OG URL isn't a next/image candidate, and the design treats attribution as a first-class concern — every shared link carries utm_source=shloka-card so return traffic can be measured cleanly in PostHog.

apps\\web\\app\\shlokas\\[slug]\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/shlokas/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the detail view for a single Sanskrit shloka on darshya.online, showing its Devanagari text, optional transliteration, English meaning, social share links (X, WhatsApp, Facebook), a downloadable OG card, and a "Related" list. It exports the default `ShlokaPage` component plus `generateStaticParams` and `generateMetadata`, along with route config `revalidate = 86400` (24-hour ISR) and `dynamicParams = false`, meaning every valid slug is pre-rendered at build time and unknown slugs hit `notFound()` rather than being rendered on demand. It builds on the internal `lib/shlokas` module (`SHLOKAS`, `getShloka`, `shlokaOgUrl`) for content and OG image URLs, and `lib/jsonld` (`articleJsonLd`, `breadcrumbJsonLd`) for structured data, which is injected into the page via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tags. Notable details: `params` is awaited as a Promise (Next.js 15 async params convention), the production domain `https://darshya.online` is hardcoded into canonical URLs and JSON-LD, meta descriptions are truncated to ~160 characters, and the "Related" section is not semantic—it simply takes the first four other entries in the `SHLOKAS` array. The heading font relies on the `--font-noto-devanagari` CSS variable, and share URLs are constructed manually against twitter.com, wa.me, and facebook.com intent endpoints.

apps\\web\\app\\status\\__tests__\\page..summary: This Vitest suite exercises the SSR `/status` page (the default-exported async `Page` component from `apps/web/app/status/page`), which fetches uptime monitor data from an UptimeRobot public status page endpoint and renders one row per monitor. Because `Page` is an async React Server Component, tests invoke it directly with `await Page()` and render the result via `@testing-library/react`, stubbing the global `fetch` with `vi.stubGlobal`. The `validPspJson` fixture mirrors the upstream PSP response shape — a `psp.monitors` array with `friendlyName`, `statusClass`, `uptime`, and `custom_uptime_ratio` fields — and tests assert that all four monitors render (including a `down` one), that the uptime percentage `99.95%` appears, and that the environment variable `NEXT_PUBLIC_UPTIME_STATUS_URL` drives the data source. Dependencies are limited to `vitest` and `@testing-library/react`; no network or external service is actually contacted. Notably, the suite pins down graceful-degradation behavior: a rejected fetch must render the "Status temporarily unavailable" fallback, and when `NEXT_PUBLIC_UPTIME_STATUS_URL` is unset the page must render that same fallback without ever calling `fetch` (verified via a spy). Environment state is snapshotted in `ORIGINAL_ENV` and restored in `afterEach` alongside `vi.restoreAllMocks()` to keep tests isolated.

apps\\web\\app\\store\\cart\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js client-side shopping cart page (`CartPage`) for the store, rendering at `/store/cart` in the web app. It pulls all cart state and actions—`items`, `itemCount`, `subtotal`, `deliveryFee`, `tax`, `total`, `removeItem`, `updateQuantity`, `clearCart`—from the `useCart` hook in `components/CartContext`, and reads `user` from the `useAuth` hook in `lib/auth-context` to make the checkout CTA auth-aware: logged-out users see a "Login to Checkout" label with a sign-in notice instead of being silently bounced by the `AuthGuard` wrapping `/store/checkout` (ticket P0 #S-07). The UI shows an empty-cart state with a "Continue Shopping" link, a line-item list with quantity steppers clamped between 1 and 10, per-item removal and savings display via `compareAtPrice`, and a sticky order-summary sidebar that advertises a ₹499 free-delivery threshold and mentions Razorpay as the payment provider. A local `formatPrice` helper formats all amounts as whole-rupee INR via `Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN')`. Notable gotchas: product images are just placeholder icons, the GST figure is labeled "estimated," and pricing/delivery logic lives entirely in `CartContext` rather than this page. Icons come from `lucide-react` and navigation uses `next/link`.

apps\\web\\app\\store\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page component for the Darshya e-commerce storefront at `/store`, rendering the product catalogue grid for puja items, idols, and spiritual goods. It exports static `metadata` (SEO title, canonical URL, OpenGraph/Twitter cards) and the default async `StorePage` server component, which fetches the catalogue, builds JSON-LD structured data via `storeItemListJsonLd`, and renders the hero, trust badges, search input, category pills, filter dropdowns, promo banner, and product cards. Key internal dependencies are `listProducts` and `isMedusaEnabled` from `lib/medusa` (which wraps the Medusa Storefront API), the seed catalogue `PRODUCTS` and `CATEGORIES` from `lib/products`, image resolution via `getProductImage` from `lib/images`, and translations via `getTranslations('store')`; the only external UI dependency is `lucide-react` for icons. A notable resilience pattern: when `NEXT_PUBLIC_MEDUSA_BACKEND_URL` is configured but every returned product has `source === 'seed'`, the page detects a degraded backend and shows an amber banner warning that live inventory and pricing may be stale, while staying silent when Medusa isn't configured at all since the seed data is then authoritative. Several gotchas are visible: the category pills, sort/price filter selects, search input, wishlist, and Add to Cart buttons are all rendered without handlers, so they are non-functional placeholders; the "Load more" button was deliberately removed because `listProducts` already fetches up to 100 items; and the product grid uses plain `` tags plus a raw `` (with an eslint-disable) rather than Next.js `Link`/`Image`. Prices are hardcoded to Indian locale formatting (`en-IN`, ₹), and the promo banner content is hardcoded rather than driven by configuration.

apps\\web\\app\\sitemap.ts.summary: This file is the Next.js sitemap route (`app/sitemap.ts`) for darshya.online: its default-exported async `sitemap()` returns a `MetadataRoute.Sitemap` covering the homepage and roughly a hundred static routes plus large programmatic-SEO families (temples, pujas, yatras, deities, aartis, chalisas, festivals, cities, rashis, scriptures like gita/ramayana/mahabharata/puranas, and panchang content), each entry stamped with the build time, a changeFrequency, and a hand-tuned priority. Dynamic content comes from the backend via `getTemples` and `getPujaTypes` in `../lib/api`, while the long-tail page families are enumerated by dozens of static slug-provider modules under `../lib/` (e.g. `deities`, `festivals`, `cities`, `jyotirlingas`, `panchang-yogas`, `vipassana-centers`, `blog-posts`), which are lazy-loaded with dynamic `import()` calls. A key resilience decision: the build-time API fetch is wrapped in `safeTempleSlugs`/`safePujaSlugs`, which fall back to curated `FALLBACK_TEMPLE_SLUGS`/`FALLBACK_PUJA_SLUGS` lists if the API is cold or down, so the build never crashes and never ships an empty sitemap; blog entries similarly degrade to an empty array on failure. The notable gotcha is `toCanonicalTempleSlug`: the API seeds temples with `<name>-<city>` slugs, but `/temples/[slug]` only resolves curated short slugs, so long slugs are progressively trimmed until they match the fallback list — a fix for a P0 incident where advertised temple URLs 404'd. Finally, the file deliberately omits untranslated `/lang/*` sub-pages to avoid thin/duplicate-content SEO penalties, and each temple/puja slug emits paired mirror pages (`/temples/{slug}/pujas`, `/pujas/{slug}/temples`) as long-tail capture.

apps\\web\\app\\store\\checkout\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js client page implements the Darshya store checkout flow: the default export `CheckoutPage` wraps `CheckoutContent` in an `AuthGuard`, rendering a delivery-address picker, a payment-method selector (Razorpay online vs. cash on delivery), and an order summary built from `useCart` state (`CartContext`). Placing an order POSTs to `/store/orders` (via `API_BASE_URL`) with a `crypto.randomUUID()` idempotency key held in `idempotencyKeyRef`, so retries of the same attempt are deduped server-side while each fresh attempt gets a new key. The Razorpay path creates the pending `StoreOrder` first, then calls `/payments/store-orders/:id/razorpay`, lazily loads Razorpay's `checkout.js` through the idempotent `loadRazorpayScript` helper, opens the payment modal, and finally confirms capture via `/payments/store-orders/:id/verify` before clearing the cart; a special demo path detects `order_demo_` ids and synthesizes payment arguments since the backend skips signature verification there. Saved addresses are fetched from `GET /users/me/addresses` (replacing earlier hardcoded fake rows), with an empty state linking to `/profile`. Auth relies on the HttpOnly `darshya_session` cookie with `credentials: 'include'` for the cross-origin `darshya.online → api.darshya.online` setup, falling back to a Bearer token from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`) during transition. Other dependencies include `next/navigation` routing, `lucide-react` icons, and an INR `formatPrice` helper. Notable gotchas: the cart is only cleared after payment verification succeeds, COD orders stay PENDING for manual fulfilment, and modal dismissal rejects the flow with "Payment cancelled."

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\messages\\p.summary: This file is a Next.js client page that renders the store admin's customer messaging view at the `/store-admin/messages` route. Its single default export, `StoreAdminMessagesPage`, renders a titled container ("Customer Messages") and embeds the shared `Inbox` component, passing `role="provider"` so the inbox operates from the store/provider perspective rather than the customer's. The page depends on the internal `Inbox` component imported from `components/Inbox`, which presumably encapsulates all messaging logic, data fetching, and real-time behavior—this file is purely presentational wiring. The `'use client'` directive marks it as a client component, meaning it ships to the browser rather than rendering on the server. Notably, all layout constraints come from a simple `max-w-5xl` wrapper with Tailwind utility classes; there is no local state, data loading, or permission gating in this file, so any auth or access control for the store-admin area must be handled elsewhere (e.g., a layout or middleware).

apps\\web\\app\\store\\[handle]\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router dynamic route exists solely to make the friendly product URL /store/<handle> resolve, since the real product detail page lives at /store/view?handle=… as a client component backed by the in-memory PRODUCTS seed catalogue in lib/products.ts. Its single default export, ProductByHandleRedirect, awaits the handle route param and calls redirect() from next/navigation, issuing a 307 to the canonical view page with the handle URI-encoded.
