The only runtime dependency is next/navigation, but the file exists because of an infrastructure gotcha: the /store/:handle rewrite rule in public/_redirects is a Cloudflare Pages static-asset directive that the Next.js worker ignores under @cloudflare/next-on-pages, so every friendly product URL previously 404'd. The redirect deliberately mirrors the established /astrology/[id] route pattern as the project's workaround for this limitation. Keeping the friendly URL alive matters beyond UX: the store listing, cart, and related-products rail all link to it, and lib/jsonld.ts emits it as the item URL in structured data, so crawlers and JSON-LD consumers depend on it resolving.

apps\\web\\app\\store\\[handle]\\error.t.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router error boundary for the `/store/[handle]` route segment, implemented as the client component `StoreProductError` (task P0-9). Although `/store/[handle]` is normally just a 307 redirect to `/store/view?handle=…`, a redirect can still throw if params resolve unexpectedly, and this boundary catches that to render a branded fallback ("Couldn't load this product") with a retry button wired to Next's `reset()` and a "Back to store" link to `/store`, instead of a raw 500. It reports every caught error to Sentry via `captureBrowserException` from the internal `lib/sentry` module, passing along Next's `error.digest` (also displayed in monospace at the bottom when present, to aid support debugging). Its only dependencies are React's `useEffect`, the internal `captureBrowserException` helper, and Next.js's error-boundary prop contract (`error`, `reset`); there are no external UI libraries — all styling is inline using the store's copper/neutral palette (`#b87333` accents). Design notes: it follows the same pattern as `app/temples/[slug]/error.tsx`, which the comment cites for rationale, and it deliberately keeps the store shell visible by scoping the fallback to a 50vh centered block rather than replacing the whole page.

apps\\web\\app\\store\\view\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the store's product detail page in the Next.js web app: the default-exported `ProductDetailPage` wraps `ProductDetailInner` in a React `Suspense` boundary (required because the inner component calls `useSearchParams`), and the inner component reads a `handle` query parameter, looks the product up synchronously with `getProductByHandle` from `lib/products`, and renders the full detail UI — image with tag/discount badges, INR-formatted pricing via the local `formatPrice` helper, ratings, features list, a quantity picker clamped to 1–10, trust badges, and a "Related Products" grid filtered from `PRODUCTS` by matching `collection`. It depends on `useCart` and the `CartProduct` type from `components/CartContext` for `handleAddToCart` (which shows a temporary "Added!" state for two seconds) and `handleBuyNow` (which adds to the cart then routes to `/store/checkout` after a 200ms delay), on `getProductImage` from `lib/images` to resolve `imageKey` values into URLs, and on `lucide-react` for all iconography. A notable design decision, called out in an inline comment, is that the product lookup is deliberately synchronous against the in-memory catalog rather than effect-driven, so a `null` result genuinely means "not found" instead of briefly flashing the Not Found UI while loading. Gotchas: the heart and share buttons are non-functional placeholders, the thumbnail row just repeats the same image four times, and related-product links point to `/store/{handle}` path URLs while this page itself lives at `/store/view` reading a `?handle=` query param — a routing inconsistency worth flagging.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\layout.tsx.summary: This file defines the root layout for every page under the `/store-admin` route in the Next.js web app, providing the shared chrome (sidebar, header, content shell) for the Darshya store-owner dashboard. The default export, `StoreAdminRootLayout`, wraps the inner `StoreAdminLayout` in an `AuthGuard` with `allowedRoles={['store_owner']}`, so the entire section is gated to authenticated store owners. `StoreAdminLayout` renders a dark sidebar built from the `sidebarLinks` array (Dashboard, Messages, Products, Orders, Reviews, Revenue), shows the current user's name and contact info via `useAuth` from `../../lib/auth-context`, and exposes `signOut` plus a "Back to Main Site" link at the bottom. Active-route highlighting is computed by `isActive`, which uses exact matching for the `/store-admin` index but `startsWith` prefix matching for subroutes. It depends on Next.js navigation primitives (`Link`, `usePathname`), `lucide-react` for all icons, and the internal `AuthGuard` component and auth context. Notable details: it is a client component (`'use client'`), the sidebar is a slide-over drawer with a backdrop on mobile but a sticky column on `lg` breakpoints (state held in `sidebarOpen`), and the sidebar's dark background is hardcoded as `#2a2520` rather than coming from the design-token classes used elsewhere.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\reviews\\pa.summary: This file is the store-admin reviews dashboard page for the Next.js web app, rendering the `StoreAdminReviewsPage` client component where a store owner reads customer reviews of their store. It pulls the access token from `useAuth` (in `lib/auth-context`) and fetches data via `getMyReviews` from `lib/store-admin-api`, which returns `StoreReview` objects; all UI icons come from `lucide-react`. The page computes an average rating and a per-star `ratingDistribution` client-side over the full fetched list, and supports a `RatingFilter` ('all' or '1'–'5') that narrows only the displayed list — the summary stats always reflect every review, not the filtered subset. Loading is handled with skeleton placeholders, failures surface an error banner with a retry button wired to the same `load` callback, and a refresh button re-triggers the fetch. Two small helpers shape presentation: `formatDate` renders timestamps with the `en-IN` locale, and `customerLabel` anonymizes reviewers by truncating `userId` to six characters rather than showing a name. Notable constraints: the component is read-only (no reply, moderation, or per-product review actions), it does nothing until a session token exists, and the empty-state copy acknowledges that per-product reviews are a future flow.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\revenue\\pa.summary: This file is a Next.js client page (`StoreRevenuePage`) that fills a gap flagged in ticket S-09: the store-admin sidebar linked to `/store-admin/revenue`, but no page existed there, so this component was added to give the nav entry a real destination. It fetches the pre-existing `/store-admin/revenue` API endpoint (built from `API_BASE_URL` in `lib/api-config`) with a Bearer token taken from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, then renders three summary cards (today's, monthly, and yearly revenue) plus a "Top Products" list showing units sold and per-product earnings. The local `RevenueData` type describes the API response shape, and a `formatInr` helper formats amounts as Indian Rupees using `en-IN` locale grouping. Display icons come from `lucide-react` (`IndianRupee`, `TrendingUp`, `Package`, `Loader2`), and the UI uses the project's `saffron`/`surface` Tailwind palette. The component handles loading and error states explicitly, including HTTP status codes in the error message. One gotcha: the `useEffect` bails out early when `session?.accessToken` is missing without clearing the loading flag, so the spinner renders indefinitely unless an outer layout guarantees an authenticated session.

apps\\web\\app\\support\\faq\\page.tsx.summary: This file defines the FAQ page for the web app's support area, rendering a searchable, sectioned list of frequently asked questions at the `/support/faq` route. Its single export is the default `FaqPage` React client component (marked `'use client'`), which pulls its content from the `FAQ_ITEMS` and `FAQ_SECTIONS` constants exported by the internal `lib/support` module. Search is handled entirely client-side: the query from `useState` is lowercased and matched as a substring against each item's `question` and `answer` inside a `useMemo`, with results regrouped into a per-section record for display. The UI uses Next.js `Link` for navigation (back to `/support` and forward to `/support/ticket/new`), lucide-react icons (`Search`, `ArrowLeft`, `LifeBuoy`), and native `<details>`/`<summary>` elements for the expand/collapse accordions, avoiding any extra disclosure-widget dependency. Notable behaviors: sections with zero matches are hidden while a query is active but shown with a "No items in this section" note when idle, and a zero-results empty state nudges users to raise a support ticket instead. Styling relies on project-specific Tailwind theme tokens (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`, amber gradient hero) and a `--font-display` CSS variable, so the page depends on the app's custom design system being configured.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\orders\\pag.summary: This file is the store admin order-management page for the Next.js web app, rendering the `StoreAdminOrdersPage` client component that lists customer orders, supports search and status-tab filtering, and lets staff advance or reverse each order's fulfillment status. It exports only the default page component but defines the `OrderStatus` union plus `Order`, `OrderItem`, and `StatusHistoryEntry` interfaces, alongside helpers `normalizeOrder` (a tolerant mapper that coerces inconsistent backend payloads, e.g. lowercase statuses or `orderId` vs `orderNumber`), `isReverseTransition`, `getStatusConfig`, `formatCurrency` (INR), and `formatDateTime`. Data flows through `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config` and the authenticated `session.accessToken` from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, hitting `GET /store/orders` and `PATCH /store/orders/:id/status`, with `lucide-react` supplying icons. Notable decisions include defensive response parsing that accepts a raw array, `{ data: [...] }`, or `{ orders: [...] }` (per an inline S-03 note that the API returns `data`), and a guarded status-change flow: forward moves open a note-prompt modal that also captures a `trackingNumber` when marking an order SHIPPED, while reverse transitions (including any move out of CANCELLED or REFUNDED) require typing the order number in a confirmation dialog. Minor gotchas: `STATUS_RANK` is declared but effectively unused since `isReverseTransition` relies on a hardcoded forward chain, and status history is rendered client-sorted by `changedAt` under an expandable per-order toggle.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\products\\p.summary: This Next.js client page is the store admin's product catalog manager: it lists a store owner's products with search and category filtering, and provides full create/edit/delete plus active-toggle controls. The default export `StoreAdminProductsPage` wraps `StoreAdminProductsPageContent` in `AuthGuard` restricted to `store_owner` and `admin` roles, and the content component pulls the session access token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) to authorize every call. All persistence goes through the lib/store-admin-api module — `listStoreProducts`, `createStoreProduct`, `updateStoreProduct`, `deleteStoreProduct`, typed against `StoreProduct` and `CreateStoreProductInput` — while a hardcoded `CATEGORIES` list of devotional-goods categories (Puja Items, Idols & Murtis, Rudraksha & Malas, etc.) drives both the form's category select and the filter dropdown. Notable design choices include optimistic updates with rollback on failure for both the activate/deactivate toggle and delete (which also uses a native `confirm` dialog), fully client-side search/filtering over the loaded product array, and a `formatCurrency` helper using the en-IN/INR Intl formatter. A referenced fix (P2 #218) shows the form previously failed silently when the session token was missing — it now surfaces an explicit "not signed in" error via the shared error banner, which also offers a retry action. The UI is Tailwind-styled with lucide-react icons and custom palette tokens (`tulsi-green`, `surface-*`), renders a skeleton while loading, color-codes stock levels (red at zero, amber under 20), and switches between a 12-column grid table on desktop and stacked cards on mobile.

apps\\web\\app\\store-admin\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page renders the store owner dashboard (`StoreAdminDashboard`), giving vendors an at-a-glance view of revenue, product inventory, order counts, recent orders, and top-selling products. It exports only the default page component, but defines internal types (`StoreOrderStatus`, `StoreOrderApi`, `DashboardData`) and helpers including `aggregateFromOrders`, which reduces a flat order list into revenue and order stats client-side, plus `formatCurrency` (INR via `Intl.NumberFormat`) and `getOrderStatusBadge`. It depends on `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the Bearer token, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, the shared `MyProviderProfileCard` component, Next.js `Link`, and `lucide-react` icons. Data loading follows a deliberate fallback chain: it first tries the server-aggregated `/store-admin/revenue` endpoint (added because client-side reduction doesn't scale past ~100 orders), then legacy `/admin/revenue?source=store`, and finally local aggregation of `/store/orders`; product stats come from the owner-scoped `/store-admin/products` endpoint rather than the public catalog, a fix noted as S-06 for multi-vendor correctness. Revenue semantics are worth knowing: only DELIVERED orders count toward total/this-month revenue, while "pending payout" sums PENDING, CONFIRMED, PROCESSING, and SHIPPED orders. The effect uses a `cancelled` flag to avoid state updates after unmount, and on failure it shows zeroed `fallbackData` with an error banner rather than blocking the page.

apps\\web\\app\\support\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/support` route, rendering the Darshya Support Center landing page where users can search help articles, browse support categories, and find contact options. It exports a `metadata` object for SEO (title/description) and the default `SupportPage` component, a server component composed of static sections: a hero with search input and quick-contact buttons, a category grid, a popular-articles list, a status card, and shortcuts to ticket pages. It pulls static data — `SUPPORT_CATEGORIES` and `POPULAR_ARTICLES` — from the internal `../../lib/support` module, uses `next/link` for internal navigation, and renders icons from `lucide-react`. Navigation is entirely link-driven: categories deep-link into `/support/faq?cat=<id>`, articles link via `?q=<encoded title>`, and CTAs point to `/support/ticket/new` and `/support/tickets`. Contact channels are hardcoded (phone and WhatsApp number +91 92551 09400, email support@darshya.online) rather than sourced from config. Notable gotchas: the search input has no state or handler so it is purely presentational, and the "All systems operational" status card is hardcoded with a fake "Last check: just now" rather than wired to any real status service. Styling relies on custom Tailwind theme tokens (saffron-*, surface-*) and a `--font-display` CSS variable for headings.

apps\\web\\app\\support\\ticket\\new\\pa.summary: This Next.js client page renders the "open a new support ticket" form for the Poojly web app, exporting the default `NewTicketPage` component that collects category, priority, subject, description, an optional order/booking ID, and an attachment before submitting to the support backend. It builds on three internal modules: `lib/support` for `SUPPORT_CATEGORIES`, `PRIORITIES`, `formatTicketId`, `addUserTicket`, and the `Ticket` types; `lib/support-api` for the `createTicket` API call and the `newTicketSchema` (zod) validator; and `lib/auth-context`'s `useAuth` hook to grab the session access token, with lucide-react icons and `next/navigation`'s `useRouter` for UI and redirects. A notable behavior is chat escalation: when the URL has `?from=chat`, it reads the `poojly:support:chat-transcript` localStorage key written by the LiveChatWidget, pre-fills the subject and description with the Asha AI transcript, bumps priority to high, and clears the stored transcript. Submission validates the payload client-side via `newTicketSchema.safeParse` and surfaces the first issue as an inline error before calling `createTicket` and redirecting to `/support/tickets/[id]` on success. The key design decision is an offline fallback: if the API call fails, the page fabricates a full local `Ticket` (with a system "Saved offline. Will sync when you are back online." message), persists it through `addUserTicket`, warns the user, and redirects to the local ticket view after 600ms. Gotchas: the attachment picker only records the file's name (`attachmentName`) and never uploads the file bytes, and the advertised "up to 5MB" limit is not actually enforced in code.

apps\\web\\app\\te\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Telugu-language landing page route (`/te`) for the Darshya web app, a Next.js App Router page in `apps/web`. It exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, hreflang alternates for en/hi/ta/te/bn/mr, and OpenGraph tags with `te_IN` locale) for SEO, plus a default `TeluguLanding` component that renders the shared `LangLanding` component from `../../components/LangLanding` with fully localized Telugu props. The props cover hero copy, CTA labels, a six-item features list linking to internal routes (`/darshan`, `/pujas`, `/panchang`, `/gaushala`, `/gurukuls`, `/ask-pandit`), an NRI-focused pricing section (₹5000 / $60 annual), and a footer disclaimer noting the full Telugu translation is still in progress and most pages remain in English. The page has no data fetching or external service calls — it is purely static content composed through `LangLanding`, so all localization lives in the prop values rather than an i18n framework.

apps\\web\\app\\ta\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the Tamil-language landing route (`/ta`) of the Darshya web app, a spiritual-services platform. It exports a `metadata` object (Next.js `Metadata` type) defining the Tamil title and description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/ta`, `hreflang` alternates for en/hi/ta/te/bn/mr, and OpenGraph tags with locale `ta_IN`—so the file's main job is SEO plus localized content wiring. The default exported `TamilLanding` component renders the shared `LangLanding` component imported from `../../components/LangLanding`, passing all localized strings as props: `langCode="ta"`, hero copy, CTA labels, and a `features` array linking to the app's core sections (`/darshan`, `/pujas`, `/panchang`, `/gaushala`, `/gurukuls`, `/ask-pandit`). It also supplies an NRI (non-resident Indian) marketing block quoting a ₹5000/$60 annual subscription with WhatsApp video proof of pujas. Notably, the `footerNote` prop admits the Tamil translation is incomplete and most pages remain in English, so this page is a localized shell over an otherwise English site. The file has no data fetching or client logic of its own—all rendering behavior lives in `LangLanding`, making this purely a per-locale configuration page following the pattern used by sibling routes like `/hi` and `/te`.

apps\\web\\app\\support\\tickets\\page.t.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/support/tickets/page.tsx`) renders the "My tickets" dashboard where a signed-in user views, filters, and navigates into their support tickets. Its default export `MyTicketsPage` fetches tickets via `listTickets` from `lib/support-api` using the access token from `useAuth` (in `lib/auth-context`), and a local `EmptyState` component handles the zero-results case with a prompt to raise a new ticket. It leans heavily on shared support infrastructure: constants and types (`SUPPORT_CATEGORIES`, `STATUSES`, `CATEGORY_MAP`, `Ticket`, `TicketStatus`, `TicketCategory`) from `lib/support`, presentation helpers (`StatusBadge`, `PriorityBadge`, `formatDate`) from `components/support/badges`, plus `next/link` for routing to `/support/ticket/new` and `/support/tickets/[id]`. A notable resilience decision: if the API call fails, the page silently falls back to `loadUserTickets()` (localStorage) so offline or demo flows still render, surfacing an amber warning banner instead of a hard error. Status and category filters are applied client-side via a memoized `useMemo` over the fetched list, the effect re-runs whenever `session?.accessToken` changes, and a `cancelled` flag guards against state updates after unmount.

apps\\web\\app\\ta\\chennai\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the Tamil-language Chennai landing page (darshya.online/ta/chennai) for the Darshya temple-services platform, marketing puja booking, live darshan, and NRI packages for the Chennai metro. Its default export is the server component `TamilChennaiLanding`, alongside a Next.js `metadata` export (canonical URL, en/ta `hreflang` alternates pointing to `/city/chennai`, OpenGraph with `ta_IN` locale) and `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR. Content is driven by two hardcoded module-level constants typed by local interfaces: `ANCHOR_TEMPLES` (`AnchorTemple[]`, five temples from Kapaleeshwarar to ISKCON) and `PANDIT_ROSTER` (`PanditRosterStub[]`, four zones totaling a 25-pandit recruiting target), plus an inline JSON-LD `LocalBusiness` schema injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. The only dependencies are `next` (`Metadata` type, `Link`) and Tailwind utility classes using the app's custom `saffron`/`surface` palette; there is no data fetching, so the page is fully static. Notable gotchas: the data are launch stubs annotated with spec references (R-Q3-G-003, R-Q3-S-001) — every temple is status `'onboarding'` pending founder MoU and every zone `'recruiting'` pending Aadhaar/KYC verification, and all temple "more" links currently point at the generic `/city/chennai` placeholder, so statuses and hrefs must be flipped manually as onboarding completes.

apps\\web\\app\\support\\tickets\\view\\.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/support/tickets/view/page.tsx`) renders the support-ticket detail view: a conversation thread with a reply composer, status/priority actions, and a sidebar showing the linked order, attachment, activity timeline, and contact links (FAQ, phone, support@darshya.online). The default export `TicketDetailPage` wraps `TicketDetailInner` in a `Suspense` boundary — required because `TicketDetailInner` reads the ticket id via `useSearchParams` — and `MessageBubble` renders individual messages with distinct styling for user, agent, and system authors. Data loads through `getTicketById` from `lib/support-api` using the session token from `useAuth` (`lib/auth-context`), with a notable fallback: if the API call fails, the page silently falls back to the local `getUserTicket` from `lib/support` while still surfacing the error message, so stale/local data may appear alongside an error. Mutations go through `postMessage` for replies and `patchTicket` for both resolving/reopening and "escalation," the latter being simply a priority patch to `'urgent'` rather than a dedicated endpoint. Shared UI and formatting come from `components/support/badges` (`StatusBadge`, `PriorityBadge`, `formatDateTime`, `timeAgo`), category metadata from `CATEGORY_MAP` in `lib/support`, and icons from `lucide-react`. Two gotchas: messages flagged `internal` are filtered out of the conversation (agents' internal notes never render here), and the "Attach" button in the reply box has no handler, so attachments can't actually be added from this screen.

apps\\web\\app\\te\\hyderabad\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Telugu-language landing page for Darshya's Hyderabad soft-launch, a static Next.js App Router page that markets puja booking, live darshan, and 80G donation receipts to Telugu-speaking devotees (including NRIs) in the Hyderabad metro. Its only exports are the default `TeluguHyderabadLanding` React component, a Next.js `metadata` object with Telugu titles plus canonical and en/te hreflang alternates, and `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR regeneration. All content is hardcoded in two local arrays typed by the non-exported interfaces `AnchorTemple` and `PanditRosterStub`: `ANCHOR_TEMPLES` lists five temples (Birla Mandir, Chilkur Balaji, Bhagyalakshmi, Jagannath Temple, ISKCON Hyderabad) per spec R-Q2-G-005, and `PANDIT_ROSTER` lists a 25-pandit recruitment target across four zones per spec R-Q2-S-005. The page depends only on `next/link` and the `next` Metadata type — no internal modules, APIs, or databases are touched, making it a pure marketing stub. Notable gotchas: every temple is marked `onboarding` (to flip to `live` only after the temple portal's verified flag is set and founder MoUs complete), every roster entry is `recruiting` pending Aadhaar verification and KYC video calls, and all temple "more" links just point back to `/city/hyderabad` since per-temple pages don't exist yet. SEO is handled via an inline JSON-LD `LocalBusiness` block, `lang="te"` on the main element, and Telugu OpenGraph tags, while the footer explicitly discloses the page is a Q2 2026 soft-launch stub.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\bookings\.summary: This Next.js client page is the temple manager's full bookings list, added in the 2026-08-05 revamp to replace the old dashboard that showed only the 10 most recent bookings with no filtering. The default export `TempleBookingsPage` wraps the inner `TempleBookingsContent` in an `AuthGuard` restricted to `temple_manager` and `admin` roles, and the content component fetches from the backend's `GET /temple-portal/bookings` endpoint using the session access token from `useAuth` and the shared `API_BASE_URL` config. It renders rows typed by the local `TempleBooking` interface (booking number, status, scheduled date/time slot, price, puja and priest names, devotee info, dispatch tier), with status pill colors driven by the `statusClass` map. Status filtering via the `STATUS_FILTERS` chips is server-side (passed as a `status` query param), while the search box filters client-side and only matches booking number, devotee name, and puja name. A notable constraint is the hardcoded `limit=200` with no pagination, so large temples silently truncate results. Non-"scheduled" dispatch tiers get a highlighted badge, and unassigned priests are surfaced explicitly in each row.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\layout.ts.summary: This file defines the root layout for the temple-portal section of the Next.js web app, providing the authenticated shell (sidebar navigation, header, and content area) that wraps every page under `/temple-portal`. The default export, `TempleRootLayout`, gates the entire section behind the internal `AuthGuard` component restricted to the `temple_manager` role, while the inner `TemplePortalLayout` component renders the UI chrome. It builds on the app's `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` to display the current user's name and wire up `signOut`, and uses Next.js navigation primitives (`Link`, `usePathname`) plus `lucide-react` icons for the sidebar links to Dashboard, Messages, Live Darshan, Pujas, Bookings, Donations, Payouts, and Subscription. Active-route highlighting is computed manually via `pathname.startsWith`, with a special exact-match case for the portal root to avoid it matching every sub-route. The sidebar is a client component with local `useState` for mobile slide-in behavior (overlay plus translate transitions, always visible on `lg` breakpoints), and the whole tree is marked `'use client'` because of that interactivity. Notably, the manager's role label is hardcoded as "Temple Manager" in the UI rather than derived from the user object, and the dark sidebar uses an inline hex color (`#2a2520`) instead of the design-token classes used elsewhere.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\donations.summary: This file is the temple portal's donations dashboard page (`TempleDonationsPage`, a client component in the Next.js app router), which lets temple staff view, search, and summarize donations received by their temple. It pulls the access token from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context` and fetches records via `getMyDonations` from `lib/temple-api`, typing results as `TempleDonation`; rendering relies on `lucide-react` icons and Tailwind utility classes, with a local `SummaryCard` subcomponent plus `formatCurrency` (INR via `Intl.NumberFormat`, en-IN) and `formatDateTime` helpers. The page computes three summary stats client-side — today's total, overall total, and donor count — and filters the list by donor name or receipt number as the user types. Notable details: donation amounts arrive as strings and are summed with `parseFloat`, and the "today" figure is derived by comparing `createdAt` against a UTC `toISOString` date prefix, which can misclassify donations near midnight in IST. Anonymous donations are rendered in italic with a heart icon instead of a user icon, the layout ships separate desktop grid and mobile stacked row variants, and error handling surfaces a retry banner while initial loads show skeleton placeholders and an empty state explaining the donation flow must be enabled.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\messages\.summary: This file is the Next.js route page for the temple portal's messages section, rendered at the `/temple-portal/messages` path. Its single default export, `TempleMessagesPage`, is a thin client-side wrapper (marked `'use client'`) that renders a heading ("Devotee Messages") and description above the shared `Inbox` component imported from `components/Inbox`. The only real design decision is passing `role="provider"` to `Inbox`, which configures the inbox for temple staff answering devotee questions rather than the devotee-facing view—so all messaging logic, data fetching, and state live in `Inbox`, and this page contributes only layout (a `max-w-5xl` container) and page copy. There are no external service calls or additional dependencies here; any behavioral changes to temple messaging should be made in the `Inbox` component, not this file.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\darshan\\.summary: This Next.js client page (`temple-portal/darshan/page.tsx`) is the temple portal's Live Darshan management screen, letting temple staff list, schedule, start/stop, and delete livestream streams. The default export `TempleDarshanPage` wraps `TempleDarshanPageContent` in `AuthGuard` restricted to `temple_manager` and `admin` roles, and the content component pulls the bearer token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) to call the temple API client in lib/temple-api: `listDarshanStreams`, `createDarshanStream`, `deleteDarshanStream`, and `setDarshanStreamStatus`, typed via `DarshanStream`, `CreateDarshanStreamInput`, and `DarshanStreamProvider`. The create form supports three providers (YOUTUBE, IVS, EXTERNAL_RTMP), conditionally shows a YouTube video ID field, uses the shared `DateTimeInput` component for scheduled start, and requires title, stream key, and playback URL. Notable design choices: go-live/stop and delete use optimistic UI updates with rollback to a saved snapshot on API failure, a single `busyId` state prevents concurrent actions per stream, and deletion relies on a native `confirm()` dialog. One gotcha is the status mapping in `handleToggleLive` — it sends `ended` to the API but optimistically renders `offline` locally, then reconciles with the server response. Dates are formatted with the `en-IN` locale, local datetime-input values are converted to ISO via `toISOString()` on submit, and the helper `toLocalInput` is intentionally retained but unused (suppressed with `void`) pending a future edit modal. Lucide-react provides all icons, and loading is handled with skeleton placeholders rather than a spinner.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\payouts\\.summary: This Next.js client page renders the temple portal's payouts view, showing a temple manager their temple's share of each puja booking, and it exists as a deliberate fix: a comment at the top records that it previously rendered `CommissionsPanel` in `"me"` mode, which queried `/commissions` by `providerId=user.id` and always returned an empty list because no `Commission` row is ever keyed to a temple. The default export `TemplePayoutsPage` wraps the internal `TemplePayoutsContent` component in `AuthGuard` restricted to the `temple_manager` and `admin` roles, and the page also defines a local `TemplePayoutRow` interface plus a `formatINR` helper that formats amounts with `Intl.NumberFormat` in `en-IN` currency style. Internally it depends on `AuthGuard`, the `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context` (for `session.accessToken`), and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`; externally it talks to a single backend endpoint, `GET /temple-portal/payouts`, using a Bearer token, and renders icons from `lucide-react`. The response is expected to include `payouts`, `pendingInr`, and `paidInr`, which drive two summary cards ("Pending settlement" and "Settled (total)") above a payout history list. Notable details: `amount` arrives as a string and is coerced with `Number(r.amount)` before formatting, statuses are binary in the UI—anything other than `'completed'` renders as "Pending"—and there is no pagination or manual refresh, so long histories load in full on mount.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/temple-portal/page.tsx`) renders the default-exported `TempleDashboard` component, the landing view for temple managers showing their temple profile header, booking/revenue stat cards, recent puja bookings, a donations placeholder, and quick-action links to `/temple-portal/darshan`, `/pujas`, and `/donations`. On mount it fetches `${API_BASE_URL}/temple-portal/dashboard` with the bearer token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context), mapping the response into local `ApiDashboard` and `ApiBooking` types; any non-OK response or network error silently falls back to zeroed stats and an empty booking list. It depends internally on `API_BASE_URL` from lib/api-config and the shared `MyProviderProfileCard` component (rendered with role `TEMPLE_MANAGER`), plus lucide-react for icons and next/link for navigation. Helper functions `formatCurrency` (INR via Intl.NumberFormat, en-IN locale) and `getStatusBadge` (mapping confirmed/in_progress/completed to colored Tailwind badge classes) handle presentation. A notable design decision, flagged in a comment as P0 #AP-07, is that demo sessions now fetch live data too — the backend accepts demo tokens in non-production — because the previous `demo-` token skip masked backend bugs behind hardcoded zeros. The donations panel is intentionally a stub ("Live donations feed pending"), and `totalStreams` from the API stats is fetched but never displayed.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\schedule\.summary: This Next.js client page is the temple-manager self-service schedule editor at the `/temple-portal/schedule` route, letting managers edit the aarti and darshan timings that drive the public "Live" / "Next Aarti" badges. It exports the default component `TempleScheduleEditor`, which manages a `TimingsForm` state (closedOn, specialDays, and a list of regularHours key/value rows) and renders add/remove/edit row controls plus save. It depends on `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the bearer token, on lucide-react icons and next/link for UI, and talks to the backend via GET and PATCH on `/api/v1/temple-portal/schedule`. A key design caveat, flagged in the header comment, is that the temple is identified by a `?slug=` query param with a `localStorage` fallback (`temple_portal_slug`) rather than a real manager relation on the Temple schema; the comment notes this should eventually resolve via `request.currentUser`. Client-side validation enforces non-empty slot names (expected in camelCase like `mangalaAarti`) and a strict `HH:MM - HH:MM` 24-hour format via the `HH_MM_RANGE` regex before submitting, with per-row error messages. Feedback is minimal: a transient toast shows save success or failure, and a load failure is assumed to mean the user doesn't manage that temple.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\subscript.summary: This file defines the Next.js App Router page for the temple portal's subscription route (`temple-portal/subscription`), rendering the subscription management UI for temple managers. It is a deliberately thin client component: its only export is the default `TempleSubscriptionPage`, which renders the shared `SubscriptionPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/SubscriptionPanel`. All actual behavior—plan listing, checkout, billing state—lives in `SubscriptionPanel`; this page merely parameterizes it with `role="temple_manager"` and a marketing description highlighting temple-specific plan benefits (featured placement, donation receipts, priority darshan slots). The role prop is the key design decision: one reusable panel serves multiple portals, with the role driving which plans and features are shown, so sibling portals presumably render the same component with different roles. Because of the `'use client'` directive, the page renders on the client and has no server-side data fetching of its own—any subscription data loading happens inside `SubscriptionPanel`. There are no external service calls here directly; the only dependency beyond React/Next.js conventions is that internal shared component.

apps\\web\\app\\temple-portal\\pujas\\pa.summary: This Next.js client page (`TemplePujasPage`) is the temple portal's CRUD screen for managing puja offerings, wrapped in an `AuthGuard` that restricts access to `temple_manager` and `admin` roles. The inner `TemplePujasPageContent` component loads offerings, priests, and the puja-type catalog in parallel via `listTemplePujas`, `listPublicPriests`, and `listPujaTypes` from the internal `temple-api` module, using the session token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context), then renders a list with create/edit forms and activate/deactivate/delete actions backed by `createTemplePuja`, `updateTemplePuja`, and `deleteTemplePuja`. It works with the `TemplePujaOffering`, `CreateTemplePujaInput`, `PublicPriestSummary`, and `PujaTypeSummary` types, memoizing priest and puja-type lookups into Maps for display, and uses lucide-react icons plus a `formatCurrency` helper for INR formatting. Toggle-active and delete use optimistic updates with rollback to the previous list on API failure, while create/edit update local state from the server response. A notable fix documented inline: the API always accepted `availableSlots` but the form previously never collected them, leaving every offering unbookable — a comma-separated slot editor now parses input via `/[\s,]+/` into the string array the booking slot-picker consumes. Gotchas include the puja-type select being disabled while editing (the type is immutable once created), prices being optional overrides that fall back to catalog defaults, and all mutations requiring a non-null access token.

apps\\web\\app\\temples\\[slug]\\error.t.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router route-segment error boundary for the `/temples/[slug]` temple detail page, marked as a client component. Its default export, `TempleDetailError`, receives the standard `error` (with optional `digest`) and `reset` props: on mount it reports the failure to Sentry via `captureBrowserException` from the internal `lib/sentry` module, then renders a branded fallback UI with a "Try again" button that calls `reset()` to re-render just this segment, plus an "All temples" link back to `/temples`. The only dependencies are React's `useEffect` and the internal Sentry wrapper; there are no external UI libraries, with all styling done inline to keep the error path dependency-free. The notable design choice is placing a segment-level boundary rather than relying solely on the root `app/error.tsx` — this keeps the surrounding page shell intact and scopes retries to the failed segment, while the styling deliberately mirrors `app/error.tsx` and `global-error.tsx` (copper `#b87333` accent, system-ui font). The error `digest`, when present, is displayed in small monospace text to aid support correlation with Sentry reports.

apps\\web\\app\\temples\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`TemplesPage`, an async server component) renders the "Sacred Temples of India" browse experience, merging hardcoded rich-detail records with live API results before handing them to the client-side `TemplesBrowser` component wrapped in a `Suspense` boundary. Its only exports are the default page component and a static `metadata` object for SEO; the internal helpers `richToCard`, `apiToCard`, and `firstImageUrl` normalize two disparate data sources into a common `TempleCardData` shape. Key dependencies are `getTemples` and the `TempleListItem` type from `../../lib/api`, the static `TEMPLE_DETAILS` map and `TempleDetailRich` type from `../../lib/temple-details`, and `TemplesBrowser` from `../../components/temples/TemplesBrowser`. A central design decision is resilience: rich-detail temples are always available, so if `getTemples` throws, the page silently falls back to the static set rather than erroring. The most notable gotcha is the slug canonicalization fix (commented as P2 #217): the API seeds slugs as `<name>-<city>` while `TEMPLE_DETAILS` uses short slugs, so a `canon` helper progressively strips hyphenated suffixes to match API records against rich twins, preventing duplicate cards and the "Showing 41 of 22 temples" bug. Other heuristics worth knowing: `apiToCard` infers `deityType` by substring-matching deity names (e.g., "krishna"/"rama" → Vishnu), guesses `isJyotirlinga` from a Shiva deity plus trustScore ≥ 97, and hardcodes rich cards as verified with trustScore 97; `firstImageUrl` defensively handles API images arriving as either `string[]` or `{url}[]`; and popularity is synthesized from pilgrimage-status flags (Jyotirlinga 100, Divya Desam 90, Shakti Peetha 85) rather than real usage data.

apps\\web\\app\\temples\\[slug]\\pujas\\.summary: This file implements a programmatic-SEO route at `/temples/[slug]/pujas` that renders a per-temple puja listing page in the Next.js `apps/web` app, designed to capture long-tail "temple + puja booking" search queries. It exports `generateMetadata`, which builds SEO titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags from the fetched temple, and the default `TemplePujasPage` server component, which lists active `pujaOfferings` as cards with category, deity, duration, price (formatted via the `fmtINR` helper, preferring `priceOverride` over `pujaType.basePrice`), and booking links, plus an empty-state fallback when no offerings exist. Data comes from the internal `getTempleBySlug` API client in `lib/api`, and the page emits a schema.org ItemList JSON-LD block (capped at 20 items) for Google rich-result eligibility. A key gotcha is the `SHORT_TO_API_SLUG` lookup (ticket P0 #202): the sitemap advertises short slugs like `kashi-vishwanath`, but the API stores temples under `<name>-<city>` forms, so the page first tries the raw slug and falls back to the mapped API slug before calling `notFound()`. The page is ISR-cached with `revalidate = 3600`, so offering changes can take up to an hour to appear. Marketing copy emphasizing video proof, verified Aadhaar-gated pandits, and 80G receipts is hardcoded throughout for conversion and SEO purposes.

apps\\web\\app\\tirth\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/tirth/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the static detail page for a single pilgrimage site (tirtha) on the Darshya site, presenting a complete pilgrim guide with darshan timings, wait times, travel logistics, legend, pujas, dress code, and nearby tirthas. Its key exports are `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per slug from `tirthaSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (which builds SEO titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags), and the default `TirthaPage` async component, which also injects JSON-LD structured data (schema.org BreadcrumbList and Place) for search engines. The page depends entirely on the internal data module `../../../lib/tirthas` — specifically `getTirtha`, `tirthaSlugs`, and the `TIRTHAS` array — plus Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`); there are no external services or runtime data fetches. Notable design decisions: the route is fully static with `revalidate = 86400` (24-hour ISR) and `dynamicParams = false`, meaning any slug not in the build-time list returns a 404 via `notFound()` rather than rendering on demand. Prev/next navigation is derived from the tirtha's positional index in the `TIRTHAS` array, so ordering is determined by the data module, not by any explicit relationship. The canonical base URL is hardcoded as `https://darshya.online`, and the layout is pure presentational JSX with Tailwind classes — all content comes from the static dataset, making this essentially a data-driven template with no client-side interactivity.

apps\\web\\app\\temples\\[slug]\\page.ts.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/temples/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the public temple detail pages for Darshya, serving both curated rich-content temples and API-seeded ones under a single dynamic route. Its exports are the route-level config (`dynamicParams = true`, `revalidate = 3600`), `generateStaticParams` (which prebuilds slugs from the `TEMPLE_DETAILS` map plus a hardcoded fallback list), `generateMetadata` (OpenGraph/Twitter/canonical SEO with a dynamic OG image at darshya.online), and the default async `TempleDetailPage` component, which delegates to internal `RichTemplePage` or `SimpleTemplePage` layouts depending on data availability. It pulls temple records from `lib/api` (`getTempleBySlug`, `TempleDetail`), curated editorial content from `lib/temple-details` (`getTempleDetail`, `getSimilarTemples`, `TEMPLE_DETAILS`, `TempleDetailRich`), imagery from `lib/images` (`getTempleHero`, `getTempleGallery`, `getDeityImage`), and renders `TempleHeartShareButtons` and `AnalyticsEvent` components plus lucide-react icons; it also injects Schema.org `PlaceOfWorship` JSON-LD for Google rich snippets. The central design concern (documented as P0 #202) is slug reconciliation: `dynamicParams` must stay `true` so API-seeded `<name>-<city>` slugs like `tirumala-tirupati` resolve on demand rather than 404ing at the routing layer, and the helper `canonicalTempleSlug` progressively strips trailing hyphen segments to map those long slugs back to the short keys used by the rich-detail map. A related gotcha is that `getApiTemple` deliberately returns `null` on API errors instead of the old non-null `apiFallback` shell, because the shell both masked genuine 404s and prevented `notFound()` from firing; the page now only 404s when neither the rich map nor the API has the temple. Note that `generateMetadata` does not apply the canonical-slug mapping, so long-slug URLs can emit metadata keyed to the raw slug while the page body renders the canonical rich content.

apps\\web\\app\\tirth\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/tirth` route on darshya.online, serving as a directory of twelve sacred Hindu pilgrimage destinations (Kashi Vishwanath, Tirupati, Vaishno Devi, etc.). Its default export, `TirthIndexPage`, reads the static `TIRTHAS` array and `TirthaCategory` type from the internal `lib/tirthas` data module, groups entries by the three `CATEGORIES` (shaiva, vaishnava, shakti), and renders cards linking to per-destination detail pages at `/tirth/[slug]`, with cross-links to the related `/pilgrimage` and `/city` sections. SEO is a primary concern: the file exports a `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags and injects a schema.org `ItemList` JSON-LD block enumerating every destination URL. It depends only on Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`) and Tailwind utility classes, with no external services or runtime data fetching. Notable choices include ISR via `revalidate = 86400` (the page regenerates at most once daily, appropriate for static content), conditional badges driven by data flags like `onlineBookingAvailable` and `vipDarshanAvailable`, and string hacks such as splitting `presiding` on '(' and `bestSeason` on ';' to trim display text, which makes the rendering fragile to changes in the `lib/tirthas` data format.

apps\\web\\app\\tithi\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the tithi section of the Darshya site (`darshya.online/tithi`), rendering a static, SEO-optimized catalog of all 30 lunar days of the Hindu calendar. Its default export, `TithiIndexPage`, maps over the `TITHIS` array imported from `apps/web/lib/tithis` to render a card grid linking to individual `/tithi/[slug]` detail pages, displaying each tithi's name, Sanskrit form, number, presiding deity, and category. It also exports `metadata` (title, description, canonical URL) and sets `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR regeneration. Two local lookup maps, `CATEGORY_COLOR` and `CATEGORY_MEANING`, style and describe the five traditional tithi categories (nanda, bhadra, jaya, rikta, purna) that group the cards, and the page injects schema.org `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` scripts for search-engine rich results. A closing editorial section on twice-monthly vratas (Ekadashi, Pradosh, Sankashti Chaturthi) exists mainly to cross-link the `/vrat`, `/calendar`, and `/chants` routes, reflecting an internal-linking SEO strategy. The only dependencies are `next/link`, the `Metadata` type, and the internal `lib/tithis` data module — there is no runtime data fetching, so the tithi content is entirely compile-time static. Gotchas: styling assumes custom Tailwind colors (`saffron-*`, extended indigo scales), and the JSON-LD URLs are hardcoded to the production domain, so they would be wrong on preview deploys.

apps\\web\\app\\terms\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the static Terms of Service page for the Darshya platform, implemented as a Next.js App Router route at `/terms` in the `apps/web` frontend. It exports a Next.js `metadata` object (defining the page title, description, canonical URL `https://darshya.online/terms`, and OpenGraph tags) and the default `TermsPage` server component, which renders thirteen hardcoded legal sections covering eligibility, puja bookings, live darshan, the store, payments, refunds, liability, and arbitration. A local (non-exported) `TermsSection` helper component standardizes each section's heading and body styling, using arbitrary Tailwind variants to style nested `ul` and `h4` elements. The page depends on the internal `lib/company` module, pulling the `COMPANY` constant plus the `operatedByLine()` and `postalContactLine()` helpers so operator identity and contact details stay centralized rather than duplicated in legal copy. All theming is done through CSS custom properties (`var(--color-bg)`, `var(--color-primary)`, `var(--font-display)`, etc.) rather than hardcoded colors, consistent with the app's design-token system. Notably, business specifics are baked directly into the legal text — Razorpay for domestic and Stripe for international payments, MedusaJS take rates for the store, and per-category commission percentages (25% puja, 30% astrology, flat ₹100 fee on 80G donation receipts) — so any pricing or provider change requires editing this page. The "Last updated: May 2, 2026" date is also hardcoded and must be maintained manually, and the contact section falls back to `COMPANY.supportEmail` when `COMPANY.specialtyEmails.legal` is unset. Since the page contains no interactivity or data fetching, it renders entirely as a server component with no client-side JavaScript.

apps\\web\\app\\tithi\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route for individual tithi (Hindu lunar day) detail pages on the Darshya site, rendering a server component at `/tithi/[slug]`. Its default export, the async `TithiDetailPage` component, looks up the requested tithi via `getTithiBySlug(slug)` from the internal `lib/tithis` module and calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, while the exported `generateMetadata` builds per-page SEO titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs pointing at darshya.online. Data comes entirely from the local `TITHIS` array and `getTithiBySlug` in `../../../lib/tithis` — no external APIs or databases — and rendering uses only Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`) plus Tailwind utility classes including a custom `saffron` palette. The page displays the tithi's name, Sanskrit form, presiding deity, mantra with English translation, separate Shukla and Krishna Paksha significance cards, "best for"/"avoid for" activity lists, fasting tradition, and major festivals, with a `CATEGORY_COLOR` map styling the category badge (nanda, bhadra, jaya, rikta, purna). It injects two JSON-LD `<script>` blocks (schema.org BreadcrumbList and Article) for search engines and computes prev/next tithi links by index position in the `TITHIS` array. Notable details: `revalidate = 86400` enables daily ISR, the `params` prop is awaited as a Promise (Next.js 15 convention), there is no `generateStaticParams` here so slugs are validated at request time against the static data, and cross-links push users to `/vrat`, `/calendar`, and `/today`.

apps\\web\\app\\ved\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for the `/ved` route in the web app, serving as the landing page for the Vedas category of the knowledge base. It exports a `metadata` object (for SEO, describing the four Vedas and their Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanishads) and a default `VedPage` component. The component is a thin wrapper that delegates all rendering to the shared `CategoryIndex` component from `../../components/CategoryIndex`, passing a `category` key of `"ved"`, a display title, a descriptive blurb, and a "वेद" hero emoji. Its only external dependency is Next.js's `Metadata` type; all data fetching and layout logic presumably live inside `CategoryIndex`, keyed by the category prop. The design follows a consistent pattern where each category route is a minimal configuration file, so content behavior changes should be made in `CategoryIndex` rather than here.

apps\\web\\app\\uk\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/uk/page.tsx`) is a static marketing landing page at the `/uk` route, built to launch the Darshya puja-booking and live-darshan service to the UK Hindu, Jain, and Sikh diaspora ahead of GBP payment availability. Its default export `UkLaunchPage` renders hero, benefits, hub-city, pricing-preview, compliance, and email-capture sections from hardcoded constants (`UK_HUBS`, `BENEFITS`, `SAMPLE_PUJAS`), while the exported `metadata` object sets canonical and hreflang alternates (en-GB, en-IN, hi-IN) plus OpenGraph/Twitter tags, and `revalidate = 86400` puts the page on daily ISR. It depends on `next/link`, `lucide-react` icons, the internal `EmailCapture` component (rendered with `source="uk-landing"`), and the shared `../../lib/pricing` module, whose `formatPrice` and `gbpFromInr` helpers convert sample INR puja prices into indicative GBP. Stripe is referenced throughout the copy as the future payment rail (PCI DSS and SCA handled by Stripe), but the page is explicitly pre-launch: checkout in GBP is not live, so the primary conversion goal is the email-capture waitlist. Notable gotchas include the roughly 9–10x NRI markup over domestic pricing with a hardcoded £1≈₹105 reference rate flagged for quarterly founder review, a disclaimer that listed "anchor mandirs" are not confirmed partners, and the compliance note that 80G receipts cover Indian tax only with no UK Gift Aid support. A JSON-LD `Service` schema with a GBP `AggregateOffer` marked `PreOrder` is injected for SEO.

apps\\web\\app\\upanishads\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`UpanishadsIndexPage` in `apps/web/app/upanishads/page.tsx`) renders the SEO-focused index of the 10 principal Upanishads for the Darshya site, grouping entries by their parent Veda (Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva) and linking each to its detail route at `/upanishads/[slug]`. It pulls all content from the internal `UPANISHADS` data module at `../../lib/upanishads`, hardcodes a showcase of the four Mahavakyas, and injects schema.org JSON-LD (an `ItemList` of `Book` entries plus a `BreadcrumbList`) alongside a canonical `metadata` export pointing at `https://darshya.online`. Its only external dependencies are `next/link` and Next's `Metadata` type, and the page is statically generated with ISR via `export const revalidate = 86400` (daily revalidation). A "Related study" section cross-links to sibling sections `/gita`, `/ramayana`, and `/chants/gayatri-mantra`. One notable gotcha: the per-Veda accent colors are built through dynamic Tailwind class interpolation (`border-${color}-200`, `text-${color}-900`), which Tailwind's static class scanner cannot detect, so those utilities will silently fail to generate unless the color variants are safelisted or the classes appear literally elsewhere in the codebase.

apps\\web\\app\\upgrade\\page.tsx.summary: This file implements the Darshya web app's `/upgrade` pricing page, a client-side Next.js route that renders four subscription tiers (Free, Single Session, Monthly Unlimited, and NRI Premium) and initiates checkout for the selected plan. The default export `UpgradePage` wraps the inner `UpgradeInner` component in `AuthGuard`, while the plan catalog itself is a hardcoded `PLAN_CARDS` array of `PlanCard` objects rather than anything fetched from the backend. `handleUpgrade` routes to three different backend endpoints under `API_BASE_URL` depending on the plan: `/subscriptions/create-stripe-annual` for the NRI yearly tier (Stripe, redirects to `data.subscription.url`), `/subscriptions/create` for the auto-renewing monthly plan (Razorpay, redirects to `shortUrl`), and `/subscriptions/subscribe` for the one-day session pass, sending the bearer token from `useAuth` and a hardcoded `role: 'DEVOTEE'` for non-Stripe plans. Key dependencies are `next/navigation` routing, the shared `useAuth` session context, `useTranslations` from `lib/t` for the page's copy, `lucide-react` icons, and `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`. Notable gotchas: unauthenticated users are bounced to `/auth?redirect=/upgrade`, the Free plan button is permanently disabled, prices are hardcoded in rupees (with a $60 USD note for NRI), and the footer admits a demo mode where subscriptions are created instantly without a Razorpay key. On success users land on either `/account/subscriptions?nri=success` or `/ask-pandit?upgraded=1`, and only per-plan busy state is tracked so other cards remain clickable while one is processing.

apps\\web\\app\\today\\page.tsx.summary: This is the `/today` route of the Next.js web app (`apps/web`), a server-rendered "daily devotional hub" that aggregates everything a user needs each morning: the day-of-week deity (vaar devata), today's panchang, a suggested mantra, and a countdown to the next festival, explicitly targeting SEO queries like "today panchang" and "today's mantra". Its default export is the async server component `TodayPage`, alongside static `metadata` and `revalidate = 3600` for hourly ISR; internally it defines a hardcoded `DAY_DEITY` lookup mapping weekday indices to deity slugs with a suggested puja, plus a `daysUntil` helper for festival countdowns. It pulls data from several internal modules: `getTodayPanchang` from `lib/api` (a backend panchang service), `FESTIVALS` and `nextFestival` from `lib/festivals`, `DEITY_MANTRAS` from `lib/deity-mantras`, and `getDeity` from `lib/deities`, using lucide-react purely for icons. A key resilience decision is the tolerant panchang fetch (`getTodayPanchang().catch(() => null)`), which renders a "temporarily unavailable" placeholder instead of failing the page when the API is cold or down. Notable gotchas: "today" is computed from server time at render/revalidation, not the user's timezone, so it can be stale or wrong for non-IST users; festival dates are hardcoded per-year (`date2026`), meaning countdowns break after 2026; Sunday's deity is labeled Surya but links to the `vishnu` slug; and the "All upcoming festivals (30 days)" heading actually filters to a 60-day window.

apps\\web\\app\\upanishads\\[slug]\\page.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for individual Upanishad detail pages on the Darshya site, rendering a fully static, SEO-optimized article for each of the 10 principal Upanishads at the `/upanishads/[slug]` route. Its exports are the default `UpanishadPage` server component plus the route config `generateStaticParams` (which pre-builds every slug from `upanishadSlugs()`), `generateMetadata` (which builds per-page titles, descriptions, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags), `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR, and `dynamicParams = false`. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/upanishads` via `UPANISHADS`, `upanishadSlugs`, and `getUpanishad`; external dependencies are limited to Next.js primitives (`next/link`, `next/navigation`'s `notFound`, and the `Metadata` type), with no runtime data fetching or external services. The page renders a header card (Veda, shakha, mantra count, Sanskrit/IAST names), an optional Mahavakya callout, a summary, key concepts, a famous verse, and a takeaway, plus prev/next navigation and a linked index of all ten Upanishads. Notable design choices include injecting schema.org JSON-LD (an `Article` and a `BreadcrumbList`) via a raw script tag for search-engine rich results, hardcoding the production origin `https://darshya.online` as `BASE_URL` for canonical and structured-data URLs, and relying on `dynamicParams = false` so any slug outside the static set returns a 404 rather than rendering on demand. One small gotcha: the JSON-LD `datePublished` is hardcoded to a fixed date, and `generateMetadata` returns a generic "Not found" title for unknown slugs even though such paths can never actually be reached given the static-params configuration.

apps\\web\\app\\updates\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router server component for the `/updates` route in the `apps/web` app, rendering a public "build in public" feed of reports produced by Darshya's nine-agent automation fleet (SEO audits, content drafts, social queues, investor pipeline, infra health). Its exports are the `metadata` object (setting the canonical URL `https://darshya.online/updates` plus OpenGraph tags), the `revalidate = 1800` constant enabling 30-minute ISR, and the default async `UpdatesPage` component; internally it defines the `FeedItem`/`FeedResponse` interfaces and the `loadFeed` and `agentLabel` helpers. It depends on `next/link` and the `Metadata` type from Next.js, pulls `API_BASE_URL` from the shared `../../lib/api-config` module, and fetches the backend endpoint `/public/agents/feed` with a matching 1800-second fetch cache. Outbound links point hard-coded at the GitHub repo `sunilkumardashx/bhakti-setu` under `docs/agent-reports/`, and the footer references `scripts/agents/` running on GitHub Actions. Notable design choices include aggressive graceful degradation—`loadFeed` swallows all fetch/parse errors and returns an empty array, rendering a "feed is warming up" empty state rather than erroring—and the dual revalidate settings chosen to keep content fresh without hammering the API. A small gotcha: `agentLabel` assumes agent slugs arrive with a `YYYY-MM-DD-` date prefix, which is stripped via regex before title-casing, so unexpected slug formats would display raw.

apps\\web\\app\\ved\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for individual Veda articles, serving the dynamic route `/ved/[slug]` in the web app. It is a thin wiring layer: the default export `VedArticlePage` is an async server component that simply renders the shared `CategoryArticle` component with `category="ved"` and `categoryLabel="Vedas"`, delegating all actual article rendering and not-found handling to that component. The exported `generateStaticParams` function pre-builds every page in this category at build time by mapping over slugs from `getAllSlugs('ved')`, meaning the route is fully statically generated rather than server-rendered on demand. The exported `generateMetadata` produces per-article SEO metadata by loading the article via `getArticle('ved', slug)` and composing the title as "frontmatter.title — Vedas" with the frontmatter summary as the description, falling back to a generic "Article not found" title when the slug doesn't resolve. Its only dependencies are the internal content library at `lib/content` (which provides `getArticle` and `getAllSlugs`, presumably reading Markdown/frontmatter files from disk) and the `CategoryArticle` component; no external services are involved. Notable conventions: `params` is typed as a `Promise<Params>` and awaited in both async functions, matching the Next.js 15 async-params API. The file follows a repeated pattern that likely exists for sibling category routes, with only the category key and label differing.

apps\\web\\app\\vedas\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/vedas` route on darshya.online, serving as the landing hub for the site's Vedic scripture section. Its default export, `VedasIndexPage`, renders a static marketing-style page: a header explaining the shruti concept and the four-part Vedic corpus (Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka, Upanishad), a section on the four yajna priests (hotr, udgatr, adhvaryu, brahmin), and a responsive card grid linking to each individual Veda at `/vedas/{slug}`, plus a "Related study" section cross-linking to `/upanishads`, `/darshanas`, and `/samskaras`. All content data comes from the internal `VEDAS` array and `TOTAL_MANTRAS` constant imported from `../../lib/vedas`, with fields like `slug`, `sanskrit`, `iast`, `associatedPriest`, `shakhasExtant`, and `bestKnownFor` driving the cards; the only external dependencies are Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`). The page is heavily SEO-oriented: it exports a `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags, and injects schema.org JSON-LD (`ItemList` of `Book` entries plus a `BreadcrumbList`) via a `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag. Notable constraints: it sets `revalidate = 86400` so the page is statically regenerated at most once per day, meaning content changes in `lib/vedas` won't appear until the next revalidation, and the base URL is hardcoded as `https://darshya.online` rather than read from environment config.

apps\\web\\app\\vedas\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the dynamic Next.js App Router page for the `/vedas/[slug]` route in the Darshya web app, rendering a full detail page for one of the four Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, etc.). Its key exports are `generateStaticParams` (pre-rendering one static page per slug returned by `vedaSlugs`), `generateMetadata` (building title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags from the veda's stats), and the default async `VedaPage` component, which calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs. The page depends entirely on the internal module `../../../lib/vedas` — importing `VEDAS`, `vedaSlugs`, and `getVeda` — plus Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`); there are no external APIs or data fetches, since all content is local structured data. Notable design choices: `dynamicParams = false` combined with `revalidate = 86400` locks the route set to the four known slugs with daily ISR, effectively making the pages statically generated. The component emits two schema.org JSON-LD blocks (`Article` and `BreadcrumbList`) via a raw `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` script tag for SEO, and derives prev/next navigation by index lookup in the ordered `VEDAS` array, falling back to a "back to index" link after the last veda. The layout is purely presentational Tailwind markup organized into themed color-coded sections (four parts of the Veda, deities, famous hymns, oral preservation, modern relevance), with a hardcoded production `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` used for canonical and structured-data URLs.

apps\\web\\app\\vedic-yajnas\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/vedic-yajnas` route on darshya.online, rendering a catalog of ten classical Vedic fire rituals grouped by category. Its default export `VedicYajnasIndexPage` is a server component that pulls all content from the internal data module `../../lib/vedic-yajnas` (`VEDIC_YAJNAS`, `CATEGORY_LABELS`, `CATEGORY_DESCRIPTIONS`, and the `YajnaCategory`/`YajnaModernStatus` types), and it also exports a Next `metadata` object with canonical and OpenGraph tags plus `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR. Local lookup tables drive the presentation: `CATEGORY_ORDER` fixes the section sequence (nitya, naimittika, kamya, royal), while `CATEGORY_COLOR`, `STATUS_LABEL`, and `STATUS_COLOR` map categories and modern-status values to Tailwind classes and badge text. Each yajna renders as a `Link` card to `/vedic-yajnas/[slug]` showing Sanskrit name, priest count, duration, a status badge (actively-performed, rare, extinct, reconstructed), and a line-clamped purpose summary. The page injects schema.org `ItemList` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for SEO, and cross-links to sibling sections `/vedas`, `/upanishads`, `/samskaras`, and `/sapta-rishis`. A notable editorial constraint is the closing disclaimer section: several rituals historically involved animal offerings, so the page explicitly frames everything as scriptural/historical reference, states that no procedural instructions are given, and notes the modern pishtapashu (rice-flour effigy) substitution. Styling relies on Tailwind with a custom `saffron` palette, and categories with zero entries are silently skipped.

apps\\web\\app\\vrat\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/vrat/[slug]/page.tsx`) statically generates the detail page for each Hindu fasting observance (vrat), rendering sections like significance, fasting rules, rituals (puja vidhi), prasad, benefits, mantra, and the vrat katha story, plus a booking CTA linking to `/ask-pandit` and `/today`. Its exports are the default async server component `VratDetail`, along with `generateStaticParams` and `generateMetadata`, which build per-slug SEO metadata including canonical URLs and OpenGraph tags under the hardcoded `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/vrats` via the `VRATS` array and the `vratSlugs()` and `getVrat()` helpers; there are no external service calls, only Next.js primitives (`Link`, `notFound`) and Tailwind styling with a custom saffron/surface palette. A private `jsonLd()` helper injects schema.org `BreadcrumbList` and `Article` structured data via a raw `<script>` tag, with a hardcoded `datePublished` of 2026-05-27. Full prerendering is enforced with `dynamicParams = false` and `revalidate = 86400`, so any slug not in `vratSlugs()` 404s at the routing layer, making the component's own `notFound()` call largely redundant. Page navigation derives prev/next from the item's index in `VRATS` (so ordering depends on array order), and the "related vrats" strip picks up to three other entries sharing the same `category`, with badge colors and labels mapped through the `catBadge`/`catLabel` records. One minor gotcha: meta descriptions are built by blindly truncating fields with `slice()`, which can cut words mid-sentence.

apps\\web\\app\\vrat\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router index page for the `/vrat` route on darshya.online, rendering a curated guide to ten major Hindu fasting observances (vrats) grouped by category. Its default export, the `VratIndex` server component, renders a header, four category sections (lunar, seasonal, family, weekly) defined in the local `sections` array, and cross-promotional CTAs linking to `/today` (panchang hub), `/ask-pandit` (pandit booking), and `/pujas`; it also exports Next.js `metadata` with canonical and OpenGraph tags and sets `revalidate = 86400` for daily ISR. Content comes entirely from the internal data module `../../lib/vrats`, specifically the `VRATS` array and the `vratsByCategory` selector, with `next/link` used for client navigation — there are no external services or runtime data fetching. SEO is a clear priority: the local `itemListJsonLd()` helper builds a schema.org ItemList of all vrat detail URLs injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and `BASE_URL` is hardcoded to `https://darshya.online` rather than read from environment config, which is a portability gotcha. Styling relies on Tailwind with a custom palette (saffron, surface, indigo, emerald, pink), and the `catColor` record maps each category key to card border/background classes — so adding a new category in `lib/vrats` requires updating `sections` and `catColor` here or cards will silently lose styling. Minor quirks include trimming parenthetical text from `v.frequency` for display and clamping `significance` to three lines with `line-clamp-3`.

apps\\web\\app\\vedic-yajnas\\[slug]\\pa.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router detail page for a single Vedic yajna, routed at `/vedic-yajnas/[slug]`, and exists to render a fully static, SEO-optimized article about one ritual from the catalog. Its default export, the async server component `VedicYajnaDetailPage`, resolves the awaited `slug` param via `getVedicYajna` and calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, then renders breadcrumb navigation, a header with category chip and Sanskrit name, stat cards (duration, priests required), and sections for purpose, deities invoked, mantra source, material offerings, modern status, and historical significance, plus prev/next links computed by index position in the `VEDIC_YAJNAS` array and a "jump to any yajna" link cloud. The exported `generateMetadata` builds per-page title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags, while `revalidate = 86400` sets 24-hour ISR caching. All content comes from the internal module `lib/vedic-yajnas` (`VEDIC_YAJNAS`, `getVedicYajna`, `CATEGORY_LABELS`, `CATEGORY_DESCRIPTIONS`, and the `YajnaModernStatus` type); the only external dependencies are `next`, `next/link`, and `next/navigation`, with no runtime data fetching. Notable details include local `STATUS_LABEL`/`STATUS_COLOR` maps that color-code the four modern-status values (actively-performed, rare, extinct, reconstructed), hardcoded `BASE_URL` of `https://darshya.online` used for canonical and JSON-LD URLs, and embedded schema.org `Article` plus `BreadcrumbList` structured data injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Purpose text is truncated to 160–220 characters for meta and JSON-LD descriptions, and the page explicitly disclaims providing procedural ritual instruction despite listing prescribed material offerings.

apps\\web\\app\\waitlist\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the `/waitlist` route of the Darshya web app (`apps/web`), a Next.js App Router server component that renders the early-access signup landing page. It exports a `metadata` object for SEO ("Early-access waitlist") and the default async `WaitlistPage` component, which renders a marketing hero pitching the first 1000 devotee spots and embeds the client-side `WaitlistForm` inside a styled card. Its only real dependencies are the `Metadata` type from `next` and the sibling `./WaitlistForm` component, to which it passes three props: `initialRef` (a referral code extracted from the awaited `searchParams` query string, per the Next.js 15 async-searchParams convention), plus two hardcoded constants, `TOP_CITIES` (20 Indian cities) and `DEITIES` (seven options including "Other"). Notable design choices include defensive handling of the `ref` param (coercing non-strings to an empty string), theming entirely through CSS custom properties like `--color-primary` and `--color-bg` with inline hex fallbacks rather than Tailwind color tokens, and a consent footnote about occasional emails. The page itself contains no data-fetching or submission logic — all signup behavior lives in `WaitlistForm`.

apps\\web\\app\\waitlist\\WaitlistForm.t.summary: WaitlistForm.tsx is a client-side React component ('use client') in the Next.js web app that renders the public waitlist signup form and handles its submission end to end. Its single default export, WaitlistForm, receives initialRef (a referral code baked into a hidden referredByCode field) plus cities and deities arrays that populate the city and preferred-deity dropdowns, and it manages submission state with useState and navigation with useRouter from next/navigation. On submit it builds a JSON payload from FormData — trimming strings, converting empty optional fields to undefined so they are omitted, reading the two opt-in checkboxes, and hardcoding source to 'web_waitlist_page' — then POSTs it to /api/v1/waitlist on the backend API. The API base URL comes from the NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL environment variable with a hardcoded fallback to https://api.darshya.online, which is worth noting since a missing env var silently points the build at production. On a successful response containing referralCode it redirects the browser to /waitlist/welcome?code=..., while server-provided error messages (json.error) or network failures are surfaced inline in an error banner. Notable details: the panchangOptIn checkbox defaults to checked (opt-out rather than opt-in), whatsappOptIn defaults off, and styling relies on CSS custom properties like --color-primary and --color-bg with literal hex fallbacks so the component renders sanely even outside the themed layout.

apps\\web\\app\\weddings\\packages\\page.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for `/weddings/packages`, a static marketing page that displays three fixed wedding service tiers — Basic (₹15,000), Premium (₹50,000), and Royal (₹2,00,000) — for the Darshya Vedic wedding platform. Its sole export is the default `PackagesPage` React server component, plus a static `metadata` export for SEO; package data lives in a hardcoded `PACKAGES` constant typed by a local `Package` interface, not fetched from any backend. The only dependencies are `next/link` for client-side navigation and the `next` `Metadata` type, with all styling done via Tailwind utility classes. Each tier card routes to `/weddings/inquiry?package=<tier>`, so the page acts as a pricing funnel into the inquiry flow, with the Premium tier visually flagged via the optional `popular` boolean. Notable gotchas: pricing and feature copy are fully hardcoded (any price change requires a code edit and redeploy), prices are preformatted display strings rather than numeric values, and the NRI surcharge is mentioned only in prose — there is no pricing logic or localization anywhere in this file.

apps\\web\\app\\waitlist\\welcome\\page..summary: This file is a Next.js App Router client page (`apps/web/app/waitlist/welcome/page.tsx`) that serves as the Darshya waitlist post-signup welcome screen: it reads a referral `code` from the URL, displays the user's rank, total signups, and referral count, and provides referral-link sharing tools. The default export `WaitlistWelcomePage` wraps the inner `WelcomeContent` component in a React `Suspense` boundary, which is required because `WelcomeContent` calls `useSearchParams` from `next/navigation`; a local `Stats` interface types the rank/total/referralCount payload.
