Data comes from `GET /api/v1/waitlist/stats?code=...` on the backend at `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online`), fetched with `cache: 'no-store'`, and the page also integrates with external share targets — WhatsApp via `wa.me`, Twitter/X intent, and the Facebook sharer — plus `navigator.clipboard` for copy-to-clipboard. A notable design decision is the polling strategy documented in the "Phase D P1 #2" comment: stats refresh on a 60-second `setInterval` (reduced from 10s) that is paused when the tab is hidden via a `visibilitychange` listener, with cleanup that clears the interval, removes the listener, and sets a `cancelled` flag to prevent state updates after unmount. Gotchas include an error state when the `code` query param is missing, a silently-swallowed clipboard failure fallback, and an SSR-safe `shareUrl` that falls back to `https://darshya.online` when `window` is unavailable. Styling relies on CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--font-display`, etc.) with hardcoded fallbacks rather than a component library.

apps\\web\\app\\weddings\\inquiry\\page..summary: This is a Next.js client-side page at `/weddings/inquiry` that renders the Darshya wedding inquiry form, letting prospective clients submit contact details, wedding date, package tier, guest count, budget, and a message, which it POSTs as JSON to the backend at `${apiBase()}/weddings/inquiry`. The default-exported `InquiryPage` provides the page shell and wraps the inner `InquiryForm` component in a `Suspense` boundary — a Next.js requirement because the form calls `useSearchParams` from `next/navigation` to read a `package` query param, which preselects the tier only if it matches the whitelist of basic, premium, or royal. A small `apiBase()` helper normalizes the `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` env var (defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online`), appending `/api/v1` if not already present. Internally it depends on React state and the shared `DateInput` component from `components/ui` for the optional wedding date field. Notable details: form state tracks a status of idle/sending/sent/error to drive the submit button, error banner, and a thank-you confirmation screen; before submission it strips empty optional fields (weddingDate, package, guests, budget, message) from the payload so only provided values reach the API; and guests/budget are captured as strings with no numeric coercion before sending.

apps\\web\\app\\waitlist\\confirm\\page..summary: This Next.js server page is the landing target for waitlist email-confirmation links: it exists to confirm a user's pending waitlist row the moment they click the link, without rendering any client UI. Its single export, the async server component `WaitlistConfirmPage`, reads the `code` query param (Next.js's promise-based `searchParams`), calls the backend at `${NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL}/api/v1/waitlist/confirm?code=...` — defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online` — and expects the API to flip the row to CONFIRMED and respond with a 302 to `/waitlist/welcome` carrying the referralCode. The only dependency is `redirect` from `next/navigation`; it talks to the external waitlist API but otherwise has no internal module imports. Key design choices are doing the confirmation entirely server-side so the API call fires immediately on link click with no UI flash, using `redirect: 'manual'` and `cache: 'no-store'` on the fetch so the 302 is captured rather than followed or cached, and failing safe to `/waitlist` whenever the code is missing or the request errors. One notable gotcha: because Next's `redirect()` works by throwing a special NEXT_REDIRECT error, calling it inside the try block means the catch-all swallows it, so the success path that should send users to the API-supplied welcome URL instead falls through to the plain `/waitlist` fallback.

apps\\web\\app\\weddings\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router landing page for Darshya's Vedic Hindu wedding planning service, served at the `/weddings` route. It exports a `metadata` object (Next.js `Metadata` type) carrying SEO title, description, and OpenGraph tags, plus the default `WeddingsPage` component, a pure server-rendered marketing page built only on `next/link` and Tailwind classes with no data fetching or client interactivity. A `jsonLd` constant embeds schema.org `Service` structured data via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, advertising three offers — Basic (₹15,000, pandit only), Premium (₹50,000, pandit + samagri + muhurat), and Royal (₹2,00,000, 4-day ceremony) — with the provider Organization set to darshya.online and areaServed India. All page content (feature cards, package tiers, testimonials, and a 10-step wedding planner list) is hardcoded inline rather than pulled from a CMS or API, so any copy change requires a code edit. The page funnels users to sibling routes `/weddings/muhurat`, `/weddings/packages`, and `/weddings/inquiry`, and links to a static printable asset at `/weddings/planner.pdf`. Visually it commits to an amber/stone palette with serif headings and a `min-h-[100dvh]` gradient layout, consistent with a static, SEO-first acquisition page.

apps\\web\\app\\weddings\\muhurat\\page..summary: This file is the client-side Next.js page (`MuhuratPage`, default export) for the "Find your muhurat" feature, which collects bride and groom birth details plus a wedding date window and displays ranked auspicious marriage dates computed by classical Vedic rules. It POSTs the form to the backend endpoint `/weddings/muhurat`, resolved through the local `apiBase()` helper, which reads `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`, falls back to `https://api.darshya.online`, and ensures an `/api/v1` suffix. The response is typed via the local `MuhuratResponse` and `Candidate` interfaces: each candidate carries a date, nakshatra, rashi, tithi, an `abhijitMuhurat` time window, a score out of 100, and human-readable `reasons` and `warnings`, while the top-level response includes computed nakshatras and a `mangalikFlag` that triggers a parihara puja recommendation when either partner is Mangalik. A notable design choice is that the bride/groom nakshatra selects are optional overrides — empty values are deleted from the request body so the server computes them from date and time of birth (which default to 06:30 and 07:00 respectively, with location defaulting to Delhi). The page depends only on React state, Next's `Link`, and the shared internal `DateInput` component from `components/ui/DateInput`; there is no auth or state-management layer. Results render as a "Top 10 muhurats" list formatted with the `en-IN` locale (dates parsed as UTC midnight), followed by a conversion CTA linking to `/weddings/inquiry` for booking a wedding planner.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\instructors\\[.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`/wellness/instructors/[id]`) that renders a statically generated instructor detail page for the wellness section, showing the instructor's profile, bio, certifications, available time slots, reviews, and tiered session pricing. It embeds a hardcoded `instructors` record (IDs `inst-001` through `inst-008`, spanning yoga, meditation, and vipassana categories) that the comment notes "mirrors API," so all content is baked in at build time rather than fetched. Its key exports are `generateStaticParams` (which pre-renders one page per instructor ID), `generateMetadata` (building SEO title/description from the instructor's name, specialties, and bio), and the default async `InstructorDetailPage` server component. Dependencies include `next/link` and the `Metadata` type from Next.js, `lucide-react` icons (Star, Award, Clock, Globe, ArrowLeft), the shared `ScrollReveal` wrapper that drives scroll animations via `data-reveal` attributes, and the co-located `WellnessEnrolButton` client component used for the "Book Consultation" and per-plan "Book Now" calls to action. Notable decisions: pricing tiers are derived from `pricePerSession` (5-pack at 4.5× and 10-pack at 8×, marketed as 10% and 20% savings) with the 5-pack visually highlighted; unknown IDs render an inline "Instructor not found" UI with a back link instead of calling Next's `notFound()`; and breadcrumbs route back to a category-specific page (`/wellness/yoga`, `/wellness/meditation`, or `/wellness/vipassana`). Gotchas include the duplication of instructor data between this page and the API (they can drift apart), the available-slot buttons being purely presentational with no booking behavior, and the use of the Next 15 convention where `params` is a Promise that must be awaited. Theming is handled entirely through CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--color-surface)`.

`WellnessEnrolButton.tsx` is a client component in the Next.js web app (`apps/web`) that renders the enrol CTA on the `/wellness/instructors/[id]` detail page; rather than charging money, it opens an inline modal that captures the user's email, optional name, and phone and posts them as a lead to `${API_BASE_URL}/waitlist`. The default-exported `WellnessEnrolButton` accepts `instructorId`, `instructorName`, a `plan` union (`consultation | single | pack5 | pack10`), optional `price`, a `variant` style flag, and a `label`, with an internal `PLAN_LABEL` map for human-readable plan names. It depends on `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, the `ArrowRight` icon from `lucide-react`, and a fire-and-forget dynamic import of `lib/posthog` to capture a `wellness_enrol_intent` analytics event after a successful submission. The header comment frames this as an intentional "honest fallback": the real Razorpay checkout lives in `wellness-sessions.ts` but needs a per-session database row that the static instructor catalog lacks, so enrolment is routed through lead capture until a session picker ships in MVP2. Every lead carries a deterministic `source` tag of the form `wellness-enrol-{instructorId}-{plan}` for attribution, and `whatsappOptIn` is implicitly set to true whenever a phone number is provided — a consent assumption worth flagging. Validation is minimal (just checking the email contains `@`), submission errors surface the API's `message` field, and the modal is hand-rolled with a fixed overlay and CSS-variable theming rather than a shared dialog component. A small footer disclaimer tells users that live Razorpay checkout activates after instructor verification and that no charge occurs today.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\meditation\\pa.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page component (`apps/web/app/wellness/meditation/page.tsx`) that renders a static marketing and discovery page for the wellness app's meditation vertical. It exports a `metadata` object for SEO (title and description) and a default `MeditationPage` server component composed of hardcoded content sections: a hero, five meditation style cards (`meditationTypes`), featured teacher profiles (`instructors`), a non-functional audio player mockup, a 21-day challenge roadmap (`challengeDays`), bookable live sessions (`upcomingSessions`), and a closing CTA. Its only internal dependency is the `ScrollReveal` wrapper component, which animates children via `data-reveal` and `data-delay` attributes scattered throughout the markup; otherwise it relies on `next/link` for navigation, `next`'s `Metadata` type, and `lucide-react` for icons. All data is inline mock content — instructor cards link to `/wellness/instructors/[id]` pages using fixed IDs like `inst-003`, and the CTAs cross-link sibling pages `/wellness/yoga` and `/wellness/vipassana`. Notable design choices include heavy use of CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, etc.) mixed with Tailwind utilities for theming, pricing displayed in rupees, and a purely presentational player whose play/skip buttons have no handlers, signaling this page is a visual placeholder pending real session and booking data.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the wellness landing page for the Darshya web app, a Next.js App Router route at `/wellness` that showcases yoga, meditation, and Vipassana offerings and funnels visitors toward category pages, instructor profiles, and bookings. Its only exports are the Next.js `metadata` object (SEO title/description) and the default `WellnessPage` React component, which renders a hero, three practice category cards, featured instructors, upcoming live sessions, a benefits grid, a CTA, and an `ApprovedProvidersStrip` (imported from `../../components/ApprovedProvidersStrip`) configured with `type="wellness"`. The whole page is wrapped in the internal `ScrollReveal` component, which drives the scroll-triggered animations declared via `data-reveal` and `data-delay` attributes throughout the markup. External dependencies are limited to `next/link` for navigation and `lucide-react` icons (Sun, Wind, Eye, Heart, Calendar, etc.); notably, there is no data fetching — `categories`, `featuredInstructors`, `upcomingSessions`, and `benefits` are hardcoded module-level constants, so instructor IDs like `inst-001` and session dates are static mock content. Styling relies entirely on CSS custom properties (`var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-surface)`, etc.) rather than a theme utility, and a small helper `getCategoryBadgeColor` maps each practice category to badge colors. One behavioral gotcha: session cards flag scarcity with red styling only when `spotsLeft <= 5`, and instructor avatars are derived from name initials rather than images.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\vipassana\\cen.summary: This Next.js App Router page renders the Vipassana center directory at `/wellness/vipassana/centers`, listing meditation centers grouped by region as an SEO-optimized index for the darshya.online site. Its default export, the `VipassanaCentersIndexPage` server component, is accompanied by a static `metadata` export (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph) and `revalidate = 86400`, meaning the page is statically rendered and refreshed at most once per day via ISR. All content comes from the internal data module `lib/vipassana-centers`, which supplies the `VIPASSANA_CENTERS` array plus the `LINEAGE_LABEL` and `REGION_LABEL` lookup maps; the only external dependencies are Next.js primitives (`Metadata`, `Link`), with no runtime service calls. Centers are grouped client-side into a fixed `REGION_KEYS` ordering (india, usa-canada, uk-europe, asia-pacific), with empty regions filtered out, and each card links to a detail route at `/wellness/vipassana/centers/{slug}` while displaying lineage badges colored via the `LINEAGE_ACCENT` map, optional capacity, and an `isFlagshipCenter` marker. For search visibility the page injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks—an `ItemList` enumerating every center URL and a `BreadcrumbList`—and hardcodes `BASE_URL` as `https://darshya.online` for canonical and structured-data links. A notable positioning constraint is stated directly in the copy: the site is a discovery and preparation resource, not a booking middleman, so applications are deferred to external dhamma.org subdomains and partner sites. The page also hardcodes editorial recommendations for specific flagship centers (Dhamma Giri, Dhamma Pattana, Dhamma Sota, Dhamma Dhara, Dhamma Dīpa) and cross-links to the `/wellness/vipassana/learn` page as an onboarding funnel.

This file is the Next.js App Router page that renders the detail view for a single Vipassana meditation center at the dynamic route `/wellness/vipassana/centers/[slug]`, fully statically generated via `generateStaticParams` (sourced from `centerSlugs()`) with `dynamicParams = false` so unknown slugs 404 and ISR revalidating daily (`revalidate = 86400`). Its exports are `generateStaticParams`, `generateMetadata` (which builds canonical and OpenGraph tags against the hardcoded `BASE_URL` of https://darshya.online), and the default async server component `VipassanaCenterDetailPage`, which resolves the center with `getCenter(slug)` and calls `notFound()` on misses. All data comes from the internal `lib/vipassana-centers` module (`VIPASSANA_CENTERS`, `getCenter`, `centerSlugs`, plus the `LINEAGE_LABEL` and `REGION_LABEL` lookup maps); there is no database or external API call at runtime. The page emits three schema.org JSON-LD blocks (BreadcrumbList, Place, Article) for SEO, and renders a breadcrumb trail, a stats grid (founded year, capacity, tradition, languages), travel info (nearest airport/railway, climate, best season), first-timer guidance, up to three related centers in the same region, and prev/next navigation computed by array index in `VIPASSANA_CENTERS`. A notable product constraint baked into the UI: Darshya deliberately does not handle bookings — the apply section links out to each center's `bookingUrl` and `officialUrl` with `target="_blank"`, emphasizing that courses are donation-based and applications are reviewed by the centers themselves.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\vipassana\\pag.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router landing page for the Vipassana meditation hub at `/wellness/vipassana`, serving as a content-rich entry point that explains the S.N. Goenka 10-day retreat tradition and funnels visitors toward center discovery. Its only exports are the `metadata` object (SEO title and description) and the default `VipassanaPage` React component, which renders a hero, an educational "What is Vipassana" section with a three-phase course timeline, a grid of featured retreat centers, a hardcoded `preparationGuide` array, a `faqs` accordion, and a closing CTA. Center data comes from the internal `lib/vipassana-centers` module via `FLAGSHIP_CENTERS` (rendered as the six featured cards) and `VIPASSANA_CENTERS` (used only for the total directory count), while animations rely on the internal `ScrollReveal` wrapper component reading `data-reveal`/`data-delay` attributes, and icons come from `lucide-react`. A key design stance is explicit in the copy: Darshya is a discovery resource, not a booking middleman, so each center card links its `bookingUrl` externally to dhamma.org while internal `next/link` routes point to `/wellness/vipassana/centers`, per-center detail pages at `centers/${c.slug}`, and a `/wellness/vipassana/learn` guide. Notable implementation details include purely static, in-file content (no data fetching), client-side truncation of center summaries at 180 characters, FAQ accordions built from native `<details>`/`<summary>` elements rather than a JS library, reveal delays capped at 4 via `Math.min(i + 1, 4)`, and theming done entirely through CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--color-surface)`.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\vipassana\\lea.summary: This file is a static Next.js App Router page (apps/web/app/wellness/vipassana/learn/page.tsx) that renders Darshya's long-form editorial guide to the 10-day Vipassana meditation course in the S.N. Goenka tradition — covering the day-by-day journey, daily schedule, code of discipline, food rules, course variations, FAQs, and post-course practice. Its exports are the default `VipassanaLearnPage` server component, a `metadata` object (canonical URL, OpenGraph article tags under `BASE_URL` https://darshya.online), and `revalidate = 86400`, which puts the page on daily ISR. The only dependencies are `next/metadata` and `next/link`; there is no data fetching, no client-side state, and no internal module imports — all copy is hardcoded inline, including the `SECTIONS` array that drives the anchor-linked table of contents. SEO is a clear priority: the component injects schema.org `BreadcrumbList` and `Article` JSON-LD via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and pairs it with an on-page breadcrumb nav. Notable design points: all content is presentational markup styled with Tailwind plus custom theme tokens (`saffron-*`, amber/emerald section accents), sections use `scroll-mt-20` so anchor jumps clear the header, and the closing CTA routes users to internal routes `/wellness/vipassana/centers` and `/wellness/vipassana` plus the external dhamma.org. The main gotcha is that every content change requires editing this file and redeploying, since nothing is sourced from a CMS or data layer.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\earning.summary: This file defines the Next.js App Router page for the `/wellness-portal/earnings` route in the web app, presenting wellness practitioners with a view of their own earnings. Its sole export is the default `WellnessEarningsPage` component, a thin client-side wrapper that renders the shared `CommissionsPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/CommissionsPanel`. The panel is configured with `mode="me"`, which scopes the displayed data to the currently authenticated user rather than an administrative or platform-wide view, along with a title of "Earnings" and copy clarifying that figures reflect net earnings after platform commission on completed sessions. The file contains no data-fetching or business logic of its own — all querying, calculations, and UI behavior live inside `CommissionsPanel`, making this page a pure composition/routing entry point. The `'use client'` directive is required because the underlying panel presumably relies on React state and effects, so the page opts into client rendering at the route boundary. One gotcha: the import uses a relative path (`../../../components/CommissionsPanel`) rather than a path alias, so moving the page deeper in the route tree would silently break the import resolution.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness\\yoga\\page.tsx.summary: This file is a Next.js App Router page (`YogaPage`, default export) that renders the static marketing landing page for the yoga vertical of a wellness app at `/wellness/yoga`, covering five sections: a hero with anchor CTAs, yoga style cards (`yogaTypes`), instructor profiles (`instructors`), a morning/evening class schedule (`schedule`), a recorded `videoLibrary` grid, and a closing CTA. It exports a Next.js `metadata` object for SEO and relies on three things: `next/link` for navigation, `lucide-react` icons (Sun, Flame, Moon, Play, etc.), and the internal `ScrollReveal` wrapper from `components/ScrollReveal`, which animates sections via `data-reveal`/`data-delay` attributes on plain elements. A key design fact is that every piece of content — styles, six instructors, eight class slots, six videos — is hardcoded as in-module constant arrays rather than fetched from any API or database, so the page is fully static with no data layer. Instructor cards link to `/wellness/instructors/${inst.id}` using string IDs like `inst-001`, meaning those identifiers must stay in sync with the instructor detail route, while the "Book" buttons in the schedule and the video thumbnails are presentational only (no handlers, no playback). Theming is done entirely through CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, etc.) with inline styles, and one small behavioral detail is that schedule cards turn the "spots left" label red (`#b91c1c`) when `spots <= 5` to signal scarcity.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\message.summary: This file defines the messages page for the wellness portal section of the Next.js web app, rendering at the `/wellness-portal/messages` route. Its single default export, `WellnessMessagesPage`, is a client component that renders a page header ("Student Messages") and embeds the shared `Inbox` component imported from `components/Inbox`, passing `role="provider"` so the inbox operates in the practitioner-facing mode rather than a student-facing one. The page is marked `'use client'`, meaning it ships as a client-side React component, though all real messaging behavior—chat threads, live sessions, data fetching—lives inside `Inbox`, making this file a thin routing/layout wrapper. The layout constrains content width with a `max-w-5xl` container and uses Tailwind utility classes for typography, consistent with the app's utility-first styling approach. The key design decision is the role-based `Inbox` reuse: the same component presumably serves multiple audiences, with the `role` prop acting as the behavioral switch, so any provider-specific messaging logic should be traced there rather than in this page.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\layout..summary: This file defines the root layout for the instructor-facing wellness portal in the Next.js web app, providing the persistent chrome — dark themed sidebar, top header, and content area — that wraps every page under `/wellness-portal`. The default export `WellnessRootLayout` wraps the inner `WellnessPortalLayout` component in `AuthGuard` with `allowedRoles={['wellness_instructor']}`, so the entire route tree is gated to wellness instructors before any page content renders. Navigation is driven by a static `sidebarLinks` array mapping routes (Dashboard, Messages, Sessions, Students, Earnings, Subscription, Profile) to `lucide-react` icons, with active-state highlighting computed by `isActive`, which requires an exact match for the portal root but uses `pathname.startsWith` for subroutes. It depends on the internal `AuthGuard` component and the `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context`, which supplies the current user's `fullName` for the sidebar identity block and the `signOut` handler, plus `next/navigation`'s `usePathname` for route awareness. Because it relies on hooks and local `sidebarOpen` state, the whole module is marked `'use client'`, meaning everything under the wellness portal renders client-side. The sidebar is responsive: on mobile it slides in as a fixed overlay with a dismissible backdrop, while at the `lg` breakpoint it becomes a sticky column, and its background is hardcoded to `#2a2520` with emerald accent styling rather than pulled from a theme token. A "Back to Main Site" link provides an escape hatch to the public homepage, and the layout assumes the auth context has already resolved by the time `AuthGuard` lets children through, so `user` may still be null-safe-fallback-rendered as "Instructor".

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\subscri.summary: This file is the Next.js client-side route page for the wellness portal's subscription section, living at the app route `wellness-portal/subscription`. Its sole default export, `WellnessSubscriptionPage`, is a thin wrapper that renders the shared `SubscriptionPanel` component imported from `apps/web/components/SubscriptionPanel`, passing the fixed role `"wellness_instructor"` and a description string highlighting group session capacity, lower commission, and live class hosting. The page contains no state, data fetching, or business logic of its own — all subscription behavior (plan selection, billing, payments) is delegated to `SubscriptionPanel`, which presumably branches on the `role` prop. The `'use client'` directive marks it as a client component, required because the underlying panel is interactive. The design follows a role-parameterized reuse pattern where each portal (wellness, and presumably others) mounts the same panel with role-specific copy, so any changes to subscription flows should be made in `SubscriptionPanel` rather than here.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\page.ts.summary: This file is the default-export `WellnessDashboard` page component for the `/wellness-portal` route of the Next.js web app, serving as the landing overview for wellness instructors (welcome header, stats, upcoming sessions list, and quick-action links to `/wellness-portal/sessions` and `/wellness-portal/students`). It fetches two read-only resources with `@tanstack/react-query`'s `useQuery` — the dashboard payload typed as `ApiWellnessDashboard` from `${API_BASE_URL}/wellness-portal/dashboard` and KYC status from `${API_BASE_URL}/provider-kyc` — sending the bearer token from `useAuth` (auth-context) and building the URL from `API_BASE_URL` in `lib/api-config`. Rendered building blocks are the internal components `MyProviderProfileCard`, `EarningsCard`, and `KycStatusBadge`, plus `lucide-react` icons and `next/link`, with local helpers `formatCurrency` (INR), `formatTime`, and `formatDate`. A `useMemo` derives `kycState`/`kycReason` from the KYC query (defaulting to `'unsubmitted'` until resolution), replacing an older imperative `useEffect`/`setState` chain — comments reference migration ticket P1-17 and note that queries use `retry: false` and stay in an error/no-data state on failure so the UI falls back to zero-valued stats and an empty-sessions placeholder. One notable detail: an optional `instructorShare`/`platformRate` split note renders beneath the earnings card, defaulting the platform cut to 20% when absent.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\student.summary: This file is the Students page of the wellness portal (a Next.js client component exported as `WellnessStudentsPage`), letting a wellness instructor view devotees who have enrolled in their sessions. It fetches data via `getMyStudents` from `lib/wellness-api`, passing the access token obtained from `useAuth` in `lib/auth-context`, and renders each `WellnessStudent` as a card showing name, an Attended/Enrolled badge derived from `hasAttended`, contact links, the `lastSession` title, enrollment date (formatted by the local `formatDate` helper using the `en-IN` locale), and total `sessionCount`. The UI supports client-side text search over name and email, an all/attended/enrolled filter toggle, a manual refresh button, a retryable error banner, skeleton placeholders during initial load, and an empty-state message, with all icons coming from `lucide-react`. Notable constraints: filtering and search happen entirely in memory with no pagination, so the page depends on the API returning the full roster; loading is silently skipped when no token exists; phone links strip whitespace for the `tel:` href; and the render assumes `lastSession` is always populated, so a student without any session record could cause a runtime error.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\profile.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/wellness-portal/profile/page.tsx`) is the wellness portal's instructor profile editor, letting instructors view and update their public-facing details: display name, bio, years of experience, per-session price in INR, certifications, and specialties. The default export `WellnessProfilePage` wraps the internal `Content` component in `AuthGuard` restricted to the `wellness_instructor` and `admin` roles, while a small `Card` helper component renders each editable section; the `WellnessProfile` interface and the hardcoded `ALL_CERTIFICATIONS` and `ALL_SPECIALTIES` lists define the data shape and the fixed taxonomies instructors pick from via toggle pills rather than free text. It depends on `useAuth` from `lib/auth-context` for the session access token, `AuthGuard` for role gating, `API_BASE_URL` from `lib/api-config`, and lucide-react icons, and it talks to two backend endpoints: the profile is loaded from GET `/wellness-portal/dashboard` (notably, there is no dedicated profile GET) and saved via PATCH to `/wellness-portal/profile`. Notable quirks: the `rating` and `approved` fields are display-only — instructors can see their star rating and approval status but cannot edit them, and they are excluded from the PATCH body. Client-side validation only requires a non-empty display name, and an empty bio is sent as `undefined` so it is omitted from the request. Load errors are swallowed silently with a fallback that pre-fills `displayName` from `user.fullName`, whereas save errors surface in an inline alert; the "Saved!" confirmation auto-dismisses after three seconds and is reset by any subsequent field edit via `updateField`.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\companion\\[id]\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`app/yatra/companion/[id]/page.tsx`) renders the detail view for a single travel companion in the yatra (pilgrimage) booking section of the web app, fully statically generated at build time. It exports `generateStaticParams`, which pre-renders one page per entry in the `companions` array, `generateMetadata` for per-companion SEO titles/descriptions, and the default async server component `CompanionDetailPage`, which calls `notFound()` for unknown ids. All data comes from the internal `lib/yatra-data` module (`companions`, `getCompanionById`, `formatINR`) — there is no backend or database call — while UI is built with `lucide-react` icons, the shared `ScrollReveal` wrapper, and inline styles driven by CSS custom property design tokens. The page shows the companion's profile header (avatar initials, rating stars, Aadhaar/background/medical verification badges), bio, languages, specializations, past yatras, reviews, and tiered pricing. Notably, the 30-day availability calendar is synthetic: availability is derived deterministically from the companion's `availability` status using modulo patterns on the day index, not real booking data, so it will misrepresent actual capacity. Pricing tiers are hardcoded (5% off for 6–10 day yatras, 10% off for 11+ days), and both booking CTAs simply route back to `/yatra` (with a hardcoded `tel:+919255109400` advisor link), indicating the actual reservation flow lives elsewhere or is not yet implemented.

apps\\web\\app\\wellness-portal\\session.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/wellness-portal/sessions/page.tsx`) is the wellness portal's session management screen, letting instructors create, edit, cancel/reactivate, delete, and attach live-class room links to their wellness sessions (yoga, meditation, vipassana, pranayama). The default export `WellnessSessionsPage` wraps `WellnessSessionsPageContent` in `AuthGuard` restricted to the `wellness_instructor` and `admin` roles, and the content component drives all state through the token from `useAuth` (lib/auth-context) and the `wellness-api` client module — specifically `listMySessions`, `createWellnessSession`, `updateWellnessSession`, `deleteWellnessSession`, and `setWellnessSessionRoom`, plus the `WellnessSession`, `WellnessSessionType`, and `WellnessSessionStatus` types. UI dependencies are limited to `lucide-react` icons, the shared `AuthGuard`, and `DateTimeInput` from components/ui/DateInput; live classes rely on Jitsi, with `handleSaveRoom` auto-generating a `https://meet.jit.si/darshya-wellness-<id>` URL when the instructor leaves the room field blank. Notably, the room-URL editor was added because the backend `/sessions/:id/room` endpoint previously had no UI, and the code reads `roomUrl` via a type cast, hinting the field is missing from the `WellnessSession` type. Delete and status-toggle operations use optimistic updates with rollback on API failure, and the toggle only cycles SCHEDULED ↔ CANCELLED (COMPLETED sessions are locked). A helper `toLocalInput` converts UTC ISO timestamps to `datetime-local` format explicitly to avoid adding date-fns, and formatting helpers enforce Indian conventions (INR currency, en-IN dates). Form handling is plain controlled-component state with `parseInt`/`parseFloat` fallbacks, so validation is minimal beyond HTML required/min/max attributes.

apps\\web\\app\\why-darshya\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page for `/why-darshya`, a static marketing page that pitches the Darshya devotional app against competitors Sri Mandir, Utsav, AstroSage, and AppsForBharat. Its only exports are the `metadata` object (SEO title, description, canonical URL, and OpenGraph tags pointing at `https://darshya.online`), a `revalidate = 86400` constant enabling daily ISR, and the default `WhyDarshya` React component. All content is hard-coded in-module: the `ROWS` array (typed by the local `Row` interface) drives a 14-row feature comparison table covering video proof, NRI pricing, 80G receipts, gaushala seva, and more, while `PILLARS` lists four brand values like "Zero VC pressure" and "NRI is a first-class customer." Two small helpers support rendering: `comparisonJsonLd()` builds a schema.org WebPage payload injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and `cellStyle()` maps the ✓/~/✗ glyph prefixes to Tailwind text colors. Dependencies are minimal — just `next` types and `next/link` for CTAs to `/pujas` and `/faqs` — with no data fetching, CMS, or shared components. Notable choices include the deliberately candid "Where competitors lead" section conceding ground to rivals (a trust-building marketing tactic), a horizontally scrollable table with a sticky first column for mobile, and a legend dated "May 2026" with a corrections mailto, meaning all comparison claims are baked into source and require a redeploy to update.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\book\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js client page for the `/yatra/book` route, implementing a five-step booking wizard (Trip, Package, Add-ons, Travelers, Review) for pilgrimage packages. Its default export wraps the main `BookYatraInner` component in `Suspense` (required because it reads `slug` and `tier` via `useSearchParams`), and it defines the `Traveler` and `BookingData` types plus small presentational helpers like `AddOnRow` and `Row`. It builds on internal modules `lib/yatra-data` (`getYatraBySlug`, `formatINR`) and the `components/ui/DateInput` component, and talks to an external backend by POSTing the final payload to `${NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL}/api/v1/yatra-inquiry/` (defaulting to `https://api.darshya.online`), from which it expects a `referenceId`. Despite a "Review & pay" step, no payment is actually collected — the flow only submits an inquiry and promises an invoice by email within 24 hours, with a failure fallback directing users to yatra@darshya.online. Notable design choices include persisting the in-progress draft to localStorage under `yatra-booking-{slug}` and appending submitted inquiries to a `yatra-inquiries` localStorage list (presumably read by `/profile/yatra-bookings`), so booking history is entirely client-side. Pricing is computed client-side in `priceBreakdown` with hardcoded add-on rates (helicopter 8000/person, puja 2100, companion 3500/day, insurance 500/person), a 5% GST, and a fixed INR→USD conversion of 83, all of which could drift from server-side pricing. Other gotchas: the travelers array is auto-synced to `travelersCount` via an effect (capped at 12), step gating is handled by the `canContinue` IIFE with per-step validation, and the helicopter add-on only renders when `yatra.helicopterAvailable` is true.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\companion\\page.t.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`CompanionListingPage` at `apps/web/app/yatra/companion/page.tsx`) renders the `/yatra/companion` marketing and listing route where users browse verified travel companions who assist elderly pilgrims on sacred journeys, and it exports a `metadata` object for SEO. The page pulls its entire companion roster from the internal `companions` array in `lib/yatra-data` and formats prices with the sibling `formatINR` helper, so there is no client-side fetching or backend call — it behaves as a static server component. Each companion card renders avatar initials, an availability pill (available/limited/busy with color-mixed badges), a five-star rating from `c.rating`, languages, specializations, verification badges for `c.verified.aadhaar`, `c.verified.background`, and `c.verified.medical`, and a per-day price, with a `next/link` CTA routing to the detail page at `/yatra/companion/${c.id}`. The layout is a sequence of hardcoded content sections — hero, three-step "how it works," the companion grid, trust guarantees, an upfront-payment explainer ("companion is paid upfront by Darshya"), a FAQ built on native `details`/`summary` elements, and a final CTA with a `tel:` link to an advisor. Animation is handled declaratively by wrapping everything in the internal `ScrollReveal` component and sprinkling `data-reveal`/`data-delay` attributes rather than using per-component animation logic. Styling mixes Tailwind utility classes with inline styles driven by CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, etc.), meaning theming depends entirely on those design tokens being defined upstream. Gotchas: the heading hardcodes "8 verified travel companions" so it will drift from the actual `companions.length` if the data changes, the phone number `+919255109400` and the ₹2,800 starting price are hardcoded literals, and all icons come from `lucide-react`.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\[slug]\\error.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js route-segment error boundary for the `/yatra/[slug]` pilgrimage-package detail page, catching render errors so a single broken page doesn't crash the whole app. Its default export, the client component `YatraDetailError`, receives the thrown `error` (with optional `digest`) and a `reset` callback, reports the exception to Sentry via `captureBrowserException` from `lib/sentry` inside a `useEffect` keyed on the error, and renders an inline-styled fallback UI with a "Try again" button that calls `reset()` to re-render the segment plus a link back to the `/yatra` listing. The only notable dependencies are React and the internal `lib/sentry` wrapper; no external UI library is used, with all styling done via inline styles in the site's copper/neutral palette. Design notes: the `'use client'` directive is required since error boundaries must be client components, the error digest is surfaced in monospace for support correlation, and the header comment marks this as task P0-9 and points to `app/temples/[slug]/error.tsx` as the reference implementation it mirrors.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\destinations\\pag.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router listing page for pilgrimage destinations at `/yatra/destinations`, rendering a hero banner plus a responsive card grid of India's top yatra sites. Its default export, the async server component `YatraDestinationsPage`, maps over the static `yatraDestinations` data array from `lib/yatra-destinations` and renders one linked card per destination, showing hero image, name, state, duration, region, a two-line `shortDescription`, and a starting price formatted via `formatINRPrice`. It also exports a static `metadata` object with SEO title, description, canonical URL (`https://darshya.online/yatra/destinations`), and OpenGraph fields targeting the Darshya brand. Copy is internationalized through `getTranslations` from `lib/t`, using the `yatra` namespace for labels like `destinationsTitle` and `viewDetails` (the `common` namespace is fetched as `tCommon` but never used — a minor dead-code gotcha). External dependencies are limited to `next/link` for navigation to `/yatra/destinations/[slug]` detail pages and `lucide-react` icons (Mountain, Calendar, MapPin, ArrowRight); there is no backend or data-fetching call since destinations come from a hardcoded module. Styling relies entirely on CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--color-primary`, `--font-display`, etc.) with inline styles, plus Tailwind utility classes for layout, and card images use native `img` tags with `loading="lazy"` rather than `next/image`. Because the page is a pure server component over static data, it prerenders cheaply, but any new destination requires editing `lib/yatra-destinations` rather than a CMS.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\destinations\\[sl.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router detail page for individual pilgrimage destinations in the Darshya yatra section, statically generating one page per slug returned by `destinationSlugs()` from the internal `lib/yatra-destinations` module. Its `generateStaticParams` enables full static generation, while `generateMetadata` produces SEO metadata (canonical URL, OpenGraph, Twitter card) pointing at darshya.online, and the default `YatraDestinationDetailPage` server component calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs and injects a schema.org `TouristAttraction` JSON-LD block. The page renders a hero image, descriptive sections (best time to visit, how to reach, what to expect) sourced from `getDestinationBySlug`, and a monetization sidebar listing affiliate partners defined in `PARTNER_LABELS` (MakeMyTrip, Goibibo, IRCTC Tourism, keyed by the `AffiliatePartner` type). Affiliate clicks route through the tracked redirect endpoint `/api/v1/affiliate/click` with `rel="nofollow sponsored noopener"` and an explicit commission disclosure, marking this sidebar as the revenue mechanism. Dependencies are minimal: `lucide-react` icons, `next/link` and `next/navigation`, plus formatting helper `formatINRPrice`. Notable details include the Next.js 15-style `params: Promise` signature, use of a plain `` tag rather than `next/image`, CSS custom properties (`--color-bg`, `--font-display`) for theming, and a `hasFullContent` flag that shows a "coming soon" placeholder for destinations lacking complete itineraries.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Yatra hub page (`YatraHubPage`, the default export) for the Next.js web app — a client-rendered landing and browse experience for "Dharmic Yatra" pilgrimage packages, with a hero section, trust badges, a filterable card grid of yatras, a travel-companion promotional section, and a custom-trip CTA linking to `/yatra/plan` and `/yatra/companion`. It pulls all content from the internal `lib/yatra-data` module (`yatras`, `formatINR`, `durationBuckets`, `budgetBuckets`, `regionOptions`, and the `YatraRegion` type) and wraps everything in the shared `ScrollReveal` component, using `data-reveal` attributes for scroll animations; icons come from `lucide-react` and navigation from `next/link`. Filtering is done entirely client-side via `useState` and `useMemo`, matching each yatra's region, duration bucket, and starting price. A notable gotcha: the budget filter hardcodes price thresholds (₹40,000 and ₹1,00,000) inline instead of delegating to `budgetBuckets` the way duration filtering uses `durationBuckets`, so the two sources could drift apart. The internal `HeroBento` component hardcodes lookups for the slugs `char-dham`, `amarnath`, and `tirupati-south` and silently renders nothing if any is missing from the dataset. Styling relies on CSS custom properties (`var(--color-primary)`, `var(--color-surface)`, etc.) rather than a utility framework, and images use plain `` tags with lazy loading rather than `next/image`.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\[slug]\\book\\pag.summary: This Next.js App Router page exists purely as an SEO-friendly per-package booking entry point: given a yatra slug like `char-dham` or `shirdi-sai`, it emits package-specific metadata and then immediately redirects the user into the canonical multi-step booking flow at `/yatra/book?slug=...`. The default-exported `PerPackageBookPage` server component awaits the route params, looks the slug up via `getYatraBySlug` from the internal `lib/yatra-data` module, calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs, and otherwise issues a `redirect()` (both from `next/navigation`). The exported `generateMetadata` function builds the `<title>`, a marketing-flavored description interpolating `yatra.durationDays` and a rupee price formatted with the `en-IN` locale, and a self-referencing canonical URL. It also exports `revalidate = 86400`, so the route is statically rendered and revalidated daily via ISR. Notably, the file deliberately contains no booking UI of its own — the comment ties it to success criterion R-Q2-P-003, which requires five per-package routes (char-dham, vaishno-devi, tirupati-south, ayodhya-kashi, shirdi-sai) to resolve end-to-end into the shared flow. Razorpay is mentioned only as checkout copy in the metadata, not as an actual dependency, and the code uses the Next.js 15 convention of awaiting the `params` promise.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\plan\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js client page (`apps/web/app/yatra/plan/page.tsx`) implements the "Custom Trip Planner" wizard for Darshya's pilgrimage (yatra) booking flow, default-exporting `CustomPlanPage`, which walks users through six steps — destinations, dates, travelers, preferences, special needs, and review — before showing a generated itinerary on a seventh pseudo-step. The `PlanData` type centralizes form state (destination site ids, date range, adult/senior counts, budget/pace/transport/stay enums, special-needs tags, free-text notes), and small presentational helpers `CounterRow`, `Section`, `ChipButton`, and `ReviewRow` render the step UIs. It pulls `sacredSites` and `formatINR` from `lib/yatra-data`, uses the shared `ScrollReveal` wrapper and `DateInput` UI component, and relies on lucide-react icons and Next.js `Link` for navigation back to `/yatra`. Notably, despite UI copy claiming an "AI will generate" the itinerary, `handleGenerate` is entirely local: it fakes latency with an 1800ms `setTimeout` and builds days from simple heuristics — a pace-derived `sitesPerDay` rate (0.5/0.8/1.2) chunks the selected destinations between fixed arrival and departure days, with leftover days filled as "Free day" entries. The price estimate is equally hardcoded, multiplying a per-person-per-day rate (₹3,800/₹7,200/₹15,000 by budget tier) by duration and headcount, with no backend call anywhere in the flow. Gotchas include a minimum enforced trip length of 3 days, `durationDays` clamped to at least 1 when dates are set, step gating via the `canContinue` check (at least one destination, valid dates, at least one traveler), and a step-7 state that lives outside the `STEPS` array so the stepper and nav buttons hide once results render. The "Request Advisor Quote" button on the result panel is currently a dead-end UI element with no handler attached.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra\\[slug]\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router dynamic route (`/yatra/[slug]`) that renders the full detail page for a single pilgrimage trip in the Darshya booking site. It exports `generateStaticParams` to pre-render one static page per entry in the `yatras` array, an async `generateMetadata` for per-trip SEO titles/descriptions, and the default `YatraDetailPage` async server component, which calls `notFound()` for unknown slugs. All content is sourced locally from `../../../lib/yatra-data` (`getYatraBySlug`, `yatras`, `formatINR`) — there are no backend or database calls — and presentation relies on the internal `ScrollReveal` component plus `lucide-react` icons, with styling done via CSS custom properties like `var(--color-primary)`. The page computes lowest/highest package prices to emit a schema.org `TouristTrip` JSON-LD block with an `AggregateOffer` and per-tier `Offer` entries pointing to `/yatra/{slug}/book?tier={tier}`. Sections rendered include a hero, route/places sidebar, day-by-day itinerary, gallery, inclusions/exclusions, three package tiers (with the `standard` tier hardcoded as "MOST POPULAR"), conditional helicopter availability, reviews, FAQs, and a final booking CTA. Notable gotchas: the popular add-ons list (puja, prasad delivery, recording, insurance) is hardcoded inline rather than data-driven, difficulty badge colors are mapped through a fixed lookup, and several prices (helicopter from ₹8,000, ₹5,000 booking advance) are literal constants in the markup.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra-packages\\page.tsx.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router listing page for Darshya's curated multi-day pilgrimage tours, rendering a marketing hero plus a responsive grid of package cards that link to `/yatra-packages/[slug]` detail pages. It exports static SEO `metadata` (canonical URL, OpenGraph) and a default async server component `YatraPackagesPage`, supported by the `YatraPackage` interface and the `fetchPackages()` helper. Data comes from the Darshya backend REST endpoint `/api/v1/yatra-packages`, whose base URL is resolved from `API_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a hardcoded fallback to `https://api.darshya.online`; the UI relies on Tailwind utilities, CSS design tokens (`--color-bg`, `--color-primary`, etc.), and lucide-react icons. Notable choices: the fetch uses ISR with `next: { revalidate: 300 }` (5-minute cache) and fails soft — any error or non-OK response yields an empty list and a "run the seed script" placeholder rather than an error page. Gotchas include a hardcoded Wikimedia Commons fallback hero image when `hero_image` is null, use of a plain `` tag instead of `next/image`, an unused `MapPin` import, and several interface fields (`departure_dates`, `destination_slug`, `price_usd`) that are fetched but never rendered here. Seats remaining are computed inline as `max_group_size - current_group_size`, and prices are formatted per the `en-IN` locale.

apps\\web\\components\\AartiOptIn.tsx.summary: AartiOptIn.tsx is a client-side React component for the web app that lets signed-in users toggle push-notification reminders fired 15 minutes before live aartis at followed temples. Its single default export, the `AartiOptIn` component, accepts a `variant` prop ('inline' renders a compact Bell/BellOff button from lucide-react, 'card' renders a bordered explainer card) and exposes `enable`/`disable` flows internally. On enable, it reads the access token from the `poojly_session` localStorage entry (throwing a sign-in error for anonymous visitors), fetches a VAPID public key from `${API_BASE_URL}/notifications/vapid-public-key`, registers the `/sw.js` service worker, requests `Notification` permission, subscribes via `reg.pushManager.subscribe` (with `urlBase64ToUint8Array` converting the key), and POSTs the subscription endpoint as an opaque `deviceToken` to `/notifications/register-token` along with platform (from `detectPlatform` UA-sniffing), language, and `aartiOptIn: true`; disable reverses this via `/notifications/unregister-token` and `sub.unsubscribe()`. Dependencies are minimal: `API_BASE_URL` from the internal `../lib/api-config` module, lucide-react icons, and browser Push API/Service Worker APIs—no Firebase SDK on web. A notable design decision is that the web build reuses the push subscription endpoint as the `deviceToken` string so the same API contract serves native iOS/Android clients passing real FCM tokens. Gotchas include the component rendering nothing until the `darshya_aarti_opt_in` localStorage flag hydrates (avoiding SSR mismatch), the hard requirement for an account before any push registration, and silent swallowing of unsubscribe failures during disable.

apps\\web\\app\\yatra-packages\\[slug]\\.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`apps/web/app/yatra-packages/[slug]/page.tsx`) renders the public detail page for a single pilgrimage package, combining data fetching, SEO metadata, and the booking entry point in one async server component. Its local `fetchPackage` helper calls the Darshya backend REST API at `/api/v1/yatra-packages/{slug}` — resolved from `API_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with a hardcoded fallback of `https://api.darshya.online` — and normalizes the base URL whether or not it already ends in `/api/v1`, caching responses with a 300-second ISR revalidation. The exported `generateMetadata` builds canonical and OpenGraph tags (including hero image) for the package, while the default `YatraPackageDetailPage` component 404s via `notFound()` on missing data and otherwise renders a hero banner, a sorted day-by-day itinerary, includes/excludes lists, a JSON-LD `TouristTrip` schema block, and a sticky booking sidebar with departure dates and INR/USD dual pricing that links to `/yatra-packages/[slug]/book`. The only notable dependencies are Next.js primitives (`next/link`, `next/navigation`, `Metadata`) and `lucide-react` icons; styling relies on global CSS variables like `var(--color-primary)` and `var(--font-display)` rather than a component library. Two gotchas stand out: the itinerary keys are sorted with a plain `localeCompare`, so keys like `day10` will order before `day2`, and seat-availability urgency ("Only N seats left") is computed at render time from `max_group_size - current_group_size`, meaning it can be up to five minutes stale under ISR. The local `YatraPackage` interface duplicates the backend's response shape rather than importing a shared type, so schema drift between API and frontend must be watched.

apps\\web\\app\\yoga-sutras\\[pada]\\pag.summary: This file is the Next.js App Router page that renders one static detail page per pada (chapter) of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras at the route `/yoga-sutras/[pada]`, part of the Darshya marketing/content site. Its key exports are `generateStaticParams`, which pre-builds all routes from `padaSlugs()`, `generateMetadata`, which produces SEO titles, canonical URLs, and OpenGraph tags from pada data, and the default `YogaSutraPadaPage` server component, which renders the pada's Sanskrit/English/IAST titles, summary, key concepts, practice pillars, key sutras with translations and commentary, plus prev/next and "all 4 padas" navigation. It depends entirely on the internal module `lib/yoga-sutras`, which provides the `YOGA_SUTRAS` dataset, `padaSlugs`, and `getPada` lookup; the only external framework dependency is Next.js itself (`Link`, `notFound`, `Metadata`), with styling done via Tailwind utility classes including a custom `saffron` palette. Notable design choices include `dynamicParams = false` combined with `notFound()` so unknown slugs hard-404, ISR with `revalidate = 86400` for daily regeneration, hardcoded `BASE_URL` (`https://darshya.online`) used in canonical and JSON-LD URLs, and embedded schema.org `Article` and `BreadcrumbList` JSON-LD injected via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for rich search results — including a hardcoded `datePublished` of 2026-05-27 that will need manual maintenance.

apps\\web\\components\\AdSenseScript.tsx.summary: This file defines `AdSenseScript`, a client component responsible for injecting the Google AdSense loader (`adsbygoogle.js` from pagead2.googlesyndication.com) into the page. Its default-exported function reads the publisher client ID from the `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_CLIENT` environment variable and renders a Next.js `Script` tag pointing at the AdSense loader URL with that ID encoded via `encodeURIComponent`. The only dependency is `next/script`, used with the `afterInteractive` strategy so the ad script loads post-hydration without blocking interactivity, plus `crossOrigin="anonymous"` on the tag. A key design decision is the silent no-op: when the env var is unset the component returns null, so ad loading can be disabled per-environment without touching call sites. Notably, premium-user suppression is deliberately not handled here — the file's comment points to the sibling `AdSlot` component, which gates ads at the individual slot level, meaning this loader mounts globally whenever a client ID is configured.

apps\\web\\app\\yoga-sutras\\page.tsx.summary: This Next.js App Router page (`YogaSutrasIndexPage`) is the static index/landing page for the Patanjali Yoga Sutras section of the Darshya site, rendering an overview of the four padas, a hardcoded grid of the eight limbs of Ashtanga Yoga, and cross-links to related study sections (`/upanishads`, `/gita`, `/chants/om-namah-shivaya`). Its data comes entirely from the internal `lib/yoga-sutras` module via the `YOGA_SUTRAS` array and `TOTAL_SUTRAS` constant; the only external dependency is Next.js itself (`Metadata`, `Link`), with no runtime fetches or services. Besides the default page component, it exports a `metadata` object (title, description, canonical URL, OpenGraph) targeting the production `BASE_URL` `https://darshya.online`, and a `revalidate = 86400` setting that makes the page ISR-cached for 24 hours. For SEO it injects two schema.org JSON-LD blocks — an `ItemList` of `Chapter` entries built from `YOGA_SUTRAS` and a `BreadcrumbList` — via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Each pada card links to `/yoga-sutras/${p.slug}` and is color-themed by indexing the `PADA_COLORS` tuple (`indigo`, `saffron`, `emerald`, `rose`). A notable gotcha: the card styling interpolates Tailwind classes dynamically (e.g. `border-${color}-200`, `text-${color}-900`), which Tailwind's static class scanner cannot detect, so these utilities will be missing from the production CSS unless they are safelisted or generated elsewhere. The eight-limbs content and intro copy are hardcoded JSX rather than data-driven, and `BASE_URL` is duplicated inline rather than imported from shared config.

apps\\web\\components\\AdSlot.tsx.summary: AdSlot.tsx is a client component in the web app that renders a Google AdSense ad unit, deciding whether an ad should appear at all before emitting the standard `ins.adsbygoogle` markup. Its default export `AdSlot` accepts a `slotId`, a `format` (typed as `AdSlotFormat`: horizontal, vertical, square, or in-feed), an optional accessibility `label`, and a `className`; the format drives both a min-height style map (`FORMAT_STYLE`) and the `data-ad-format` attribute map (`FORMAT_DATA_ATTR`, which translates square to "rectangle" and in-feed to "fluid"). Internally it depends on the `useIsPremium` hook to hide ads from paying users, and externally on the AdSense loader script (referred to as AdSenseScript) which bootstraps the `window.adsbygoogle` array that the component pushes to. Configuration comes entirely from build-time environment variables: `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_CLIENT` plus a per-slot lookup by convention, `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_SLOT_<slotId>`, and the component renders nothing if either is missing. A notable design decision is the "ad quarantine" mechanism: if any ancestor element carries `data-ad-quarantine="true"`, ads are suppressed for that subtree to keep advertising away from sensitive content such as antim sanskar pages. Other gotchas include a `pushedRef` guard so the ad push happens only once, a try/catch around the push so network or CSP failures never crash rendering, a deliberately local `AdsByGoogle` type to avoid leaking an ambient global declaration, and a visible "Advertisement" caption with `role="complementary"` for both accessibility and AdSense policy compliance.

apps\\web\\components\\AuthGuard.tsx.summary: AuthGuard.tsx is a client-side React component in the web app that gates protected pages behind authentication and role checks. Its default export, the `AuthGuard` component, accepts `children`, an optional `fallback` shown while auth state loads, and an optional `allowedRoles` array restricting access to specific `UserRole` values. It depends on the internal `../lib/auth-context` module, consuming the `useAuth` hook for `isAuthenticated`, `isLoading`, and `user` state, plus the `getRoleDashboardPath` helper and `UserRole` type for role-based routing. Unauthenticated visitors are sent to `/auth/login` with the current path encoded as a `redirect` query parameter so they can be returned after signing in, while logged-in users with the wrong role are redirected to their own portal via `getRoleDashboardPath`. Notably, navigation is done with hard `window.location.href` assignments rather than Next.js router pushes, causing full page reloads on redirect. During loading or any pending redirect the component renders a saffron-themed full-screen `Spinner` (with a distinct "Redirecting to your portal..." message for wrong-role users), so protected content never flashes before the redirect completes.

apps\\web\\components\\Analytics.tsx.summary: This file defines the web app's client-side PostHog analytics integration as a Next.js client component. It exports a single `Analytics` component that renders an internal `AnalyticsInner` inside a React `Suspense` boundary — required because `AnalyticsInner` calls `useSearchParams` from `next/navigation`, which Next.js App Router mandates be wrapped in Suspense to avoid deopting pages to client-side rendering. On mount, it lazily injects the PostHog snippet (`array.js`) via a dynamically created script tag rather than bundling the library, then calls `window.posthog.init` with `capture_pageview` disabled, `capture_pageleave` and `autocapture` enabled, and `localStorage+cookie` persistence; a second effect manually fires `$pageview` events with `$current_url` whenever `usePathname` or the search params change, since automatic pageview capture is off. The component depends on `next/navigation` hooks and the `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST` environment variables, and it treats `lib/posthog.ts` as the single source of truth for the `Window.posthog` type. Notable gotchas: the host defaults to the EU endpoint (`https://eu.i.posthog.com`) specifically to match `lib/posthog.ts` and prevent double-initialization splitting events across two PostHog projects, and the init effect early-returns if `window.posthog` already exists or no key is configured. The component renders `null` and exists purely for side effects, so it is intended to be mounted once near the app root.

apps\\web\\components\\AnalyticsEvent.ts.summary: This file defines `AnalyticsEvent`, a client component that fires a single PostHog analytics event on mount and renders nothing, letting Server Components (such as the `/temples/[slug]` page) emit a client-side ping without restructuring the page. Its default-exported component accepts an `event` name, an optional `properties` bag typed as `EventProps` (a record of string/number/boolean values), and an optional `dedupeKey`. Rather than importing `posthog-js` directly, it talks to the globally injected `window.posthog`, so it depends on PostHog being initialized elsewhere via `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`. Defensive design is the main theme: a `typeof window` and `window.posthog` existence check plus a blanket try/catch make analytics a silent no-op in demo or preview environments where the key is missing, on the principle that tracking must never break the page. Deduplication is handled with a `useRef` keyed on `dedupeKey ?? event`, so re-renders with churning prop identities won't double-count, though this also means changing `properties` alone (despite being in the effect's dependency array) will not re-fire the event. Before capture, undefined and null property values are stripped so PostHog receives a clean payload.

apps\\web\\components\\AiChatMessage.tsx.summary: This file defines the chat message UI for an AI scripture assistant in the web app, rendering both user and assistant chat bubbles with distinct styling. Its default export, `AiChatMessage`, takes a role, content, optional timestamp, streaming flag, and an exported `Citation` type describing scripture references with Sanskrit, transliteration, English, and Hindi fields; assistant messages additionally render a hardcoded "Om" avatar, a streaming cursor, a clipboard copy button (via `navigator.clipboard.writeText`), and expandable `CitationCard` components for scripture references. Rather than pulling in a markdown library, it ships a hand-rolled renderer (`renderMarkdown` and `renderInlineMarkdown`) supporting a small subset: `##`/`###` headings, bullet and numbered lists, bold, italic, and inline code. Its only external dependency is `lucide-react` for icons (ChevronDown, ChevronUp, Copy, Check, BookOpen); styling relies on Tailwind with custom theme tokens like the `saffron` palette, `surface` grays, `gradient-saffron`, and a Devanagari font variable (`--font-noto-devanagari`) for Sanskrit and Hindi text. Notable constraints: citations and the copy button are suppressed while `isStreaming` is true, the italic regex relies on lookbehind assertions (which older Safari versions lack), and safety against XSS comes implicitly from React's text escaping rather than any sanitization.

apps\\web\\components\\AiChat.tsx.summary: AiChat.tsx is the main client-side chat component for Darshya's "Pandit Ji" AI spiritual guidance feature, rendering the message list, composer, and a usage-quota banner while orchestrating the full send/stream/persist lifecycle. The default-exported `AiChat` component accepts `conversationId`, `accessToken`, `language`, and callbacks (`onConversationCreated`, `onConversationUpdated`) so a parent sidebar can track conversation state; an internal `EmptyState` component shows suggested questions that feed back into `handleSend`. It talks to the backend at `API_BASE_URL` (from `../lib/api-config`) via two endpoints: `POST /ai/chat`, whose SSE stream is parsed manually with a `ReadableStream` reader into `text`, `metadata` (citations), `done`, and `error` events, and `GET /ai/usage`, which powers the plan/remaining-messages indicator shown only to authenticated users. Messages are persisted to localStorage through `../lib/conversation-store` (`createConversation`, `addMessage`, `getConversation`), and each bubble is rendered by the sibling `AiChatMessage` component, which supplies the `Citation` type. Notable gotchas: an HTTP 402 response triggers paywall handling that swaps the assistant placeholder for an upgrade prompt, and any network/auth failure falls back to `getLocalDemoResponse`, which keyword-matches against the hardcoded `LOCAL_DEMO_TOPICS` scripture responses and fakes a typing effect with 12ms delays. The conversation-loading effect deliberately skips reloading when `conversationId` matches the locally created one so in-flight streamed tokens aren't wiped, and `scrollToBottom` manipulates the inner container's `scrollTop` directly to avoid triggering Next.js window scrolling. The upgrade nudge appears when the paywall fired or when free-plan remaining drops to ≤2 (session plan ≤5), linking to `/upgrade`.

apps\\web\\components\\ApprovedProviders.summary: This file defines `ApprovedProvidersStrip`, an async Next.js server component for the Darshya web app that renders a homepage-style section of vetted service providers — pandits, stores, astrologers, wellness instructors, gaushalas, and temples — as a responsive card grid. It fetches data server-side via `getApprovedProviders` from `../lib/api` (using the `ProviderListingType` and `ApprovedProvider` types), and renders each card with `ProviderBadge` and `RatingDisplay` from `./provider/ProviderBadge`, plus `next/link` navigation and `lucide-react` icons. Lookup tables `TYPE_LABEL` and `DETAIL_PATH` map each provider type to its plural label and detail route, while helpers `getDisplayName` and `getPriceLabel` pick the type-specific name field (e.g. `templeName`, `storeName`, `displayName`) and format pricing in ₹ with `en-IN` locale — though prices are only shown for pandit (per puja), astrologer (per minute), and wellness (per session). A notable gotcha: `showWhenEmpty` defaults to true so admins and developers see a dashed "No approved providers yet" placeholder with an "Apply to be listed" signup link, whereas production callers can pass false to hide the section entirely. The rating logic falls back from `ratingAvg` to a legacy `rating` field, and the "View all" link uses a different path scheme (`/${type}`) than `DETAIL_PATH`, which is inconsistent for astrologer (`/astrologer` vs `/astrology/...`) and wellness listings. Specialties are capped at two chips with a "+N" overflow counter, and each card deep-links to the provider's detail page.

apps\\web\\components\\AudioPlayer.tsx.summary: AudioPlayer.tsx is a client-side React component (marked 'use client', likely Next.js) that renders a styled in-page audio player for track playback, apparently in a devotional/spiritual content app given its `deity`, `type`, and saffron-themed props. It exports the `AudioPlayerProps` interface and a default `AudioPlayer` component that accepts title, artist, audioUrl, imageUrl, duration, and an `onEnded` callback. Rather than using a media library, it drives the browser's native `HTMLAudioElement` via `new Audio()` inside a `useEffect`, wiring `timeupdate`, `loadedmetadata`, and `ended` listeners, and depends only on React and `lucide-react` icons. The UI supports play/pause, click-to-seek on a progress bar, volume/mute controls, and an expandable/collapsible layout with a mini player mode; when `audioUrl` is null it renders an "Audio coming soon" placeholder card instead. Notable gotchas: the 32-bar "waveform" is purely decorative—heights are generated once with `Math.random()` and are not derived from actual audio data. The `audioUrl` effect intentionally suppresses `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`, so volume changes made after creation are applied via a separate effect rather than recreating the element. The `duration` prop is only an initial estimate that gets corrected once `loadedmetadata` fires, and `play()` promise rejections are silently swallowed, so autoplay-policy failures surface only as the UI showing "paused" state.

apps\\web\\components\\BookingStatusTrac.summary: BookingStatusTracker.tsx is a client-side React component in the web app that visualizes a booking's fulfillment progress as a multi-step tracker. It exports the `BookingStatus` union type (booked, priest_assigned, in_progress, completed, video_uploaded, delivered) and a default `BookingStatusTracker` component that accepts a `currentStatus` and an optional `timestamps` map, rendering a fixed six-step `STEPS` array with icons from lucide-react. Its only external dependency is lucide-react; styling relies on the project's custom Tailwind theme colors (tulsi-green for completed steps, saffron-500 for the active step, surface grays for pending). Notable design decisions include rendering two entirely separate layouts — a horizontal stepper with a gradient progress connector for desktop (`hidden md:block`) and a vertical timeline for mobile (`md:hidden`) — driven purely by responsive CSS rather than a shared adaptive layout. Completed steps swap their step icon for a CheckCircle2, the current step pulses via `animate-pulse`, and the desktop progress bar width is computed as `currentIndex / (STEPS.length - 1)`, so a status not found in STEPS (index -1) silently yields 0% progress. Timestamps are formatted with the hardcoded `en-IN` locale (day, short month, 2-digit time), assuming ISO-parseable date strings with no error handling for invalid input.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ChapterNav.summary: ChapterNav.tsx is a presentational React component in the web app that renders previous/next navigation between chapters of a book, plus a central "Contents" link back to the book's table of contents. It exports a single component, `ChapterNav`, which takes a `bookSlug` and nullable `prev`/`next` chapter objects typed as `ChapterSummary` from the `@poojly/shared` package. Navigation is built on Next.js `Link` for client-side routing to `/content/books/{bookSlug}/{chapterSlug}` paths, and icons come from `lucide-react` (ChevronLeft, ChevronRight, BookOpen). Styling is pure Tailwind utility classes using the project's custom `surface` and `saffron` color palettes, with the "next" button visually emphasized (filled saffron) over the muted "previous" button to guide readers forward. A notable detail is that when `prev` or `next` is null (first/last chapter), an empty `<span />` placeholder keeps the three-column flex layout intact rather than collapsing.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\BookCard.t.summary: `BookCard` is a presentational React component in the Next.js web app that renders a single clickable book tile, linking to `/content/books/{book.slug}` via `next/link`. It accepts a `BookManifest` object from the shared `@poojly/shared` package and displays the cover image, optional Sanskrit title (rendered with the `--font-noto-devanagari` CSS variable), title, subtitle, translator credit, and a unit count. A key piece of logic is that it handles two content structures: books with `structure === "kandas"` (e.g., the Ramayana) sum `sargaCount` across the `kandas` array and label the total as "sargas", while standard books just use `book.chapters.length` labeled as "chapters". Notably, it deliberately bypasses `next/image` optimization in favor of a plain `img` tag with lazy loading, suppressing the `@next/next/no-img-element` lint rule—likely to avoid optimization costs or config for external cover URLs. Styling relies on the project's custom Tailwind palette (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`) with hover scale and shadow transitions. All secondary metadata (Sanskrit title, subtitle, translator) is conditionally rendered, so the component tolerates sparse manifests without layout breakage.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ChapterTOC.summary: ChapterTOC.tsx is a presentational React component in the web app that renders a book's table of contents as a grid of links to individual chapter pages. Its single exported component, `ChapterTOC`, takes a `BookManifest` (imported from the internal `@poojly/shared` package) and branches on the manifest's `structure` field: books organized as "kandas" render one `<section>` per kanda—showing the kanda's name, optional Sanskrit name in the Noto Devanagari font, and description—with chapters filtered by matching `c.kanda` to the kanda slug, while all other books fall through to a flat chapter list. The unexported helper `ChapterList` does the actual rendering, producing an ordered grid where each chapter is a `next/link` pointing to `/content/books/{book.slug}/{chapter.slug}`, displaying the chapter number, title, and a compact status badge derived from content-completeness flags: "stub" for `placeholder`, "partial" for `partial`, or a verse count like "42v" when `verseCount` is present. The only dependencies are Next.js's `Link` for client-side navigation and the shared `BookManifest` type, with styling done entirely via Tailwind utility classes in the app's saffron/surface palette. A notable design point is that kanda grouping is purely a filtering concern over the flat `chapters` array rather than a nested data structure, and empty kandas would still render a header with an empty list since there's no guard against a kanda having zero matching chapters.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ContinueRe.summary: This file defines `ContinueReadingCTA`, a client-side React component in the web app (`apps/web`) that renders a "Continue reading" button on a book page, deep-linking the user back to the chapter they last reached. It takes a single `bookSlug` prop, checks authentication via the local `useAuth` hook from `lib/auth-context`, and fetches the reader's saved position through the `useReadingProgress` hook exported by the internal `@poojly/api-client` package, passing `isAuthenticated` so the query only runs for signed-in users. The rendered link points to `/content/books/{bookSlug}/{progress.chapterSlug}` using `next/link`, displays the chapter number and rounded `scrollPercent`, and is styled with Tailwind's custom `saffron` palette plus a `BookOpen` icon from `lucide-react`. A key design decision is that the component returns `null` while progress is loading or when no progress exists, so parent pages can include it unconditionally without handling empty states themselves. Notably, the resume target comes from server-persisted progress (`chapterSlug`, `chapterNumber`, `scrollPercent`), meaning the CTA reflects cross-device reading state rather than local storage. The main gotcha is that anonymous users will never see the button, since the progress query is gated on authentication.

apps\\web\\components\\CartContext.tsx.summary: This file implements client-side shopping cart state for the web app as a React context, exposed through the `CartProvider` component and the `useCart` hook. It defines the exported `CartProduct` and `CartItem` types plus the internal `CartContextValue` interface describing the cart's data and operations (`addItem`, `removeItem`, `updateQuantity`, `clearCart`) and UI drawer controls (`openCart`, `closeCart`, `toggleCart`). Cart contents persist to browser localStorage under the `poojly_cart` key, with a `hydrated` flag ensuring storage is only written after the initial load so SSR doesn't clobber saved data, and all storage access is wrapped in silent try/catch for environments where localStorage is unavailable. Derived pricing is computed inline: a flat ₹49 delivery fee waived at subtotals of ₹499 or more, 5% tax, and a summed total, though `freeDelivery` on `CartProduct` is captured but never used in the fee calculation.
