Notable constraints include a hard quantity cap of 10 per item, quantity updates below 1 being ignored rather than removing the item, cart item IDs generated via `Date.now()` (potential collision risk), and `addItem` automatically opening the cart drawer as a side effect.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\Verse.tsx.summary: This file defines the presentational React component used to render a single verse in the poojly web app's book reader. It exports one component, `Verse`, which takes a `Verse` object and the user's `ReaderPreferences` (both types imported from the internal `@poojly/shared` package) and renders the verse number plus up to three text layers — Sanskrit, transliteration, and English translation. Each layer is gated on both the corresponding preference flag (`showSanskrit`, `showTransliteration`, `showEnglish`) and the field actually being present on the verse, so missing data or disabled preferences simply omit that section. Commentary, by contrast, renders whenever `verse.commentary` exists, regardless of reader preferences. The component has no state, data fetching, or external service dependencies — it is a pure function of its props. A notable design detail is that the root `<article>` carries a stable anchor id (`verse-{number}`) and a `data-verse` attribute, which other reader features (deep-linking, scroll restoration, or verse highlighting) presumably rely on, so renaming those hooks would break callers. Styling is entirely class-driven (`reader-verse`, `reader-sanskrit`, etc.) with `whitespace-pre-line` preserving line breaks from the source text, meaning formatting lives in global CSS rather than this file.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ScrollProg.summary: `ScrollProgressBar.tsx` is a client component in the web app's books feature that renders a thin fixed-position reading-progress indicator showing how far the user has scrolled through the page. Its single export, `ScrollProgressBar`, accepts an optional `onChange` callback that receives the current scroll percent (0–100) so parent components—such as a book reader tracking reading position—can react to progress changes. It depends only on React's `useEffect`/`useState` and the browser DOM: it computes percentage from `document.documentElement` scroll metrics and listens to window `scroll` and `resize` events. Scroll handling is throttled via `requestAnimationFrame` (canceling any pending frame before scheduling a new one) and both listeners are registered with `passive: true`, keeping scroll performance smooth; cleanup removes listeners and cancels the animation frame. The bar is styled with Tailwind—fixed at `top-14` (positioning it just below the app header), `z-40`, `pointer-events-none`, and filled with the custom `bg-saffron-500` color—while a width transition smooths visual updates. Accessibility is handled via `role="progressbar"` with rounded `aria-valuenow` and a "Reading progress" label. One gotcha: because `onChange` is in the effect's dependency array, callers passing an inline (non-memoized) callback will cause the effect to tear down and re-subscribe listeners on every render.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ReaderCont.summary: `ReaderControls.tsx` is a client component in the web app's books feature that renders a floating settings panel for the scripture reader, letting users adjust display preferences via a fixed bottom-right button that expands into a dialog. The exported `ReaderControls` component receives a `ReaderPreferences` object and an `onChange` callback as props, making it fully controlled — all preference state lives in the parent, which is responsible for persisting it, while only the panel's open/closed state is held locally. It offers three controls: a theme picker cycling through `THEMES` (saffron, sepia, night), a four-step font-size picker from `SIZES` (sm through xl), and toggle switches for `showSanskrit`, `showTransliteration`, and `showEnglish`. It depends on `lucide-react` for icons and imports the `ReaderPreferences`, `ReaderTheme`, and `ReaderFontSize` types from the `@poojly/shared` package, keeping preference semantics shared across the monorepo. A non-exported `Toggle` helper implements an accessible switch using `role="switch"` and `aria-checked`, and the main panel uses `role="dialog"` with `aria-pressed` on option buttons, so accessibility is handled manually rather than via a UI library. Styling is pure Tailwind with custom `saffron-*` and `surface-*` design tokens, and the panel is hard-coded to `fixed bottom-6 right-6 z-50`, so it overlays page content globally. Notably, the file exports a `__testing` object exposing the `THEMES` and `SIZES` constants, a deliberate hook so tests can iterate the same option lists the UI renders.

apps\\web\\components\\books\\ReaderClie.summary: This client component (`"use client"`) implements the chapter reading screen for the web app: it renders a chapter's header (book title, chapter number, Sanskrit title, subtitle, translator, plus partial/placeholder banners), the verse list, previous/next navigation, a scroll progress bar, and floating reader controls for theme and font size. The sole export is `ReaderClient`, which takes a `Chapter`, the book title, and `prev`/`next` `ChapterSummary` links; internal helpers `loadPrefs`/`savePrefs` persist `ReaderPreferences` to localStorage under the key `poojly_reader_prefs`, merging stored values over `DEFAULT_READER_PREFERENCES` from `@poojly/shared`. It builds on `@poojly/shared` for types and defaults, `@poojly/api-client`'s `useReadingProgress` hook to save scroll-percent progress, the app's `useAuth` context (`../../lib/auth-context`) to determine whether progress should be persisted for the signed-in user, and sibling components `Verse`, `ChapterNav`, `ScrollProgressBar`, and `ReaderControls`. Notable design choices: theme and font size are applied via `data-reader-theme`/`data-reader-font-size` attributes rather than inline styles, leaving presentation to CSS; preferences initialize from defaults and hydrate from localStorage in a mount `useEffect` (with `typeof window` guards) to stay SSR-safe and avoid hydration mismatch; and scroll changes from `ScrollProgressBar` are forwarded to `save` with book/chapter slugs as the progress payload. The component also encodes a content-integrity stance—placeholder chapters show a banner stating "We do not fabricate Sanskrit text"—and gracefully handles empty verse lists and localStorage parse/write failures by falling back to defaults.

apps\\web\\components\\CategoryIndex.tsx.summary: This file defines CategoryIndex, a React server component for the Next.js web app that renders the landing page for a knowledge-base category such as philosophy or scripture. It accepts a KnowledgeCategory, title, description, and optional heroEmoji (defaulting to "Om"), then calls getAllArticles from the internal lib/content module to load all published articles in that category and groups them in-memory by their frontmatter subTopic field, falling back to an "Overview" bucket when no subtopic is set. The page renders a hero header with an article-count badge, an embedded DailyVerse component, and one section per subtopic containing a responsive grid of Link cards (next/link) that route to /{category}/{slug} and display each article's title, summary, and readingMinutes, with lucide-react supplying the BookOpen and Clock icons. Notable details: grouping relies on a JavaScript Map, so section ordering follows first-appearance order of subtopics rather than any explicit sort; an empty-state message ("Content publishing soon") is shown when a category has no articles; and styling is entirely Tailwind utility classes using custom saffron and surface color tokens.

apps\\web\\components\\CartDrawer.tsx.summary: CartDrawer.tsx is a client-side React component in the Next.js web app (`apps/web`) that renders the store's slide-in shopping cart panel, including item list, quantity controls, price breakdown, and checkout actions. Its single default export, the `CartDrawer` component, pulls all cart state and actions—`items`, `itemCount`, `subtotal`, `deliveryFee`, `tax`, `total`, `removeItem`, `updateQuantity`, `isOpen`, and `closeCart`—from the `useCart` hook provided by the sibling `CartContext` module, so it contains no cart logic of its own. A private `formatPrice` helper formats amounts as whole-rupee INR via `Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN')`, reflecting an India-focused storefront (also seen in the GST estimate line). External dependencies are limited to `next/link` for navigation to `/store`, `/store/cart`, and `/store/checkout`, and `lucide-react` for icons. Notable behaviors: the component returns `null` when closed, closes on Escape keypress and backdrop click, and locks body scroll (`document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden'`) while open, cleaning both up in a `useEffect`. Business rules are hardcoded in the UI—quantity is clamped between 1 and 10, and a free-delivery nudge appears when `subtotal` is below ₹499. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with a custom palette (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`, `tulsi-green`) plus an `animate-in slide-in-from-right` entrance, and it layers above the page with fixed z-indexes of 60 (backdrop) and 70 (drawer). Product images are placeholders only—the drawer always renders a gradient box with a `ShoppingBag` icon rather than actual product thumbnails.

apps\\web\\components\\CategoryArticle.t.summary: CategoryArticle is a React server component in the Next.js web app that renders a complete knowledge-base article page for a given `KnowledgeCategory` and slug. It loads the article synchronously via `getArticle(category, slug)` from the internal `../lib/content` module, triggering a 404 through `notFound()` from `next/navigation` when the slug doesn't resolve, and it calls `getAllArticles(category)` to resolve the `frontmatter.related` slug list into real article entries, silently dropping any that don't match. The page renders a back link using `categoryLabel`, a header driven by frontmatter fields (`subTopic`, `title`, `summary`, `readingMinutes`), the MDX body through the sibling `MdxRender` component (which also receives `frontmatter.glossaryTerms` for inline term linking), plus conditionally rendered Sources and Related sections that only appear when the frontmatter provides them. External dependencies are limited to `next/link` for client navigation and `lucide-react` for the Clock and ArrowLeft icons; all content comes from the local content library rather than a remote service, implying static generation at build time. A notable gotcha is the `filter(Boolean) as typeof all` cast, which masks potential type unsoundness if related slugs reference missing articles, and related links are built manually as `/${category}/${slug}` rather than through a shared routing helper.

apps\\web\\components\\CategoryMegaMenu..summary: `CategoryMegaMenu.tsx` is a client-side presentational component that renders the desktop mega-menu panel shown beneath a `CategoryNav` trigger in the web app. Its single export, `CategoryMegaMenu`, takes a `Category` object (plus optional `onItemClick` and `labelledBy` props for close handling and ARIA wiring) and renders either a specialized layout or a default one. If the category is `library` and has populated `subGroups`, it delegates entirely to `LibraryMegaPanel`; otherwise it renders a two-column grid of `next/link` menu items with descriptions, topped by a label/tagline header and followed by an optional featured tile at the bottom. It depends on the `AccentColor` and `Category` types from `../lib/category-tree` and on the sibling `LibraryMegaPanel` component, with Next.js `Link` (prefetch enabled) as the only external import beyond React. A static `ACCENT` record maps each of the four accent colors (saffron, indigo, emerald, amber) to a full set of Tailwind class strings covering hover, focus-ring, and featured-tile styling, defaulting to saffron when `accentColor` is unset. Notable constraints: the library branch ignores the outer wrapper's card styling since `LibraryMegaPanel` owns its own four-column layout, all classes are hardcoded literals so Tailwind's compiler can see them (no dynamic class interpolation), and the component is purely presentational — all open/close and keyboard behavior must be managed by the consuming trigger via `aria-labelledby` and `onItemClick`.

apps\\web\\components\\ClientOnly.tsx.summary: This file defines `ClientOnly`, a small client-side React utility component in the web app's shared components folder, created to prevent hydration mismatches between server-rendered and browser-rendered output. It accepts `children` plus an optional `fallback` prop (defaulting to `null`, so the slot renders empty during SSR) and only renders the children once a `useEffect`-driven `mounted` state flag flips to true after the component mounts in the browser. Its sole dependencies are `useEffect`, `useState`, and the `ReactNode` type from the `react` package, and the `'use client'` directive marks it as a client component in the Next.js App Router sense. The intended use, per the docblock, is to wrap any node whose value differs between SSR and client — examples called out include `new Date()`, `Math.random()`, `localStorage`, and `window.matchMedia`. A notable gotcha is that the default `null` fallback collapses layout space until hydration completes, so callers needing to avoid layout shift must pass an explicit placeholder via `fallback`.

apps\\web\\components\\CommissionBanner..summary: CommissionBanner is a client-side React component in the web app that displays a provider's current subscription plan and commission rate, while nudging them toward a higher-tier plan with a lower commission. It accepts `currentPlanId` and `role` props and derives everything else from the internal pricing library (`../lib/pricing`), using `getPlanById`, `getUpgradePlan`, `getCommissionRate`, and `formatPrice` along with the `PlanId` and `ProviderRole` types. When an upgrade plan exists, it shows the potential commission reduction alongside the upgrade plan's monthly price and renders a call-to-action link to `/settings/subscription`. The component uses lucide-react icons (`Percent`, `ArrowUpRight`) and relies heavily on CSS custom properties like `--color-primary` and `--color-text` for theming, so it inherits whatever design tokens the app defines. Notably, it performs no data fetching of its own — plan and commission logic live entirely in the pricing module, making this purely a presentational wrapper around that domain logic.

apps\\web\\components\\CloudflareAnalyti.summary: This file provides the `CloudflareAnalytics` React component, which injects the Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon script into the Next.js web app (`apps/web`). Its sole purpose is privacy-first, cookieless site analytics, which comes free with Cloudflare Pages hosting. The component reads the public environment variable `NEXT_PUBLIC_CLOUDFLARE_BEACON_TOKEN` and, if it is unset, returns null so analytics are silently disabled in environments without a configured token. When a token is present, it renders a deferred script tag pointing at Cloudflare's hosted beacon (`static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js`) and passes the token to it via a JSON-serialized `data-cf-beacon` attribute. It has no internal dependencies beyond React/Next.js conventions and talks only to the external Cloudflare Insights service. Notable design points: the opt-in env-var gating means the component is safe to mount unconditionally (e.g., in the root layout) without leaking requests in local or staging environments, and the comment documents exactly where to obtain the token in the Cloudflare dashboard (Analytics & Logs → Web Analytics).

apps\\web\\components\\ChannelAttributio.summary: `ChannelAttribution` (in `apps/web/components/ChannelAttribution.tsx`) is a renderless React client component that captures first-touch marketing attribution so signup analytics can segment users by acquisition channel (Reddit, Twitter, WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram), per the playbook `docs/marketing/100-signups-5-channels-playbook.md` (requirement R-Q1-M-012). Its single exported component, `ChannelAttribution`, runs a one-shot `useEffect` that parses `utm_source`, `ref`, and the standard `utm_*` params from `window.location.search`, normalizes them via the internal helpers `normalizeUtmSource` and `deriveChannelFromRef` (backed by the `REF_PREFIX_MAP` lookup that aliases prefixes like `tw`, `wa`, `tg`, and `x`), and builds an `Attribution` record. The record is persisted to `localStorage` under the key `darshya_attr` and pushed into PostHog as a super property through `window.posthog.register`, plus a one-time `attribution_captured` event via `window.posthog.capture`, so every subsequent analytics event carries the channel. Its only dependencies are React, the browser APIs `URLSearchParams` and `localStorage`, and a globally loaded PostHog snippet (`window.posthog`), which is checked defensively before use. A key design rule is first-touch-wins: if a stored attribution already has a `signup_channel`, new URL params never overwrite it, and the stored value is simply re-registered with PostHog on each fresh page load (also covering the case where the snippet loads late or a signup happens in another tab). Other gotchas include the `utm_source`-over-`ref` precedence, truncation of captured values via `pickString` (64–128 chars), and silent try/catch around `localStorage` to survive quota or privacy-mode failures.

apps\\web\\components\\CommissionsPanel..summary: CommissionsPanel.tsx is a client-side React component in the apps/web frontend that renders a table of commission records — net payouts to providers after platform commission on completed bookings. It exports a single CommissionsPanel component with a mode prop: 'me' fetches the logged-in provider's records via listMyCommissions, while 'admin' fetches every commission across providers via listCommissions, both from the internal lib/commission-api module, authenticating with the session access token from lib/auth-context's useAuth hook. In 'me' mode it also renders three SummaryCard tiles (total earned, pending amount, last payout) computed client-side with useMemo, and admin mode adds a Provider column showing providerName and providerRole. A row of status filter pills (all, pending, processing, paid, failed, on_hold) filters the already-fetched list locally rather than re-querying the API. Money is formatted as whole-rupee INR via Intl.NumberFormat with the en-IN locale, and nullish fields consistently fall back to an em-dash, with netAmount falling back to amount in the summary math. The component handles loading, error, and empty states, uses a cancelled flag in its useEffect to avoid setting state after unmount, and depends on lucide-react for icons and Tailwind utility classes (including a custom saffron/surface palette) for styling.

apps\\web\\components\\CategoryNav.tsx.summary: CategoryNav.tsx is a client component that renders the desktop-only mega-menu navigation bar, hidden below the `md` breakpoint (mobile uses `MobileNavV2` instead, so this must only be rendered inside an `md:` block). It maps over `CATEGORY_TREE` from `../lib/category-tree` to render one trigger button per `CategoryKey`, and mounts a `CategoryMegaMenu` panel for whichever category is open, using `ChevronDown` from `lucide-react` as the affordance icon. Its single export, `CategoryNav` (also the default export), manages all open/close state locally via `openKey` plus ref-held timers and a `triggerRefs` map keyed by category. Interaction is deliberately hybrid: hover opens a panel after a 120ms delay and closes 120ms after the pointer leaves both trigger and panel (the grace period permits mouse travel into the fixed-positioned panel), while keyboard focus opens immediately, click toggles, Escape closes and returns focus to the originating trigger, and outside mousedown closes. A notable gotcha is the `suppressFocusOpenRef` flag, which briefly blocks the trigger's `onFocus` handler after Escape-driven refocus so the just-closed panel doesn't instantly re-open; the flag clears on the next event-loop tick. Keyboard support follows menu-bar conventions, with ArrowRight/ArrowLeft cycling focus across triggers and ArrowDown/Enter/Space opening the focused category, and ARIA wiring (`aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `labelledBy`) ties triggers to panels using `useId`-generated IDs. The panel is `fixed` at a hard-coded `top-16`, which implicitly couples it to the site header height, and the `library` category special-cases a wider 1120px panel versus the default 640px. All timers are cleared on unmount, so the component is self-cleaning despite its window-level listeners.

apps\\web\\components\\DailyVerse.tsx.summary: DailyVerse.tsx is a presentational React component in the web app that renders a "Verse of the Day" card, displaying a Sanskrit verse alongside its transliteration, English translation, and source/reference. Its single default export, the `DailyVerse` component, takes no props and derives all content by calling `getVerseForDate()` from the internal `../lib/daily-verse` module, which presumably selects a verse deterministically based on the current date. The component has no external runtime dependencies beyond React and styles itself entirely with Tailwind utility classes, relying on custom theme tokens such as `saffron-50/100/700`, `amber-50`, and the `surface` palette, plus a `font-serif` class for the Sanskrit text. Notably, it has no `"use client"` directive, no state, and no effects, so it renders as a server component — meaning the verse is resolved at render time, and if the page is statically generated the displayed verse will be frozen at build time unless the route uses revalidation or dynamic rendering. The `whitespace-pre-line` class on the Sanskrit paragraph indicates the underlying verse data may contain intentional line breaks that the component preserves verbatim.

apps\\web\\components\\CookieBanner.tsx.summary: This file implements the cookie consent banner for the Darshya web app, a Next.js client component that collects and persists user consent for DPDP/UK-GDPR compliance. The default-exported `CookieBanner` component renders a bottom-anchored dialog with "Accept all," "Reject all," and a granular "Manage preferences" panel covering three `ConsentCategory` values — essential (always on), analytics, and marketing — while the exported helpers `getStoredConsent` and `hasConsent` let other modules check consent before loading trackers; the UI text indicates these gates guard PostHog, Cloudflare Web Analytics, Google Ads, and Meta retargeting. Consent is stored as a `ConsentState` object in `localStorage` under `STORAGE_KEY` ("darshya_cookie_consent_v1"), and `persistConsent` broadcasts a `darshya:consent-changed` CustomEvent on `window` so listeners elsewhere in the app can react without a prop or context dependency. Notable design decisions include version-based invalidation (`CONSENT_VERSION` mismatch discards stored consent), automatic re-prompting after `REPROMPT_DAYS` (365), SSR safety via `typeof window` guards, and silent swallowing of storage errors (quota or privacy-mode failures). A key gotcha: `hasConsent` fails closed for analytics and marketing but returns true for essential when no consent record exists, so the banner must appear on first visit for anything non-essential to ever activate. The component depends only on React (`useEffect`, `useState`) and browser APIs, with styling via Tailwind utility classes plus CSS variable fallbacks (`--color-primary`, `--color-border`).

apps\\web\\components\\ContentPageHeader.summary: ContentPageHeader is a client-side React component (Next.js `'use client'`) that renders the banner section of the `/content` listing page in the apps/web frontend: a saffron-gradient hero with a localized title and subtitle, a language switcher, and a search bar. Its default export, the `ContentPageHeader` component, accepts `currentType` and `currentSearch` props to reflect active filters. It builds on the sibling `LanguageSwitcher` module, importing the `LanguageSwitcher` component plus the `CONTENT_LABELS` lookup and `SupportedLanguage` type for English/Hindi strings, and uses the `Search` icon from lucide-react; styling is Tailwind utility classes with a custom saffron/temple-gold palette. Language preference is hydrated from `localStorage` under the key `poojly_language` inside a `useEffect` (guarded to only accept `'en'` or `'hi'`), which avoids SSR mismatch by always rendering `'en'` on first paint. Notably, the search box is a plain HTML form doing a GET submission to `/content`, preserving `currentType` via a hidden input so filter state lives in the URL and results can be server-rendered rather than fetched client-side. One gotcha: `onLanguageChange` only updates local state and never writes back to `localStorage` in this file, so persistence of a language change must happen inside `LanguageSwitcher` itself or the selection won't survive a reload.

apps\\web\\components\\DarshanPlayer.tsx.summary: DarshanPlayer.tsx is a client-side React component in the Darshya web app that renders a temple's live darshan (video streaming) player, adapting its UI across three states: a premium-lock paywall with an upgrade link to /pricing, a "Stream Starting Soon" placeholder keyed off scheduledStart, and the live playable view. Its exports are the default DarshanPlayer component plus the DarshanPlayerProps interface, which carries stream metadata such as streamUrl, templeName, templeSlug, isLive, viewerCount, isPremium, currentEvent, and templeCity/templeDeity/templeImage for labeling. The only dependencies are react (useState) and lucide-react for icons — there is no video library; playback is delegated entirely to a YouTube embed iframe, detected by the internal isYouTubeEmbed helper which matches youtube.com/embed and youtube-nocookie.com/embed URLs. A notable workaround is the autoplay handling: the iframe always loads with autoplay=1 and mute=1 to satisfy browser autoplay policies, and a "Tap to unmute" overlay button flips the URL to mute=0, which deliberately reloads the iframe to unmute. Fullscreen is faked with CSS (fixed inset-0 z-[100]) rather than the browser Fullscreen API, so it won't cover browser chrome. Gotchas: non-YouTube stream URLs are never actually played (the component falls back to a static "Stream offline" placeholder), overlays use pointer-events-none so YouTube's own controls remain clickable, and the custom fullscreen button is hidden until hover/focus to avoid clashing with the iframe's native controls.

apps\\web\\components\\DarshanScheduleRe.summary: This file defines `DarshanScheduleRemindButton`, a client-side React component that lets users toggle a "remind me" bell for an item on the darshan schedule, identified by a `reminderId` prop and described by a `label` prop. The default-exported component tracks its on/off state in `useState`, persists the set of active reminder IDs as a JSON string array in `window.localStorage` under the key `poojly_darshan_reminders`, and shows a self-dismissing toast (via `role="status"` / `aria-live="polite"`) for three seconds after each toggle. Its only external dependency is the `Bell` icon from `lucide-react`; it has no backend or API calls, so reminders are purely device-local and never synced or used to trigger actual notifications. Helper functions `readReminders` and `writeReminders` defensively guard against SSR (`typeof window === 'undefined'`), malformed JSON, and localStorage failures, silently falling back to an empty list or no-op writes—useful for private browsing or quota errors but meaning corrupted state is quietly discarded. Styling relies on project-specific Tailwind theme tokens (`text-saffron-600`, `fill-saffron-500`, `text-surface-600`, `shadow-warm-md`), and accessibility is handled with `aria-pressed` and dynamic `aria-label` text. One gotcha: because state initializes on mount via `useEffect`, the button always renders in the "off" state during SSR and first paint, then flips after hydration if a reminder exists.

apps\\web\\components\\dashboard\\Devote.summary: DevoteeTodaySection.tsx is a client-side React component that renders the "Today" engagement block on the devotee dashboard, replacing four previously hardcoded mock widgets (Darshan History, Saved Temples, Chat History, Store Orders) with live data. Its default export, DevoteeTodaySection, displays a two-column grid of four cards: a Today's Panchang strip (tithi, nakshatra, sunrise/sunset, Rahu Kaal, festivals), a rashi-personalized Daily Horoscope, a Continue Reading resume row (implemented by the internal ContinueReadingCard component with progress bars), and a real Store Orders list, plus a shared EmptyHint fallback component. It depends on useAuth from lib/auth-context for the user's rashi, locationCity, and session access token, on API_BASE_URL from lib/api-config, and on lucide-react icons, calling four backend routes: GET /panchang/today (city-aware, public), GET /astrology/horoscope/daily (only when the user has a moon sign), GET /store/orders?limit=3 (authenticated), and GET /me/reading-progress?limit=3 (authenticated). A core design principle is "never fake data": every card degrades to a graceful EmptyHint with a call-to-action link (e.g., prompting the user to set their rashi in /profile) rather than showing placeholder content. Fetches are fired in parallel via Promise.allSettled with per-request .catch guards so one failing endpoint never blocks the others, and a cancelled flag guards all setState calls against unmount races. A notable gotcha: the orders fetch tolerates two response shapes (j.orders or j.data), and ContinueReadingCard normalizes both camelCase and snake_case fields (bookSlug/book_slug, scrollPercent/scroll_percent) from the reading-progress route, deriving display titles by de-slugging book slugs and building resume hrefs as /content/{bookSlug}/{chapterSlug}. The horoscope fetch silently skips entirely when the user has no rashi, and the orders and reading-progress fetches skip when there's no access token, so logged-out viewers see only the public panchang card populate.

apps\\web\\components\\DarshanBrowser.ts.summary: DarshanBrowser.tsx is a Next.js client component (the default export `DarshanBrowser`) that renders the browsable catalog of temple livestream ("darshan") content, split into a "Live Now" grid, a "Next Aarti" chip row driven by `upcomingNotes`, and an "Upcoming Streams" grid with per-stream reminder buttons. It receives `liveStreams` and `scheduledStreams` as `DarshanStream` objects typed in `../lib/api`, and resolves card imagery through helpers in `../lib/images` (`getTempleHero`, `getDeityImage`, `wikiThumb`), with `templeImageFor` falling back from the temple's first image to a slug-based hero to a deity-based stock image that defaults to `lord-shiva` when no keyword matches. Client-side filtering is handled by `matchesQuery`, `matchesDeity`, and `matchesRegion` against hardcoded `DEITY_OPTIONS` and a `REGION_CITIES` lookup, which means temples whose city isn't in those lists can never match a region filter, and deity matching relies on substring checks after stripping "lord"/"goddess" prefixes. Reminders are purely local: `readReminders`/`writeReminders` persist stream IDs to localStorage under `poojly_darshan_reminders` (guarded for SSR), and `toggleReminder` fires a transient toast rather than any backend or push notification. The component injects an `AdSlot` in-feed ad spanning the full grid width after every fourth live card, links cards via `streamHref` (preferring `temple.slug` over `stream.id` for the `/darshan/...` route), and decorates the UI with lucide-react icons and countdown labels formatted by `formatStartsIn`.

apps\\web\\components\\EmailCapture.tsx.summary: This client-side React component provides a reusable one-field email capture form that any landing surface (home hero, NRI page, upgrade paywall) can drop in to collect waitlist signups. The default export `EmailCapture` accepts a required `source` prop for funnel attribution plus optional `title`, `subtitle`, `cta`, `successMessage`, and a `variant` toggle between a styled `card` layout and a compact `inline` form. On submit it POSTs the lowercased, trimmed email along with the source tag and a hardcoded `panchangOptIn: true` flag to the backend's `/waitlist` endpoint, using the `API_BASE_URL` constant from the internal `../lib/api-config` module. After a successful response it lazily imports `../lib/posthog` and fires a best-effort `email_capture_submitted` analytics event, silently ignoring any failure so analytics never block the UX. The component is deliberately a thin wrapper: the backend endpoint is idempotent (duplicate emails return the existing row), so no client-side dedup is attempted. Local state (`email`, `busy`, `done`, `error`) drives three render paths — form, loading-disabled button, and a success confirmation panel — with only a minimal client-side check that the input contains an `@`. Styling relies on the project's Tailwind theme tokens (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`), and error messages from the API's JSON `message` field are surfaced verbatim when available.

apps\\web\\components\\DeferredClientWid.summary: This file defines `DeferredClientWidgets`, a client-side wrapper that lazy-loads non-critical overlay UI—`CartDrawer`, `LiveChatWidget`, `StickyAartiCta`, `HeaderScrollShadow`, and `CookieBanner`—via Next.js `dynamic()` imports with `ssr: false` and a null loading fallback. Its purpose is performance: all five widgets are invisible on first paint and only appear after user interaction, so excluding them from the server-rendered initial bundle speeds up every route. The `'use client'` directive exists specifically because the consuming layout is a Server Component, which cannot legally call `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` itself—this wrapper is the workaround for that constraint. It depends only on `next/dynamic` and sibling components within `apps/web/components` (including `home/StickyAartiCta`), with no external services called directly. Compliance is a notable concern: `CookieBanner` implements GDPR/UK DPA consent with ICO-mandated reject-all parity and re-prompts users every 12 months (tracked as R-Q3-L-002). A key gotcha documented inline is that `WhatsAppButton` was deliberately removed (Phase D-5) because its chat FAB collided with `LiveChatWidget`, which is now the canonical chat surface (AI Asha + Claude API + escalate-to-ticket flow); WhatsApp remains reachable through the Ask Pandit nav chip, `/contact`, and `/support/ticket/new`.

apps\\web\\components\\DonationForm.tsx.summary: This file defines `DonationForm`, a client-side React component (default export, with the `DonationFormProps` interface) that renders the complete donation checkout flow for a temple or gaushala on the Darshya platform: amount preset selection, donor details (name, email, phone, PAN, dedication), validation, payment, and a success screen showing the 80G receipt number. It depends on the internal `useAuth` hook from `../lib/auth-context` for the authenticated session and pre-filling donor fields, and `API_BASE_URL` from `../lib/api-config` to call the backend endpoints `POST /donations/create-order` and `POST /donations/verify`, which bookend a Razorpay payment; Razorpay's `checkout.js` is loaded lazily at runtime from `https://checkout.razorpay.com/v1/checkout.js` via the `loadRazorpay` helper rather than bundled. The flow is three-phase: create a server-side order, open the Razorpay modal with a narrowly-typed global `Razorpay` constructor (deliberately avoiding `any`), then verify the signature server-side in the `handler` callback before showing success. Notable constraints: the component mirrors backend limits client-side (`MIN_INR` 101, `MAX_INR` 1,000,000, matching `apps/api/src/routes/donations.ts`), enforces PAN only for donations of ₹2,000 or more per 80G tax rules, and validates Indian phone numbers as 10 digits starting 6–9, trimming the `+91` prefix when pre-filling from `user.phone`. A key gotcha is that the backend field `gaushalaId` is reused as an opaque cause id for both temples and gaushalas, and the Razorpay key falls back to `NEXT_PUBLIC_RAZORPAY_KEY_ID`, the server-provided `keyId`, or the literal `rzp_test_demo`. Unauthenticated submitters are redirected to `/auth/login` with a return URL, and verification failures after a successful charge deliberately surface the Razorpay payment id with instructions to email support@darshya.online for manual reconciliation.

apps\\web\\components\\ForYouSection.tsx.summary: ForYouSection.tsx is a client-side React component that renders the "For You Today" homepage section, displaying up to four personalized spiritual content cards (aarti, mantra, article, festival special) with type badges, hover play overlays, durations, and links to /content/{slug}. Its default export is the ForYouSection component; internally it defines the PersonalizedContentItem and PersonalizedContent interfaces plus a TYPE_CONFIG map that assigns lucide-react icons, colors, and Listen/Read actions per content type, with unknown types defaulting to the article config via getTypeConfig. The component builds on API_BASE_URL from ../lib/api-config and the lucide-react icon set, and talks to two backend endpoints: the authenticated GET /ai/personalize-content and the unauthenticated GET /content/daily. A notable design decision is the three-tier resilience strategy in fetchPersonalizedContent: it first attempts personalized picks by manually parsing the bs_access_token cookie into a Bearer header, falls back to generic daily content when the user is anonymous or the AI call fails, and finally renders hardcoded FALLBACK_CONTENT (e.g., "Om Jai Jagdish Hare", "Gayatri Mantra - 108 times") on network error, in which case an amber AlertCircle banner notes that popular picks are being shown. Gotchas include the manual cookie parsing (with decodeURIComponent on the token), the fact that imageUrl is defined on items but never rendered (thumbnails are always gradient placeholders with an icon), and an error state that still displays fallback items rather than hiding the section. Loading is handled with a four-card pulse skeleton grid that mirrors the final layout.

apps\\web\\components\\GlobalSearch.tsx.summary: This file provides GlobalSearch, the site-wide search dropdown component for the Next.js web app, letting users query temples, pujas, and editorial content from the header. It exports the single GlobalSearch React component (typed locally against SearchResult and SearchResponse interfaces), which fetches from the backend `${API_BASE_URL}/search` endpoint imported from `../lib/api-config`, passing the query plus a limit of 5 and rendering grouped Temples, Pujas, and Content sections as next/link navigation items. External dependencies are limited to React hooks, next/link for client-side routing, and lucide-react icons (Search, X, Loader2). Notable behaviors include a 200ms debounced fetch that only fires for queries of at least two characters, a "/" global keyboard shortcut that opens the dropdown (suppressed when focus is inside form fields or contentEditable elements), and placeholder text that rotates through ROTATING_PLACEHOLDERS every 3.5 seconds to showcase search categories. The trigger is responsive: a full pill with keyboard hint at xl breakpoints and up, an icon-only button below that, and the open state renders as a full-screen dimmed overlay on mobile but an anchored 420px dropdown on sm and larger screens. Gotchas worth knowing: network failures are swallowed silently so stale results remain visible, the dropdown closes on outside mousedown, Escape, or link navigation, and the empty state suggests sample queries (Tirumala, Hanuman Chalisa, Rudrabhishek) when fewer than two characters are typed.

apps\\web\\components\\GlossaryTooltip.t.summary: GlossaryTooltip.tsx is a client-side React component in the apps/web Next.js application that renders an inline glossary term with an on-demand definition popup. Its default export, the GlossaryTooltip component, takes a `term` string and a `GlossaryEntry` object (imported from the sibling module `../lib/glossary`) and displays the term as a dotted-underline button that toggles a tooltip via local `useState`, opening on mouse hover or click and closing on mouse leave. The tooltip shows the entry's term, an optional Devanagari rendering, and its meaning, making it the UI surface for whatever content pipeline produces `GlossaryEntry` records. It depends only on React and the internal glossary library — no external services — and is marked `'use client'` because of its interactive state. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with custom `saffron` and `surface` color tokens, so it assumes those exist in the project's Tailwind config. Notable details: the popup is absolutely positioned within a relative inline span (so layout depends on surrounding flow content and a `z-50` stacking context), and the button includes an `aria-label` for accessibility, though the hover-only dismissal means touch users must rely on the click toggle.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\ConsultStri.summary: This file defines `ConsultStrip`, the default-exported React component that renders the "Talk to an expert" section on the home page, presenting three consultation entry points as clickable cards: Ask Pandit (AI Q&A), Talk to an Astrologer (paid live calls), and Wedding Muhurat. Card content and per-card styling are driven by a static `CARDS` array typed by the internal `ConsultCard` type, which carries href, copy, a Lucide icon component, and optional color overrides plus an `emphasis` flag that gives the first card a gradient background and primary-colored border. It depends on `next/link` for client-side navigation, `lucide-react` for icons, and the internal `TextReveal` motion component from `../motion/TextReveal` for the animated section heading. Notable choices include theming entirely through CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-surface`, `--color-text`, etc.) so the strip adapts to the design system, disabling link prefetching (`prefetch={false}`) presumably to avoid loading the destination routes eagerly, and accessibility touches like `aria-labelledby`, `aria-hidden` decorative icons, and `focus-visible` ring styles; the layout is a responsive grid collapsing from three columns to one on mobile.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\HeroCopyVar.summary: HeroCopyVariant.tsx is a client component that runs the `hero_copy_v2` A/B experiment on the home page hero, choosing between a server-supplied control copy (Sanskrit-anchored title and subtitle passed as props) and a hard-coded "benefit" variant aimed at NRI and first-time devotees. It relies on the internal `useExperiment` hook from `../../lib/experiments`, which resolves the variant and fires exactly one `experiment_exposure` analytics event per page view (PostHog is the implied analytics backend per the file's comments). The component exports a single default function accepting `controlTitle1`, `controlTitle2`, `controlSubtitle`, and an optional `children` render-prop that receives the resolved copy plus the variant tag, letting callers customize markup while keeping experiment logic centralized. A notable design decision is that the benefit copy is hard-coded in this file rather than translated, deliberately so PostHog never has to manage untranslated keys, while control copy stays server-rendered for i18n. The default render path tags the wrapper with `data-experiment` and `data-variant` attributes for debugging and styles the headline with CSS custom properties (`--font-display`, `--color-primary`, `--color-text-muted`). The experiment's success criterion, noted in the header comment, is 100+ exposures per variant before calling a winner (tracked as requirement R-Q1-E-009).

apps\\web\\components\\home\\ContinueJou.summary: This file defines `ContinueJourneyCard`, a client-side React component for the web app's home page that nudges returning users back toward their chosen onboarding intent (e.g. "Live Darshan", "Book a Puja", "Ask a Pandit") via a dismissible banner card. The default export wraps its rendering in `OnboardingGate`, imported along with the `PrimaryIntent` type from the sibling module `./_useOnboardingSafe`, which acts as a safety boundary so the card silently renders nothing if the underlying onboarding hook is unavailable (the code comments note the hook may land in a parallel PR). Internally, a static `INTENT_MAP` translates non-null intents (`darshan`, `puja`, `wisdom`, `consult`) into label/href pairs, while the presentational `Card` component renders the banner using `next/link` (with prefetch disabled) and `lucide-react` icons, styled entirely through CSS custom properties like `--color-primary` and `--font-display`. Notable design decisions: the card renders nothing when no `primaryIntent` is recorded or when the intent is `'explore'`, since that intent has no guided destination; and the dismiss handler is defensive, preferring `api.clearIntent` but falling back to `api.setPrimaryIntent(null)`, deliberately clearing only the stored intent while leaving language and NRI flags to the real hook.

apps\\web\\components\\HeaderScrollShado.summary: `HeaderScrollShadow.tsx` is a client component in the Next.js web app (`apps/web`) that adds an Apple-style scroll shadow to the site header. Its single default export, `HeaderScrollShadow`, renders nothing (`null`) and instead uses React's `useEffect`/`useState` to listen for window scroll events, toggling an `is-scrolled` class on the `header[data-scroll-shadow]` element whenever `window.scrollY` crosses an 8px threshold; the actual border and saturation fade are handled by CSS rules following the Josh Comeau backdrop-filter recipe. It exists as a separate component because `layout.tsx` is a server component and cannot use hooks, so this is mounted as a sibling and manipulates the header through direct DOM access rather than refs or props. Dependencies are minimal: only React and browser APIs (`document.querySelector`, `window.addEventListener`). Notable details: the scroll listener is registered with `{ passive: true }` for performance, the component silently no-ops if no matching header is found, and because `scrolled` is in the effect's dependency array, the listener is torn down and re-registered on every threshold crossing — a minor inefficiency offset by the guard that skips redundant state updates.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\NriLaneAbTe.summary: **NriLaneAbTest.tsx** implements the client-side A/B experiment `nri_lane_above_fold`, which tests whether placing an NRI gift-puja promotional card above the fold outperforms the existing below-fold placement. It exports a single default React component `NriLaneAbTest` that takes a `slot` prop (`'above' | 'below'`); the page mounts it twice — once near the top and once at the historical NRI strip location — and each instance renders its content only when the resolved variant matches its own slot, otherwise returning null. The component depends on the internal `useExperiment` hook from `../../lib/experiments` to resolve the variant (defaulting to `'below'`, meaning hidden), and uses `next/link` for navigation to `/gift` plus `Gift` and `ArrowRight` icons from `lucide-react`. A key design constraint is that exposure events must not double-fire despite the double mounting: `useExperiment` guards by experiment key so only the first mount records exposure, which is why the slot is a prop rather than two separate components. Rendered output is a gradient-styled banner linking to `/gift` (with `prefetch={false}`), carrying `data-experiment`, `data-variant`, and `data-slot` attributes for analytics verification, and inline styles reference the CSS variable `--color-bg` for theming.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\TrustStrip..summary: TrustStrip.tsx is a presentational React component for the web app's home page that renders a horizontal strip of trust signals—such as "200+ verified temples," "500+ vetted pandits," "₹0 hidden fees," "80G receipt available," and "Live video proof"—intended to build user confidence near the top of the page. Its only export is the default `TrustStrip` component, backed by a local `TrustItem` type and a hardcoded `ITEMS` array, so the content is static and not driven by any API or CMS. The sole external dependency is `lucide-react`, from which it imports the Shield, Users, BadgeCheck, FileCheck, and Video icons. Styling is done entirely through CSS custom properties (e.g., `--color-surface-offset`, `--color-border`, `--color-primary`, `--color-text-faint`) rather than hardcoded colors, meaning the strip adapts to the app's theming system. Notable details: it is a server-safe component with no state or client-side interactivity, uses an accessible `aria-label` on the section and `aria-hidden` on decorative icons and dot separators, and the dot separators between items are hidden on small screens (`hidden sm:inline`) where items wrap.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\IntentTrio..summary: IntentTrio.tsx is a client-side homepage section that presents three entry-point cards—Live Darshan (/darshan), Book a Puja (/pujas), and Ask a Pandit (/ask-pandit)—so first-time visitors can self-select a journey. The default-exported `IntentTrio` wraps the inner `TrioCards` renderer in `OnboardingGate` (from the sibling module `_useOnboardingSafe`) and returns null when the user's onboarding data already contains a `primaryIntent`, meaning the section only appears for users who haven't declared an intent; the gate's `fallback` renders the cards while onboarding state loads. Card content is hardcoded in a typed `CARDS` array (`IntentCard` type) with per-card icon colors, and icons come from `lucide-react` (Video, Flame, MessageCircleQuestion, ArrowRight). Every card click fires a PostHog `intent_card_click` event via the `capture` helper from `lib/posthog`, tagged with the card's lane and href. Notable details: Next.js `Link` uses `prefetch={false}` (likely to avoid eager-loading three routes on the landing page), theming is done through CSS custom properties like `--color-surface` and `--color-text-muted` rather than Tailwind color classes, and accessibility is handled with a visually hidden `aria-labelledby` heading and focus-visible rings on each card link.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\NextFestiva.summary: NextFestivalStrip.tsx is a homepage conversion component for the Next.js web app that renders an above-the-fold banner highlighting the next upcoming Hindu festival, complete with a days-until countdown and a call-to-action to book a related puja. Its default export, the NextFestivalStrip component, pulls data synchronously from the nextFestival() function in the internal lib/festivals module, which reads a static festival calendar — so the strip renders with zero network cost. A local daysUntil() helper computes the countdown by normalizing today's date to a UTC midnight and diffing against the festival's date2026 field, mapping the result to labels like "Today," "Tomorrow," or "In N days" (negative values collapse to "Recently"). The UI links to /festival/[slug] for details and, when available, promotes the first entry of the festival's pujasAvailable array as a booking button pointing at /pujas/[slug], formatting the slug into readable text. It depends only on next/link for client-side navigation and lucide-react for the Calendar and ArrowRight icons, with no other runtime services. Notable gotchas: the component returns null when no upcoming festival exists, so callers must tolerate an absent strip; the countdown is pinned to the hardcoded date2026 field, meaning the calendar data is year-specific and will need updating (or a nextFestival() that handles year rollover) after 2026; and styling relies on a custom --color-surface CSS variable plus a saffron/amber Tailwind palette.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\ShopStrip.t.summary: ShopStrip.tsx is a presentational Next.js component that renders a "Shop" preview strip on the home page, showcasing a handful of store products (prasad, idols, books, sacred items) as cards linking into the store. Its single default export, ShopStrip, maps over a hardcoded PRODUCTS constant typed by the local Product type (name, category, price, href, accentColor) and renders them in a responsive 2-column/4-column grid, with a header built from the internal motion component TextReveal and a mobile-only "Visit store" CTA button. Dependencies are next/link for navigation, lucide-react for the ShoppingBag and ArrowRight icons, and the sibling module ../motion/TextReveal for animated heading text. Notable design choices: the product data is fully static with no API call, and every card links to the generic /store route rather than individual product pages, so the strip is a teaser rather than a real catalog. All card links set prefetch={false} to avoid unnecessary prefetching of the store page. Styling is driven entirely by CSS custom properties (--color-surface, --color-primary, --color-text, etc.) plus per-product accentColor values for prices and arrows, and the section carries accessibility touches like aria-labelledby, focus-visible rings, and aria-hidden on decorative icons.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\WorshipStri.summary: WorshipStrip.tsx is a presentational React component for the Next.js web app's home page that renders a "Worship" section of four promotional cards linking to core product routes: /darshan (live aarti streaming), /pujas (ritual booking), /gaushala (cow sponsorship), and /donations (80G tax-deductible giving). Its only export is the default `WorshipStrip` component, and it defines a local `WorshipCard` type plus a hardcoded `CARDS` array that inlines marketing copy and pricing (e.g., "Rudrabhishek at Kashi, ₹1,100"), so content changes require editing this file rather than a CMS. Card imagery comes from internal image-registry helpers `getTempleHero` and `getDeityImage` in `../../lib/images`, keyed by temple/deity slugs like 'jagannath-puri' and 'krishna', while icons (Video, Flame, Heart, Gift, ArrowRight) come from lucide-react and the section heading animates via the internal `TextReveal` motion component. Theming is driven entirely by CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-text`, `--font-display`, etc.) rather than Tailwind color classes, which keeps the strip consistent with the app's design-token system. Notable choices include `prefetch={false}` on every Next Link to avoid eager route loading, lazy-loaded plain `img` tags instead of `next/image`, an animated "LIVE" badge on the darshan card, and a responsive 1/2/4-column grid layout.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\WisdomStrip.summary: WisdomStrip.tsx defines the default-exported `WisdomStrip` React component, a homepage section that routes users to the app's daily-wisdom features: panchang, sacred texts, and aarti/mantra audio. It renders three navigation cards driven by a hardcoded `CARDS` array typed by the local `WisdomCard` type (which bundles href, copy, a lucide icon component, and per-card hex colors), linking to `/panchang`, `/content/books`, and `/content`, plus a separate pill-style link to `/astrology/horoscope` beneath the grid. Dependencies are minimal: `next/link` for client-side navigation, `lucide-react` for the Calendar, BookOpen, Music, Moon, and ArrowRight icons, and the internal `TextReveal` motion component for the animated section heading. Styling mixes two approaches — theme CSS variables like `--color-surface`, `--color-bg`, and `--color-text` for layout surfaces, but hardcoded hex values (e.g. `#4F46E5`, `#EEF2FF`) for icons and CTA accents, so these cards won't fully adapt to theme changes. Every `Link` sets `prefetch={false}`, a deliberate choice to avoid eager prefetching of these routes on the homepage. Two gotchas: the section's `aria-labelledby="wisdom-strip-heading"` references an id that no element in the JSX actually carries, so the accessibility hook is broken, and the heading copy promises "horoscope" even though horoscope has no card — only the small footer pill.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\StickyAarti.summary: StickyAartiCta is a client-side React component for the web app's home page that renders a floating pill-shaped reminder counting down to the next temple aarti, deep-linking to the /today schedule page. It exports a single default component, StickyAartiCta, supported by internal helpers nowInIST, nextAartiFrom, and formatCountdown, plus the hardcoded AARTI_SLOTS schedule (Mangal, Shringar, Sandhya, and Shayan Aarti). Its only dependencies are React hooks, next/link for navigation, and lucide-react icons (Flame, X, ArrowRight); it talks to no backend services. The countdown is anchored to Asia/Kolkata via Intl.DateTimeFormat rather than the user's local timezone — note that nowInIST rebuilds the IST parts as a local Date, so the math only works because both now and target are constructed the same way, giving a wall-clock difference. Visibility is gated on scrolling past SHOW_AFTER_PX (800px) and the component is hidden on small screens via the hidden md:block classes. Dismissal is persisted per browser tab using sessionStorage under the darshya:sticky-aarti-cta:dismissed key, so it resets each new session. A one-second interval drives re-renders through a tick state (forced through a useMemo with an eslint-disable), and the timer explicitly pauses on visibilitychange when the tab is hidden — a deliberate battery-drain fix referenced in the code as "Phase D P1 #8".

apps\\web\\components\\home\\YatraStrip..summary: YatraStrip is a presentational React component that renders a homepage section promoting pilgrimage travel packages, displaying three hardcoded destination cards—Char Dham, Vaishno Devi, and Tirupati—with hero images, region labels, and starting prices. The default-exported YatraStrip function maps over an internal DESTINATIONS array of the local Destination type and wraps each card in a Next.js Link pointing to /yatra/destinations. Its dependencies are minimal: next/link for client navigation, Mountain and ArrowRight icons from lucide-react, and the internal getTempleHero helper from lib/images to resolve destination imagery by slug. Notable details include prefetch={false} on every link to avoid eagerly loading the destinations route, lazy-loaded and async-decoded img tags rather than next/image, and styling that mixes Tailwind utilities with inline CSS variables (var(--color-bg), var(--color-border), var(--font-display)) plus hardcoded emerald hex values. Because all three cards share the same href and the data is static in-file, adding or personalizing destinations requires editing this component directly rather than any CMS or API.

apps\\web\\components\\HomeHeroCta.tsx.summary: HomeHeroCta.tsx is a client-side React component that renders the primary call-to-action button in the home page hero, with both its text/destination and background color driven by concurrent A/B experiments. Its single export, `HomeHeroCta`, resolves the `home-hero-cta-text` feature flag via the internal `useFeatureFlag` hook (from `../lib/feature-flags`) to choose between a "control" variant ("Explore Temples" linking to `/temples`) and a "watch-darshan" variant ("Watch Live Darshan" linking to `/darshan`), falling back to the control for any unknown variant value. Independently, it calls `useExperiment` (from `../lib/experiments`) with the `cta_color_test` key to pick a background color — saffron (`var(--color-primary)`, #E16318) or indigo (#4F46E5) — deliberately stacked so the two experiments run without conflicting, with exposure captured by the hook. Externally it depends on `next/link` for navigation and `lucide-react` for the `ArrowRight` icon. Notable design choices include restricting colors to the brand palette (matching the home category strip) so the experiment can never select an off-system color, and emitting `data-experiment`, `data-variant`, and `data-cta-color` attributes on the rendered link for analytics attribution. The file is marked `'use client'` since it relies on client-side flag hooks, and comments note it serves as the legacy A/B seed (layer AL) for the experimentation system.

apps\\web\\components\\Inbox.tsx.summary: This file implements a shared messaging inbox React component (`Inbox`) reused across seven portal routes (devotee /messages plus priest, astrologer, wellness, temple, gaushala, and store-admin message pages), with a `role` prop that tells the backend which side of each conversation to filter. The only export is `Inbox`; internally it renders a conversation list plus a `Thread` subcomponent for the active chat and a `RatingBar` for post-call reviews. It depends on `useAuth` from `../lib/auth-context` for the bearer token, `API_BASE_URL` from `../lib/api-config`, Next.js `Link`, lucide-react icons, and a REST API exposing `/conversations`, `/conversations/:id/messages`, `/conversations/:id/read`, `/conversations/:id/start-call`, and `/ratings`; video calls link out to the existing `/consultation/[room]` page that embeds Jitsi. Both the list and the open thread poll every 3 seconds, but polling pauses when the tab is hidden and the list stops entirely after three consecutive 401/403 responses to avoid hammering the API with an expired token. Message fetching is incremental via a `since` cursor keyed off server time, with client-side dedupe by message id because the manual refetch after sending can overlap with the scheduled poll. The rating prompt is devotee-side only, appears after a system message matching "Call ended," and pre-fills any existing rating fetched from `/ratings/:conversationId` so users see or update their prior submission rather than a blank form.

apps\\web\\components\\home\\_useOnboard.summary: This client-side file provides a defensive adapter for consuming an onboarding hook that ships in a parallel PR and may not exist at build time. It exports the types `PrimaryIntent` (a union of intent strings like `'darshan'`, `'puja'`, `'wisdom'`), `OnboardingData`, and `OnboardingApi`, plus the `OnboardingGate` component, which dynamically imports `../../lib/use-onboarding`, resolves either a named `useOnboarding` or default export, and renders its children render-prop with a normalized API only once the hook is available (otherwise rendering the `fallback`). Its only dependencies are React's `useEffect`/`useState` and the optional internal `apps/web/lib/use-onboarding` module, loaded via a cached `loadHook()` that tri-states between unattempted, unavailable, and resolved. The key design decision is preserving the Rules of Hooks: the real hook is invoked only inside the inner `HookCaller` component, which `OnboardingGate` mounts solely after the hook function is confirmed to exist, and the code carefully wraps function values in thunks when calling `setHook` so React doesn't invoke the stored hook as a lazy initializer or updater. A notable gotcha it handles is shape drift in the real hook — `HookCaller` prefers explicit `clearIntent`/`setPrimaryIntent` helpers but falls back to synthesizing them from a `set(partial)` method, and any error during hook invocation degrades gracefully to `{ data: null }`.

apps\\web\\components\\JitsiCallButton.t.summary: JitsiCallButton.tsx is a Next.js client component in apps/web/components that renders a "Join 1:1 Call" button linking devotee and provider into a shared Jitsi video room for a given booking. Its default export, the JitsiCallButton component, accepts a JitsiCallButtonProps object (bookingId, scheduledAt, optional variant and label) and produces a deterministic room URL of the form meet.jit.si/darshya-<bookingId> via the internal roomUrl helper, so both parties land in the same room without any coordination. The internal withinCallWindow helper gates availability to a two-hour window on either side of scheduledAt (TWO_HOURS_MS), rendering a disabled button with explanatory text outside that window and an anchor tag opening the room in a new tab inside it. The only external dependencies are the Video icon from lucide-react and the free public meet.jit.si service; styling relies on Tailwind theme tokens like saffron-600 and surface-700 plus the --color-border CSS variable. Notable design tradeoffs: there is no call authentication — security rests on the room name being an opaque booking-derived string, and the time window is enforced only client-side, so a determined user could join early. The file's header comment explicitly documents the intended hardening path: swap to a JWT-issuing API endpoint that signs room and expiry claims with a JITSI_JWT_SECRET when paid, auth-gated rooms become necessary. Authorization is delegated upward — the parent component is expected to render this button only when the caller already has booking context. Finally, the window check fails open: a null or unparseable scheduledAt allows the call, on the assumption the parent UI can override.

apps\\web\\components\\LessonCard.tsx.summary: LessonCard is a presentational React component in the Next.js web app (apps/web) that renders a single lesson entry in the Sanskrit learning curriculum, showing its difficulty level, estimated duration, completion state, and score. It default-exports the `LessonCard` function, which takes a `Props` object with `id`, `title`, `subtitle`, `level` ('beginner' | 'intermediate' | 'advanced'), `minutes`, and optional `locked`, `completed`, and `score` flags. Its only dependencies are `next/link` for client-side navigation and `lucide-react` for the `Lock`, `CheckCircle2`, and `Circle` status icons. The key behavioral decision is access gating at the UI level: when `locked` is true the card renders as a plain non-interactive div, but otherwise it wraps the content in a `Link` pointing to `/learn-sanskrit/lesson/${id}`. Visual state is driven entirely by Tailwind utility classes — a `LEVEL_COLOR` lookup maps each difficulty tier to emerald/amber/purple badge colors, completed cards get an emerald border and display the `score` percentage, and available cards use a custom `saffron` accent on hover, indicating a project-specific Tailwind theme with custom `surface` and `saffron` palette tokens. Note that the `Props` interface itself is not exported, so consumers cannot easily reuse the type.

apps\\web\\components\\LangLanding.tsx.summary: LangLanding.tsx is a presentational React component that serves as the shared page shell for the localized landing pages at /hi, /ta, /te, /bn, and /mr. It exports the `LangLandingProps` interface (langCode, langTag, hero strings, CTA labels, a `features` array, NRI-section copy, and footer strings) and the `LangLanding` component, which renders the header, hero, feature-card grid, NRI promo section, and footer while setting the `lang` attribute on the root `<main>`. Its only dependency is `next/link`; all text is supplied by the per-language route files, so this component contains no translation logic itself. A key design decision is that internal links deliberately point to canonical English routes (`/`, `/pujas`, `/darshan`, `/nri`) rather than nonexistent `/lang/*` subpaths, since only the landing pages have been translated. Styling relies on Tailwind utility classes with the project's custom `saffron` and `surface` color tokens. One gotcha: the `featureSectionLabel` and `langTag` props are declared in the interface but never actually rendered by the component, so they appear to be reserved for metadata or future use.

apps\\web\\components\\LibraryMegaPanel..summary: This file defines `LibraryMegaPanel`, a presentational React component (exported both named and as default) that renders a wide 4-column mega-menu panel for the Library section of the `apps/web` Next.js frontend. It receives a `Category` object (typed via `../lib/category-tree`) plus an optional `onItemClick` callback, and renders that category's `subGroups` as columns: each with an uppercase heading, a list of `Link` items, and a "Browse all" hub link (`g.hubHref`/`g.hubLabel`) with a `ChevronRight` icon from `lucide-react`, followed by a bottom strip linking to `/discover` for "Browse all 500+ guides." Dependencies are minimal — `next/link` for client-side navigation, `lucide-react` for icons, and Tailwind utility classes for styling. Design-wise it is a wider variant of the default `CategoryMegaMenu` (960px vs 640px per the doc comment) and invokes `onItemClick` on every link so the parent can dismiss the menu on navigation. One gotcha: the comment promises a fallback to a flat items grid when no `subGroups` exist, but the implementation just maps over `category.subGroups ?? []`, so a category with only flat items would render an empty grid.

apps\\web\\components\\ListYourBusinessD.summary: This file defines a client-side navigation dropdown for the Next.js web app that lets business owners (temples, priests, astrologers, yoga/wellness teachers, and gaushala operators) jump to the onboarding pages where they can list their services. Its single export, `ListYourBusinessDropdown`, renders a "List your business" button that toggles a menu of hard-coded `businessLinks` pointing to routes like `/list-temple`, `/become-priest`, `/become-astrologer`, `/become-wellness`, and `/list-gaushala`, with each menu item implemented as a `next/link` `Link`. It depends only on React hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, `useRef`), Next.js routing, and the `Briefcase`/`ChevronDown` icons from `lucide-react`, with styling done via Tailwind utility classes using the app's `surface` color palette. The component is marked `'use client'` because it manages open/close state and attaches global `mousedown` and `keydown` listeners—registered only while the menu is open—to close the dropdown on outside clicks or the Escape key, and it sets `aria-expanded`/`aria-haspopup`/`role="menu"` attributes for accessibility. A notable constraint is that the entire widget is hidden below the `lg` breakpoint (`hidden lg:block`), so mobile navigation must surface these links elsewhere; the dropdown is also rendered conditionally rather than animated in/out, with the chevron rotation providing the only transition.

apps\\web\\components\\LanguageSwitcher..summary: This Next.js client component (`'use client'`) provides the bilingual language switcher for the Poojly web app, supporting English and Hindi via the exported `SupportedLanguage` union type (`'en' | 'hi'`). The default-exported `LanguageSwitcher` component renders in two modes: a `compact` icon-button that toggles directly between languages, and a dropdown variant built with `lucide-react` icons (`Globe`, `ChevronDown`, `Check`) that closes on outside clicks (tracked via `dropdownRef`) and the Escape key. Selection state is hybrid controlled/uncontrolled: it honors the `currentLanguage` prop and `onLanguageChange` callback when provided, but otherwise self-manages and persists the choice to `localStorage` under the key `poojly_language`, which is read on mount to restore the preference. The file also exports `CONTENT_LABELS`, a `Record<SupportedLanguage, Record<string, string>>` containing all English and Hindi UI strings for the devotional content library page (titles, search placeholder, content-type labels like aarti/chalisa/mantra), effectively doubling as a lightweight i18n dictionary rather than using a dedicated localization module. Notable gotchas: it writes to `localStorage` on every selection even in controlled mode, the Hindi strings are stored as escaped unicode sequences, and styling depends on custom Tailwind theme tokens (`saffron-*`, `surface-*`) defined elsewhere in the design system. Its only external dependency is `lucide-react`; everything else is standard React.

apps\\web\\components\\Logo.tsx.summary: This file defines the Darshya brand logo as inline SVG React components for the web app. It exports `Logo`, which renders a stylized shikhara (temple peak) silhouette enclosing a diya and flame, and `LogoWithText`, which pairs the mark with the "Darshya" wordmark where the final syllable is highlighted in a saffron tone. Both components share the `LogoProps` interface accepting optional `size` (default 28), `className`, and `color` (default `#EA580C`, an orange) props. There are no external dependencies beyond React JSX and no imports; styling hooks rely on project utility classes such as `text-surface-800` and `text-saffron-600`, implying a Tailwind-based design system with custom color tokens. Notably, the logo is built from hardcoded SVG path data on a 48×48 viewBox so it scales cleanly from favicon to display sizes, and while the shikhara/gateway strokes follow the configurable `color` prop, the diya and flame use fixed gold/amber fills (`#D4A438`, `#F59E0B`, `#FDE68A`), so the mark is not truly single-color despite the comment claiming otherwise.

apps\\web\\components\\MobileBottomTabs..summary: This file defines `MobileBottomTabs`, the fixed bottom navigation bar shown only on mobile viewports (`md:hidden`) in the Next.js web app. It exports the component as both a named and default export, rendering four tabs — Home, Book, Library, and Profile — driven by a static `TABS` config where each entry declares an href, a `lucide-react` icon, route prefixes for active-state matching, and a per-lane active color. It builds on `next/link` for routing and `usePathname` from `next/navigation` to compute the active tab via the `isActive` helper, which does exact matching for the root and prefix matching elsewhere; notably the Library tab absorbs a long list of content routes (`/vedas`, `/mantra`, `/tithi`, etc.), reflecting a consolidation from a former 5-tab layout where Darshan had its own tab. The Book tab is flagged `primary` and rendered as an elevated saffron (`bg-saffron-600`) circular button that overflows the bar, making booking the visual call-to-action. The component returns null on `/auth/` and `/checkout/` paths so it doesn't compete with form CTAs, and it respects device safe areas via `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`. Two small gotchas: the JSDoc still says "Fixed 5-tab" and lists Darshan even though the code ships four tabs, and the `Video` icon import is unused.

apps\\web\\components\\motion\\ParallaxL.summary: `ParallaxLayer.tsx` is a client-side React component in the web app's motion toolkit that wraps children in a div and applies a scroll-driven parallax translation based on the element's distance from the viewport center. Its single default export, the `ParallaxLayer` component, accepts `children`, a `speed` multiplier (default 0.15), an optional `className`, and a `maxOffset` clamp (default 80px) that bounds how far the layer can drift. It depends only on React (`useEffect`, `useRef`) and standard browser APIs — `window.matchMedia`, `getBoundingClientRect`, and `requestAnimationFrame` — with no external libraries. Notable design decisions include respecting the `prefers-reduced-motion` media query by zeroing the transform and skipping listeners entirely, throttling scroll/resize handling through `requestAnimationFrame` so updates run at most once per frame, and using passive listeners plus `willChange: 'transform'` with `translate3d` for GPU-friendly animation. Gotchas: the reduced-motion preference is only checked once on mount (changes aren't observed), the effect re-runs when `speed` or `maxOffset` change, and there's a redundant `window === undefined` guard inside `useEffect`, which never executes server-side anyway.

apps\\web\\components\\motion\\ScrambleR.summary: ScrambleReveal.tsx is a client-side React component in the web app's motion library that renders text with an Apple-style character-scramble animation, where each glyph cycles through random alphanumeric characters before snapping to its final form as the element scrolls into view. Its single default export, the ScrambleReveal component, accepts a string as children plus optional props for the rendered tag (h1–h4, p, or span), per-character stagger delay (default 35ms), and scramble duration (default 600ms). It depends only on React core hooks (useRef, useState, useEffect, useMemo) and browser APIs — IntersectionObserver, requestAnimationFrame, matchMedia, and performance.now — with no external animation libraries. Key design choices include triggering the animation once via IntersectionObserver at a 30% visibility threshold, computing per-character lock times as charIndex × stagger + duration to create the staggered "text snaps together" effect, and exempting whitespace and punctuation from scrambling so word shapes stay readable during the animation. Accessibility is handled deliberately: the full text is exposed via aria-label while the animated span is aria-hidden, and users with prefers-reduced-motion (or browsers lacking IntersectionObserver) see the final text instantly with no animation.

apps\\web\\components\\MobileNav.tsx.summary: MobileNav.tsx exports the `MobileNav` React client component, a mobile-only hamburger button and slide-in drawer that consolidates every desktop navigation destination—`primaryLinks`, `moreLinks`, `accountLinks`, and `supportLinks`—into one menu, topped with a highlighted "Ask Pandit" CTA linking to `/ask-pandit`. It is built on `next/link` for routing and `lucide-react` for icons, with two unexported helper components, `NavSection` (a labeled group heading) and `DrawerLink` (a 44px-minimum touch target row with an optional icon and chevron). The key design decision is rendering the drawer and backdrop through `createPortal` into `document.body` after a `mounted` state gate, because the parent `<header>` uses z-50 with backdrop-blur, which creates a stacking context that would otherwise trap the drawer behind page content. Z-indexes are deliberately stacked at z-[100] (backdrop) and z-[101] (drawer) to sit above the fixed header and the `LiveChatWidget` floating button (z-[60]). While open, the component locks body scroll via `document.body.style.overflow` and closes on the Escape key, backdrop click, or any link navigation. Everything is hidden at the `md` breakpoint and up (`md:hidden`), since the desktop nav takes over there, so this component exists purely for small screens.

apps\\web\\components\\MdxRender.tsx.summary: `MdxRender.tsx` is a hand-rolled, dependency-free Markdown renderer for the web app: despite the name, it uses no MDX or markdown library, instead parsing the `body` prop line-by-line into block elements (h1–h3 headings, fenced code blocks, blockquotes, unordered and ordered lists, paragraphs) and a regex pass (`renderInline`) for inline bold, italic, inline code, and links, emitting React elements styled with the app's Tailwind `surface`/`saffron` palette. Its default export `MdxRender` accepts `body` and an optional `glossaryTerms` list; the helper `renderPlain` splits plain-text segments into words and, when a lowercased word matches the glossary set, looks it up via `lookupTerm` from `../lib/glossary` and wraps it in the `GlossaryTooltip` component. Its only dependencies are React, the sibling `GlossaryTooltip` component, and the `lib/glossary` module. Notable constraints: inline formatting is single-pass with no nesting (e.g., no bold inside links), lists support only one level, and inline code contents are rendered verbatim without further parsing; glossary matching is exact-word and case-insensitive, so multiword terms or inflected forms won't be tooltipped.
