External links (those starting with `http`) automatically get `target="_blank"` and `rel="noreferrer"`, and the block parser is stateful by line index, so any line not matching a known prefix is folded into the current paragraph.

apps\\web\\components\\LiveChatWidget.ts.summary: LiveChatWidget.tsx is a client-side React component for the Next.js web app that renders "Asha," Darshya's floating AI support chat widget, letting customers ask about puja bookings, darshan, yatra, and refunds from any page. It exports the `LiveChatWidget` component (both named and default) along with internal `ChatMessage` and `QuickAction` types describing messages and suggested action chips. The widget POSTs each user message plus the last 10 messages of history to `${API_BASE}/api/v1/support/chat` — where `API_BASE` is derived from `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` with trailing slashes and any `/api/v{n}` suffix stripped to avoid double-prefixing — and it depends on `next/navigation` (`usePathname`, `useRouter`), `next/link`, `lucide-react` icons, and the local `findAutoReply` helper from `../lib/support`. A key resilience decision is the 15-second `AbortController` timeout with a local keyword-matching fallback (including hardcoded greeting handling and suggestion links to `/pujas`, `/darshan`, `/yatra`) when the AI endpoint is unreachable. If the backend signals `escalate`, the widget saves a plain-text transcript to localStorage under `poojly:support:chat-transcript` and routes to `/support/ticket/new?from=chat` so the ticket form can pre-fill it — note the legacy "poojly" key prefix despite Darshya branding. The component deliberately renders nothing on provider and admin routes (`/admin`, `/astrologer-portal`, `/temple-portal`, `/store-admin`, `/wellness-portal`, `/gaushala-portal`, `/priest`, `/provider-kyc`) because WhatsApp is the designated support channel for providers. Other gotchas: conversation state lives only in component memory (resetting to the static `WELCOME` message on remount), the `WELCOME` timestamp is computed once at module load, and quick-suggestion chips appear only before the first user message.

apps\\web\\components\\MobileNavV2.tsx.summary: MobileNavV2.tsx is a client component in apps/web/components that provides the mobile-only navigation for the Darshya web app: a hamburger toggle that opens a full-screen sheet containing a sticky header (logo, close button, search input), single-open category accordions, an auth-aware account section, help links, and a sticky "Ask Pandit" CTA. It exports MobileNavV2 as both a named and default export. Navigation content is driven by CATEGORY_TREE and the CategoryKey type from ../lib/category-tree, while the useAuth hook from ../lib/auth-context switches the account links between ACCOUNT_LINKS_AUTHED (dashboard/bookings/profile) and ACCOUNT_LINKS_GUEST (sign-in/bookings); icons come from lucide-react and routing from next/link. Notably, the sheet is rendered via createPortal into document.body — gated by a mounted flag to avoid SSR hydration issues — specifically to escape the fixed header's stacking context, and it mirrors MobileNav.tsx's body scroll-lock and Escape-to-close behavior. Two gotchas worth knowing: the accordion is strictly single-open and clicking the already-active category cannot collapse it (setActiveKey always sets, never toggles), and search submission does a hard navigation via window.location.href to /content?q= rather than using the Next.js router, per the in-code comment that this is the most reliable existing target. The sheet stays mounted off-screen (translate-x-full with pointer-events-none) instead of unmounting, and everything is hidden at the md breakpoint and up.

apps\\web\\components\\MoreDropdown.tsx.summary: This file defines the `MoreDropdown` React component, a client-side navigation element that renders a "More" overflow menu in the desktop header of the Next.js web app, linking to secondary routes such as `/nri`, `/yatra`, `/panchang`, `/gaushala`, `/donations`, `/astrology`, and `/wellness`. The sole export, `MoreDropdown`, is a stateless-ish presentational component whose only local state is whether the menu is open. It builds on `next/link` for client-side navigation and draws all its icons (`ChevronDown`, `Globe2`, `Mountain`, `Calendar`, `Heart`, `Moon`, `Leaf`) from `lucide-react`, with styling done via Tailwind utility classes using the project's `surface` color palette. A key design decision is that open/close is driven by React state rather than a CSS `:hover` rule, deliberately so the menu works on touch devices where hover never fires. The component attaches `mousedown` and `keydown` listeners on `window` only while the menu is open, closing it on outside clicks (checked against a `containerRef`) or the Escape key, and it also closes after any link is clicked to avoid a stale menu post-navigation. Accessibility is handled with `aria-expanded`, `aria-haspopup="menu"`, and `role="menu"`/`menuitem` semantics, plus a rotating chevron as a visual state cue. Because it is marked `'use client'` and relies on window event listeners, it must be rendered as a client component within the app's header tree.

apps\\web\\components\\motion\\StickyHea.summary: StickyHeadlinePin is a client-side React component that renders an Apple-style scroll-pinned headline section: a 180vh outer wrapper provides scroll runway while a sticky inner container holds the headline centered in the viewport as the user scrolls past. The default export accepts a `headline` string plus optional `children` body content and a `className` override. It tracks scroll progress (0–1) across the runway via a passive `scroll`/`resize` listener throttled with `requestAnimationFrame`, then maps that progress to an opacity/scale/translateY curve — fade in over the first 30%, hold through the middle 40%, fade out over the last 30% — applied inline to an `h2` styled with the `--font-display`, `--color-text`, and `--color-text-muted` CSS custom properties. It has no external dependencies beyond React itself; all measurement is done with `getBoundingClientRect` on the outer ref. Accessibility is handled by checking `prefers-reduced-motion` on mount and falling back to a static, fully visible render with no scroll binding. One gotcha: `reducedRef` is a ref read during render, so the reduced-motion branch only takes effect after the mount effect runs, meaning SSR/first paint always assumes full motion.

apps\\web\\components\\motion\\TextRevea.summary: `TextReveal.tsx` is a client-side React component (apps/web) that renders a string as individually animated words, fading and sliding each word up into place when the element scrolls into the viewport. Its default export, `TextReveal`, accepts the `TextRevealProps` interface: the text `children`, an `as` prop constrained to the `AsTag` union (`h1`–`h4` or `p`) so the semantic heading level is preserved, plus `className`, a base `delay`, and a per-word `stagger` (default 60ms). It has no internal or external library dependencies beyond React itself — animation is pure CSS transitions driven by the browser's `IntersectionObserver` API, with a 0.3 intersection-ratio threshold that fires once and disconnects, and a graceful fallback that reveals text immediately if `IntersectionObserver` is unavailable. Notable design decisions: the full string is exposed via `aria-label` on the wrapper while each animated word span is `aria-hidden`, keeping screen readers unaffected by the per-word splitting. A subtle gotcha is the whitespace handling — because `inline-block` on animated spans would collapse trailing spaces, inter-word spaces are rendered as separate text-node siblings of each word span so line wrapping and visible gaps are preserved. The animation uses a fixed `cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1)` easing over 600ms with `willChange` hints, and since it's a pure client component with no reduced-motion check, consumers on motion-sensitive pages should be aware the transition always plays.

apps\\web\\components\\NavCartButton.tsx.summary: NavCartButton.tsx is a client-side React component that renders the shopping-cart button in the app's navigation bar, giving users a one-click way to open the cart drawer and a live count of its contents. Its single default export, the NavCartButton component, pulls itemCount and toggleCart from the internal useCart hook provided by CartContext, so it stays in sync with cart state without managing any state itself. It depends on the lucide-react library for the ShoppingBag icon and on the sibling CartContext module for cart state. Notable details: the count badge renders only when itemCount is greater than zero and caps its display at "99+" to avoid layout breakage with large numbers, and the aria-label embeds the item count for screen-reader accessibility. Styling is done entirely with Tailwind utility classes using the project's saffron/surface color palette, and the "use client" directive is required since the component relies on React context and event handlers.

apps\\web\\components\\NavAuthButton.tsx.summary: This client component renders the navbar's auth-aware control: it shows a loading spinner while session state resolves, a "Sign In" link to `/auth/login` for anonymous visitors, and an avatar-plus-name dropdown menu for signed-in users. The default-exported `NavAuthButton` pulls `user`, `isAuthenticated`, `isLoading`, and `signOut` from the `useAuth` hook and uses the sibling helpers `getRoleLabel` and `getRoleDashboardPath` from `../lib/auth-context` to personalize the menu by role. The dropdown renders a dashboard link plus role-conditional entries—`/bookings` and `/store/cart` for devotees, `/priest` for priests, `/store-admin` for store owners, and `/astrology` for astrologers—each with a lucide-react icon and a color-coded role badge from the local `roleBadgeColors` map. Two notable integration points: the "Restart guided tour" item (hidden for admins) communicates with the onboarding system by dispatching a `darshya:open-onboarding` `CustomEvent` on `window` rather than importing it, and sign-out awaits `signOut()` before forcing a hard navigation to `/` via `window.location.href`. Minor gotchas include the control being hidden on small screens (`hidden sm:inline-flex`), a fallback to a two-letter initials avatar when `avatarUrl` is missing, a default role of `'devotee'` when the user record lacks one, and click-outside dismissal implemented with a `mousedown` listener against a `menuRef`.

apps\\web\\components\\MyProviderProfile.summary: MyProviderProfileCard is a client-side React component in the Next.js web app that renders a dashboard card summarizing the logged-in provider's marketplace profile for a given role. It accepts a `role` (one of the backend MarketplaceRole values such as PANDIT, STORE_OWNER, or TEMPLE_MANAGER), an `onboardingSlug`, and an optional `publicListingType`, then fetches the profile from the backend endpoint `GET /onboarding/provider?role=...` using `API_BASE_URL` and the bearer token from the `useAuth` session context. Depending on state it shows a loading spinner, an amber "complete onboarding" prompt linking to `/onboarding/view`, or the profile summary with an approval badge ("Live on Darshya" vs "Pending approval"), an edit link, and a link to the public listing page. Key dependencies are `next/link`, lucide-react icons, the internal `auth-context` module, and `api-config`. Notable gotchas: demo sessions (tokens prefixed with `demo-`) skip the fetch and always show the onboarding prompt; the display name is role-specific via `getDisplayName` (templeName, storeName, displayName, or gaushalaName); store owners pass `publicListingType: null` and so never get a public-profile link; and the public URL has a hard-coded special case mapping `pandit` to the plural route `/pandits/[id]`.

apps\\web\\components\\OnboardingTrigger.summary: OnboardingTrigger is a client component that decides when the onboarding modal appears in the web app. Its default export renders nothing most of the time, but auto-opens the OnboardingModal after a 1500ms delay (FIRST_RUN_DELAY_MS) when the useOnboarding hook reports both isFirstRun and isFlagEnabled, a delay chosen so the modal doesn't compete with Largest Contentful Paint on initial load. It also supports manual reopening by listening for a custom window event named 'darshya:open-onboarding' (OPEN_EVENT), which other UI like the NavAuthButton menu or mobile drawer can dispatch to summon the modal without direct coupling. The modal itself is loaded via next/dynamic with ssr: false, keeping it out of the server-rendered bundle since it only matters client-side. Key dependencies are the internal useOnboarding hook from ../lib/use-onboarding (which supplies the feature-flag and first-run state) and the lazily imported OnboardingModal component. One subtle behavior: the render guard returns null only when the flag is disabled AND the modal isn't open, so a manually dispatched open event will still show the modal even when the onboarding feature flag is off.

apps\\web\\components\\NotificationPromp.summary: This file defines `NotificationPrompt`, a client-side React component that prompts signed-in users to enable web push notifications for darshan and festival reminders. It renders a fixed bottom-right card whose visibility is driven by a small state machine (`hidden` → `prompt` → `busy` → `error`), appearing only when the browser supports `serviceWorker`/`PushManager`, notification permission is still "default", an access token exists in the `poojly_session` localStorage entry, and the user hasn't dismissed the prompt within the last 7 days (tracked via the `darshya_push_dismissed_at` key); it also waits 4 seconds after mount to avoid flashing on first paint. On opt-in it fetches the VAPID public key from `${API_BASE_URL}/notifications/vapid-public-key`, registers `/sw.js`, requests `Notification` permission, subscribes via `reg.pushManager.subscribe` (converting the URL-safe base64 key with the internal `urlBase64ToUint8Array` helper), and POSTs the subscription to `/notifications/subscribe` with a Bearer token. Dependencies are minimal: `lucide-react` icons (`Bell`, `BellOff`, `X`) and the shared `API_BASE_URL` from `../lib/api-config`, plus browser Push/Notification APIs. Notable gotchas: failures (including permission denial) persist a dismissal timestamp so users aren't re-prompted on every navigation, and error toasts auto-hide after 6 seconds; the server can effectively disable the feature by returning `enabled: false` from the VAPID endpoint; and the localStorage keys are inconsistently namespaced (`poojly_session` vs `darshya_push_dismissed_at`), suggesting a product rename that could bite anyone reading or clearing stored state.

apps\\web\\components\\profile\\AddressM.summary: AddressManager.tsx is a client-side React component rendered on the /profile page that gives devotees a UI for managing delivery addresses (used for prasad delivery and at-home puja visits), closing a gap where the backend address endpoints existed but had no frontend. It default-exports the AddressManager component and defines a local Address interface (id, label, line1/line2, city, state, pincode, country, isDefault); there are no other exports. It depends on the useAuth hook from lib/auth-context for the session access token, API_BASE_URL from lib/api-config, and lucide-react icons, and it talks directly to the backend REST endpoints GET/POST /users/me/addresses plus PATCH and DELETE /users/me/addresses/:id using bearer-token fetch calls rather than a shared API client. Notable behaviors: the first address a user creates is automatically submitted with isDefault set to true, deletion updates local state optimistically while setDefault triggers a full reload, and load/save failures silently keep the existing list while only surfacing errors for the add form. Gotchas include that the form never collects country even though the Address type includes it (so the backend must supply a default), validation is client-side only (line1, city, state, pincode required), and there is no edit flow — users can only add, delete, or mark an address default.

apps\\web\\components\\OnboardingModal.t.summary: This file defines the default-exported `OnboardingModal` React component, a three-step first-run wizard for the web app that captures a new user's primary intent, preferred language, and India-vs-NRI location to personalize their experience. It reads and persists state through the `useOnboarding` hook and the `OnboardingIntent`/`OnboardingLang` types from `../lib/onboarding-store`, resuming at the step stored in `data.currentStep` if the user previously abandoned the flow. Step 1 (`Step1`) offers five intents (darshan, puja, wisdom, consult, explore) rendered from `INTENT_OPTIONS` with `lucide-react` icons; Step 2 (`Step2`) lists six languages but only English and Hindi are marked `active`, with the rest shown as "coming soon"; Step 3 (`Step3`) asks where the user is based to drive currency display. On completion (`handleSelectNri`) it stamps `completedAt`, closes, and hard-navigates via `window.location.assign` to the intent-matching route such as `/darshan` or `/ask-pandit`. Analytics are deliberately decoupled: a local `track()` helper dispatches `darshya:posthog` CustomEvents on `window` (e.g. `onboarding_opened`, `onboarding_completed`) rather than importing PostHog directly. A notable back-compat gotcha is that language selection also writes `ONBOARDING_LANGUAGE_KEY` directly to `localStorage` because the separate `LanguageSwitcher` component reads that key rather than the onboarding store. The component also implements modal hygiene manually — body scroll locking, Escape-to-close, a Tab focus trap, and deferred auto-focus of the dialog — and renders nothing when `open` is false.

apps\\web\\components\\provider\\Earning.summary: EarningsCard.tsx is a client-side presentational component for the provider dashboard that renders a three-tile summary of a provider's earnings. Its default export, the `EarningsCard` component, accepts `totalPaid`, `pending`, `thisMonth`, an optional `currency` (INR or USD, defaulting to INR), and a `loading` flag, then displays stat cards labeled "Paid out," "Pending payout," and "This month." A private `fmt` helper formats amounts with `Intl.NumberFormat` using the `en-IN` or `en-US` locale and zero fraction digits, rendering an em-dash for null or undefined values and an ellipsis while loading. The only external dependency is `lucide-react`, which supplies the `CheckCircle2`, `Clock`, and `TrendingUp` icons, while styling relies on project-specific Tailwind theme tokens such as `tulsi-green`, `saffron`, and `surface`. Notably, the component is purely presentational—it fetches no data itself—so a parent must supply the earnings figures, and all amounts are displayed as whole-currency values with no decimal precision.

apps\\web\\components\\provider\\KycStat.summary: This file defines `KycStatusBadge`, a client-side React component in the provider dashboard that displays a provider's KYC (Aadhaar verification) status as a small colored pill. It accepts a `state` prop typed as `KycState` (`verified`, `pending`, `unsubmitted`, or `rejected`), an optional `reason` string shown beneath the badge in red (typically a rejection explanation), and an optional `href` that defaults to `/provider/kyc`. The component maps each state to a label, Tailwind color classes, and an icon from `lucide-react` (`ShieldCheck`, `Clock`, or `AlertCircle`) via a static `CFG` lookup record, using the project's custom `tulsi-green` design token for the verified state. It depends on `next/link` for navigation and standard Tailwind utility styling, with no internal module imports. A notable design decision is that only non-verified states render as clickable links directing the provider to the KYC submission/resubmission page, while the verified badge is inert text; this makes the badge double as a call-to-action for completing or fixing KYC, which is framed as a prerequisite for payout.

apps\\web\\components\\provider\\Provide.summary: This client-side React module renders verification-tier badges for every provider type on the Darshya platform (priests, astrologers, wellness practitioners, stores, temple managers). Its main exports are the `ProviderTier` union type, the pure `computeProviderTier` function that derives a tier from `aadhaarVerified`, `ratingAvg`, and `ratingCount`, the default `ProviderBadge` pill component (which accepts either a precomputed `tier` prop or raw inputs, with `tier` winning when both are given), and a reusable `RatingDisplay` component that renders a compact star-and-count summary or a "No ratings yet" fallback. Its only external dependency is `lucide-react` for the `ShieldCheck`, `Award`, and `Sparkles` icons, with styling done via Tailwind utility classes in `xs`/`sm` sizes. A key design decision is that tiers are computed on-the-fly at render time rather than stored in a cached database column, so a freshly reviewed provider shows the correct badge on the next page load; the underlying rating aggregates are maintained by `booking.service` when devotees submit post-puja reviews. All tiers are gated on Aadhaar verification (unverified providers always get `none` and the component renders `null`), with thresholds of 100+ ratings at ≥4.5 average for `elite`, 20+ at ≥4.5 for `top_rated`, and 5+ at ≥4.0 for `verified`. Callers should note that providing neither `tier` nor the raw inputs silently yields no badge, since missing values default to zero.

apps\\web\\components\\provider\\Booking.summary: BookingRow.tsx is a presentational client component that renders a single booking as a clickable list row for the provider-facing pages of the Next.js web app. The default-exported `BookingRow` takes all display data via its `Props` (href, title, subtitle, schedule date/time, amount, status label/class, and currency) and wraps the whole row in a `next/link` `Link`, showing a Flame icon avatar from lucide-react, the title with an optional status pill, location and schedule metadata with MapPin and Calendar icons, and a right-aligned amount with an ArrowRight chevron. It has three private formatting helpers: `fmtCur` uses `Intl.NumberFormat` with en-IN/en-US locales and zero fraction digits for INR/USD amounts, `fmtDate` renders dates in en-IN short format, and `fmtTime` converts 24-hour "HH:MM" strings to 12-hour AM/PM form. A notable gotcha guard: `fmtDate` appends `T00:00:00` to date-only strings before constructing a `Date`, preventing UTC parsing from shifting the displayed day in negative-offset timezones. The component is purely dumb — it does no data fetching and holds no state — and defaults to INR with an en-IN locale, reflecting the India-first audience. Callers can override the status badge styling through `statusClass` (falling back to neutral surface colors), and styling relies on custom Tailwind tokens like `saffron-50` and `surface-800` from the app's design system. One subtle behavior: the amount block renders whenever `amount !== undefined`, so an explicitly null amount still displays the block with a dash from `fmtCur` rather than hiding entirely.

apps\\web\\components\\QueryProvider.tsx.summary: `apps/web/components/QueryProvider.tsx` is a client-side wrapper component that wires TanStack Query into the Next.js web app's component tree, so any descendant can use hooks like `useQuery` and `useMutation`. Its single export, `QueryProvider`, takes `children` and renders a `QueryClientProvider` from `@tanstack/react-query`, supplying a configured `QueryClient` instance. The file depends only on React (`useState`, `ReactNode`) and the `@tanstack/react-query` package, with no internal module imports. The `"use client"` directive is required because the component uses React state and context, which cannot run in Next.js server components. A notable design decision is creating the `QueryClient` inside a `useState` initializer: this lazily constructs one stable client per component mount, preventing the cache from being recreated (and wiped) on re-renders and avoiding shared state leakage across requests during SSR — the pattern recommended for App Router setups. Default query behavior is tuned globally here: data stays fresh for 60 seconds (`staleTime`), automatic refetching on window focus is disabled, and failed queries retry only once, so callers inherit conservative, low-churn fetching unless they override it per query.

apps\\web\\components\\provider\\VideoPr.summary: VideoProofUpload is a client-side React component in the provider dashboard that lets a provider attach proof-of-service video to a booking, either by direct file upload or by pasting an external link. It is the default export and takes bookingId, an optional bucket (defaulting to `booking-proofs`), an existingUrl to short-circuit into an "already uploaded" state, and an onUploaded callback that receives the final public URL. Direct uploads go through getSupabaseBrowserClient from `../../lib/supabase` to Supabase Storage, writing to a `${bookingId}/${Date.now()}.${ext}` path with upsert disabled and deriving the shareable link via getPublicUrl; storage was migrated from Cloudflare R2 to Supabase, and the bucket must already exist with suitable RLS policies. Files are validated client-side against a whitelist of MP4, WebM, MOV, and MKV MIME types and a 200MB cap (MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB), with no server-side enforcement visible here. A notable degradation path checks NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY at render time: if either is missing, the dropzone is replaced with an amber notice and only the manual URL input (intended for YouTube, Drive, etc.) is offered, though the manual input is shown alongside uploads regardless. UI is built with Tailwind using the project's custom saffron/tulsi-green/surface palette and lucide-react icons, and since getPublicUrl is used, the component implicitly assumes the bucket is publicly readable.

apps\\web\\components\\Quiz.tsx.summary: This file provides `Quiz`, a client-side React component (`'use client'`) for rendering an interactive multiple-choice quiz in the web app, along with the exported `QuizQuestion` interface that defines each question's text, `options`, `correct` index, and optional `explanation`. The component walks users through one question at a time using local `useState` (`idx`, `selected`, `answers`, `done`), locks the option buttons once a choice is made, immediately highlights correct/incorrect answers, shows the explanation, and then advances via a Next/Finish button. On completion it displays a score summary with per-question pass/fail markers and a Retake button that resets all state, and it reports the final result through the optional `onComplete(score, total)` callback prop. It depends only on React itself; styling is pure Tailwind utility classes using the project's custom `saffron` and `surface` palette tokens, with no backend calls or persistence. Notable gotchas: all progress is ephemeral component state (refreshing or unmounting loses answers and nothing is saved server-side), the score is recomputed in two places (the `done` render branch and the Finish handler), the correct answer is revealed immediately after any selection, and the code relies on non-null assertions like `questions[idx]!`, so passing an empty `questions` array would crash.

apps\\web\\components\\PujaRecommendatio.summary: PujaRecommendationWidget is a client-side React component in the Next.js web app that renders personalized puja (ritual) recommendations for signed-in users. It obtains auth state via `useAuth` from `../lib/auth-context`, then calls two backend endpoints using `API_BASE_URL` from `../lib/api-config`: `GET /users/me` to check whether the profile has a `rashi` or `nakshatra`, and `POST /ai/recommend-puja` (optionally passing a `lifeEvent`) to fetch AI-generated suggestions shaped by the `PujaRecommendation` interface (puja name/slug, deity, reason, date, price range, temple slug). The component gates its UI in three states: unauthenticated users get a sign-in prompt linking to `/auth/login`, users lacking astrological profile fields get a "complete profile" prompt linking to `/profile`, and everyone else sees up to three recommendation cards with deity-specific badge colors from the `DEITY_COLORS` map and "Book Now" links to `/pujas/{pujaSlug}/book?temple={templeSlug}`. A `LIFE_EVENTS` dropdown (career, health, marriage, graha_shanti, etc.) lets users re-fetch recommendations for specific occasions, and changing it re-triggers `fetchRecommendations` via its callback dependency. Notable design choices: the profile check fails open (`setHasProfile(true)`) when `/users/me` errors, so a flaky endpoint never blocks recommendations; loading shows skeleton placeholders; and a retryable error state handles API failures. Icons come from `lucide-react`, and styling is Tailwind with custom `saffron`/`surface`/`temple-gold` palette classes.

apps\\web\\components\\ReferralCapture.t.summary: ReferralCapture.tsx is a client-side React component that renders nothing but implements the web app's referral-attribution flow: it captures a `?ref=CODE` query parameter from any page into a 30-day cookie (`darshya_ref`), then automatically claims it via a POST to the backend's `/referrals/claim` endpoint once the user authenticates. The single exported component, `ReferralCapture`, relies on `useAuth` from `../lib/auth-context` for session state and `API_BASE_URL` from `../lib/api-config` to reach the API, plus a lazily imported `../lib/posthog` module to fire a `referral_claim_signed_up` analytics event on successful new claims. Code capture is sanitized (uppercased, alphanumeric-only, 4–16 characters) and follows last-touch-wins semantics — a newer `?ref=` overwrites the existing cookie and resets the localStorage claim flag so the new code can be claimed. Claiming is designed to be idempotent: a `useRef` guard prevents duplicate calls within a mount, a localStorage flag (`darshya_ref_claimed`) prevents repeats across sessions, and the server endpoint itself dedupes, with HTTP 201, 200, and 400 (self-referral) all treated as terminal "done" states. Notably, demo tokens (those starting with `demo-`) are skipped since the API rejects them, the `Secure` cookie attribute is only set over HTTPS, and network failures are silently swallowed so the claim simply retries on a future session.

apps\\web\\components\\RoadmapRail.tsx.summary: `RoadmapRail.tsx` is a client-side React component that renders a scroll-driven product roadmap section for the web app. Its default export `RoadmapRail` accepts a `milestones` array (typed by the exported `Milestone` interface and `MilestoneIconKey` union) and presents it two ways: on desktop (`hidden md:block`) as a sticky-pinned horizontal rail where a tall outer wrapper (`N * 85vh`) converts vertical scroll into horizontal translation of cards that snap to a centered "You are here" playhead, with the background cross-fading between per-milestone gradients; on mobile as `MobileStack`, a vertical timeline whose active card is tracked via `IntersectionObserver` because the horizontal pin would conflict with native touch scrolling. Internal helpers include `RailCard` (individual milestone card with accent-tinted styling), `StatusPill` (renders shipped/now/planned/vision badges), and `jumpToMilestone` (computes a scroll target from section geometry so progress dots can deep-link to a milestone). The only external dependency beyond React is `lucide-react`, whose icons populate the `ICONS` map; styling relies on Tailwind with custom theme tokens like `saffron-*`, `surface-*`, and `font-display`. Notable constraints: scroll updates are throttled through `requestAnimationFrame`, users with `prefers-reduced-motion` get a static first milestone with no scroll listeners attached, and the card geometry is hardcoded (24rem cards with a 4rem gap forming a 28rem stride), so the centering padding and translate math assume those values stay in sync.

apps\\web\\components\\StreakBadge.tsx.summary: StreakBadge.tsx is a presentational React component in the web app that renders a pill-shaped badge displaying a user's day streak, complete with a Flame icon from the lucide-react library. It exports a single default component, StreakBadge, which accepts a required days count, an optional longest streak value, and an optional size prop ('sm', 'md', or 'lg', defaulting to 'md') that maps to a fixed lookup of Tailwind CSS utility classes for padding, text size, and icon dimensions. The component has no internal dependencies beyond lucide-react and relies entirely on Tailwind for styling. A notable design decision is the active/inactive visual state: when days is greater than zero the badge gets an orange-to-red gradient background, otherwise it renders in muted surface tones, and the longest streak is surfaced only through a native title tooltip rather than visible text. It also handles pluralization inline, rendering "1 day" versus "N days" based on the count.

apps\\web\\components\\SentryErrorBounda.summary: This file defines `SentryErrorBoundary`, a React error boundary for the web app (`apps/web`) that catches errors thrown anywhere in its child render tree and reports them to Sentry. It exports a single class component — required because React's error boundary lifecycle methods (`getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`) are only available on class components — which accepts `children` and an optional `fallback` prop. When a descendant component throws during rendering, `componentDidCatch` forwards the error to `captureBrowserException` from the internal `../lib/sentry` module, attaching the React `componentStack` as context, and the boundary swaps its children for a fallback UI. If no custom `fallback` is provided, it renders a minimal inline-styled "Something went wrong. Please refresh." message using system fonts, deliberately avoiding any app components that might themselves be broken. The file is marked `'use client'`, and its stated purpose is to catch render-tree errors that never reach Next.js's `global-error` handler, making it a complement to — not a replacement for — the framework-level error page. A notable constraint is that the boundary is a one-shot latch: once `hasError` flips to true there is no reset mechanism, so the user must refresh to recover.

apps\\web\\components\\ScrollReveal.tsx.summary: ScrollReveal.tsx is a client-side React component (default export `ScrollReveal`) that wraps page content and orchestrates all scroll-driven animation for the web app: reveal-on-scroll, text highlighting, animated number counters, parallax, and a scroll progress bar. It renders only its children and does all work inside a single mount-time `useEffect`, using four IntersectionObservers (`revealObserver` for `[data-reveal]` elements, `highlightObserver` for `.text-highlight`, `counterObserver` for `[data-counter]`, and `parallaxVisibilityObserver` for `[data-parallax]`) plus a passive, rAF-throttled scroll listener guarded by a `ticking` flag. Its only dependency is React itself — all animation is hand-rolled with DOM APIs, including `animateCounter`, which parses an optional ₹/$ prefix and suffix off the target value and eases the number over 1200ms with cubic ease-out. A key performance design decision is that parallax transforms are only computed for elements flagged visible by a dedicated observer with a 200px viewport buffer, so off-screen elements never trigger `getBoundingClientRect` reads or style writes; reveal/highlight/counter observers also self-unobserve after first activation. The component honors `prefers-reduced-motion` by skipping parallax registration entirely and snapping counters straight to their final value. A notable gotcha is that it queries `document` globally rather than scoping to its own subtree, so it will animate matching elements anywhere on the page — and only those present at mount time, meaning dynamically injected `[data-reveal]` or `[data-parallax]` nodes are never observed.

apps\\web\\components\\ServiceWorkerRegi.summary: `ServiceWorkerRegister.tsx` is a client-side React component whose sole job is to register the `/sw.js` service worker unconditionally on first visit, so the offline page and push-notification contract are active even before a user opts into notifications — a requirement traced to KPI R-Q2-E-016. It exports a single component, `ServiceWorkerRegister`, which renders nothing and performs registration inside a `useEffect`. Its only dependencies are React (`useEffect`) and the browser's Service Worker and `requestIdleCallback` APIs; it talks to no internal modules or external services. Notable design choices: registration is deferred to browser idle time (falling back to a 1500ms `setTimeout` when `requestIdleCallback` is unavailable) so the SW install doesn't compete with first-paint network traffic. It is safe to mount on every page because `navigator.serviceWorker.register()` is idempotent, and it guards against SSR (`typeof window === "undefined"`) and unsupported browsers. Failures — e.g. private browsing mode — are swallowed silently since they are considered non-fatal.

apps\\web\\components\\SentryProvider.ts.summary: This file provides `SentryProvider`, a renderless React client component in the Next.js web app whose sole job is to bootstrap Sentry error tracking in the browser. On mount, it invokes `initSentryBrowser` from the internal `../lib/sentry` module and renders nothing, so it can be dropped into the app tree (typically the root layout) without affecting the UI. Its only dependencies are React's `useEffect` and that internal sentry helper, which presumably wraps the Sentry SDK itself. The `'use client'` directive is required because initialization must happen in the browser, not during server-side rendering. The empty dependency array guarantees initialization runs exactly once per mount, and deferring the call to an effect rather than module scope keeps Sentry setup out of the server bundle and ensures it only executes in a real browser environment. Note that it returns `null`, so despite the "Provider" name it provides no React context — it is purely a side-effect component.

apps\\web\\components\\StripeClientSecre.summary: This client component renders an embedded Stripe Payment Element checkout for bookings where the server supplies a payment `clientSecret` but no hosted checkout URL. Its sole export, `StripeClientSecretCheckout`, takes a `clientSecret`, `bookingNumber`, `returnUrl`, and an `onMailtoFallback` callback; internally it defines a `CheckoutForm` that calls `stripe.confirmPayment` with the supplied return URL to handle SCA redirects, displaying inline error messages and a processing spinner via `Loader2` from lucide-react. It builds on `@stripe/stripe-js` (`loadStripe`) and `@stripe/react-stripe-js` (`Elements`, `PaymentElement`, `useStripe`, `useElements`), with the `Elements` provider configured with a custom `appearance` theme (saffron primary color, 8px radius) and the `PaymentElement` set to a tabs layout with Apple Pay and Google Pay wallets auto-detected. A key design decision is graceful degradation: the module reads `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` at load time, and if absent it renders an amber warning card that hands off to the mailto fallback instead of crashing, so the booking flow still completes via email support. The Stripe instance is memoized in a module-level singleton `stripePromise` to avoid re-initialization across renders, and the submit button stays disabled until both `stripe` and `elements` report ready. The header comment notes this file completes the Sprint 3 "Stripe Elements full Provider" item, meaning the only remaining integration work is environment wiring of the publishable key.

apps\\web\\components\\SelfOnboardPageSh.summary: This file defines `SelfOnboardPageShell`, a presentational React layout component in the web app that wraps self-service onboarding pages—apparently for partners (likely priests or service providers) applying to join the Darshya marketplace. It accepts an `eyebrow` label, `title`, `subtitle`, a list of `benefits` (title/body pairs), and a `formCard` ReactNode, then renders a centered hero header, a responsive benefit-card grid (up to four columns), the injected form inside a styled card, and a hardcoded "What happens next" section describing a 48-hour partnerships review, verification call, and profile go-live. Its only dependency is React's `ReactNode` type; there are no internal module imports, data fetching, or state. Theming is done entirely through CSS custom properties (`--color-primary`, `--color-bg`, `--color-text`, `--color-surface`, `--color-border`, `--font-display`) with warm-toned fallback hex values, so the shell adapts to whatever theme tokens the host app defines. Layout uses Tailwind utilities, with `min-h-[calc(100vh-3.5rem)]` implying a fixed 3.5rem global header above it. Notable constraints: the "What happens next" copy is baked in and not customizable per consumer, benefit cards are keyed by `title` (duplicate titles would break React keys), and the fixed three-step process text means this shell is only suitable for flows matching that review pipeline.

apps\\web\\components\\TempleHeartShareB.summary: TempleHeartShareButtons is a client-side React component that renders floating "favorite" (heart) and share buttons on a temple detail page, plus a transient toast notification. Its single default export takes a temple `slug` and `templeName` and manages favoriting entirely client-side: favorites are persisted as a JSON string array in `window.localStorage` under the key `poojly_favorite_temples`, with defensive parsing and silent no-ops on storage failures (quota, disabled storage, SSR). Sharing prefers the Web Share API (`navigator.share`) with the current `window.location.href`, falling back to `navigator.clipboard.writeText` when the API is unavailable or the user cancels, and reporting the outcome via a toast that auto-dismisses after three seconds. It depends only on React hooks and the `lucide-react` icons `Heart` and `Share2`, with styling via Tailwind utility classes including a custom `bg-surface-800` token. Notable details: there is no backend sync for favorites, so state is per-device and per-browser; accessibility is handled with `aria-pressed`, `aria-label`, and an `aria-live` toast region; and there is a branding inconsistency — the storage key references "poojly" while the share text and fallback URL reference "Darshya"/`darshya.online`, suggesting a rebrand.

apps\\web\\components\\SelfOnboardForm.t.summary: SelfOnboardForm.tsx is a client component in the Next.js web app (apps/web) that renders the self-service application form prospective providers — temples, priests, astrologers, wellness instructors, and gaushalas — use to request onboarding onto the platform. The default export SelfOnboardForm accepts a role (typed as the exported OnboardRole union), a ctaLabel, and an extraFields ReactNode slot, renders the shared contact fields (fullName, email, phone, city, state), and POSTs the collected data as JSON to `${NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL}/api/v1/leads/self-onboard`, defaulting to https://api.darshya.online. The companion exports ExtraInput, ExtraSelect, and ExtraCheckbox are pre-styled field primitives meant to be composed into the extraFields slot so each role-specific page can add its own questions without duplicating submission logic. The file depends only on React (useState, FormEvent) and the browser fetch API — no internal modules, form libraries, or validation packages. Submission builds the payload from FormData, trimming strings and silently dropping empty values, injects the role into the body, and expects the backend to answer with `{ ok, leadId?, error? }`, surfacing json.error on any failure. Styling is done via inline styles keyed to CSS custom properties (--color-primary, --color-bg, --color-border, --color-text) with hardcoded fallbacks, so the form inherits page theming while Tailwind classes handle only layout. Gotchas worth noting: validation is limited to HTML required/type attributes, checkboxes submit the literal string "yes", and on success the form resets and shows a fixed "review within 48 hours" message.

apps\\web\\components\\SubscriptionPanel.summary: `SubscriptionPanel.tsx` is a client-side React component that renders the marketplace subscription UI for the Darshya web app, letting providers browse plans for their role, view their current subscription, subscribe, or cancel. It exports a single `SubscriptionPanel` component (parameterized by a `ProviderRole` with optional title/description), supported internally by a `StatusPill` badge and `formatINR`/`formatDate` helpers that localize prices and dates to Indian conventions. It depends on `useAuth` from `../lib/auth-context` for the session token and user prefill data, and on `../lib/subscription-api` for `listPlans`, `getMySubscription`, `subscribeToPlan`, `cancelMySubscription`, and `openRazorpayCheckout`, plus the `SubscriptionPlan` and `MarketplaceSubscription` types; Razorpay is the external payment service it integrates with. The subscribe flow first creates a subscription server-side, then attempts to open the Razorpay checkout modal, falling back to opening the returned `shortUrl` in a new tab when the modal can't load or isn't applicable, and refreshes the local subscription state on payment success. Notable details: plan listing failures are swallowed so the page still renders with an empty-state message, the cancel button only appears when status is `active`, plan cards derive their CTA state from whether the plan is the current one, and commission override plus max-listings are always surfaced as headline features alongside any custom `features` list.

apps\\web\\components\\support\\badges.t.summary: This file provides the presentational badge components and date-formatting helpers used across the support-ticket UI in the web app. It exports `StatusBadge` and `PriorityBadge`, two small React components that render a styled pill by looking up Tailwind class strings and human-readable labels in the `STATUS_CLASS`/`STATUS_LABEL` and `PRIORITY_CLASS`/`PRIORITY_LABEL` maps, keyed by the `TicketStatus` and `TicketPriority` union types imported from the internal `lib/support` module. It also exports `formatDate` and `formatDateTime`, which format ISO strings with the hard-coded `en-IN` locale, and `timeAgo`, which renders relative timestamps ("just now", minutes/hours/days) and falls back to `formatDate` once a ticket is older than 30 days. There are no external runtime dependencies beyond React and the native `Date` API; styling relies on Tailwind utilities including a custom `surface-*` color palette. Because the maps are typed as `Record<TicketStatus, string>` and `Record<TicketPriority, string>`, TypeScript enforces exhaustiveness—adding a new status or priority in `lib/support` will fail compilation until these tables are updated, which is a deliberate safety net but also a coupling to remember. All components are pure and client-safe, with no state or side effects.

apps\\web\\components\\ui\\CityAutocompl.summary: CityAutocomplete.tsx is a client-side React component (default-exported as `CityAutocomplete`) that provides an accessible combobox-style input for selecting a city, primarily from an Indian city database. It is a thin UI layer over the internal `lib/indian-cities` module, relying on its `findCity` search function, `formatCityLabel` helper, and `CityRecord` type, plus `lucide-react` icons (`MapPin`, `AlertTriangle`) for visual affordances — all searching is local and synchronous, so there is no network call or debounce logic. The component exposes a controlled `Props` interface (`value`, `onChange`, optional `placeholder`, `required`, `className`) and communicates selection upward only through `onChange(city | null)`. Notable behaviors: any keystroke after a selection clears it via `onChange(null)`, forcing the parent to treat free-text input as uncommitted; a "city not found" amber warning appears once the query reaches three characters with zero results, steering users to pick from the list; and a green confirmation chip showing `formatCityLabel(value)` renders beneath the input when a selection exists. Accessibility is handled deliberately with `role="combobox"`/`listbox`/`option`, `aria-activedescendant`, and full keyboard support (Arrow keys, Enter, Escape, and Tab-to-select), while dropdown dismissal relies on a document-level `mousedown` listener and options use `onMouseDown` rather than `onClick` so selection fires before input blur. Each suggestion row also displays formatted latitude/longitude and appends the country code for non-`IN` records, signaling the dataset is India-centric but not India-exclusive.

apps\\web\\components\\temples\\TemplesB.summary: TemplesBrowser.tsx is a Next.js client component that renders the temple discovery page — a hero with search, a filter bar, and a responsive grid of temple cards linking to `/temples/[slug]` detail pages. Its main export is the `TemplesBrowser` component, which receives a pre-fetched `temples` array and `total` count (filtering happens entirely client-side, so the parent page must supply the full dataset), along with the types `DeityTypeFilter`, `SortMode`, and the `TempleCardData` interface describing each card's fields; a private `TempleCard` subcomponent renders individual cards with badges for Jyotirlinga, Shakti Peetha, Divya Desam, Verified, and live-darshan status plus viewer counts formatted with the `en-IN` locale. It depends on `next/navigation` hooks, `lucide-react` icons, and the internal `lib/images` module, whose `getTempleHero`, `getDeityImage`, and `wikiThumb` helpers power a three-level image fallback chain (temple `imageUrl`, then a slug-based hero lookup, then a generic deity image via `deityFallbackKey`) resized to 800px Wikimedia thumbnails. Notable design choices include a 200ms debounced mirror of the search input (filtering reads `debouncedSearch`, not the raw state) to avoid re-filtering 200+ temples per keystroke, and bidirectional URL synchronization — filters initialize from `useSearchParams` and are written back via `router.replace` with `scroll: false`, making filtered views shareable without navigation jank. Sorting supports popularity (default), alphabetical, and state modes via `localeCompare`, and the state dropdown options are derived from the data itself rather than hardcoded. One gotcha: `TempleCardData` includes `trustScore`, `tradition`, and `hasRichDetail` fields that the card never renders, so they exist only for upstream data shaping.

apps\\web\\components\\ui\\DateInput.tsx.summary: This file provides the app's branded date-picking components, deliberately avoiding any native browser calendar by rendering a `type="text"` input paired with a fully custom React popover grid—no `type="date"` anywhere in the DOM, so Chrome's native picker can never appear. The main export, `DateInput` (also the default export), accepts an ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` value and `onChange` callback via `DateInputProps`, but displays and accepts typed input in `DD/MM/YYYY` format, with internal helpers `formatForDisplay`, `parseFromDisplay`, `toIso`, `parseIso`, and `isInRange` handling conversion and lexicographic min/max bound checks. The popover offers month chevron navigation, a year dropdown spanning 1900 through current year + 5, today/selected highlighting, out-of-range disabling, Clear and Today footer actions, and closes on outside click via a `mousedown` listener on `containerRef`. A second export, `DateTimeInput`, composes `DateInput` with a native `type="time"` field side by side, committing a combined `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM` string only once both parts are filled. Dependencies are minimal: React hooks and `lucide-react` icons (`CalendarDays`, `ChevronLeft`, `ChevronRight`), styled with the project's saffron/surface Tailwind design tokens. Notable gotchas: invalid or out-of-range text reverts to the last valid value on blur, and `DateTimeInput` silently drops changes until both date and time are present.

apps\\web\\components\\useIsPremium.ts.summary: This file defines a client-side React hook, `useIsPremium`, whose job is to decide whether the current user qualifies for premium treatment—chiefly to mute ad rendering—returning a plain boolean. It pulls the current user via `useAuth` from the internal `../lib/auth-context` module and immediately returns false for anonymous visitors, so logged-out users always see ads. The hook checks the user's `subscriptionTier` against an internal `PREMIUM_TIERS` Set containing 'pro', 'premium', 'bhakti_pass', and 'annual_ratna', where 'premium' is retained only for backward compatibility with older accounts and Bhakti Pass/Pro map to the ₹499/mo and ₹5000/yr plans noted in the comment. As a secondary path, it also honors a duck-typed `isNriPremium` boolean flag, accessed through an inline type cast, which signals that this field may not be part of the formally typed user model in `auth-context`. Notable gotchas: the file requires the `'use client'` directive because it depends on React context, all premium logic is hardcoded client-side with no server verification, and any new subscription tier must be added to `PREMIUM_TIERS` here or ads will incorrectly render for those subscribers.

apps\\web\\components\\WhatsAppButton.ts.summary: This file provides a floating WhatsApp contact button for the Next.js web app, letting visitors open a pre-addressed chat with the Darshya support team in a single tap. It default-exports a single client component, `WhatsAppButton`, which renders a fixed circular anchor (`<a>`) linking to a `wa.me` deep link that pre-fills the greeting "Namaste! I have a question about Darshya." via `encodeURIComponent`. The destination number comes from the `NEXT_PUBLIC_WHATSAPP_NUMBER` environment variable, falling back to a hardcoded Indian number (919255109400) when unset — worth noting since the fallback silently ships a real phone number. Its only external dependency is the `MessageCircle` icon from `lucide-react`, styled with the WhatsApp brand green (#25D366). The component is marked `'use client'` though it contains no interactivity beyond the link itself. Positioning is a deliberate constraint: it sits fixed at `bottom-20` with `z-[59]`, suggesting it is intentionally stacked above other floating UI (and below modals at z-60+), so layout changes to other floating elements could cause overlap. The link opens in a new tab with `rel="noopener noreferrer"` and carries an `aria-label` for accessibility.

apps\\web\\components\\VedicTimeline.tsx.summary: VedicTimeline.tsx is a purely presentational React component in the apps/web frontend that renders a static vertical timeline titled "Timeline of Sanatan Dharm," summarizing roughly 3,500 years of Vedic and Hindu religious history. Its single default export, VedicTimeline, maps over a hardcoded ERAS array — typed by a local Era interface with period, name, and description fields — containing nine entries spanning from the Early Vedic/Rigvedic period (~1500 BCE) through the Brahmana, Upanishadic, Sutra, Classical, Puranic/Bhakti, and Medieval Bhakti eras to the modern revival. The component has no props, state, hooks, or data fetching; its only real dependency is the Tailwind CSS utility system, and it relies on custom theme tokens (saffron-200/500/700, surface-600/900), so it will break visually if those palette extensions are removed from the Tailwind config. Styling constructs the timeline effect with a left border on the ordered list plus absolutely positioned dot markers per entry. Notable gotchas: all content is editorialized and hardcoded in-file rather than sourced from a CMS or data layer (so updates require code changes), and list items use the array index as a React key, which is safe only because the data is static and never reordered.

apps\\web\\components\\YouTubeEmbed.tsx.summary: This file defines `YouTubeEmbed`, a small React component in the web app's component library that renders a responsive YouTube video player given a raw URL. It accepts a `url` and optional `title` prop, and relies on the unexported helper `getYouTubeId`, which extracts the 11-character video ID from watch, youtu.be, or embed-style URLs via regex matching. The component has no internal module dependencies beyond React itself, styling via Tailwind utility classes, and the external YouTube iframe embed service. Notably, it embeds via the privacy-enhanced `youtube-nocookie.com` domain with `rel=0` and `modestbranding=1` parameters to limit tracking and related-video noise. The player maintains a 16:9 aspect ratio using the classic `paddingBottom: "56.25%"` CSS trick and sets `loading="lazy"` on the iframe to defer loading offscreen embeds. One gotcha: if the URL doesn't match any recognized YouTube pattern, the component silently renders nothing rather than surfacing an error or fallback UI.

apps\\web\\components\\YouTubeDarshanPla.summary: This file defines `YouTubeDarshanPlayer`, the default-exported React client component (marked `'use client'`) in the `apps/web` Next.js app that embeds live temple "darshan" video streams via YouTube iframes. It accepts three optional props—`videoId`, `channelId`, and `attribution`—and resolves them with a fallback chain: a specific `videoId` produces a privacy-enhanced `youtube-nocookie.com` embed with `modestbranding=1`, `controls=1`, and `rel=0` parameters; otherwise a `channelId` falls back to YouTube's generic `live_stream?channel=` embed; if neither exists, it renders a static "Stream offline" placeholder instead of a player. The component has no internal-module or external-library dependencies beyond React and Tailwind utility classes (`aspect-video`, `bg-surface-100`, etc.) for styling the 16:9 responsive container. Notable design choices include preferring the no-cookie YouTube domain to limit tracking of devotional-site visitors, enabling `allowFullScreen` and standard iframe permissions for playback, and conditionally rendering an attribution line crediting the live source and noting the stream is "Operated by temple trust"—a likely legal/transparency requirement. The main gotcha is that all props are nullable, so callers must tolerate the offline state, and the `channelId` live-stream embed uses the standard `youtube.com` domain rather than the no-cookie variant.

apps\\web\\components\\VoicePanditButton.summary: VoicePanditButton.tsx is a client-side React component ("use client") implementing the R-Q3-E-001 Voice AI Pandit v1 push-to-talk widget: the user holds a saffron mic button to record audio with the browser MediaRecorder API, releases to POST base64-encoded audio to /api/v1/voice-pandit/turn on the backend (NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL, defaulting to https://api.darshya.online), then autoplays the returned mp3 and renders the transcript/reply pair. The default-exported VoicePanditButton accepts a language prop ('en' | 'hi') and manages a status state machine ('idle' | 'recording' | 'uploading' | 'playing' | 'error') via refs for the MediaRecorder, audio chunks, mic stream, and playback Audio element; a private blobToBase64 helper strips the data: prefix before upload, and the TurnResponse type captures transcript, reply, audioBase64, latency_ms, an stt/llm/tts breakdown_ms, and a demo flag. Its only hard dependencies are react and lucide-react icons (Mic, Square, Loader2, Volume2); PostHog analytics are optional, fired defensively through window.posthog.capture with events like voice_pandit_session_started, voice_pandit_turn_complete, and voice_pandit_session_error. Notable design decisions target the sub-3-second mic-stop-to-first-audio-frame latency budget: the getUserMedia stream is reused across turns to avoid ~200 ms re-acquisition cost, and the MIME type is negotiated from a candidate list (webm/opus first, mp4 for Safari) via MediaRecorder.isTypeSupported. Gotchas include autoplay blocking (playback failure silently returns to idle rather than erroring), mouse-leave during a hold auto-sends the recording, touch handlers preventDefault to avoid double-firing with mouse events, and mic tracks are released only on unmount.

apps\\web\\e2e\\capture-pitch.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright spec is a marketing capture suite, not a regression test: it drives the live site (defaulting to https://darshya.online, overridable via the `PITCH_BASE_URL` environment variable) through the product's golden flows and saves numbered PNG keyframes plus 1920x1080 MP4 video into a `pitch-captures/` directory, which are then assembled into the investor walkthrough video and the `/pitch` interactive deck. It exports no reusable API; its building blocks are a `test.describe('pitch capture — golden flows')` block containing twelve sequential tests (01-home-hero through 12-ai-chat) and a private `snap()` helper that writes viewport screenshots to `OUT_DIR`. It depends on `@playwright/test` for the browser runner and on Node built-ins (`node:path`, `node:fs`, `node:url`) for output directory management, and it exercises the web app's main public routes: `/temples`, `/pujas`, `/darshan`, `/panchang`, `/astrology`, `/gaushala`, `/store`, `/yatra`, and the Asha AI chat widget. Notable design choices include `test.use` settings that force a 1080p viewport with video and screenshots always on but tracing off, a generous 120-second per-test timeout, and fixed `waitForTimeout` sleeps instead of semantic waits, since visual polish matters more than speed here. Gotchas: several tests silently no-op when a selector finds nothing (e.g. no temple links or chat button), so captures can be missing without failing, the AI chat test fills a question but never submits it, and the suite hits the production site, so its output depends on live content and availability.

apps\\web\\e2e\\debug-screenshot.spec.ts.summary: This file is a Playwright end-to-end debugging spec whose sole purpose is to capture a full-page screenshot of the app's home page for visual inspection. It defines a single test, "capture home page," which navigates to `http://localhost:3000`, waits for network idle plus a hard-coded 2-second delay, and saves the result to `debug-home.png`. Its only dependency is the `@playwright/test` package, and it exports nothing for other modules to consume. Notable gotchas: the test assumes a dev server is already running on port 3000, relies on a brittle fixed timeout rather than waiting for specific elements, and writes its artifact to a relative path, making it a manual debugging utility rather than an assertion-based regression test.

apps\\web\\e2e\\asha-chat.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec (`apps/web/e2e/asha-chat.spec.ts`) validates the "Asha" AI support chat widget in the web app, running against `http://localhost:3000` with `@playwright/test`. It covers the widget's core behaviors: normal messages must never surface the "couldn't reach the AI service" error, a greeting like "Hi" should get a friendly "Namaste" reply without escalation, a puja-booking question should return an action chip linking to `/pujas`, and refund requests above ₹5,000 or explicit "talk to human" asks should trigger escalation via a "Talk to Human Agent" button. One test verifies the escalation handoff end-to-end: clicking that button navigates to `/support/ticket/new?from=chat`, where the subject ("Escalated from AI chat") and description are prefilled from the chat transcript. The spec depends on the chat widget's DOM contract — an `aria-label="Open live chat"` button and a textarea whose placeholder contains "Darshya" — plus the ticket-creation page and the `/pujas` route. Notable gotchas: the `beforeEach` retries the open button up to five times to avoid clicking before React hydration completes, tests rely on fixed `waitForTimeout` delays rather than deterministic waits, and the transcript is handed to the ticket form via localStorage, which is why the test pauses after navigation for the client component to hydrate.

apps\\web\\lib\\api-config.ts.summary: This module provides the single source of truth for the Fastify backend's base URL in the Next.js web app, exporting one constant, `API_BASE_URL`. The value is resolved at module load from the `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` environment variable, falling back to the production default `https://api.darshya.online` when unset. A small `resolve()` helper normalizes the value by stripping any trailing slash and appending the `/api/v1` prefix if it isn't already present, so consumers can write paths like `${API_BASE_URL}/ai/chat` without worrying about versioning or duplicate slashes. A deliberate design decision, noted in the header comment, is that this lives in its own module separate from `lib/supabase.ts` specifically so that components needing only the backend URL don't pull the heavy `@supabase/supabase-js` dependency into the client bundle. The file has no runtime dependencies of its own—just `process.env` access—making it safe to import anywhere in the app. One gotcha: because it relies on a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable, the value is inlined at build time, so changing the backend URL requires a rebuild rather than just a redeploy.

apps\\web\\e2e\\capture-demo-video.spec..summary: This Playwright spec exists to record a single continuous 1080p demo video of the Darshya product's "golden path" for KYC reviewers (Razorpay, Stripe, WhatsApp Meta), Reddit marketing, and investor outreach — deliberately one long browser session producing one MP4, in contrast to the sibling capture-pitch.spec.ts which splits footage into 12 clips for pitch-deck slides. It exports nothing; its single test, "darshya demo — golden path single session," uses two local helpers, `pause` (fixed waits that make navigation look natural on camera) and `snap` (saves 16 numbered keyframe PNGs into the `demo-keyframes/` directory). The walkthrough visits the home hero, `/temples` and a temple detail page, `/pujas` and a puja booking form, `/darshan` live streaming, `/astrology` where it types a question into the AI Pandit "Asha" chat, `/gaushala` (80G donations), the `/nri` premium landing, and `/upgrade` pricing tiers before returning home. Its only real dependency is `@playwright/test` plus Node's `fs`/`path`/`url` modules; it runs against a live deployment via the `DEMO_BASE_URL` env var (defaulting to https://darshya.online) rather than a local dev server, and the raw `video.webm` output is meant to be converted to MP4 by `scripts/build-demo-video.sh` using ffmpeg. Notable gotchas: it is not a genuine test — the only assertion is `expect(true).toBe(true)` — so it passes even if pages break, and all element interactions are guarded with `.count()` checks and swallowed `.catch()` calls so a missing chat button or link never fails the recording. The 300-second timeout, hardcoded multi-second `waitForTimeout` pauses, and disabled tracing are all deliberate choices to prioritize a smooth, human-looking video over speed or diagnostic detail. It is invoked headed on the chromium project via `pnpm --filter @poojly/web exec playwright test`.

apps\\web\\lib\\aarti-schedules.ts.summary: This module provides per-temple aarti schedules in IST so the live-darshan detail page (`/darshan/[id]`) can render an accurate "LIVE NOW" marker and today's schedule instead of a single static timetable. It exports the `AartiSlot` and `TempleAartiSchedule` types, the `AARTI_SCHEDULES` constant covering ten temples (e.g. `mahakaleshwar`, `tirupati`, `golden-temple`), the `getScheduleForTemple` lookup, the `nowMinutesIST` clock helper, and the `currentAartiState` / `nextAartiLabel` functions that compute the current slot, next slot, countdown minutes, and completed/upcoming lists for UI labels like "LIVE NOW — Mangala Aarti". A private `SLUG_INDEX` map resolves both canonical slugs and aliases (such as `mahakaleshwar-ujjain`) to the same schedule, and `mkSlot` converts display times into minutes-since-midnight for comparison. There are no external library dependencies; the only runtime reliance is `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with the `Asia/Kolkata` zone. A key design decision is that `nowMinutesIST` derives IST time via locale formatting rather than `Date.getTimezoneOffset`, making it safe on edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers whose host clock is UTC. The "live" window is a half-open interval from slot start to start plus `durationMin`, and when all slots finish, `currentAartiState` wraps past midnight to report tomorrow's first slot as next. Times were hand-verified against official temple websites as of 2026-05 with a stated ±30 minute drift tolerance, and a daily `temple-link-validator` agent is expected to flag published schedule changes rather than this file self-updating.

apps\\web\\lib\\admin-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed client for the admin backend, wrapping the `/admin/*` REST endpoints exposed at `API_BASE_URL` (imported from `./api-config`) so admin pages never hand-roll fetch calls. It exports the dual role vocabularies `BackendRole` (Prisma enum values like `PANDIT`) and `UiRole` (lowercase UI strings like `priest`) plus the bidirectional lookup maps `backendToUiRole` and `uiToBackendRole`, which page code uses to translate between API payloads and display/filter values. The main data functions are `getUsers` (with limit/page/role/search query params), `getPendingApprovals`, `patchUser` (approve/block/role updates via PATCH), `getDashboard`, `getRevenue`, and `getReports`, each returning a corresponding response type (`UsersResponse`, `PendingApprovalsResponse`, `DashboardResponse`, `RevenueResponse`, `ReportsResponse`) and authenticating via a Bearer token through the `authHeaders` helper. A notable design choice is `describeFailure`, which parses the API's `{ error, message }` failure bodies and appends the detail to thrown Errors so the UI shows real diagnostics rather than bare status codes. The file also ships CSV export utilities — `rowsToCsv` with proper escaping of quotes, commas, and newlines via `escapeCsvCell`, and `downloadCsv`, which builds a Blob anchor download but silently no-ops when `window` is undefined, keeping it safe for server-side rendering. Every function takes the token as an explicit argument rather than reading auth state itself, so callers remain responsible for token sourcing.

apps\\web\\lib\\ashta-lakshmi.ts.summary: This file is a static content data module for the web app's devotional section, cataloging the Ashta Lakshmi — the eight manifestations of Goddess Lakshmi — with an explicit SEO aim (the header names target queries like "ashta lakshmi names" and "dhana lakshmi mantra"). It exports the `AshtaLakshmi` interface describing each deity (slug, iconography, vahana, beeja and primary mantras in Sanskrit plus English transliteration, benefit, best day, festival, vrata practice, associated temple, and origin story), the `ASHTA_LAKSHMIS` array holding all eight entries, the `getAshtaLakshmiBySlug` lookup helper, and `ASHTA_LAKSHMI_SLUGS`, a precomputed slug list presumably used for static route generation. The module has zero imports and no runtime dependencies — it is pure typed data consumed by page components elsewhere in `apps/web`. The design favors slugs as stable keys for routing and lookups, and the per-entry `number` field preserves canonical ordering independent of array position. One small gotcha: Gaja Lakshmi's `beejaMantra` is identical to her `primaryMantra` rather than a distinct seed syllable formula, and the `storyOrigin` narratives mix scripture with regional legend, so consumers should treat that field as content copy rather than verified citation.

apps\\web\\lib\\aartis.ts.summary: This file is a static data module that powers the `/aarti/[slug]` programmatic SEO pages in the Next.js web app, targeting long-tail searches like "shiv aarti lyrics" and "om jai jagdish lyrics." It exports the `AartiInfo` interface and a single `AARTIS` array containing public-domain devotional aarti texts for deities including Vishnu (Om Jai Jagdish Hare), Shiva, Ganesha, Lakshmi, Durga, Hanuman, Sai Baba, Krishna, Saraswati, Jagannath, Kali, Surya, Satyanarayan, and Kala Bhairava. Each `AartiInfo` entry pairs Devanagari verses (`lyricsHindi`) with line-matched Roman transliterations (`lyricsTransliteration`), plus an English `meaning`, `whenSung` timing guidance, `durationMinutes`, and `description`. The module has no runtime dependencies — it's a pure typed constant with no imports, fetching, or logic, so pages simply read from the array. Two fields act as graph edges into the rest of the site: the optional `deitySlug` links entries to deity pages (with several aartis sharing slugs like `vishnu` or `devi`), and `relatedPujas` holds puja slugs such as `satyanarayan-puja` and `rudrabhishek` for cross-linking. A notable gotcha is that `sai-baba-aarti` omits `deitySlug` since Sai Baba isn't a canonical deity, and `bhairav-aarti` reuses the `shiva` deity slug. The checked-in file appears truncated mid-entry inside the Bhairav aarti's Hindi lyrics, so any consumer reading it must tolerate that boundary or the full dataset lives elsewhere.

apps\\web\\lib\\astrologer-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed client for the astrologer portal's availability feature, wrapping two backend endpoints under `API_BASE_URL` (imported from `./api-config`). It exports `getAvailability`, which fetches the `AstrologerProfile.availability` blob via `/astrologer-portal/dashboard` (noted as the only endpoint that currently returns the profile), and `updateAvailability`, which PATCHes a new blob to `/astrologer-portal/availability`; both take an optional bearer token that `authHeaders` converts into an `Authorization` header. The exported types include the deliberately loose `AvailabilityJson` (typed as `unknown`), the more structured `DaySlots` and `WeekAvailability` shapes the UI layers on top, and `AstrologerDashboard` for the dashboard response. A key design constraint is that availability is a free-form JSON blob whose shape is owned by the UI while the backend (see `apps/api/src/routes/astrologer-portal.ts`) stores up to 64KB unmodified, so this client performs no validation. Both functions throw `Error`s enriched by the `describeFailure` helper, which extracts `message` or `error` fields from failed responses and appends the HTTP status for easier debugging.

apps\\web\\lib\\api.ts.summary: This file is the server-side data-access layer for the Next.js web app (`apps/web`), used by Server Components to query the Fastify backend during SSR via a single internal `serverFetch` helper that applies a 4-second `AbortController` timeout, Next.js ISR options (`revalidate` defaulting to 60s, cache tags, `no-store` opt-out), and error handling. `resolveApiBase()` picks the backend origin from `API_URL` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` (covering both Node SSR and Cloudflare Pages edge runtimes), falls back to the production Render deployment at `api.darshya.online`, and appends `/api/v1` when missing. Because the API's paginated envelope (`{ temples: [...], total, page, ... }`) differs from the web's `PaginatedResponse<T>` shape, `normalizePaginated()` rewrites responses at the boundary, and similar adapters exist in `getTodayPanchang()` (converting the `shubhMuhurat` object into a `{name, start, end}` array) and `getApprovedProviders()` (accepting either envelope and swallowing failures so listing strips can render an empty state when the API is down). Exports are organized by domain: temple functions (`getTemples`, `getTempleBySlug`, `getTempleReviews` with types `TempleListItem`, `TempleDetail`, `TempleReview`), puja types (`getPujaTypes`), content (`getContent`, `getContentBySlugApi`, `getDailyContent`), panchang (`getTodayPanchang`, `getUpcomingFestivals`), live darshan (`getLiveDarshan`, `getScheduledDarshan`, returning `DarshanStream` with YouTube/IVS provider fields), and public provider listings (`getApprovedProviders` for `ProviderListingType` values like `pandit`, `store`, `gaushala`). Each fetcher sets per-resource cache tags (e.g. `temples`, `temple-${slug}`, `daily-content`) so routes can be revalidated granularly. Notable gotchas: `TempleImage` is a union of plain string URLs and legacy `{url, alt, type}` objects, so consumers must normalize before rendering, and prices are serialized as strings (`basePrice`, `nriPrice`, `priceOverride`) rather than numbers. The only real dependency is the Fastify API itself plus Next.js's extended `fetch` caching semantics; there are no third-party libraries involved.

apps\\web\\lib\\books.ts.summary: This file is the server-only data layer for the book-reading feature in the web app: it loads book content stored as static JSON files under `public/books` at request time, a layout chosen so the code works identically in static export and edge runtimes since the files ship with the bundle. It exports `listBookSlugs` to enumerate available books, `loadManifest` and `loadAllManifests` to read per-book `manifest.json` files, `loadChapter` to fetch individual chapter JSON, and the pure helpers `nextChapter` and `prevChapter` for navigating a manifest's chapter list. Its only external dependency beyond Node's `fs`/`path` is the `@poojly/shared` package, which supplies the `BookManifest`, `Chapter`, and `ChapterSummary` types, and the `server-only` import guards against accidental client-side bundling. A notable security decision is that all slugs pass through `safeBookSlug`/`safeChapterSlug` regex validation (with an explicit `..` rejection) to prevent path traversal before touching the filesystem. Chapter slugs support a compound form like `bala/sarga-1`, which maps to a nested `kandas/<kanda>/sargas/<sarga>.json` directory convention, while simple slugs resolve to `chapters/<slug>.json`. All read failures are swallowed and surfaced as `null` (or an empty list), so callers must handle missing content gracefully. The `__testing` export exposes the slug validators and `BOOKS_ROOT` purely as a test surface.

apps\\web\\lib\\blog-posts.ts.summary: This module is the data layer for the blog section of the web app: because the edge runtime on Cloudflare Pages cannot read the filesystem, it fetches blog posts at request time from the `docs/agent-reports/blog-drafts/` directory of the `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu` GitHub repo, via the GitHub Contents API plus `raw.githubusercontent.com` downloads, following the same pattern as the `/changelog` feature. It exports the `BlogPost` interface (slug, date, title, excerpt, raw markdown body, and GitHub source URL) along with three async functions: `listBlogPosts()` returns all posts sorted newest-first, `getBlogPost(slug)` finds one post by slug, and `blogPostSlugs()` returns slugs for static route generation. Internal helpers enforce conventions: `parseFilename` requires the `YYYY-MM-DD-slug.md` (or `.mdx`) naming scheme, `extractTitle` pulls the first H1 or humanizes the slug, and `extractExcerpt` strips frontmatter, headings, and code fences to build a 220-character preview from the first paragraph. All fetches use Next.js's `next: { revalidate: 3600 }` for one-hour ISR-style caching, so new posts can take up to an hour to appear. A notable gotcha is that `getBlogPost` and `blogPostSlugs` both call `listBlogPosts`, meaning a single-post view downloads every post's content — cheap at small volume but N+1 by design. Error handling is deliberately silent: any network or API failure yields an empty array or null rather than throwing, so upstream GitHub outages degrade the blog to empty instead of erroring the page.
