It exports the `Nakshatra` interface — which models each mansion with a `slug`, English and Devanagari names, ruling `lord` and `deity`, `gana` constrained to the union 'Deva' | 'Manushya' | 'Rakshasa', zodiac `range`, plus pre-written SEO copy fields (`meaning`, `qualities`, `career`, `compatibility`, `spiritualPractice`) — and the `NAKSHATRAS` constant array holding all 27 fully populated entries from Ashwini through Revati. Two helper functions support routing: `nakshatraSlugs()` returns all slugs for static path generation, and `getNakshatra(slug)` looks up a single entry, returning `undefined` for unknown slugs so pages must handle the not-found case. The module has zero imports and no runtime dependencies — it is pure compile-time data, meaning content changes require a redeploy but lookups are free. Notable details: `padas` is typed as the literal `4` rather than a general number, and compatibility guidance is stored as unstructured prose strings rather than normalized references to other slugs, so cross-linking between nakshatras cannot be derived programmatically from this data alone.

apps\\web\\lib\\markdown.ts.summary: This file is a dependency-free, hand-rolled markdown-to-HTML converter built to render devotional content in the web app. It exports two functions: `markdownToHtml`, which transforms markdown (headings, bold, italic, lists, links, images, blockquotes, fenced code blocks, horizontal rules) into an HTML string, and `renderContentBody`, a wrapper that returns the body unchanged if it already looks like HTML and otherwise delegates to `markdownToHtml`. Internally it leans on two helpers: `processInline`, which applies inline substitutions in a deliberate order (inline code first, then images, links, bold, italic) so earlier replacements aren't mangled by later passes, and `sanitizeUrl`, an allowlist filter permitting only http(s), mailto, tel, anchor, and relative URLs — it strips javascript:/data:/vbscript: vectors because the output is injected into the DOM via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Notable design choices include pre-extracting fenced code blocks into placeholder tokens so their contents bypass all other processing, a preprocessing pass that splits bold spans crossing newlines, and a line-by-line state machine that tracks open paragraph, list, and blockquote elements to emit balanced tags. The generated markup hardcodes Tailwind utility classes from the app's palette (surface-*, saffron-*), and external links get `target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"` unless they point at darshya.online. Gotchas worth knowing: the HTML detection in `renderContentBody` is a shallow heuristic that only recognizes bodies starting with `<h`, `<p`, or `<div`, and the regex-based parsing is intentionally not spec-compliant, so nested or edge-case markdown may render imperfectly.

apps\\web\\lib\\muhurats.ts.summary: This file is a pure static data module — the canonical catalog of Vedic muhurats (auspicious and inauspicious time windows) that powers the site's programmatic SEO pages at `/muhurat/[slug]`, targeting long-tail queries like "rahu kalam today" and "vivah muhurta 2026". It exports the `Muhurat` interface — describing each entry's slug, Devanagari `sanskritName`, `category` union, `bestFor`/`avoid` activity lists, and prose fields for `spiritualSignificance`, `howToCalculate`, and `modernApplication` — plus the `MUHURATS` constant array holding entries such as `brahma-muhurta`, `abhijit-muhurta`, `rahu-kalam`, `gulika-kalam`, `vivah-muhurta`, `griha-pravesh-muhurta`, the choghadiya windows, and the siddhi/pushkar yogas. There are no imports or runtime dependencies: it is hand-authored content consumed elsewhere by the web app's route handlers, with in-text cross-references to other product surfaces like the Darshya panchang and `/ask-pandit`. A notable design consequence is that all timing and calculation logic is stored as descriptive prose rather than computable data, so any live computation of these windows must happen in a separate panchang/astronomy module. Gotchas visible in the code include a redundant `category` union with overlapping values (`daily`, `daily-auspicious`, `auspicious`, `special`), an inline admission that the Rahu Kalam mnemonic is wrong and must be verified against a panchang, and content accuracy that rests entirely on manual curation rather than any validated source.

apps\\web\\lib\\nakshatra-finder.ts.summary: This module computes a newborn's birth nakshatra (lunar mansion), pada, and rashi from a date of birth, local time, and timezone offset, serving the namakaran (name-giving) and basic kundli features of the web app. Its sole public entry point is `findNakshatra`, which takes a `NakshatraFinderInput` (`dob` as YYYY-MM-DD, `time` as HH:MM, and `timezoneOffset` in hours) and returns a `NakshatraFinderResult` — carrying the Julian day, tropical and sidereal moon longitudes, ayanamsa, the resolved `Nakshatra` object, pada (1–4), and rashi — or `null` when input validation fails rather than throwing. It also exports `TIMEZONE_OPTIONS`, a curated list of UTC offsets for the UI dropdown. Internally it depends only on the `NAKSHATRAS` table and `Nakshatra` type from the sibling `./nakshatras` module and uses no external libraries or services; all astronomy is done in-process via an abridged Jean Meeus "Astronomical Algorithms" implementation (chapter 7 Julian day, chapter 47 moon longitude with only the top 11 perturbation terms). The key design tradeoff is precision: the simplified lunar longitude is accurate to roughly 0.3°, which the file's header notes is ample given each nakshatra spans 13.33° and each pada 3.33°, but it explicitly disclaims muhurat-grade ceremonial accuracy and recommends pandit verification. Similarly, `lahiriAyanamsa` is a linear fit anchored at J2000.0 and only valid for 2000–2050, and date handling is done manually (regex parsing plus a hand-rolled `daysInMonth` rollover when local-to-UTC conversion crosses midnight) instead of using Date or a timezone library, so callers must supply the correct historical offset themselves.

apps\\web\\lib\\lal-kitab.ts.summary: This file is a pure-data module for the Lal Kitab tradition of Vedic astrology (attributed to Pt. Roop Chand Joshi's 1939–52 Granthavali): it maps grahas to houses and life problems and prescribes Farman remedies, deliberately containing no astronomy or computation. It exports the GrahaCode union (surya through ketu), the Graha metadata type (nature, element, ruling weekday, metal, color, gemstone, deity, generalUpay, significance) with the nine-entry GRAHAS constant, plus the LifeProblem union and ProblemDef type behind the PROBLEMS constant, which maps twelve life issues (career, marriage, health, legal-case, and so on) to the grahas most commonly afflicting them. The HouseEffect type captures a per-house verdict ('auspicious' | 'neutral' | 'troubling'), effect text, and a specific upay. Internally, RAW_EFFECTS stores twelve verdict/effect/upay rows per GrahaCode (the 9 × 12 = 108 effect cells), while the private houseLabel helper resolves Sanskrit bhava names from HOUSE_SANSKRIT by positional index — a structural gotcha, since array order encodes the house number and reordering rows would silently corrupt the mapping. The module has no imports or external dependencies and is meant to be consumed by other apps/web code that computes chart positions and performs the lookups; the truncated tail presumably assembles and exports the full HouseEffect table from RAW_EFFECTS. Finally, the remedy strings are traditional prescriptive content (donations, deity worship, household items like jaggery, copper, and mustard oil), so consuming UI should frame them as cultural guidance rather than medical, legal, or financial advice.

apps\\web\\lib\\navaratna.ts.summary: This file is a pure data module that defines the nine Navaratna (sacred Vedic gems, one per Nava-Graha planet) and exists to power the `/navaratna` programmatic SEO route family, statically generated via `generateStaticParams` in `apps/web/app/navaratna/`. It exports the `NavaratnaGem` interface, which types a rich per-gem record (names in English, Sanskrit Devanagari, and Hindi, plus mineralogy, wearing instructions, mantras, benefits, contraindications, pricing, and quality indicators), along with the `NAVARATNA` constant array holding all nine fully-populated gem entries, the derived `NAVARATNA_SLUGS` list for static param generation, and the `getNavaratnaBySlug` lookup helper for page rendering. The module has no external or internal dependencies — it is self-contained static content consumed by the route layer. A key design decision is the `planetSlug` field on each record (e.g. `surya`, `brihaspati`, `rahu`), which deliberately mirrors the slugs of the nava-graha route family so gem pages can cross-link to their planet pages and strengthen the SEO graph. Content is authored to target long-tail queries ("ruby for sun benefits", "neelam side effects"), evident in fields like `sideEffectsIfWrong`, `averagePriceRange`, `trialDuration`, and `substitutes`. A gotcha for maintainers: lookup returns `undefined` for unknown slugs, so callers must handle misses, and there is no runtime validation tying `planetSlug` values to actual nava-graha routes, so renames on either side must be kept in sync manually.

apps\\web\\lib\\navadurga.ts.summary: This file is a dependency-free static data module that catalogs the Navadurga — the nine forms of Durga worshipped across the nine days of Navratri — for the web app. Its centerpiece is the `NAVADURGA` array, where each entry conforms to the `NavadurgaForm` interface and bundles a day's full devotional metadata: `slug` (constrained by the `NavadurgaSlug` union type), `day` (typed as the literal range 1–9), Sanskrit and transliterated names, `color`/`colorHex` (Tailwind-palette hexes, implying UI theming), ruling `planet`, `mount`, `weapons`, `prasad`, `mantra`/`beejMantra`, `story`, `iconography`, `blessing`, `chakra`, plus `forDevotees` and `doNotDo` guidance lists. Two lookup helpers, `getNavadurga(slug)` and `getNavadurgaByDay(day)`, do simple linear `find`s over the array and return `undefined` on miss, so callers must handle absent results. The file also exports `NAVRATRI_TYPES`, an `as const` array describing the four Navratri observances (Sharad, Chaitra, and the two tantric Gupt Navratris) with season, lunar month, and significance. There are no imports or external service calls — it is pure content, effectively an in-code CMS. One gotcha: Skandamata's `blessing` string contains a mojibake character ("sant�n prapti", likely "santān prapti"), signaling an encoding slip worth fixing. Also note the chakra mapping is not one-to-one — both Kalaratri (day 7) and Siddhidatri (day 9) claim Sahasrāra, so consumers shouldn't index chakras by day.

apps\\web\\lib\\numerology.ts.summary: This file is the pure-function numerology computation engine for the web app's `/astrology/numerology` calculator, with no external dependencies. It implements two letter-mapping systems — Pythagorean (`PYTH_VALUES`, mod-9 of alphabet position) and Chaldean (`CHALDEAN_VALUES`, the Babylonian mapping that omits 9 as sacred) — and exports calculators for five number kinds: `lifePath` (digit sum of the DOB, returned with a reduction trace string), `birthdayNumber`, `nameChaldean`, `nameSoulUrge` (Pythagorean sum of vowels only), and `namePersonality` (consonants only). The main entry point is `computeNumerology(dob, name)`, which returns a `NumerologyResult` bundling all five numbers plus their `NumberMeaning` interpretations (title, element, ruling planet, strengths, challenges, careers, lucky days/colors, and a Vedic `spiritualNote` for each of 1–9 and master numbers 11/22/33), or null if the DOB is invalid. A key design rule is that the internal `reduce` helper preserves master numbers 11/22/33 rather than reducing them further, per the Sepharial/Cheiro convention noted in the header. Gotchas: `lifePath` accepts YYYY-MM-DD, DD/MM/YYYY, or DD-MM-YYYY but only checks digit length (8+), and `birthdayNumber` returns 0 for unparseable dates, which then maps to `getMeaning`'s fallback of meaning 1. `ALL_NUMBERS` and `listAllMeanings()` support UI dropdowns and SEO listing pages.

apps\\web\\lib\\nava-grahas.ts.summary: This file is the static content model for the nine Vedic planets (Nava-Graha), existing purely as typed data to power the programmatic SEO route family under apps/web/app/nava-graha/, which statically generates one page per graha via generateStaticParams. It exports two things: the NavaGrahaInfo interface, which defines the ~35-field shape of a planet record (identity slugs, Sanskrit/Devanagari names, gemstone and metal, mantras in three forms, yantra, presiding deity, fasting and charity guidance, positive/negative indications, remedies, and the mahadashaYears dasha length), and the NAVA_GRAHAS constant array holding the nine populated records — surya, chandra, mangal, budh, brihaspati, shukra, shani, rahu, and ketu. The file has no imports or runtime dependencies; it is consumed by the /nava-graha routes and implicitly couples to a sibling rashi dataset, since fields like rulingRashis, exaltationRashi, and debilitationRashi store rashi slugs, while friends/enemies/neutrals store graha slugs for cross-linking between planet pages. Notable design choices include the header comment documenting target long-tail keywords ("shani sade sati remedy", "guru chandal yoga"), making the SEO intent explicit in source, and the repeated safety caveats baked into remedy and gemstone copy — especially shani's blue sapphire entry flagged "HIGH RISK — test first" — which guard against harmful gem recommendations. The shadow planets rahu and ketu break the pattern slightly with empty rulingRashis arrays and school-dependent co-rulership notes, and the mahadashaYears values (6 through 20) collectively encode the 120-year Vimshottari dasha cycle, which downstream pages likely use for mahadasha-duration content.

apps\\web\\lib\\panchang-karanas.ts.summary: This file is a static data module defining the 11 karanas — the fifth anga of the Hindu Panchang, each a half-tithi unit — for use across the web app, with scriptural sourcing from Surya Siddhanta, Muhurta Chintamani, and Brihat Samhita noted in comments. Its central export is the `PANCHANG_KARANAS` array of `PanchangKarana` objects, each carrying a slug, number, Sanskrit name, deity, `chara`/`sthira` category, auspiciousness `nature`, muhurta guidance (`bestFor`/`avoidFor`), and a bilingual mantra. Lookup and presentation helpers include `getKarana(slug)`, the pre-filtered constant lists `CHARA_KARANAS`, `STHIRA_KARANAS`, `AUSPICIOUS_KARANAS`, and `INAUSPICIOUS_KARANAS`, and `natureColor(nature)`, which maps nature to Tailwind-style color names (emerald, rose, amber) for UI rendering. The module has no runtime dependencies — it is pure TypeScript data with no imports, no API calls, and no calculation logic; the karana-to-slot astronomy (the 7 chara karanas repeating across 56 half-tithi slots versus the 4 fixed sthira slots near Amavasya and Shukla Pratipada) lives only in comments, so consumers must compute the active karana elsewhere. A notable domain decision is flagging Vishti (Bhadra) as the universally inauspicious karana with an extensive `avoidFor` list, while Kintughna is the sole auspicious sthira karana. Because categories and natures are encoded as string-literal union types on the interface, the derived filtered lists stay type-safe and will not silently drift if entries are edited.

apps\\web\\lib\\onboarding-store.ts.summary: This file is the client-side state store for the first-run guided onboarding flow in the web app, persisting the user's `OnboardingState` (primaryIntent, lang, isNri, completedAt, currentStep, version) to `window.localStorage`. It exports the `OnboardingIntent`, `OnboardingLang`, and `OnboardingState` types, the constants `ONBOARDING_STORAGE_KEY`, `ONBOARDING_LANGUAGE_KEY`, and `ONBOARDING_EVENT`, plus the functions `getOnboarding`, `setOnboarding` (a partial merge that always forces version 1), `clearOnboarding`, and the `isOnboardingFlagEnabled` feature-flag check gated on `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ONBOARDING_V1 === '1'`. It has no external library dependencies, but it is built to feed React 18's `useSyncExternalStore` and signals changes by dispatching a `darshya:onboarding-changed` `CustomEvent` on `window` after every write or clear. Two hard constraints stand out: the storage key must remain `poojly_onboarding_v1` forever (the legacy `poojly_*` namespace predates the bhaktisetu rename, so bumping it requires a migration), and the onboarding modal ships dark by default until the flag is flipped in layout integration. The module is deliberately defensive: every accessor short-circuits during SSR when `window` is undefined, `normalize` rejects malformed payloads and sweeps corrupt JSON from storage, and write failures (quota, serialization) are swallowed silently. Most critically, `getOnboarding` maintains a `cachedRaw`/`cachedSnapshot` memo so `getSnapshot()` returns a stable reference — without this, React 18 detects a changing snapshot and loops into the `SentryErrorBoundary` fallback.

apps\\web\\lib\\pancha-bhoota.ts.summary: This file is a static content data module for the "Pancha Bhoota" feature in the `apps/web` app, cataloging the five elemental Shiva temples of South India (Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Ether) as hardcoded TypeScript rather than pulling from a database or CMS. It exports the `PanchaBhootaTemple` interface, which defines a rich 21-field schema covering religious details (presiding deity, linga form, mantra in Sanskrit and English, associated saint), practical pilgrimage info (nearest airport, best season), and explanatory content (why the temple represents its element, significance). The main export is the `PANCHA_BHOOTA` constant array containing five fully populated entries — Ekambareshwarar, Jambukeshwarar, Arunachaleshwar, Srikalahasti, and Chidambaram Nataraja — along with a derived `PANCHA_BHOOTA_SLUGS` array and a `getPanchaBhootaBySlug(slug)` helper that does a linear `find` and returns `undefined` on misses. The module has zero dependencies, internal or external, making it safe to import from server or client components. Notable design choices: the `slug` field (e.g., `'arunachaleshwar-thiruvannamalai'`) plus the precomputed slug list strongly suggest usage for static route generation or sitemap/SEO purposes in a Next.js app, the `number` field enforces the canonical element ordering, and content is bilingual with Devanagari strings embedded directly. The gotcha is that all content is maintained by hand in code, so any correction to temple facts, festivals, or travel details requires a code edit and redeploy rather than a content update.

apps\\web\\lib\\pitra-dosh.ts.summary: This file is a static domain-knowledge module for the web app that models Pitra Dosh, a Vedic-astrology ancestral-karma affliction, as queryable TypeScript data. It exports the `DoshSeverity` and `LifeArea` union types, the `PitraDoshType` and `SymptomChecker` interfaces, three data constants (`PITRA_DOSH_TYPES` cataloguing five doshas such as `surya-pitra-dosh` and `rahu-pitra-dosh` with houses, symptoms, remedies, and bilingual mantras; `SYMPTOM_CHECKERS` mapping six life areas like `progeny` and `marriage` to self-identifiable indicators and likely dosh slugs; and `UNIVERSAL_REMEDIES` listing rituals like Pitru Paksha Shradh and Gaya Shradh), plus three lookup helpers: `getDoshType`, `getSymptomChecker`, and `diagnoseBySymptom`, which resolves a symptom category into its linked dosh records. The module has no runtime dependencies or external service calls — it is pure embedded content referencing classical sources (Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra, Garuda Purana) in comments. Notable design points: entities are linked loosely by slug strings rather than object references, with `diagnoseBySymptom` using a type-guard filter to drop unresolved slugs, and all lookups return `undefined` rather than throwing on missing keys. One gotcha is that user-facing strings contain HTML entities like `'` rather than literal apostrophes, so consumers must render them as HTML or decode them. The data is entirely hardcoded, so adding a new dosh type requires editing this file and keeping the `likelyDosh` slug arrays in sync manually.

apps\\web\\lib\\posthog.ts.summary: This file is the web app's env-or-noop PostHog analytics loader, designed to be imported unconditionally from the root layout and to activate only when NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY is set. It exports PostHogScript, a component that injects the standard PostHog js-lite snippet via next/script with the afterInteractive strategy so initialization never blocks LCP, along with thin capture, identify, and reset wrappers that silently no-op on the server or when PostHog was never loaded. Its only dependencies are next/script, React's createElement, and the global window.posthog stub typed via a declared Window interface. Notable choices include defaulting the API host to the EU region endpoint (overridable via NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_HOST) for GDPR-friendly storage, configuring person_profiles: 'identified_only' with pageview and pageleave capture enabled, and relying on the stubbed snippet's command queue so calls made before array.js loads are still buffered rather than dropped.

apps\\web\\lib\\pilgrimage-circuits.ts.summary: This file is a static data module that powers the web app's programmatic-SEO landing pages for multi-temple Hindu pilgrimage itineraries (Char Dham, 12 Jyotirlinga, Panch Kedar, etc.), targeting high commercial-intent searches like "char dham yatra package" and funneling visitors toward the yatra inquiry form. It exports two TypeScript interfaces — `CircuitStop` (a single temple stop with deity, state, best months, and an optional `templeSlug` linking to a `/temples/{slug}` detail page) and `PilgrimageCircuit` (a full itinerary with slug, Sanskrit name, region, duration range, starting price in INR, difficulty, ordered stops, significance text, and practical tips) — plus the `CIRCUITS` constant array containing the actual circuit records. There are no imports or runtime dependencies; it is pure typed data consumed by page components in `apps/web`, with internal linking expressed only through optional string slugs (`templeSlug`, `relatedYatra`) that must match real `/temples/{slug}` and `/yatra/{slug}` routes to avoid dead links. Notable conventions: `shortDesc` is capped at ~140 characters to serve directly as a meta description, `longDesc` is a ~400-word SEO body, and `region`/`difficulty` are string-literal unions rather than enums. One gotcha: the header comment claims "8 canonical circuits," but the file actually defines more (Panch Prayag, Dwadasha Aditya, and likely others in the truncated portion), so the comment is stale and any code relying on a fixed count should use `CIRCUITS.length` instead.

apps\\web\\lib\\pandit-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed API client for all pandit (priest) functionality, wrapping fetch calls against the backend at `API_BASE_URL` imported from `./api-config`. It exports the `Offering`, `PriestSummary`, `PriestWithOfferings`, and `PriestReview` types plus input types `CreateOfferingInput`/`UpdateOfferingInput`, along with two groups of functions: bearer-token-authenticated CRUD for the priest dashboard (`listMyOfferings`, `createOffering`, `updateOffering`, `deleteOffering`, `toggleOfferingActive` against `/priest/pujas`, and `getMyReviews` against `/priest/reviews`), and unauthenticated server-side fetchers `getPublicPriests` (with `specialization`/`deity` query filters) and `getPublicPriest` for the public directory. Shared helpers `authHeaders` and `describeFailure` attach optional Authorization headers and enrich thrown errors with the response body's `message`/`error` fields and HTTP status. Two serialization gotchas are documented: `Offering.basePrice` arrives as a string because Prisma Decimals serialize to JSON strings, so callers must `parseFloat` before arithmetic, and `PriestReview.providerId` holds the priest's User UUID rather than `Priest.id`, with no devotee name joined so the UI falls back to a generic label. The public fetchers rely on Next.js fetch caching (`revalidate: 300` for the list, `60` for the detail) and deliberately swallow failures — `getPublicPriests` returns an empty array on any error, while `getPublicPriest` returns null on 404 or other non-OK statuses so pages can invoke `notFound()`.

apps\\web\\lib\\pricing.ts.summary: This file is the single source of truth for the Darshya platform's revenue model, defining subscription plans and commission structures for the web app. It exports the `PlanId` and `ProviderRole` union types (six provider roles from pandit to gaushala), the `Plan`, `PlanFeature`, and `CommissionRate` interfaces, plus two data constants: `PLANS` (four monthly INR tiers — Free, Basic ₹499, Pro ₹1499, Enterprise ₹4999 — each with listing limits and a commission override) and `COMMISSION_RATES` (a per-role, per-plan rate matrix where, notably, the plan-level `commissionOverride` values mirror but don't automatically drive the `rates` records, so the two must be kept in sync manually). Helper functions include `getPlanById` and `getPlanFeatures` (throwing on unknown IDs), `getCommissionRate(role, planId)`, `getUpgradePlan` for the linear upgrade path, `formatPrice` (Intl.NumberFormat-based INR/USD/GBP formatting with an optional currency-code suffix for NRI checkout ambiguity), and `gbpFromInr`, which implements the NRI premium pricing rule. There are no external dependencies beyond the standard `Intl` API, and no internal imports — it's a pure constants-and-helpers module meant to be consumed by checkout, listing, and dashboard code. Key gotchas: `gbpFromInr` hardcodes a ₹105/GBP reference rate with a 10x multiplier and rounds to the nearest £5, requiring quarterly founder review rather than live FX data, and it returns 0 for non-positive input; also `maxListings: null` signals unlimited, so consumers must null-check rather than treat it as zero.

apps\\web\\lib\\panchang-yogas.ts.summary: This file is a static reference dataset for the 27 nitya yogas, the fourth anga (limb) of the Hindu Panchang, intended to power muhurta/auspicious-timing features in the web app. It exports the `PanchangYoga` interface, the `PANCHANG_YOGAS` constant array containing one entry per yoga, a `getYoga(slug)` lookup helper, and precomputed `INAUSPICIOUS_YOGAS` and `AUSPICIOUS_YOGAS` slug lists for quick filtering. Each yoga record carries a slug, canonical number (1–27), Sanskrit name, presiding deity, a `nature` classification (auspicious, inauspicious, or mixed), a prose `effect` description, `bestFor`/`avoidFor` activity lists, a `firstPart` field capturing intra-day timing nuances (e.g., Atiganda is only dangerous for its first 6 ghatikas), and a deity mantra in both Devanagari and romanized form. The header comment documents the traditional calculation rule — yoga index equals (Sun longitude + Moon longitude) divided by 13°20′ — and cites classical sources (Brihat Samhita, Muhurta Chintamani, Kalaprakashika), though the file itself contains no computation logic. It has zero imports and no external dependencies, making it a pure data module that other panchang modules presumably combine with live Sun/Moon longitude calculations. One gotcha: the header comment claims 9 yogas are inauspicious, but the data marks only 8 as `inauspicious` (Vishkambha is classified as `mixed`), so consumers relying on `INAUSPICIOUS_YOGAS` should be aware it omits Vishkambha despite its partially adverse first 72 minutes. Consumers should also note that "avoid" guidance for several inauspicious yogas applies only to an initial ghatika window encoded as free text in `firstPart`, not as structured time ranges.

apps\\web\\lib\\ramayana-kandas.ts.summary: This file is a static data module powering programmatic SEO pages about the Valmiki Ramayana's seven kandas (books) in the apps/web application. It exports the RamayanaKanda interface, which structures each book with a URL slug, Sanskrit and IAST names, sarga (chapter) count, setting, narrative summary, key episodes, central character, and a moral takeaway, plus the RAMAYANA_KANDAS constant array holding all seven records from bala-kanda through uttara-kanda. Helper exports include kandaSlugs() for enumerating routes (likely for static path generation), getKanda(slug) for lookup by slug, and the derived TOTAL_SARGAS constant summing chapter counts to 645. The module has no runtime dependencies — it imports nothing and is pure in-memory data, so pages consume it at build time without any database or external service. Notable constraints flagged in comments: sarga counts follow the canonical Valmiki edition while episode lists are only representative, and the Uttara Kanda entry acknowledges scholarly debate over its authenticity while retaining it as received tradition.

apps\\web\\lib\\products.ts.summary: `apps/web/lib/products.ts` is the static product catalog for the Bhakti Store web app, serving as the single source of truth shared by both the product listing and product detail pages. It exports the `Product` interface (id, handle, title, price, compareAtPrice, discount, rating, reviewCount, inStock, freeDelivery, sku, imageKey, and more), the `PRODUCTS` array containing 24 hardcoded products organized into 8 collections (Puja Essentials, Rudraksha & Malas, Idols & Murtis, Puja Samagri, Books & Scriptures, Spiritual Jewellery, Organic & Natural, Home Temple & Decor), the `CATEGORIES` constant pairing each collection slug with a display name and computed product count, and the `getProductByHandle` lookup helper. The module has zero dependencies — no internal imports, external libraries, or backend services — making it entirely self-contained mock data rather than a real inventory source. Notable design choices include pricing in INR with pre-computed `discount` percentages, an `imageKey` field that references image assets indirectly rather than embedding URLs (so consumers must resolve keys to actual images), and `CATEGORIES` counts computed by filtering `PRODUCTS` at module load, which keeps counts in sync automatically but means the catalog is fixed at build time. A gotcha for consumers: `getProductByHandle` returns `undefined` for unknown handles, so detail pages must handle the not-found case explicitly.

apps\\web\\lib\\pancha-pakshi.ts.summary: This file is the static domain-data module for the web app's Pancha Pakshi (five-bird) Vedic/Tamil astrology feature, providing reference content rather than any timing or cycle computation. Its core export is `PANCHA_PAKSHI_BIRDS`, a hardcoded array of five `PanchaPakshiBird` records (vulture, owl, crow, cock, peacock) each carrying deity, `PakshiElement`, planet, direction, lucky colors/days, personality, strengths, weaknesses, careers, compatibility/incompatibility slugs, `birthNakshatras`, mantras, and remedies; the `ACTIVITIES` array describes the five `PakshiActivity` states ('rules' through 'dies') with a quality ranking from 'best' to 'worst'. Lookup helpers `getBird` and `getBirdByNakshatra` find birds by slug or by exact case-insensitive nakshatra name, and `ALL_NAKSHATRAS_FOR_DROPDOWN` exposes a deduplicated sorted list of all 27 nakshatras for form inputs. `ELEMENT_COLOR` and `ACTIVITY_COLOR` map elements and activity qualities to Tailwind CSS class strings, coupling this otherwise pure-data module directly to the UI layer. The file has no imports or external dependencies — it is entirely self-contained constants and types. One notable gotcha: the `birthNakshatras` lists overlap across birds (Punarvasu, Magha, Anuradha, and Uttara Bhadrapada each appear under two birds), so `getBirdByNakshatra` silently returns whichever bird comes first in array order, making the nakshatra-to-bird mapping ambiguous for those four stars. Additionally, nakshatra matching is exact string equality after lowercasing, so alternate spellings will fail to resolve.

apps\\web\\lib\\rashi-profiles.ts.summary: This file is a static data module that provides deep trait, career, compatibility, health, and spiritual profiles for the twelve Vedic zodiac signs (rashis), powering the programmatic-SEO pages at `/rashi/[slug]` in the web app. It exports the `RashiProfile` interface — defining fields like `sanskritName`, `quality`, `luckyDay`, `gemstone`, `career`, `compatibility`, `healthTendencies`, `spiritualPractice`, and `beejMantra` — along with the `RASHI_PROFILES` constant array holding one hardcoded record per sign, plus two lookup helpers: `getRashiProfile(slug)` for fetching a single profile and `rashiProfileSlugs()` for enumerating all slugs (useful for static route generation). It is explicitly a companion to `lib/rashis.ts`, which carries the horoscope-focused data, and keys its records by the same English slug (`aries`, `taurus`, etc.) used by `RashiInfo.rashi` there so the two datasets join cleanly. The module has no runtime dependencies — it is pure TypeScript data with typed literals (e.g., the `quality` union of Cardinal/Fixed/Mutable) and no external API or database calls. A notable design point is that each rashi's profile embeds cross-references to other signs by both English and Sanskrit names inside the free-text `compatibility` field, so relationship data exists only as prose rather than structured edges. Because all content is inlined, updating any profile requires a code change and redeploy, and `getRashiProfile` returns `undefined` for unknown slugs, meaning callers must handle the miss case.

apps\\web\\lib\\puranas.ts.summary: This file is a dependency-free static reference data module cataloging the 18 Mahapuranas of Hindu tradition for the web app. It exports the `PuranaAlignment` union type ('sattvic' | 'rajasic' | 'tamasic'), the `Purana` interface (number, slug, Sanskrit and IAST names, alignment, presiding deity, verse count, themes, notable stories, and reader-guidance fields like `whyRead` and `bestKnownFor`), and the `PURANAS` array containing all 18 hardcoded entries from Brahma Purana through Brahmanda Purana. Utility exports include `TOTAL_VERSES` (a reduced sum of all `verseCount` fields, roughly 400,000), `puranaSlugs()` for enumerating route-friendly identifiers, `getPurana(slug)` for single-record lookup, and `ALIGNMENT_LABELS` mapping each guna classification to a display string. Notably, the module has zero imports — no database, CMS, or external library — so all content is baked into the bundle at build time and any textual correction requires a code change and redeploy. The classification scheme follows the traditional Padma Purana division of six sattvic (Vaishnava), six rajasic (Brahma), and six tamasic (Shaiva) puranas, though individual entries take liberties (e.g., Markandeya is classified rajasic despite presiding deity Devi, and several "Mixed"-deity texts land in tamasic). The `presidingDeity` field is constrained to five literal values ('Vishnu' | 'Shiva' | 'Brahma' | 'Devi' | 'Mixed'), and `getPurana` returns `undefined` for unknown slugs, so consumers must handle the missing case — the linear `find` lookup is fine at 18 records but worth noting if the dataset grows.

apps\\web\\lib\\release.ts.summary: This module (apps/web/lib/release.ts, requirement R-Q2-E-015) is the single source of truth for the build's Sentry release identifier, which is injected at build time as NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_RELEASE in the format `darshya@<sha>` by the .github/workflows/sentry-release.yml GitHub Actions workflow. It exports three helpers: getRelease(), which returns the env var or the fallback string 'dev' when unset (local dev and preview deploys); getReleaseShortSha(), which extracts a seven-character SHA suffix for display surfaces like the footer build-id badge; and hasReleaseTag(), which reports whether the build came from the tagged-release workflow and is used to gate UI such as a "report a bug" link wired to the Sentry user-feedback widget. Its only real dependency is Next.js build-time inlining of NEXT_PUBLIC_ environment variables, plus the external Sentry release-tracking pipeline. A key design decision is the 'dev' fallback, which guarantees downstream consumers (footer badge, window.onerror beacon, server-component logging) never crash on a missing env var. Note the intentional gap: the Sentry workflow only fires on `git tag v*` pushes, so non-tagged builds deliberately carry no release tag, and getReleaseShortSha() degrades to returning 'dev' or a truncated prefix when the expected `name@sha` format is absent.

apps\\web\\lib\\sacred-mountains.ts.summary: This file is a static content-data module for the web app's "sacred mountains" section, explicitly positioned as distinct from the `/tirth` (temple destinations) and `/pilgrimage` (multi-stop circuits) sections and aimed at long-tail SEO queries like "{mountain} parikrama" or "{mountain} legend". It exports the `MountainAccess` union type (`'vehicle' | 'trek' | 'spiritual-only'`), the `SacredMountain` interface, the `SACRED_MOUNTAINS` array of ten hand-authored entries (from Mount Kailash to the cosmological Mount Meru), and two lookup helpers, `sacredMountainSlugs()` and `getSacredMountain(slug)`, presumably for route generation and page rendering. The module has zero imports — it is pure typed data with no runtime dependencies, though it cross-references other content domains through `deitySlug` (linking to deity pages like `shiva` or `kartikeya`) and `nearbyTirthas` (slugs of tirth entries), making it a join point in the content graph. Notable design choices include `height: number | null` to accommodate the non-geographic Mount Meru, the optional `templeAtSummit` field, and the `modernAccess` classification which encodes whether a mountain is drivable, trek-only, or worshipped without climbing (e.g., Govardhan and Arunachala are circumambulated, never summited). Each entry bundles practical pilgrimage logistics (`pilgrimRoute`, `bestSeason`) with Puranic narrative (`legend`, `significance`), so consumers get both travel-guide and mythological content from a single record. Because the data is hardcoded, adding a mountain requires a code change and redeploy, and slug consistency with the tirth and deity datasets is maintained by convention rather than enforced by the compiler.

apps\\web\\lib\\rashis.ts.summary: This file is the canonical zodiac (rashi) data dictionary for the web app, powering the programmatic-SEO route `/astrology/horoscope/[rashi]` plus an existing client-side horoscope page, targeting long-tail queries like "aries horoscope today" and "mesh rashifal". It exports the `RashiInfo` interface (bilingual Hindi/English fields covering daily prediction, career, love, health, lucky number/color/direction, mantra, ruling planet, element, and an overall rating) and the `RASHIS` constant, a hardcoded array of all twelve signs. Three helper functions sit on top: `getRashi(slug)` for lookup by URL slug, `rashiSlugs()` which returns all slugs (presumably for `generateStaticParams`), and `pujasForRashi(r)` which maps a rashi's ruling planet to suggested puja slugs to drive cross-linking into `/pujas/[slug]`. The module has zero dependencies — it is pure static data with no imports, API calls, or date logic. The notable gotcha is that the "daily" horoscope content is fully static: predictions never change by date, so every visitor sees identical text regardless of the day. Additionally, all `symbol` fields are empty strings awaiting assets, and `pujasForRashi` relies on brittle case-insensitive substring matching against the `rulingPlanet` string (e.g. "mars"/"mangal") and returns hardcoded slugs like `navgraha-puja` and `maha-mrityunjaya` that must stay in sync with the pujas catalog or the cross-links will 404.

apps\\web\\lib\\rahu-kalam.ts.summary: This module computes the three daily inauspicious windows of Vedic muhurat shastra — Rahu Kalam, Yamaganda, and Gulika Kalam — for a given date and location, returning them as a `RahuKalamDay` object consumed by the web app's panchang features. Its main export, `computeRahuKalam(input, asOf?)`, takes a `RahuKalamInput` (date, lat/lng, timezone offset, city) and an optional reference instant, then splits the sunrise-to-sunset arc into eight equal octets and places each dosha according to per-weekday lookup tables (`RAHU_OCTET`, `YAMAGANDA_OCTET`, `GULIKA_OCTET`, indexed Sunday-first and sourced from Brihat Samhita / Muhurta Chintamani). Each `DoshaWindow` carries display metadata — English label, Sanskrit name, ruling deity, and an "avoid" advisory string — via the exported `DOSHA_LABEL`, `DOSHA_SANSKRIT`, `DOSHA_RULER`, and `DOSHA_AVOID` maps, plus timing fields and an `isCurrent` flag; the result also surfaces `currentDosha` and `nextDosha` pointers. Rather than computing solar events itself, it depends entirely on the sibling `./choghadiya` module, borrowing sunrise/sunset from `computeChoghadiya`'s day-period boundaries and re-exporting `CITY_OPTIONS` for the UI. Notable gotchas: local "now" is derived by manually shifting the timestamp by `tz` hours and reading UTC fields (so `isCurrent`/`nextDosha` only populate when the requested date is today in that timezone), `nextDosha` never wraps into the following day, and the function returns null when the underlying choghadiya computation fails, the day arc is non-positive, or the weekday can't be resolved.

apps\\web\\lib\\sacred-rivers.ts.summary: This file is a static content-data module powering a programmatic-SEO surface for queries like "sacred rivers of india" and "saraswati river vedic," cataloguing the Sapta Sindhu plus supplementary rivers of Bharat. It exports the `SacredRiver` interface (capturing slug, Sanskrit name, length, origin/mouth, states, goddess identity, sacred ghats, legends, spiritual significance, pilgrim season, and scriptural references), the `SACRED_RIVERS` constant holding ten hardcoded entries from `ganga` through `tapti`, and two lookup helpers: `sacredRiverSlugs()` for enumerating routes (likely for static page generation) and `getSacredRiver(slug)` for fetching a single record. The module has no runtime dependencies or external service calls — all content lives inline as typed TypeScript data rather than in a database or CMS. Its main internal coupling is to `lib/tirthas.ts`: the `majorTirthas` field stores slug strings meant to cross-link to tirtha pages, enabling a content graph between rivers and the pilgrimage sites on their banks. Notable gotchas: `majorTirthas` is an unvalidated string array with no compile-time guarantee the slugs exist in the tirthas module, and three rivers (`sindhu`, `brahmaputra`, `tapti`) ship with empty arrays, so consumers must handle the no-cross-link case. The optional `goddessSlug` field similarly implies a related goddesses collection that isn't referenced by module path here. Content is editorially rich and SEO-oriented, so updates require code changes and redeployment rather than a content pipeline.

apps\\web\\lib\\sacred-trees.ts.summary: This file is a static content catalog of sacred trees in Hinduism for the web app, exporting the `SacredTree` interface and a twelve-entry `SACRED_TREES` array covering species like Peepal, Banyan, Bilva, Tulsi, and Kadamba. Each `SacredTree` record bundles a URL `slug`, English/Sanskrit/botanical names, an `associatedDeity` with an optional `deitySlug` cross-reference (e.g. `vishnu`, `shiva`, `krishna`) that presumably links into a separate deities module, plus rich descriptive fields: `spiritualSignificance`, ritual `uses`, puranic `legend`, an optional `mantraIfAny` in Devanagari, an auspicious `plantingMuhurta`, and geographic `foundIn` regions. Two helper functions round out the API: `sacredTreeSlugs()` returns all slugs (useful for static route generation), and `getSacredTree(slug)` performs a linear lookup returning `undefined` for misses. The file has no runtime dependencies — it is pure TypeScript data — making it safe to import from both server and client components. Notable gotchas: `deitySlug` is absent on entries whose deity has no dedicated page (Neem, Ashoka, Sandalwood), lookups are O(n) array scans rather than a map (fine at this size), and all content is hardcoded, so adding a tree means editing source and redeploying rather than touching a CMS.

apps\\web\\lib\\rudrakshas.ts.summary: This file is a static content catalog for Rudraksha prayer beads, part of the web app's lib data layer, built to power SEO-targeted informational pages for queries like "{mukhi} rudraksha benefits" and "rudraksha for {planet/dosha}" per the header comment. It exports three things: the `RudrakshaCategory` union type ('standard' | 'rare' | 'special'), the `Rudraksha` interface describing one bead, and the `RUDRAKSHAS` array holding 14 numbered mukhi varieties (1–14) plus special variants like Ganesh, Gauri-Shankar, Trijuti, and Sawar. Each `Rudraksha` record carries a URL `slug`, `mukhi` count, deity and planet associations, a Sanskrit `mantra` with romanized `mantraTranslit`, `benefits`, wearing guidance (`whoShouldWear`, `notRecommendedFor`, `wearingDay`, `wearingHand`), an `energising` ritual, sourcing `origin`, and a mythological `storyOrigin` — enough structured content to render a full detail page per bead. The file has no imports or runtime dependencies; it is pure typed data consumed elsewhere by the web app (likely route generators or page components). A notable design quirk is that `mukhi` is typed as `number | string` so special non-numbered variants fit the same schema, and the `category` field lets consumers filter premium 'rare' beads from universally wearable 'standard' ones like the 5-mukhi. The content mixes devotional claims with health claims (e.g., BP control, curing ailments), which is worth flagging as a compliance consideration for downstream rendering.

apps\\web\\lib\\sankalp.ts.summary: This file powers the `/sankalp` interactive vow tool in the web app, generating the formal Sanskrit declaration of intent traditionally recited before a puja, vrat, or donation. It exports two static datasets — `GOTRAS` (15 rishi lineages as `Gotra` records) and `INTENTS` (10 `SankalpIntent` records pairing Devanagari intent phrases with English glosses and recommended puja names) — plus lookup helpers `getGotra` and `getIntent`. The main entry point is `buildSankalp`, which takes a `SankalpInput` (yajamana name, gotra slug, optional nakshatra/rashi, city, intent slug, date) and returns a `SankalpOutput` with the full declaration rendered in three parallel forms: `sanskritFull`, `iastFull`, and `englishFull`, assembled via template strings and private `transliterateMasa`/`transliteratePaksha`/`transliterateTithi` lookup tables. Supporting date helpers `approximateTithi`, `approximateMasa`, and `vaaraName` derive lunar-calendar fields from a JavaScript `Date`. The module is fully self-contained with no imports or external services. The key gotcha is accuracy: tithi is approximated from the calendar day-of-month, masa from the month index, and Vikram Samvat as Gregorian year + 57, so the output is a ceremonial approximation rather than a true panchang calculation — integrating a real ephemeris would be needed for astrologically correct results.

apps\\web\\lib\\sapta-rishis.ts.summary: This file is a static content module that defines the canonical dataset for the Sapta Rishis (the seven great Vedic sages) in the web app, pairing each sage with rich encyclopedic metadata — Sanskrit and IAST names, gotra, consort, sons, associated Ursa Major star (with Bayer designation), Rigvedic mandala authorship, pilgrimage sites (tirthas), story summaries, teachings, scriptures, and modern relevance. It exports the `Rishi` type describing this roughly twenty-field record, the `SAPTA_RISHIS` constant array holding the seven hardcoded entries (Atri, Bharadvaja, Gautama, Jamadagni, Kashyapa, Vasishtha, Vishvamitra), and two lookup helpers: `rishiSlugs()`, which returns all URL slugs (likely for static route generation such as Next.js `generateStaticParams`), and `getRishi(slug)`, which finds a single rishi by slug and returns `undefined` on a miss. The module has zero dependencies — it is pure typed data with no imports, I/O, or external services, making it safe to use in both server and client components. Notable details: `hymnsCount` and `rishiOfMandala` are optional fields since Gautama, Jamadagni, and Kashyapa lack fixed mandala attributions, and the `slug` field serves as the sole lookup key, so consumers must handle the not-found case from `getRishi`. Because all content is inline, any editorial correction requires a code change and redeploy rather than a CMS update.

apps\\web\\lib\\sanskrit-lessons-catalog.summary: This file is a static, in-code content catalog for the web app's Sanskrit learning feature, holding the lesson text and quiz data that a lesson UI presumably renders. It defines two exported types — `SanskritLessonQuiz` (a multiple-choice question whose `correct` field is a numeric index into `options`, with an optional `explanation`) and `SanskritLesson` (id, title, subtitle, difficulty `level`, estimated `minutes`, plus `intro` and `body` strings) — alongside the `LESSONS` constant, which currently hardcodes three beginner lessons covering Devanagari vowels, consonants, and the word "namaste." Two accessor functions are exported: `getLesson(id)` does a linear `find` over the array, and `getAllLessons()` returns a shallow copy via `slice()` so callers can't mutate the module-level data. The file has zero imports and no external dependencies — it's pure TypeScript data, meaning there's no CMS or database behind the lessons and adding content requires editing and redeploying this file. Notably, each lesson's `body` is markdown-formatted text (headers, bold, bullet lists) with embedded Devanagari Unicode, so the consuming component must render markdown and handle Indic script correctly. The quiz format is minimal — no per-option feedback or multi-answer support — and with only three lessons the linear lookup in `getLesson` is fine, though a Map would be warranted if the catalog grows.

apps\\web\\lib\\sapta-mathruka.ts.summary: This file is a dependency-free static data module that catalogs the Sapta Matrika (Seven Mother Goddesses) for the web app, serving as the single source of truth for content pages about each deity. It exports the `SaptaMathruka` TypeScript interface, the `SAPTA_MATHRUKA` array containing seven hardcoded records (Brahmani, Vaishnavi, Maheshwari, Indrani, Kaumari, Varahi, and Chamunda), the derived `SAPTA_MATHRUKA_SLUGS` list, and a `getSaptaMathrukaBySlug` lookup helper that returns `undefined` for unknown slugs. Each record bundles iconographic details (consortDeity, vahana, weapons, color, direction), devotional practice fields (beejaMantra, primaryMantra with English transliteration, vrataPractice, bestDay), narrative content (storyOrigin, benefit), and an associatedTemple reference. The slug-based design with a precomputed slug array strongly suggests consumption by dynamic routes (e.g., Next.js `generateStaticParams`) for per-goddess pages. Notable constraints: all content is hardcoded rather than fetched from a CMS or database, so updates require code changes; Sanskrit text is stored inline alongside transliterations with no i18n abstraction; and there are no imports at all, making this a pure leaf module in the dependency graph.

apps\\web\\lib\\samskaras.ts.summary: This file is a static content catalog for the web app documenting the 16 Hindu samskaras (life-cycle sacraments), from Garbhadhana at conception through Antyeshti at death. It exports the `Samskara` and `SamskaraStage` types, the canonical `SAMSKARAS` array where each entry carries a number, slug, Sanskrit and IAST names, life stage, timing, purpose, ritual summary, key elements, officiant, modern relevance, and an optional scriptural reference, plus the `STAGE_LABELS` map that ties the five stages (prenatal, childhood, student, householder, final) to display names referencing the ashrama system. Two lightweight accessors, `samskaraSlugs()` and `getSamskara(slug)`, support slug-based routing and detail-page lookup, and `TOTAL_SAMSKARAS` exposes the count. The module has no dependencies — it is pure hand-curated data with no database, CMS, or external service behind it. A notable design choice is that content lives directly in TypeScript, so adding or editing a samskara requires a code change and redeploy; consumers should treat the array as the single source of truth and always resolve entries via `getSamskara` rather than hardcoding slugs, and note that `scripturalReference` is optional and only present on a few entries such as Garbhadhana, Upanayana, Vivaha, and Antyeshti.

apps\\web\\lib\\search-index.ts.summary: This file provides lightweight in-memory keyword search over the knowledge base for the web app. Its module, `apps/web/lib/search-index.ts`, exports a `SearchHit` interface (a `SearchIndexEntry` augmented with a numeric `score`) and a single function, `searchKnowledge(query, limit = 20)`, which ranks index entries against a user query and returns the top matches. It depends entirely on the sibling `./content` module, calling `buildSearchIndex()` to obtain the entries and reusing the `SearchIndexEntry` type; there are no external libraries or services involved. The scoring is deliberately simple: the query is lowercased and split into tokens, every token must appear somewhere in an entry's combined title, summary, subTopic, and slug (AND semantics — a single missing token zeroes the score), title matches are weighted 3 points while summary matches add 1 extra. Results are sorted by descending score with `localeCompare` on title as a deterministic tie-breaker, then truncated to `limit` (default 20). Notable gotchas: matching is plain substring-based with no stemming, fuzzy tolerance, or field boosting beyond the hardcoded title weight, and `buildSearchIndex()` is invoked on every query, so performance depends on whether that function caches its result in the `content` module.

apps\\web\\lib\\sentry.ts.summary: This file provides lightweight, client-side error reporting for the Next.js web app by integrating Sentry without bundling the Sentry npm package. It exports two functions: `initSentryBrowser`, which lazily injects the pinned Sentry browser SDK (version 8.55.0) from `browser.sentry-cdn.com` as an async script tag and initializes it once loaded, and `captureBrowserException`, which forwards errors to `window.Sentry.captureException` with optional context attached as `extra`. A module-level `initialized` flag plus a global `Window.Sentry` interface declaration make initialization idempotent and type-safe. The only dependencies are the Sentry CDN bundle and environment variables: `NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN` (required—init is a silent no-op without it), `NEXT_PUBLIC_ENV`, and `NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_RELEASE`. Notable design choices include privacy-conscious defaults (`sendDefaultPii: false`), a low 5% `tracesSampleRate`, and graceful degradation: both functions no-op during server-side rendering, and `captureBrowserException` silently drops errors if the CDN script hasn't finished loading, so early-page-load exceptions may be lost.

apps\\web\\lib\\store-admin-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed client for the store-owner admin backend, wrapping fetch calls against API_BASE_URL (from ./api-config) with Bearer-token auth via the authHeaders helper and uniform error messages via describeFailure, which appends the server's message or error field to a status-coded fallback. It exports two type families: StoreReview with its fetcher getMyReviews, and StoreProduct plus CreateStoreProductInput/UpdateStoreProductInput with full CRUD (listStoreProducts, createStoreProduct, updateStoreProduct, deleteStoreProduct) against /store-admin/products. A key gotcha is that reviews are fetched from /store/reviews — mounted under /api/v1/store rather than /store-admin — and because the Review model has no productId column yet, reviews are provider-level buckets and the UI must render an empty state until the schema migration lands. Another constraint: StoreProduct.price is typed as a string because Prisma Decimal serializes to JSON as a string, so callers must apply Number() before any arithmetic.

apps\\web\\lib\\supabase.ts.summary: This file centralizes Supabase client construction for the Next.js web app, providing separate factories for browser and server contexts along with the backend API base URL. `getSupabaseBrowserClient()` returns a lazily-initialized singleton `SupabaseClient` configured with session persistence, automatic token refresh, and URL-based session detection, while `getSupabaseServerClient(accessToken?)` intentionally creates a fresh client per call—with no persistence—because Next.js Server Components and API routes must not share auth state across requests. Both factories build on `createClient` from `@supabase/supabase-js` and read `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` from the environment; since only the anon key is used, all access is governed by row-level security policies. The server variant optionally forwards a user's access token as an `Authorization: Bearer` header so RLS evaluates per-user on server-initiated queries. The file also exports `API_BASE_URL`, defaulting to `http://localhost:4000/api/v1` when `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` is unset, which points at the Fastify backend. A subtle gotcha: the non-null assertions on the env vars mean a missing configuration will fail at runtime rather than at build time.

apps\\web\\lib\\subscription-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's client-side SDK for the marketplace subscription system, wrapping the backend REST routes under `/api/v1/subscriptions` (plans, my, subscribe, cancel) plus an admin listing endpoint, using `API_BASE_URL` from `./api-config` as the base and Bearer-token auth via the `authHeaders` helper. It exports the domain types `ProviderRole`, `SubscriptionStatus`, `SubscriptionPlan`, `MarketplaceSubscription`, and `SubscribeResponse`, along with functions `listPlans`, `getMySubscription`, `subscribeToPlan`, `cancelMySubscription`, and the admin-only `listAllSubscriptions`. Beyond plain data fetching, it also drives the payment flow: `loadRazorpayScript` lazily injects Razorpay's `checkout.js` from the CDN exactly once (via a cached promise), and `openRazorpayCheckout` opens the recurring-subscription checkout modal with `onSuccess`/`onDismiss` callbacks. A notable design choice is defensive payload handling — `unwrapPlans` and `unwrapSub` tolerate multiple response envelope shapes (bare arrays, `{plans}`, `{data}`, `{subscription}`), and `getMySubscription` treats 404 as "no subscription" rather than an error, reflecting the file's stated goal of degrading gracefully so demo/offline flows don't crash. Other gotchas: every fetch uses `cache: 'no-store'`, error messages are extracted from the server's JSON `message` field when available, and the Razorpay helpers are SSR-safe, returning `false` when `window` is undefined. The external dependency is Razorpay's hosted checkout script; internally it depends only on `api-config`.

apps\\web\\lib\\support-api.ts.summary: This file is the browser-side client for the support tickets backend, bundling both the HTTP calls and the Zod validation schemas used by support UI forms. It exports three schemas with inferred types — newTicketSchema/NewTicketInput for ticket creation (subject, body, a fixed category enum like 'puja' or 'payments', priority, optional orderId and attachmentName), replySchema/ReplyInput for posting messages with an optional internal flag, and patchTicketSchema/PatchTicketInput for admin edits to status, priority, and assignedTo — plus five async functions (listTickets, getTicketById, createTicket, patchTicket, postMessage) that hit the /support/tickets REST endpoints under API_BASE_URL. It depends on the internal api-config module for the base URL, imports the Ticket, TicketCategory, TicketPriority, and TicketStatus types from the sibling support module (re-exporting them so callers need only one import), and uses zod and the global fetch API. Notable details: authentication is an optional Bearer token passed per call via authHeaders rather than stored state, the asJson helper prefers server-supplied error messages when throwing, and the unwrapTicket/unwrapTickets helpers defensively normalize several possible response envelope shapes ({ticket}, {tickets}, {data}, or bare arrays). Reads use cache: 'no-store' to avoid stale ticket data, and listTickets supports an ?all=true admin flag to fetch every user's tickets rather than just the caller's own.

apps\\web\\lib\\sade-sati.ts.summary: This module computes Vedic Sade Sati and Dhaiya (Kantaka Shani) periods — Saturn's 7.5-year transit across the 12th/1st/2nd rashis from the natal Moon, plus the lighter 4th- and 8th-house dhaiya transits — following Brihat Parashara/Phaladeepika conventions. Its main export, `computeSadeSati(input, asOfDate?)`, takes a `NakshatraFinderInput`, derives the natal Moon rashi via `findNakshatra` from the sibling `./nakshatra-finder` module (returning null if that lookup fails), and returns a `SadeSatiResult` containing every non-'normal' `SadeSatiPhase` from birth to age 90 with start/end dates, ages, current-phase flags, and a human-readable `reasoning` string. Other exports include the `SadeSatiPhaseKind` union ('rising' | 'peak' | 'setting' | 'dhaiya-4th' | 'dhaiya-8th' | 'normal'), remediation content constants `SADE_SATI_REMEDIES` and `SADE_SATI_DOS_DONTS`, the label/description maps re-exported as `PHASE_KIND_LABEL` and `PHASE_KIND_DESCRIPTION`, and `SATURN_DAYS_PER_RASHI`. There are no external dependencies: Saturn's tropical longitude comes from a simplified Meeus VSOP87 truncation in `saturnTropicalLongitude` (~1° accuracy), corrected to sidereal with a linear Lahiri ayanamsa fit that intentionally mirrors nakshatra-finder — acceptable only because rashis are 30° wide. Phase boundaries are detected by stepping Saturn forward in 30-day increments and bisecting any rashi change to ~1-day precision, but since only sample endpoints are compared, a retrograde double-crossing inside a single window would be silently missed. All dates flow through Julian Day math at UT 00:00 as YYYY-MM-DD strings, and `isCurrent` is decided by lexicographic ISO string comparison, which is safe only because of the zero-padded format.

apps\\web\\lib\\shlokas.ts.summary: This file is the seed shloka catalogue for the web app — a curated, static list of Sanskrit verses (Bhagavad Gita, Upanishads, Vedic suktas, stotras, and Patanjali) bundled directly into the frontend with no imports or external dependencies. It exports the `Shloka` type (fields: `slug`, `source`, `text` in Devanagari, optional IAST `translit`, English `meaning`, and `tags`) and the `SHLOKAS` array containing roughly forty entries. Each entry's `slug` is a stable identifier consumed by `/shlokas/<slug>` share URLs and by the social-queue agent's output, so the file's header comment lays down a strict append-only rule: new shlokas may be added, but entries must never be deleted or re-ordered, because slugs underpin existing backlinks and SEO. The curation is deliberately small and non-controversial to keep the launch surface SEO-clean. A notable gotcha is that the data violates its own uniqueness assumption in at least two places — `gita-9-22` and `gita-18-66` each appear twice with different `source` labels and `tags` — which would make slug-based lookups or routing ambiguous for any consumer that indexes `SHLOKAS` by slug. Additionally, some slugs alias the same verse under different names (e.g. `shanti-mantra` versus `asatoma-sadgamaya-pavamana`), which is intentional but worth knowing when deduplicating content. The `meaning` field is inconsistent in depth, ranging from plain translations to long interpretive commentaries in later entries, so UI consumers should not assume uniform length.

apps\\web\\lib\\shubh-muhurat.ts.summary: This file implements a composite "Shubh Muhurat" (auspicious timing) finder that ranks time windows for twelve life events—marriage, griha-pravesh, vehicle purchase, surgery, and so on—by layering scores from three already-existing modules rather than doing any new astronomy. Its single main export, `computeShubhMuhurat`, calls `computeChoghadiya`, `computeHora`, and `computeRahuKalam` (from `./choghadiya`, `./hora`, and `./rahu-kalam` respectively), returning `null` if any of them fail, and otherwise scoring each Hora window (~60-minute slots, used as the natural grid) by summing a `CHOGH_SCORE` lookup for the Choghadiya active at the slot's midpoint, a planet-match bonus based on the event's `idealPlanets` ordering from the exported `EVENT_OPTIONS` table, a −50 penalty per overlap with Rahu Kalam/Yamaganda/Gulika windows, and a small daytime bonus, all clamped to 0–100. It also exports the `EventType` union plus the `MuhuratInput`, `MuhuratWindow`, and `MuhuratResult` types, the latter bundling the top six windows (sorted by score), all scored windows with `excellent`/`good`/`fair`/`avoid` verdicts, and the raw `ChoghadiyaDay`, `HoraDay`, and `RahuKalamDay` payloads for diagnostics. Notable gotchas: night windows that wrap past midnight are handled by normalizing minutes against 1440, but the Rahu overlap check for wrapped windows only tests up to midnight since Rahu Kalam is day-only; an unknown `event` silently falls back to the `'general'` preset; and each window carries human-readable `reasons` and `warnings` chips intended for direct UI display.

apps\\web\\lib\\support.ts.summary: This file is the client-side support and customer-care data layer for the Darshya web app, providing everything the support UI needs without a backend: ticket types, canned content, mock replies, and localStorage persistence. It exports the core domain types — `Ticket`, `TicketMessage`, `TicketActivity`, `TicketStatus`, `TicketPriority`, and `TicketCategory` (covering the app's eight verticals from puja to yatra) — along with display metadata in `SUPPORT_CATEGORIES`, `CATEGORY_MAP`, `PRIORITIES`, and `STATUSES`. Ticket persistence is handled by `loadUserTickets`, `saveUserTickets`, `addUserTicket`, `updateUserTicket`, and `getUserTicket`, all reading and writing a versioned localStorage key (`poojly:support:tickets:v1`), while `formatTicketId` mints human-readable IDs like `BS-TKT-48213`. For admin views it ships `SAMPLE_ADMIN_TICKETS`, ten hardcoded realistic tickets with message threads and activity logs, and `generateAgentReply` produces templated per-category agent responses using a random name from `randomAgentName`. The live-chat side is served by `AUTO_REPLY_RULES` and `findAutoReply`, a naive lowercase substring matcher over keyword lists, plus a large `FAQ_ITEMS` catalog organized into sections. The file has no external dependencies — it is pure TypeScript using only `window.localStorage` and `Date.now()`. Notable gotchas: every storage helper guards against SSR with a `typeof window === 'undefined'` check and silently swallows JSON parse/write errors; ticket IDs are just the last five digits of a timestamp, so collisions are plausible; and `findAutoReply` returns the first matching rule, making the order of `AUTO_REPLY_RULES` semantically significant (e.g. "hi" matches greetings before any longer keyword is considered). Everything here is mock/local data, so any real ticketing backend would replace these helpers wholesale.

apps\\web\\lib\\t.ts.summary: This file is a minimal, type-safe translation utility for the web app, providing localized string lookups keyed off the English message catalog in `./i18n/en.json`. It derives a `Messages` type from that JSON and exposes a `Translator` per namespace: a callable that maps a key to its string (falling back to the key itself when the value is missing or not a string) plus a `raw` method that returns the untyped dictionary value. Three factories are exported — `getTranslations` (async, returning a resolved Promise), `useTranslations`, and `t` — all of which synchronously build a namespace-scoped translator via the internal `build` function. The only dependency is the internal `en.json` file; there are no external i18n libraries involved. Notably, the API deliberately mirrors next-intl's `getTranslations`/`useTranslations` signatures, presumably so a real i18n library could be swapped in later without changing call sites. Gotchas: only English is supported with no locale negotiation, `useTranslations` is not an actual React hook despite its name, and each call rebuilds the translator closure rather than caching it.

apps\\web\\lib\\temple-details.ts.summary: This file is a static content store that supplies rich, editorial-style detail pages for individual temples in the Darshya web app, keyed by temple slug, with the header comment noting that slugs absent here should fall back to basic API data. It exports the `DeityType` union (Shiva, Vishnu, Shakti, Ganesha, Sikh, Other), the `PujaOffering` interface describing a bookable puja with INR price, duration, and spiritual benefit, the comprehensive `TempleDetailRich` interface, and the central `TEMPLE_DETAILS` record holding one full entry per temple (e.g. `kashi-vishwanath`, `somnath`, `mahakaleshwar`, `omkareshwar`). Each `TempleDetailRich` entry bundles history, significance, deity description, festivals, opening hours, dress code, travel logistics, accommodation, rules, nearby attractions, testimonials, and FAQs, plus flags like `isJyotirlinga` and links to `officialWebsite`, `officialBookingUrl`, and `officialDarshanBookingUrl`. The module has no imports or runtime dependencies — it is pure typed data consumed by temple page components. A key design decision is that content is hardcoded in source rather than fetched from a CMS, so adding or editing a temple requires a code change and redeploy. The `bookExternal` flag on `PujaOffering` is an important gotcha: when true, booking must be handed off to the temple's official website rather than completed in-app, reflecting that some services (like Mahakaleshwar's Bhasma Aarti) are only sold through official channels. Prices are stored as raw INR numbers, and several entries emphasize queue-avoidance products (Sugam Darshan, VIP darshan) that align with the app's booking flow.

apps\\web\\lib\\temple-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed API client for the temple portal, wrapping the backend's `/temple-portal/*` routes plus a couple of public catalog endpoints, and building all URLs from `API_BASE_URL` imported from `./api-config`. It exports `getMyDonations` for the donor history view; full CRUD for temple puja offerings (`listTemplePujas`, `createTemplePuja`, `updateTemplePuja`, `deleteTemplePuja`) typed around `TemplePujaOffering`; and parallel CRUD for live darshan streams (`listDarshanStreams`, `createDarshanStream`, `updateDarshanStream`, `deleteDarshanStream`) plus a dedicated `setDarshanStreamStatus` for lifecycle transitions. It also provides unauthenticated lookups `listPublicPriests` and `listPujaTypes` to populate form dropdowns, returning `PublicPriestSummary` and `PujaTypeSummary` shapes. A key gotcha is documented up front: donations are currently gaushala-only in the Prisma schema, so `getMyDonations` always yields an empty array until a `TempleDonation` model ships, and the `TempleDonation` interface is forward-compatible speculation. Because Prisma `Decimal` fields serialize as strings, money fields like `amount`, `priceOverride`, and `nriPrice` are typed as strings rather than numbers. Error handling is deliberately inconsistent: portal mutations throw enriched errors via the `describeFailure` helper, while the two public list functions silently return `[]` on failure, and `listPujaTypes` tolerates three different response envelope shapes (`pujaTypes`, `data`, `items`). Note also that `authHeaders` accepts an undefined token and simply omits the `Authorization` header, and the status patch type `DarshanStreamStatusPatch` ('scheduled' | 'live' | 'ended') intentionally differs from the stored `DarshanStreamStatus` ('offline' | 'live' | 'scheduled').

apps\\web\\lib\\shakti-peeths.ts.summary: This file is a hand-curated, pure-data TypeScript module cataloging the 51 Shakti Peeths — pilgrimage sites from the Sati legend per the Devi Bhagavata and Pithanirnaya — and its header comment makes the purpose explicit: fueling SEO-targeted content pages for queries like "{name} shakti peeth" and "shakti peeth in {state}". It exports three entities: the `ShaktiPeethCountry` union type ('India' | 'Nepal' | 'Bangladesh' | 'Sri Lanka' | 'Pakistan' | 'Tibet'), the `ShaktiPeeth` interface with roughly twenty fields covering both mythology (bodyPart, devi, bhairava, legend, significance) and travel logistics (darshanTimings, howToReach, primaryPujas, modernAccess, estimatedDailyVisitors), and the `SHAKTI_PEETHS` constant array holding one object literal per site, from Kamakhya through Srisailam and onward. The module has zero imports, no runtime logic, and no external service calls, so it is safe to consume from any rendering layer in the web app. A key design decision is that even structured-sounding data — timings, seasons, visitor counts, booking URLs — is stored as free-form display strings rather than typed values, meaning the catalog supports content rendering but not filtering, scheduling, or validation. The data carries editorial caveats inline rather than as flags: Chintpurni's bodyPart notes conflicting traditions, multiple entries repeat "Right hand" as the body part, and politically sensitive sites like Sharada Peeth (inaccessible in PoK), Hinglaj Mata (Pakistan permits required), and Manasarovar (MEA yatra registration) encode access restrictions in prose fields. The provided excerpt truncates mid-entry at number 25, so consumers should expect the full file to continue to the promised 51 entries.

apps\\web\\lib\\use-premium.ts.summary: This file defines `useIsPremium`, a client-side React hook that determines whether the currently signed-in user holds a premium subscription, returning an `{ isPremium, loading }` pair for gating UI. It consumes `useAuth` from `./auth-context` to read `isAuthenticated` and the session's `accessToken`, then calls the backend endpoint `GET /subscriptions/is-premium` (base URL from `API_BASE_URL` in `./api-config`) with a Bearer token, defaulting to non-premium whenever the user is unauthenticated or the request fails. The hook is the single client-side source of truth for premium status across several features noted in the header comment: the AQ ad-gate, the NRI surcharge bypass, priority-booking gating, and the M3 AI astro paywall waiver. Notable design choices include a `cancelled` flag inside the effect to prevent state updates after unmount or token change, and a fail-closed posture where network or server errors silently resolve to `isPremium: false` rather than surfacing an error to the caller. Because it depends on the auth session, the fetch re-runs whenever `isAuthenticated` or the access token changes, so consumers should expect `loading` to cycle on login/logout transitions.

apps\\web\\lib\\tithis.ts.summary: This file is a static data module for the `apps/web` frontend that catalogs the tithis (lunar days) of the Hindu calendar, providing the content backing for panchang/calendar pages. It exports the `Tithi` interface — describing slug, tithi number, English and Sanskrit names, presiding deity, the five-fold classical `category` union ('nanda' | 'bhadra' | 'jaya' | 'rikta' | 'purna'), separate `shuklaSignificance`/`krishnaSignificance` texts for the waxing and waning fortnights, auspicious/inauspicious activity lists, fasting traditions, associated festivals, and a mantra in Devanagari plus romanized form — and the `TITHIS` constant array holding one fully-populated record per tithi. The array has no imports or runtime dependencies; it is pure hardcoded content meant to be imported directly by page components or lookup helpers elsewhere in the app. A notable structural choice is the dual representation: there is one generic entry per tithi (e.g. `pratipada`, `ekadashi`, `purnima`, `amavasya`) plus additional paksha-specific entries (e.g. `shukla-pratipada` vs `krishna-pratipada`) where observances diverge sharply between fortnights, so consumers must decide which slug convention to query. The `number` field follows the traditional 30-tithi lunar month, so `amavasya` is numbered 30 while `purnima` is 15, which matters for any sorting or lookup logic. Because everything is inlined as literal data, content edits require code changes and redeploys, and the generic and paksha-specific records duplicate some festival and fasting text (with occasional category inconsistencies, e.g. `panchami` as 'purna' vs `shukla-panchami` as 'bhadra'), which is a maintenance gotcha for the team.

apps\\web\\lib\\tirthas.ts.summary: This file is a static content-data module for the web app's single-destination sacred site pages, explicitly scoped (per its header comment) to individual tirthas rather than multi-stop `/pilgrimage` circuits, and curated to capture SEO queries like "tirupati darshan slot booking" and "amarnath yatra registration." It exports three things: the `TirthaCategory` union type (`'shaiva' | 'vaishnava' | 'shakti' | 'jain' | 'sikh' | 'syncretic'`), the `Tirtha` interface describing one destination across roughly two dozen fields (slug, presiding deity, `darshanTimings`, `averageWaitTime`, `howToReach`, `dressCode`, `photoPolicy`, `legend`, `modernRelevance`, etc.), and the `TIRTHAS` constant array holding hand-written records for major sites including Kashi Vishwanath, Tirupati Balaji, Vaishno Devi, Somnath, Jagannath Puri, Amarnath, Rameswaram, Badrinath, Kedarnath, Dwarka, Mahakaleshwar Ujjain, and Ayodhya Ram Mandir. The module has zero imports — it is pure typed data with no internal or external dependencies, presumably consumed by route handlers or page components elsewhere in `apps/web` that render one page per `slug`. A notable design choice is that even numeric-ish values (`estimatedDailyVisitors`, `averageWaitTime`) are stored as free-text strings, so the data supports display but not structured filtering or comparison; only `vipDarshanAvailable` and `onlineBookingAvailable` are booleans. The `TirthaCategory` type anticipates `jain`, `sikh`, and `syncretic` entries that don't yet appear in the visible data, suggesting planned expansion. The main gotcha is freshness: everything is hardcoded editorial content (visitor counts, post-2021 corridor expansions, 2024 ropeway and bridge openings, booking URLs), so timings, prices, and infrastructure claims will silently go stale unless someone manually maintains the array.

apps\\web\\lib\\vastu.ts.summary: This file is a pure, dependency-free Vastu Shastra scoring engine for the web app: it evaluates whether rooms are placed in auspicious compass directions according to classical sources (Mayamatam, Vishwakarma Prakash, Brihat Samhita), with no astronomy or external calls involved. It exports two static datasets — `DISHAS`, describing the eight directions with deity, ruling planet, element, and nature, and `ROOMS`, which maps each of the fifteen `RoomType` values to its `ideal`, `acceptable`, and `avoid` direction lists plus a one-line shastric justification — along with lookup helpers `getDisha` and `getRoom` that silently fall back to the first entry when given an unknown code.
