The main entry point is `computeVastu`, which takes a `VastuInput` (house facing plus chosen direction per room) and returns a `VastuResult` containing per-room `Placement` scores, an overall 0–100 score computed as a simple mean, human-readable `strengths` and `dosha` strings, and a verdict bucketed at thresholds of 80/65/45. Scoring in the internal `scoreSingle` uses a baseline of 50, adding 40 for ideal, 20 for acceptable, subtracting 10 for unlisted ("neutral") directions and 50 for avoid, then clamping to 0–100 — so a neutral placement actually scores below the baseline, which is worth knowing when interpreting results. `suggestIdealLayout` builds a canonical ideal floor plan by taking each room's first ideal direction. Key types consumers will use are `Direction`, `Disha`, `RoomType`, `RoomDef`, `Placement`, `VastuInput`, and `VastuResult`. Notable constraints: the model is intentionally simplistic (no weighting by room importance, no interaction between facing and placement), Sanskrit strings are embedded directly as Devanagari literals, and the non-null assertions in the fallback lookups assume `DISHAS` and `ROOMS` are never empty.

apps\\web\\lib\\upanishads.ts.summary: This file is a static data module in the web app's `lib` directory that powers programmatic-SEO pages about the Upanishads, explicitly following the same pattern as the sibling modules `gita-chapters.ts` and `ramayana-kandas.ts`. It exports the `UpanishadInfo` interface and a single `UPANISHADS` constant array of hand-authored records, each carrying a URL `slug`, English/Sanskrit/IAST names, Vedic affiliation (`veda` constrained to the union 'Rig' | 'Sama' | 'Yajur' | 'Atharva', plus a free-text `vedaShakha` recension), `mantraCount`, `centralTheme`, a long-form `summary`, `keyConcepts`, a required `famousVerse` with Sanskrit, transliteration, translation and reference, an optional `mahavakya` (great-saying) in the same shape, and a pithy `takeaway` for display. The module has no runtime dependencies — it imports nothing and is pure typed content meant to be consumed by page components that render one SEO route per slug. A notable discrepancy is that the header comment advertises the "10 principal Upanishads (Dashopanishads)" while the array actually extends well beyond the classical ten (adding Svetasvatara, Kaushitaki, Maitri, Yoga Tattva, Yoga Kundalini, and likely more in the truncated portion), so consumers should not assume a fixed count of ten. Data-quality gotchas include `mantraCount: 0` for the prose-heavy Taittiriya entry (a sentinel rather than a real count) and the optional `mahavakya`, which is present on only some records, so renderers must handle its absence. Because all content is inline string data, any correction or addition requires a code edit and redeploy rather than a CMS change.

apps\\web\\lib\\use-onboarding.ts.summary: This file defines `useOnboarding`, a client-side React hook that lets components read and mutate the persisted onboarding flow state (current step, dismissal, etc.) managed by the sibling module `./onboarding-store`. It re-exposes the store's `OnboardingState` through the exported `UseOnboarding` type and returns `{ data, set, reset, isFirstRun, isFlagEnabled }`, where `set` and `reset` are stable callbacks delegating to `setOnboarding` and `clearOnboarding`. The hook is built on React's `useSyncExternalStore`, with a `subscribe` function that listens to both the app-level `ONBOARDING_EVENT` and the browser's cross-tab `storage` event so multiple mounted consumers (e.g. the `NavAuthButton` menu and the onboarding modal) and multiple tabs stay in sync. SSR is handled explicitly: `subscribe` no-ops when `window` is undefined and `getServerSnapshot` returns `null`, which matters because the underlying store reads from `localStorage`. Two derived conveniences are computed on each render: `isFirstRun` is true when there is no stored state or `currentStep < 3` (hard-coding step 3 as the completion threshold), and `isFlagEnabled` reflects the `isOnboardingFlagEnabled()` feature-flag check from the store module. The file is marked `'use client'` for Next.js and has no external dependencies beyond React itself. A gotcha worth noting: because `isFirstRun` treats missing state as first run, any logic that clears onboarding storage will cause the flow to restart.

apps\\web\\lib\\vedas.ts.summary: This file is a static content module for the `apps/web` frontend that hardcodes descriptive data about the four Vedas rather than fetching it from a database or CMS. It exports the `Veda` type, a wide interface covering each text's identity fields (slug, name, Sanskrit, IAST transliteration), statistics (totalMantras, shakha counts), and long-form content (summary, fourParts breakdown of samhita/brahmana/aranyaka/upanishad, principalUpanishads, famousHymns, oralPreservation, modernRelevance). The main export is the `VEDAS` array containing four fully populated records — `rigveda`, `samaveda`, `yajurveda`, and `atharvaveda` — which serves as the single source of truth for Veda-related pages. Two helper functions support routing and lookup: `vedaSlugs()` returns all slugs (likely consumed by Next.js `generateStaticParams` for static page generation), and `getVeda(slug)` finds a single record, returning `undefined` for unknown slugs so callers must handle the not-found case. A derived constant `TOTAL_MANTRAS` aggregates the mantra counts across all four Vedas at module load. The file has zero imports and no external dependencies, making it a self-contained data layer. A notable tradeoff is that all editorial content lives in source code, so any content correction requires a code change and redeploy rather than a CMS edit.

apps\\web\\lib\\vipassana-centers.ts.summary: This file is a hand-curated static catalog of Vipassana meditation centers for the web app, exporting the `VipassanaCenter` interface, the `VipassanaLineage` and `VipassanaRegion` union types, and the `VIPASSANA_CENTERS` constant array that holds the actual records. Each center record carries identity fields (`slug`, `name`, `city`, `state`, `country`), classification (`region`, `lineage`, optional `isFlagshipCenter`), practical planning data (`nearestAirport`, `nearestRailway`, `climate`, `bestSeason`, `languagesTaught`, `capacity`), outbound links (`officialUrl`, `bookingUrl`, mostly `*.dhamma.org` subdomains), and long-form editorial prose in `summary` and `notesForFirstTimers` aimed at content/SEO pages. The dataset is dominated by Goenka-tradition Dhamma centers in India (Dhamma Giri, Dhamma Pattana, Dhamma Khetta, etc.) plus flagship centers abroad (Dhamma Dhara, Dhamma Dīpa, Dhamma Bhumi) and a few non-Goenka venues like Tushita Meditation Centre, Root Institute, and Bodhi Zendo. There are no imports, functions, or runtime dependencies — it is pure typed data consumed by other modules in `apps/web`. Notable gotchas: optional fields (`foundedYear`, `capacity`, `nearestRailway`) are populated inconsistently across records, the `mahasi` and `imc-lineage` lineage values appear unused in the visible data, and Bodhi Zendo — explicitly described as Zen, "not Vipassana strictly" — is tagged with the `thai-forest` lineage, suggesting the taxonomy is loose and consumers should not treat `lineage` as strictly accurate. Because everything is hardcoded, adding or updating a center requires a code change and redeploy rather than a CMS edit.

apps\\web\\lib\\vedic-months.ts.summary: This file is a static reference dataset for the twelve Hindu lunar (Vedic) calendar months, living in the web app's shared lib folder. It exports the `VedicMonth` interface, which models each month with fields for slug, ordinal number, English and Sanskrit names, approximate Gregorian range, season (`ritu`), presiding Aditya and deity, major festivals, major vratas (fasts/observances), ritual character, religious significance, and a mantra in both Devanagari and transliterated English. The main export, `VEDIC_MONTHS`, is a hardcoded array of twelve records from Chaitra through Phalguna, along with `VEDIC_MONTH_SLUGS` (a derived list of slug strings, likely for route validation or static path generation) and `getVedicMonthBySlug`, a simple lookup helper returning a month or `undefined`. The file has zero imports — it depends on no internal modules, external libraries, or services, making it a pure in-repo content source. A notable design choice is that all content is manually curated and embedded directly in code rather than fetched from a CMS or database, so updates require a code change and redeploy. Consumers should also note that `gregorianRange` is approximate (lunar months shift year to year) and that the data embeds specific traditional claims (e.g., Purana citations), so it functions as editorial content rather than computed calendrical logic.

apps\\web\\lib\\vedic-yajnas.ts.summary: This file is a static content module that catalogs Vedic fire-sacrifices (yajnas) for the web app, pairing scholarly descriptions with structured metadata. It defines the `YajnaCategory` union type (nitya, naimittika, kamya, royal) and the `YajnaModernStatus` union (actively-performed, rare, extinct, reconstructed), the `VedicYajna` interface describing each rite (slug, priests required, duration, deities, mantra sources, material offerings, historical significance, modern relevance), and the human-readable `CATEGORY_LABELS` and `CATEGORY_DESCRIPTIONS` maps used for UI rendering. The core export is the `VEDIC_YAJNAS` array containing ten hard-coded entries — from Agnihotra through Ashvamedha, Rajasuya, and Gosava — while `vedicYajnaSlugs()` and `getVedicYajna(slug)` are lookup helpers clearly shaped for static route generation and detail pages. The module has zero imports: no internal dependencies, no external libraries or services, so all content lives inline and any edit requires a code change and redeploy. A notable design decision is the careful editorial handling of extinct animal-offering rites: entries like Ashvamedha, Rajasuya, and Pashubandha carry explicit disclaimers that they are scriptural-historical references only and note modern substitutions such as the pishtapashu flour effigy. One small gotcha: the `reconstructed` status is declared in the type but never used by any entry, so consumers shouldn't assume it appears in the data.

apps\\web\\lib\\vedic-astrology.ts.summary: This file is a self-contained, client-side Vedic astrology engine that computes sidereal (Lahiri ayanamsa) birth charts entirely in TypeScript with no external dependencies or API calls — all planetary math is done locally using simplified astronomical algorithms accurate to roughly 1–2 degrees for the Sun and Moon and coarser for other planets. Its low-level exported functions handle the computational pipeline: `toJulianDay` converts civil dates to Julian Day numbers, `getLahiriAyanamsa` computes precession (a comment notes a fixed 100× unit bug in the precession rate), `tropicalToSidereal` adjusts longitudes, and `getSunLongitude`, `getMoonLongitude`, and `getPlanetLongitude` produce tropical positions for the seven classical planets plus the lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu. The exported types describe the output model: `PlanetPosition` (with sign, house, nakshatra, dignity status, retrograde flag), `HouseInfo`, `NavamsaHouse`, `DashaPeriod`, `BhuktiPeriod`, `DoshaInfo`, and the aggregate `KundliData` result. Internal helpers derive the ascendant from latitude/longitude via local sidereal time (`getAscendant`), map longitudes to the 27 nakshatras and their padas, assign planetary dignity (`getPlanetStatus`), detect retrograde motion by sampling positions a half-day apart, compute the 120-year Vimshottari dasha sequence from the Moon's nakshatra lord (`calculateDashas`), and flag four afflictions in `detectDoshas` — Manglik, Kaal Sarp, Sade Sati, and Pitra Dosha — each with severity and remedy text in English and Hindi. A key constraint is the hardcoded `CITY_COORDS` table, which only covers major Indian cities (all assumed UTC+5:5), so births elsewhere fall back to default coordinates. Notable simplifications to be aware of when extending it: Mercury and Venus are modeled as sinusoidal elongation arcs around the Sun rather than true orbits, Rahu/Ketu use mean node motion, and Sade Sati is checked against the natal Saturn position rather than the current transit.

apps\\web\\lib\\wellness-api.ts.summary: This file is the web app's typed API client for the instructor-facing wellness portal, wrapping the backend's student-roster and session-management endpoints. It exports types mirroring the server responses — `WellnessStudent` (with nested `WellnessStudentSession`), `WellnessSession`, the `WellnessSessionType`/`WellnessSessionStatus` unions, and the `CreateWellnessSessionInput`/`UpdateWellnessSessionInput` payloads — alongside functions `getMyStudents`, `listMySessions`, `createWellnessSession`, `updateWellnessSession`, `deleteWellnessSession`, and `setWellnessSessionRoom`. Everything is built on `API_BASE_URL` from `./api-config` and calls the NestJS backend routes `/wellness-portal/students` and `/wellness/sessions` (implemented in `apps/api/src/routes/wellness-sessions.ts`) using plain `fetch` with an optional Bearer token via the `authHeaders` helper. A shared `describeFailure` helper enriches thrown errors by pulling `message` or `error` fields out of non-OK JSON responses. Two serialization gotchas are documented in comments: `WellnessSession.priceInr` arrives as a string because Prisma Decimal serializes to JSON as text, so callers must `Number()` it before arithmetic, and `scheduledAt` is an ISO string rather than a `Date`. The `setWellnessSessionRoom` function was added in the 2026-08 wellness revamp to expose the previously unreachable `PATCH /sessions/:id/room` endpoint, letting instructors attach a Jitsi live-class URL from the UI.

apps\\web\\lib\\vrats.ts.summary: This file is a static content dataset that powers the programmatic-SEO pages at `/vrat/[slug]` in the web app, targeting long-tail search queries like "ekadashi vrat" and "karva chauth vidhi." It exports the `Vrat` TypeScript interface, which defines a rich per-vrat schema (slug, English and Devanagari names, a `category` union of 'weekly' | 'lunar' | 'seasonal' | 'family', deity, significance, fastingRules and rituals bullet lists, prasad, timing fields, mantra, and a storyOrigin katha summary), plus the `VRATS` constant array holding the curated entries. The visible data covers major observances — `ekadashi`, `pradosh`, `shivratri`, `karva-chauth`, `navratri`, `janmashtami`, `ganesh-chaturthi`, `satyanarayan`, `hartalika-teej`, `monday-vrat`, `purnima-vrat`, and `amavasya-vrat` — with the file truncated mid-entry. There are no imports or runtime dependencies: it is pure hand-authored data consumed directly by the route that renders each slug's page. Notable design choices include deliberately consistent content shapes (roughly 50-word significance blurbs, 60-word origin stories, 4–6 bullets per list) to keep generated pages uniform for SEO, and slugs that double as URL segments, so adding a new vrat is purely a data-edit with no routing or schema work. One gotcha: because all copy is inlined strings, any content fix requires a code change and redeploy rather than a CMS update.

apps\\web\\lib\\yatra-data.ts.summary: This file is the hardcoded content source for Darshya's "Dharmic Yatra" pilgrimage feature, providing realistic seed data for 9 yatra packages, 8 travel companions, and 30+ sacred sites rather than fetching from a database or CMS. It defines the domain model through exported types and interfaces — `YatraRegion`, `YatraDifficulty`, `YatraBudgetTier`, `Yatra`, `YatraItineraryDay`, `YatraPackageTier`, `YatraReview`, `YatraFaq`, `TravelCompanion`, and `SacredSite` — and exposes the main `yatras` array, which includes full itineraries, three-tier pricing (economy/standard/premium in INR), reviews, and FAQs for packages like Char Dham, Do Dham, 12 Jyotirlingas, and the 4 Dhams of India. Its only internal dependency is the `./images` module, using `getTempleHero` and `getDeityImage` to resolve hero and gallery images by slug, while a private `meals` constant standardizes sattvic meal-plan strings across itinerary days. Notable design choices include the consistent three-tier package structure with named tiers (e.g., Sharda/Shraddha/Divya), a `helicopterAvailable` flag and optional helicopter pricing for Himalayan routes, and domain-specific quirks like Kedarnath being excluded from the Jyotirlinga circuit as a seasonal add-on. The main gotcha is that everything is static and inlined — at 24k+ characters and counting, this is effectively a mock database that any future CMS migration will need to replace.

apps\\web\\playwright.config.ts.summary: This file configures Playwright end-to-end testing for the web app, exporting a single `defineConfig` object consumed by the `@playwright/test` runner. Tests live in the `./e2e` directory and run against `http://localhost:3000`, the presumed local dev server for the apps/web frontend. The only external dependency is `@playwright/test`, from which it imports `defineConfig` and the `devices` presets. Behavior branches on the `CI` environment variable: CI runs forbid `.only` tests, retry failures twice, and serialize execution to a single worker, while local runs execute fully parallel with no retries. Each test has a 30-second timeout with 10 seconds for assertions, traces are captured on first retry, and screenshots are taken only on failure. Notably, only the chromium project (Desktop Chrome) is configured — no Firefox or WebKit coverage — and the config assumes the app server is already running on port 3000 since no `webServer` block is defined.

apps\\web\\middleware.ts.summary: This Next.js edge middleware for the apps/web portal is a server-side session gate (audit remediation P1-16) that redirects fully logged-out users away from portal pages before the shell renders. Its exported `middleware` function checks whether the request path falls under `PORTAL_PREFIXES` (/admin, /priest, /store-admin, /astrologer-portal, /wellness-portal, /gaushala-portal) and, if so, calls the internal `hasSession` helper, which treats a session as existing iff the `poojly_user` cookie is present and non-empty; requests with no cookie get a 307 redirect to /auth/login with the original path preserved in a `redirect` query param for post-login bounce-back. The exported `config` object's matcher restricts the middleware to those same portal paths, leaving public and auth routes untouched. It depends only on `next/server` (NextResponse, NextRequest) and on the `poojly_user` cookie written client-side by `setCookie` in lib/auth-context.tsx. The critical design decision is that the middleware deliberately ignores the `role` field inside that cookie, because the cookie is plain, unsigned, non-HttpOnly JSON and therefore user-spoofable — gating on it would let an attacker forge `role:'admin'`. Real authorization lives elsewhere: the portal APIs authenticate every call server-side against the session/JWT, and the client-side `AuthGuard` in lib/auth-context renders the correct portal shell only after server role confirmation. In other words, this file is defence-in-depth plus UX polish — it prevents a flash of gated chrome for logged-out users, but any user with any cookie passes the gate, so it must never be treated as the security boundary.

apps\\web\\postcss.config.mjs.summary: This file is the PostCSS configuration for the `apps/web` package, and it exists solely to wire Tailwind CSS into the build's stylesheet pipeline. It exports a single default config object typed against `import('postcss-load-config').Config`, which registers just one plugin: `@tailwindcss/postcss` — the official Tailwind CSS v4 PostCSS adapter that compiles Tailwind directives and utility classes into plain CSS at build time. Its only external dependencies are PostCSS itself (via the `postcss-load-config` typing convention) and the `@tailwindcss/postcss` package. Notable design points: the config is intentionally minimal with no plugin options passed, meaning Tailwind runs with defaults and auto-detection of content, reflecting Tailwind v4's configuration-less philosophy where theme customization typically lives in CSS rather than a `tailwind.config` file. Build tools in `apps/web` (such as Next.js) pick this file up automatically by convention, so any change here affects all CSS processed in that app.

apps\\web\\lib\\yatra-destinations.ts.summary: This file is the data layer for lightweight SEO landing pages promoting pilgrimage (yatra) destinations, designed to rank for high-intent queries like "vaishno devi yatra package" and route clicks to booking partners through `/api/v1/affiliate/click` for 5–10% commission — explicitly distinct from the full curated packages in `yatra-data.ts`. It exports the `AffiliatePartner` union type (`'makemytrip' | 'goibibo' | 'irctc'`), the `AffiliatePartnerLink` and `YatraDestination` interfaces, and the `yatraDestinations` array covering ten destinations (Vaishno Devi, Tirupati, Char Dham, Shirdi, Kashi, Amarnath, Kailash Mansarovar, Rameshwaram-Madurai, Dwarka-Somnath, Ujjain). Each destination carries SEO fields (`shortDescription` constrained to ≤140 chars for meta descriptions, a ~200-word `longDescription`), practical details (price, duration, best season, how to reach), hero images hotlinked from Unsplash, and a `hasFullContent` flag that tells the renderer whether to show the full page or an abbreviated placeholder version. The private `partnersFor` helper builds three `AffiliatePartnerLink` entries per destination from the `MMT`, `GOIBIBO`, and `IRCTC` base-URL constants, URL-encoding the search slug into MakeMyTrip and Goibibo query strings. A key gotcha is that partner URLs contain no affiliate IDs yet — setup is deferred to `docs/yatra-affiliate-setup.md` — so clicks currently earn nothing until tracking parameters are added. The file has no runtime dependencies and is pure static content; note the header comment's claim that five destinations are placeholders is already stale, since entries like Amarnath and Kailash Mansarovar ship with `hasFullContent: true` and complete descriptions.

apps\\web\\lib\\yoga-sutras.ts.summary: This file is a self-contained static content module that encodes Patanjali's Yoga Sutras for the web app — it exists to give pages and components a typed, structured source of truth about the text's four chapters (padas) without needing a database or API. Its main exports are the `YogaPada` type, which models each chapter with Sanskrit (Devanagari), IAST transliteration, English titles, concept lists, and curated `keySutras` with optional commentary, and the `YOGA_SUTRAS` constant holding all four padas: Samadhi, Sadhana, Vibhuti, and Kaivalya. Two small helpers, `padaSlugs()` and `getPada(slug)`, support slug-based routing or lookups, with `getPada` returning `undefined` for unknown slugs, and `TOTAL_SUTRAS` derives the canonical count of 196 by reducing over `sutraCount`. The file has zero dependencies — no imports, internal or external — making it a pure data layer. Notable design choices include constraining `YogaPada.number` to the literal union `1 | 2 | 3 | 4` for type safety, and making `practicePillars` optional, which is exercised in practice since the fourth pada (Kaivalya) omits it, reflecting that it describes liberation rather than practice. Consumers should treat the data as read-only editorial content; adding a fifth pada or changing counts would require a deliberate edit since the type system and the `TOTAL_SUTRAS` comment both assume the traditional four-chapter, 196-sutra structure.

apps\\web\\next.config.ts.summary: This file is the Next.js configuration for the `apps/web` frontend, defining how the app is built, bundled, cached, and deployed. It sets `output: 'standalone'` to produce a self-contained `server.js` for self-hosting on Render's Node free tier (the OpenNext/Cloudflare Workers path was abandoned because the server-function bundle exceeded the 3 MiB free limit), and enables `transpilePackages` for the monorepo's internal `@poojly/ui`, `@poojly/shared`, and `@poojly/api-client` workspace packages. Notable workarounds include `typescript.ignoreBuildErrors` (pnpm hoists conflicting `@types/react` 18/19 versions, so real type-checking is deferred to `turbo type-check` in CI), a custom webpack `extensionAlias` mapping `.js` to `.ts`/`.tsx` to resolve NodeNext-style imports in workspace packages, and `images.unoptimized` kept deliberately to avoid sharp's CPU/RAM cost on the free tier. The config whitelists remote image hosts (`**.supabase.co`, `**.cloudfront.net`, Unsplash, Wikimedia, archive.org, Pexels, YouTube), sets `experimental.optimizePackageImports` for tree-shaking `lucide-react`, `date-fns`, `@tanstack/react-query`, `recharts`, `framer-motion`, and others, and strips console calls (except `error`/`warn`) in production. It declares one permanent redirect from `/kundli` to `/astrology/kundli` and per-route `Cache-Control` headers: immutable year-long caching for static assets and `/_next/static`, 5-minute `s-maxage` with 1-day stale-while-revalidate for `/temples/:slug`, `/pujas/:slug`, and `/yatra/destinations/:slug`, and hourly refresh for `sitemap.xml`/`robots.txt`. Browser-side Sentry (`@sentry/nextjs`) was removed entirely because it broke the old Cloudflare adapter builds, `productionBrowserSourceMaps` stays off until the Sentry release pipeline is wired up, and server-side Sentry on the Render API via `@sentry/node` remains active.

apps\\web\\next-env.d.ts.summary: This is the auto-generated TypeScript environment declaration file for the `apps/web` Next.js application, existing solely to pull Next.js ambient types into the project's compilation. It exports nothing itself; instead it contains three reference directives that load the core `next` type package, the `next/image-types/global` declarations that let TypeScript accept static image imports and the Image component's global JSX types, and the generated `./.next/types/routes.d.ts` file that powers Next.js's typed-routes feature. Its only dependencies are the `next` npm package and Next's own build output, since `routes.d.ts` is produced inside `.next` when the dev server or a build runs. The main gotcha is stated in the file itself: it must not be hand-edited because Next.js regenerates it automatically, so it should be committed as-is and left alone. A practical consequence is that the typed-routes reference will be unresolved on a fresh checkout until `next dev` or `next build` has run at least once, which is normal and expected.

apps\\web\\public\\sw.js.summary: This file is the Darshya web app's service worker (`apps/web/public/sw.js`), responsible for two things: Web Push notification handling and a minimal offline fallback for page navigations. It registers handlers for the standard service worker lifecycle and events — `install` (precaches the `/offline` shell into the `darshya-offline-v1` cache), `activate` (purges stale `darshya-offline-*` cache versions and claims clients), `fetch` (network-first strategy for GET navigation requests, falling back to a cached page, then the `/offline` page, then an inline 503 HTML response), `push` (parses the JSON payload and calls `self.registration.showNotification` with title, body, icon, tag, and a target URL), and `notificationclick` (focuses an existing window matching the URL or opens a new one via `clients.openWindow`). It has no internal module imports and depends only on browser platform APIs: the Cache Storage API, the Push API, and the Clients API, serving the Next.js frontend deployed on Cloudflare Pages. Key design decisions: precache failure is deliberately swallowed so it never blocks installation, and the worker intentionally avoids aggressive app-shell caching because Next.js/Cloudflare Pages manage their own caching and competing layers cause stale-UI bugs — the offline page is only a floor. Although the offline fallback was spec'd (R-Q2-E-016) for `/pujas/*` and `/darshan/*` routes, the implementation applies it globally to all navigations, and push payloads that aren't valid JSON degrade gracefully to a plain-text notification titled "Darshya" with `/logo.svg` as the default icon.

apps\\web\\vitest.setup.ts.summary: `apps/web/vitest.setup.ts` is the shared test-environment bootstrap for the web app's Vitest suite, loaded before tests run to configure the DOM testing environment. It exports nothing itself; instead it registers a global `afterEach` hook that calls `cleanup` from `@testing-library/react` to unmount rendered components between tests and `vi.restoreAllMocks` from `vitest` to reset spies, preventing state leakage across test cases. It imports `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest` purely for side effects, which adds DOM assertion matchers like `toBeInTheDocument` to Vitest's expect. A notable gotcha-handling decision: because jsdom lacks `window.matchMedia`, the file polyfills it with a stub whose listener methods are `vi.fn()` mocks that always report `matches: false`, so components using media-query hooks won't crash. Similarly, if `globalThis.fetch` is missing, it installs a bare `vi.fn()` placeholder so components that fetch on mount don't throw, though tests wanting real responses must mock it themselves. The file depends on the external libraries `vitest`, `@testing-library/react`, and `@testing-library/jest-dom`.

apps\\web\\types\\global.d.ts.summary: This ambient declaration file exists solely to give TypeScript type information for third-party analytics globals that external scripts attach to `window`, so that guarded calls like `if (window.fbq) window.fbq(...)` compile without falling back to `any`. It exports nothing at runtime (the `export {}` is only there to make the file a module, which is required for `declare global` augmentation to work) and instead extends the global `Window` interface with four optional members: `dataLayer` and `gtag` for Google Analytics 4, and `fbq` plus its `_fbq` alias for the Meta (Facebook) Pixel. The `fbq` type is a callable intersection that also carries the pixel's well-known sub-properties (`callMethod`, `queue`, `loaded`, `version`, `push`), and `_fbq` is defined via the `Window['fbq']` lookup type so the two stay in sync. The file has no internal dependencies; it describes globals populated at runtime by the external gtag.js and fbevents.js loader scripts. A notable design constraint is that every property is optional, reflecting the codebase's env-or-noop integration pattern where a given analytics vendor may never load, and the deliberate use of `unknown` rather than `any` keeps call sites type-safe without prescribing argument shapes for third-party APIs.

apps\\web\\scripts\\indexnow-ping.ts.summary: This standalone script (tagged R-Q3-M-014) exists to notify the IndexNow search-indexing service whenever new city+puja landing pages go live on darshya.online. It has no exports; instead it defines and immediately invokes an internal async `ping()` function that builds a URL list by mapping `CITY_PUJA_SLUGS` (imported from `../lib/city-pujas`) into `/puja/{city}/{puja}` paths and POSTs them as JSON to `https://api.indexnow.org/IndexNow`. The request body includes the host, the `INDEXNOW_KEY` environment variable (a 32-character hex string), a `keyLocation` pointing at a verification file, and the full URL list. A key operational gotcha is the manual founder prerequisite: besides setting `INDEXNOW_KEY`, someone must host a matching plain-text key file at `apps/web/public/{INDEXNOW_KEY}.txt`, which Cloudflare Pages serves as a static asset so IndexNow can verify ownership. The script follows an explicit env-or-noop design: if the key is missing it logs a warning and exits 0 rather than failing the deploy pipeline. Similarly, only HTTP 200/202 counts as success, while non-2xx responses and network errors are merely warned about, never thrown. It is intended to be run manually or in CI via `tsx` with the environment variable set.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\AdSlot.test.tsx.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the behavior of the `AdSlot` component in `apps/web/components/AdSlot`, a Google AdSense wrapper that conditionally renders ad placements. It mocks the sibling `useIsPremium` hook via `vi.mock` so tests can toggle premium status, and asserts that the component renders nothing for premium users or when the `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_CLIENT` or slot-specific `NEXT_PUBLIC_ADSENSE_SLOT_*` environment variables are absent. For the happy path it checks that `AdSlot` renders a `complementary` landmark labeled "advertisement", honors a custom `label` prop, and stamps a `data-ad-slot` attribute matching the `slotId` prop. A notable case confirms the "quarantine" feature: ads mounted inside a subtree marked `data-ad-quarantine` suppress the live `ins.adsbygoogle` element, with a comment noting that jsdom runs effects synchronously so the quarantined render returns null. The suite stubs `window.adsbygoogle` and mutates `process.env` per test, restoring the original environment in `afterEach` to avoid cross-test leakage. Dependencies are limited to `vitest`, `@testing-library/react`, and the two internal modules under test; no network or real AdSense script is involved.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\astrologer-portal-.summary: This Vitest test file is a regression guard for bug AP-07 in the astrologer-portal dashboard: previously the page skipped its API fetch whenever the session token started with `demo-`, leaving demo users stuck on hardcoded ZERO_STATS and hiding backend issues. Its two tests verify that `AstrologerDashboard` (imported from `../app/astrologer-portal/page`) now fires the fetch to `/astrologer-portal/dashboard` with the demo Bearer token in the Authorization header, and that the rendered "Total Consultations" card shows the API-returned value (42) rather than the zero fallback. It depends on Vitest and `@testing-library/react`, and stubs several internal modules via `vi.mock`: `../lib/auth-context` (its `useAuth` hook is replaced with a controllable mock returning a demo session), `../lib/api-config` (pinning `API_BASE_URL` to a sentinel), and the heavy child components `MyProviderProfileCard`, `provider/EarningsCard`, and `provider/KycStatusBadge` (rendered as inert divs to isolate the dashboard's own fetch). A notable design choice is the deliberate isolation strategy: by mocking auth, config, and all fetch-hungry children, the suite asserts purely on the dashboard's fetch behavior, with a global `fetch` spy installed per test and restored in `afterEach`. The file's header comment also documents the fix contract—that the backend accepts demo tokens in non-production environments—so future changes to demo-session handling don't silently reintroduce the skip.

apps\\web\\vitest.config.ts.summary: This file is the Vitest configuration for the `apps/web` Next.js application, exporting a `defineConfig` object that controls how unit and component tests are discovered and executed. It enables automatic JSX transformation via esbuild, turns on test globals, runs tests in the `happy-dom` environment with `./vitest.setup.ts` as a setup file, disables CSS processing, and limits test discovery to `__tests__/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}` files at the app root and nested under `app/`. The `resolve.alias` section maps the `@` import prefix to the app directory and redirects the `server-only` package — a Next.js runtime guard that pnpm does not hoist into `apps/web` — to a no-op stub at `./__tests__/__stubs__/server-only.ts` so server-only modules can load under Vitest. The most significant design decision is a set of aliases pinning `react`, `react-dom`, `react-dom/client`, the JSX runtimes (`react/jsx-runtime`, `react/jsx-dev-runtime`), and `scheduler` to exact physical copies inside the pnpm `.pnpm` store (React 19.2.5, scheduler 0.27.0). This works around the pnpm workspace installing multiple byte-identical but physically distinct React copies (plus a stale 18.3.1 hoisted at the worktree root), which Node treats as separate module instances and which otherwise breaks the hooks dispatcher, producing "Invalid hook call" errors when `@testing-library/react` renders components. A notable gotcha: alias entries are deliberately ordered most-specific first so `react-dom/client` matches before the broader `react-dom` entry.

apps\\web\\scripts\\build-search-index.m.summary: This build script generates a static client-side search index for the web app: it scans MDX files under the `content` directory in three hardcoded categories (`sanskrit`, `ved`, `sanatan`), extracts frontmatter metadata, and writes the results as compact JSON to `public/search-index.json` so it ships as a servable static asset. Its main exported logic is internal rather than exported—`parseFrontmatter` is a hand-rolled YAML-ish parser supporting only flat `key: value` pairs, quoted strings (via `stripQ`), and simple `- item` arrays, and each index entry carries `category`, `slug`, `title`, `summary`, and `subTopic`. It depends solely on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`)—no external YAML or globbing libraries—so it runs as a zero-dependency pre-build step. Notable gotchas: the custom parser silently ignores anything it doesn't recognize (nested YAML, multiline scalars), files lacking `slug` or `title` frontmatter are skipped without warning, and paths resolve from `process.cwd()`, meaning the script must be run from the `apps/web` root.

apps\\web\\scripts\\stitch-pitch-video.s.summary: This bash script stitches a 60-second investor pitch reel (`darshya-demo-reel.mp4`) for the Darshya web app by combining pre-recorded product screen captures with generated narration and music, outputting to `apps/web/public/pitch/video`. Its single helper, `make_clip`, trims each `.webm` capture, letterboxes it to 1920x1080, and burns in brand lower-third captions via ffmpeg's `drawtext`; around that it builds a cream-and-saffron intro/outro card sequence, a ken-burns `zoompan` on the `07-panchang.png` still, and chains all fourteen clips with 0.4s `xfade` crossfades whose offsets are computed in awk. Externally it depends on ffmpeg 6+ and the Python `edge-tts` package (Microsoft Edge's `en-IN-NeerjaExpressiveNeural` voice at −5% rate) reading the script from `pitch-vo-script.txt`, while inputs are the numbered captures under `apps/web/public/pitch/video` and `img`. Audio is fully procedural: a tanpura-style drone synthesized from three detuned sine waves (146.83/220/293.66 Hz) is lowpass-filtered, loudness-normalized, and ducked ~10dB under the voice-over via `amix`, with the VO delayed 2.5s to clear the intro. Notable constraints: the brand palette constants (SAFFRON `0xb87333`, INK, CREAM) are hand-duplicated from `apps/web/app/globals.css` and must be kept in sync manually; `FONT_ESC` hardcodes the Windows path `C:\Windows\Fonts\arialbd.ttf`, so the script is effectively Windows-only despite being bash; and the voice-over is cached at `apps/web/scripts/build/vo.mp3`, meaning edits to the narration script are silently ignored until that file is deleted. The script must be run from the monorepo root, honors an `FFMPEG` env override, and uses `-shortest` plus a computed `total_dur` to land within its 60s ±1s target.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\CartContext.test.t.summary: This Vitest test suite verifies the shopping-cart state logic exposed by `CartProvider` and the `useCart` hook from `../components/CartContext`, using `renderHook` and `act` from `@testing-library/react` with a shared `CartProduct` fixture. It covers the cart's full lifecycle: starting empty, adding items, merging duplicate adds by product id, removing items, updating quantities, clearing the cart, and toggling the drawer via `isOpen`/`toggleCart`. Beyond basic behavior, the tests pin down several business rules: quantities are capped at 10 per product, a flat delivery fee of 49 applies but is waived once the subtotal reaches 500, tax is computed as 5% of the subtotal, `updateQuantity` silently ignores values below 1, and `clearCart` also closes the drawer. Each test clears `localStorage` in `beforeEach`, indicating the context persists cart state to browser storage and that tests must be isolated from it. The file has no exports of its own; its dependencies are vitest, React Testing Library, and the internal `CartContext` component module.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\astrologer-revamp..summary: This Vitest file provides lightweight regression guards for the astrologer portal revamp, verifying two fixes via static source-text assertions rather than rendered-component tests. Using `readFileSync` from `node:fs` and `path.resolve` against `__dirname`, it reads the portal's source files and greps them with `expect(...).toContain` checks. The first suite confirms the dashboard at `app/astrologer-portal/page.tsx` exposes a go-online presence toggle — asserting the source references the `/astrologer-portal/online` endpoint and a `toggleOnline` handler. The second suite guards the earnings fix by checking `app/astrologer-portal/earnings/page.tsx` reads the astrologer-own `/astrologer-portal/earnings` endpoint and no longer references the dead `/admin/commissions` route or the `CommissionsPanel` component. Its only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and Node's `fs`/`path` builtins; nothing is rendered or mocked. The notable design tradeoff is that these are brittle string-matching tests: they catch reintroduction of the old admin route but can pass or fail on incidental source changes, so they complement rather than replace behavioral coverage.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\ChannelAttribution.summary: This is the Vitest suite for the `ChannelAttribution` React component in `apps/web`, verifying how the app captures marketing attribution from URL parameters into `localStorage` and PostHog. It builds on `vitest`, `@testing-library/react` (running under happy-dom, with `window.history.replaceState` used to rewrite the URL), and stubs the global `window.posthog` object to assert on `register` and `capture` calls without a real analytics client. The tests document the component's contract: `utm_source` (with `x` aliased to `twitter`) and `ref` parameters prefixed `tw_`, `wa_`, `tg_`, or `ig_` map to a `signup_channel` of twitter, whatsapp, telegram, or instagram, and captured attribution is persisted under the `darshya_attr` storage key with a `first_touch_at` timestamp, while PostHog receives a `register` call plus an `attribution_captured` capture event only on first capture. Key behavioral constraints asserted here: first-touch attribution wins, so an existing stored record is re-registered rather than overwritten by new URL params (and no duplicate capture fires); the component no-ops silently when no attribution params exist; it tolerates a missing PostHog global without throwing; and oversized UTM fields are truncated to 128 characters. Notably, the tests rely on rendering the component multiple times across cleared storage rather than unmounting, so they implicitly treat each render as a fresh attribution evaluation.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\CategoryNav.test.t.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the behavior of the `CategoryNav` component from `../components/CategoryNav`, using `@testing-library/react` (`render`, `screen`, `fireEvent`, `within`) to simulate user interaction in jsdom. It covers five behaviors: all category triggers from `CATEGORY_TREE` (imported from `../lib/category-tree`) render as buttons, no menu is open initially (asserted via `role="menu"` absence and `aria-expanded="false"`), clicking a trigger opens the mega-menu and shows the first item of that category, pressing Escape on `window` closes the menu, and clicking the same trigger twice toggles it shut. The tests lean on ARIA roles and attributes rather than DOM structure, which enforces accessibility semantics as part of the contract. Two coupling gotchas stand out: the suite hard-asserts `CATEGORY_TREE` has exactly 5 entries and assumes the first category is "Worship" (using `CATEGORY_TREE[0].items[0].label` and the "Library" label), so changes to the data in `category-tree` will break tests even if `CategoryNav` itself is fine. It also implicitly documents that the Escape handler lives on `window`, a design detail of the component worth knowing.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\books.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite validates the server-side books content loader in `apps/web/lib/books`, covering slug sanitization, on-disk manifest/chapter reads, and chapter navigation helpers. Because the module under test is guarded by the `server-only` package, the suite mocks that import so vitest can load it, then exercises the internal `safeBookSlug` and `safeChapterSlug` functions exposed via a `__testing` export, asserting they accept known lowercase slugs and compound chapter paths like `bala/sarga-1` while throwing on path-traversal inputs (`../etc`, `foo/../bar`) and uppercase characters. The disk-read tests are effectively integration tests: they call `listBookSlugs`, `loadManifest`, `loadAllManifests`, and `loadChapter` against real content, expecting exactly three books (`bhagavad-gita` with 18 chapters, `ramayana` whose first kanda reports 77 sargas, and `upanishads` whose `isha` chapter has 18 non-placeholder verses), so the suite will fail if the content directory is missing or restructured. Unknown-book handling is verified by passing `not-a-book` cast `as never` and expecting a null result, indicating the loader's type signature doesn't naturally admit invalid slugs. Navigation logic is tested separately with a hand-built `BookManifest` stub (typed from `@poojly/shared`), confirming `nextChapter` and `prevChapter` walk the `chapters` array in order and return null at the boundaries. Dependencies are minimal: `vitest`, the `server-only` mock, the sibling `lib/books` module, and the shared `BookManifest` type.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\city-pujas.test.ts.summary: This Vitest test suite enforces SEO and content invariants for requirement R-Q3-M-014 on the city-plus-puja landing page dataset exported from `apps/web/lib/city-pujas.ts`. It imports `CITY_PUJAS`, `CITY_PUJA_SLUGS`, and the `getCityPuja` lookup helper, then asserts the dataset ships exactly 10 entries with unique `city/puja` slug pairs, that `CITY_PUJA_SLUGS` stays in sync with `CITY_PUJAS`, and that every `relatedSlug` resolves to a real sibling entry via `getCityPuja`. It also validates SEO metadata — `metaTitle` capped at 60 characters, `metaDescription` within a length window, and `heroAlt` text containing the city display name — plus content completeness (at least 3 FAQs and 4 samagri items per entry) and positive `priceInr`/`priceUsd` pricing fields. The only dependency beyond Vitest itself is the internal `city-pujas` module; there are no external services involved. One notable discrepancy: the meta-description test is titled "140-160 chars" but the assertions actually enforce a looser 120–170 character bound, so the test name overstates the constraint.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\company.test.ts.summary: This Vitest test suite verifies the company-identity helpers exported from apps/web/lib/company, which centralize legal and contact details for the Darshya web app. It pins the brand constants on the COMPANY object (brand "Darshya", domain "darshya.online") and exercises the operatedByLine and postalContactLine functions, confirming that when the business is not incorporated, operatedByLine returns an "independently-operated" notice containing COMPANY.supportEmail while postalContactLine returns null. The suite also locks in refund-policy values on COMPANY.refunds, asserting freeCancellationHoursBeforeService stays at 24 and refundSettlementDays remains a string. The tests depend only on vitest and the internal company module, with no external services involved. A notable gotcha: the expectations encode the current non-incorporated state of the business, so they will deliberately fail if the company later incorporates and the helpers start returning corporate legal entity details, forcing an intentional test update alongside the compliance copy change.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\CookieBanner.test..summary: This Vitest test suite validates the GDPR/UK DPA cookie consent flow (requirement R-Q3-L-002) implemented in the `CookieBanner` component in `apps/web/components/CookieBanner`, exercising it via React Testing Library's `render`, `screen`, and `fireEvent` helpers against a cleared `localStorage`. It imports the default `CookieBanner` component plus the named helpers `getStoredConsent` and `hasConsent`, which are the module's public API for reading consent state elsewhere in the app. The tests cover first-visit banner display, the Reject-all and Accept-all paths, granular toggling through the Manage-preferences dialog (where the essential checkbox is intentionally disabled and analytics/marketing are the first two enabled checkboxes), and suppression of the banner when valid stored consent exists. Consent is persisted under the `darshya_cookie_consent_v1` localStorage key as an object with `essential`, `analytics`, `marketing`, `acceptedAt`, and `version` fields. Notable behavioral constraints verified here: `hasConsent('essential')` always defaults to true even with nothing stored, consent older than one year is treated as expired, and records whose `version` doesn't match the current schema (version 1) are discarded, forcing users to re-consent after policy updates.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\booking-fixes-phas.summary: This Vitest file contains Phase 0 regression guards for the 2026-08-04 booking revamp, verifying that previously dead or broken UI wiring in the booking flow stays fixed by failing CI if a refactor reintroduces the bugs. Rather than rendering components, it reads the actual page sources with Node's `readFileSync` (via a local `read` helper) and asserts on string/regex patterns, a deliberate choice because the pages are heavy client components with auth/query dependencies and the defects were simple "wired or not" issues that source assertions catch deterministically. The "devotee booking fixes" suite covers three pages: `app/bookings/page.tsx` must wire its Cancel button through `handleCancel` to the `/cancel` endpoint, `app/checkout/success/page.tsx` must link to `/bookings` instead of the dead `/profile/bookings` route, and `app/bookings/view/page.tsx` must expose a Reschedule action via `handleReschedule` hitting `/reschedule`. The "pandit portal fixes" suite checks that `app/priest/bookings/page.tsx` renders a Decline action wired to `handleAction(booking.id, 'reject')` (surfacing the previously UI-less PATCH `/priest/bookings/:id/reject` API, with a `reject: 'confirmed'` status mapping) and that `app/priest/page.tsx` has an on-duty toggle calling `/priest/availability`. Its only dependencies are `vitest`, `node:fs`, and `node:path`, with no mocks or test harness. The main gotcha is brittleness: assertions like the exact `onClick={() => handleCancel(booking.id)}` regex can break from innocent formatting changes even when the behavior is correct.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\csr-match.test.tsx.summary: This Vitest suite validates the CSR Match landing page component `CsrMatchPage` (imported from `app/csr-match/page`) against requirement R-Q4-M-007, using `@testing-library/react` with a mocked `global.fetch` that stubs a successful lead response. The tests pin down the page's marketing and conversion behavior: the hero must display "2x Match" copy, an interactive calculator must triple an employee pledge (₹1,00,000 input renders a ₹3,00,000 total in the `total-impact` test id), and a signup form must expose four required labeled fields — company name, CSR head email, CSR budget bracket, and expected match cap. It also verifies a transparency dashboard section renders exactly three placeholder `temple-card` elements, and that submitting the form issues a POST to the internal endpoint `/api/csr-match/leads` with the company name in the body. Notably, the suite depends on specific accessibility labels and `data-testid` hooks in the page component, so renaming labels or test ids will break these tests even if behavior is unchanged; it also asserts Indian-style number formatting (3,00,000), coupling tests to locale-specific rendering.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\JitsiCallButton.te.summary: This is a Vitest test suite (apps/web/__tests__/JitsiCallButton.test.tsx) that verifies the behavior of the JitsiCallButton React component, which renders a "Join 1:1 Call" link to a Jitsi Meet room for a booking. It uses @testing-library/react's render and screen queries with vitest assertions to cover nine scenarios: the link is enabled only within a 2-hour window around the scheduled time, renders as a disabled button with explanatory text when the booking is long past or far in the future, and treats null or unparseable scheduledAt values as open (fail-open behavior delegated to a UI parent override). The tests also pin down several contract details of the component: room URLs follow the deterministic pattern meet.jit.si/darshya-{bookingId}, links open in a new tab with noopener for security, a custom label prop overrides the default text, and styling variants default to a primary "bg-saffron-600" treatment while the secondary variant uses a bordered style instead. Notably, the suite documents that invalid date input errs toward enabling the call rather than blocking it, which is an intentional permissive design choice worth preserving. The only internal dependency is the component under test at ../components/JitsiCallButton; no mocking or network services are involved.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\gau-seva-revamp.te.summary: This Vitest suite, `gau-seva-revamp.test.tsx`, acts as a regression guard for the 2026-08-05 Gau Seva (cow adoption) revamp in the `apps/web` Next.js app, ensuring adoption-plan CTAs actually reach the donation flow. Rather than rendering components, it uses `readFileSync` from `node:fs` and `path.resolve` to read source files as text and asserts on regex/string patterns. The first describe block verifies that `app/gaushala/[id]/page.tsx` renders plan cards as `<Link>` elements into `/donations?causeId=...&planId=${encodeURIComponent(plan.id)}` and that the old dead no-op `<button key={plan.id}>` markup is gone. The second block checks that `app/donations/page.tsx` defines a `PLAN_AMOUNTS` lookup (including a `plan_monthly` entry) and passes a derived `planAmount` down, and that `components/DonationForm.tsx` accepts a `planAmount` prop used via `planAmount ?? presets` to pre-select the donation amount. Its only dependency is `vitest` plus Node builtins; the code under test spans the gaushala detail page, the donations page, and the shared `DonationForm` component. The notable gotcha is that these are brittle source-grep assertions, not behavioral tests — they can pass while the UI is broken and can fail on innocent refactors like reformatting or renaming, so they document intended wiring rather than verify it.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\OnboardingModal.te.summary: This Vitest test suite validates the `OnboardingModal` React component, a three-step first-run wizard (intent picker, language selection, and an "Outside India"/NRI question) for the web app. It has no exports of its own; it exercises the component from `../components/OnboardingModal` and the persistence helpers `getOnboarding`, `ONBOARDING_STORAGE_KEY`, and `ONBOARDING_LANGUAGE_KEY` from `../lib/onboarding-store`, using `@testing-library/react` for rendering and events and `vitest` for mocking. The tests cover rendering suppression when `open` is false, step advancement and Back navigation, incremental persistence to `window.localStorage` (intent saved at step 1, language written both to the onboarding record and a standalone language key at step 2), disabled languages like Tamil not advancing the flow, and completion stamping `completedAt` and `isNri` before invoking `onClose`. Two notable behaviors are pinned down: both the Skip button and the X close button dismiss the modal while preserving partially collected state rather than clearing storage. A setup gotcha worth noting is that `beforeEach` clears localStorage and stubs `window.location.assign` with a `vi.fn()` because jsdom would otherwise throw on the post-completion redirect.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\experiments.test.t.summary: This Vitest suite is a contract test ("spec lock" R-Q1-E-009) that freezes the shape of the `ACTIVE_EXPERIMENTS` registry exported from `apps/web/lib/experiments`, guarding the A/B testing configuration against accidental edits. It asserts that the registry exposes exactly three PostHog feature-flag keys — `cta_color_test`, `hero_copy_v2`, and `nri_lane_above_fold` — because an external orchestrator's KPI counting depends on precisely those flags, so adding, renaming, or removing one will fail the build. Beyond the key list, it enforces structural invariants: every experiment must ship at least two variants (one acting as control), and every variant name must match the PostHog-compatible pattern of lowercase alphanumerics, underscores, and hyphens. It also pins the exact ordered variant arrays for each experiment — `hero_copy_v2` is `['control', 'benefit']`, `cta_color_test` is `['saffron', 'indigo']`, and `nri_lane_above_fold` is `['below', 'above']` — meaning even reordering variants is treated as a breaking change. The only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and the internal `../lib/experiments` module; PostHog itself is not called, only its naming requirements are encoded. A notable gotcha is that the key comparison sorts before asserting, so key order in the source is free, but variant order is locked. Teams adding a new experiment must update this test deliberately, which is the intended friction of the spec-lock pattern.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\devotee-today-sect.summary: This Vitest suite is a set of regression guards for the devotee dashboard revamp (dated 2026-08-05), verifying that the dashboard no longer ships hardcoded mock widgets and instead fetches live data. Rather than rendering components, it reads `app/dashboard/page.tsx` and `components/dashboard/DevoteeTodaySection.tsx` as raw text via node's `readFileSync` and asserts on string presence or absence. Specifically, it checks that `page.tsx` no longer contains the old fake demo rows ("Kashi Vishwanath", "Somnath Jyotirlinga", "Brass Diya Set + Agarbatti", "Rudraksha Mala (5 mukhi)", "Best muhurat for griha pravesh?") and that it mounts the new `DevoteeTodaySection` component. It then verifies `DevoteeTodaySection.tsx` calls the live API endpoints `/panchang/today`, `/astrology/horoscope/daily`, `/me/reading-progress`, and `/store/orders`, personalizes the horoscope via the devotee's rashi (`horoscope/daily?sign=`), and contains no leftover fake data arrays. Its only dependencies are `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and the node built-ins `fs` and `path`. The notable design tradeoff is that these are grep-style source-text assertions rather than behavioral tests: they run fast with no DOM, network mocking, or component rendering, but they're brittle — any rename of an endpoint, string, or component will fail the suite even if runtime behavior is correct.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\images.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite validates the image-URL utilities in `apps/web/lib/images`, which centralize how the web app builds and selects remote image URLs. It covers `wikiThumb` (and its alias `wikiResize`), which rewrites Wikimedia Commons URLs by snapping requested widths up to a fixed "ladder" of steps (e.g. 330, 500, 960, capping at 3840px), constructs thumb URLs from Commons originals, and appends `.png` when thumbnailing SVGs per Wikimedia convention. It also tests `resizeImage`, which rewrites Unsplash `w`/`h`/`q` query params for named presets like `hero` (1600×900 at q85) and `card` while routing Wikimedia URLs through `wikiResize`. The higher-level getters — `getTempleHero`, `getTempleThumbnail`, `getTempleGallery`, `getDeityImage` (with a `square` variant), `getPujaImage`, `getProductImage`, `getHeroImage`, `getFestivalImage`, `getContentImage`, `getAstrologerImage`, and generic `getImage` — are verified to pull slug-keyed URLs from the exported `IMAGES` registry. Notable behaviors pinned by the tests: unknown slugs and categories fall back to a default Wikimedia image rather than failing, unknown temple galleries return an empty array, and astrologer images cycle deterministically through a gendered pool by modulo index. The only external dependency is Vitest; the suite exercises no network calls, asserting purely on URL string transformations against Wikimedia Commons and Unsplash URL formats.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\pricing.test.ts.summary: This Vitest test suite validates the pricing utilities exported from `apps/web/lib/pricing`, which power the web app's subscription plan display and commission logic. It exercises `getPlanById`, `getPlanFeatures`, `getCommissionRate`, `formatPrice`, and `getUpgradePlan`, along with the `PLANS` and `COMMISSION_RATES` data tables themselves. The tests confirm concrete business rules: commission rates differ by role (e.g., `pandit` on the `pro` plan pays 15%, `temple` on `enterprise` pays 5%), prices are formatted in INR with "Free" for zero, and plans ascend from `free` through `basic` to `enterprise`, with `getUpgradePlan` returning null at the top tier. Data-integrity checks lock in structural invariants — exactly four plans ordered by ascending price and at least six commission rate entries — so accidental reordering or deletion of plans fails the build. A notable contract enforced here is the error behavior: `getPlanById` and `getCommissionRate` throw on unknown inputs, while `getUpgradePlan` gracefully returns null for unknown plans, an asymmetry callers must respect. The file depends only on `vitest` and the internal `../lib/pricing` module, with no external services involved.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\onboarding-store.t.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the behavior of the `onboarding-store` module (`apps/web/lib/onboarding-store`), which persists multi-step onboarding progress to `localStorage` under `ONBOARDING_STORAGE_KEY`. It exercises the store's exported API — `getOnboarding`, `setOnboarding`, `clearOnboarding`, `isOnboardingFlagEnabled`, and the `ONBOARDING_STORAGE_KEY` constant — confirming that `setOnboarding` merges partial updates rather than replacing state and that reads backfill unset fields (`lang`, `isNri`, `completedAt`) with `null` while stamping `version: 1`. A key documented contract is the self-healing read path: `getOnboarding` returns `null` and deletes the stored entry when the JSON is corrupt, the schema `version` mismatches, or a field fails validation (e.g. an unrecognized `primaryIntent`). The suite also pins down the feature-flag semantics of `isOnboardingFlagEnabled`, which is true only when `NEXT_PUBLIC_ONBOARDING_V1` equals the literal string `"1"` (not `"true"` or empty). Dependencies are limited to `vitest` globals (`describe`, `it`, `expect`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach`) plus jsdom's `window.localStorage`; tests snapshot and restore `process.env` and clear storage between cases. Notably, the SSR-safety test deletes `globalThis.window` mid-run, documenting that the implementation checks for the browser environment dynamically per call rather than at module load, so no re-import is needed.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\products.test.ts.summary: This Vitest suite validates the static product catalogue exposed by the `lib/products` module in the `apps/web` app, acting as a data-integrity guard rather than a behavioral test. It imports `PRODUCTS`, `CATEGORIES`, and `getProductByHandle` and asserts that the catalogue and category list are non-empty, that every product `id` and `handle` is unique (handles presumably serve as URL slugs), and that pricing invariants hold — `compareAtPrice` never falls below `price` and `discount` stays within 0–100. It also covers `getProductByHandle`, confirming it returns the exact matching product object for a known handle and `undefined` for an unknown one. The only external dependency is `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`); there is no mocking, I/O, or service interaction, so all assertions run purely in memory against the static data. The suite is a useful regression net: any catalogue edit that introduces a duplicate slug, a malformed discount, or inverted pricing will fail CI before reaching the storefront.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\release.test.ts.summary: This Vitest test suite validates the release-tagging utilities exported from `apps/web/lib/release`, namely `getRelease`, `getReleaseShortSha`, and `hasReleaseTag`, under the requirement label "R-Q2-E-015 release surface." It verifies that all three helpers fall back to a `'dev'` identifier when the `NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_RELEASE` environment variable is unset, ensuring local builds carry no Sentry release tag. The tests confirm that a Sentry-style tag in the form `darshya@<sha>` is parsed so `getReleaseShortSha` extracts the first seven characters of the commit SHA while `getRelease` returns the full tag, and that a plain version tag like `v1.2.3` (no `@` separator) is passed through unchanged yet still counts as a valid release via `hasReleaseTag`. The only dependencies are `vitest` itself and the internal `lib/release` module, with no external services touched. A notable design detail is the careful save-and-restore of `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_RELEASE` in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks, which prevents test pollution of the environment for other suites running in the same process.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\ReaderControls.tes.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the `ReaderControls` component from `apps/web/components/books/ReaderControls`, which renders a hidden-until-triggered reader settings dialog for adjusting theme, font size, and Sanskrit visibility. It exercises the component's controlled API — a `prefs` prop typed as `ReaderPreferences` and an `onChange` callback emitting partial preference updates — using `DEFAULT_READER_PREFERENCES` from the `@poojly/shared` package as the baseline fixture. The tests also pin the internal `__testing` export, asserting that `THEMES` contains exactly the keys `saffron`, `sepia`, and `night` and that `SIZES` is `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, so those option lists are part of the tested contract. Accessibility semantics are treated as the public interface: the suite locates controls by ARIA roles (`dialog`, `switch`, `button`) and checks `aria-checked` on the Sanskrit toggle and `aria-pressed` on the font-size buttons. The tests are built with `vitest` and `@testing-library/react`, using `vi.fn()` spies to capture `onChange` payloads. One notable coupling: the font-size test selects buttons by index within `getAllByRole('button', { name: 'Aa' })`, so it implicitly depends on the fixed sm/md/lg/xl render order of the size buttons.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\reading-progress-h.summary: This Vitest test suite verifies the localStorage persistence helpers behind the reading-progress feature, exercising the `__testing` export surface of the `@poojly/api-client` package rather than a UI hook directly. It covers the round-trip behavior of `writeLocal` and `readLocal`, confirming that a missing entry returns null, that progress rows (keyed by `bookSlug` and carrying `chapterSlug`, `chapterNumber`, `scrollPercent`, optional `lastVerse`, and an ISO `updatedAt`) persist per book, and that `readAllLocal` returns a map spanning multiple books. The tests also pin two important contract details: writing a second row for the same book overwrites the previous chapter's progress (so only one position is kept per book), and the underlying storage key retains the legacy prefix `poojly_reading_progress` via `STORAGE_KEY`. Finally, the suite locks in `FLUSH_THROTTLE_MS` at 5,000 ms, documenting that local writes are throttled to five-second intervals, and uses `clearLocalAll` in `beforeEach` to isolate each case. Dependencies are minimal — just `vitest` and `@poojly/api-client` — so the suite effectively serves as a regression guard for the storage format and throttling constants that sync logic elsewhere relies on.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\seo\\no-internal-4.summary: This Vitest file is a regression guard for the "SIDE-FIX-SEO-404" incident, ensuring that previously promoted long-tail content slugs (like `om-jai-jagdish-hare-aarti` and `ganesh-chalisa`) can no longer silently 404 in the Next.js app under `apps/web`. It imports the route-segment config directly from `../../app/content/[slug]/page` (`dynamicParams` and `generateStaticParams`) and from `../../app/darshan/[id]/page` (`dynamicParams`), treating those Next.js exports as an enforceable contract. The suite asserts three things: that `/content/[slug]` sets `dynamicParams = true` so unknown slugs render a graceful loading fallback instead of a hard 404, that `/darshan/[id]` keeps `dynamicParams = true` so future refactors can't regress it, and that every slug in the `PREVIOUSLY_BROKEN_CONTENT_SLUGS` constant (six aarti and chalisa slugs from the 2026-06-10 broken-link audit) appears in the static-params allow-list returned by `generateStaticParams`. Its only dependencies are `vitest` and the two page modules under test, with no network or filesystem access. Notably, the test deliberately enforces only the technical fix — the underlying content backfill (200+ word histories, 40-verse chalisas) is an editorial task tracked separately in `docs/cto/SIDE-FIX-SEO-404-handoff.md`. A gotcha for maintainers is that the test couples itself to Next.js file-convention exports, so any refactor that renames or restructures those page modules will break the import even if runtime behavior is unchanged.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\ServiceWorkerRegis.summary: This test file verifies the behavior of the `ServiceWorkerRegister` component from `apps/web/components/ServiceWorkerRegister`, ensuring it registers the `/sw.js` service worker only when the browser supports it. It uses vitest (`describe`, `it`, `expect`, `vi`) together with `@testing-library/react`'s `render`, and runs in a happy-dom environment, as hinted by comments about the navigator Proxy. Two local helpers, `installServiceWorker` and `uninstallServiceWorker`, mock `window.navigator.serviceWorker` with a `vi.fn()`-based `register` stub and clean it up after each test. The three test cases cover the happy path (register called with `/sw.js`), graceful no-op when the serviceWorker API is missing, and swallowing of a rejected registration promise so errors never bubble to the app. A notable design point is the `beforeEach` hook that replaces `window.requestIdleCallback` with a synchronous stub, since the component defers registration to idle time and tests cannot wait for real idle callbacks. Another gotcha is the cleanup fallback: because happy-dom's navigator may be a Proxy that refuses `delete`, `uninstallServiceWorker` catches the failure and instead redefines the property as `undefined`. Overall the suite documents the component's contract — register on idle when supported, stay silent otherwise — without touching any network or real service worker infrastructure.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\store-revamp.test..summary: This Vitest suite contains regression guards for the 2026-08-05 store-owner revamp, verifying that previously identified dead or fake UI was actually removed from the storefront. Rather than rendering components, it uses `readFileSync` from `node:fs` (with `node:path` for resolution) to read page sources as text and assert on string presence or absence — a cheap but brittle approach that can break on trivial refactors like renaming a constant. The checkout tests require `app/store/checkout/page.tsx` to fetch addresses from the `/users/me/addresses` backend endpoint, forbid the old hardcoded `SAVED_ADDRESSES` fake rows (including the literal strings "Lotus Garden Apartments" and "Whitefield"), and require the Add New Address link to point at `/profile`. A catalog test confirms `app/store/page.tsx` no longer renders the dead "Load More Products" button, and an orders test checks that `app/store-admin/orders/page.tsx` captures a `trackingNumber` when transitioning an order to `SHIPPED` status. The suite has no exports; its only dependencies are `vitest` globals (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and Node built-ins.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\seo\\puja-book-rou.summary: This Vitest file is a regression guard ensuring the `/pujas/[slug]/book` route never 404s again: after a 2026-07-11 incident where path-style booking links from puja pages broke (the booking UI actually lives at `/pujas/book` reading a `slug` search param), `app/pujas/[slug]/book/page.tsx` was added to redirect to `/pujas/book?slug=...&temple=...`, and this suite locks that behavior in. It dynamically imports the route module and invokes its default export with Promise-wrapped `params` and `searchParams` (matching Next.js 15's async request API), relying on the fact that `next/navigation`'s `redirect()` throws rather than returns. The helper `redirectUrlFromError` parses the thrown error's `digest` field, which follows Next.js's internal `NEXT_REDIRECT;<type>;<url>;<status>` semicolon format, while `renderBookRoute` wraps the invocation and asserts the throw actually happens. The tests cover module existence, slug forwarding (`maha-mrityunjaya` → `/pujas/book?slug=maha-mrityunjaya`), optional `temple` query forwarding, and URL-encoding of slugs/temples containing spaces. The notable gotcha is the dependence on the undocumented `NEXT_REDIRECT` digest shape, so a Next.js upgrade changing that format would break these tests even if the route still works; conversely, deleting the route or dropping slug/temple forwarding will now fail the build instead of silently reintroducing the 404.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\__stubs__\\server-.summary: This file is a test-environment stub that replaces the `server-only` npm package from Next.js when running under vitest. The real `server-only` package exists as a build-time guard: it throws an error if imported into a client bundle, preventing server-side code (secrets, database access, etc.) from leaking to the browser. Because vitest has no server/client compilation split, importing any module that depends on `server-only` would fail, so the test configuration aliases the package to this no-op module. It exports nothing (`export {}`) and has no dependencies; its only purpose is to satisfy the module resolver. A notable gotcha is that this stub silently disables the safety check during tests, so a client-side import of server-only code would not be caught by the test suite — only by an actual Next.js build.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\useIsPremium.test..summary: This Vitest suite verifies the behavior of the `useIsPremium` hook exported from `apps/web/components/useIsPremium`, which decides whether the signed-in user has premium access. It mocks the `useAuth` hook from `apps/web/lib/auth-context` via `vi.mock` and a resettable `useAuthMock` function, so each test can inject a different user object without standing up a real auth provider, and renders the hook with `renderHook` from `@testing-library/react`. The tests document the hook's contract: it returns false when no user is signed in or the user's `subscriptionTier` is `'free'`, and true for the paid tiers `'pro'`, `'bhakti_pass'`, `'annual_ratna'`, and the legacy `'premium'` value kept for backward compatibility. A notable gotcha captured here is the NRI override: an `isNriPremium` flag grants premium even on the free tier, but only when it is strictly the boolean `true` — the string `'true'` is explicitly rejected, indicating the hook uses a strict equality check rather than truthiness. Dependencies are limited to `vitest` and `@testing-library/react`; no network or backend services are involved.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\wellness-revamp.te.summary: This file is a Vitest regression suite guarding the "Wellness instructor revamp (2026-08-05)" in the `apps/web` app, ensuring two previously broken instructor features stay fixed. Rather than rendering components, it reads source files as text via a `read` helper built on `node:fs` (`readFileSync`) and `node:path`, then asserts on their contents. The first describe block verifies that the once-unreachable live-room editor now exists: `lib/wellness-api.ts` must export `setWellnessSessionRoom` hitting the `/sessions/:id/room` endpoint, and `app/wellness-portal/sessions/page.tsx` must surface a Set-room UI (matching strings like "Set live-class room link") for what used to be a curl-only operation. The second block checks that `app/wellness-portal/page.tsx` displays instructor-share earnings (matching `instructorShare` or "You keep") instead of the gross figure previously shown. Its only dependencies are Vitest's `describe`/`it`/`expect` plus Node built-ins, with no React testing library involved. The notable trade-off is that these are source-text string assertions, so they guard against the features being deleted or renamed but won't catch behavioral or rendering bugs, and they will fail on innocent refactors that change the matched literals.

apps\\web\\__tests__\\temple-revamp.test.summary: This Vitest suite provides regression guards for the temple manager revamp dated 2026-08-05, verifying that two previously-missing features stay implemented in the temple portal. It exports nothing itself; its two describe blocks check that the puja offering form in `app/temple-portal/pujas/page.tsx` collects available time slots (via `formSlots` state, an "Available Time Slots" UI section, submission as `availableSlots`, and edit-mode pre-fill through `setFormSlots(slots)`), and that a dedicated bookings list exists at `app/temple-portal/bookings/page.tsx` with a corresponding `/temple-portal/bookings` link in the portal sidebar `app/temple-portal/layout.tsx`, replacing the old dashboard top-10-only view. Its only dependencies are `vitest` (describe/it/expect) and Node's `node:fs` `readFileSync` plus `node:path`, wrapped in a small `read` helper that resolves sibling source files relative to the test. The notable design choice is that these are source-grep tests: they read files as text and assert on substrings and regexes rather than rendering components or exercising behavior, which makes them cheap and fast but brittle — harmless refactors like renaming a variable or rewording the label will fail them, and matching source text does not prove the feature actually works at runtime.

docs\\google-auth-cutover-2026-04-28.sql.summary: This is a one-off migration script (`docs/google-auth-cutover-2026-04-28.sql`) for the Darshya project, dated 2026-04-28, intended to be run manually once in the Supabase SQL editor against the production database. Its single schema change drops the NOT NULL constraint on the `phone` column of the `users` table so that Google Sign-In users — who authenticate with only an email and no phone number — can be inserted alongside existing phone-by-OTP users. The script depends on Supabase/Postgres and relies on the `information_schema.columns` catalog for a verification SELECT that runs inside the same transaction, letting the operator confirm `phone_nullable = 'YES'` before choosing COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A key design point documented in the header is that the `@unique` constraint on `phone` is deliberately preserved, because Postgres unique indexes permit multiple NULL values, so phone-number exclusivity for OTP accounts is unaffected while many Google users can share a NULL phone.
