The main gotcha is operational: the file is not part of an automated migration pipeline, must be executed manually and exactly once, and the verify-then-commit flow only works if the person running it reads the SELECT output before committing.

commitlint.config.js.summary: This file is the root commitlint configuration for the poojly monorepo, enforcing the Conventional Commits v1.0.0 message format (`type(scope): subject`) on every pull request via the `.github/workflows/commitlint.yml` GitHub Actions workflow, which runs it through npx with a cached layer to avoid install overhead. Its single export is a config object that extends the external `@commitlint/config-conventional` preset rather than replacing it, layering project-specific rules on top of the standard type set. The most notable customization is the `type-enum` rule, which adds a project-specific `security` type used by Darshya audit commits (e.g., `security(secrets): …`); per the comments, this type is treated as advisory (`release: false`) so it never triggers an automatic version bump. An `ignores` predicate skips Git-generated merge commits (anything matching `/^Merge\b/`), since those appear when a branch merges main mid-history and their embedded messages are already linted on their own PRs. Style enforcement includes lowercase scopes via `scope-case` (catching drift like `Feat(API):`), imperative lowercase subjects with no trailing period via `subject-case` and `subject-full-stop`, a 100-character `header-max-length` for scannability, and a softer warning-level 200-character `body-max-line-length`. The expected scopes map to monorepo areas such as api, web, admin, mobile, prisma, render, cf, ci, and agents. A practical gotcha: because enforcement is server-side in CI (~15–20s per run on the free tier), nothing here blocks commits locally, so contributors only learn about violations at PR time.

docs\\prod-cutover-2026-04-28.sql.summary: This is a one-time production cutover migration script for Darshya (dated 2026-04-28), designed to be run manually in the Supabase SQL editor or via psql against `$DATABASE_URL`, executing atomically inside a single transaction. It performs three operations: creating the `provider_kyc` table (the KYC stage-2 schema storing Aadhaar last-four/hash, PAN, and bank details keyed by `user_id` with a foreign key to `users` and `ON DELETE CASCADE`), deleting two contaminated rows—a `pandit_profiles` record and a `PANDIT` entry in `user_role_assignments`—left behind when a smoke-test signup for devotee@demo.com fell through to demo-mode, and running verification SELECTs that must return `('provider_kyc', 0, 0, 0)` before commit. The schema enforces format via CHECK constraints: regex validation on `pan_number`, `bank_ifsc`, and `aadhaar_last4`, plus a `provider_kyc_verified_idx` index on the `verified` flag to support verification-queue queries. Notable design choices include the use of `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` for idempotency on re-runs, and an in-transaction verification pattern where the operator is expected to run `ROLLBACK` instead of `COMMIT` if the expected counts don't match, since PostgreSQL DDL is transactional. The script references application-side context: the data corruption it cleans up was fixed in commit e9ff02f, which made the onboarding and provider-kyc routes check the access-token prefix to prevent demo-mode fall-through. A practical gotcha is that the verification is manual—the script commits unconditionally, so a human must actually read the SELECT output and decide whether to roll back.

docs\\chat-archive\\_export.py.summary: This is a standalone batch-export utility that converts Claude Code session transcripts from JSONL into human-readable markdown archives. It reads every `.jsonl` file under the hardcoded `SRC_DIR` (`C:\Users\DELL\.claude\projects\E--NewClaude`) and, via `render_session`, writes one markdown file per session plus a sortable `INDEX.md` summary table into `OUT_DIR` (`E:\NewClaude\bhaktisetu\docs\chat-archive`). The pipeline hinges on `extract_text_blocks`, which normalizes message content (text, thinking, tool_use, tool_result, image blocks) into a uniform list of dicts, and `summarize_tool_input`, which renders known tools like Read, Edit, Bash, Grep, and WebFetch as one-line argument summaries. A key design choice is that user and assistant prose is kept verbatim while tool calls and results are collapsed to truncated previews (governed by `MAX_TOOL_RESULT_PREVIEW` and `MAX_TOOL_INPUT_PREVIEW`), and thinking blocks are hidden inside collapsible `<details>` tags capped at 2000 chars, all to keep long sessions readable. The script distinguishes genuine user prompts from `tool_result`-wrapper messages by checking block kinds, handles `isApiErrorMessage` assistant entries specially, and skips unrecognized record types like permission-mode and file-history-snapshot. Session header stats (message counts, timestamps, working directories, git branches, first prompt) are collected during the single pass and backfilled into a placeholder before writing. It uses only the Python standard library (json, pathlib, datetime) and forces stdout to UTF-8 for emoji output, but note the gotchas: both paths are hardcoded to one Windows machine, malformed JSONL lines are silently skipped, and the script is intended to be run manually rather than imported.

docs\\agent-reports\\bug-audit-rerun\\_m.summary: `_merge.js` is a standalone Node.js utility script (run via `node _merge.js`, exporting nothing) that consolidates the per-domain bug audit results in `docs/agent-reports/bug-audit-rerun/` into a single deduplicated report. It reads every sibling `.json` file not prefixed with an underscore, parses out each file's `findings` array, tags every finding with a `_domain` field taken from the parent document's `domain` property, and lowercases `severity` before bucketing findings into critical/high/medium/low/info counts. A notable workaround: if `JSON.parse` fails, it repairs lone backslashes (invalid regex escapes embedded in strings) with a regex substitution and rewrites the corrected file back to disk, skipping only unrecoverable files. Deduplication uses a normalized key built from `file` plus `title` (lowercased, stripped of non-alphanumerics, truncated to 140 characters), which means near-identical titles in the same file collapse and overlong keys could theoretically cause false-positive collisions. It prints per-domain totals, pre- and post-dedup severity tallies, and full listings of critical, high, and medium findings, then writes the surviving set to `_MERGED_ALL.json` in the same directory — a filename whose underscore prefix deliberately excludes it from re-ingestion on subsequent runs. The script depends only on Node's built-in `fs` module and assumes each input JSON follows the `{ domain, findings[] }` shape produced by the individual audit agents.

e2e\\content-darshan.spec.ts.summary: This file is a Playwright end-to-end test suite that smoke-tests three public-facing sections of the app: the Content Hub, Live Darshan streaming pages, and the Panchang (Hindu calendar) page. It uses the `test` and `expect` APIs from `@playwright/test` to drive a real browser against routes like `/content`, `/darshan`, and `/panchang`. The Content Hub tests verify that the listing page renders the "Aarti" and "Chalisa" tabs and that a detail route (`/content/hanuman-chalisa`) returns HTTP 200. The Live Darshan tests check that the heading contains "Darshan", that at least one "LIVE" badge and one stream card mentioning Varanasi, Tirumala, or Mumbai is present, and that `/darshan/live-1` responds with 200. The single Panchang test only asserts that the page shows a "Tithi" label. Notable gotchas: tests rely on hard-coded seeded data (the slug `live-1` and specific city names), so they will fail against a database lacking those fixtures, and the stream-card selector loosely matches any element whose class contains "rounded", which could produce false positives if the UI's styling changes.

e2e\\astrology.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec smoke-tests the astrology section of the application, verifying that its main pages load and render key content. Using the `test` and `expect` APIs from `@playwright/test`, it groups five checks under the `Astrology` describe block: the `/astrology` hub must render an `h1` and at least one astrologer price matching the `₹\d+/min` pattern, astrologer cards must show a "Chat Now" call-to-action as a proxy for online status, and the profile (`/astrology/astro_001`), kundli (`/astrology/kundli`), and horoscope (`/astrology/horoscope`) routes must each return HTTP 200. The suite depends only on Playwright and a running app server; it has no internal module imports or exports. Notable constraints include a hardcoded astrologer ID (`astro_001`) that presumes seeded test data, and reliance on visible-text selectors (pricing in rupees-per-minute, "Chat Now"), which makes the tests sensitive to copy and locale changes. The assertions are shallow smoke checks—status codes and first-match visibility—rather than deep functional validation of chat or kundli generation.

docs\\roadmap\\setup\\supabase-readonly-.summary: This one-time setup script provisions a read-only Postgres role named `claude_readonly` on Supabase, intended to be run manually in the Supabase SQL editor as superuser before wiring the resulting connection string into the `SUPABASE_READONLY_URL` env var. It exists as defense-in-depth for the darshya-mcp server (Claude Code MCP) and the ARE KPI scraper: the server's `loadEnv()` prefers `DIRECT_URL` from the environment, and `.mcp.json` maps `${env:SUPABASE_READONLY_URL}` into it, so even a bypass of the application-level `guard.ts` write-protection cannot mutate data at the database layer. The script grants `CONNECT` on the `postgres` database, `USAGE` on the `public` schema, and `SELECT` on all existing tables, plus an `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` clause so future tables are automatically readable — a deliberate choice to keep the role from breaking as the schema evolves. It depends only on standard Postgres catalog views (`pg_roles`, `information_schema.role_table_grants`) for its built-in verification queries, and references `docs/engineering/R-Q1-E-014` and `docs/engineering/darshya-mcp-handoff.md` as the governing design docs. Notable gotchas: the `REPLACE_WITH_STRONG_RANDOM_PWD` placeholder must be substituted before running (suggested via `openssl rand -base64 24`), the connection string must use the direct host `db.<ref>.supabase.co` rather than the pooled connection, and the optional `DATABASE_URL_READONLY` GitHub Actions secret enables the same role in CI. The file closes with a commented revocation sequence (`REVOKE` grants then `DROP ROLE`) for teardown.

e2e\\auth.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec, `e2e/auth.spec.ts`, verifies the authentication flow of the Poojly web app, focusing on the `/auth/login` page and the demo sign-in path. It contains a single `test.describe('Authentication')` block with five tests: the login page renders the Poojly branding, a phone input (`input[type="tel"]` or `input#phone`), and a "Send OTP" button; the "Demo Sign In" button exists; clicking it redirects to `/dashboard` within a 10-second `waitForURL` timeout; the dashboard greets the hardcoded demo user "Arjun"; and the `/profile` page returns HTTP 200 after demo login. Its only dependency is `@playwright/test`, and it exercises the app's own routes rather than any external service, implying a demo-mode auth bypass exists alongside the real phone-plus-OTP flow. Notable issues: the "demo sign-in redirects" and "dashboard shows user info" tests are near-duplicates, and the profile test calls `page.goto('/profile')` twice in a row, making the first navigation redundant. The suite also relies heavily on brittle text-based selectors (`text=Arjun`, `text=Send OTP`) and `.first()` to resolve strict-mode ambiguities, so copy changes or duplicate strings will break it.

e2e\\mobile-demo.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec (`e2e/mobile-demo.spec.ts`) is a smoke-test suite that verifies the app's mobile preview routes and cross-platform demo page actually load. The `Mobile Preview & Demo` describe block contains six tests, each navigating to a route with `page.goto` and asserting the HTTP response status is 200. Covered routes are `/mobile` (home), `/mobile/temples`, `/mobile/darshan`, `/mobile/content`, `/mobile/profile`, and `/demo` (the combined iOS + Android demo page). Its only dependency is `@playwright/test`, specifically `test` and `expect`, and it relies on Playwright's configured `baseURL` since all paths are relative. A notable limitation is that these are pure availability checks: they confirm the server responds with 200 but assert nothing about page content, rendering, or behavior, so they would pass even if the screens render blank or broken.

e2e\\gaushala.spec.ts.summary: This is a Playwright end-to-end test suite verifying the gaushala (cow adoption) feature of the site. Its single `test.describe` block, "Gaushala / Cow Adoption", contains four tests: the `/gaushala` listing page renders a heading and at least one gaushala card (checked via the text "Vrindavan"), adoption plan pricing appears (₹51 and ₹3,000 tiers), at least three cow images with alt attributes load, and the detail route `/gaushala/cow_001` returns HTTP 200. The only dependency is `@playwright/test`, and the tests run against the application's public pages rather than mocked services. Notable gotchas: the tests are tightly coupled to seed data — specific names, prices, and the hardcoded cow ID `cow_001` must exist in the environment or the suite fails — and the final test calls `page.goto` twice, discarding the first navigation's response, which is redundant and slightly wasteful. Assertions are intentionally shallow (visibility and status code only), so the suite acts as a smoke check rather than a functional validation of the adoption flow.

e2e\\priest.spec.ts.summary: This file is a Playwright end-to-end smoke test suite for the priest-facing portal, verifying that four routes—`/priest` (dashboard), `/priest/bookings`, `/priest/payouts`, and `/priest/profile`—each return an HTTP 200 status when loaded. It exports no functions itself; everything is registered through the `test.describe`/`test` API imported from the external `@playwright/test` library, which must be configured with a `baseURL` elsewhere (typically `playwright.config.ts`) for the relative paths to resolve. The tests are intentionally shallow: they assert only response status, not page content, role-based access, or rendered components, so they catch routing and server errors but not broken UIs. A notable gotcha is that none of the tests set up authentication state, implying either the priest pages are publicly reachable in the test environment or an authenticated storage state is supplied globally—otherwise these assertions would fail against a guarded app.

e2e\\navigation.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end suite, `Navigation & Layout`, smoke-tests the Poojly web app's basic shell and route health rather than deep user flows. It has no exports; it registers six tests via `test.describe` from `@playwright/test`, covering the home page title (`/Poojly/`), visibility of the `nav[aria-label="Main navigation"]` landmark, desktop nav links to `/temples`, `/pujas`, and `/store`, and presence of the `footer` element. Two route-inventory tests then iterate hardcoded lists: thirteen public routes (including `/panchang`, `/gaushala`, `/astrology`, `/ask-pandit`, `/auth/login`) must each return HTTP 200, while auth-protected routes (`/bookings`, `/dashboard`, `/profile`) are only required to not return 500. Its only dependency is `@playwright/test`, run against a live server with no fixtures, mocks, or auth setup. Notable design choices: the protected-route check is deliberately lenient (treating redirects and 200s as equally valid and even defaulting a missing response to 200), those pages use the faster `domcontentloaded` wait, and the duplicated route arrays serve as a de facto registry of the app's public surface—so new pages must be added manually or they go untested.

e2e\\store.spec.ts.summary: This file is a Playwright end-to-end test suite that smoke-tests the storefront's core pages. It uses the `test` and `expect` fixtures from `@playwright/test` to define a `Store` describe block with five tests: the `/store` listing page must render a visible `h1` and at least five rupee-formatted prices (matched via a `₹[\d,]+` text selector) plus at least five images with `alt` attributes, while the product detail page (`/store/premium-brass-puja-thali-set`), `/store/cart`, and `/store/checkout` must each return HTTP 200. The suite has no internal module dependencies—it talks only to a running application server, whose base URL is presumably configured in Playwright's config. Notable choices: assertions are loose existence/count checks rather than content validation, the tests assume seeded data with at least five products priced in rupees (an India-focused storefront), and one test hardcodes a specific product slug, which will break if that seed product is renamed or removed.

e2e\\pujas-booking.spec.ts.summary: This file is a Playwright end-to-end test suite named "Pujas & Booking" that smoke-tests the temple site's puja listing, detail, and booking flows against a running server. It uses the `test` and `expect` APIs from `@playwright/test` and declares no exports — its behavior is entirely side-effect registration of five test cases. The suite verifies that `/pujas` renders a visible `h1` and at least three rupee-priced (₹) puja cards, that the `/pujas/rudrabhishek` detail page returns HTTP 200 with a heading, and that the booking wizard at `/pujas/rudrabhishek/book`, the `/bookings` list, and a booking detail at `/bookings/demo-001` all return 200. The tests depend on seeded fixture data — specifically a puja with slug `rudrabhishek` and a booking with id `demo-001` — so they will fail against an unseeded environment. Notably these are shallow smoke checks (status codes and element visibility only), with no form interaction, authentication, or payment-flow coverage despite the wizard routes being under test.

e2e\\temples.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end test suite, defined in `e2e/temples.spec.ts` via `@playwright/test`, validates the temples browsing experience of the web app. The `Temples` test group covers five scenarios: the `/temples` listing page renders its heading and at least three temple cards (located by `a[href^="/temples/"]` anchors), cards contain real images rather than placeholders, filter controls (a `select` dropdown and a search `input`) are present, clicking a card navigates to a detail page matching `/temples/.+`, and the detail page for the hardcoded slug `/temples/kashi-vishwanath` shows its heading, a gallery with at least three images, an "Available Pujas" section, and a "Book Now" call-to-action. It depends only on the Playwright test runner and a running instance of the app, with no internal module imports. Notable assumptions baked into the tests include a minimum of three seeded temples with images, the presence of the specific "Kashi Vishwanath" fixture data, and a filter UI that renders a `select` element — so the suite is coupled to both seed data and current DOM structure and will break if either changes.

packages\\analytics\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the entirety of `@poojly/analytics`, a thin TypeScript wrapper around the `posthog-js` SDK that centralises all product analytics for the platform behind a small, domain-specific API. It exports the `AnalyticsConfig`, `UserTraits`, and `EventProperties` types, plus initialisation and core functions: `initAnalytics` (call once at startup), `identifyUser`, `resetUser`, `trackEvent`, `trackPageView`, `setSuperProperties`, `isFeatureEnabled`, `getFeatureFlag`, and `setGroup` for PostHog group analytics (e.g., temples, families). The `AnalyticsEvents` constant provides pre-typed helpers for business events spanning the booking flow, payments, temple and content views, live darshan streams, search, and subscriptions, each mapping to a snake_case PostHog event name. Its sole external dependency is `posthog-js`; the default host is PostHog's US cloud unless `posthogHost` overrides it. Notable design decisions: page views are captured manually (`capture_pageview: false`) because the app is an SPA, identity persistence uses `localStorage+cookie`, autocapture and session recording are on, and module-level `isInitialised`/`isDisabled` flags make every function a safe no-op when analytics is disabled, uninitialised, or running server-side (SSR) — with feature flag getters falling back to `false`/`undefined` in those states.

packages\\api-client\\src\\client.ts.summary: This file is the core of the `@poojly/api-client` package: a singleton-configured, fetch-based HTTP client that centralizes auth token injection, timeouts, error normalization, and optional response validation for all API traffic. Callers initialize it once at startup via `initApiClient(config)` with an `ApiClientConfig` (base URL, `getAuthToken` callback, default headers, timeout, and an `onUnauthorised` hook), then make requests through the exported `api` object's method shortcuts (`api.get`, `api.post`, `api.put`, `api.patch`, `api.delete`). Errors are always surfaced as `ApiClientError`, which wraps the `ApiError`/`ApiResponse` envelope types imported from `@poojly/shared` and distinguishes timeouts (`REQUEST_TIMEOUT`), network failures (`NETWORK_ERROR`), and schema mismatches (`RESPONSE_SHAPE_MISMATCH`). A notable design choice is the `ZodSchema<T>` interface, which structurally mirrors zod's `.parse()` so callers can pass real zod schemas (via `RequestOptions.schema`) without this package taking a hard runtime dependency on zod; combined with `parseEnvelope`, it can validate and unwrap the `data` field of an `ApiResponse<T>` envelope, falling back to an unchecked cast when omitted. Other gotchas: the client config is module-level mutable state (requests throw if `initApiClient` was never called), timeouts are implemented with `AbortController`, and a latch (`unauthorisedInProgress`, ticket P1-46) ensures a burst of concurrent 401s fires `onUnauthorised` only once, with handler errors swallowed so the original 401 is what callers see.

packages\\api-client\\src\\client.test.t.summary: This vitest suite unit-tests the API client in `packages/api-client/src/client.ts` by mocking `globalThis.fetch`, exercising the core `request<T>()` branches behind the `api.get/post/delete` verb helpers. Local helpers `mockFetch`, `jsonResponse`, and `nthCallInit` install fake fetch implementations and inspect the `RequestInit` of each call, while `beforeEach` re-runs `initApiClient({ baseUrl })` because the client stores module-level config that would otherwise leak between tests. Coverage spans the happy path (parsed JSON returned as `T`, `Authorization: Bearer` injection via the `getAuthToken` callback, `noAuth` opt-out, 204 responses returning `undefined`) and the error taxonomy: aborts become `ApiClientError` with code `REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (408), fetch rejections become `NETWORK_ERROR` (status 0), and failed `schema.parse` calls become `RESPONSE_SHAPE_MISMATCH` (422). A notable behavioral contract is the 401 `onUnauthorised` latch (ticket P1-46): the tests prove that a burst of concurrent 401s collapses into a single handler invocation while the handler is in-flight, using a gate promise to hold the handler open. The schema tests (P0-3a) also pin down that `parseEnvelope: true` unwraps the `ApiResponse` envelope so `schema.parse` receives the inner `data`, and that omitting `schema` preserves the unchecked as-`T` cast fallback. Gotchas worth noting: the timeout test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` with a synchronously-attached rejection handler to avoid unhandled rejections while advancing timers, and `afterEach` restores real timers and mocks.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\portal.summary: This file in `@poojly/api-client` provides React Query hooks that fetch dashboard and supporting-list data for five role-specific portal UIs: astrologer, store-admin, gaushala, temple, and wellness. It exports one hook per endpoint — `useAstrologerDashboard`, `useStoreAdminDashboard`, `useStoreAdminReviews`, `useStoreAdminRevenue`, `useGaushalaDashboard`, `useGaushalaPortalDonations`, `useGaushalaVolunteers`, `useTempleDashboard`, `useTemplePortalDonations`, `useWellnessDashboard`, and `useWellnessStudents` — each paired with an exported response interface describing the expected payload (stats blocks, donation lists, volunteer rosters, student lists, etc.). Everything is built on the shared `api` client from `../client.js` and `@tanstack/react-query`'s `useQuery`, with all requests hitting `/api/v1/`-prefixed routes like `/api/v1/gaushala-portal/donations` to match the server's active mounts. A notable deliberate design choice is that the response types are intentionally permissive — nearly every field is optional — because the server returns role-specific records that the mobile UI narrows downstream, and the authors explicitly rejected tightening types here to avoid ripple changes whenever the server adds fields. All hooks are read-only queries with simple two-part query keys like `["store-admin", "revenue"]`, so there is no mutation, pagination, or cache-invalidation logic in this layer.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\index..summary: This file is the React Query hooks layer of the `@poojly/api-client` package, exposing a complete set of typed data-fetching hooks for the Poojly platform's frontend apps. It exports a hierarchical `queryKeys` factory (namespaced by temples, pujas, bookings, content, panchang, darshan, and user) alongside query hooks such as `useTemples`, `useTemple`, `usePujas`, `useBookings`, `usePanchang`, `useDarshan`, and `useUserProfile`, plus mutation hooks like `useCreateBooking`, `useCancelBooking`, `useCreateReview`, `useUpdateProfile`, and `useCreateAddress`. Every hook delegates HTTP calls to the shared `api` client from `../client.js`, uses endpoint builders from `API_ENDPOINTS` and domain types (`Temple`, `PujaBooking`, `DailyPanchang`, `CreateBooking`, etc.) imported from `@poojly/shared`, and builds on `@tanstack/react-query` primitives (`useQuery`, `useMutation`, `useQueryClient`). Detail hooks guard against empty identifiers via `enabled: !!slug` (or id), while mutations invalidate the relevant `queryKeys` namespaces on success to keep cached lists fresh. Caching policy is tuned per resource: `usePujaCategories` and `useFeaturedContent` use a 5-minute staleTime, `usePanchangByDate` caches historical data indefinitely, and the live darshan hooks poll with `refetchInterval` (30s for the stream list, 15s for a single stream). A recurring pattern is accepting caller-supplied `UseQueryOptions`/`UseMutationOptions` (minus `queryKey`/`queryFn`) and spreading them last, so consumers can override defaults — including, notably, the built-in invalidation callbacks.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\auth.t.summary: This file is the auth layer of the `@poojly/api-client` package, exposing a set of TanStack React Query hooks that wrap the `/api/v1/auth/*` endpoints of the backend (whose response shapes in `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts` it mirrors). It exports type definitions for `UserRole`, `AuthSession`, `AuthUser`, and the request/response pairs for each endpoint, followed by hooks `useSignInWithOtp` and `useVerifyOtp` for phone-OTP login, `useSignInWithCredentials` and `useSignUp` for email/password flows, `useRefreshToken` for session renewal, `useLogout`, and `useMe` for fetching the current user profile. All hooks delegate HTTP calls to the shared `api` client imported from `../client.js` and accept standard `UseMutationOptions`/`UseQueryOptions` so callers can attach callbacks or override behavior. A key convention is passing `{ noAuth: true }` on pre-authentication endpoints (OTP, login, signup, refresh) so the client skips attaching an access token, while `useLogout` notably sends the `accessToken` explicitly in its request body rather than relying on headers. `useMe` is the only query (fixed query key `["auth", "me"]`) and takes an `enabled` boolean as its first argument, letting consumers gate the profile fetch on session availability. Consumers must manually handle token storage and `expiresAt` bookkeeping, since the hooks return session payloads but do not persist them.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\consul.summary: This file in the `@poojly/api-client` package provides React Query hooks for the newer per-minute astrologer consultation lifecycle, which is backed by the `AstrologerConsultation` table and the `/api/v1/consultation/*` REST endpoints. It exports two hooks: `useMyConsultations`, which fetches a devotee's consultation history and upcoming sessions via `GET /api/v1/consultation/mine`, and `useCancelConsultation`, a mutation that POSTs to `/api/v1/consultation/:id/cancel` and reports refund eligibility per business rule #5. Supporting types include `ConsultationStatus` (a union of "pending_payment", "confirmed", "completed", "cancelled" that remains open to other strings), the `MyConsultation` interface (notably carrying `roomName` and `jitsiUrl` fields for Jitsi video sessions), `MyConsultationsResponse`, `CancelConsultationResponse`, and the `consultationKeys` cache-key factory. The hooks build on `@tanstack/react-query` (`useQuery`, `useMutation`, `useQueryClient`) and the shared internal `api` client from `../client.js`. A key design point, flagged prominently in the header, is that these hooks deliberately wrap the new consultation API rather than the legacy `/astrology/consultations` endpoint handled by `useAstrologyConsultations` in `wave-1-4.ts`, so the two must not be conflated. On successful cancellation, the mutation invalidates `consultationKeys.all` to refresh any cached consultation data, and the `CancelConsultationResponse` tolerates idempotent cancels through its `alreadyCancelled` flag.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\readin.summary: This file in the `@poojly/api-client` package implements hybrid reading-progress tracking: anonymous users persist to `localStorage` under the legacy `poojly_reading_progress` key (kept for back-compat despite the bhaktisetu/darshya rebrand), while authenticated users sync to the `/api/v1/me/reading-progress` REST endpoints. Its main exports are `useReadingProgress(bookSlug)`, which returns the current `ReadingProgress` plus a throttled `save()` and manual `flushNow()`; `useAllReadingProgress()`, which merges server and local rows with server winning per `bookSlug`; and `useMergeAnonReadingProgress()`, meant to be called once on login to push buffered local rows to the server (last-write-wins, so safe to re-call). It also exports `readingProgressKeys` for cache management, the `UseReadingProgressOptions` interface (whose `isAuthenticated` flag switches storage modes), and a `__testing` object exposing the storage helpers and constants. It builds on the package's internal `api` client and `ApiClientError` from `../client.js`, the `ReadingProgress` type from `@poojly/shared`, `@tanstack/react-query` for caching, and React (imported under `@ts-ignore` because it's a peer dependency typed by the host app). Notable design choices include write-local-first mutations for instant offline-capable UI, a 5-second throttle (`FLUSH_THROTTLE_MS`) using refs and a trailing `setTimeout` so rapid scroll saves coalesce, and a `beforeunload` listener that flushes any pending progress so the final scroll position is never lost. All storage helpers are SSR-safe via `typeof window` guards and swallow JSON/quota errors. Gotchas: a 401 `ApiClientError` silently falls back to localStorage rather than failing, local data is deliberately not cleared after the login merge (it remains as a cache fallback), and queries use a 60-second `staleTime`.

packages\\api-client\\vitest.config.ts.summary: This file is the Vitest test-runner configuration for the `api-client` package, defining how unit tests are discovered and executed. Its sole export is a default configuration object created with `defineConfig` from the `vitest/config` module, which provides type-checked config authoring. The configuration enables `globals: true`, so test functions like `describe`, `it`, and `expect` are available without explicit imports, and sets `environment: 'node'`, meaning tests run in a plain Node.js context rather than a browser-like DOM environment. Test discovery is restricted to files matching `src/**/*.test.ts`, so only colocated test files under the package's `src` directory are picked up. The only dependency is Vitest itself; there are no coverage, mocking, or alias settings, indicating the package relies on Vitest defaults beyond these basics. A practical gotcha is that tests needing browser APIs (e.g., `fetch` polyfills or DOM) would need per-file environment overrides or additional setup not present here.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\provid.summary: This file is the read-side data-fetching layer of the `@poojly/api-client` package, exposing a family of React hooks that wrap `@tanstack/react-query`'s `useQuery` for five product domains: Astrology, Wellness, Gaushala, the Priest Portal, and the Admin Portal. Every hook delegates HTTP work to the shared `api` client imported from `../client.js`, hitting GET endpoints under `/api/v1/` (e.g. `/api/v1/astrology/astrologers`, `/api/v1/priest/dashboard`, `/api/v1/admin/users`), so the file depends on both the internal client module and the external react-query library. Key exports include domain types — `Astrologer`, `WellnessInstructor`, `WellnessSession`, `WellnessProgram`, `Gaushala`, `Cow`, `AdoptionPlan`, `PriestDashboard`, `PriestBooking`, `PriestPayout`, `AdminDashboard`, and `AdminUser` — alongside hooks such as `useAstrologers`, `useAstrologer`, `useHoroscope`, `useWellnessSessions`, `useGaushalas`, `useCows`, `useAdoptionPlans`, `usePriestBookings`, `useAdminUsers`, and `useAdminPendingApprovals`. Query keys are consistently namespaced by domain (e.g. `["astrology", "astrologers", params]`, `["admin", "users", params]`), which keeps cache invalidation predictable across the app. Parameterized hooks like `useAstrologer` and `useHoroscope` guard execution with `enabled: !!id`, and every hook accepts an options bag typed as `Omit<UseQueryOptions<...>, "queryKey" | "queryFn">` so callers can tune caching behavior without overriding the fetch logic. A notable gotcha is that several responses — `useHoroscope`, `usePriestProfile`, and `useAdminRevenue` — are typed as `unknown`, signaling unsettled backend contracts that consumers must narrow themselves. The file is strictly read-only: there are no mutations here, so any write operations for these domains must live elsewhere in the package.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\wave-1.summary: This file in `@poojly/api-client` defines the "Wave 1-4" batch of React hooks, exposing data-fetching and mutation operations for store orders, support tickets, wellness sessions, astrology consultations, admin commissions, subscriptions, and donations. Every hook is built on `@tanstack/react-query`'s `useQuery`/`useMutation` and routes HTTP calls through the shared `api` client imported from `../client.js`, with mutations calling `qc.invalidateQueries` on success to refresh the relevant query-key namespace (e.g. `["storeOrders"]`, `["supportTickets"]`, `["wellnessSessions"]`). Key exports include list/detail pairs like `useStoreOrders`/`useStoreOrder` and `useSupportTickets`/`useSupportTicket`, plus action mutations such as `useUpdateStoreOrderStatus`, `useAddTicketMessage`, `useEnrollWellnessSession`, `useVerifyWellnessEnrollment`, `useSetWellnessRoom`, `useUpdateConsultation`, `useStartConsultationCall`, `useSubscribe`, `useCancelSubscription`, and the donation payment pair `useCreateDonationOrder`/`useVerifyDonation` (which notably skip cache invalidation, presumably because they redirect to an external payment flow). A notable naming gotcha: the wellness list hook is called `useWellnessSessionsV2` because `useWellnessSessions` already exists in `hooks/providers.js` as a mock-data variant, while these hooks target the real Prisma-backed `/wellness/sessions` routes. Detail queries guard with `enabled: !!id` to avoid firing on empty identifiers, and response payloads are loosely typed as `unknown`, leaving shape validation to consumers. Filterable queries (`useSupportTickets`, `useAstrologyConsultations`, `useAdminCommissions`, `useSubscriptionPlans`) build query strings from optional params and include the params object in the query key so each filter combination caches independently. The file talks only to first-party REST endpoints under `/store`, `/support`, `/wellness`, `/astrology`, `/admin`, `/subscriptions`, and `/donations`, with no direct third-party service calls.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\store..summary: This file is the store/products hook module of the `@poojly/api-client` package, exposing React Query hooks that let UI components fetch and mutate storefront data without touching HTTP details directly. It exports domain types (`Product`, `Collection`, `CartItem`, `Cart`, `Order`), a `storeQueryKeys` factory for consistent cache keys, query hooks `useProducts`, `useProduct`, `useCollections`, and `useCart`, plus mutation hooks `useAddToCart`, `useUpdateCartItem`, and `useRemoveCartItem`. Everything builds on `@tanstack/react-query` and the package's internal `api` client from `../client.js`, which it calls against REST endpoints under `/api/v1/store/`. Each hook accepts caller-supplied `options` typed via `Omit<UseQueryOptions, "queryKey" | "queryFn">` (or the mutation equivalent), so consumers can tune behavior without overriding the built-in key or fetcher. Notable choices: search/filter params are baked into the products query key for per-filter caching, `useProduct` is gated with `enabled: !!handle` to avoid firing on empty handles, and `useCollections` sets a 5-minute `staleTime` since collections change rarely. All three cart mutations invalidate `storeQueryKeys.cart` through `useQueryClient` so the cart refreshes after any change. One loose end: the `Order` type and `storeQueryKeys.order` key are exported but no corresponding order-fetching hook exists yet, suggesting planned or missing functionality.

packages\\api-client\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the barrel export for the `@poojly/api-client` package — it defines the package's entire public surface by re-exporting the core client and every React Query hook so consumers can import everything from a single entry point. From `./client.js` it exposes the low-level HTTP layer: the `api` client object, the `initApiClient` initializer, the `ApiClientError` class, and the `ApiClientConfig` and `RequestOptions` types. The bulk of the file re-exports domain-organized hooks: temple, puja, booking, content, panchang, darshan, and user hooks plus shared `queryKeys` from `./hooks/index.js`; OTP/credential auth hooks and their request/response types from `./hooks/auth.js`; store/cart hooks and `storeQueryKeys` from `./hooks/store.js`; and provider-portal hooks for astrologers, wellness, gaushalas, priests, and admins from `./hooks/providers.js`. Later feature work is layered in explicitly named modules: `./hooks/wave-1-4.js` (store orders, support tickets, wellness v2, astrology consultations, commissions, subscriptions, donations) and `./hooks/wave-5.js` (kundli generation, horoscopes, yatra packages, muhurat finding, wedding inquiries, Stripe premium), along with dashboard hooks for each stakeholder portal from `./hooks/portals.js`, the consultation lifecycle hooks from `./hooks/consultations.js`, and reading-progress tracking (including anonymous-progress merging and a `__testing` export) from `./hooks/reading-progress.js`. A notable design trait is that the module organization mirrors feature delivery waves rather than pure domain boundaries, and each submodule also re-exports its own TypeScript types and query-key factories, so consumers get a fully typed API surface with consistent cache-key helpers.

packages\\api-client\\src\\hooks\\wave-5.summary: This file is the "Wave 5" hook module of the `@poojly/api-client` package, providing React Query hooks for mobile-parity work tracked as TD10: kundli generation, daily horoscopes, yatra packages, curated yatra destinations, wedding muhurat search and inquiries, and the Stripe annual premium upgrade for NRI users. It builds on `@tanstack/react-query`'s `useQuery`/`useMutation` and the internal `api` HTTP client from `../client.js`, with every endpoint hardcoded using the explicit `/api/v1/` prefix to match the active server mounts. Exported hooks include `useGenerateKundli` and `useDailyHoroscope` (astrology), `useYatraPackages`, `useYatraPackage`, and `useBookYatraPackage` (bookable tour packages returning a `bookingNumber`), `useYatraList` and `useYatra` (curated destinations), `useFindMuhurats` and `useCreateWeddingInquiry` (weddings), plus `useCreateStripeAnnual` and `useIsPremium` (subscriptions). Each hook ships with its own TypeScript interfaces such as `KundliInput`, `YatraPackage`, `YatraBookInput`, `MuhuratInput`, `WeddingMuhurat`, and `WeddingInquiry`. Query hooks gate on required identifiers via `enabled: !!slug`/`!!sign`, and accept optional `UseQueryOptions` overrides (e.g., `useDailyHoroscope`). Notable looseness: several response payloads are typed as `unknown` (kundli, horoscope, `departure_dates`, and the muhurat response which may be a wrapped object or a bare array), so consumers must narrow types themselves. There is no cache invalidation wiring for the booking/inquiry mutations, and prices arrive as `string | number` unions, reflecting inconsistent server serialization.

packages\\shared\\src\\constants\\index..summary: This Vitest test file guards the shared API_ENDPOINTS constants map (exported from packages/shared/src/constants/index.ts) against drift from the actual backend routes. It exists because of a past regression where AUTH_REQUEST_OTP pointed at /api/v1/auth/otp/request while the real route in apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts was /auth/send-otp. The first test pins the four auth endpoints (AUTH_REQUEST_OTP, AUTH_VERIFY_OTP, AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN, AUTH_LOGOUT) to exact string literals matching the Express auth router mounted at /api/v1/auth. The second test iterates every entry in API_ENDPOINTS, invoking path-builder functions with a placeholder 'sample' argument and treating literals as-is, asserting each resolves to a non-empty string rooted at /api/v1 and collecting all violations into one failure message. It deliberately checks only path shape, not route resolution or argument substitution, making it a lightweight structural sanity check rather than an integration test. A design gotcha it encodes: path builders are assumed to take exactly one string id/slug argument, so any future endpoint requiring multiple parameters would need the harness updated.

packages\\shared\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the public entry point (barrel export) for the `@poojly/shared` package, which aggregates the shared code used across the Poojly monorepo. It defines no logic of its own; instead it re-exports everything from four internal submodules: `./types/index.js`, `./validators/index.js`, `./constants/index.js`, and `./utils/index.js`. Consumers of the package import any shared type, validator, constant, or utility directly from `@poojly/shared` without needing to know the internal folder layout. The use of `.js` extensions in the export paths indicates the package targets ESM-compliant module resolution (e.g., NodeNext), so internal barrels must exist in each of the four directories for the build to succeed. Because it is a wildcard re-export surface, any new export added to the underlying modules automatically becomes part of the public API — a convenience that also means name collisions between submodules would break the build.

packages\\shared\\src\\constants\\index..summary: This file is the shared constants module for the `@poojly/shared` package, centralizing domain enums, lookup tables, and API route definitions so every app in the monorepo (web, mobile, api) references the same values. Its key exports are `BOOKING_STATUSES` (an eight-state booking lifecycle map with labels, colors, and descriptions, plus the derived `BookingStatusKey` type), `PUJA_CATEGORIES` and `TRADITIONS` (Hindu puja types and sectarian traditions with Hindi labels), `LANGUAGES` (twelve supported Indian languages), and `SUBSCRIPTION_PLANS` (the FREE, DEVOTEE, PREMIUM, and FAMILY tiers with INR/USD pricing, feature lists, and usage limits). The most consequential export is `API_ENDPOINTS`, which hardcodes the REST paths of the backend — including parameterized builder functions like `TEMPLE_BY_SLUG(slug)` and `BOOKING_CANCEL(id)` — with comments explicitly cross-referencing `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`, meaning this file must be kept in sync with the server router by hand. It also exports operational limits (`MAX_DEVOTEE_NAMES`, `MIN_BOOKING_ADVANCE_HOURS`, `OTP_LENGTH`, `OTP_EXPIRY_SECONDS`, `SUPPORTED_IMAGE_TYPES`) and the `INDIAN_STATES` list. The module has zero imports and no runtime dependencies, making it safe to consume from any package. Notable gotchas: everything is frozen with `as const` so consumers get literal types rather than `string`, subscription limits use `-1` as an "unlimited" sentinel that callers must special-case, and the puja endpoints point at `/pujas/types/*` rather than the intuitive `/pujas/*`, reflecting a server-side routing quirk.

packages\\shared\\src\\types\\books.ts.summary: This file is the shared domain model for the books/reader feature of the `@poojly/shared` package, containing only type declarations and one constant—no runtime logic or external dependencies. It models scripture content hierarchically: a `BookManifest` describes a book with its `BookStructure` (either flat `"chapters"` or nested `"kandas"`, accommodating texts like the Ramayana), an optional list of `Kanda` divisions, and lightweight `ChapterSummary` entries, while the full `Chapter` type carries the actual `Verse` array with optional Sanskrit, transliteration, English, Hindi, and commentary fields per verse. The `BookLanguage` union (`"sa" | "en" | "hi"`) reflects the trilingual nature of the content. A notable design decision is the explicit support for incomplete content via `placeholder`/`partial` flags and `shippedVerses` counts on chapters, letting the UI represent works that are only partially digitized. For the reading experience, `ReadingProgress` persists per-chapter scroll position and last-read verse, and `ReaderPreferences` captures theme (`ReaderTheme`: saffron, sepia, night), font size, and per-language visibility toggles, with `DEFAULT_READER_PREFERENCES` providing the shipped defaults. Because these types live in the shared package, they serve as the contract between content sources, API layers, and reader UI components across the monorepo.

packages\\shared\\vitest.config.ts.summary: This file is the Vitest test configuration for the `packages/shared` package, defining how the package's unit tests are discovered and executed. It exports a single default configuration created with `defineConfig` from `vitest/config`, the only external dependency. The config enables `globals: true`, so test functions like `describe`, `it`, and `expect` are available without explicit imports, and sets `environment: 'node'` so tests run in a plain Node.js context rather than a browser-emulated one like jsdom — appropriate since this is a shared utilities package with no DOM dependencies. Test discovery is restricted via `include` to files matching `src/**/*.test.ts`, meaning tests are expected to be colocated with source files under the `src` directory and must use the `.test.ts` suffix; files named otherwise (e.g., `.spec.ts`) will be silently ignored. There are no coverage, mock, or alias settings, so the package relies entirely on Vitest defaults beyond these three options.

packages\\shared\\src\\utils\\index.ts.summary: This file is the shared utility barrel for the `@poojly/shared` package, providing domain-agnostic formatting, string, and pricing helpers used across the Poojly booking platform's apps. Its exports include `formatPrice` (locale-aware INR/USD currency display via the native `Intl.NumberFormat` API, defaulting to Indian formatting with zero minimum fraction digits), `formatDate` (en-IN date formatting with a `relative` option backed by the private `getRelativeTime` helper), `generateBookingNumber` (producing IDs in the BS-YYYYMMDD-XXXXX pattern using an unambiguous character set that excludes 0/O/1/I), `isNriUser` (treating any country code other than IN/IND/INDIA as non-resident Indian), and `calculateBookingPrice` (multiplying base price by devotee count, applying a default 1.5x NRI multiplier and optional percentage discount). Presentational helpers `getDeityIcon` (mapping Hindu deity names like shiva, ganesha, and venkateswara to icon identifiers with an "om" fallback), `slugify`, `truncate`, `titleCase`, `parseTime`, and `buildQueryString` round out the module. The file has zero external dependencies, relying only on built-in `Intl` and `URLSearchParams` APIs, which keeps it portable across client and server runtimes. Notable gotchas: `parseTime` silently coerces malformed input to zero rather than throwing, `generateBookingNumber` uses `Math.random` so IDs are not cryptographically unique, and the relative-time month/year math uses rough 30-day approximations.

packages\\shared\\src\\types\\index.ts.summary: This file is the central domain-type barrel for the `@poojly/shared` package, defining the shared TypeScript contracts used across the Poojly platform (a Hindu puja-booking and devotional-content app) so that API, web, and mobile consumers all speak the same schema. It exports enums covering lifecycle and classification states — `BookingStatus`, `PaymentStatus`, `PaymentMethod`, `PayoutStatus`, `SubscriptionTier`, `SubscriptionStatus`, `StreamStatus`, `ContentType`, and `Tradition` (Hindu denominations like SHAIVA and VAISHNAVA) — plus core entity interfaces: `User`/`UserAddress`, `Temple` (with nested `TemplePriest` and `TemplePujaOffering`), `Priest`, `PujaType`, `PujaBooking`/`BookingReview`, `Payment`/`PriestPayout`, `ContentItem`, `DailyPanchang`, `LiveDarshanStream`, and `Subscription`. It also defines the API transport contract via generic `ApiResponse<T>`, `PaginatedResponse<T>`, `ApiError`, and `ValidationError`, and query/filter types such as `TempleSearchParams`, `PujaSearchParams`, `BookingFilterParams`, and `ContentFilterParams` extending `PaginationParams`, and re-exports additional types from `./books.js`. The file has no runtime dependencies — it is pure type declarations meant to be imported by other packages in the monorepo. Notable design decisions include dual-currency support baked into every monetary entity (`priceInr`/`priceUsd` with a literal `"INR" | "USD"` currency union, plus explicit `nriPriceUsd` for non-resident Indians), parallel payment-provider fields on `Payment` and `Subscription` for both Razorpay and Stripe, and phone-number-first user identity with devotional attributes like gotra, nakshatra, and rashi. One gotcha: entities carry both foreign-key IDs and optional embedded relations (e.g., `priestId` alongside `priest?`), and `TemplePriest` embeds `Priest` which embeds `User`, so deeply nested serialization or circular references are possible if API payloads populate every relation.

packages\\shared\\src\\validators\\index.summary: This vitest suite validates the zod request schemas exported by `packages/shared/src/validators/index.js`, the shared validation layer for what is evidently a temple/puja booking platform. It exercises eight schemas via `safeParse`: `phoneOtpRequestSchema` and `phoneOtpVerifySchema` (E.164-style phone numbers, 6-digit OTP), `updateProfileSchema` (optional profile fields including a `tradition` enum spanning SHAIVA through SIKH), `createAddressSchema`, `createBookingSchema` (UUID foreign keys, future-only `scheduledDate`, 1–10 devotee names), `createReviewSchema` (integer rating 1–5), plus `searchQuerySchema` and `paginationSchema`. The only external dependency is `vitest`; all assertions target the sibling `index.js` module, so the suite doubles as executable documentation of the schemas' contracts. The tests pin down several India-first defaults worth knowing: `countryCode` defaults to `+91`, address `country` to `IN`, and booking `currency` to `INR` (with USD also accepted but EUR rejected). They also confirm coercion behavior in `paginationSchema` and `searchQuerySchema`, where string query params like `page: '3'` are coerced to numbers, capped at `pageSize` 100, and `sortOrder` defaults to `desc`. Boundary coverage is thorough — min/max lengths, past-date rejection, and empty-input rejection — though one test is misleadingly named "accepts today's date" while actually building a tomorrow date, suggesting same-day bookings may not truly be supported.

packages\\shared\\src\\validators\\readi.summary: This file defines Zod validation schemas for the reading-progress feature in the shared package, ensuring that client-supplied progress data is well-formed before it reaches the API or database. It exports two schemas: `readingProgressUpsertSchema`, which validates a full progress write (bookSlug, chapterSlug, chapterNumber, scrollPercent, and an optional lastVerse), and `readingProgressQuerySchema`, which validates a lookup by bookSlug alone. It also exports the inferred TypeScript types `ReadingProgressUpsert` and `ReadingProgressQuery`, so compile-time types and runtime validation stay in sync automatically via `z.infer`. The only dependency is the external `zod` library; there are no internal module imports. A shared `SLUG_REGEX` constrains both slug fields to lowercase alphanumeric strings up to 128 characters that may contain hyphens and slashes but must start with a letter or digit, which prevents path-injection-style values. Numeric bounds are deliberately conservative: `chapterNumber` and `lastVerse` must be positive integers capped at 10,000, and `scrollPercent` is clamped to the 0–100 range. Notably, `lastVerse` is optional on upserts, so consumers must handle its absence, and the query schema only supports single-book lookups rather than listing progress across all books.

packages\\shared\\src\\utils\\index.test.summary: This Vitest suite verifies the shared utility module at packages/shared/src/utils/index.ts, which provides formatting, text, and pricing helpers for the booking platform. It exercises formatPrice (en-IN/INR defaults, Indian digit grouping like "12,50,000", USD decimals, compact notation), formatDate (medium/full/long/short/time presets plus a custom "relative" mode yielding "just now", "10m ago", "yesterday", "3d ago", "2w ago"), and generateBookingNumber, which must match the BS-YYYYMMDD-XXXXX pattern with a suffix drawn from an alphabet that excludes ambiguous characters 0, O, 1, and I. It also pins down isNriUser (case/whitespace-insensitive matching of IN, IND, and India as domestic, everything else NRI), getDeityIcon (deity-name-to-icon mapping with aliases like ganesh/ganesha and balaji/venkateswara, falling back to "om"), and string helpers slugify, truncate (ellipsis-aware, trims trailing space), buildQueryString (drops undefined/null/empty values but preserves 0 and false, returns empty string when nothing qualifies), titleCase, and parseTime. The pricing tests document calculateBookingPrice as basePrice × devoteeCount with a default NRI multiplier of 1.5, optional discount percentage, and rounding to two decimals. The only external dependency is vitest; note that vi, beforeEach, and afterEach are imported but never used, suggesting leftover scaffolding. The suite serves as executable documentation of business rules — booking-number format, NRI pricing, and deity iconography — so regressions in any of these contracts will fail here.

packages\\shared\\src\\validators\\index.summary: This file is the validators barrel for the `@poojly/shared` package, defining the Zod schemas that both client and server use to validate incoming data for a puja booking platform. It exports primitive schemas (`phoneSchema`, `indianPostalCodeSchema`) plus request-level schemas and their inferred TypeScript types for phone OTP auth (`phoneOtpRequestSchema`, `phoneOtpVerifySchema`), user profiles (`updateProfileSchema`, `UpdateProfile`), addresses (`createAddressSchema`), bookings (`createBookingSchema`, `CreateBooking`), reviews (`createReviewSchema`), search (`searchQuerySchema`), and generic pagination (`paginationSchema`), and it re-exports everything from the sibling `./reading-progress.js` module. Its only external dependency is the `zod` library; there are no service calls or internal imports beyond the reading-progress re-export. The domain is clearly India-centric: `countryCode` defaults to `"+91"`, `createAddressSchema.country` defaults to `"IN"`, `createBookingSchema.currency` defaults to `"INR"` with only INR/USD allowed, and the `tradition` enum lists Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Sikh denominations. Notable details: `searchQuerySchema` and `paginationSchema` use `z.coerce.number()` so they can parse string query params directly, many fields rely on `.default()` so inferred output types differ from raw input, and `createBookingSchema.scheduledDate` carries a `.refine` that rejects past dates relative to the server's clock (a runtime-dependent check worth remembering in tests). The phone regex is a loose E.164-style pattern rather than a strict one, and the `.js` extension on the re-export indicates the package compiles to ESM with explicit extensions.

packages\\ui\\src\\components\\Badge.tsx.summary: This file defines the Badge component for the `@poojly/ui` component library, rendering small inline status/label pills used across the app, with special support for displaying booking statuses. It exports the `Badge` React component (a `forwardRef` span wrapper), the underlying `badgeVariants` style definition, and the `bookingStatusVariantMap` lookup table. Styling is built with `class-variance-authority` (cva) using Tailwind utility classes, and class merging relies on the `cn` helper imported from the package's own `../index.js` barrel. The variant system includes generic color variants (default, saffron, success, warning, error, info, purple, gold, outline) plus a dedicated set mirroring the booking lifecycle (pending, confirmed, priestAssigned, inProgress, completed, cancelled, refunded, failed). A key design feature is the `bookingStatus` prop, which automatically maps a `BookingStatus` enum string (e.g. `PRIEST_ASSIGNED`) to the matching variant via `bookingStatusVariantMap`, falling back to "default" for unknown values; when provided, it overrides the manually passed `variant` prop. Additional props include `dot` (a small colored indicator circle using `bg-current` so it inherits the variant's text color) and `icon` for a leading React node, with three size options (sm, md, lg) defaulting to md. One gotcha: `bookingStatus` is typed as a plain `string` rather than the actual `BookingStatus` enum, so invalid values silently degrade to the default style rather than producing a type error.

packages\\ui\\src\\components\\Card.tsx.summary: This file defines the Card component family for the `@poojly/ui` design system package, providing the standard container primitive used to group related content across the application. It exports six `React.forwardRef` components: the root `Card` (a styled `div` with optional `hoverable` and `elevated` props for a hover lift effect and a warmer `#FFFDF7` surface color), plus the compositional subcomponents `CardHeader`, `CardTitle`, `CardDescription`, `CardContent`, and `CardFooter`. The only dependencies are React itself and the internal `cn` class-merge utility imported from the package's `../index.js` barrel. Styling is pure Tailwind utility classes in a stone-toned palette (`rounded-xl`, `border-stone-200`, `shadow-sm`), with each component accepting a `className` override that `cn` merges after the defaults so consumers can extend styles without fighting specificity. Notably, the design mirrors the shadcn/ui convention of composable card parts with explicit `displayName` assignments for devtools, and the footer hardcodes a top border with `mt-2 pt-4` spacing, meaning layout is opinionated rather than prop-configurable beyond className overrides.

playwright.config.ts.summary: This file is the Playwright test runner configuration for the project's end-to-end test suite, exporting a single `defineConfig` object from `@playwright/test`. It targets a live deployment, defaulting `baseURL` to `https://darshya.online` unless overridden by the `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` environment variable, and discovers specs matching `e2e/**/*.spec.ts` or `tests/e2e/**/*.spec.ts` from the repo root. Tests run serially (`workers: 1`, `fullyParallel: false`) with 2 retries, a 60-second test timeout, and a 10-second assertion timeout, and `test.only` is forbidden in CI. Two browser projects are defined — Desktop Chrome (`chromium`) and iPhone 13 emulation (`mobile-safari`) — using Playwright's built-in `devices` presets. Failures are debuggable via traces captured on first retry plus screenshots and videos retained only on failure, reported through both an HTML report written to `playwright-report` and a console list reporter. Notably, `ignoreHTTPSErrors` is enabled, which relaxes TLS validation against the target environment and is worth remembering when diagnosing certificate-related behavior.

packages\\ui\\src\\index.ts.summary: This file is the public entry point (barrel export) for the `@poojly/ui` package, defining everything consumers of the design system can import. Its only locally defined export is `cn`, a utility that merges class names by combining `clsx` for conditional class composition with `twMerge` from `tailwind-merge` to resolve conflicting Tailwind CSS utilities (e.g., later padding classes overriding earlier ones). The rest of the file re-exports the component library's public surface: `Button` and `ButtonProps` from `./components/Button.js`, `Card` plus its `CardHeader`, `CardContent`, and `CardFooter` subcomponents from `./components/Card.js`, `Badge` and `BadgeProps` from `./components/Badge.js`, and the `theme` object from `./primitives/theme.js`. Externally it depends on the `clsx` and `tailwind-merge` libraries, both industry-standard choices for Tailwind-based component styling. Notable design choices include using explicit `.js` extensions on relative imports, indicating the package targets ESM/NodeNext module resolution, and isolating type re-exports with the `type` modifier so they erase cleanly at compile time. Because this is the sole public API surface, any new component must be re-exported here to be consumable, making this file the control point for the package's API contract.

packages\\ui\\src\\primitives\\theme.ts.summary: This file defines the design-token theme for the `@poojly/ui` package, a spiritual saffron-based design system, and serves as the single source of truth for the brand saffron color (`saffron.500 = #E16318`) that web (`apps/web/globals.css`), mobile (`apps/mobile/lib/theme.ts`), and remotion (`apps/remotion-pitch/src/tokens.ts`) themes are expected to derive from rather than hardcode. It exports a single `theme` constant (declared `as const`) plus a derived `Theme` type alias. The token set covers six color palettes — saffron, sindoor (red), tulsi (green), stone (neutral), gold, and mystic (purple) — along with semantic colors (success, warning, error, info), surface/background tones, spacing, borderRadius, fontSize with paired line-heights, fontFamily stacks (including Noto Serif Devanagari and Noto Sans Devanagari for Indic script), shadows, animation durations/easings, and a zIndex scale. The file has no runtime dependencies; it is pure data intended to be consumed by styling layers across the monorepo. A notable gotcha is that the `shadows.glow` value hardcodes the saffron RGBA (`rgba(225, 99, 24, 0.3)`) rather than referencing the token, so it must be kept in sync with `saffron.500` manually. The `as const` assertion makes all values deeply readonly literal types, enabling precise type inference for consumers of the `Theme` type.

packages\\ui\\src\\components\\Button.ts.summary: This file defines the `Button` component for the `@poojly/ui` design system, providing a single styled button with variant, size, loading, and icon support for consumers across the app. It exports the `Button` component (a `React.forwardRef` wrapper around a native `<button>`), the `ButtonProps` interface, and the underlying `buttonVariants` style map so callers can reuse button styling on other elements. Styling is built with `class-variance-authority` (`cva`) and merged via the `cn` utility imported from the package index (`../index.js`), relying on Tailwind classes that reference a custom `saffron-*` color palette defined in the project's Tailwind theme. Six visual variants are supported (primary, secondary, ghost, destructive, outline, link) plus five sizes (sm through xl, and a square `icon` size) and a `fullWidth` flag, with primary/md as defaults. The `isLoading` prop disables the button, sets `aria-busy`, swaps `leftIcon` for an inline animated SVG spinner, and suppresses `rightIcon`, keeping the label visible during loading. One notable gotcha: `asChild` is declared in `ButtonProps` (presumably for a future Radix Slot-style composition) but is never destructured or implemented, so it leaks through `...props` onto the DOM element as an unknown attribute — treat it as unavailable until wired up.

scripts\\agents\\broken-link.mjs.summary: This file is a standalone Node.js agent script (`broken-link.mjs`) that runs a daily broken-link audit against the production site: it fetches a set of seed pages (e.g. `/temples`, `/pujas`, `/store`), extracts every internal `href` via regex, then issues HEAD requests to each link and reports 4xx/5xx responses, timeouts, and slow responses (≥3000 ms) as a Markdown report written to `docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-broken-link.md`. It exports nothing; its only entry point is the `run()` function executed at module load, with helper functions `head()` (timed HEAD fetch with an 8-second `AbortController` timeout) and `extractLinks()` (regex-based link extraction that normalizes protocol-relative and root-relative URLs). It depends entirely on the sibling internal module `./_lib.mjs` for `fetchText`, `writeReport`, `upsertLog`, `WEB_BASE`, and `TODAY`, and deliberately uses no external libraries or paid services — link parsing is a simple regex rather than an HTML parser, which is a known fragility. Notable design choices: requests are made sequentially (not in parallel) to be a "polite citizen" against the site's own infrastructure, total links are hard-capped at `MAX_LINKS = 200` per run, seed pages that themselves return ≥400 are silently skipped, and the script exits with code 1 on fatal error so cron/CI can detect failure.

scripts\\agents\\agent-issue-filer.mjs.summary: This script closes the loop between detection and action for the agent suite: it reads today's markdown reports from `docs/agent-reports` (produced by `uptime-pinger`, `broken-link`, and `schema-validator`), extracts critical signals via regex-based parsers (`extractUptimeSignals`, `extractBrokenLinkSignals`, `extractSchemaSignals`), and files GitHub issues through the REST API using helpers `ghFetch`, `listOpenAutoIssues`, and `fileIssue`. It depends only on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`), the shared `./_lib.mjs` module (`writeReport`, `TODAY`), and the GitHub API, targeting the repo in `GH_REPO` (default `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu`). The generic `processReport` pipeline handles read → extract → dedup → file for each source, and `main` writes its own summary report via `writeReport('agent-issue-filer', ...)`. Idempotency is the central design decision: each issue body embeds a `fingerprint:<source>:<hash>` tag (a Java-style string hash rendered in base36), and the script skips filing if any open issue labeled `agent-auto-filed` already carries that fingerprint — meaning an identical signal set never re-files, and closing an issue re-arms it. Like its sibling agents, it follows the env-or-noop pattern: without `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` it logs a skip report instead of failing, making it safe to wire into `agents-daily.yml`. Notable gotchas: the extractors are tightly coupled to the exact markdown table/heading formats of the upstream reports, broken-link signals are hard-capped at 10 per run, and only reports whose filenames start with today's date are considered.

scripts\\agents\\backlinks-monitor.mjs.summary: This script is a scheduled backlinks monitor that tracks external domains mentioning darshya.online by scraping DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint (`duckduckgo.com/html/`) with a set of hardcoded QUERIES that use quoted brand terms plus `-site:` exclusions, since DuckDuckGo ignores the `link:` operator. It has no exports; the internal pipeline consists of `extractLinks` (regex-parses anchor hrefs into a domain set, filtering out search-engine and own domains), `probeDdg` (fetches one query via `fetchText` with a 1.5s polite delay between calls), `loadState`/`saveState` (persist snapshots as JSON to `docs/agent-reports/_backlinks-monitor-state.json`), and `main`, which diffs today's domains against prior state to compute new and lost backlinks, updates per-domain `lastSeen` timestamps, and emits a Markdown report through `writeReport('backlinks-monitor', md)`. Its only internal dependency is `./_lib.mjs` (`writeReport`, `fetchText`, `TODAY`), alongside `node:fs` and `node:path`; it talks to DuckDuckGo over plain HTTP with no API keys. Notable caveats: the header comment advertises Bing `linkfromdomain:` probes but no Bing code actually exists, detection is explicitly heuristic and prone to false positives, an empty result set may indicate rate-limiting rather than zero backlinks, and the process exits with code 1 on any fatal error so CI/scheduler runs surface failures.

scripts\\agents\\booking-quality-monitor.summary: This script is an hourly ops monitor that detects SLA-overdue puja bookings — any booking whose scheduledDate is at least 24 hours in the past while the pandit still hasn't uploaded a videoProofUrl, which is mandatory under business rule #1 and represents a refund/trust risk. Its main() routine calls the internal admin endpoint /api/v1/admin/ops/sla-overdue-bookings (authenticated via the CRON_AUTH_TOKEN query param against API_BASE) and files one rolling GitHub issue per breach signature using the ghFetch/fileIssue helpers, labeling them agent-auto-filed, booking-quality, and P0 with instructions to WhatsApp the pandits and force-cancel plus auto-refund anything past 72 hours. Duplicate filings are avoided by a fingerprint() function that hashes the sorted bookingNumbers into a base36 signature embedded in the issue body as an "sla-overdue:<fp>" marker, which findOpenSlaIssue() matches against existing open issues before creating a new one. It builds on the shared internal module ./_lib.mjs (importing writeReport, TODAY, and API_BASE) and talks externally to the GitHub REST API for the repo configured by GH_REPO (defaulting to XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu). Notable gotchas: the script is designed to no-op gracefully — if CRON_AUTH_TOKEN is missing it writes a skip report instead of failing, and without GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN it still writes a markdown report via writeReport but files no issue. Other defensive choices include a 15-second AbortSignal.timeout on the feed fetch, silent failure swallowing in ghFetch (returning status 0 on network errors), and truncation of breach listings to 25 rows in the issue and 15 in the report.

scripts\\agents\\cold-temple-outreach.mj.summary: This is a daily cron script that runs cold email outreach to prospective temple partners for the Darshya platform, hard-capped at 25 leads per run to stay within Resend's free-tier limits (25/day × 30 ≈ 750/month, under the 100/day ceiling). It polls the internal admin endpoint `/api/v1/admin/ops/cold-temples` (authenticated via `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN`) for NEW Lead rows with role=TEMPLE and `lastContactedAt=null`, sends each a personalized partnership pitch through the Resend API, then POSTs the successful IDs to `/api/v1/admin/ops/mark-contacted` so leads flip NEW → EMAILED and reruns stay idempotent. The key internal functions are `emailHtml` (builds the pitch with an escaped name/city and a UTM-tagged `/list-temple` onboarding link), `sendEmail` (Resend HTTP client), `markContacted`, and `main` (orchestration plus a 500ms throttle between sends); a Markdown run report is emitted via `writeReport` imported from the shared `./_lib.mjs` module along with `TODAY`, `API_BASE`, and `WEB_BASE`. External dependencies are limited to the Resend email API and the Darshya admin ops API, configured through `RESEND_API_KEY`, `RESEND_FROM`, and `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` environment variables. Notable design choices: personalization is deliberately template-only (city in subject, name in opener) with no LLM involved, trading customization for zero spend and deterministic deliverability; all lead-supplied strings pass through `escapeHtml` to prevent injection into the email body; and the script degrades gracefully — it writes a "skipped" report when `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` is missing and flags in the report when `RESEND_API_KEY` is unset so sends silently no-op rather than crash.

scripts\\agents\\cold-temple-outreach-v2.summary: This script is version 2 of the cold-temple outreach cron job (roadmap item R-Q1-M-014), which emails NEW temple leads with bodies personalized by deity tradition, region, city tier, and nearest festival — deterministically, with no LLM spend. Its `main()` fetches leads from the internal endpoint `/api/v1/admin/ops/cold-temples` (capped at 25 per run), generates each email via `buildPersonalizedEmail` from the sibling module `cold-temple-outreach-v2-personalize.mjs`, sends through the Resend API via the local `sendEmail` helper, and then calls `markContacted` to POST the contacted lead IDs to `/api/v1/admin/ops/mark-contacted`, flipping their status NEW → EMAILED so re-runs are idempotent. Internal dependencies are `writeReport`, `TODAY`, and `API_BASE` from `_lib.mjs`; external dependencies are the Resend email service (`RESEND_API_KEY`, `RESEND_FROM`) and the backend admin API authenticated by `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN`. Sends run serially with a 500ms gap to respect Resend free-tier limits (25/day, ~750/month). The script degrades gracefully: it writes a skip report when `CRON_AUTH_TOKEN` is missing and records sends as skipped when `RESEND_API_KEY` is absent. Each run emits a markdown report containing the KPI counter `email_v2_personalized_sent` plus deity-class and region breakdowns, designed to feed a manual KPI rollup in `_manual-kpis.yml`. A noted caveat is that cumulative source attribution in the lead table depends on future API-side tracking of `contactSource = 'cold-temple-outreach-v2'`.

scripts\\agents\\competitor-feature-watc.summary: This script is a weekly competitor intelligence agent that scrapes the live product surfaces of SriMandir, Utsav, AstroSage, and AppsForBharat (hardcoded in the `SURFACES` array) and diffs each page against the previous snapshot to surface new SKUs, price changes, and added or removed offerings — complementing the RSS-based `competitor-watch` agent by tracking what competitors ship rather than what they announce. The core pipeline is `fingerprint(html)`, which extracts a page signature of H1–H3 heading text plus price-like strings via regex (capped at 50 headings and 30 prices), and `diff(prev, curr)`, a set-based comparison producing new/removed headings and prices. State persistence lives in `loadState`/`saveState`, which read and write `docs/agent-reports/_competitor-feature-watcher-state.json`; deleting that file resets the baseline, and the first run for any URL is captured as baseline-only with no diff reported. The main `run()` loop fetches each surface sequentially, stores the new fingerprint with a `capturedAt` timestamp, renders a Markdown summary (including net-change counts, per-surface diffs truncated to 15 items, an errors section, and a "How to act" playbook), then publishes it via `writeReport('competitor-features', md)` and records a one-line tally with `upsertLog`. Its only dependencies are `node:fs` and the sibling `_lib.mjs` module, which supplies `fetchText`, `writeReport`, `upsertLog`, and `TODAY`. Notable constraints: it uses plain HTTP fetches with regex parsing rather than a headless browser, so JavaScript-rendered content will be missed, non-200 responses are logged as errors and skipped without retry, and any fatal error exits the process with code 1.

scripts\\agents\\cold-temple-outreach-v2.summary: This file is a deterministic, LLM-free cold-outreach email generator (campaign R-Q1-M-014) that builds a per-temple personalized subject line and HTML body for Darshya, an NRI temple-seva marketplace, so that no two temples receive identical boilerplate while the same temple always gets identical output across runs for QA diffing. Its main exports are `buildPersonalizedEmail` (the top-level entry returning subject, html, and classification metadata), plus `buildSubject` and `buildBodyHtml`, supported by classifiers `classifyDeity`, `classifyRegion`, and `classifyCityTier` that bucket a lead into deity families (shiva, vishnu, devi, ganesha, hanuman, ayyappa, generic), geographic regions (north/south/west/east/central/unknown), and city tiers (tier1, tier2, pilgrim). Template selection uses `stableHash`, an FNV-1a hash of the temple's id/deity/region/tier tuple, fed into `pickTemplate` to index into the `DEITY_HOOKS`, `REGION_CONTEXT`, `CITY_TIER_VALUE`, and `FESTIVAL_HINTS` banks — the key design decision being zero LLM spend combined with run-to-run stability. The module has no npm imports and makes no network calls; its only external dependency is `process.env.WEB_BASE` (defaulting to https://darshya.online), used to build the UTM-tagged `/list-temple` onboarding link. All lead-supplied values pass through `escapeHtml` before interpolation into the body, mitigating injection from untrusted lead data. Notable gotchas: the regex-based deity classifier can misclassify (e.g. matching "ram" inside unrelated words is guarded by `\b`, but ambiguous deities fall through to `generic`), empty or malformed lead fields degrade silently to 'generic'/'unknown' fallbacks, and despite a comment claiming runtime festival computation, `FESTIVAL_HINTS` are static month ranges — so template freshness requires editing the banks or changing the hash seed.

scripts\\agents\\competitor-watch.mjs.summary: This Node CLI script monitors public RSS/Atom feeds from four competitors — Sri Mandir, AppsForBharat, Utsav, and AstroSage — and emits a Markdown report listing only items that are new since the previous run, treating each new post as a competitive signal (feature launch, blog post, press, pricing change).
