scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\preflight.mjs.summary: `scripts/agents/roadmap/preflight.mjs` is a one-shot readiness probe meant to run before the first ARE Orchestrator dry-run: it live-tests each external dependency the orchestrator needs and exits 0 (GO) or 1 (NO-GO) based on the results. It exports nothing; its structure is a `CHECKS` array of six probes plus a `main()` runner that prints pass/fail/skip per check and summarizes. The probes cover: the Anthropic API via `@anthropic-ai/sdk` (using `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`), Supabase Postgres via `pg` (`DATABASE_URL_READONLY` with `SUPABASE_DIRECT_URL` as fallback), PostHog project access, Render service listing, Cloudflare token verification (all three via plain `fetch` against their REST APIs), and GitHub access via the local `gh` CLI. Each check is wrapped in a 15-second `Promise.race` timeout, and HTTP checks use 10-second `AbortSignal` timeouts. Notable gotchas: the Anthropic probe mirrors the model-selection logic in `_anthropic-client.mjs`, deliberately choosing `blackboxai/z-ai/glm-5.2` instead of `claude-opus-4-7` when the base URL points at the Blackbox proxy, because that proxy 403s on Claude models. The exit-code semantics are nuanced — failures are NO-GO, all-skipped is NO-GO, but partially skipped is a "PARTIAL GO" that still exits 0, since skipped checks will be exercised later in the GitHub Actions cron where the secrets exist.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\finalize.mjs.summary: This script is the finalize step of the roadmap agent pipeline: it scans recent commits for `Closes: Q-...` trailers and archives the matching roadmap queue entries from `docs/roadmap/queue` into month-bucketed folders under `docs/roadmap/done/YYYY-MM`. Its main entry point, `main()`, is supported by `getRecentClosesTrailers()`, which pulls commit messages either from the GitHub Actions event payload at `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` or, as a local fallback, from `git log -10` via `execSync`, and by `verifyContract()`, which is currently a stub that always returns passed=true with real curl/SQL/test verification deferred to Phase 6. Queue files are matched by parsing their YAML frontmatter with `js-yaml` and comparing the `queueId` field; on a match, the script stamps `verifiedAt` and appends to `shippedCommits` in the frontmatter, writes the updated file to the done directory, and removes the original with a best-effort `git rm` so the move lands atomically in the surrounding commit. If verification were to fail, it would instead write an alert file to `docs/roadmap/_alerts` and skip the move. Key gotchas: the regex only matches trailers at line start in the exact `Closes: Q-<id>` format, unmatched queueIds only produce warnings, and since verification is a no-op stub, every closed item is currently archived on trust with a note recommending manual verification.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\queue-list.mjs.summary: This standalone Node CLI script prints a quick console report of pending work in the roadmap queue by scanning markdown files in `docs/roadmap/queue` and displaying up to ten unconsumed items as a fixed-width table. It exports nothing; running it reads each `.md` file, extracts the YAML frontmatter block with a regex, parses it via `js-yaml`, and keeps only entries lacking a `consumedAt` timestamp. Its dependencies are limited to Node built-ins (`readFileSync`, `readdirSync`, `existsSync` from `node:fs`, and `join` from `node:path`) plus the external `js-yaml` package. For each surviving item it prints `queueId`, `role`, `priority`, `estMinutes`, `itemId`, and a truncated 50-character `itemTitle`, prefixed by a total unconsumed queue-depth count. Notable behaviors: it exits with code 0 (not an error) when the queue directory is missing, silently skips files with absent or malformed frontmatter via an empty catch, and relies on alphabetical filename sorting to determine display order, so filename conventions control which items surface in the top ten.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_decision-prom.summary: This Vitest test file validates the `scripts/agents/roadmap/_decision-prompt.mjs` module, which assembles the LLM prompt and tool definitions for a "Master Orchestrator" roadmap-decision agent. It checks three exports: `DECISION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` (verified to be a substantial multi-line string mentioning "Opus 4.7", all 12 sub-agent roles such as cto-agent, cfo-agent, and geo-agent, plus free-tier budget doctrine like CF 500 / GH 2000 minutes and founder-blocker discipline), `DECISION_TOOLS` (asserted to be exactly four tools — `spawn_subagent`, `defer_to_founder`, `kill_item`, and `write_decision_note` — each with a name, description, and object-typed `input_schema` with required fields, and the spawn tool's role enum having 12 values), and `buildDecisionUserMessage` (verified to compile cycle timestamp, backlog counts, GitHub/Cloudflare budget percentages, item IDs, fired tripwires, and founder blockers into the user prompt). The only external dependency is Vitest; the tests rely on regex and substring matching rather than snapshot comparison, so they pin key semantic content without constraining exact prompt wording. The fixture context object also documents the expected shape of the orchestrator's cycle state (budget percentages, status buckets, queue depth, tripwires), which is useful for anyone consuming this module.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\queue-pick.mjs.summary: This standalone Node CLI script (`scripts/agents/roadmap/queue-pick.mjs`) selects a work item from the roadmap queue — a folder of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter under `docs/roadmap/queue` — marks it consumed in place, and prints the item body to stdout for an agent to act on. The selection mode comes from a single positional argument: `next` takes the first unconsumed file (alphabetically sorted), `next-<role>` filters by the frontmatter `role` field, and anything else is matched against the `queueId` or `itemId` frontmatter keys. When an item is picked, the script stamps `consumedAt`, `consumedBy: 'claude-code'`, and `consumedInSessionId` (read from the `CLAUDE_SESSION_ID` environment variable, falling back to `unknown-session`) back into the file, explicitly mirroring the behavior of the PowerShell counterpart `queue-pop.ps1`. Its output is framed in HTML comments, including a reminder to append a `Closes: <queueId>` trailer on commit so the queue item can be cross-referenced in git history. Dependencies are minimal: `node:fs`, `node:path`, and `js-yaml` for frontmatter parsing. Notable gotchas: it always exits 0 — emitting only an HTML comment when the queue directory is missing or nothing matches — so callers must parse stdout rather than rely on exit codes; "next" means alphabetically first unconsumed file, not chronologically first; and rewriting via `yaml.dump` may reformat the original frontmatter, with no file locking to guard against concurrent picks.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_agent-fleet-s.summary: This script compiles the daily markdown reports of a roughly 38-agent automation fleet into a single compact JSON digest so the downstream Decision Agent (fed via signal-context) can review fleet activity without reading full reports. Its sole export, `summarizeFleet()`, scans `docs/agent-reports/` for files matching the `YYYY-MM-DD-{agent}.md` convention (with an optional `-Nh` suffix), keeps only the latest report per agent via string date comparison, and truncates each report to a 1500-character excerpt governed by `MAX_EXCERPT`. It relies only on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:url`) and two internal helpers: `findLatestPerAgent()` for the daily reports and `findLatestAdvisory()`, which pulls the newest ISO-week folder (`YYYY-Www`) under `docs/roadmap/advisory/` to include weekly CXO role advisories. A hard-coded `AGENT_TO_SECTOR` table routes each agent to an executive sector (cmo, cfo, cto, cpo, sales, cs, hr, it, founder), producing a `bySector` rollup where each entry is further trimmed to 500 characters; agents missing from the table silently fall into an `unmapped` bucket, which is the main maintenance gotcha as new agents are added. The module is dual-mode: it detects direct CLI invocation by comparing `realpathSync` of `import.meta.url` against `process.argv[1]`, and only then writes the result to `docs/roadmap/_sector-summaries.json` — importing it as a module produces no side effects. Note the internal variable is misspelled `byector` though the emitted JSON key is correctly `bySector`, and the truncation marker `...[truncated]` is appended when reports exceed the excerpt cap.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_anthropic-cli.summary: This Vitest test suite (`_anthropic-client.test.mjs`) verifies the behavior of `callOpus47` and `ModelRejectedError` from the sibling module `_anthropic-client.mjs`, part of the `scripts/agents/roadmap` tooling. It uses mocked Anthropic SDK clients (injected via a `client` option) to confirm the "no silent swap" guard: a 403 rejection — whether a "Free tier" or "Only open-source models are supported" message — throws `ModelRejectedError` without retrying, and unverified model overrides like `claude-sonnet-4-5` in `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` are rejected before any API call. The suite also pins model auto-selection logic: when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` contains "blackbox" the default is `blackboxai/z-ai/glm-5.2`, otherwise it falls back to `claude-opus-4-7`. Retry behavior is covered too — up to three attempts on 5xx errors with a configurable `retryDelayMs` — along with the streaming auto-switch that routes requests with `maxTokens >= 8192` (or explicit `stream: true`) to `messages.stream()` instead of `messages.create()`, including reconstruction of `tool_use` blocks from streaming `input_json_delta` partial JSON. A final describe block checks API-key fallback resolution, verifying that `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_BLACKBOX_PROXY` is side-mirrored into `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` only when the latter is unset. Tests carefully isolate host environment state (`ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, and four key-related env vars) via `beforeEach`/`afterEach` save-and-restore, and the only external dependency is `vitest` itself.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_decision-prom.summary: This module is a dependency-free prompt-definition file that compiles the system prompt, tool schemas, and per-cycle user message for the Decision Agent, the "Master Orchestrator" of the Bhaktisetu/Darshya virtual company that runs on a 6-hour cycle to pick which roadmap items advance next. It exports three things: `DECISION_SYSTEM_PROMPT`, the persona-and-rules text that ranks work by revenue-impact/hour, enforces role-diversity coverage across twelve sub-agent roles (cto-agent, cmo-agent, sales-agent, cs-agent, legal-agent, researcher, geo-agent, etc.), and cites sources of truth like `docs/roadmap/_index.json`, `docs/free-tier-budgets.md`, and `docs/activation-gates.md`; `DECISION_TOOLS`, the JSON tool schemas for `spawn_subagent`, `defer_to_founder`, `kill_item`, and `write_decision_note`; and `buildDecisionUserMessage(signalContext)`, which renders the cycle's KPI snapshot — backlog counts, GH/CF budget percentages, queue depth, fired tripwires, ready-to-ship and founder-blocked items — into the user turn with the full `signalContext` JSON embedded. The module has no imports and is pure prompt-engineering data, loaded once per cycle by the roadmap orchestrator, which the comments indicate runs as a Render bg-worker with no timeout cap. Hard constraints baked into the prompt include never spawning founder-blocked work, never exceeding free-tier budgets (CF 500 builds/mo, GH 2000 min/mo, Resend 100/day), never re-spawning items already in `queue.itemIds`, and always calling `write_decision_note` exactly once as the final tool call or the cycle is recorded as broken. A notable gotcha is an internal inconsistency: the prose says to spawn 3–7 sub-agents of 1–3 itemIds each, while the tool section caps spawning at 2–4 per cycle with 1–2 items bundled, and the `spawn_subagent` schema itself allows 1–3 itemIds — consumers should treat the schema and the 2–4 budget cap as the operative limits.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_bulk-create.m.summary: This file is a one-shot bulk-import CLI that converts a CSV of roadmap items into individual markdown files with YAML frontmatter under `ITEMS_ROOT/{quarter}/{category}/`, where `ITEMS_ROOT` comes from the sibling internal module `./_lib.mjs`. It takes the CSV path from `process.argv[2]` (defaulting to `docs/roadmap/_bulk-input.csv`) and is built entirely on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`) with no external dependencies. The key internal functions are `parseCsv`, a hand-rolled RFC-4180 parser that handles quoted fields, escaped double-quotes, and strips a UTF-8 BOM; `itemMd`, which renders the markdown template with frontmatter covering id, KPI block, revenue_impact, dependencies (`depends_on`, `blocks`, `tags` parsed as semicolon lists), and placeholder body sections; plus `yamlStr` and `slugify` helpers for YAML escaping and filename slugs. Before writing anything, it runs three fail-fast pre-scans that exit with code 1: a duplicate-id check, an id-format regex (`R-(Q[1-4]|Y\d-Q[1-4])-[A-Z]+-\d{3}`), and a cross-check that the id's category letter matches the `CATEGORY_LETTERS` map (e.g. engineering→E, marketing→M, sales→SA). Files are written as `{seq}-{slugified-title}.md` and existing files are silently skipped, so re-runs are idempotent at the file level, though rows missing id, quarter, or category are also skipped. A notable design decision is that all generated items are emitted with `status: planned`, `agent_assignable: true`, and placeholder content (`kpi.query` set to "TBD-populate-before-orchestrator-go-live", empty `agent_brief.context_files`), because the script is explicitly a seeding step whose output is meant to be fleshed out later by a first orchestrator/sub-agent cycle.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_anthropic-cli.summary: This module is a hardened wrapper around the `@anthropic-ai/sdk` client for the roadmap agent pipeline (used by the roadmap orchestrator and Decision Agent), enforcing a "no-silent-swap" model guarantee. Its main export, `callOpus47` — a historical name, since it now resolves to `blackboxai/z-ai/glm-5.2` when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at the open-source-only Blackbox proxy and `claude-opus-4-7` for direct API access — sends a messages request with optional system prompt, tools, and temperature, and the companion `ModelRejectedError` is thrown either when `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` names anything outside a hardcoded verified-model whitelist or when the proxy returns a 403, with no fallback permitted so the workflow halts. Retry policy is deliberate: exponential backoff (2s/8s/30s, or a uniform caller-supplied `retryDelayMs`) applies only to 5xx and 429 responses, while all other 4xx errors throw immediately. Because the SDK warns that long non-streaming calls can exceed 10 minutes, the wrapper auto-switches to streaming when `maxTokens >= 8192` or `stream: true`, and the internal `collectStream` helper accumulates text and `tool_use` blocks into the exact response shape of `messages.create()` so downstream parsing stays unchanged. API-key resolution is defensive, probing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_BLACKBOX_PROXY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, and `CLAUDE_API_KEY`, then side-mirroring the result into `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` so the SDK's internal env lookup also succeeds. Notable gotchas: `temperature` is deprecated on Opus 4.7 and omitted unless explicitly set, env vars are read at call time rather than module load so tests can override them, and callers may inject their own `client` instance to bypass construction entirely.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_index-build.m.summary: This script generates the compact `docs/roadmap/_index.json` manifest consumed by the Orchestrator, aggregating frontmatter from every roadmap item markdown file under `docs/roadmap/items/`. Its single export, `buildIndex(itemsRoot = ITEMS_ROOT)`, walks the items tree, parses each file's frontmatter, and returns a timestamped object with an `items` array; when run directly (`node scripts/agents/roadmap/_index-build.mjs`) it writes the result to disk. It builds entirely on the sibling internal module `./_lib.mjs`, which supplies `walk`, `parseFrontmatter`, and `ITEMS_ROOT`, plus Node's built-in `node:fs` and `node:url`—no external dependencies. The central design decision is context economy: verbose fields are stripped from the index, notably the markdown body and `agent_brief.prompt_skeleton`, while `agent_brief.context_files` is deliberately retained so consumers can still filter by relevant files. Each entry gets a `_file` property with backslashes normalized to forward slashes for cross-platform path consistency. Malformed frontmatter is handled leniently—the file is skipped with a console warning rather than aborting the build. CLI execution is gated behind a `realpathSync` comparison of `import.meta.url` against `process.argv[1]`, so importing `buildIndex` programmatically never triggers a write.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_index-build.t.summary: This Vitest test file verifies the behavior of `buildIndex` from the sibling module `_index-build.mjs`, which compiles roadmap item markdown files into a compact index. Its single test case builds a temporary fixture on disk — creating `items/Q1/engineering/001-foo.md` with full YAML frontmatter (id `R-Q1-E-001`, kpi, revenue_impact, agent_brief, and so on) plus a markdown body — then runs `buildIndex` against the fixture's `items` directory. It asserts that the resulting index contains exactly one parsed item with the correct id, and confirms the compaction contract: the markdown body is excluded and `agent_brief.prompt_skeleton` is stripped from the emitted entry. Dependencies are limited to `vitest` (describe/it/expect) and Node built-ins — `node:fs` (`mkdtempSync`, `mkdirSync`, `writeFileSync`, `rmSync`), `node:os` (`tmpdir`), and `node:path` (`join`) — with no external services involved. Notable details: the fixture lives in a unique temp directory prefixed `are-test-`, cleanup happens in a `finally` block via a forced recursive `rmSync` so the test can't leave residue, and the hardcoded `created_at`/`updated_at` of 2026-06-10 suggests the schema is date-sensitive but the test does not exercise date logic.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_experiment-tr.summary: This module tracks A/B-style experiments registered in the roadmap system: it reads the `_experiments.yml` registry from `ROADMAP_ROOT` (imported from `./_lib.mjs`), fetches each experiment's PostHog insight via the PostHog REST API, decides whether a winning variant has emerged, and — when run as a CLI — writes the compiled results to `_experiments-state.json`, which feeds signal-context so a downstream Decision Agent can reshuffle roadmap item priorities. The sole export is the async `trackExperiments()`, supported by two internal helpers: `fetchPosthogInsight(insightId, fetchFn)`, which calls `https://app.posthog.com/api/projects/{projectId}/insights/{insightId}/` with bearer auth from the `POSTHOG_PERSONAL_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` env vars, and `decideWinner(exp, series)`, which evaluates variant series against per-experiment thresholds. Dependencies are minimal — Node's fs/path/url modules, `js-yaml` for parsing the registry, and the sibling `_lib.mjs` — with global fetch used for HTTP. A notable design choice is graceful degradation: instead of throwing, the tracker marks experiments `stale` with an error reason when env vars are missing, the insight ID is still the `posthog-insight-TBD` placeholder, the request fails, or the 10-second `AbortSignal.timeout` fires. The winner logic is explicitly a stub — it simply sorts variants by raw count, requires total samples to meet `min_sample_per_variant * variants.length`, and demands uplift over the runner-up exceed `target_uplift_pct`, with no statistical-significance testing. Other gotchas: `fetchFn` is injectable for testing, CLI execution is detected via `realpathSync` comparison of `import.meta.url` against `process.argv[1]` (so importing the module never writes the state file), and the summary output reports counts of decided versus under-sampled experiments for quick triage.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-manual.te.summary: This is a Vitest test suite for the `scrapeManual` function exported by `_kpi-manual.mjs`, which reads manually curated KPI values from a YAML file. The suite creates a temporary `_manual-kpis.yml` fixture in the system temp directory (via `mkdtempSync` on `node:os.tmpdir()`) containing a `last_updated` date and a `values` map, then cleans it up after the run. Its two test cases cover the happy path — a metric present in the YAML returns its numeric value with `stale: false` and a `fetchedAt` timestamp — and the miss path, where an unknown metric yields a stale result carrying an error message matching "no manual value". Dependencies are limited to vitest's `describe/it/expect/beforeAll/afterAll`, Node's `fs`, `os`, and `path` modules, and the module under test. Notably, `scrapeManual` is async and accepts an injectable `yamlPath` option, which is what makes the test hermetic without mocking the filesystem. The cleanup in `afterAll` only deletes the YAML file, not the temp directory itself.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-posthog.t.summary: This vitest test file validates the `scrapePosthog` function exported from the sibling module `_kpi-posthog.mjs`, which fetches KPI metric values from the PostHog analytics API. Using an injectable `fetch` stub (passed via an options object), the suite covers three scenarios: a successful API response returning a numeric value (asserting the result includes the metric name, value 42, a `fetchedAt` timestamp, and `stale: false`), an HTTP 5xx server error, and a network timeout simulated via an `AbortError`. In both failure cases, the tests assert that the function degrades gracefully by marking the result `stale: true` and attaching an error message referencing the status code or abort reason, rather than throwing. The file depends only on `vitest` for test infrastructure and the internal `scrapePosthog` scraper. A notable design implication is that `scrapePosthog` supports dependency injection of `fetch`, and its contract guarantees per-item results with stale flags so dashboard consumers can tolerate partial API outages.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-posthog.m.summary: This module is a PostHog KPI scraper for the roadmap agent tooling, responsible for turning roadmap items whose `kpi.query` field holds a PostHog insight ID into concrete metric readings. Its single export, `scrapePosthog(items, { fetch })`, iterates the given items, calls `https://app.posthog.com/api/projects/{POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID}/insights/{insightId}/` with a Bearer token from `POSTHOG_PERSONAL_API_KEY`, and returns one result per item shaped as `{metric, value, stale, fetchedAt, error?}`. Value extraction prefers a numeric `result[0].count` and otherwise falls back to the last point of the `result[0].data` time series. The only dependencies are the global `fetch` (injectable via options for testing) and the two environment variables; the PostHog host is hardcoded to `app.posthog.com`, so self-hosted instances are not supported. The defining design choice is fail-soft behavior: every request is wrapped in try/catch with a 10-second `AbortSignal.timeout`, and any failure—HTTP error, missing value, or exception—yields a `stale: true` entry rather than throwing, so callers always get a complete array. One gotcha: a missing API key is not detected up front; the request is sent with an empty Bearer token and surfaces only as an HTTP error on each item.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-render.mj.summary: This file is the Render KPI scraper for the roadmap agent scripts: it fetches the latest deploy status for Render-hosted services so roadmap items can report live health metrics. Its single export, `scrapeRender(items, { fetch })`, accepts roadmap items whose `kpi.query` is either a bare Render service ID or a JSON string like `{"serviceId":"srv-x","field":"finishedAt"}` (defaulting the field to `status`), and returns one result object per item containing `metric`, `value`, `stale`, `fetchedAt`, and optionally `error`. It calls the Render REST API at `api.render.com/v1/services/{serviceId}/deploys?limit=1`, authenticating with a Bearer token from the `RENDER_API_KEY` environment variable, and allows dependency injection of a custom `fetch` for testing. Notable design choices: it is deliberately fail-soft — every failure mode (missing API key, malformed query JSON, non-OK HTTP status, missing field, network exception) yields a `stale: true` entry rather than throwing, so callers never need try/catch. Each request carries a 10-second timeout via `AbortSignal.timeout(10000)` to prevent a hung Render API from stalling the scrape. The parser also defensively handles the Render API's inconsistent response shape, unwrapping either a raw deploy object or a `{deploy: {...}}` wrapper from the first array element.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-cf.test.m.summary: This Vitest test file verifies `scrapeCfAnalytics` from the sibling module `_kpi-cf.mjs`, which scrapes Cloudflare GraphQL analytics KPIs. It injects a fake `fetch` via an options object to test three scenarios: a successful GraphQL response yields a numeric value with `stale: false` and a `fetchedAt` timestamp; a missing `CF_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` environment variable short-circuits before any network call and returns `stale: true` with a matching error; and a malformed GraphQL response containing an `errors` array also returns `stale: true` with a defined error. Each test uses a KPI item with `source: 'cf'` and metric `pages_builds`. The suite depends on Vitest's `describe`/`it`/`expect` and mutates `process.env` per test, so the token is explicitly set or deleted to control the code path.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-gh.test.m.summary: This vitest suite verifies `scrapeGhRepo` from the sibling module `scripts/agents/roadmap/_kpi-gh.mjs`, which collects KPI metrics by running GitHub CLI (`gh`) shell queries. It injects fake `exec` implementations to cover three behaviors: numeric stdout (e.g. `42\n`) is parsed into a numeric `value` with `stale: false` and a `fetchedAt` timestamp; a non-zero exit (thrown error with `status`) yields `stale: true` plus the error message; and non-numeric output is returned as a raw string value rather than being coerced or rejected. The suite's only external dependency is `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`), and it relies on `scrapeGhRepo` accepting an `{ exec }` options object, which is the dependency-injection seam that lets the tests avoid spawning real `gh` processes. The fixtures model KPI items shaped as `{ kpi: { source: 'gh', metric, query } }`, documenting the expected input contract of the module under test.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-cf.mjs.summary: This module scrapes KPI metrics from the Cloudflare Analytics GraphQL API for the roadmap agents pipeline. Its sole export, `scrapeCfAnalytics(items, { fetch? })`, iterates over items carrying `kpi.metric` and `kpi.query` fields, POSTs each query to `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/graphql/`, and returns an array of `{metric, value, stale, fetchedAt, error?}` result objects. Authentication comes from the `CF_ANALYTICS_TOKEN` environment variable sent as a Bearer token, and an internal helper `findNumericTolerantly` recursively walks the GraphQL `data` payload to extract the first finite numeric value, coercing numeric strings along the way. Notable design choices: the function never throws to its caller — missing tokens, HTTP failures, GraphQL errors, empty numeric results, and exceptions are all converted into `stale: true` entries with an `error` message, so one bad metric can't sink a batch. Requests are capped by a hardcoded 10-second `AbortSignal.timeout`, and `fetch` is injectable via options (defaulting to `globalThis.fetch`) to keep the module testable without network access. Because numeric extraction is positional rather than schema-aware, queries returning multiple numbers will silently yield only the first one found.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-render.te.summary: This Vitest test suite verifies the contract of `scrapeRender` from the sibling module `_kpi-render.mjs`, which is the scraper responsible for pulling KPI values (such as `api_status`) from the Render API for roadmap items whose `kpi.source` is `render`. It depends only on `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`) and the module under test, stubbing the HTTP layer by injecting a fake `fetch` through an options object rather than mocking network calls globally. The three cases pin down the happy path (a 200 response yields the latest deploy's `status` as the metric value with `stale: false` and a defined `fetchedAt` timestamp) and two failure modes (an HTTP 503 response and a missing `RENDER_API_KEY` environment variable), both of which must resolve to a result marked `stale: true` with a descriptive `error` string instead of throwing. Notably, the missing-key test asserts that `fetch` is never invoked, confirming the scraper short-circuits before any network call when credentials are absent. A subtle gotcha is that the tests mutate `process.env.RENDER_API_KEY` directly — setting it in the first two tests and deleting it in the third — so the suite relies on sequential execution order and could pollute the environment for other tests in the same worker. The fixtures also reveal the item shape `scrapeRender` expects: `kpi.query` carries the Render service ID (e.g., `srv-abc123`), and the API response is treated as an array of deploys ordered so the first entry is the latest.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-gh.mjs.summary: This file is a GitHub KPI scraper for the roadmap agent tooling: it executes per-item shell commands (typically `gh` CLI calls piped through grep/wc/jq) to collect repository metrics and normalizes the results. Its single export, `scrapeGhRepo(items, { exec? })`, reads `it.kpi.metric` and `it.kpi.query` from each item, runs the query, and resolves to an array of `{metric, value, stale, fetchedAt, error?}` records. The only internal dependency is `execSync` from `node:child_process`, plus the external `gh` CLI that the queries assume is installed and authenticated. Results are parsed tolerantly — output that converts to a finite number is returned as a number, otherwise the raw trimmed string is kept — and the function never throws: failures are captured per-item as `{stale: true, error}` entries, so one bad query can't sink the batch. Every command runs under a hard 10-second timeout, and an injectable `exec` parameter allows tests to substitute a fake runner. Two gotchas stand out: the header comment says `execFileSync` but the code actually imports `execSync`, meaning queries run through a shell (a mismatch, and a trust assumption since KPI queries are executed as arbitrary shell pipelines), and stale entries omit both `value` and `fetchedAt`, so consumers must handle that shape.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-manual.mj.summary: This file is a manual KPI scraper for the roadmap agent tooling: it reads hand-maintained metric values from `docs/roadmap/_manual-kpis.yml` so KPIs that cannot be fetched automatically still flow through the same pipeline as live scrapers. Its single export, `scrapeManual(items, { yamlPath })`, takes KPI items (each carrying `it.kpi.metric`) and returns one result per item in the shared scraper shape `{metric, value, stale, fetchedAt, error?}`, marking entries `stale: true` with a "no manual value" error whenever the metric is missing, null, or the file failed to load. An internal helper, `parseManualYaml`, implements a deliberately minimal line-based YAML reader that only understands the file's expected shape — a `values:` block of indented `key: scalar` lines — coercing null, booleans, numbers, and quoted strings while stripping comments. The only dependencies are `node:fs` (`readFileSync`) and `node:path` (`resolve`); notably it avoids pulling in a real YAML library, so anything beyond flat scalars (nested maps, lists, anchors) will silently not parse. A key design decision is that it never throws: file-read failures are captured once and fanned out into per-item stale results, keeping the aggregator resilient. One gotcha is that the default path resolves against `process.cwd()`, so the caller's working directory determines whether the file is found unless `yamlPath` is passed explicitly.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-scraper.t.summary: This is the Vitest test suite for the KPI aggregation module `_kpi-scraper.mjs`, exercising its exported `scrapeAllKpis` function. It verifies that KPI items are routed by their `kpi.source` field to dependency-injected scraper functions (`scrapeManualFn`, `scrapeCfFn`, `scrapeSupabaseFn`), with results persisted to a JSON cache file keyed by `source:metric` pairs (e.g. `manual:foo`). The suite covers the cache semantics in detail: fresh entries are served with a `cached: true` flag without invoking scrapers, `forceRefresh: true` bypasses the cache, and stale entries are re-fetched — with per-source TTLs, notably a 24-hour TTL for the `cf_analytics` (Cloudflare Analytics) source versus a shorter default (a 2-hour-old manual entry is treated as expired). It also confirms partial-failure tolerance: a rejecting `scrapeSupabaseFn` does not prevent manual KPI results from being returned. Dependencies are limited to `vitest` (`describe`, `it`, `expect`, `vi`, `beforeEach`) and Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:os`), with each test isolating itself by writing a fresh `_kpi-cache.json` into a `mkdtempSync`-created temp directory. A notable setup constraint is that the cache file must exist upfront with the shape `{"lastFullRefresh":null,"entries":{}}`, implying the scraper expects a pre-initialized cache rather than creating one.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-scraper.m.summary: This file is the KPI scraping orchestrator for the roadmap agent: its single export, `scrapeAllKpis(items, opts)`, fans metric requests out to six per-source scraper modules (`_kpi-supabase.mjs`, `_kpi-posthog.mjs`, `_kpi-render.mjs`, `_kpi-cf.mjs`, `_kpi-gh.mjs`, `_kpi-manual.mjs`) and merges the results with a JSON cache persisted at `docs/roadmap/_kpi-cache.json` via node's `fs`. Items are grouped by `kpi.source`; entries whose cached `fetchedAt` is still within a per-source TTL (default 1 hour, 6 hours for `render_logs`, 24 hours for `cf_analytics`) are served from cache without re-scraping, unless `forceRefresh` is set. All six scrapers run concurrently under `Promise.allSettled`, so a failing source only logs a warning and yields zero rows rather than aborting the run. A notable safeguard is the `withTimeout` helper, which races each scraper against a 90-second hard wall—added after a "cycle 11" postmortem where TLS/socket hangs caused silent 49-minute stalls—and the timer is `unref`'d so it can't keep the event loop alive. Cache reads and writes are both wrapped in try/catch as best-effort, so a corrupt or unwritable cache never crashes the scrape. All scraper functions are injectable through `opts` (e.g. `scrapeSupabaseFn`), making the orchestrator testable without live credentials for Supabase, PostHog, Render, Cloudflare Analytics, or GitHub.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_lib.mjs.summary: This module is the shared helper library for the roadmap agent utilities living under `scripts/agents/roadmap/_*.mjs`, providing common filesystem and frontmatter handling so each script doesn't reimplement it. It exports two path constants, `ITEMS_ROOT` (`docs/roadmap/items`) and `ROADMAP_ROOT` (`docs/roadmap`), plus three functions: `walk(dir)`, which recursively collects all `.md` files under a directory; `parseFrontmatter(content)`, which extracts and parses the YAML frontmatter block from markdown content; and `readItemFrontmatter(filepath)`, a convenience wrapper that reads a file from disk and returns its parsed frontmatter. It is written as pure Node ESM using only `node:fs` and `node:path`, with `js-yaml` as its single external dependency. Notable behavioral details: `walk` silently returns an empty array when the target directory doesn't exist rather than throwing, while `parseFrontmatter` does throw a hard error if the content lacks a leading `---` delimited frontmatter block, so callers can assume a returned value is always valid parsed YAML.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-supabase..summary: This module is a read-only KPI scraper that runs metric queries from roadmap items against a Supabase/Postgres database and returns per-metric results as `{metric, value, stale, fetchedAt, error?}` objects, guaranteeing it never throws to its caller — any failure simply yields `stale: true` with an error message. Its main export, `scrapeSupabase(items, { pool? })`, iterates items carrying `kpi.query` and `kpi.metric` fields, classifies each query via `classifyQuery`, executes the real ones, and coerces the first column of the first row to a number when possible. `classifyQuery` sorts raw query strings into four kinds — `sql`, `unpopulated` (TBD/TODO/MANUAL/PLACEHOLDER/FIXME/XXX sentinels matched by `UNPOPULATED_RE`), `manual_ref` (lowercase `manual:docs/...` pointers tracked by humans), and `rejected` — deliberately giving unpopulated sentinels a benign error code instead of the security-toned "not SELECT-only" message so dashboards aren't spooked. Safety enforcement lives in `isSelectOnly`, which requires the statement to start with SELECT or WITH and then crudely rejects it if any DML/DDL keyword from `DML_DDL_KEYWORDS` appears anywhere (catching `DROP` after a semicolon or `DELETE` in a subquery), while `stripSqlComments` removes line and block comments first so keywords mentioned in comments don't false-positive. The only external dependency is the `pg` (node-postgres) library, with connections built from `DATABASE_URL_READONLY` falling back to `SUPABASE_DIRECT_URL`. Notable constraints: the pool is capped at 3 connections with a 5-second `statement_timeout` per query, and if the caller supplies its own pool it is reused, otherwise the module creates and ends its own. One gotcha documented inline is the case-sensitivity split between the uppercase `MANUAL:` sentinel (unpopulated) and lowercase `manual:` doc references, which are matched in that order inside `classifyQuery`.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_lock.mjs.summary: This module implements a file-based JSON lock for the roadmap orchestrator, extracted from roadmap-orchestrator.mjs so the acquire/check/release lifecycle can be unit-tested against a temporary lock file. Its sole export is the `createLock` factory, which returns an object with `checkLock`, `acquireLock`, `releaseLock`, plus the resolved `lockPath` and `ttlMs`; `acquireLock(cycleId)` writes the cycle id, timestamp, and pid, `checkLock()` returns the live lock or null, and `releaseLock()` marks the file released. It depends only on `node:fs` (existsSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync) — there are no external libraries or services involved. The default configuration targets docs/roadmap/_lock.json with a 15-minute TTL, while tests inject `{ lockPath, ttlMs, pid }` to use a temp file with a tight expiry. Notably, `checkLock` collapses four failure modes — missing file, unparseable JSON, a `released: true` flag, and age exceeding the TTL — into a single null result, logging a warning when it overrides a stale lock. `releaseLock` is deliberately idempotent and uses synchronous writeFileSync wrapped in a try/catch so it is safe to invoke from a signal handler during orchestrator shutdown.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_kpi-supabase..summary: This is a vitest test suite for `scripts/agents/roadmap/_kpi-supabase.mjs`, the module that scrapes KPI metrics from a Supabase Postgres database for the roadmap agent. It exercises four exported functions: `isSelectOnly` (a SQL safety gate that accepts SELECT and WITH/CTE statements while rejecting INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER, and GRANT, including DML hidden in subqueries or after semicolons), `stripSqlComments` (removes line and block comments so a benign comment containing "DROP" doesn't trip the guard), `classifyQuery` (sorts a KPI's query string into `sql`, `unpopulated`, `manual_ref`, or `rejected` buckets), and `scrapeSupabase` (the end-to-end scrape path). The only dependency is vitest; no real database is used because `scrapeSupabase` accepts an injectable `pool`, which the tests replace with a fake that either resolves rows or rejects, letting them verify that connection failures yield `{ stale: true, error }` results, that non-SELECT queries are refused before ever touching the pool, and that successful queries return the first row's numeric value with a `fetchedAt` timestamp. A notable behavioral contract pinned down here is the distinction between editorial placeholders and security violations: queries containing TBD, TODO, MANUAL, or empty/null values must surface an "unpopulated" error rather than the "SELECT-only" rejection message, and `manual:docs/...` references must produce a "manual KPI" error instead. The suite thereby documents the module's fail-soft design — every failure mode produces a stale result with a descriptive error rather than throwing — and its defense-in-depth stance of classifying and validating SQL before execution.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_tripwire-eval.summary: This module provides a sandboxed JavaScript evaluator for "tripwire" conditions, part of the roadmap agent tooling under `scripts/agents/roadmap/`. Its single export, `evalTripwires(tripwires, ctx)`, evaluates each tripwire's `condition` string against a supplied context object and returns the subset that fired, each annotated with an ISO `firedAt` timestamp. Sandboxing is achieved by compiling each condition with `new Function` in strict mode: safe globals listed in `ALLOWED_GLOBALS` (Math, Object, Array, JSON, Date) are passed in as parameters, while dangerous globals in `BLOCKED_GLOBALS` (globalThis, global, Function, process, require, window, self) are shadowed by parameter names bound to `undefined` to block sandbox escapes. The input context is defensively deep-frozen via a JSON round-trip, which also strips any functions from it. Notable constraints: `import` and `eval` cannot be shadowed as parameter names (the code relies on strict mode and the `new Function` environment to neutralize them), and evaluation errors are caught per-tripwire, logged via `console.warn`, and treated as non-firing rather than aborting the batch.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_subagent-runn.summary: This vitest suite verifies `runSubagent` from `_subagent-runner.mjs`, which turns an Opus LLM response into structured roadmap queue files. It injects a mocked `opusFn` and asserts the returned `{ queueFiles, errors, usage }` contract: parsing YAML-frontmatter-plus-markdown chunks separated by `---END-QUEUE-FILE---`, splitting multi-item output, rejecting malformed chunks or ones missing `queueId`/`itemId`, catching Opus failures (e.g. a proxy 403) into `errors` with null `usage` instead of throwing, and filtering the prompt so only requested `itemIds` reach the model. A second describe block locks in the "0-queue-write fix (2026-07-31)": because glm-5.2 doesn't reliably emit the legacy end-marker text format, sub-agents now emit each queue file via a `write_queue` tool_use block — the same structured-output mechanism the Decision Agent uses — and the tests confirm tool_use blocks are preferred even over non-conforming text, multiple blocks map one-per-item, blocks missing required fields are flagged as errors, and legacy text parsing still works as a fallback. The notable design points are the dependency-injected `opusFn` (making the runner model-agnostic and unit-testable) and the dual-format parsing strategy that preserves backward compatibility while routing around unreliable model formatting.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_signal-contex.summary: This Vitest suite pins down the contract of `buildSignalContext` exported by `_signal-context.mjs`, the module that compresses raw roadmap state into the compact signal context consumed by roadmap agents. It verifies that items are aggregated into `byStatus`, `byCategory`, `byPriority`, and `byOwnerRole` count maps, and that the `readyToShip` list ranks agent-assignable, unblocked planned items by revenue-per-hour (`revenue_impact.amount_inr` divided by `est_hours`). A notable behavioral constraint it locks in: the `depends_on` DAG only unblocks a dependent item when its dependency reaches `verified` status — a dependency stuck at `shipped` still excludes the item from `readyToShip`. The suite also covers founder-blocked items being surfaced in `founderBlocked` with a computed `daysOpen` age, KPI arrays being reshaped into a metric-keyed object preserving `value` and `stale` flags, and queue metrics (`depth`, `oldestAgeHours`, `byRole`) derived from `emittedAt` timestamps. Budget normalization is tested too: raw `ghMinutes`/`cfBuilds` usage is converted into tripwire-compatible `ghMinutesMonth`/`cfBuildsMonth`/`renderHoursMonth` entries with computed `pct` values and zero-filled defaults, while `firedTripwires` passes through unchanged. Finally, it asserts the `cycle` metadata (UTC `dayOfMonth`, `dayOfWeek`, and ISO `ts`) is derived from the injected `now` timestamp, with a comment noting a spec correction about the weekday. The only dependencies are `vitest` and the sibling module under test; all inputs are deterministic fixtures with fixed dates.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_subagent-runn.summary: This module implements the sub-agent runner for the roadmap orchestration pipeline: it spawns a role-specific Opus 4.7 worker (via `callOpus47` from `./_anthropic-client.mjs`) to compose one Claude Code queue file per roadmap item, then returns the parsed queue files plus any errors and token usage. The sole export, `runSubagent({ role, itemIds, briefing, items, cycleId, opusFn })`, filters `items` to `itemIds`, serializes them to YAML (using `js-yaml`) into a single user message, and sends it with the `SUBAGENT_SYSTEM(role)` prompt and the `WRITE_QUEUE_TOOL` tool definition; `opusFn` is injectable for testing. The preferred output path is structured output: the model must emit each queue file as a `write_queue` tool_use block (frontmatter fields plus a markdown `body`), which the runner extracts from `response.content` — a deliberate fix for a bug where glm-5.2 failed to reliably emit the legacy `---END-QUEUE-FILE---` plus YAML-frontmatter text format, causing silent "0 queue files" cycles. A legacy fallback parser for that text format is retained and used only when no tool_use blocks arrive. Any block missing `queueId` or `itemId` is dropped with an error message rather than aborting the batch. Failure handling is designed for graceful degradation: Opus errors (proxy 403, ModelRejected) and timeouts are caught and returned as `{ queueFiles: [], errors: [...], usage: null }` so the orchestrator can tolerate partial sub-agent failure. Resource budgets are intentionally tight — 12,000 max tokens and an 8-minute wall-clock timeout (`PER_SUBAGENT_TIMEOUT_MS`, raced via `Promise.race` with an unref'd timer), trimmed from 16k/12min specifically to survive Render free-tier container restarts observed in cycle 8.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_tripwire-eval.summary: This Vitest test suite validates `evalTripwires` from the sibling module `_tripwire-eval.mjs`, which evaluates declarative tripwire conditions against a runtime context object (covering budget, external errors, and queue depth) for the roadmap agent system. The tests confirm legitimate tripwires fire correctly, such as the budget-threshold tripwire T-A at over 60% CF builds and the T-T009-RBALANCE rule that detects role over-spawn using a Math.max over Object.values ratio above 0.6, while falsy conditions stay silent. A major focus is sandbox security: dedicated cases assert that malicious conditions attempting process.exit, require('fs'), globalThis.process access, or nested Function-constructor eval are all blocked and never fire. The suite also verifies robustness behaviors: malformed conditions like '))))' return empty results instead of throwing, fired tripwires receive an ISO-format firedAt timestamp, and the ctx object is frozen (or cloned) so conditions attempting mutation cannot leak changes back to the caller. Notably, the sandbox tests rely on the implicit guarantee that a failed sandbox would kill the test process itself, making test execution proof of containment.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_signal-contex.summary: This module compresses the full ARE (autonomous roadmap engine) state — roadmap items, KPIs, work queue, budgets, and fired tripwires — into the signal-context object that feeds the Decision Agent, per spec §7. Its main export, `buildSignalContext`, derives decision-ready views: a `readyToShip` list of up to 20 planned, agent-assignable, unblocked items whose dependencies are all verified, ranked by revenue-per-hour (`revenue_impact.amount_inr / est_hours`); a `founderBlocked` list with `daysOpen` computed from `created_at`; KPIs re-keyed by metric; queue depth and oldest-age stats; and UTC cycle timing (dayOfMonth/dayOfWeek) used downstream for monthly and weekly triggers. The internal `normalizeBudget` helper reshapes raw budget snapshots (`ghMinutes`, `cfBuilds`, `renderHours`) into the `*Month` shape tripwires expect, computing `pct` with a divide-by-zero guard and defaulting Render usage to the free-tier 750 hrs/mo when untracked. The second export, `trimSignalContext`, enforces a token budget using the 1-token-≈-4-chars heuristic: if serialized JSON exceeds 100KB it progressively drops `sectorDocs.bySector` excerpts, then `external.experiments.results` detail, then truncates `lastAnthropicError` to 500 chars, with an emergency pass over the 180KB hard ceiling that deletes `verticals` and `founderState` entirely; every trim is recorded in a `_trim` metadata block. The file has no imports — it's pure transformation logic with no I/O — depending only on the caller supplying correctly shaped state (e.g., it assumes `revenue_impact`, `est_hours`, and `emittedAt` exist, so malformed items would produce NaN sort keys or ages). A notable gotcha is that trimming preserves counts but silently discards detail, so consumers must check `_trim.drops` and the `_excerptDropped`/`_resultsDropped` flags before assuming full context is present.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap\\_validate-item.summary: This CLI script (no exports; run directly with Node) validates the YAML frontmatter of every markdown roadmap item under `docs/roadmap/items` against a fixed schema, exiting with code 1 on any validation error so it can gate CI or orchestrator runs. It relies on the shared sibling module `_lib.mjs` for `walk`, `parseFrontmatter`, and the `ITEMS_ROOT` constant, plus `node:fs` for file reads, and aborts early if `ITEMS_ROOT` doesn't exist. Per-file checks enforce a 20-field REQUIRED list (with a small NULLABLE whitelist like `founder_blocker` and `shipped_at`), enum membership for `category`, `owner_role`, `priority`, and `status`, the nested `kpi` object's sub-keys (`metric`, `target`, `source`, `query`), and the item id format `R-(Q[1-4]|Y\d-Q[1-4])-[A-Z]+-\d{3}` — the header comment documents the category-letter codes (E, M, S, SA, F, L, H, CS, IT, G, P) used in those ids. A second pass builds a global id-to-files map to catch ID collisions across the whole tree, which per-file checks alone would miss. Notably, unpopulated TBD placeholders in `kpi.query`, `success_criteria`, and `agent_brief.prompt_skeleton` produce warnings rather than errors, so the script passes while flagging fields that the comments say must be filled before orchestrator go-live.

scripts\\agents\\route-manifest.test.mjs.summary: This test file verifies the behavior of the sibling module `route-manifest.mjs`, specifically its exported `buildRouteManifest` and `resolveProbe` functions. Using the built-in `node:test` runner and `node:assert/strict`, it builds a temporary directory tree (via `fs.mkdtempSync` in the OS temp dir) populated with stub Next.js App Router files: a root `page.tsx`, a static `pujas/page.tsx`, named dynamic segments like `calendar/[month]/page.tsx` and `gita/[chapter]/page.tsx`, and a catch-all `docs/[...rest]/page.tsx`. The single test then asserts that `resolveProbe` returns true for the root path, static paths, dynamically parameterized paths such as `/calendar/march`, and multi-segment catch-all paths like `/docs/a/b/c`, while returning false for an unmatched route such as `/nope/missing`. Its only dependencies are Node core modules (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:os`) plus the module under test, so it runs without external packages. A notable gotcha: the test creates a temp directory but never cleans it up, leaving residue in the OS temp folder after runs.

scripts\\agents\\route-manifest.mjs.summary: This script builds a route manifest for the Next.js App Router application under `apps/web/app` by recursively scanning the filesystem for `page.tsx` files, turning each containing directory into a route pattern paired with a compiled `RegExp`. It exports two functions: `buildRouteManifest(appDir)`, which performs the scan and returns an array of `{ pattern, regex }` entries, and `resolveProbe(manifest, url)`, which normalizes a candidate URL (stripping leading and trailing slashes) and reports whether it matches any manifest entry. Two internal helpers do the heavy lifting: the generator `walk` recursively yields every `page.tsx` path, and `patternToRegex` converts a route pattern into a case-sensitive regex, mapping dynamic segments like `[month]` to `[^/]+`, catch-alls like `[...slug]` to the greedy `(?:[^/]+/)*[^/]+`, and regex-escaping static segments. It depends only on Node built-ins (`node:fs` and `node:path`) and has no external library or service dependencies. The central design decision is that the manifest is derived directly from the filesystem rather than hand-maintained, so it cannot drift when developers add new named params or catch-all routes. Notable details: matching tolerates an optional trailing slash via `/?$`, patterns are built with forward slashes regardless of OS separator, and there is no deduplication or support for Next.js route groups (parenthesized folders), intercepting routes, or `index`-style special files beyond `page.tsx`.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap-orchestrator.te.summary: This Vitest suite provides regression coverage for the orchestrator's file-lock lifecycle (acquire / check / release), exercising the `createLock` factory exported from `./roadmap/_lock.mjs` — a module that was deliberately extracted from the monolithic `roadmap-orchestrator.mjs` specifically so the lock behavior could be unit-tested. Its central purpose is to lock in the SIGTERM stale-lock fix: the signal handlers in `roadmap-orchestrator.mjs` call `releaseLock()` on cancel, and these tests prove that a released lock reads as "no lock" to `checkLock`, so a killed cycle can't block the next tight-retry cron for up to the 15-minute `LOCK_MAX_AGE_MS` TTL. The suite verifies that `checkLock` returns null when no file exists, that `acquireLock(cycleId)` produces a live lock carrying `cycleId`, `acquiredAt`, and numeric `pid`, that `releaseLock` writes a `released: true` marker, is idempotent across double invocation, and is a safe no-op when no lock file exists. It also covers the self-heal paths: a lock older than its `ttlMs` (simulating a silent Render kill with no signal handler run) is treated as stale and reclaimed, and a corrupt/unparseable lock file is treated as absent rather than crashing. Additional defensive cases confirm a fresh `acquireLock` after a release reclaims cleanly and that a `released: true` lock never reads as live regardless of age. The only dependencies are Vitest (`describe`/`it`/`expect`) and Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:os`, `node:path`), with each test isolated via a fresh `mkdtempSync` temp directory under the OS tmpdir that is force-removed in `afterEach`. A notable design constraint is that staleness is simulated by backdating `acquiredAt` in the JSON lock file rather than by sleeping, keeping the suite fast while still exercising the TTL comparison.

scripts\\agents\\run-all.mjs.summary: `scripts/agents/run-all.mjs` is a sequential orchestrator that executes the entire fleet of agent scripts, and is invoked by the daily GitHub Actions workflow. It exports nothing; as an executable Node script it uses `spawnSync` from `node:child_process` to run each agent as a child `node scripts/agents/<name>.mjs` process with inherited stdio. The built-in `ALL` roster covers thirteen agents — `seo-audit`, `content-pipeline`, `lead-gen`, `investor-pipeline`, `growth-metrics`, `social-queue`, `onboarding-drip`, `pr-outreach`, `health-smoke`, `broken-link`, `gsc-submitter`, `founder-tweet-draft`, and `content-publisher` — but passing agent names as CLI arguments runs only that subset. Each agent is capped by a 240-second `timeout`, after which the child is killed and counted as failed. Notably, execution is strictly sequential rather than parallel, a failure in one agent does not stop the rest of the fleet, and the script tallies failures and exits with code 1 if any agent failed so the CI job is marked red. One minor gotcha: when a child is killed by the timeout, `r.status` is `null`, so the logged exit code will read "exit null" rather than a real signal or code.

scripts\\agents\\rss-to-thread.mjs.summary: This Node CLI script is the build-in-public engine of the Darshya agent fleet: it reads the day's agent reports from `docs/agent-reports/` and turns them into a copy/paste X (Twitter) thread draft plus a LinkedIn post draft, writing the result back as its own dated report. Its key functions are `todaysReports()`, which globs markdown files prefixed with `TODAY` and derives each agent's name from the filename; `extractStat()`, which pulls a headline number from each report body via regexes matching patterns like bolded counts near words such as "broken", "mentions", or "leads", falling back to counting bullet items; and `buildThread()`/`buildLinkedIn()`, which assemble the drafts with per-agent emoji from `emojiFor()` and title-cased names from `humanizeAgent()`. It depends only on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`) and the sibling internal module `_lib.mjs`, which supplies `writeReport`, `upsertLog`, `TODAY`, and `REPORT_DIR` — notably it never calls the X or LinkedIn APIs, so a human still reviews and posts manually. Tweets are hard-truncated at 270 characters, the thread caps at five agents (six for LinkedIn), and the script filters out its own report to avoid self-reference. Two gotchas stand out: the stat-extraction regexes are coupled to the exact phrasing other fleet agents use in their reports, so format changes upstream silently degrade output to the bullet-count fallback, and if no reports exist yet it writes a placeholder note (suggesting cron hasn't fired) rather than failing.

scripts\\agents\\run-orchestrator-bg.mjs.summary: This script is a wrapper launched by Render's bg-spawn to run one roadmap-orchestrator cycle end-to-end: it hard-resets the repo to origin/main, executes `scripts/agents/roadmap-orchestrator.mjs`, then commits and pushes any changes under `docs/roadmap/` back to GitHub. Its only entry point is `main()`, supported by `log()` (timestamped stdout plus append to `LOG_PATH`, defaulting to `/tmp`) and `run()` (a `execSync` helper that captures output and errors), with behavior driven by env vars `CYCLE_ID`, `GH_ORCHESTRATOR_PAT`, `GH_REPO` (default `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu`), and `DRY_RUN`, while `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `SUPABASE_DIRECT_URL` are passed through to the child orchestrator. It depends only on Node builtins (`node:child_process`, `node:fs`) and talks externally to GitHub over PAT-authenticated HTTPS, running on Render's infrastructure. Notable design choices revolve around secret hygiene: the PAT is never passed through `run()`—`spawnSync` is invoked directly for `git remote set-url` and `git push` so the token stays out of logs, and error output is scrubbed via `replace(PAT, '<REDACTED>')`. The origin remote is re-established idempotently (set-url with an add fallback) because Render rebuilds wipe `.git/config`, a workaround for a documented fetch failure from cycle C-20260611T2025. Constraints include a hard 60-minute `spawnSync` timeout sized against Render's 750-hour free-tier budget, `[skip ci]` in commit messages to avoid CI loops, staging only `docs/roadmap/`, and a single fetch-rebase-retry on push failure. Exit codes propagate the orchestrator's status, with exit 1 for a missing PAT and exit 2 for a failed push retry.

scripts\\agents\\seo-audit.mjs.summary: This is a standalone Node agent script (`scripts/agents/seo-audit.mjs`) that runs a daily SEO audit against the live site and writes a Markdown report to `docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-seo-audit.md` via `writeReport`. Its entry point `run()` fetches each path in the hardcoded `CORE_PAGES` list, extracts the `<title>` and meta description/OG tags using the regex helpers `extractTitle` and `extractMeta`, counts unique internal links per page with `countInternalLinks`, and flags issues with codes like `TITLE_TOO_SHORT`, `DESC_MISSING_OR_SHORT`, and `FEW_INTERNAL_LINKS`. It also verifies `/sitemap.xml` (must contain `<urlset`) and `/robots.txt` (checks for a `Sitemap:` directive), then detects "orphan" core pages that no other core page links to. The report includes a summary, a per-page table, excerpts for the first five failing pages, a static `KEYWORDS` list (informational only — rankings are meant to be tracked manually in Google Search Console, not checked by the script), and auto-generated action items. It depends entirely on the shared sibling module `_lib.mjs` for `fetchText`, `writeReport`, `WEB_BASE`, and `TODAY`, and talks only to the deployed site over plain HTTP — no external SEO APIs. Notable gotchas: HTML parsing is purely regex-based, so malformed or attribute-reordered meta tags will be missed; orphan detection is limited to links among the 18 core pages rather than the whole crawl graph; and `fetchJson` is imported but never used. The script exits 0 on success and prints a JSON summary of passing/failing counts, making it suitable for scheduled CI or cron execution.

scripts\\agents\\schema-validator.mjs.summary: This daily-run agent script validates schema.org structured data across roughly eighty high-value pages of the site, fetching each URL listed in the hardcoded TARGETS array and checking that the expected JSON-LD types (ItemList, BreadcrumbList, Article, FAQPage, TouristTrip, Place, Organization, WebSite, and similar) are present and minimally well-formed. It depends on the shared internal module ./_lib.mjs for fetchText (HTTP fetching against WEB_BASE), writeReport (persisting the markdown report), and the TODAY constant, and talks only to the site's own web server — no external services. The main() loop probes each target with a 250 ms politeness delay between requests, then classifies results into fully valid versus broken pages and emits a markdown report with a summary, per-page issue details, and an all-pages table via writeReport('schema-validator', md). The pipeline is split into extractJsonLd (regex-pulls application/ld+json script blocks and JSON-parses them), validate (checks for @context pointing at schema.org, presence of @type, and a small set of type-specific required fields like itemListElement, mainEntity, headline, and name), and probe (ties fetching, extraction, and expectation-matching together per URL). Notable gotchas: JSON-LD extraction is regex-based rather than a real HTML parse, and validation only inspects top-level @type values, so blocks wrapped in an @graph array would be misread as type "unknown" and expected types would report missing. Pages with an empty expected list (like /today, /shloka-card, /launch) are still checked for parse errors and HTTP status. The script exits with code 1 on fatal error and is designed to re-run daily via the fleet cron, treating any non-200 response as an issue with all expected types marked missing.

scripts\\agents\\social-queue-buffer-csv.summary: This standalone Node script converts the social-queue agent's markdown output into a Buffer Bulk Upload CSV: it scans `docs/agent-reports` for the newest `YYYY-MM-DD-social-queue.md` file (produced by `social-queue.mjs`), parses each post's date, IST time slot, type, and body via regex, and writes a per-platform CSV to `docs/marketing/buffer-21-social-posts.csv`. Key functions include `findLatestSocialQueueReport` and `parseReport` for ingestion, `slotToIso` for converting IST slots into ISO 8601 timestamps with a hardcoded `+05:30` offset, `platformsForType` for routing (Twitter gets all posts; LinkedIn only `NRI`/`gurukul`/`founder`; Instagram only `shloka`/`temple`/`gaushala`), and the `adaptForTwitter`/`adaptForLinkedin`/`adaptForInstagram` trio which respectively truncate to 280 chars while preserving trailing hashtags, prepend founder-voice intros with a Darshya promo footer, and append Reel-style CTAs. It has zero external dependencies, using only `node:fs` and `node:path`, and prints a per-platform/per-type summary table to stdout. Notable gotchas: the parsing regex is tightly coupled to the upstream report template (CRLF is normalized, but any heading-format drift causes a hard "template drift" failure when zero posts parse), and the script throws if no prior social-queue report exists, so `social-queue.mjs` must run first.

scripts\\agents\\temple-link-validator.m.summary: This script is a scheduled validation agent that HEAD-probes every `officialWebsite`, `officialBookingUrl`, and `officialDarshanBookingUrl` stored in `apps/web/lib/temple-details.ts` to catch dead or broken temple links before devotees hit them mid-booking. It parses the TypeScript source as plain text with regex (rather than importing it), walking slug-by-slug to extract each temple record's three URL fields, then probes each URL sequentially with a 10-second `AbortController` timeout and a 300ms delay between requests to stay polite to government temple endpoints. The `probe` function falls back from HEAD to GET when servers return 405/403 or time out, since some temple boards block HEAD requests, and it uses `redirect: 'manual'` so 3xx responses are surfaced as their own category instead of being silently followed. Results are classified by `classify` into OK, REDIRECT, BROKEN, SERVER_ERROR, or TIMEOUT verdicts and rendered into a prioritized markdown report (P1 broken, P2 redirects) via `writeReport` and `upsertLog` from the shared `./_lib.mjs` helper, written to `docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-temple-link-validator.md`. A notable gotcha is the parser's heuristic: it distinguishes top-level temple records from nested puja objects by requiring a `name:` field in the block, so any record lacking that field would be silently skipped. The script depends only on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`) plus the internal `_lib.mjs` reporting utilities, and is designed to run as a weekly cron.

scripts\\agents\\seo-internal-linker.mjs.summary: This file is a standalone Node CLI agent (run directly, exports nothing) that audits internal linking for SEO: it crawls a hardcoded list of seed surfaces (SEEDS, e.g. `/pujas`, `/temples`, `/deity`), extracts outbound links from each page's HTML, and builds an inbound-link graph for a curated list of high-value programmatic landing pages (TARGETS such as `/deity/shiva`, `/festival/diwali`, `/city/varanasi`). It classifies each target as orphan (0 inbound links), weak (1), or healthy (≥2), generates heuristic fix suggestions via `guessLinkSource` (which maps URL prefixes to recommended linking surfaces like index pages and related deity pages), and writes a dated Markdown report to `docs/agent-reports/` through `writeReport`. Its only internal dependency is the sibling module `./_lib.mjs`, which supplies `fetchText`, `writeReport`, `WEB_BASE`, and `TODAY`; it talks to the live site over HTTP and has no external libraries. Notable gotchas: `extractLinks` uses a regex over raw HTML rather than a real parser, so it only matches simple `href` attributes and misses links rendered client-side; seeds are fetched sequentially rather than in parallel, making runs slower as SEEDS grows; and self-links are explicitly excluded from the inbound count. The script prints a JSON summary and uses explicit `process.exit` codes, so it is designed to slot into scheduled CI/cron agent runs.

scripts\\agents\\social-content-multiple.summary: This Node.js agent script generates Darshya's daily multi-channel social media content pack deterministically — no LLM — producing 5 X drafts, 3 LinkedIn posts, and 3 Instagram captions that promote darshya.online, and it supersedes the older founder-tweet-draft, rss-to-thread, and content-publisher agents. It builds context in `main` by finding the next upcoming festival from the hardcoded `FESTIVALS_2026` list (via `nextFestival`/`daysUntil`), counting live URLs by fetching `sitemap.xml` from `WEB_BASE` (`getSitemapUrlCount`, with a silent fallback to 0 on failure), and scanning `docs/agent-reports` for the past 7 days of fleet reports (`recentReports`). That context is fed into the `X_TEMPLATES`, `LINKEDIN_TEMPLATES`, and `INSTA_TEMPLATES` function arrays, whose rendered output is checked against platform character caps by `xStatus`, `liStatus`, and `igStatus` — though these only annotate drafts with ✓/⚠/✗ labels rather than truncating. Everything funnels through the shared internal module `./_lib.mjs`, using `writeReport` to emit `docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-social-content-multiplexer.md`, `upsertLog` for a one-line run summary, and `TODAY`/`fetchText` helpers; only `node:fs` and `node:path` are used otherwise. Because templates are pure functions of the date-driven context, output is reproducible for a given day, giving the founder a fresh copy-paste queue with cadence guidance appended. Two gotchas stand out: the festival calendar duplicates data whose stated authority is `apps/web/lib/festivals.ts` and will go stale after 2026 (with `nextFestival` wrapping around to the first entry), and the header's claim of day-of-year template seeding is slightly misleading since all templates render every run — only the context values change daily.

scripts\\agents\\support-intent-triage.m.summary: This file implements the `support-intent-triage` agent, an hourly cron job that reads inbound support tickets from the append-only JSONL inbox `docs/agent-reports/_inbound-tickets.jsonl` and classifies each by intent — refund, abuse, booking-status, payment, technical, or general — using an ordered list of keyword regex heuristics in `RULES` via the `classify()` function. Its key internal pieces are `readInbound()` (parses JSONL, silently skipping malformed lines and tickets missing `id`/`text`), `loadState()`/`saveState()` (persist processed ticket IDs in `_support-intent-state.json` so each ticket is triaged exactly once), and `ghFileIssue()` (posts to the GitHub Issues API for repo `GH_REPO`, defaulting to `XI1568-raghav/bhaktisetu`). P0 intents (refund, abuse) trigger a single combined GitHub issue per run labeled `agent-auto-filed`, `support`, `P0`, capped at 25 tickets; everything else is aggregated into a daily markdown report via `writeReport` imported from the sibling module `./_lib.mjs` (alongside `TODAY` and `isoNow`) for batched founder response. Dependencies are minimal — `node:fs`, `node:path`, global `fetch` to `api.github.com`, and the `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` env var, with issue filing gracefully skipped when no token is present. Notable design choices: the inbox is deliberately a plain file rather than a webhook so future WhatsApp or email parsers can append to it without coupling to this agent, and the agent intentionally runs "no-op-but-alive" until that hook ships so its cron slot is already established. A gotcha worth noting: classification is first-match-wins over `RULES`, so ordering determines priority when multiple intents match.

scripts\\agents\\roadmap-orchestrator.mj.summary: This is the master entry point of the roadmap automation pipeline, invoked by cron every 6 hours: `main()` ingests the roadmap index via `buildIndex`, scrapes KPIs (`scrapeAllKpis`), builds a signal context (`buildSignalContext`), evaluates tripwires (`evalTripwires`), calls an LLM Decision Agent through `callOpus47` with `DECISION_SYSTEM_PROMPT`/`DECISION_TOOLS`, fans out sub-agents with `runSubagent`, and writes queue files and decision notes under `docs/roadmap/`. It exports nothing — it is a self-executing script whose helpers (`raceWithWall`, `writeAlert`, `readQueue`, `readResumeState`/`saveResumeState`) exist only to support that flow. Its dependencies are the sibling modules in `scripts/agents/roadmap/` (`_kpi-scraper.mjs`, `_tripwire-eval.mjs`, `_signal-context.mjs`, `_decision-prompt.mjs`, `_subagent-runner.mjs`, `_anthropic-client.mjs`, `_index-build.mjs`, `_lock.mjs`, plus lazily imported `_agent-fleet-summary.mjs` and `_experiment-tracker.mjs`), `js-yaml` for queue frontmatter, the Anthropic API reached through a proxy (comments reference glm-5.2 on Blackbox), and PostHog via the experiment tracker. The dominant design concern is surviving unreliable infrastructure: a file lock (`createLock`, 15-minute TTL) prevents overlapping cron runs and is released from SIGTERM/SIGINT/uncaughtException handlers, while a checkpointed resume state (`_cycle-resume.json`) lets a Render mid-cycle kill reuse the Decision Agent's spawn plan instead of paying for another Opus call. Timing is engineered around the GitHub Actions 50-minute ceiling — `raceWithWall` uses `.unref()`'d, cleared timers because a dangling handle once left Node idle 45 minutes past completion (the same reason `main()` ends in an explicit `process.exit(0)`), the spawn plan is hard-capped at 4 sub-agents run at concurrency 2, and the KPI, experiment, and Decision phases have 5-minute, 60-second, and 10-minute wall budgets respectively. Hard-stop paths exist for safety: tripwire T-005 (Anthropic proxy blocked) and `ModelRejectedError` both write an alert and exit with code 2. Several guards compensate for glm-5.2's unreliable tool calling — a synthesized default `decisionNote` when `write_decision_note` is never invoked, an alert on cycles producing zero spawns/defers/kills, and persisted alerts when `runSubagent` returns errors or unparseable output so silent zero-queue-file cycles stay diagnosable. Finally, `DRY_RUN=true` redirects queue and decision writes to `docs/roadmap/_dryrun/`, letting the whole cycle be exercised without touching production artifacts.

scripts\\agents\\social-queue.mjs.summary: This is a standalone Node CLI script, `scripts/agents/social-queue.mjs`, that acts as the "Social Agent" for the Darshya platform (darshya.online): it generates a 7-day queue of 21 draft social posts (7 days × 3 daily `SLOTS` at 9:00/13:00/19:00 IST) for Twitter, LinkedIn, and Instagram, then writes them as a markdown report via `writeReport('social-queue', body)` to `docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-social-queue.md`. It deliberately does no posting — the user is expected to paste drafts into Buffer, Hootsuite, Typefully, or Metricool, and the report itself documents which hook types suit which platform (e.g., NRI/gurukul/founder for LinkedIn, shloka/temple/gaushala for Instagram). Content comes from seven hardcoded `HOOKS` templates (shloka, practice, temple, NRI, gurukul, gaushala, founder) filled from static `TEMPLE_FACTS`, `MANTRAS`, and `WEEKDAYS` arrays, with hooks rotated deterministically by `(d * SLOTS.length + s) % HOOKS.length`. Its only internal dependency is `./_lib.mjs`, from which it imports `writeReport`, `TODAY`, and `isoNow`; notably `fetchJson` and `API_BASE` are also imported but never used, so the script makes no network calls and has no external library dependencies. Gotchas: the shloka placeholder is always filled with the same hardcoded verse (Satyameva Jayate, Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.6) rather than rotating, and the founder-update fields (`{weeklyWin}`, `{weeklyLearning}`, `{weeklyAsk}`) are left as literal parenthetical fill-in prompts for a human to complete. The single `run()` function does all the work and exits with code 1 on failure.

scripts\\agents\\validate-fleet-report.m.summary: This is a standalone Node.js CLI script that validates fleet agent JSON reports against `docs/agent-reports/fleet-report.schema.json`, run by the agents-daily workflow before its "Commit reports" step so malformed reports never get committed, and also runnable locally via `node scripts/agents/validate-fleet-report.mjs <report.json>`. Its core is an internal recursive `validate(value, schema, path)` function — a hand-rolled minimal JSON Schema draft-07 validator supporting only the keywords the schema actually uses (type, const, enum, required, additionalProperties, properties, items, pattern, minLength/maxLength, minimum/maximum). The only dependencies are Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:url`); the no-external-deps choice is deliberate, noted in a comment as a free-tier constraint that avoids pulling in a library like Ajv. Exit codes are part of the contract: 0 for valid, 1 for invalid or unreadable input/schema, 2 for missing CLI argument, with violations printed to stderr in JSONPath-style notation (`$.findings[0]`). Notable gotchas include the special-casing of arrays in `typeof` checks, bailing out of child validation when a type check fails, and the validator being incomplete by design — it will silently ignore any schema keywords outside its supported subset, so schema authors must stay within that vocabulary.

scripts\\agents\\uptime-pinger.mjs.summary: This Node.js script is a daily uptime monitor that probes 14 critical surfaces—public web pages (home, pujas, temples, darshan, panchang, sitemap.xml, feed.xml, robots.txt) and API endpoints (/healthz, temples, puja-types)—recording HTTP status and latency, then writing a dated Markdown report to docs/agent-reports via writeReport. It's explicitly scoped to availability rather than performance, complementing the separate lighthouse-weekly agent. The core logic lives in three functions: ping, which performs a GET with a custom darshya-uptime-pinger user agent and a 10-second hard cap via AbortSignal.timeout; classify, which buckets each result as DOWN (5xx or network failure), ERROR (4xx), SLOW (over 3000ms), or OK; and main, which orchestrates the run and renders summary counts, an "Action required" table for failures, and a full results table with emoji badges. It depends on the internal ./_lib.mjs module for WEB_BASE, API_BASE, and writeReport, and otherwise uses only native fetch—no external packages. Notable design choices: requests are made serially with a 200ms delay to avoid hammering the team's own infrastructure, error messages are truncated to 200 characters, and the report notes that latency is measured from a GitHub Actions runner so it includes runner-to-origin round-trip time. The SLOW_MS threshold of 3000ms and the 10s timeout are hardcoded constants, so tuning cadence or sensitivity requires editing the file directly.

scripts\\agents\\_lib.mjs.summary: This module is the shared helper library for the agent fleet scripts under `scripts/agents`, written as pure Node ESM with zero external dependencies.
