It exports the `REPORT_DIR` constant (`docs/agent-reports`) and `TODAY` date stamp, plus `writeReport(agentName, body, { suffix })`, which writes a dated markdown report file and returns its path, and `upsertLog(name, line)`, which prepends a timestamped bullet to a persistent per-agent log file (`_<name>-log.md`) while preserving its header. For network access it provides `fetchJson` and `fetchText`, thin wrappers around global `fetch` that tag requests with the `darshya-agent/1.0` user agent and never throw — failures return `{ status: 0, ... }` objects instead, so callers must check `status` rather than rely on try/catch. `fetchJson` also tolerates non-JSON responses by returning the raw `text` alongside a null `json`. Finally, it exports `WEB_BASE` and `API_BASE`, defaulting to `https://darshya.online` and `https://api.darshya.online` but overridable via environment variables, which lets the fleet point at staging or local deployments. Notable gotchas: `TODAY` is computed once at module load (so long-running processes crossing midnight get stale filenames), and `upsertLog` assumes the log's first two lines are a header it should keep on top.

scripts\\agents\\__tests__\\blog-draft-f.summary: This Vitest suite validates "deity-of-day-cluster" blog drafts stored as Markdown files in docs/agent-reports/blog-drafts/, enforcing the SEO/content spec referenced in the header comment (a roadmap queue spec under docs/roadmap/_dryrun). It has no exports; instead it scans the drafts directory at load time with a hand-rolled frontmatter parser (parseFrontmatter) that handles quoted strings and bracket-style arrays, then filters to files whose tags include 'deity-of-day-cluster' and dynamically generates a describe block per matching draft. Each draft is checked for eight required frontmatter fields (title, slug, target_keyword, meta_description, tags, deity, weekday, week_number), a meta_description of exactly 140–160 characters, body links to /deity/, /pujas/, and /aarti/ routes, and a body word count between 800 and 1500. Its only dependencies are vitest and Node built-ins (fs, path, url) — it deliberately avoids a real YAML parser, so the naive regex-based parsing could misread nested or multiline frontmatter values. A notable gotcha is the intentionally "vacuous green" design: if the drafts directory is missing or contains no cluster drafts, the suite passes trivially, so a green run does not prove any drafts exist.

scripts\\agents\\weekly-digest.mjs.summary: This script generates Darshya's internal weekly founder digest, a Sunday-run rollup (skippable via `FORCE=1`) that contrasts with the external `weekly-investor-update` by focusing on what needs attention: agent failures, uptime regressions, broken links, keyword losses, and competitor changes. It exports nothing itself; its main entry point orchestrates snapshot helpers (`uptimeSnapshot`, `brokenLinkSnapshot`, `schemaSnapshot`, `competitorSnapshot`, `backlinkSnapshot`, `keywordSnapshot`) that mine prior agent artifacts, then `buildActionItems` converts findings into a severity-tagged (P0/P1/P2) punch list rendered as a markdown report via `writeReport`. Its only internal dependency is `./_lib.mjs` (`writeReport`, `REPORT_DIR`, `TODAY`), plus `node:fs` and `node:path`; it talks to no external services, reading exclusively from the local report directory. Two reader strategies are used: `readLatest` regex-scrapes the most recent markdown report per agent (e.g. counting `DOWN`/`SLOW` in uptime-pinger output), while `readState` parses `_<name>-state.json` files from stateful agents like `keyword-rank-tracker` and `competitor-feature-watcher`. A notable fragility is that the regex extraction tightly couples this digest to the exact phrasing of sibling agents' reports, so output format changes there silently zero out metrics here. The keyword tracker logic flags a loss when a rank disappears or drops five or more positions week-over-week, and `fleetActivity` counts per-agent report files over the trailing seven days to populate an activity table. Thresholds are hardcoded—e.g. more than two SLOW surfaces triggers a P2—and missing data degrades gracefully to "_no recent report_" rows rather than failing.

scripts\\agents\\__tests__\\cold-temple-.summary: This Vitest suite (tagged R-Q1-M-014) verifies the cold-temple-outreach-v2-personalize module, which generates personalized outreach emails for temple leads. Its central promise is anti-boilerplate determinism: two leads with different attributes must never receive identical body text, while the same lead re-processed must produce byte-identical output, making results safe to diff and re-test. The suite exercises the module's exported classifiers — classifyDeity (Shiva/Vishnu/Devi/Ganesha/Hanuman/Ayyappa alias families with a generic fallback), classifyRegion (north/south/west/east/central/unknown from state and city), and classifyCityTier (tier1/pilgrim/tier2) — plus the stableHash and pickTemplate helpers that seed deterministic template selection from a lead's id. It then validates buildSubject and buildBodyHtml, asserting that deity-tradition language (Rudrabhishek for Shiva, Navratri for Devi) and region context lines vary appropriately, that UTM parameters (utm_source=cold-outreach-v2, utm_campaign=per-temple, deity=, region=) are embedded for downstream tracking, and that dynamic fields are HTML-escaped to prevent injection. The end-to-end buildPersonalizedEmail tests confirm that a fleet of 10 distinct temples yields 10 unique bodies (with subjects allowed occasional collisions since they share deity+city template seeds), and that an empty lead still returns valid output with generic/unknown classifications rather than throwing — null-lead skipping is explicitly deemed outside this module's responsibility. The only dependency is vitest, imported alongside the sibling module under test.

scripts\\agents\\__tests__\\cs-sla-track.summary: This is the Vitest test suite for `scripts/agents/cs-sla-tracker.mjs`, exercising its two exports, `computeSla` and `percentile`, which compute first-response-time SLA statistics for customer support tickets. The `percentile` tests pin down edge cases — null on empty input, the single-element case, and specific p50/p90 values on small arrays. The `computeSla` tests use a fixed clock (`nowMs`, June 2026) to verify behavior: empty ticket lists yield a zero cohort with null percentiles, tickets older than the configurable `windowDays` (default 7) are excluded from the cohort, and channel aliases are normalized — `wa` maps to whatsapp, `resend` to email, and `livechat` to chat. They also confirm that tickets missing `firstResponseAt` are counted as `pending` rather than sampled, that `met_sla` counts responses within the 120-minute `sla_target_minutes` threshold, and that tickets with a `firstResponseAt` earlier than `receivedAt` are dropped from the latency sample while remaining in the cohort. The only dependency is vitest itself, with the tracker module under test imported as a sibling file. Notably, the suite documents that p90 of ten evenly spaced values resolves to 91, revealing the tracker's percentile interpolation method.

scripts\\agents\\weekly-investor-update..summary: This Node.js script generates a weekly investor update by synthesizing the past seven days of git activity and agent-fleet reports into a markdown file (docs/agent-reports/YYYY-MM-DD-weekly-investor-update.md) suitable for emailing investors. Its entry point `main()` is gated by `isSunday()`, skipping all other days unless the FORCE=1 environment variable is set; helper functions include `lastNDays()`, `gitCommitsLastWeek()` (which shells out to `git log` via `execSync` and parses hash/subject/author/date), `classifyCommit()` (buckets subjects by conventional-commit prefixes like feat/fix/docs into categories), `collectAgentReports()` (scans REPORT_DIR for dated .md files, skipping underscore-prefixed state files), and `summarizeKeywordRank()` (reads `_keyword-rank-tracker-state.json` to compute week-over-week SEO ranking deltas and top-10 counts). It depends on the sibling internal module `./_lib.mjs` for `writeReport`, `REPORT_DIR`, and `TODAY`, plus Node builtins `node:fs`, `node:path`, and `node:child_process`; it talks to no external services beyond the local git CLI. Notable design choices: the report is a draft, with the "Next week — focus" and "Asks" sections left as placeholders for the founder to fill in before sending; output is capped at 12 features and 8 fixes to keep the update scannable; and all failure modes degrade gracefully — git errors yield an empty commit list and missing or thin SEO state (fewer than two days of history) simply omits the SEO snapshot section.

scripts\\agents\\x-engagement-digest.mjs.summary: This executable Node script (no exports; it runs `main()` directly) generates a daily X/Twitter engagement digest for the `@darshya_app` handle (overridable via the `X_HANDLE` env var), so the founder can triage mentions against a reply SLA. It fetches public mention data by scraping Nitter RSS search feeds, rotating through the hardcoded `NITTER_HOSTS` mirrors (`nitter.privacydev.net`, `nitter.poast.org`, `nitter.lucabased.xyz`) until one returns parseable items, avoiding the paid X API entirely. Incoming tweets are deduplicated against a persisted state file (`_x-engagement-digest-state.json`, seen IDs capped at 500) and sorted by the regex-based `classify()` function into five sentiment buckets — issue, question, praise, comparison, other — each rendered as a report section with its own SLA (issues 4h, questions 24h, praise as quote-tweet candidates, comparisons as competitor intel). The digest markdown is emitted through `writeReport` from the shared internal helper `./_lib.mjs`, which also supplies `REPORT_DIR`; otherwise the only dependencies are `node:fs`, `node:path`, and global `fetch`. Notable fragilities: `parseRssItems` hand-parses XML with regexes rather than a parser, mirror availability is volatile so the host list needs periodic maintenance, and although the header comment promises an RSS.app or stub fallback, the code actually just records `mentionSource = 'none'` and writes a "skipped" note when every mirror is down. Volume is deliberately capped — 30 mentions fetched, 10 questions and 5 praise items shown — to keep the report scannable.

scripts\\agents\\__tests__\\nri-fb-ads-p.summary: This Vitest suite validates the contents of a generated marketing deliverable — the "NRI FB Ads launch pack" under `docs/agent-reports/cmo/2026-03-nri-fb-ads-launch-pack` — rather than testing executable code, effectively acting as a contract check that the CMO agent's output artifacts exist and meet spec. It verifies that the pack directory contains a README with the $50 budget split and 7-day plan, exactly three creative briefs matching `CREATIVE_IDS` (gift-puja-nri, live-darshan-nri, 80g-receipt-nri), two audience JSON specs for `AUDIENCE_IDS` (us-hindu-25-45, uk-hindu-25-45), a utm-plan.md with at least six URL variants (3 creatives × 2 audiences), a posthog-events.md funnel defining `nri_landing_view`, `gift_puja_click`, `checkout_start`, and `order_placed`, plus launch-checklist.md and kill-criteria.md mentioning CPA and CTR thresholds. Each creative brief is checked for Facebook compliance: frontmatter headline ≤40 chars, primary_text ≤125 chars, description ≤30 chars, a CTA, an image prompt, and UTM-tagged landing URLs with `utm_source=facebook`, `utm_medium=cpc`, `utm_campaign=nri-q1-feb-2026`, and per-creative `utm_content`. Its only dependencies are vitest and Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`), via helper functions `readCreative` and `frontmatter`. Notable gotchas: the `frontmatter` helper is a naive line-based key:value parser rather than real YAML, so it will break on multiline or nested values, and `PACK_DIR` is resolved from `process.cwd()`, meaning the suite only works when run from the repository root. Audience specs are hard-coded to ages 25–45 with at least three interests, so any legitimate targeting change requires editing the test.

scripts\\backup\\supabase-backup.mjs.summary: This script automates daily Postgres backups of the Supabase database, dumping via `pg_dump` in custom format and uploading the result to Supabase Storage (with an S3-compatible swap possible via env), as specified in roadmap item R-Q2-IT-003. Its main entry point is `runBackup()`, which orchestrates the dump, SHA256 hashing, upload, and an optional heartbeat POST to a healthchecks.io-style `HEARTBEAT_URL`, while the exported pure helpers `buildPgDumpArgs()` and `buildBackupKey()` construct the CLI arguments and the date-partitioned object key (`backups/YYYY/MM/DD/bhaktisetu-<ISO>.dump`) and are unit-tested in `scripts/backup/test/backup.test.mjs`. It depends only on Node built-ins (`child_process`, `fs`, `crypto`, `os`, `path`) plus the external `pg_dump` binary and the Supabase Storage REST endpoint at `/storage/v1/object/{bucket}/{key}`, authenticated with the `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` JWT. A notable design decision is the env gate: if `SUPABASE_DB_URL`, `SUPABASE_URL`, or `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` are missing, the script no-ops with exit 0 and a structured JSON log so CI stays green before secrets are configured. All output is single-line JSON for GitHub Actions parsing, with distinct exit codes (2/3/4) marking pg_dump, hashing, and upload failures. Gotchas include requiring Node 20+ for streaming fetch with `duplex: 'half'`, replacing colons in timestamps because they're illegal in many object-store keys, and the strict warning that the service-role key must never ship to the client.

scripts\\build-demo-video.sh.summary: This Bash script automates production of the Darshya golden-path demo video used as KYC evidence for Razorpay, Stripe, and WhatsApp Meta verification, plus Reddit and investor outreach. It runs a four-step pipeline: executes the Playwright spec `e2e/capture-demo-video.spec.ts` in headed Chromium against the target in `DEMO_BASE_URL` (defaulting to https://darshya.online), locates the resulting `.webm` under `apps/web/test-results/`, transcodes it to H.264 MP4 via ffmpeg, and extracts a poster JPG from the 8-second mark. Outputs are date-stamped files (`darshya-demo-YYYYMMDD.mp4` and a `-poster.jpg`) written to `docs/demo-video/`. Dependencies are ffmpeg on PATH and the `@poojly/web` workspace's Playwright with Chromium installed via pnpm. Notable gotchas: the script wipes `test-results/` beforehand so exactly one `.webm` exists to find, and it deliberately injects a silent AAC audio track rather than stripping audio because uploaders like LinkedIn reject audio-less files; the video is also scaled and padded to a fixed 1920x1080 with faststart enabled for web playback.

scripts\\backup\\prune-old-backups.mjs.summary: This Node.js ESM script is a retention pruner for database backups stored in Supabase Storage: it lists everything under the `backups/` prefix in the `db-backups` bucket (overridable via `SUPABASE_BACKUP_BUCKET`) and deletes all but the newest entries. It exports two things: `pickOldBackups`, a pure function kept side-effect-free specifically so vitest can test it, and `runPrune`, the orchestrating entrypoint that is also invoked when the file is run directly. The only external service is the Supabase Storage REST API, called with raw `fetch` against the `object/list` and `object/delete` endpoints using `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`; it builds on no internal modules but mirrors the env-gate pattern of the sibling `supabase-backup.mjs`, exiting 0 as a logged no-op when those credentials are absent. A notable semantic decision: despite the "RETENTION_DAYS" naming, `pickOldBackups` keeps the N newest dumps sorted by `created_at` (default 30) rather than comparing against calendar age, so missed runs can't cause over-deletion, and items with unparseable timestamps are defensively neither retained nor pruned. Because Supabase's list endpoint returns only one folder level at a time, `listAllBackups` manually walks the YYYY/MM/DD directory hierarchy before issuing a single batch DELETE of all stale paths. Failures are reported as structured JSON with distinct exit codes (2 for list errors, 3 for delete errors, 1 for unhandled), which makes the script friendly to scheduled CI/cron monitoring.

scripts\\backup\\test\\backup.test.mjs.summary: This file is a Vitest test suite for the backup scripts `scripts/backup/supabase-backup.mjs` and `scripts/backup/prune-old-backups.mjs`, written as pure unit tests that never invoke real `pg_dump` or talk to Supabase. It covers three exported helpers: `buildPgDumpArgs`, which must emit the `--no-owner`, `--no-privileges`, and `--format=custom` flags with the dump path after `-f` and the database URL as the trailing positional argument, and must throw when the database URL is missing or empty; `buildBackupKey`, which must produce storage keys shaped like `backups/YYYY/MM/DD/bhaktisetu-<ISO-timestamp>.dump` with zero-padded months and days; and `pickOldBackups`, which implements the retention policy by selecting entries older than a given day count (30 in the tests) for deletion. The retention tests generate fake Supabase Storage list entries (with `name`, `created_at`, and `path` fields mimicking the real API output) to verify that 35 dated dumps yield exactly 5 deletions, that lists of 30 or fewer entries produce no deletions, and that entries lacking a `created_at` timestamp are defensively skipped. Notable constraints encoded here: the timestamp in keys has colons and dots replaced with dashes for storage safety, the age comparison uses a one-millisecond tolerance against the 30-day threshold, and the tests serve as executable documentation of the backup naming convention and prune behavior expected by the production scripts.

scripts\\agents\\__tests__\\twitter-thre.summary: This Vitest spec validates the "founder Twitter pack" content deliverable tracked as requirement R-Q2-M-012, asserting structural and content rules against markdown files under docs/agent-reports/cmo/2026-05-founder-twitter-pack rather than testing executable code. It defines two local helpers — parseFrontmatter, a minimal regex-based parser for simple `key: value` frontmatter (no nested YAML or arrays), and listThreads, which filters pack files against the `thread-W[1-4]-[1-3]-*.md` naming convention — then runs assertions for the full 4-week × 3-threads-per-week matrix of 12 files. Per-thread rules cover required frontmatter fields (hook capped at 280 characters, tweet_count between 5 and 12, topic, cta, schedule_week in 1–4, schedule_day_hint, and target_audience restricted to india, nri, or generic) plus a 280-character limit on every numbered `N/M` tweet line in the body. Portfolio-level checks enforce an audience mix of at least 4 NRI, at least 6 India, and at most 2 generic threads, and require the supporting docs README.md, cadence.md, engagement-playbook.md, success-criteria-update.md, and metrics-tracker.md to exist, with success-criteria-update.md specifically required to have its "Populate during first sub-agent emission cycle" placeholder replaced by at least four bullet points. The only dependencies are vitest and node builtins (fs, path), and because PACK_DIR resolves from process.cwd(), the suite must be run from the repository root. One notable gotcha: the tweet-length test's comment claims the `N/M` prefix is stripped before counting, but the assertion actually measures the full line including that prefix, so tweets pass only if they fit within 280 characters with the prefix included.

scripts\\build-og-default.mjs.summary: This standalone build script generates the Darshya brand's default Open Graph social card, rendering an inline HTML template to a 1200x630 PNG at `apps/web/public/og/default.png` via a headless Chromium screenshot. It dynamically imports `playwright-core` from the local pnpm store and launches it against an explicit Chrome executable, waits for `networkidle` and `document.fonts.ready` so the Google Fonts (Fraunces, Inter, Tiro Devanagari Sanskrit) load, then captures a clipped screenshot and writes it with `writeFileSync`. The card design itself is embedded as a template literal: a saffron-to-amber gradient, a large watermark ॐ glyph, the "Darshya" wordmark, a tagline, four feature pills (Live Darshan, Puja Booking, Vedic Astrology, 80G Receipts), and the darshya.online URL. It exports nothing and is meant to be run manually with `node scripts/build-og-default.mjs`. The major gotcha is portability: the `PW_CORE`, `CHROME`, and `OUT` constants are hardcoded absolute Windows paths tied to one developer machine, so the script will break in CI or on other machines without edits. It also requires network access at render time for the Google Fonts import, meaning offline runs will silently produce a card with fallback fonts.

scripts\\build-audit-pdf.mjs.summary: This standalone Node script converts a hardcoded markdown file (Darshya-Audit-Report-V3-2026-05-14.md) into a styled A4 PDF (Darshya-Audit-Report.pdf) by rendering HTML in headless Chromium. It deliberately avoids `npm install`: it imports `playwright-core`'s `index.mjs` directly from a pnpm-store path via `pathToFileURL` and points `chromium.launch` at a system Chrome executable, with all paths (E:/NewClaude/..., C:/Users/DELL/...) hardcoded to one Windows machine, so the script is not portable. Rather than pulling in a markdown library, it implements a minimal converter: `escapeHtml` handles entity escaping, `inline` processes code spans, bold, italic, and links (protecting backtick code contents with placeholder tokens before escaping), and `mdToHtml` handles fenced code blocks, pipe tables, headings, horizontal rules, flat ordered/unordered lists, and paragraphs. Table rendering destructures rows as `[head, , ...body]` to skip the separator row, and the generated HTML is wrapped in a print-oriented template with an orange/amber theme, `page-break-inside: avoid` on tables and pre blocks, and Chromium's `headerTemplate`/`footerTemplate` supplying "Page X of Y" numbering. Notable gotchas: the parser only covers the subset of markdown the V3 report uses (no nested lists or blockquotes, despite blockquote CSS existing), the `flushList` IIFE is dead code shadowed by the later `listType`/`closeList` implementation, and the ` C<n> ` code-span placeholder could collide with literal text matching that pattern. Rendering uses `page.setContent`, `emulateMedia({ media: 'print' })`, and `page.pdf` with `printBackground: true` and explicit A4 margins.

scripts\\finance\\unit-econ-refresh.mjs.summary: This standalone Node script (`scripts/finance/unit-econ-refresh.mjs`, roadmap item R-Q2-F-002) refreshes blended unit economics — CAC, LTV, and payback months — across acquisition channels, split into `domestic` (INR) and `nri` (USD) cohorts. It reads a static baseline from `docs/finance/unit-econ-channel-data.json`, computes volume-weighted blends via `computeBlended` (weighted by `monthly_acquired_target`, payback rounded up to whole months), and evaluates guardrail thresholds in `checkTripwires` against `blended_nri_cac_usd_max` and `blended_domestic_payback_months_max`. `fetchPostHogCohort` follows the repo's env-or-noop pattern: with `POSTHOG_PERSONAL_API_KEY` and `POSTHOG_PROJECT_ID` set it would query the PostHog cohorts API, but that query is unimplemented, so it currently always returns an advisory and every snapshot is marked `stale` with the baseline labeled as the source. Running with `--write` persists a dated snapshot to `docs/agent-reports/unit-econ/`; tripwire breaches log a warning and exit with code 2, while stale (baseline-only) snapshots exit 0 but explicitly keep the KPI `unit_econ_dashboard_live` at 0 until a real PostHog refresh lands.

scripts\\cs\\build-macros-yaml.mjs.summary: This Node.js ESM script generates `docs/agent-reports/cs/macros/multilingual-macros-v1.yaml`, a customer-support macro catalog for the Bhaktisetu product covering 40 intents (M001–M040) across five categories — billing, onboarding, content, account, and escalation — each with template variables like `{user_name}` and `{order_id}`. It exports no reusable API; the internal `build()` function assembles YAML as raw text lines, `escapeYamlString()` sanitizes double-quoted scalars, `regional()` fabricates the ta/te/bn/mr entries, and `main()` writes the file via `node:fs/promises`. The only dependencies are Node builtins (`fs/promises`, `path`, `url`) — notably, no YAML library is used despite emitting YAML. English templates come from the `INTENTS` array and production-grade formal Hindi from the `HI` map, but the Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, and Marathi versions are a deliberate shortcut: `regional()` just prepends a translated salutation to the stripped English body and marks each with a REVIEW comment, so they are placeholders, not real translations, and must be replaced by native speakers before any customer-facing deploy. The header ties the artifact to requirement R-Q2-CS-003 and points reviewers to `docs/agent-reports/cs/macros/DEPLOY-RUNBOOK.md` for the review checklist. Because `generated_at` embeds a fresh timestamp on every run, the output is not byte-reproducible across builds.

scripts\\dev.sh.summary: This bash script is the project's one-command dev launcher for the Poojly monorepo: it kills stale processes, wipes the build cache, and starts both apps in a clean state. It first frees ports 3000 and 4000 by finding listeners via netstat and terminating them with taskkill (falling back to Unix kill), then force-deletes the apps/web/.next directory — using both rm -rf and cmd.exe rmdir — because a stale .next cache is cited as the top cause of "Internal Server Error" during development. It then backgrounds the API from apps/api via npx tsx src/server.ts on port 4000 and the web app from apps/web via npx next dev on port 3000, ending with wait so a single Ctrl+C stops both servers. The script depends only on npx, tsx, and Next.js, but is clearly written for a Windows/Git Bash hybrid environment given the taskkill //F and cmd.exe invocations. Notable constraints: turbopack is deliberately omitted from next dev due to a known bug with pnpm workspaces and Next 15.5, and startup relies on fixed sleep delays (1.5s for the API) rather than health checks, so slow machines may race.

scripts\\build-pitch-deck-pdf.mjs.summary: This standalone Node.js ESM build script (it exports nothing) converts the HTML slide deck docs/client-pitch-deck.html into docs/client-pitch-deck.pdf at a fixed 1280×720 (16:9) page size. It dynamically imports playwright-core from a hardcoded pnpm store path (playwright-core@1.59.1) and launches Chromium with an explicit executablePath pointing at a specific chrome.exe in the local ms-playwright cache, rather than resolving Playwright through normal package imports. The page is loaded via a file:// URL with networkidle and a 90-second timeout, then switched to print-media emulation, and the script awaits document.fonts.ready so the Fraunces, Inter, and Tiro Devanagari web fonts fully load before capture. The PDF is emitted with printBackground enabled, zero margins, and preferCSSPageSize so the deck's own @page CSS governs the final dimensions. The main gotcha is portability: every path—node_modules, the Chrome binary, the input HTML, and the output PDF—is an absolute Windows path under E:/NewClaude/bhaktisetu tied to one user's machine, so the script breaks anywhere else without edits. The browser instance is closed in a finally block to guarantee cleanup even on failure.

scripts\\inject-video-urls.mjs.summary: `scripts/inject-video-urls.mjs` is a one-off Node.js migration script that injects YouTube `videoUrl` values into the Prisma seed file `apps/api/prisma/content-data.ts` by rewriting the source text in place. It hardcodes a `VIDEO_URLS` lookup table mapping roughly 22 content slugs (aartis, chalisis, mantras, and guide articles such as `om-jai-jagdish-hare-aarti` and `twelve-jyotirlingas-pilgrimage-guide`) to their YouTube watch URLs, then for each slug locates the matching object literal via string search for `slug: '<slug>',`. For each matched item it bounds the object by regexing for the next `},\n{` or `},\n];` delimiter, skips items that already contain a `videoUrl:` key, and otherwise splices a `videoUrl` line immediately after the existing `audioUrl: null,` line. The script depends only on `node:fs` (`readFileSync`/`writeFileSync`) and has no external services or internal imports. Notable gotchas: it relies entirely on fragile textual conventions — exact slug formatting, the literal `audioUrl: null,` placeholder, and specific closing-brace whitespace — so it will silently miscount or warn if the seed file's formatting drifts, and it is idempotent only because of the `videoUrl:` presence check. It logs per-slug progress and a final injected/skipped tally, and it mutates the seed file directly rather than going through Prisma or a database migration.

scripts\\cs\\render-macros.mjs.summary: This Node.js ESM script renders the customer-service macro catalog from `docs/agent-reports/cs/macros/multilingual-macros-v1.yaml` into platform-specific artifacts under `docs/agent-reports/cs/macros/rendered/`: per-language per-intent WhatsApp `.txt` files in Wati positional-placeholder format (`{{1}}`, `{{2}}`), a Freshdesk bulk-import `macros.json` where variables become `{{ticket.var}}`, a Zoho `macros.csv` with one row per macro-language pair, and a `manifest.json` index. Its exported, testable helpers are `parseMacroYaml` (a hand-rolled parser supporting only the v1 schema subset — a fragility if the YAML format evolves), `validateMacros` (enforces version 1, `M\d{3}` IDs, and that every declared variable placeholder appears in all six `REQUIRED_LANGS`: en, hi, ta, te, bn, mr), `detectForeignScript` (flags Devanagari characters leaking into Tamil/Telugu/Bengali text via Unicode block ranges), and the three `renderForWati`/`renderForFreshdesk`/`renderForZohoCsv` formatters. It depends only on Node built-ins (`node:fs/promises`, `node:path`, `node:url`) with no external packages or services. Notable guardrails: the driver hard-exits on "ASCII leaks" (20+ consecutive Latin characters in ta/te/bn/mr, indicating untranslated English), while foreign-script issues only produce warnings in the manifest. Gotchas include the output directory being wiped and recreated on every run, and the Zoho CSV escaping only double-quotes in the body — commas or newlines in intent/category fields are not quoted, which could corrupt rows.

scripts\\cs\\__tests__\\render-macros.te.summary: This Vitest suite (`scripts/cs/__tests__/render-macros.test.mjs`) verifies the multilingual customer-service macro pipeline implemented in `scripts/cs/render-macros.mjs`, exercising its exports `parseMacroYaml`, `validateMacros`, `detectForeignScript`, `renderForWati`, `renderForFreshdesk`, and `renderForZohoCsv`. Rather than mocking data, it loads the real shipped fixture `docs/agent-reports/cs/macros/multilingual-macros-v1.yaml` via `node:fs` and asserts it contains exactly 40 macros with unique `M###`-format IDs and complete non-empty translations across the six required languages (`en`, `hi`, `ta`, `te`, `bn`, `mr` — the `REQUIRED_LANGS` constant), so the suite doubles as a CI gate on the data file itself. It checks the renderer contracts: `renderForWati` rewrites `{var}` placeholders into Wati's positional `{{N}}` form using declaration order from the `varMap`, `renderForFreshdesk` emits one `send_reply` action per language with variables rewritten to `{{ticket.user_name}}` dotted notation, and `renderForZohoCsv` emits one row per language with CSV double-quote escaping. The `detectForeignScript` tests confirm Unicode-block guards that flag Devanagari characters leaking into Tamil, Telugu, or Bengali text while permitting them in Hindi and Marathi and tolerating ASCII placeholders plus the rupee symbol. Negative tests deep-clone the parsed YAML with `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` and assert `validateMacros` throws errors matching `/missing\/empty/`, `/variable \{user_name\} missing/`, and `/bad id/` when translations are blank, placeholders are dropped, or IDs are malformed. Only dependencies are `vitest` and Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:url`), keeping the suite hermetic apart from the live YAML fixture.

scripts\\load-test\\diwali-spike.js.summary: This k6 load test script simulates the Diwali-night traffic spike for the Darshya platform (roadmap item R-Q4-E-004), ramping to 100K concurrent virtual users in staged phases and holding that peak for 60 minutes, with explicit warnings to run only against the staging environment (api-staging.darshya.online) at 80% prod capacity. Its key exports are the k6 `options` object (ramping-vus scenario, latency/error thresholds like p95 < 400ms and <0.5% failures, and k6 Cloud region distribution weighted 60% Mumbai), the default virtual-user function that randomly dispatches among four weighted behavior flows (browseFlow 50%, darshanFlow 25%, bookingFlow 15%, pandithAskFlow 10%), and `handleSummary`, which writes results to docs/load-test/diwali-spike-summary.json plus a formatted stdout report. It depends entirely on the k6 runtime (`k6/http`, `k6`, `k6/metrics`) and exercises public REST endpoints under `/api/v1/` such as temples, pujas, and darshan, plus web pages on the staging frontend. Notable design choices include custom Trend metrics (bookingDuration, darshanDuration) and a Rate metric (errorRate) layered on top of built-in HTTP metrics, a behavior mix justified by PostHog funnel data, the deliberate omission of POST requests in pandithAskFlow to avoid rate limits and LLM costs, and a low-cost distributed-run option using five AWS Lightsail nodes instead of k6 Cloud.

scripts\\fix-store-service-images.mjs.summary: This is a one-off Node.js maintenance script that bulk-rewrites product image URLs inside `apps/api/src/services/store.service.ts`, a hardcoded product catalog for a Hindu puja-goods store. It exports nothing; its core is the `HANDLE_TO_URL` lookup mapping 24 product handles (e.g. `premium-brass-puja-thali-set`, `brass-krishna-playing-flute`) to replacement images, mixing full Wikimedia Commons URLs with bare Unsplash-style photo IDs like `photo-1541795083-1b160cf4f3d7` that the catalog's `img()` helper presumably resolves. Its only dependency is `node:fs` (`readFileSync`/`writeFileSync`), and it performs crude string surgery rather than AST manipulation: for each handle it locates `handle: '<name>',` via `indexOf`, then regex-searches forward for the next `images: [img('url', 'alt')]` line and swaps in the new URL while preserving the existing alt text. Notable gotchas: the regex only matches entries with exactly one `img()` call using single quotes, it assumes each `images:` line appears after its handle, and the script edits the file in place with no backup, dry-run mode, or idempotency guard. Handles that aren't found simply log a warning and are skipped, with a final summary of how many of the 24 replacements succeeded.

scripts\\lint-product-specs.mjs.summary: scripts/lint-product-specs.mjs is a standalone Node ESM CLI script (run via `pnpm lint:specs` and roadmap CI) that validates every Markdown file in docs/product/specs/ and exits 1 if any check fails. It has no exports and depends only on node:fs, node:path, and node:url. Specs are routed by filename regex: files matching /antim[\s-]?sanskar/i must contain the twelve dignity-domain H2 sections in REQUIRED_H2 (Mission, Non-goals, Pandit dispatch SLA, Grief-sensitive copy review checklist, etc.), at least 12 grief-checklist bullets, at least 5 ASCII wireframe code blocks, and must not use FORBIDDEN_WORDS marketing terms like "discount", "book now", or "VIP" — though lines matching EXEMPTION_RE (e.g. Non-goals or blocklist discussions citing the words) are exempted. Files matching /wedding[\s-]?planner/i instead follow the commerce-oriented WEDDING_REQUIRED_H2 schema and face quantitative checks: at least 8 API endpoint bullets, at least 12 wireframe blocks in UI Screens, the three required data tables (wedding_event, wedding_vendor_booking, muhurat_request), all three revenue tiers (₹15,000 / ₹50,000 / ₹2,00,000) plus the 8%-12% take rate, at least two named competitors (WedMeGood, ShaadiSaga, BookMyPandit), and v1/v2 columns in the MVP Cut-line table. A notable gotcha is that specs matching neither filename pattern are linted for nothing beyond a log line, so the rules are per-domain rather than universal. The section-extraction regexes deliberately stop only at the next H2 (`^##\s[^#]`) so nested H3/H4 headings don't truncate a section. A missing or empty specs directory is treated as a vacuous pass rather than an error.

scripts\\load-test\\steady-200k.js.summary: This file is a k6 load test script modeling a steady-state day of traffic for the Darshya platform at 200K monthly active users, peaking at 50K concurrent virtual users under roadmap item R-Q4-E-004 Scenario A. It exports a k6 `options` object configuring a `ramping-vus` executor with five stages (ramping through 10K, 30K, a 50K peak labeled "evening aarti," then cooldown) plus latency and error thresholds (p95 under 400ms, p99 under 800ms, failure rate under 0.5%), and a default function that probabilistically dispatches each virtual user into one of three flows: `browseFlow` (60%, hitting the web home page and `/api/v1/temples`), `darshanFlow` (25%, hitting `/api/v1/darshan/live`), or `bookingFlow` (15%, hitting `/api/v1/pujas/types` and `/api/v1/pujas/rudrabhishek`). It depends only on the external k6 runtime (`k6/http`, `k6` for check/sleep/group, and `k6/metrics` for the custom `errors` Rate) and targets staging environments via the `BASE_URL` and `WEB_URL` environment variables, defaulting to api-staging.darshya.online and staging.darshya.online. Notable design choices include a 2–7 second randomized think-time between iterations to keep load steadier than a spike test, the 25% concurrency-to-MAU assumption baked into the peak target, and the use of short-circuit `check(...) || errorRate.add(1)` so failed checks feed the custom error metric that has its own 1% threshold. The script is read-only—it only issues GET requests, so it validates read-path capacity rather than write or booking-transaction throughput.

scripts\\issue-b2b-key.ts.summary: `scripts/issue-b2b-key.ts` is a standalone CLI utility (run via `pnpm tsx`, requirement tag R-Q3-E-007) that provisions API keys for B2B partners of the Darshya platform. It takes `--org` and `--email` flags (both mandatory) plus optional `--scopes` and `--rpm` overrides, then uses `node:crypto` to mint a public `keyPrefix` (`dk_live_<8-hex>`) and a one-time secret `fullKey` (`dk_live_<8-hex>_<32-hex>`), storing only the SHA-256 `keyHash`. Default entitlements are 60 requests per minute and five read scopes (`read:temples`, `read:bookings`, `read:pandits`, `read:donations`, `read:darshan-schedule`). The script's only dependencies are Node built-ins (`node:crypto`, `node:process`); it has no runtime imports from the app. Notably, despite the header comment claiming it writes to the Prisma `B2BApiKey` table "when DB available," the implementation never touches Prisma — it always prints a raw SQL INSERT for `b2b_api_keys` plus a curl test snippet hitting `https://api.darshya.online/api/v1/b2b/ping` with the `X-Darshya-Key` header. Two gotchas: the full key is unrecoverable after the run (only its hash persists), and the emitted SQL interpolates org, email, and scopes without escaping, so values containing quotes would produce broken or injectable statements.

scripts\\load-tests\\50k-concurrent-mau..summary: This k6 load-test script (requirement R-Q3-E-006) validates that the Darshya API and its Render auto-scaling can sustain 50,000 concurrent virtual users representing projected Q3 monthly-active-user load, with PASS gates of under 1% failed requests and p95/p99 latency under 1500/3000 ms feeding the KPI `scale_test_max_concurrent`. It exports a k6 `options` object with stage/threshold profiles (`smoke` at 200 VUs for CI gating, `midscale` at 5K, and the 45-minute `full` ramp to 50K with a 15-minute hold), a default VU function, and a `handleSummary` hook that writes a JSON report to `docs/agent-reports/scale-test-latest.json`. It depends only on the external k6 runtime modules (`k6/http`, `k6`, `k6/metrics`) and targets the API at `BASE_URL` (defaulting to `https://api-staging.darshya.online`), hitting read-only endpoints—`/api/v1/pujas/types`, `/api/v1/panchang/today`, `/health`, and `/api/v1/search`—in a weighted 60/20/15/5 traffic mix modeling the "Aarti" devotee persona. Custom `Rate` and `Trend` metrics (`errors`, `health_latency_ms`, `listing_latency_ms`) supplement k6's built-ins, and checks accept HTTP 200 or 401 with a non-empty body. Notable constraints: authenticated write and booking paths are deliberately excluded because they require a live Razorpay handshake that would pollute the payment provider (covered instead by `booking-flow-smoke.k6.js`), and the header warns that Render's free tier will throttle far below 50K, so the full soak requires a paid plan or sandbox API copy per `docs/engineering/R-Q3-E-006-handoff.md`.

scripts\\regression-check.sh.summary: This file is a Bash script, `scripts/regression-check.sh`, that serves as a one-shot regression gate for the POOJLY monorepo, verifying that the codebase type-checks, builds, and passes unit tests before changes are shipped. It exports no functions or types; instead it runs three sequential Turbo pipeline commands via `pnpm turbo`: `type-check`, `build`, and `test`, which fan out across all apps and packages in the workspace. Its only dependencies are the Bash shell, the pnpm package manager, and Turborepo, with the actual per-package check logic delegated to each workspace's own scripts. The notable design decision is the use of `set -e`, which aborts the script immediately on the first failing step, so a type error prevents a wasted build and a build failure prevents a wasted test run — making it fast-failing but meaning later stages never execute if an earlier one breaks. It produces only console progress output and no reports or artifacts, so it functions as a lightweight local or CI smoke check rather than a full test harness.

scripts\\mcp-smoke.mjs.summary: `scripts/mcp-smoke.mjs` is a CI-friendly smoke test that verifies the built darshya MCP server (`apps/darshya-mcp/dist/index.js`, from the `@darshya/mcp` package) actually boots and exposes exactly the six expected read-only tools: `funnel_today`, `kpi_snapshot`, `agent_reports`, `agent_report_read`, `prod_health`, and `recent_commits`. It spawns the server as a child process via `node:child_process.spawn`, speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdio — sending `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, and `tools/list` (id 2) up front — then parses stdout for the id:2 response and compares the sorted tool names against the expected list. Its only dependencies are Node built-ins (`node:child_process` and `node:fs`, the latter used to check the server build exists and fail fast with a helpful build hint); it is normally invoked via `pnpm mcp:smoke`, which builds the server first. Notable design choices include inheriting the child's stderr so server diagnostics land directly in CI logs, defensively skipping blank or non-JSON stdout lines, and guaranteeing termination through a 5-second timeout, a `close` handler, and an `exited` flag that prevents double-finish — ensuring the script can never hang a pipeline. It prints a single `MCP SMOKE: PASS/FAIL` line and exits 0 or 1 accordingly.

scripts\\sales\\seed-antim-pandits.ts.summary: This script (spec R-Q4-S-007) is a stub seed loader intended to populate the Supabase table `antim_sanskar_pandits` with rows from `seeds/antim-pandits-prospects.csv`, marking each with `verification_status='pending'`. It currently does naive comma-split parsing of the CSV (rather than the planned `csv-parse/sync`), reports the row count, and exits cleanly if `DATABASE_URL` is unset or the schema is missing, leaving the actual `pg` Pool upsert logic commented out as a founder TODO. The intended behavior is upsert on the `phone` unique key with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, skipping rows with blank phone or `founder-collect-onsite` notes. It is blocked on three external dependencies: the missing `supabase/migrations/` directory and table DDL, the absent `signal-context/kpi-collectors.yaml` collector registry (with `scripts/agents/roadmap/_kpi-supabase.mjs` as a fallback path), and the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable. Run via `pnpm tsx scripts/sales/seed-antim-pandits.ts`; note the script exits with code 0 on missing env config, so CI or automation should not treat that as success of an actual seed.

scripts\\seed-wedding-vendors.ts.summary: This script (R-Q4-S-009) is a one-off seed loader that populates the `wedding_vendors` table in Supabase with prospect vendors parsed from `seeds/wedding-vendors-prospects.csv`, inserting every row with `verification_status = 'pending'` so the founder can later run a verification rubric and flip statuses manually. Its core pieces are the `Row` type (constraining `vendor_type` to photographer, caterer, or decorator), a hand-rolled `parseCsv` function that skips malformed lines and rows missing `business_name` or `vendor_type`, and a `main` routine that dedupes on the (business_name, vendor_type) pair before inserting. It depends only on Node's `fs`/`path` built-ins and lazily imports the `pg` client (a dev dependency) to talk to Postgres via `DATABASE_URL` or `SUPABASE_DIRECT_URL`. Notable design choices: when no database URL is set the script degrades gracefully to a dry run that logs parsed row counts per vendor type and exits 0 rather than failing, and the naive CSV parser splits on commas only, so any field containing a comma will silently corrupt a row. Empty optional fields (`service_city`, `instagram_handle`, `notes_for_outreach`) are normalized to SQL NULL on insert. The script is idempotent by virtue of its existence check, making reruns safe.

scripts\\preflight-cf-pages.sh.summary: This bash script is a pre-push guard that replicates the production Cloudflare Pages build locally for the Next.js app in `apps/web`, catching CF-only failures—such as non-edge routes using dynamic features or a `middleware.ts` forcing all routes onto the edge runtime—that a plain `next build` would miss. It exits 0 when a push is safe and 1 when the push would break the CF Pages deploy, printing the tail of `/tmp/preflight-cf-build.log` plus common fixes on failure. Change detection is layered: it checks the `WEB_CHANGED_RANGE` env var (set by a pre-push hook), then staged and working-tree git diffs for paths under `apps/web/`, skipping entirely with a hint to set `FORCE=1` if nothing matches. The build pipeline runs `pnpm exec next build` followed by `pnpm dlx @cloudflare/next-on-pages`, so it depends on pnpm, git, and the Vercel/Cloudflare toolchain. A notable gotcha is its platform branching: on Windows (MINGW/MSYS/CYGWIN/Git Bash) it skips both builds—citing `.next` race/ENOTEMPTY issues and the fact that `@cloudflare/next-on-pages` spawns the Vercel CLI, which crashes outside Linux/WSL—and falls back to a static audit instead. That audit greps `apps/web/app` for hot patterns (`searchParams`, imports from `next/headers`, `revalidate = 0`) and fails if any matching file lacks an `export const runtime = 'edge'` declaration, or if `apps/web/middleware.ts` exists at all, since middleware forces every non-static route onto the edge runtime. The header comments instruct running it before every push touching `apps/web/**`, and the full build path is expected to run in CI/Linux even when Windows users only get the static check.

scripts\\sales\\canada-pandit\\__tests__.summary: This Vitest suite guards the hand-authored lead-seed CSV `data/leads/canada-pandits-2026-06.csv`, which contains prospective Canadian pandit (Hindu priest) contacts for a sales outreach campaign, enforcing the requirements tagged R-Q3-S-007. It exports nothing; instead its `describe('canada-pandits CSV seed')` block reads the real file at test time via `node:fs` `readFileSync` and asserts that the data has at least 50 rows, meets a city distribution floor (Toronto ≥ 20, Vancouver ≥ 10, Brampton ≥ 5), marks at least 10 rows with `outreach_status=queued` for the first batch send, populates `temple_affiliation`, `city`, and `province` on every row, and matches an exact 12-column header spec including fields like `source_url`, `language_preference`, and `first_contact_at`. The only dependencies are `vitest`, `node:fs`, and `node:path` — there are no internal module imports, since the suite tests a data artifact rather than code. The notable gotcha is the deliberately naive parser: rows are split on bare commas with no quote handling, which the authors justify in a comment by controlling the CSV by hand, so any future seed value containing an embedded comma will silently corrupt the column mapping and produce confusing test failures. Because the tests couple directly to the on-disk data file, editing the CSV is effectively a code change that CI will validate.

This Vitest test suite validates the markdown outreach templates for the canada-pandit sales campaign (spec R-Q3-S-007), reading outreach-email-en.md, outreach-email-hi.md, outreach-whatsapp.md, and followup-day5.md from the parent directory via a small `read()` helper built on node:fs and node:path. Rather than exporting anything, it encodes content and compliance invariants: the English and Hindi emails must include `{first_name}`, `{temple_name}`, and `{city}` merge placeholders, and every template's call-to-action must link to `/become-pandit`. It enforces Canadian CASL compliance by requiring a "Reply STOP" footer and a Bhaktisetu sender address in the emails and the day-5 follow-up, and it blocks hard pricing claims (matching `$`, `CAD`, `USD`, or `₹` amounts) across all templates until the payment rail is live. Bilingual support is checked by asserting the Hindi template contains both `## Devanagari` and `## Romanized` sections and that early-access partner language appears in English, Devanagari, or romanized form. The WhatsApp template is additionally constrained to under 400 characters, measured after stripping markdown header and blockquote lines so only the message body counts. Its only external dependency is vitest.

scripts\\sales\\warm-network\\__tests__\.summary: This Node.js test suite (run via `node --test`) enforces the data and content contracts for requirement R-Q1-S-014, the warm-network sales outreach artifacts, using only Node built-ins (`node:test`, `node:assert/strict`, `node:fs`, `node:path`). It verifies that `data/sales/warm-network-tracker.csv` has the expected 12-column header (`contact_name` through `notes`), and that `data/sales/warm-network-contacts-seed.csv` contains exactly 50 pre-segmented contact rows sharing that schema. It also asserts a fixed `ask_type` distribution in the seed file — 15 temple, 15 pandit, 10 gaushala, 5 donor, 5 diaspora — so the seed data cannot drift from spec without failing CI. For the WhatsApp scripts (`wa-script-temple.md`, `wa-script-pandit.md`, `wa-script-gaushala.md`) in `scripts/sales/warm-network`, it checks each has `## Hindi` and `## English` headings, a `{first_name}` personalization placeholder, and bodies under 350 characters each for WhatsApp-friendliness, plus a directory-level check that at least six markdown files exist including `email-script-formal.md`, `followup-script-day7.md`, and `README.md`. Notable gotchas: CSV parsing is a naive comma-split that assumes no quoted commas in the data, and markdown bodies are extracted with regex rather than a real parser, so structural changes to either format will break these tests.

scripts\\test-agent-summary.mjs.summary: This executable Node script (run via `pnpm test:agent`) exists to give AI agents a compact, parseable verdict on the vitest suite instead of the verbose TAP output that agents tend to misread; it is the intended input for the darshya-verify agent and the stop-verify-gate hook. It exports nothing — it spawns `pnpm exec vitest run --reporter=json` via `spawnSync` from `node:child_process`, relying only on Node built-ins (`node:fs`, `node:path`) plus the project's pnpm/vitest tooling, and accepts passthrough CLI args for scoped runs (e.g., `apps/api`). A key design decision is routing vitest's JSON through `--outputFile` into `.claude/vitest-result.json` rather than parsing stdout, because vitest interleaves its default checkmark output with the JSON blob, making `indexOf('{')`-style parsing unreliable. The script aggregates totals (total/passed/failed/skipped/duration) and collects failing test names into an `agentOutput` object with a `PASS`/`FAIL` verdict, hardcoding a `PREEXISTING` regex that excludes the known-broken `canada-pandit-prospector` test from the verdict since it fails on clean main and is not a regression. If the JSON file cannot be read (vitest crashed), it falls back to an `UNVERIFIED` verdict with 500-character tails of raw stdout/stderr. Results are persisted to `.claude/test-result.json` for downstream agents, printed to stdout, and the process exits with vitest's own exit code so CI gates correctly; the project root comes from `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` or `process.cwd()`, and the spawn has a 300-second timeout.

scripts\\verify-deploy-stack.sh.summary: `scripts/verify-deploy-stack.sh` is a pre-deploy gate that verifies the entire Darshya stack—backend API, database reachability, frontend pages, feature flags, and security headers—before allowing a push, exiting non-zero if any check fails so it can be wired into a pre-push hook. It accepts a `MODE` argument (`local` by default against localhost:3000/8787, or `prod` against darshya.online and api.darshya.online) and runs five layers of checks: `/health`, critical endpoints (`/api/v1/temples`, `/api/v1/pujas/types`, and a negative auth test expecting 400/401 from `/api/v1/auth/login`), HTTP 200s on key frontend routes (`/`, `/astrology/kundli`, `/pujas`, `/profile`), grep-based content assertions on rendered HTML, and a Content-Security-Policy header check. Its only dependencies are `bash`, `curl`, and `grep`, with three helper functions—`check` (exact-match comparison), `check_grep` (pattern must appear), and `check_grep_zero` (pattern must be absent)—tracking PASS/FAIL counters. Notable details: the feature-verification layer is regression-locked to specific UI fixes (e.g., `check_grep_zero` confirms the "See divinity. Hear devotion" StickyHeadlinePin was removed from the home page, while other checks confirm `object-cover object-center`, a "verified temples" trust strip, `py-6 md:py-8` padding, and a combobox on the kundli CityAutocomplete), and cache-busting `?v=$$` query params (PID-based) are appended to frontend URLs. One design quirk: a missing CSP header only emits a WARN (not a FAIL), so it never blocks deploys, which the script justifies as acceptable on free-tier hosting.

scripts\\ship-batch-build.mjs.summary: This standalone Node CLI script (`scripts/ship-batch-build.mjs`) assembles a 40-item work batch for the repo's roadmap "ship loop," writing a dated JSON manifest (`docs/roadmap/_ship-batch-2026-06-15-r4.json`) that downstream shipping automation consumes. It scans markdown specs in `docs/roadmap/_dryrun/queue`, dedups them by roadmap ID (keeping the latest ISO-timestamped filename, since string sort works), then tops up to `TARGET = 40` from `docs/roadmap/items/**` files whose frontmatter `status` is `in_progress`. Helper functions include `extractId` (regex-matching IDs like `R-Q1-CS-007`, `SIDE-FIX-*`, `META-*`), naive line-based parsers (`parseFrontmatter`, `parseStatus`, `parsePriority`, `parseEstHours`), `priorityRank`, and a `roundRobin` interleaver that spreads categories so the batch isn't dominated by one department. A hardcoded `EXCLUDE_IDS` set of 120+ previously shipped or rejected IDs (annotated by round R1–R3) prevents re-selecting completed work, making the script a per-round snapshot that must be manually edited each cycle. Queue items are enriched by locating their source item file via a brittle nested-ternary that maps category codes to directories (h→talent, s→sales, cs→cs, etc.) and matching zero-padded number prefixes. Dependencies are only `node:fs` and `node:path`—no external libraries—and the script assumes it runs from the repo root via `process.cwd()`. Notable gotchas: missing metadata silently defaults (est_hours→999, priority→P3), the output filename is baked in per round, and frontmatter parsing is regex-based rather than real YAML, so multi-line or nested fields would be missed.

scripts\\test\\docs-uptime-lint.sh.summary: This bash script is a documentation linter that verifies the structural integrity of the project's uptime-monitoring docs, written test-first per TDD (the header comment notes it should be RED before the docs exist and GREEN after they ship). It checks that three files exist — `docs/it/uptime-setup-checklist.md`, `docs/it/uptime-monitors.md`, and `docs/operational-context.md` — then enforces content rules: the checklist must contain at least four `### Monitor` headers and cross-link to `uptime-monitors.md`, the runbook must include a `## Escalation Policy` section, and the operational context doc must mention UptimeRobot (the monitoring service, matched case-insensitively). It also requires the production URLs `https://api.darshya.online/health`, `https://darshya.online`, and `https://darshya.online/pujas` to appear verbatim in the checklist. Failures are accumulated via the `err` helper into a `fail` flag rather than aborting on the first problem, so a single run reports every violation before exiting 1. Its only dependencies are git (to resolve the repo root via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, falling back to the current directory) and standard grep. One gotcha: the comment claims "all 4 monitor URLs" are checked, but the loop only tests three, so the fourth monitor's URL is unenforced; also `set -e` is active, which is why the `grep -c` call needs `|| true` to survive zero-match counts.

supabase\\migrations\\20260613000000_ant.summary: This Supabase migration (spec R-Q4-S-007) creates the `antim_sanskar_pandits` table, which backs the onboarding pipeline for ghat-specialist pandits who perform last-rites ceremonies. The table stores each pandit's `full_name`, a `primary_ghat` restricted by CHECK constraint to 'kashi', 'haridwar', or 'prayagraj', a unique `phone`, a `languages` text array defaulting to Hindi, and a `verification_status` field that moves through 'pending', 'in_review', 'verified', and 'rejected' (with a `verified_at` timestamp), plus a free-text `source` for tracking acquisition channel. Row-level security is enabled with two policies: `antim_pandits_admin_all` grants the `service_role` full access, while `antim_pandits_public_denied` blocks all SELECTs from `anon` and `authenticated` roles, meaning reads must go through the backend service role rather than the public Supabase client. Two indexes, `antim_pandits_status_idx` and `antim_pandits_ghat_idx`, support filtering by verification state and ghat. The file depends on Supabase's Postgres (using `gen_random_uuid()` and RLS) and can be applied either via `psql "$DATABASE_URL"` or `pnpm prisma db execute` against `apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma`. Notable gotchas flagged in the header: the team has not yet settled on a canonical migration tool, the `DATABASE_URL` must point at the Supabase direct (non-pooled) connection for DDL to succeed, and `apps/api/scripts/check-prod-tables.mjs` should be run afterward to verify the table exists in production. The whole migration is wrapped in a transaction and uses `IF NOT EXISTS`/`IF EXISTS` guards, so it is idempotent and safe to re-run.

tests\\e2e\\astro-chat.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec (`tests/e2e/astro-chat.spec.ts`) verifies the "Ask Pandit" AI chat feature and the astrology hub of the web app, using the `test`/`expect` API from `@playwright/test` against a running site. The suite "TD2: Ask Pandit free quota then paywall" contains three tests: one checks that `/ask-pandit` renders a heading and chat input; one sends five canned spiritual questions and asserts a paywall prompt (matching upgrade/subscribe/limit language) appears on the sixth message, enforcing the five-free-messages quota; and one confirms `/astrology` lists astrologers with per-minute pricing in rupees (`₹\d+/min`). Its only external dependency is the live application under test — no internal modules or fixtures are imported. Notably, the tests are written defensively for a flaky or partially implemented product: they skip entirely when the site returns a 5xx, swallow interaction errors with `.catch()`, fall back to pressing Enter if no submit button is found, use fixed 800ms waits between messages, and the paywall assertion soft-fails with a comment acknowledging the app may not yet enforce a hard paywall. The hardcoded five-message quota and 15-second visibility timeouts encode the expected product limits directly in the test.

supabase\\migrations\\20260613232547_wed.summary: This Supabase migration creates the `wedding_vendors` table, the data backbone for the Q4 multi-vendor onboarding initiative (requirement R-Q4-S-009), which targets a pipeline of 65 verified vendors split across photographers, caterers, and decorators. The table enforces vendor_type and verification_status via check constraints, with the status column modeling an outreach funnel from `pending` through `contacted`, `meeting`, `verified`, and `onboarded` (plus `rejected`), alongside fields for contact details, Instagram handle, GST number, and portfolio URL. Two indexes support the expected query patterns: a composite `wedding_vendors_type_city_idx` on (vendor_type, service_city) for segmenting outreach, and `wedding_vendors_status_idx` for funnel tracking. Row-level security is enabled with admin-only read and write policies (`wedding_vendors_admin_read`, `wedding_vendors_admin_write`) that authorize by joining against the existing `"UserRoleAssignment"` table, comparing `auth.uid()` cast to text against its `"userId"` column where role equals 'admin'. The migration depends on Supabase Auth (`auth.uid()`), the pgcrypto-backed `gen_random_uuid()`, and the pre-existing `"UserRoleAssignment"` table, so it must run after that table exists. A practical gotcha: because RLS has no permissive policy for regular users, all non-admin access—including seed scripts—must go through the `service_role` key, which bypasses RLS entirely; the `drop policy if exists` statements keep the migration safely re-runnable.

sql\\cs\\multilingual-macro-impact.sql.summary: This analytics script (ticket R-Q2-CS-003) measures whether rolling out multilingual support macros improves customer-service KPIs, and is designed to run against a data-warehouse table `cs_tickets` (columns include `created_at`, `first_response_at`, `language`, `macro_id_used`, `csat_score`, `nps_score`) at baseline, T+14 days, and T+28 days, with results pinned in Metabase as "Multilingual Macros — Impact". It contains four standalone queries: Q1 computes p50/p90 first-response minutes per language per week using `percentile_cont` over a 12-week window; Q2 reports weekly macro usage rate (`macro_id_used` non-null share) per language against a >60% regional target; Q3 compares average `csat_score` between with-macro and no-macro ticket segments over 30 days, targeting a +0.5 point lift; and Q4 builds a weekly NPS series (percent promoters minus detractors, computed via `FILTER` aggregates) for the regional-language cohort ta/te/bn/mr over 16 weeks, targeting a rise from ~32 to >40. The language set is hard-coded to ISO 639-1 codes en/hi/ta/te/bn/mr, so the file assumes upstream ETL already normalizes `language` values. The script has no internal module dependencies and no external service calls beyond the warehouse and Metabase for visualization. A notable gotcha is that all windows are relative to `now()`, so baseline and follow-up runs cover different absolute date ranges and are not directly reproducible snapshots; Q1 also silently drops tickets where `first_response_at` is null, which can flatter response-time percentiles if unanswered tickets cluster in certain languages. Division-by-zero is guarded with `NULLIF` in the percentage calculations.

tests\\e2e\\booking-flow.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec (`tests/e2e/booking-flow.spec.ts`) verifies the puja booking journey for the "TD2" suite, covering the `/pujas` listing, puja detail pages, the `/pujas/rudrabhishek/book` wizard, and a demo booking confirmation at `/bookings/demo-001`. It exports no reusable code; its only dependency is `@playwright/test`, exercising the app's own routes rather than internal modules. The suite runs in `serial` mode and includes a guard (`test.skip` on any response ≥500) so tests quietly pass when the site is down—a trade-off that keeps CI green but can mask outages. The payment test deliberately uses the "Demo Sign In" button on `/auth/login` and asserts the browser never reaches `api.razorpay.com/v1/checkout`, confirming the Razorpay demo path stays in-app without real charges. Notable assumptions baked in: the `rudrabhishek` slug and `demo-001` booking ID must exist as seed/demo data, and the detail-page test falls back to a hardcoded slug if no listing link is found, so failures in listing rendering may go undetected.

tests\\e2e\\signup-login.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec, `signup-login.spec.ts`, verifies the site's authentication flows: rendering of the signup page, presence of a demo sign-in button on the login page, demo login with role-based redirect to a dashboard, logout returning the user to a public area, and that the protected `/dashboard` route never returns a 5xx for unauthenticated visitors. It exports no reusable symbols; instead it defines a single `test.describe` block ("TD2: Signup, demo login, role redirect, logout") containing five tests built on `@playwright/test`'s `test` and `expect`. The suite depends on a running deployment of the app (routes like `/auth/signup`, `/auth/register`, `/auth/login`, `/dashboard`) and reads demo credentials from the `E2E_DEMO_EMAIL` and `E2E_DEMO_PASSWORD` environment variables, defaulting to `devotee@demo.com` / `demo123`. Notably, the tests are written to be extremely tolerant: they call `test.skip` when the site is unavailable or a signup route is missing, fall back from `/auth/signup` to `/auth/register`, and fall back from the "Demo Sign In" button to filling a plain email/password form. The assertions are deliberately soft — most `waitForURL` and `click` calls are wrapped in `.catch(() => {})` and final expectations only assert the URL matches `darshya.online|localhost` or is not an error page — so the suite functions more as a smoke/availability check than a strict correctness gate.

tests\\sales\\varanasi-temples-artifacts.summary: This Vitest test suite validates the sales onboarding artifact bundle for requirement R-Q1-S-004 (Varanasi temple outreach), asserting that the directory docs/sales/varanasi-temples contains all ten expected deliverables and that their contents meet structural contracts. It exports no reusable API; its single helper, readCsv, implements a small RFC-4180-style parser (handling quoted commas and escaped quotes) used to inspect the CSV fixtures. The suite checks that target-list.csv has at least 25 rows with required columns like temple_name, trust_name, priority_tier, and a non-empty research_source per row, and that crm-tracking.csv uses only the eight valid pipeline statuses from lead through live or dropped. It also verifies content-level requirements: verification-checklist.md must contain all 8 mandatory trust-verification gates (12A/80G certificates, PAN, bandwidth check, signed MOU, etc.), intake-form-spec.md must define at least 12 fields in a markdown table with type and required flags, and the Hindi/English outreach scripts must contain culturally appropriate greetings and the {{BOOKING_LINK}} placeholder. Dependencies are limited to vitest and Node's node:fs and node:path modules; there are no internal module imports since the tests operate purely on files in the repo's docs tree. A notable gotcha is that paths are resolved from __dirname, so the tests assume a fixed relative location of the docs folder, and the markdown field count relies on a regex matching table rows starting with a snake_case identifier, which could silently miscount if the spec's formatting changes.

tests\\e2e\\navigation.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec verifies that the site's primary navigation works across the Darshya/Poojly/Bhakti devotional platform (the title regex suggests the brand name is in flux). It contains a single `test.describe` block, "TD2: Cross-section navigation works end-to-end," with five tests: a home-page title check, a full click-through journey from home to `/temples` to a temple detail page to `/darshan` and back, a sweep of ten primary routes (`/pujas`, `/panchang`, `/store`, `/gaushala`, `/astrology`, `/ask-pandit`, etc.) asserting none return 5xx, a footer visibility check, and a mobile-only hamburger-menu probe gated on Playwright's `isMobile` fixture. Its only dependency is `@playwright/test`; there are no page objects or shared helpers, so all selectors (nav links, `h1`, `footer`, menu buttons) are inlined. A key design decision is graceful degradation: every test calls `test.skip` when the initial page load fails or returns ≥500, so the suite goes green during outages rather than alerting — useful against flaky environments but a real risk of masking downtime. Related gotchas: the temple-detail step and mobile-menu click are conditional on `locator.count()`, meaning they silently pass if the elements are absent, and the mobile trigger's `.click().catch(() => {})` swallows interaction errors entirely.

tests\\e2e\\donation-flow.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright end-to-end spec smoke-tests the Gaushala (cow adoption) donation flow and 80G tax-receipt visibility, grouped under the suite "TD2: Gaushala donation + 80G receipt". Its five tests verify that the `/gaushala` list page renders a heading and rupee pricing, that at least one cow card links to `/gaushala/*`, that the detail route `/gaushala/cow_001` surfaces a Donate/Adopt/Sponsor CTA near the ₹501 amount, that a demo donor can reach a donations page showing 80G/DR- receipt markers, and that clicking the donation CTA does not crash the page. The only dependency is `@playwright/test` (`test`, `expect`); it exercises no internal modules directly, instead driving the running site over HTTP, including the `/auth/login` "Demo Sign In" shortcut. A notable design choice is pervasive graceful degradation: tests call `test.skip` when responses are missing or return 5xx, gate visibility assertions behind `count()` checks, and use `trial: true` clicks so no real donation is ever submitted. The receipt test probes a fallback chain of candidate URLs (`/donations`, `/profile/donations`, `/dashboard?tab=donations`), making the suite resilient to routing changes but also meaning it can pass without strongly asserting any single behavior. Overall this is a tolerant availability smoke suite rather than a strict correctness test of the payment or receipt-generation logic.

vitest.config.ts.summary: This is the root Vitest configuration for the monorepo, defining how unit tests run across the API, shared packages, and repo-level scripts. It exports a single `defineConfig` (from `vitest/config`) that enables global test APIs, uses the `node` environment, and scopes discovery to `*.test.ts` files under `apps/api/src`, `apps/api/scripts`, `packages/shared/src`, `scripts/` (including `.test.mjs`), and `tests/`. Coverage uses the `v8` provider with `text` and `lcov` reporters, measured only against `apps/api/src/services/**` and `packages/shared/src/**`. A key design decision (ticket P2-37) is the deliberately minimal coverage thresholds — 1% lines/branches/statements and 40% functions — because the current baseline is only ~3% against a ~15k-line services tree, so the gates exist to catch catastrophic drops rather than enforce a real floor, and should be raised as coverage grows. Notably, `apps/web` is intentionally excluded from the root include: it has its own `vitest.config.ts` (happy-dom environment, JSX automatic runtime, React alias pinning, setup files) and runs via `pnpm --filter @poojly/web test` through turbo, so it is not silently skipped. One outstanding integration item: a `test:coverage` script still needs to be added to the root `package.json`, which is owned by another workstream (A5) and must not be added here.

tests\\sales\\wellness-instructors-artif.summary: This Vitest spec enforces structural contracts on the wellness-instructor onboarding documentation living in `docs/sales/wellness-instructors`, treating docs-as-code for requirement `R-Q1-S-010`. It asserts that nine required artifacts exist (including `README.md`, `target-list.csv`, `vetting-rubric.md`, `intake-form-spec.md`, and `crm-tracking.csv`), then validates their contents: `target-list.csv` must have exactly 11 columns in a fixed order, at least 15 candidate rows, discipline values restricted to the `ALLOWED_DISCIPLINES` enum (e.g. `hatha_yoga`, `ayurveda_practitioner`), with at least 3 Ayurveda and 8 yoga rows; `crm-tracking.csv` must have its 8-column header and at least 15 rows pre-seeded with `lead` status. It also requires `vetting-rubric.md` to declare at least six `## Gate N` sections and `intake-form-spec.md` to mention twelve mandatory field names such as `credentials_doc_url`, `hourly_rate_inr`, and `mou_signed_at`. The file depends only on `vitest` and Node's `fs`/`path` modules — no application code — and notably ships a hand-rolled `parseCsv` helper implementing RFC-4180 quote/escape handling instead of pulling in a CSV library. A key gotcha is that column order is asserted exactly and row-count thresholds are hardcoded, so any reordering or trimming of the CSVs will fail the suite.

tests\\e2e\\booking-tiers.spec.ts.summary: This Playwright spec (`@playwright/test`) provides live CTA-to-CTA end-to-end coverage of the 2026-08-04 booking revamp, exercising the devotee journey from `/pujas` through the booking wizard plus the Phase 0 fixes (D1 cancel, D2 checkout-success link, D3 priest decline, D7 reschedule) and the new T1 priest on-duty toggle, all against the deployed site at `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` (default `https://darshya.online`). The central helper `demoSignIn(page, email?, password?)` clicks the "Demo Sign In" button or fills the email form and returns a boolean rather than throwing, so callers can `test.skip` when an environment lacks a demo-auth path; a `signOut` helper is also defined. Authentication is gated on the `E2E_DEMO_EMAIL`/`E2E_DEMO_PASSWORD` variables because production disables demo sign-in (behind `NEXT_PUBLIC_ALLOW_DEMO_PAYMENTS`), while priest-side tests use `E2E_PRIEST_EMAIL`/`E2E_PRIEST_PASSWORD` and self-skip on 404/403 responses from `/priest` routes, keeping the suite green in both devotee-only and full environments. A final API smoke test hits `E2E_API_BASE` (default `https://api.darshya.online`) and asserts the dispatch routes — `/api/v1/priest/availability`, `/api/v1/priest/offers`, `/api/v1/bookings/:id/cancel-quote`, and `/api/v1/bookings/:id/reschedule` — return auth errors rather than 404. Notable defensive choices: the suite runs in serial mode with `retries: 0`, every test skips on 5xx responses, and `demoSignIn` races `waitForURL` against a hard 10-second `setTimeout` so a navigation hung by third-party scripts can never stall the run. The D1 cancel test registers its `dialog` handler before clicking and dismisses the confirm so no real booking is cancelled, and several assertions degrade gracefully to a visible `body` check when the demo account simply has no matching data.

apps\\api\\src\\services\\recurring.serv.summary: This service implements recurring devotional subscriptions (monthly gau-feeding, wellness batches, temple seva) for the API's Phase 2, capturing a devotee's subscription intent now while the actual Razorpay Subscriptions mandate/webhook integration is deferred to a later phase. It exports the `RecurringPlan` type and `RecurringPlanKind` union, a static `RECURRING_PLANS` catalog, `getRecurringPlan` for plan lookup, `createRecurringSubscription` to insert a pending subscription row, and `listMyRecurring` to fetch a user's subscriptions. Its only dependency is the internal `prisma` client from `../lib/prisma.js`, and it deliberately uses raw SQL (`$executeRawUnsafe`/`$queryRawUnsafe`) against a `recurring_subscriptions` table so the code works even before the Prisma migration/client generation lands. A key design constraint is that every plan is priced at or under ₹15,000 per transaction to stay within the UPI Autopay no-PIN limit for donation/wellness categories, which is why `upiAutopayOk` flags each plan. Notably, `listMyRecurring` swallows all errors and returns an empty array if the table doesn't exist yet, and inserts use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` with all new subscriptions created in `pending` status until a payment mandate activates them.

apps\\api\\prisma\\migrations\\202608060.summary: This Prisma migration (20260806010000_temple_payouts_push_subs, dated 2026-08-06) is an additive schema change for the API that introduces two unrelated features: temple payout tracking and persisted web-push subscriptions. It creates a `ProviderPayoutStatus` enum (pending, processing, completed, failed) and a `temple_payouts` table that records the temple administration's share of each puja booking — explicitly closing the "temple gets nothing / donation bypass" revenue gap — with foreign keys to the existing `temples` and `puja_bookings` tables and indexes on `status` and `(temple_id, status)` for payout batch queries. It also creates a `push_subscriptions` table storing web-push credentials (endpoint, p256dh, auth) per user, replacing a previously in-memory subscription store that was lost on every server restart, which enables the daily panchang push notification feature. The table enforces a unique constraint on `endpoint` to prevent duplicate subscriptions, cascades on user deletion, and includes a `panchang_opt_in` boolean that defaults to true, meaning users are opted in unless they explicitly disable it. The migration depends on pre-existing `temples`, `puja_bookings`, and `users` tables and builds on the Prisma-managed schema in apps/api. Notably, every statement is guarded — `IF NOT EXISTS` on tables and indexes, plus `DO $$ ... EXCEPTION WHEN duplicate_object` blocks around the enum and foreign keys — making the migration idempotent and safe to run on a populated database, with money stored as DECIMAL(10,2) rather than float.

apps\\web\\components\\motion\\ScrollDis.summary: ScrollDiscover.tsx is a client-side React component (default export `ScrollDiscover`) that renders the homepage's "One app, five worlds of devotion" section: a sticky, full-viewport split-panel showcase cycling through five product worlds (Worship, Library, Consult, Seva, Yatra) as the user scrolls through a tall outer runway of `N * 78` viewport heights.
